The term "Saṃgha" is also a Western [Indic] sound; it is here called the "harmonious assembly. This refers to a group of four or more who, in both principle and practice, are entirely free from conflict and contention, and are thus termed the "harmonious assembly.
Regarding the general designation "Treasure" (Ratna): these three types are all cherished and highly valued by the world, and are therefore collectively called "Treasures.
To briefly distinguish their individual characteristics, the differences between the Three Jewels and their single essence are now presented here in brief.

Regarding the vehicle and the precepts: because one has not yet realized the *tathatā-dharmadhātu*, they are not considered to be of one essence. Within the context of their distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are further divided into Great and Small.
To take the Small Vehicle as an example, according to the Sarvāstivāda, the attainment of Buddhahood consists of four stages.

First, for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one cultivates the four *pāramitās* that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), excluding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as the causes for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*). Second...

During two hundred kalpas, one cultivates the causes for the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana). In the third and final existence, after having gone forth into homelessness, one cultivates the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) to exhaust the outflows (āsrava).
One eliminates the afflictions (kleśa) of the eight stages, beginning from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).

Only by abandoning the outflowing activities of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), and by delighting in the higher [realms] while reviling the lower, can one finally sever the delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The unsurpassed stage is to be delighted in as a flow of outflows (*āsrava-vāhana*); because one lacks the capacity for it, one cannot sever [the outflows].

Under the fourth *bodhi*-tree, he cultivated thirty-four moments of mind (*citta*) and attained Buddhahood in succession. Regarding these thirty-four: the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) consists of sixteen moments of mind;

observing the four truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are the Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*); observing the two higher realms, there are the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). First, he observed...

Regarding the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): there is the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*). Next, one contemplates the suffering of the two higher realms;

there is the subsequent receptivity to suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*). These constitute the four moments of mind regarding suffering. This continues up to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), which likewise has four moments. Thus, there are sixteen moments of mind.

Among these sixteen moments of mind, the four dharma-receptivities (*dharma-kṣānti*) and the four dharma-knowledges (*dharma-jñāna*) do not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), because the afflictions of the desire realm are [already being abandoned] at the time of practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Because they have already been abandoned, the four types of subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) sever the afflictions of the truth-seeing (*darśana-heya*) of the single stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Since the afflictions of the truth-seeing of the four dhyānas and three formless attainments (*ārūpya*) have already been severed previously, they need not be severed again. Next, one severs the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
these consist of nine grades (*navaprakāra*). For the severance of each individual grade, there are two moments of mind: first, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).

There are two paths of liberation; thus, there are eighteen [moments of mind]. As for the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the eight lower stages, because they have already been severed previously when practicing dhyāna, they need not be severed again.
Among these thirty-four moments of mind, the first thirty-three are the minds of the Bodhisattva in training (*śaikṣa*), and the final one is the Buddha’s mind of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
According to their respective meanings, these are further categorized as three: the Buddha’s untainted (*anāsrava*) [mind], and so forth.

The Dharma-body, consisting of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*), is taken as the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*). The physical body born of parents and the four aggregates born of retribution are taken as the Retribution-Buddha (*vipākabuddha*).
The manifested Buddha-body that performs transformations in other realms is taken as the Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*).

According to the Mahāyāna, however, these three types are all Transformation-Buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*). Regarding the three Buddhas of the Mahāyāna: at the completion of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the Vajra-mind...

They are attained all at once later on. At that time, one abides within the five aggregates; this is the Buddha of Retribution (*vipākabuddha*). When the ninth pure consciousness—the *tathatā-dharmadhātu*—which was originally hidden, now becomes manifest, it constitutes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Through great vows of compassion, it manifests as a form-body (*rūpakāya*), being born in Tuṣita Heaven and so forth until its parinirvāṇa, serving as the Transformation-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāyabuddha*).
This is the one venerated by the present Master of the Vinaya. For now, based on the minor treatises, we have explained these matters. Next, we shall clarify the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).
There are four kinds of distinct doctrines: first, the doctrine of teaching, which refers to the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures;

second, the doctrine of principle, which refers to the Four Truths and the Noble Ones of the Three Vehicles who, by collectively contemplating the Four Truths, enter the Noble Path; third, the doctrine of practice, which refers to precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth;
fourth, the doctrine of fruition, which refers to the two kinds of nirvana: the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. Next, [the text] clarifies...

The Jewel of the Saṃgha refers to the four stages of approach and the four fruits—the assembly of Śrāvakas—as well as Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas. These do not, however, fall within the numerical category of the Saṃgha.
Because Pratyekabuddhas appear in worlds where no Buddha exists and lack rituals such as the *karmavācanā*, and because Bodhisattvas are solitary, they are not considered the Saṃgha;

rather, they are subsumed under the Jewel of the Dharma. If one speaks of them as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), the sense of "Saṃgha" may be applicable; yet they are not included within the Saṃgha defined by ritual procedures.
Third, regarding the expression of reverence, there are first four points specifically clarifying the reverence due to the Buddha: 1. The Buddha is the Teacher;

as he is about to transmit the holy teachings, how could one not manifest devotion to signify that he is present as a master to be consulted? 2. Offering in gratitude for his kindness. 3. Revealing the protocols for monks and nuns to follow in their veneration.
4. Requesting the addition of his majestic protection. There are three points regarding the reverence for the Dharma: 1. The Dharma is that which is transmitted...

The essential meaning is as follows: First, because the Saṃgha truly benefits and guides the assembly, it is likewise worthy of reverence. Second, to demonstrate the ritual for following and honoring them.

Third, to request their majestic protection. Regarding the three points of revering the Saṃgha: first, the Saṃgha possesses the merit of transmitting and upholding the Dharma, which brings benefit and profit to us;

thus, we offer support as an act of gratitude. Second, to demonstrate the ritual for following and honoring them. Third, to request their majestic protection. Next, regarding the general reverence according to the three points, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states: "To develop..."

Sentient beings maintain mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because the Three Jewels are the most auspicious, I have spoken of them at the beginning of my treatise.
Now, as for the Master of the Vinaya paying homage here: his primary intention is to expound the *Vinaya*.
Next, I shall explain the three phrases. From the crown of the head down to the feet, one brings devotion through the activity of the body; thus it is called "prostrating with the head" (*praṇāma*).
Furthermore, "prostrating" (*kai*) means to bend, and "head" (*shou*) refers to the skull; hence it is called "bowing the head" (*kai-shou*). What is the object of this veneration?

It refers to the Buddhas and various sages, who are not merely one; thus they are termed "various" (*zhū*). While it is appropriate to revere the Teacher, the inclusion of veneration for other Buddhas serves to manifest the breadth of the teaching.
The principle is uniform and the ritual procedure is non-dual; since all Buddhas are equal, one must pay them equal respect. "Buddha" is explained as before.

Regarding the phrase "above, bowing the head," it extends downward to encompass the following two items. What are those that are "reached" and "not reached"? They are the Dharma and the Saṅgha. "Dharma" is explained as before.
"Bhikṣu" refers to the cause capable of accomplishing [the goal], while "Saṅgha" refers to the community that is accomplished. These are raised together, both collectively and individually.

Therefore, it is called the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*. "Bhikṣu" is a Western (Indic) term; according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it has many meanings. First, it means a mendicant (*yācanaka*); second, it means one who begs for a purpose.

[The first] is for sustaining the body so as to cultivate the Path, thereby remaining free from wrong livelihoods (*mithyājīva*). There are four types of wrong livelihood: the first is "downward-mouthed" (*adhomukha*).

Second is seeking food by looking upward; third is seeking food from all four directions; fourth is seeking food by following others. One who is free from these four wrong livelihoods and sustains oneself through right livelihood is therefore called a *bhikṣu*.
Second, it is for the benefit of the donors: giving to the "field of the Sangha" yields the merit of a reciprocal reward;

for this reason, one must beg. Furthermore, the name is explained as follows: *bhi* means to destroy, and *kṣu* means afflictions (*kleśa*). Because one is able to destroy the afflictions, [one is a *bhikṣu*].
He is called a bhikṣu. Third, he is called "one who terrifies Māra," because he can terrify Māra and the followers of Māra; thus he is named "one who terrifies Māra.
The explanation of the bhikṣu is concluded. As for the *saṃgha*, it is explained as previously stated.

Next, the explanation of "How to Pay Reverence" is divided into three parts. First, there are two and a half verses that briefly praise the merit of the precepts and exhort one to faithfully practice them.
Second, from "Now I shall explain the meaning of the ten phrases" onwards, the benefits of the precepts are praised in detail to manifest the exhortation to faith.

Third, the final half-verse explicitly clarifies the intention of the Master of the Vinaya in offering praise and exhortation, and concludes by once again prostrating himself in reverence. This marks the end of the section.

Within the preceding brief introduction, it is further divided into four parts. First, for half a line, a general expression of reverence is made for the exposition of the *Vinaya*, so as to encourage the arising of faith in the present age and ensure that the transmission of the teachings endures for a long time.

Second, for half a line, the author reveals what has been transmitted, showing that the principles are not his own private errors; he personally received the instructions of his own teacher, Kumāralāta, and distantly inherited those of Upāli.

The final exhortation serves as the basis for transmission and preservation, establishing its credibility. Third is the "Half-Practice" section, which briefly extols the essentials of the precepts and exhorts the audience to listen attentively at this time.
Fourth is the single verse, which states that by merely following the teaching and practicing it with devotion, one will obtain benefits that are not in vain, thereby becoming a venerable elder.

First, I shall explain the initial passage, which is now being proclaimed; hence it is said, "I shall now expound. What is it that is being expounded? It is the Dharma of the Vinaya. *Vinaya* is a Western (Sanskrit) term;
in this land [of China], it is called "extinction" (*mie*) or "overcoming and extinction. Because it functions through its practice and teaching, the name is established based on its efficacy;
thus, this teaching is called the Dharma of the Vinaya. Furthermore, the name *vinaya* possesses many meanings, as explained in the *Tripiṭaka-artha*.

First, it is capable of inducing [attainment]; this is the meaning of *vinaya*. That is to say, at the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, forty-two thousand merits are induced to arise simultaneously.
Second, it is capable of teaching the purity and rectitude of body and speech; this is the meaning of *vinaya*.

That is to say, because one is free from the turbidity of karma and the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called the purity of body and speech; because they are pure and upright, it is so named.
1. It is directed toward *nirvāṇa*. 2. It has the sense of cessation (*nirodha*). This is the meaning of *vinaya*: its nature is to be free from all evils, and its activity is not non-arising;

therefore, it is called "cessation. 3. It is called *vinaya* because it leads to excellence; that is to say, it leads the worldly into the Path, leads the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle, and causes ordinary beings to enter the state of the Noble Ones, and so forth.
4. It is the practice of superior persons; this is the meaning of *vinaya*, meaning that all Noble Ones practice this together.

The Dharma comprehensively encompasses the teachings on discipline (*vinaya*), exhausting all aspects thereof. Since it possesses many meanings, the term "extinction" (*nirodha*) used here refers to that which can attain extinction;

it corresponds to the second meaning, "tending toward Nirvana," and the third meaning, "extinction" itself. However, while the scriptural teachings vary in their breadth and brevity, this *Vinaya* contains eight categories of discipline (*vinaya*).

As stated in the *Dvayāvadāna*, there are five categories of discipline in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: first, the brief version, referring to the precepts of the five groups of offenses (*pañca-pārājikādi*); second, the extensive version.
This refers to the two categories of precepts: first, the three aspects, such as the permission for the five matters granted in the country of Śroṇā;

second, the four firm points, such as the relinquishing of the five offenses upon receiving the *kaṭhina* robe; third, that which accords with the Dharma, namely the *saṃghakarma* performed in accordance with the Dharma;

fourth, the discussion of the five *vinayas* regarding the *pārājika* offenses, namely the *pratideśanīya*, *ānuśāsana*, *pratyāpatti*, *nirodha*, and *prahāṇa* *vinayas*; and fifth, the nine *vinayas* according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the first of which is the *bhikṣu-vinaya*.

1. Vinaya regarding intentional acts, such as the intentional emission of semen; 2. Vinaya regarding individuals, such as those who wander alone; 3. Vinaya regarding both [categories], such as sexual misconduct and theft; 4.
Vinaya regarding offenses, which refers to the remedies applied according to the Dharma arising from the eight origins; 5. Vinaya regarding afflictions.

Regarding the nine types of knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*) and cessation (*nirodha*) for the afflictions of the three realms and five categories: this explains the *vinaya* in terms of the cessation of afflictions.
The "sixfold *vinaya* of contact" refers to the ten precepts of training, namely the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera; these encompass future matters and are therefore called "desire" (*chanda*).
If one receives the ten precepts, one does not yet possess the full ordination (*upasampadā*); these precepts are the means (*upāya*) for attaining that full ordination and are able to encompass it.

It is named as such because it concerns future matters. Seventh is the *asaṃsṛṣṭa-vinaya* (non-contact discipline). When the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is completed, forty-two thousand rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) arise simultaneously;
since not a single precept fails to arise, it is called "non-contact. Eighth is the *ekadeśa-vinaya* (one-place discipline).

This refers to places such as those for receiving the full ordination or bathing, which serve two purposes: first, a geographical location serves as the "place," such as the exemptions granted in border regions.

These are the ten [types]. Second, there are those where the time itself constitutes the occasion (*sthāna*). For example, whereas one formerly obtained the precepts through the three refuges, one does not obtain them in this way now;

this refers to the time, meaning that during the hot season in the Middle Kingdom, [certain practices] were permitted. Ninth, there are the *sarvatra-vinaya* (universal rules), such as the prohibition against killing and so forth.

These are common trainings for all [monastics]. In the *Vinaya-śāstra*, they are categorized as the ten types of *vinaya*: namely, those for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; the complete portion and the partial portion;
those pertaining to specific locations and those pertaining to all locations; and those for the cessation of the three poisons, the cessation of offenses, and the cessation of disputes.

These enumerations—whether the teachings are extensive or concise—comprehensively encompass these disciplinary practices, leaving no aspect of their meaning unaddressed. Now, in explaining the *vinaya*, I shall cite one such category to clarify this.

This is the text. Therefore it is said: "Now I expound the Vinaya-dharma; the mastery of all practices is called the True Dharma (Saddharma). The Dharma is propagated by people, and people can master the Dharma.

Because the Dharma resides in people, it flourishes again and does not fall into ruin. Therefore it is said: 'To cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states at its beginning:
"If one wishes to establish the Buddha-Dharma, one should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya. Second, to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time...
As for "abiding," there are five [reasons]: first, not desiring to harbor doubts or regrets; second, seeking to question others;

third, acting as a refuge for monks and nuns who have broken the precepts and are terrified by their transgressions; fourth, desiring to travel and transform beings in all directions without hindrance;
and fifth, for the sake of attaining these five benefits, a man of sincere faith should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya. Having obtained these five, therefore—

It enables one to abide for a long time. Furthermore, the *Śāstra* states: "There are five benefits of upholding the Vinaya: first, one is able to uphold the precepts oneself; second, one is able to sever the doubts of others;
third, one enters the assembly without fear; fourth, one establishes the True Dharma; and fifth, the True Dharma abides for a long time. This is also said in accordance with this [text].
Regarding "the second, with Upāli as the leader": he personally consumed the teachings of the Sage; because he was the first to transmit them, he is called the "leader.
As for "and the others," this refers to the fact that all five masters were Arhats, possessing both forms of liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*). Regarding the term "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*):
a questioner asks, "Among the lineage of transmission held by the five masters, the name of Upāli does not appear. Why are they all now designated by that title? The answer is: "The five..."

The Master was proficient in both the teachings of principle (*li*) and practice (*xing*); therefore, his name is recorded. Upānanda understood the teachings of practice but did not penetrate the teachings of principle;
he was not one who fully transmitted and propagated [the Dharma], and thus his name is omitted and not made manifest.

Since this Vinaya intends solely to circulate the teachings of practice, the Master of the Vinaya cites various proofs and transmissions as its basis, thereby establishing the meaning of its credibility. Question: Why does he cite these?
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* first mentions the seven Buddhas because it lists the successive lineage of transmission from which the Upāsaka precepts were received.

Since this [text] does not personally receive the teachings directly from the Buddha’s own words, it does not cite the seven Buddhas; rather, as the precepts emerge from this [lineage], there is no need to cite them again.
Because it provides a general exposition of the transmission of the abbreviated teaching, it cites the seven Buddhas.
Next, I shall now proclaim this third [section]. Therefore, it is said: "Now, I shall briefly explain the function of praising the precepts. They extinguish evil and give rise to good;
they are supreme among the means of transcendence. This is called the essential meaning. As for those who partake of this teaching, they are not merely one, hence the term "all" (*sarve*).

They are all characterized by harmonious and upright conduct and are called "worthy ones" (*satpuruṣa*); I hope that these benevolent persons will together set aside their distractions and listen attentively. Thus, it says: "May you all listen together."

Next, regarding the explanation of the fourth [category], the "Profound Precepts" (*gambhīra-śīla*), it is explained in three ways: First, the essence of the precept’s goodness is profound and its principle is mysterious;
its moistening influence is boundless, and thus it is called "profound. Second, it is able to give rise to the profound understanding of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Third, it is able to guard against the three types of action (*trikarma*) with great gravity; therefore, it is named "profound. When taught, it necessarily reaches sentient beings, yet it does not benefit those who are not suitable vessels. This is for the sake of single-mindedness.

Because it is for one's own benefit, it is said that those who delight in upholding the precepts do so for themselves. Second, when one practices them while benefiting both oneself and others, it is called "recitation" (*svādhyāya*).

When one’s own practice is perfected and its utility is realized within oneself, it is termed "benefit" (*ātma-hita*). When one opens up what one has attained to cause others to receive its nourishment, it is termed "benefiting others" (*para-hita*).

Regarding the benefits of the precepts (*śīla*): these benefits are manifold and not limited to one. Second, by being fully endowed with the two types of conduct, one becomes venerable and is called an "Elder" (*sthavira*).

Following this, the second section provides a detailed praise of the benefits of the precepts. Although the preceding text spoke of their profound importance, their specific characteristics were not yet manifest, making them difficult [to understand].
To convey this intention, the following section extensively elucidates the characteristics of the profound essentials. This is divided into two parts.

First, there are three verses that explain the benefits of the precepts through the Dharma, citing the essential tenets to encourage practice. Since the characteristics of the Dharma are subtle and its principles are hidden and difficult to discern, they cannot be understood without the use of analogies;
therefore, from the second verse on "the various mountains" onwards, the benefits of the precepts are extensively clarified through metaphorical explanations.
Their manifestations are extraordinary. To uphold them brings benefit; the tenfold merit of such advantages is certain and not in vain. To disparage them brings harm;

one will inevitably fall into the fires and cauldrons of the three miserable realms—of this there is no doubt. Why do you not abandon what causes harm to pursue what brings benefit, and cast aside evil to practice goodness?
The initial exposition of the Dharma is divided into three parts. First, the first half-verse summarizes the number of benefits and links the teaching to its intended recipients. Second...

The two verses extensively manifest the essence of the benefits. The third half-verse concludes by establishing that the original intent of the Tathāgata’s formulation of the precepts lies precisely in these benefits.

Although the benefits of the precepts are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, why limit them to these ten? For the time being, taking a single aspect of the transformative ritual, I have briefly indicated these two sets of five;
thus, they are termed "ten. The phrases that express these benefits are called "sentences" (*pada*). The merits expressed beneath those sentences are called...

The meaning [of the preceding] has been explained. Next, the twentieth benefit is clarified. The section beginning with "the essence and characteristics" constitutes the main text; it will not be explained at length, but will be briefly categorized.
Regarding the phrase "causing the Sangha to rejoice and dwell in eternal peace": the second and third benefits encompass the Sangha, whereas the first benefit concerns those who lack faith.

First, it inspires faith; second, it causes those who already have faith to increase and expand it; third, it causes those who do not observe the precepts to abandon them; fourth, it leads those on wrong paths into the right path;
fifth, it benefits those with a sense of shame and remorse; sixth, it ensures long-term stability; seventh, it clarifies the original intent behind the establishment of the precepts;
and eighth, it serves these very purposes. Therefore, he now concludes by saying: "For this reason, the World-Honored One, Most Victorious," and so forth.

The explanation of the second metaphor consists of four parts. The first section, extending up to the point concerning Rāhula, uses a metaphor to praise how the Dharma of precepts can produce the good and extinguish evil, properly regulating the three karmas, and producing good while extinguishing evil by relying upon the teachings.

Thus, the second section, from "For what reason the king was established" up to "among the dragons," provides a metaphor for the relative gravity of the five categories of offenses. Having already understood this...
As for its characteristics: one must certainly be able to uphold it so that no evil remains unremoved and no good remains unaccumulated.

Therefore, from the third section on the lioness down to the long-abiding [jewel], this clearly explains the capacity of the precepts to generate and produce beneficial conduct; these functional capacities serve as metaphors.

Since the teaching and practice have been proclaimed, it is appropriate to exhort others to revere and cultivate them. Thus, from the fourth section on the wet nurse downward, there are metaphors for exhorting cultivation and exhorting exposition. Regarding this:
The first section contains three parts. The first consists of two verses, which use analogies to show that precepts are the foundation from which all virtuous qualities arise.

The second part, consisting of one verse, praises how precepts can eliminate afflictions (*saṃyojana*). However, the arising of good and the elimination of evil must necessarily depend upon the three types of action; only through such practice can these goals be accomplished.

Therefore, from the third section, "From the desire to cultivate goodness," onwards, the text clearly elucidates the fundamental basis for properly harmonizing the three karmas to produce goodness and extinguish evil.

The initial passage consists of two parts: the first verse uses a metaphor to show how precepts can produce goodness; the second verse cites the benefits of the aforementioned precepts to encourage their cultivation.
The first verse has an upper half that provides the metaphor and a lower half that applies it to the subject at hand. Among all the mountains, the [Sumeru]...
As for "Mī-zuì" (Most Supreme): Mount Sumeru is able to support the great earth so that it does not tilt, and all the hundred species of plants grow because of it.
Among those that support the earth, nothing surpasses Sumeru; therefore, it is called the most supreme. This is a metaphor for the merit of the practice of precepts among the ten thousand practices:
it is able to support the "great earth" of the practitioner’s body and speech, keeping them free from the transgressions of the seven types of deviant inclinations. First.

All wholesome dharmas increase by means of this; it is preeminent among all that arises through accumulation. Its significance is equal to Mount Sumeru, and thus it is the most excellent. Therefore, a sutra says:
"Relying upon and because of this precept, one attains various meditative concentrations as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering. The great ocean is vast and deep, its moisture boundless;

surpassing the hundred rivers, it is designated as the most excellent. This metaphor illustrates that the principle of the excellence of the precepts provides profound support and inexhaustible nourishment.
It transcends the myriad practices. To illustrate this, it is like the ocean; below, the teaching is cited to harmonize with the various sutras.

It unites the aforementioned various mountains, making the flowing precepts the foremost and supreme, and unites them with the aforementioned Mount Sumeru and the great ocean. If one discusses this in terms of practice, meditative concentration eliminates subtle distractions.
Wisdom severs the afflictions; therefore, it is superior. As for the roots and branches, they differ: the precepts are the root, while concentration and wisdom arise from them.

Furthermore, the precepts are superior. If distinguished according to the teachings, the two baskets (the Vinaya and Sūtra) are superior because they serve as the means for explaining concentration and wisdom. However, if one explains the fundamental practice, [wisdom is superior].

The Vinaya is supreme. That it is now called "the most excellent" is because it is the root; thus it is the most excellent. The *Yilun* (Treatise on the Parājikas) states that there are four reasons for its being "most excellent":

first, it is called "most excellent" because it excels in generating goodness; second, it is called "most excellent" because it excels among the methods for extinguishing evil; third, by relying on worldly precepts, one attains supramundane precepts;

and fourth, by relying on the precepts that transcend the mind, one masters the precepts of the mind. Since these essential practices have been proclaimed, one should diligently strive for this benefit. This is so.
The following verses are cited to exhort you toward practice: "If you can merely uphold this without letting it lapse from your mind, the foremost victory will surely be achieved without fail.
However, if you wish to attain that which is the foremost among the aforementioned practices, it cannot be achieved without upholding the precepts."
Therefore, it says "the present age," referring to the monks and nuns of the present; "future ages" refers to the monks and nuns of the future.

You should uphold these prohibitive precepts, and you will certainly obtain benefit without fail. As for the monks and nuns of the past, they no longer have the capacity to maintain the precepts; therefore, they are not exhorted.

Next, the second [section] explains the extinction of evil. When delusions arise, they are lost; when myriad burdens are incurred, they are diminished. Therefore it is said: "Eliminating fetters, one is free from obstruction.

Those who wish to cast off bonds must rely on clear wisdom (*prajñā*) as their foundation. Yet wisdom arises fundamentally from pure precepts (*śīla*). Tracing the merit back to its source, it is said:
"By this, one attains liberation. However, such liberation is not in vain; it must necessarily be protected by upholding the pure precepts. Thus, one should...

Examine one’s own transgressions and compliance; use the teachings as a standard for self-observation. By means of these precepts and instructions, verify the purity or defilement of one’s conduct throughout this entire life, until it appears with perfect clarity.
This is called "observation" (*vipaśyanā*), which is like a mirror suspended from above: whether one is handsome or ugly in a lofty hall is revealed therein.
Therefore, it is said that the mirror reflects the image of the face.
Next, the third section, "Complete Endowment," is explained. Three types of karma can produce two kinds of goodness, as described in the section on observance and transgression.

Since the mind is the root of the good and evil of body and speech, it is urged that one should examine them with care. Rāhula, for the sake of a Brahmin who treated you lightly, you endured his afflictions through your three karmas without retaliating;
you felt compassion for him. [The Buddha said: "My pain was but for a moment; why do you subject yourself to such long-term suffering?"
This is because it reveals the excellence within the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*). It is cited here to provide clarification.

Regarding the second section on the lightness and heaviness of the characteristics of offenses, there are two parts. First, the initial two verses serve as a metaphor for the arising of the teaching that expresses [the offenses].

Second, the following ten verses serve as metaphors for the characteristics of the offenses being expressed. Within the first part, there are two sections; the first consists of one and a half verses.

This is an illustration. The second half [of the verse] provides the application of the illustration. Within the illustration, there are two parts: first, one line serves as an illustration for the reason why the teaching arose;

second, half a line serves as an illustration for the purpose for which the teaching arose. This entire body of Vinaya teaching is noble and worthy of veneration, held in high esteem by the monks and nuns.

This is illustrated by the analogy of reprimanding a king; for this is the reason why this teaching arose. To say "the reason for establishing a king" refers to those who cause strife and contention in the world.

To say "because of the offenses of the bhikṣus, the multitude raised [the matter]" illustrates how the bhikṣus reported their transgressions to the Buddha and requested that the Noble One establish the precepts.
In ancient times, according to the Dharma, this analogy applies to all Buddhas of the three periods: they all wait for an offense to be committed and a request to be made before [acting].
The regulations are formulated as a comprehensive model based on ancient and modern precedents; therefore, they are said to be "in accordance with the Dharma.
Next, regarding the persons for whom these teachings are intended: the reason this extensive teaching, the sovereign of the precepts, was established is for two types of people.

First, for those who have committed an offense but are capable of repentance, so that they may recognize their ailment and know the medicine, and be provided with the methods for confession, remediation, and total eradication; hence it is said that "the offender knows the Dharma. Second, for those who are...

The essence does not transgress against people; it causes them to follow the teachings and practice them with devotion, establishing the conduct of remedial action. Therefore, it is said that those who require the Dharma achieve accomplishment.
This may be understood through the appropriate analogy.

Next, regarding the second section on the relative lightness and heaviness of the characteristics of offenses, there are two parts. First, there are two verses that provide a general analogy for the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*). Second...

Next are eight verses. Five verses provide specific analogies for the five categories [of offenses], while two verses provide a general analogy. The former provides the analogy and the latter provides the application. Within the section on the analogy, there are two parts:

the first line provides the analogy of identifying the illness and prescribing the specific medicine; the following three lines provide the analogy of administering the treatment appropriately. This constitutes one division of the Vinaya teachings.
It can explain the characteristics of offenses, distinguishing clearly between their lightness and gravity; thus it is said: "Like a physician examining various illnesses.
Within the first three phrases, the initial phrase establishes two topical headings, while the following two explain and substantiate them.

Regarding the subsequent four [phrases], those requiring confession are termed "progress" (*jin*), while the transgressions of the first category, being grave in principle and incapable of repentance, are termed "stopping" (*zhi*). There are four meanings for "progress": first, the secondary branches such as *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; [the others follow].
Second, there are the two indeterminate obstacles to the Path. Third, they are extinguished by means of conditions. Fourth, it ensures the quorum of the Saṃgha is complete.

For these reasons, it is called *śamatha* (cessation). The previously mentioned [term] also possesses these four meanings; therefore, it is named *śamatha*. Since progress and its negation accord with the proper ritual, it is said to be "attaining what is appropriate."

That which can be treated is "releasing and advancing"; that which cannot be treated is "releasing and stopping. Next, the analogy is applied: the first phrase corresponds to the first phrase, and the following three correspond to the following three.
Four matters are condensed into one phrase, corresponding to "stopping" so as to attain the proper place; that which is "untenable" is abandoned, while that which is "tenable" is rescued.

The second phrase corresponds to "advancing" so as to attain the proper place; "that which can be treated" refers to the administration of medicine. Furthermore, according to another interpretation, the correspondence is such that the first phrase corresponds to the first three characters of the [original] four.

There are thirteen matters; the remaining ones are subsumed under the two terms "all illnesses. Those that cannot be treated are not to be combined with those that can be saved; they simply belong to the category of the "gate of what is obtainable.

Those that do not require saving are not to be combined with those that proceed to the "gate of what is obtainable. These four matters encompass [the categories]. Are those that cannot be treated exhaustive? Answer: One part is exhausted by dosage.

In the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, it is based on nature that there are four that cannot be treated. Now, according to the characteristics of the teachings, we restrict it to these four; thus, they are distinguished.

Lanti-ki and others cite the *Pārājika* and the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* categories; furthermore, these exclude the two types of *ānantarya* (heinous crimes). Since they apply only to monks and not to nuns, cases such as physical contact (*sparśana*) are excluded.
Therefore, it is said that these four matters are incurable.
Next, the individual metaphors are explained. The first two verses provide the metaphors for the first category (āpatti). The following two verses provide the metaphors for the second category.
The subsequent two verses are combined with those of the third and fourth categories. Why are they combined? The answer is:

just as one fears the four offenses because one wishes to avoid fear, those who dread even minor matters lose their names [as distinct categories] because the four gates are increased; thus, the third and fourth are separated. Now, the five categories are being explained. However—

Regarding the combination of three and four: this is a division based on whether they correspond or do not correspond. Because the first of the five corresponds to the distinction between the Saṃgha and the individual, it is combined;

yet, within the Saṃgha, it is further divided according to whether there is a remedy or no remedy. Thus, there are only four analogies. However, because the first two categories differ in many respects, they are separated into one:

namely, the treatable and the untreatable, and the distinctions between the *pārājika* offenses with concealment and without concealment, as well as the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses with concealment and without concealment.

1. Concealment (*paticchādana*): All such [concealed] offenses may be expiated through confession. 2. Limiting the confession to residual offenses (*śeṣa*): For *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, one confesses for a limited period; for *pārājika* offenses involving training and repentance (*śikṣamāṇā*), one must confess for as long as one lives. 3. Concealment of residual offenses and repeated commission during confession:

If one commits a [residual] offense again while in the process of confessing it, one is subjected to the "treatment of the original day" (*mūlāpakarṣa*). If one commits a *pārājika* offense again, further confession is no longer permitted. 4. Counting versus not counting:
Although both cases involve facing the Saṃgha individually, there are many differences; therefore, two analogies must be provided for the third and fourth points. II.3.4.2.

Section. If based on the three explanations, the distinctions within one explanation should be divided into two. However, because they share many common points, they are combined into a single analogy:

first, both refer to individuals; second, both are subject to confession; third, both allow for confession whether the offense was concealed or not; fourth, both satisfy the required number of participants.

Therefore, they are joined as one illustration. Next, the initial analogy is explained. The preceding analogy is followed by its application. The first phrase is the analogy of severing one's own portion through personal conduct. Next...

The first phrase is a metaphor for the severance of the constituent factors of the Dharma; the second phrase is a metaphor for the removal and discarding of the ritual acts; the third phrase is a metaphor for impurity not remaining within purity.
If one commits an offense against the first *pārājika* rule, one is permanently obstructed for the duration of this life, and the life-force of wisdom is severed;

this is termed "death. One no longer functions as a monk worthy of treatment, and is thus called a "corpse. A corpse possesses five meanings, as will be analyzed below. Since the karma is already so grave, [one is excluded from] the pure assembly.

They were not accepted; hence it is said that "the great ocean does not receive them. A *jñapti-karman* was performed to expel and punish them, and they were driven away by a fierce wind, forever distinguished from the community.
Thus it is said that "they were cast onto the shore. This combines the second phrase of the middle section with the first phrase of the initial section.

The third [verse] combines with the lower three [lines]. The fourth [verse] exhorts the upholding [of the precepts], following the second analogy. The first half [of the verse] is an analogy for upholding; the second half is an analogy for breaking [the precepts].

Mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, and so forth, which guard and restrain the six sense faculties, are called "guarding the gates. When the practice of the antidotes is perfected, one is ultimately pure and cannot be destroyed by conditions;
this is termed "firm and secure. Because one does not fear external wrongs that would rob one of the wealth of goodness, it is said: "not..."

One grieves over the loss of wealth. The second section concerns the practice of the communal rules (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*); the meaning of the "net" is the same [as the previous]. Just as a wall may encounter conditions that cause it to be broken and ruined, one fears the loss of the wealth of precepts;

hence, it is called "anxiety and dread. The correspondence of the metaphors can be understood thus. Next, the third metaphor: the first half-line is a metaphor for breaking [the precepts], and the second half-line is a metaphor for upholding them.

The two sections on the fourth and fifth [categories of offenses] concern subtle matters of deportment (*īryāpatha*), which are easily corrupted; their meaning is the same as that of the "unbaked clay pot" (*kapāla*).
A vessel that encounters conditions leading to transgression is called "perforated and leaking. Seeing one's own faults and fearing a fall into the three miserable realms is called "sorrow.

When the practice of the precepts is successfully accomplished, it serves as a means to sustain the body; this is likened to being complete and intact. When the inner mind leaps with joy at having crossed over what was maintained [in the past], it is likened to the delight of a family circle.
This refers to first breaking [the precepts] and later upholding them, which is a metaphor for transgressing them earlier and later. This is an ornamental literary expression.
Therefore it is so. Next are the four similes. The fifth is the smallest among the offenses of the category of *pārājika* (defeats), comparable to a wildfire.
This slight evil is easy to commit, yet it must be strictly prohibited when maintaining [the precepts]; hence it says, "Be careful not to.

This means that while the continuity of wholesome thoughts is like grass and trees, a single moment of slight evil is by nature contrary and harmful; it can open the door to unwholesomeness and incinerate the wholesome mind, causing it to...

Because they manifest [in this way], it is said that they "burn away the unconditioned and leave nothing remaining. What are the five unwholesome doors? First, they can burn away one's roots of goodness;
second, they arise from evil; third, they are censured by the noble ones; fourth, they cause one to fall away from the fruits of the path; and fifth, at death, one falls into the evil realms.
In the third section, "Generating Practice and Benefits," there are two parts. The first consists of two verses: the analogy of the fool and the wise man.

The second, beginning with "In harmony," explains the generation of practice and benefits. Regarding the initial analogy of the fool and the wise man, it is intended to establish the meaning of the preceding section.

To say it "establishes the preceding" means to clarify that the transgressions of the five categories of offenses are truly fearsome; who would not stand in awe of them? There is no evil they do not commit.
Regarding what is called a "foolish person": who is it that can fear? It is one who does not avoid affliction. Regarding what is called a "wise person":

this constitutes the preceding analogy of "fearing yet not fearing. As for the statement "giving rise to the inferior": who is it that cannot maintain [the precepts]? It is the so-called foolish person.

Who is it that can maintain them? It is the so-called wise person. This constitutes the subsequent analogy of "being able to maintain" versus "being unable to maintain. The first verse is the analogy.

The following verse provides the analogy. The first half of the verse corresponds to the analogy of the fool who has no fear; the second half corresponds to the analogy of the wise person who can fear.
The grave offenses of the first category involve karmic obstructions so profound that they can destroy the Dharma-body and sever the life-force of wisdom;
they are most terrifying, like the roars of lions and tigers. Yet foolish ordinary beings, intoxicated by the three poisons, do not dread such evil.

Therefore it is said: "The intoxicated person feels no terror. This is an illustration of the heavy by means of the light; since they do not fear what is heavy, there is no need to speak of what is light.
This explains the second half of the verse. The *dukkaṭa* offense is the most minute among evils; hence it is said: "Though the cry of a small beast is faint, the wise are afraid.
Because a sense of conflict arises within them, it is said: "The sober person hears it and is struck with fear. This is an illustration of the heavy by means of the light.
If even the light [offense] is already feared, how much more so the heavy one? Next, the analogy is joined: these three types of people who remain alive correspond to the aforementioned drunkard;
all evils correspond to the lion’s roar; not being afraid corresponds to the aforementioned lack of terror; and the wise person corresponds to the aforementioned sober man.
Regarding the phrase "even with a slight evil," although the sound of a small animal is faint, one should harbor fear; upon hearing it, one becomes terrified.
Within the second section, which explains the benefit of generating the practice, there are two parts. The first consists of ten verses, which provide analogies for generating one's own practice.
The second, beginning from "as previously [stated], having first made oneself firm," correctly clarifies the ability to generate [the practice] by managing the monastic community and the assembly.
The Dharma is harmonious; one establishes the practice of the True Dharma. Regarding the first [of the three stages], there are five similes and ten verses.

The first consists of two verses, which correspond to the application of the precepts (*śīla*) and their subsequent cultivation (*anuśīla*); they serve as an antidote to practice, like excellent medicine that can cure all ailments.
The second consists of two verses, praising ethical discipline (*śīla*) as feet, capable of traversing perilous paths. The third consists of two verses.

The fourth section consists of two verses, which clarify that the nature of the precepts is to ascend, carrying the practitioner across the three realms—this is the analogy of the life-preserving float.
The fifth section consists of two verses, which illustrate the precepts as a flight of stairs, serving as the essential path for proceeding toward Nirvana.
This clearly explains that morality is like a craft; once one has completed the training and attained the resulting fruit, one does not fall into the evil destinies. This is the analogy.
Next, the first verse is explained through its metaphor, and the following verse provides the application of that metaphor. Within the metaphor, there are four lines:

the first line is the metaphor for cultivating morality with right mindfulness, because when right mindfulness is present, there is no evil from which one does not turn away. The second line clarifies the remedial practice (*pratipakṣa*).

The analogy of suppressing karma: Having suppressed the seven transgressions, ethical discipline (*śīla*) becomes pure, enabling the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), thereby severing the afflictions and delusions.
For this reason, the third phrase clarifies the analogy of the provisions for achieving the severance of fetters. Once karmic fetters are removed, one becomes serene and free from all burdens.
One realizes the great fruit and thereby brings the spirit to its natural repose. Therefore, the fourth section is the analogy of the perfection of causes resulting in the attainment of the fruit.
Through mindfulness, wisdom, equanimity, and so forth, one guards what was originally received; receiving and practicing in accordance with these, their meaning is identical to "harmony.

The practices of counteraction are not singular, hence they are called a "multitude" (*saṃgha*). Once these remedial practices are perfected, they are able to extinguish evil, which is designated as "medicine" (*bhaiṣajya*); "releasing" (*śi*) means "removing" (*chō*).
"Yi" (also) means "liang" (good). When right mindfulness is practiced to completion, one will necessarily subdue and sever the seven non-virtues; hence it is said, "removing the unwholesome.
As for those called "the sick," they are those bound and entangled by the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and various fetters (*saṃyojana*), who lie submerged within birth and death.

Once the *śīla* (precepts) are pure, one gathers and gives rise to *samādhi*. With the concentrated mind clear and still, one penetrates the principle and contemplates the mind within; this is what is meant by [the term].

It is said: "To wear [the medicine] means to resolve arising delusions and eliminate their loss; therefore, it is called 'removal' and 'healing. Once the karmic knots are removed, one attains the fruit of the path of *nirvāṇa* and thereby brings the spirit to its own natural ease;
thus it is said that 'the body is healthy and one attains peace and joy. Next, the phrases are combined according to their respective correspondences. This is the second analogy.

The first verse provides a metaphorical exposition; the subsequent verses correlate with the preceding one. The first half of the latter verse serves as a metaphor for maintaining [the precepts], while the second half serves as a metaphor for their violation.
The "Pure Heaven of Nirvāṇa" lies beyond the realm of birth and death and is termed the "distant path. Since one sets out with the resolve to proceed toward it, it is said:

"If you wish to traverse it," yet though the intention has been set forth, if one lacks the feet of the precepts, there is no means by which one may ascend. Therefore, it says: "One should protect one's own feet. The second half of the verse may be interpreted as follows:
[The practitioner] knows this. Seeking heaven or *nirvāṇa* corresponds to the first line [of the verse]; if one wishes to travel a long road, guarding the precepts corresponds to the second line.
The latter half of the verse concerns breaking the precepts. Taking the practice of upholding them as a counter-example, it corresponds to the third metaphor:
"Just as a person who can cross a river. The goodness of receiving the precepts has an upward-tending nature.
Carrying the practitioner so as not to let them sink is likened to a floating bag; protecting what was originally received is functionally identical.

Though the cycle of birth and death is shoreless and called "deep," when the reception [of the precepts] and the phenomena [of practice] mutually support one another, and the antidotes are successfully established, one need not fear drowning.
Therefore, it is said that there is no sorrow of perishing. Reaching the fruit of the other shore of *nirvāṇa*, it is called "reaching the other shore.
All sons of the Buddha should be like a person wishing to cross a river; their practice must employ the appropriate means. The precepts are fundamentally like a life-preserving float (*uḍupa*).

One must never [abandon them], for one will ultimately not [sink]. The first two lines correspond to the first two [of the following], or they may be taken together as a whole. This is the fourth analogy.
The hall of the True Dharma of Nirvāṇa provides shelter for practitioners, protecting them from the cold and heat of birth and death. It is like the Hall of Śakra;
with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one polishes and carves this hall of the True Dharma of Nirvāṇa. Hence it is said: "Adorned with a city of myriad jewels.
Since the path to the fruit arises through precepts, they are likened to steps upon which the noble and holy ones tread. Hence it is said: "The path traversed by devas and humans. Below...

This may be understood accordingly. The fifth analogy illustrates skillful means and right mindfulness. Cultivating both the preparatory and the actual stages constitutes the goodness of upholding the precepts, which is termed "skillful training in the mundane.

When the practice of upholding the precepts is perfected, its internal capacity for rectitude is called "craft" (*kī*), while its external inexhaustible wondrous application is called "art" (*śilpa*).
Since these various practices are not singular, they are referred to as "all. Once the upholding of the precepts is ultimately accomplished, one will necessarily...
One does not fall into the lower realms or suffer evil retribution, just as a person in the world who is favored by a king does not fall into poverty or low station.

Not only does one avoid falling into the three miserable paths, but one further attains the fruits of the Path, whereby the spirit finds its own contentment; therefore it is said, "By this, one attains peace and happiness.
In this verse, the first half treats the subject specifically, while the second half follows it with a general summary.

In the second section, "The Practice of Gathering the Multitude," there are two parts. First, the verse on being able to accomplish the benefit of the multitude; second, the verse on being praised by the noble ones.

Within the first part, the upper half is an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the lower half is the application to the Dharma (*dārṣṭāntika*). If one wishes to govern and protect [the community], one must necessarily obtain the characteristics of a good assembly;
hence it says, "as before. Once the assembly is harmonious and close-knit, it fulfills the function of the *saṃgha* and is not [corrupted] by an evil assembly.

Because it is destroyed, it is called "ruined from within. When evil exists outside of good, it is termed "the enemy's army. Because one submits to and follows the transformation of the Right, it is called "conquered.

When they encounter people during times of famine while begging for food, those people would give rise to arrogance and say: [“Even the disciples of the Buddha could not obtain anything.”]
When the Buddha was in the world, his disciples were fully endowed with the precepts and possessed supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). They would take that non-glutinous rice to provide for the assembly.

Regarding those who violate the tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas: when explaining the aforementioned "knowing the time," what does "knowing the time" mean? It means knowing the time when the tainted dharmas arise.
As for the statement that the precepts were subsequently formulated, it is said that there are two benefits: first, praising him as a skilled physician.
First, it cures my illness. Second, regarding what I have established, it gives rise to a heart of reverence, causing the Dharma to abide for a long time.

The Buddha, knowing that this was the time when establishing the precepts would be beneficial, therefore spoke of "knowing the time. Furthermore, if one commits an outflow (āsrava), it immediately gives rise to disputes and faults;
every passage should be understood in this way. Subsequently, the establishment of the precepts refers to the broad formulation of the various prohibitions.
The text states: "All respond to this teaching: those who wish to sever the outflows (āsrava) thereby bring forth the ten benefits. Furthermore, the subsequent passage says:

"When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he perceives the faults of the multitude and establishes the precepts for the bhikṣus; for the sake of a single purposeful benefit, he gathers the Saṃgha," and so forth.
These passages from the main body of the scripture all pertain to gradual and progressive benefits. As for the wording of the text: [if...]

Regarding those who commit offenses involving outflows (*sāsrava*): both the teaching and the practice were deficient, and only thereafter were the precepts established. Because of these offenses, the rules were expanded to remedy the deficiencies of the previous two [stages].
Question: How does one supplement the teaching and supplement the practice? Answer: When the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, he proclaimed the concise teaching (*saṃkṣipta-śāsana*).

Those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) received the teaching and practiced it without deficiency or transgression. While the prohibitions of the teaching benefited the various capacities of beings at that time, for those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*), [the situation was different]...

If one’s conduct deviates from the teachings, giving rise to what is improper, and fails to practice them accordingly, thereby causing the teachings to be ruined and rendering them useless for the present time, this is called a deficiency in the teaching (*śāsana-vaidhurya*).
This constitutes a violation of the teachings and results in the defilement of one’s original vows; this is called a deficiency in practice (*pratipatti-vaidhurya*).

Therefore, the Tathāgata established those extensive teachings to reveal the names of various evils and the essence of various virtues. These two types of teachings are mutually consistent and mutually supportive, and they further lead back to the concise [teachings].

The teachings provide benefit according to the time; in meaning, they are equivalent to "supplementary instruction" (*pūjā*). Having heard the extensive prescriptions, the censuring that reveals faults, and having repented one's transgressions, one forever severs the continuity [of misconduct].
Thus, previously arisen evil karma cannot serve as a cause, and future bitter fruits will ultimately not be experienced.

This restores the purity of the precepts and is termed "supplementary practice" (*pūjā-caryā*). Furthermore, because it is extensive, the practitioner recognizes the characteristics [of the offenses] and guards the original [vows].
That which is received is focused, pure, and more excellent than before; it serves as a continuous support and is also called "supplementing practice. Question:

If the two faults were already prohibited even before the outflows had arisen, why was the brief teaching (saṃkṣipta-śikṣā) stated directly without waiting for an offense to be requested? Answer: There are two reasons.
First, because the brief teaching is the fundamental wheel of Dharma (mūla-dharmacakra), it can be established directly without waiting for an offense; the extensive [teaching] is merely its branch.
Regarding the branches of the Wheel of Dharma: if the root has not yet been destroyed, what need is there for extensive regulations?
Therefore, one must wait until the root is already damaged before regulating the branches to repair the wheel. Because these roots and branches differ, the methods of regulation are distinct.

As for those targeted by the two abbreviated teachings, their faculties are matured, supple, and easy to transform; thus, they do not require waiting for an offense to apply the extensive teachings. This is because the faculties targeted [by the abbreviated teachings]...
Regarding the dull-witted: they are unable to avoid transgressions. The initial establishment of the precepts was necessitated by actual offenses arising from specific circumstances.

It is for this reason that, because of the differences between the sharp and the dull, the methods of regulation vary. Second, regarding the conditions for the arising or non-arising of outflows (*āsrava*):

as long as the Bhikṣu Śāriputra had not yet attained the "sharp" [faculty], he remained close to the state of non-arising; from a remote perspective, his intention was merely to remain still. Thus, the present moment has passed.

This is the section on moderation (*mātrajñatā*). Regarding the statement, "If one obtains gain and offerings, one gives rise to outflows (*āsrava*) and the like," this is a proximate explanation for the arising of outflows and a remote explanation for knowing the proper time;

it serves as the basis for the formulation of the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). This is merely a refutation; there is no [inherent] name [for such a person]. As for the proximate explanation that outflows do not arise: [it refers to one who] does not give rise to outflows.

The distant explanation may be set aside for now. If one acquires fame or even great wealth, the proximate explanation gives rise to outflows (*āsrava*), while the distant explanation involves knowing the proper time.
As for the phrase "this person," it refers to being known by others and so forth; the two [explanations] should be understood as a combined conclusion.
End of the First Fascicle of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya*.
Written by hand during the heat of the sixth month of the seventh year of the Hōei era (1710). It is my hope that from generation to generation, the Vinaya teachings may long endure in this world.
In the past, the Great Master Ganshin [Ganjin], who crossed the sea, transmitted the two schools of the Dharma—the Nanshan and the Ritsu—to Japan. It is exactly as if...
The two wings of the bird are now widely practiced in the world by the Nanshan school, whereas those who transmit the single tradition of Fali are few.
Were it not for my own descendants, how could this [teaching] have been passed down? Let those with resolve reflect upon this, reflect upon this!
At the Shantian Monastery on Mount Wei, transcribed by the śramaṇa Huìhuǎng at the end of the era after the sea [had crossed];
verified by the śramaṇa Fǎlì. Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya, Fascicle Two, Part One. Composed by the śramaṇa Fǎlì.

From here below begins the main body of the text. The reason it was able to flourish is truly because monks and nuns could not overcome their pursuit of fame and profit, extensively generating outflows (*āsrava*) and thereby corrupting the abbreviated teachings.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, in accordance with these deficiencies and transgressions, established the extensive [vinaya] to supplement them;

he then categorized the manifestations of offenses and distinguished their degrees of gravity. These prohibitions and instructions were intended for all capacities, providing benefit for the times. This was the original intent, and thus it is so named.

The True School. The essential purport of the True School does not go beyond the physical and verbal restraint of goodness, receiving and upholding [the precepts], and the lightness or gravity of transgressions.

These have been explained by many people, so they cannot be recorded in full here. There are also those who say that the regulations were established for a single era, depending on the person, time, place, and circumstances.
The preceding and succeeding sections differ. Within a single code of precepts and a single scripture, there are over six hundred segments that explain the sequence [of rules];

it is not that this meaning is absent. Now, seeking the essential principle, I shall divide them into two parts for the time being. The first two sections consist of the *Prātimokṣa* (Bases of Precepts), which detail the five categories of offenses.

This is intended to enable monks and nuns to skillfully cultivate the practice of antidotes to distance themselves from transgressions, or to maintain the practice of restraint and observance. The second *Khandhaka* (Section) follows.

The lower body, speech, and deportment constitute the various aspects of the practice of the two observances (*saṃvara*): first cessation (*virati*), then performance (*karaṇa*). This follows the sequential order of their meaning.
Alternatively, one may briefly clarify the two observances first and then extensively differentiate them later; for now, we shall proceed from the beginning. Question:

Within the primary doctrine of the higher precepts (*adhiśīla*), there are only the vows of undertaking (*samādāna*) and the subsequent rules (*anuśikṣā*). For what reason does this textual analysis focus exclusively on the two observances of cessation and performance? It seems as though it should address the specific points of the [lower] training.
According to the meaning. Answer: If one considers the sequence of following the practice of receiving [the precepts], the actual reception of the dharma is not "following" (anuvartana).

However, here we speak from the perspective of what enables a person to maintain [the discipline]; therefore, the reception of the dharma is subsumed under "active maintenance" (kriyā-dhāraṇa). The first section further divides into two: first, the maintenance through restraint for the great *saṃgha* (monks);

second, the maintenance through restraint for the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*). Regarding this, there must first be a clear distinction between two gates: first, the combination and separation of monks and nuns; second, [the distinction between] monks and nuns...

Regarding the sequence [of the five categories]: first, we shall distinguish their combination and separation. Question: The *bhikṣu* and *bhikṣuṇī* Sanghas are equal in their status as renunciants; they equally aspire for liberation, and both are fully ordained.
Since there is no difference in the titles of the precepts, why are five categories established separately? Answer: In general, the function of the precepts is to prevent wrongdoing.
In enumerating the offenses, they cannot be distinguished by the transgressions themselves, for the faults arise in people and the resulting afflictions are unequal.

Therefore, between the two assemblies (monks and nuns), there are differences in the number of articles in the five groups of rules and variations in their gravity; some rules exist in one and not in the other, and while the nature of the offense may be the same, the circumstances differ.

Because of these distinct characteristics, they cannot be governed by a single, unified regulation. Second, regarding the sequence: [this section] asks about the characteristics of the precepts for the Great Assembly of monks.

The reason it was explained first is answered as follows: it is to manifest that the man who protects, maintains, and establishes [the teaching] possesses a power superior to that [of the woman], and furthermore, because there are two distinct types—teacher and follower—and because there is a sequence of ordination for those who have left the household life. For these reasons, it is so. Within the category of *bhikṣus*, they are further divided into two.

First, the five categories [of offenses] clarify the prevention of future transgressions. Second, the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmāḥ*) eliminate and extinguish the karma of transgressions that have already arisen;

only when both the past and the present have vanished can one become truly pure and bright. Furthermore, the former section clarifies "abstaining from what is prohibited" (*śīla-virati*), while the subsequent section distinguishes "engaging in what is prescribed" (*samādāna*).

Now, in explaining the seven methods for settling disputes, if we investigate them through their underlying principles, they likewise prevent future impropriety, because they apply to both the past and the present.
Previously, it was not granted that there is an offense. How then can it be judged as "the practice of having already extinguished"?

That which has been extinguished is precisely what is to be performed. Furthermore, regarding the previous explanation: among the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), if a dispute is settled, on one hand there is the *pāyattika* (offense), and on the other hand there is the *duṣkṛta* (misdeed).
Therefore, it was said, "the practice of having already extinguished. Now, upon examining this meaning, there are many contradictions. First, the two offenses...

There are five contradictions: first, the contradiction regarding the granting [of the *pārivāsika*]; second, the contradiction regarding the three locations for the *duṣkṛta*; third, the contradiction regarding the location where the teaching was established;
fourth, the contradiction that the one hundred and one *duṣkṛtas* are not subsumed; and fifth, the contradiction with the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya that there would be only a *duṣkṛta*.

For these reasons, the current interpretation should be that whether the *parivāsa* is granted or not granted, it constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one were to act otherwise—granting it when it should not be granted—it would be only a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes a small portion of the fifth section. How could the training rules be collectively bound together as a single part?

Thus, the aforementioned [sections] form one part, and the small portion of the fifth [section] along with the seven methods of settling disputes (satta adhikaraṇasamathā) form another. The *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* is divided into two parts according to the text that establishes its fundamental principles.

Since there is this difficulty, the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* shall for now be explained according to eight textual sections. If these eight are taken as a whole, they constitute five categories of offenses, namely:

The two *naiḥsargika-pāyattikās* are combined under the category of the *śaikṣa-dharmas*; the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamathas* are combined under the category of the *aniyata-dharmas*. Because they are not yet fixed, they constitute only five [categories].
To explain these five, one must employ two gates: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition.

The general exposition is explained through four gates: first, the five categories of offenses; second, the seven groups of offenses; third, the preparatory stages; and fourth, the maintenance and violation [of precepts].
Regarding these four positions, the fifth—namely, the ultimate [offense] alone—is explained first, because it constitutes the fundamental and ultimate course of action (*karmapatha*).

Although one knows the ultimate [result], the characteristics of the preceding and succeeding attendants must also be recognized; therefore, the seven groups are distinguished so that their meanings may be weighed according to lightness or gravity.

Whether the fruits of the five or seven [categories] arise from the root or from causes, they differ merely through variations in conditions (*pratyaya*), and these cannot be fully exhausted. This is because one must thoroughly contemplate the nature of karma.

Next, the third [section] explains the three skillful means (*upāya*). Having already recognized the characteristics of transgressions and their gradations, it is logically necessary to maintain [the precepts]; therefore, this is followed by the section on observance and violation.

If one understands the five categories (*pañca-vastu*), there are four gates of explanation: first, establishing the five categories and explaining their names and meanings; second, explaining the names.
This is the title. Third, the establishment of the five bases; fourth, the clarification of the sequence.

Regarding the meaning of the first section: since the Vinaya takes the cessation of unwholesome conduct as its primary principle, it employs the disciplinary practices (*śīla*) that serve as the remedy as the subject of exposition.

As for the establishment of the five categories, this Vinaya is called the "Five Aggregates of Offenses" (*pañca-āpatti-skandha*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the five sections of offenses are established based on one [principle].
I shall now explain their names. The four *śīla* for the great *bhikṣu* [saṃgha] and the eight *śīla* for the *bhikṣuṇī* constitute the first chapter.

The thirteen *śīla* for the *bhikṣu* and the seventeen *śīla* for the *bhikṣuṇī* constitute the second chapter. The thirty-nine *śīla*, one hundred and twenty-one *śīla*, and one hundred and twenty *śīla* for the *bhikṣu*, along with the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* and one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* for the *bhikṣuṇī*—totaling two hundred and eight *śīla*—constitute the third chapter. [The rules for] the *bhikṣu*...

The four *śikṣāpada* for *bhikṣuṇīs* and the eight *gurudharma* constitute the fourth *varga*. The one hundred *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules for monks and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* methods constitute the fifth *varga*.

The one hundred *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules for *bhikṣuṇīs* constitute the fifth *varga*. As for the term "varga" (*pāda*), it is called a "varga" because people explain it by comparing the relative gravity of the offenses;
it is as commonly analyzed. Now, when we speak of a "varga," it refers to a category where the types are uniform and the meanings are similar. This is what is meant.
There are five stages; hence they are called the "Five Sections. Each possesses three types of equality: first, equality of name; second, equality of substance;

and third, equality of ultimate realization. For example, the four precepts of the first section are all named *pārājika*; their meanings regarding gravity and lightness are equal, and they are all products of deliberate thought.
Because they share these similarities, they are recorded as the first section. Other items that do not belong to this class cannot logically be considered the same. Thus it continues...
This continues up to the fifth category; the same applies to the subsequent types. Therefore, they are called "sections" (*varga*). The term "section" appears in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

This Vinaya is termed the "Fivefold Transgression of Prohibitions. Because it arises from what is improper, it is called an "offense" (*āpatti*); it is also termed the "Fivefold Aggregate of Offenses."

Because each of these offenses contains many specific instances, they are called "aggregates of offenses" (*āpatti-skandha*). Furthermore, because they must be restrained and guarded against, they are also called the "five kinds of prohibitions.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* refers to them as the "five categories," while the *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* refers to them as the "five sections. "Section" (*varga*) is a synonym for a distinct class or group.

For example, there are sixteen sections for the *pārājika* offenses, fifty-two sections for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, three hundred and sixty sections for the *sthūlātyaya*, and twelve sections for the *prāyaścittika*. These are not four.

They are subsumed under their respective sections (*varga*). All remaining offenses, those common to the *Śaikṣa* rules, and the offenses taught in the *Vasudharmā-vinaya*, are all subsumed under the category of *dukkaṭa*.
