These transgressions and the clusters of offenses, along with their titles, chapters, sections, and names—their types, meanings, and so forth—are here explained by means of a single name.
However, because the commentary on the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* circulated in this land prior to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it has caused [confusion] among those who explain [the law].

The name of the *Śīla-skandhaka* (Chapter on Ethics) is cited to explain this meaning; the meaning itself is not at fault. When explained in this manner, the offenses (*āpatti*) and their respective chapters (*skandha*) are integrated throughout the five categories.
The specific names of these five are the *pārājika* and so forth. Question: Since the practice of ethical conduct (*śīla-karman*) is the primary subject, why is it referred to as *pārājika*?
Answer: Because the practice extends across all five categories and cannot be distinguished by itself, the term is used to differentiate them by citing that which they prevent.

Because they are able to counteract [the offenses], they are called *pārājika* and so forth. This is to cite the names of that which is prevented as the names of the remedial practices (*pratipakṣa-caryā*), since the signified is named after the signifier.
Within this context, these are also termed the chapters on offenses such as *pārājika*, as well as their categories and sections.
The second is the designation by name. This designation further involves five aspects. "Pārājika" (I-yi) is designated according to its essential nature;

it is called "extreme evil" (*pārājika*). It is considered evil for three reasons: first, falling away, meaning the loss of the fruits of the Path; second, not dwelling together, because such a person is not included within either of the two Saṃghas;

and third, falling into ruin, because they enter the evil destinies. Thus, this extreme evil is termed a "person deserving punishment"; therefore, it is designated according to its essential nature. [This refers to] the Saṃgha.
"Residual" (*śeṣa*) refers to the name derived from the nature of the object. Having committed this offense, the defilements entangle the practitioner such that their pure function is not complete;

therefore, it is called "residual. Because this offense with its residue is removed through the Sangha, it is termed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Sangha-residual). This means the name is formed based on the substance [of the offense] and the object of the confession.
Alternatively, "residual" may be named after the meaning of the object. Furthermore, it is said: "Sangha" refers to the object of confession, and "va" (or "po") refers to the beginning.

This refers to *pārājika* (defeat), which involves concealment; *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting with remainder), which means that at the very end one emerges from the offense; these are named entirely according to the object of confession. *Pātayantika* (offense involving falling) has the sense of causing a person to fall;
the offense possesses this capacity, and thus the name is derived from its functional power. *Pratideśanīya* (to be confessed) is established as a designation based on its antidote;
the text says, "I now confess my fault to the Venerable One," which may also be called "receiving [the title] by being reproached for the fault. The text says, "I have committed an offense."
Regarding the "reprehensible dharma" (*sāvadya-dharma*): if it is called *duṣkṛta*, the name is derived from its full meaning; thus it is said that *duṣkṛta* means "evil action.

If it is called *śikṣāpada*, the name is derived from the injunction to train; that is, because one "should train" (*śikṣitavya*). What has been explained above concerns only the designation for the expiation of offenses (*āpatti-nirghātana*).

If, however, we consider the designation based on the practice of the precepts (*śīla-caryā*), then among the five categories of preceptual conduct, the fifth is *duṣkṛta*. Thus, the five categories of preceptual conduct are established.

The name is singular, as it denotes that which is accomplished by way of prevention. If one speaks of *śikṣā*, the name has two aspects: the first four are identical to the aforementioned names for what is prevented;
the fifth is "exhortation to training. If it is capable of expressing the teaching, the name is singular, meaning that all [names] follow from what is expressed (*vācya*).

Furthermore, regarding the previous statement that "anāpatti" (non-offense) is the opposite of "āpatti" (offense), and that "sāvaśeṣa" (with remainder) is the opposite of "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder)—let us set these aside for a moment as they cannot be used to establish a direct reversal of names.

For instance, if one were to treat the *śīla* (precepts) and *vṛtta* (conduct) as two distinct categories, how could the names of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses with remainder) within the *śīla* be reversed to correspond to the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses) and so forth within the *vṛtta*? Therefore, it is known that this is not the case.

Regarding the intention behind establishing the third [category] as five: some say it is because there are five types of medicine, and thus they are established as five sections; this interpretation may well be correct.

Alternatively, it may be that these are merely worldly regulations for the Path, such as the system of the five penal codes. Or, it may be that the Tathāgata, teaching in accordance with the faculties of beings, briefly indicated these five.
Regarding the fourth sequence: first, we shall explain the offenses to be prevented by investigating the origins of their original establishment.

As prohibitions were issued in accordance with specific transgressions, the gravity of the matters became disordered, lacking a fixed order of priority. Now, in clarifying this sequence, upon what standard does it rely?
It is because the Great Sage desired that this Dharma be fully transmitted to distant generations; thus, Upāli now specifically proclaims the correct method, doing so out of a sense of solemnity.

Light offenses are compared to those that follow. Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Upāli, relying strictly upon the sacred teachings, compiled the offenses established by the Buddha regarding death itself;

these were appropriately placed at the beginning with strict regulation. As for the remaining lighter offenses, they are arranged according to their respective grades, such that even the fifth category can be understood accordingly.
The reason for doing so is the desire to enable monks and nuns to observe their transgressions and give rise to [repentance].

One develops revulsion: first recognizing gross transgressions, and later perceiving subtle faults. One skillfully cultivates remedies to eliminate those karmic factors that obstruct the Path and to provide the resources for renunciation, thereby overcoming the hindrances to realizing the Way.
As it is said regarding the three, five, and fifteen precepts—how could these not be the golden words of the Buddha?
Thus, one knows the sequence. If we rely on the sequence of the practices that can serve as protection, the remedies for the first category constitute the root of practice;
therefore, they are explained first. This is known because if the practice of the first category is ruined, how could the four lower branches possibly arise?

Thus, it is necessary for the practice of the first category to be established so that it may give rise to the root of all other practices. Therefore, one knows that the first is the root of practice.

First, it clarifies the fundamental establishment of practice. If one does not cultivate the various dharmas of the community, the practitioner’s communal dharmas will not be perfected and the structural framework will not be established;
how then could one bring peace to the Dharma and benefit the masses? Next, it clarifies the second section: the practice of the structural framework of the communal dharmas.

Although these communal dharmas may exist, if one does not cultivate the body, speech, and the dignified deportment of movement and stillness, the structural framework is difficult to establish. Next, it clarifies...
Third is the majestic deportment of body and speech. Since such deportment is required, if one does not avoid reproach and fault, practice will be difficult to accomplish.

Fourth is the section on distancing oneself from reproach and fault. Although one may distance oneself from reproach and fault, if one does not show reverence and compliance toward the Triple Gem, one will merely eliminate transgressions through dispute;
this instead becomes an obstacle that binds one to the three realms of existence—how then could one achieve liberation? Fifth is the section on revering and complying with the Triple Gem.

The Jewel [of the Sangha] possesses matured and refined deportment; it ultimately eliminates transgressions and disputes, and its conduct proceeds toward the Path. This is based on the fundamental [nature], and for this reason, it is superior at the outset.
If, however, superiority is defined by the difficulty of renunciation, then the fifth [stage] is the most superior, down to the initial stage which is inferior.

The second section, the Sevenfold Grouping (*saptaka-puñja*), is analyzed through five gates: first, the arrangement of the seven groupings and the explanation of the meaning of the term "grouping"; second, the intention behind establishing the seven;

third, the clarification of how they receive their names; fourth, the sequence of *sthūlātyaya* offenses; and fifth, the distinction between those that enter the formal categories (*paryāya*) and those that do not.

Regarding the one who establishes the seven groups (*saptaka-nikāya*): the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* constitute the first group; the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣas] and seventeen [anīyatas] constitute the second group; all *sthūlātyaya*s constitute the third;

the one hundred and twenty and two hundred and eight [prāyaścittika*s] constitute the fourth; the four *pratideśanīya*s constitute the fifth; *duṣkṛta*s constitute the sixth; and *durbhāṣita*s constitute the seventh. These seven positions are identical across all Vinayas and Śāstras. As for what is called a "group" (*nikāya*): The term "group" (*nikāya*) refers to a collection of similar offenses.

Just as when many people gather together they are called a "group," so too, when many offenses of a similar nature are gathered together, it is called a "group. Furthermore, because these offenses are grouped according to their gravity and shared characteristics, they are termed "groups. This classification is consistent in all the Vinaya scriptures and commentaries.
As for this, various offenses are not merely one; when they are gathered together in one place, it is called a "collection" (*piṇḍa*).

If that is so, since there is no separate text for the *pāyantika* (offenses requiring expiation), why is it called a "collection"? Answer: The collection exists within the Great Teaching, or it may be assembled under a single name.

If one were to cite a single name and issue a command, there would be no *pāyantika* that would not be exhausted. Therefore, it is also called a "collection. According to the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*, the seven collections are as follows: the first is...
1. The four *pārājika* offenses. 2. The twenty-three *śeṣa* (residual) offenses. 3. The three *sthūlātyaya* offenses. 4.
All those arising from incomplete portions of the two groups [of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pāyattika*]. 5. The four *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
6. The nine and ten *pāyattika* offenses. 7. The four *pratideśanīya* offenses. 8. Those offenses not included within the six groups, as well as incomplete portions of the six groups.
Regarding the origins and the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), all [offenses] are included within the *vinaya-skandha*. This is the sequence of the seven groups (*skandha*).
As for the third group, the *sthūlātyaya*, it is because all [offenses] in the other two groups arise from incomplete parts.
Within the *pāyattika* [rules], there are two groups distinguished by whether they involve relinquishment (*pratyosaraṇa*) or non-relinquishment. The seventh group...
Regarding the phrase "not included therein" and so forth: this means that only the fundamental offenses (*maulāpatti*) constitute the first six groups;

the proximate preparations (*sāmantaka*) for the first two groups constitute the third group; and the remote and proximate preparations for the first two groups, as well as those for the latter four groups, [are excluded].
All are included within the seventh category. To understand these distinctions, we shall return to the explanation provided in the *Vinaya*.

Regarding the establishment of the seven categories in the second [section], this refers to the nature of the offenses being prevented; their essence is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*). Why is this?

It is not established based on the substance [of the act] alone, but is called the "unwholesome category" (*akuśala-rāśi*). Answer: If one considers the three categories (*tri-rāśi*) to provide a general clarification of the characteristics of karma, it is also...

It is thus designated as "a single mass of unwholesome. However, the original intent behind the formulation of the precepts was to extensively clarify the distinctions among offenses and the differentiation between their degrees of gravity.

If one were to establish them solely according to their essential nature, how could the distinction between the light and the heavy be recognized? For this reason, [the classification is established].

One cannot establish a single category. If one proceeds by dividing according to the complete [factors], they do not exceed body and speech; bodily transgressions constitute *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), while verbal transgressions constitute *dubbhāsita* (ill-spoken).

Thus, two groups should be established. As for why [only] these two are not established: because their substance contains both light and heavy [degrees of gravity], and their characteristics are likewise difficult to distinguish, two categories are not established.
Therefore, following the meaning and departing from prolixity, five groups are established. Those not subsumed within these five are returned once more to the two positions [of body and speech].

By assigning the five [categories] to the two [types of offenses], there are thus seven groups (*sapta-varga*). The distinctions between the characteristics of these offenses are coarse enough to be recognized. Question:

Since the original precepts were established by the Noble One, they are divided according to the specific transgressions as they occur; why then speak of following the meaning and departing from the detailed text? Could it be that a single dharma existed prior [to the specific instances]?

[The text] is divided into five [categories]. Therefore, one knows it is not otherwise. The answer, "following the meaning and departing from the extensive," is because there are five aspects regarding what is produced by body and speech;

these are simply the previous five, which differ from the aforementioned five. Regarding the characteristics of minor offenses (*laghu-laghu*), two are established within their respective positions, thus forming seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*).
Why must there necessarily be a prior division into five before the departure from the extensive can be clarified? Furthermore, with respect to the precepts (*śīla*)...
The establishment of the chapters and sections (*pien-chü*) and the meaning of their division are, in principle, without error.

Regarding the third point, "attaining a name," there are six ways of attaining a name; the first is when the aggregate (*pien*) corresponds to its own essential substance (*t'ang-t'i*). "Residue" (*ts'an*) refers to the sense of the object (*ching*). As for "Lan," the commentary says:

*Thūla* means "great. *Āpatti* means "obstructing the Path. This offense is a great obstruction; the Path is that which is obstructed. Thus, the name is formed based on the function of that which is obstructed.

*Pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are as explained in the five categories [of offenses]. Since the sixth and seventh groups are termed *duṣkṛta* (evil action) and *durbhāṣita* (evil speech), these names are formed by combining both meanings.
Regarding what is called "evil action" (*duṣkṛta*) and so forth: it is evil because one has performed evil; it is due to the act itself.

To incur evil and that which is called "evil action" (kaukṛtya) are both termed "evil. It is called "evil" because it is spoken of as evil; because one incurs evil through such speech, they are both termed "evil speech.

What has been analyzed above concerns only the designation of offenses. If one proceeds according to the object, and the prohibitive teaching follows the object, then the designations for what is expressed are identical.
Regarding the sequence of the fourth *sthūlātyaya*: one asks why a single offense of *sthūlātyaya* is sometimes placed in the third category and sometimes in the fifth. What is the meaning of this?
The answer is that the seven groups (*saptanikāya*) are distinguished by means of the precepts (*śīla*) and the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*).

Because the *sthūlātyaya* obstructs [the attainment of] the precepts, the practice capable of counteracting it is subsumed under the gate of the precepts; thus, it is placed in the third category. However, if one were to divide them according to a uniform mixture of categories, it must be placed in the fifth.
The reason for this is that their essence contains the distinction between the provisional (*upāya*) and the ultimate;

furthermore, they are subsumed under the "Miscellaneous Gates" (*miśra-mukha*), and since their transgressions are more numerous and their prohibitions more severe, they must be placed below the "Uniform" [category] and above the "Miscellaneous" [category], occupying the fifth position. Moreover, there is another interpretation: because they act as causes, they constitute three [categories].
There are five [categories] for the sake of the fruit; they are established to clarify the completion of others, and it is because others are completed that this is so.

Regarding the fifth point, the meaning of "entering" and "not entering," there is a twofold analysis. First, by citing the seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*) in contrast to the five offenses, one clarifies what constitutes entering and not entering.
Second, by relying on the ten sūtras of the *Prātimokṣa*, one distinguishes between entering and not entering. To explain the first method: the seven groups...
Regarding the status of offenses, they are divided into three levels. The four upper groups constitute the four transgressions (*pārājika*).

The group of *sthūlātyaya* never enters [the category of transgression]. As for the two groups of the sixth and seventh [saṃghāvaśeṣa and pāyattika], there are cases where they do and do not enter [the category of transgression].

Why, then, does *sthūlātyaya* alone not enter the five transgressions among the seven groups? What is the meaning of this? The answer is: Generally, for an offense to enter the five transgressions, it must possess three conditions: first, equality of name; second, equality of substance...
The essence is uniform. Third, the ultimate uniformity. The four categories beginning with *pārājika* all possess these meanings; therefore, they constitute four [categories].

Within the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, there is only nominal uniformity—that is, it is called a "saṃghāvaśeṣa cluster"—but it lacks the other two types of uniformity. Because it encompasses both cause and effect and includes both heavy and light offenses, it is not included among the five [categories].
What, then, is this? It is said that the "saṃghāvaśeṣa cluster" is its nominal uniformity; however, if one relies on the cause...

The results are twofold: namely, the preliminary application (*prayoga*) and the culmination (*niṣṭhā*). For example, those who assist in the schism of the Saṃgha—such as those with skins, bowls, naked bodies, flesh, or blood—are guilty of the culmination of a *pārājika*.

In the treatise, this is called a "solitary *sthūlātyaya*. The first two [categories] constitute the minor offenses, while all subsequent grave and light *sthūlātyayas* are collectively termed "preliminary applications" and also "unaccomplished offenses. A *pārājika* is termed a "grave turbidity"; these are not equal to the culmination. If, regarding...

The first two categories contain both heavy and light offenses, which are thus divided into four: first, *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses that cannot be expiated, such as the two types of *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses;

second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses before a great assembly (*mahā-saṃgha*); third, *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses before a small assembly (*parītta-saṃgha*); and fourth, *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses before a single person (*pratimukha*).

Regarding "offenses that cannot be expiated," the text states that they are like Devadatta, who ought to be expelled (*pravāsanīya*). Furthermore, the *Mātṛkā* says that among the four matters that cannot be remedied, there is...
Because these two are *ānantarya* (heinous) offenses, they cannot be expiated. If that is so, why does it say elsewhere, "One offense cannot be repented"?

Furthermore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is asked: "Who breaks the Saṃgha? It is said to be nine pure persons (*pariśuddha*). What offense do they incur? The *Daśabhāṇavāra* answers: "A *sthūlātyaya*.
How is it removed? The Buddha says: "Is it like the repentance for a *sthūlātyaya*? The answer is: "Now, explaining this meaning, it differs from what is seen in the *Daśabhāṇavāra*. As follows:

In that Vinaya, the two types of *ānantarya* (heinous offenses) are termed "light"; therefore, slandering [the Dharma] incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. It further states: "As with the repentance for a *sthūlātyaya*," from which we know that in that Vinaya, one follows the principle according to the teaching;
this is because there is no mention of the name *pārājika* (defeat). In this Vinaya, however, slandering [the Dharma] is difficult [to expiate], being equal to a *pārājika*.

Since both *ānantarya* and *pārājika* are equally subject to formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), we know that the gateway of repentance here also follows the principle and does not merely follow the literal teaching. Therefore...

Regarding the first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* that cannot be expiated, the second which requires a great assembly (*mahāsāṃghika*), and the third which requires a small assembly (*pariṣad*), the *Daśabhikṣuvinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
The Buddha said there are four types of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: namely, those bordering on a *pārājika*, which are expiated before the entire Saṃgha within the boundary (*sīmā*);

the light ones, which are expiated before four monks outside the boundary; those bordering on a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* that are grave, which are treated like a *pārājika*; and those bordering on a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* that are light. First.

Regarding the confession among human beings, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "For a *pārājika*, one should confess its gravity before a great assembly; for a light *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one should go outside the boundary and repent before four people.
The method of repentance is as described above. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, four or more people constitute a "great assembly.

If it does not say "great assembly," yet there are four or more, this serves as proof that they are so considered. Two or three people are called a "small assembly"; if one says "great assembly" [when there are fewer than four], [it is an error].
"Exclusion" refers to methods such as the confession through one's own words before the assembly (*prātimokṣa-vinaya*).

"Confession before a small group" refers to methods such as the confession through one's own words before two or three people. The "fourth, face-to-face" refers to confessing within a single individual among those who have made their own admissions.
Since there are these four stages—such as those cases where confession is impossible—they are not of equal substance. If...

The *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) is also fourfold. As in the case of the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for a group, or regarding the two causes—proximate and remote—for causing a schism in the Saṃgha, those who must confess before both the Great Assembly and a small group, as well as those subject to internal remorse (*tatsvabhāva-vijñapti*), are likewise unequal [in their status]. Why, then, is it said that there are *duṣkṛta* offenses included within the five categories of transgressions?

Answer: The original formulation of the five categories of transgressions was established in relation to the *mahābhikṣu*. Where, then, could there be a *duṣkṛta* offense involving the formal act of banishment by the Great Assembly?
The minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*) are also skillful means. Apart from these, that which is ultimately auspicious (*niṣṭhā-guṇa*) is included within the five categories.

If this is so, the *sthūlātyaya* is likewise; those who take the ultimate form as the basis for their classification do so because, within the category of *duṣkṛta*, provided the act is completed, it fully possesses the three equal factors.
For the *sthūlātyaya*, the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is excluded, yet even within the ultimate stage, there still remains a distinction between the grave and the light. Therefore—

They are not analogous. However, among the *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅) offenses, there are those that are included and those that are not. Therefore, the *pācittiya* (聚) category is broad while the [specific] articles (篇) are narrow;
because the former includes both body and speech, the articles are broad while the category is narrow.

Regarding the second section, the ten items of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* concerning what is included and what is excluded: first, the introduction to the precepts (*śikṣāpada-nidāna*) is clarified through a threefold analysis.

First, determining whether offenses are grave or light as to their inclusion or exclusion; second, distinguishing the quantity of offenses; third, explaining the conditions for the arising of transgressions.

These involve distinctions between the general and the specific, and the universal and the particular. First, to determine gravity and lightness: it is asked, "What offenses does the introduction contain, and how are they grave or light? The answer is: speaking generally...

Regarding the detailed exposition of the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts): if one remains silent when falsely claiming purity, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); if one announces [one's purity] while being impure, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

The same principle applies to the fifteen types of *Poṣadha* expositions. If there are three or fewer people present, there is only a *sthūlātyaya* and no *duṣkṛta*, because the requirement of "purity through self-declaration" is excluded.

Even if one person performs the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) and verbally declares purity, because the counterpart is absent, they commit only a *duṣkṛta*. What is now referred to as the "introduction" (*nidāna*) refers to the actual...

There is an offense. If one does not confess after being questioned three times, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for silent falsehood. As for the subsequent discussion of whether [the offense] enters [the formal category] or not:
setting aside for a moment the matter of individuals practicing the Dharma, we shall directly address the inclusion of the offense within the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* articles.

It is because of this expedient means that it does not enter [the formal category], even though it is concealed and not spoken of; thus, while it remains hidden and unspoken, the words have not yet been made manifest.
[Question: Therefore, this is a skillful means (*upāya*). Because it is a skillful means, it does not enter into the formal categories [of offenses].

If that were so, then in the case of a great lie (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*) where the body manifests signs and so forth, even if the other person understands, since one has not yet spoken it aloud, how could one incur the ultimate grave offense?

Yet, that [offense] is established as grave; this case should be the same. [Answer: Although in the case of a great lie one has not yet spoken it aloud, the meaning of the indicative sign (*liṅga*) is complete.
Those who observe his physical appearance believe that the Noble One cannot be mistaken; thus, he incurs a grave offense.

This silent falsehood involves no movement of the body, yet while among the assembly, it deceives those who are pure. Those who ought to question him do not ask him, and consequently develop the perception that he is pure.

Therefore, this is merely a skillful means. If this were so, and one had previously formed the intention to remain silent, yet later remained silent when questioned, would that not then fulfill one's original purpose?

Question: The mind should be the culmination. Answer: Although one performs the act of silence, there may still be the possibility of speaking; thus, [silence] is merely a preliminary means (*upāya*).

If that were so, when one originally forms the mind of contact (*sparśa*), there would be the possibility of it becoming heavy; therefore, contact should be the preliminary means. Answer: Because one simply forms a mind that seeks comfort, contact is the culmination.
If, later, one acts with heaviness, then a separate mind arises anew. If that were so, even when performing silence—

Question: If one intends [to speak] but does not wish to utter words, and instead uses subsequent speech to deceive, this constitutes a separate offense; it should therefore not be considered a preparatory act (*upāya*). Answer:

Since one may personally commit a grave offense without depending on physical contact, contact is the culmination [of that act]. There is no instance of false speech that does not depend on a deceptive mind;

thus, remaining silent while intending to deceive is merely a preparatory act. Because it is a preparatory act, it does not constitute a full offense (*pārājika*). Furthermore, it is categorized under minor false speech.

In the passage following the *vyañjana* (phoneme), the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is not established because it occurs within the state [of the actual path]. Since this is so for the silence of the introduction (*nidāna*), the same applies to the subsequent eight [sections].
However, contemporary commentators address only the fixed [rules] of the introduction; as for the logic of the subsequent eight sections, they are identical, and thus I shall not elaborate further.
I shall merely distinguish between entry and non-entry with respect to the *udāyin* and other [factors].
Second, the extent [of the offense] shall be explained in four sections. First, distinguishing according to the object. Question:

If one commits a single offense and passes through three interrogations, is the offense incurred individually from each member of the Saṃgha, or is it incurred collectively from the three interrogations? Answer: Silence is fundamentally a deception of the interrogation;

the offense is incurred in accordance with the interrogation. It is not individually determined for each person. This is because silence occurs precisely when there is an interrogation; where there is no interrogation, there is no silence.

Therefore it is so. Since this is the case for *tūṣṇīmbhāva* (remaining silent), the same applies to *jñapti-codanā* (informing for purification): one does not incur a separate offense based on the individual person. Second, speaking in terms of the offenses themselves:

Question—As in the introduction, there was a general question regarding those who have committed an offense and must confess; what if one commits ten offenses and remains silent, thereby deceiving the Saṃgha?

Is the offense incurred from the questioning, or is the greater offense incurred from the silence? The answer is that it is concluded solely based on the questioning and the silence, not because of the offense itself.

Since the false speech arises through the silence when the Sangha questions, and does not exist if there is no questioning, and since the condition of the questioning is one and the same, how could there be multiple instances of silence?

This is unlike the concealment of an offense, where the offense arises as one conceals it; thus, the number of offenses follows the number of times it is concealed. Furthermore, this silence constitutes a false and deceptive act.

Question: Regarding the offense of arising (*utthāna-āpatti*), it is not the offense of deception (*visaṃvādana-āpatti*) that constitutes the arising of the offense; therefore, this is determined by the question. As for concealing the original offense, one does not conceal the characteristic of clarity (*vijñapti-lakṣaṇa*);

thus, the offense follows the extent of what was concealed. The *pācittiya* for declaring oneself pure (*śuddhivāda*) is also established based on the speech itself, not based on the underlying offense.
Third, regarding the questioner: since the question is asked once and the proclamation is made three times, does this conclude one silence or conclude three silences?

The answer is that although there are three proclamations, the silence constitutes only one offense, because they together constitute a single dharma. This is like how all three requests constitute a single dharma.

If that is so, then as with the two types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) performed during the day, if there is a transgression of the mind and one abandons [the practice], why is it that there are three *thullaccaya* offenses?

It cannot be that for each individual question posed, one who possesses a deceitful mind would simultaneously give rise to three instances of silence. Answer: The method of admonishing through speech already carries a grave result;
it is possible for there to be gradations of lightness and gravity within the causal stage such that three offenses are incurred. As for this present inquiry:
I ask the assembly directly: since purity and impurity are non-existent, why must one pose a fourth question to obtain a heavy retribution?
Why is it necessary to follow the chanting of descending stages and commit many transgressions? The fourth [question] distinguishes the "many" based on the disclosure or concealment of offenses.

Regarding the ancient interpretation of the six offenses as being committed through silence in three locations—namely, the two cases of sexual contact and physical touch, the two cases of coarse behavior in private or public, and the two cases of sitting [inappropriately]—these are not present in either the introduction or the main body of the text.

Within the *niyata* (definitive) offenses, there are three instances of transgression, as each of these categories is specifically raised for questioning. Excluding the *sthūlātyaya*, all others involve transgression in two places:
within the *nidāna* (introduction) and the main body of the text (*vibhaṅga*), with the exception of only one *sthūlātyaya* among the seven methods of settling disputes (*saptadharmāḥ*).

Within the *nidāna* and the seven methods of settling disputes, there are two instances of transgression through silent falsehood. All other *sthūlātyayas* involve transgression in only one place, namely within the *nidāna*. As previously stated, regarding the six types of offenses, three...

Regarding the offense of remaining silent in two locations, this meaning is not so. There is an offense in only two locations, because within the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules, there has as yet been no actual offense;

how then could there be an offense for remaining silent? As for the inquiry within those *aniyata* rules, it means one must ask: "In the two locations—the secluded and the open—and within the four modes of deportment, is there anything that requires investigation?
It does not mean that there already exists a fixed matter such as a *pārājika* (defeat) or other offense that can be identified.
Question: When this silence arises and one understands it in this way, there are two positions: excluding the *laṅka* (stain), the remaining are reduced by two places and seven extinctions;

there is only the auspicious (*śubha*) and no stain. This has already been refuted previously. It should be administered in the presence [of the Sangha], and shall be administered in the presence; this is precisely the meaning of *śikṣā*.
Because it is subsumed under the fifth category, it is like a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for a bhikṣuṇī according to the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya; it is simply [a matter of] oneself—
Because the various dharmas are distinct, two questions must be posed, just as the five groups of *śaikṣa* rules are treated as seven questions.

If this is so, does it not conflict with the recitation of the precepts in seven or fifteen sections? The answer is that there is no conflict; since the term "various *śaikṣa* rules" is constantly heard by the Saṃgha, it already includes the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
Therefore, one cannot simply perform eight or six recitations; they must be combined to form eighteen. All [of these]...
Regarding all offenses, with the exception of the *sthūlātyaya*, the remaining are all committed through silence in two instances. If one wishes to confess them, it is sufficient to do so once.

If that is the case, while silence may be committed during the *karmavācanā* (preliminary procedure), it should not be committed during the following eight [procedures]. Answer: Silence is fundamentally in response to questioning; therefore, based on the two types of questions—the general and the specific—one commits silence in both cases.
If that is so, then confession serves as a defense against silence; in response to the two types of questions—the general and the specific—one likewise performs the two types of confession.

Lù replied: "Since the assembly already knows what has been confessed, one location is sufficient. If that is so, and the assembly already understands it clearly, why would there be an offense at two locations?
He replied: "Confession allows one to hear the precepts. Furthermore, because there is no further intent to deceive, one does not answer the questioning;

yet in all cases, one must confess. It is as if one who is without fault may hear the precepts: although one passes through the circumstances of questioning, no offense is incurred because there is no intent to deceive."
The meaning of confessing now is the same as that [previous case]; therefore, it is sufficient to confess in one place.

Furthermore, some say that once a confession has been made, if the intention to conceal subsequently arises, one must confess again at every subsequent point of questioning. This is like the rule for persons, where if one first confesses and later conceals it, [a further offense occurs].
Since it was stated that silence arises from deceptive questioning, and since there are two types of questioning, how could there not be two offenses? This precept is not like that;

because its nature differs from the [other] persons and dharmas, it is the same as the initial explanation: there is no need for a repeated confession. Furthermore, it is asked: "In this context, what is meant by 'in'?
The answer is: "In" refers to among all the precepts; if it refers to the other eight questions, it means among the offenses such as the *pārājika*s; the two *aniyata*s are likewise.
Regarding these two locations—the secluded and the exposed—among the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), is there anything that must be examined? The remainder may be understood by analogy.

If, according to the presence of an offense, one is unfit to hear the precepts, yet recites them together with others, or perhaps separately binds oneself for an improper offense, this constitutes a transgression.

Third, distinguishing the nine questions regarding their universal or limited application and their general or specific nature: the introductory question applies universally to the seven classes of offenses (*saptāpatti-varga*), as the text states that one who has committed an offense is not permitted [to participate].

Regarding the "hearing of the precepts" (*śīla-śravaṇa*): yet, as for the introductory statement, "If you have committed an offense, disclose it; if you have committed no offense, remain silent," what would not be included therein? Thus, we know that [the former] is restrictive.
Furthermore, within the section concerning the inquiry into the establishment of the teachings and so forth, it is because the categories of offenses are not exhaustive.

Moreover, the initial question is general, as it is a general inquiry without listing specific names; the subsequent eight questions are specific, as they cite the names of the offenses and the matters to be examined.
Regarding these matters, each question is distinct and does not overlap with the others. That is to say, when asking about the "raw" (yí), one does not ask about the "cooked" (cán) at all;

the same applies to the other categories such as the "cooked. Thus, we know that the beginning provides a general overview while the subsequent sections provide specific details. Furthermore, the introductory questions are intended for recollection and recognition, whereas the eight [questions] below do not involve doubt.
The separate questions regarding doubt concern not recollecting or not recognizing; this is stated according to their respective stages.

If sought by way of their meaning, the initial question does not apply to doubt and the like, because there is no silence in the case of doubt. The subsequent eight questions apply to both recollection and recognition, as well as to non-doubt and so forth.

Among all offenses, with the exception of one category of *sthūlātyaya*, the remainder are all offenses of silence committed in two locations. Furthermore, the introductory questions are general inquiries.
He then asks the following in order to examine whether the assembly is pure or impure before he intends to speak; thus, he must first ask these preliminary questions.

The eight questions that follow all inquire about the preceding points, enumerating each characteristic one by one, and only thereafter does he question the assembly. That is to say, he asks whether those present are pure regarding the aforementioned offenses.
The preceding section on whether or not to include the Preface to the Precepts (Śīlaskandha) is concluded.

Regarding the two Indefinite Rules (Aniyata), because the offense has not yet been definitively established, they are not included in the formal categories; this is not a matter of omission or inequality. As for the sevenfold Vinaya:
A small portion falls under the fifth category. Since these verses constitute a summary teaching (*saṃkṣipta-śāsana*), they are likewise not included. All other [cases] are included.
Regarding the third [category], the offenses of preparatory effort (*prayoga*)—whether grave or light—all involve three types of preparatory effort:

that which is distant has a result but is not established; that which is progressive achieves the result through its cause; and that which lacks conditions has no result and cannot be established. As for the term "distant": [Note: The source text appears to be a commentary on the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* or a related Vinaya/Abhidharma treatise concerning the classification of karmic offenses.]
This refers, for example, to concealing one's own offenses. It is not that the subsequent offense arises without depending on this concealment; thus, it is called a "preparatory act" (*prayoga*).
Since one never takes up this [concealment] to bring about that [subsequent offense], it is termed "distant. As for its essential nature, it consists solely of the final consummation (*niṣṭhā*).

The instruction regarding the *laṅgi* (the "Lanki" offense) is likewise similar. A detailed discussion of the five offenses (*pañca-āpatti*) shows that all may serve as remote conditions (*dūra-pratyaya*).

For example, claiming to have attained holiness (*āryatva*) serves as a remote condition for the offense of theft (*steya-saṃghāvaśeṣa*), because it occurs within the context of the first five *saṃghāvaśeṣas* concerning sexual misconduct (*aśubha-caryā*) and the *utkṣepaka* (expulsion).

Taking clothing, traveling together, or staying overnight [with a woman] serves as a remote condition for the first offense (*parājika*). The latter two cases may be understood by analogy with this explanation. By citing these five offenses, they serve as conditions for the *pārājika* (defeat); the remainder...
When categories are compared, there may be mutual dependence; such types as these are called "remote preparatory means" (*dūre-upāya*).

Second, regarding "approaching preparatory means": when the mind yearns for a future object and the body and speech engage in movement to construct that object and seek its accomplishment, it is therefore called "approaching.

This mental state encompasses both specific and general [intentions], and the karma extends to oneself, others, and so forth; as long as there is this seeking, it all constitutes approaching. Regarding...
The middle two gates distinguish between existence and non-existence, and between accomplishment and non-accomplishment. Regarding existence and non-existence:
one interpretation says there is no offense, because the text states that it is not accomplished as a *pārājika* (defeat), rather than stating that it has not yet been accomplished as a *pārājika*.

Even if one increases unwholesome acts at every step, there is no designation of "offense" (*pārājika*) or "merit" (*kuśala*) at each step. It is like walking toward the Buddha; at every step, there is the merit of conforming to the principle.
Virtue. Now, if one falsely pretends to commit an offense, there is a transgression at every step; yet, there is no *dukkaṭa*.

Furthermore, regarding the three *thullaccayas* for abandoning [the training] through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, this third point of rest likewise lacks the three offenses. The second interpretation holds that they both exist and do not exist, as in the case of violating exhortations and the like.

Because there is a dharma that creates an interruption, it does not depend on the cessation of the mind; therefore, it is said there are three *thullaccayas*, just as in the cases of killing or stealing.

[The text continues with: "And so forth. Originally there was no separation of the dharmas; therefore, when the evil mind ceases, one incurs the offense [of *sthūlātyaya*], and thus there is no further progression. Now it is understood that [the offense] definitely exists.

Since the text states that 'abandoning' constitutes three *sthūlātyayas*, if the bond were to cease solely through the cessation of the mind, this would contradict the initial statement that the bond constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* that does not reach the second or third [stages]."

If it reaches two or three [stages], and one speaks of "three *thullaccaya*s," there is therefore a progressive advancement; this constitutes the conclusion within the first two stages of advancement, while the third *thullaccaya* exists within the conditions.
If one considers the deficiency of the fruit, all three are deficient in their conditions. This is like the case of two people, one departing and one staying.
If a person is moving, they are called a "goer. If they are obstructed and remain stationary, they are called a "stayer.

Since it is precisely this goer who becomes this stayer, how could it be that at the time of staying one is a "stayer," while at the time of going one is not a "goer"? It is simply one and the same person;
yet, because going and staying are two distinct states, we know that with every step there is an offense (āpatti). Furthermore, why should this be limited to...?
Because there was progress toward the goal, the third *karmavācanā* was completed. At the moment the *śeṣa* (residual) offense was incurred, Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha persisted;
his mind remained unappeased, and he rejected advice, refusing to comply. Nevertheless, because the act was accomplished, the *śeṣa* offense was formally established.

Thus we know that within the causal process, whatever karma is initiated possesses its own preparatory means (*upāya*), and it does not necessarily require the cessation of the intention. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states regarding the precept against stealing: "One intends to take five *kārsāpaṇas*."

With every step taken toward committing [the offense], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). This continues up to three *kārsāpaṇas*, for which there is a *duṣkṛta*; at four *kārsāpaṇas*, there is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

and upon reaching five, one commits a *pārājika* (defeat). Furthermore, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states: "There are sixteen types of *pārājika* offenses, three types of preparatory acts (*prayoga*), and the state where the mind does not cease [from its intent].

Moreover, eight factors constitute a grave offense; following the first seven factors, for each individual factor, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. How could one possibly expect [the full offense] by merely ceasing the intention?"
Regarding the meaning: one should know that there is progress toward realization. Next, one explains success and failure. As for the "seven clusters" mentioned regarding the stages:

the first four clusters cannot achieve success for themselves, nor can they bring success to others. The latter three—*pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *duṣkṛta*—act as causes to bring success to others.

If one considers their own achievement of success, the two offenses of *pāyattika* and *duṣkṛta* may be either identical or different. This means that when a *pāyattika* serves as the cause and another *pāyattika* results from it, they are not fundamentally distinct offenses; therefore, they are classified as *pāyattika*.
It is accomplished by means of *duṣkṛta*. This is the point of distinction. If one looks at the causes in relation to one another:

that which is *sthūlātyaya* is accomplished by the first two [classes of offenses], *pāyattika* is accomplished by *duṣkṛta*, and *pratideśanīya* is accomplished by *duṣkṛta*. As for *duṣkṛta*, it is accomplished by *duṣkṛta* itself, because it is the most minor offense.

The third section concerns the preliminary preparations (*upakrama*) for the *thullaccaya* offense, analyzed through five gates: first, enumerating the categories, explaining the names, and defining their characteristics;

second, distinguishing between those that are specific (*niyata*) or non-specific (*aniyata*), as well as those that are intentional (*saṃketa*) or unintentional (*asaṃketa*); third, distinguishing the variations based on the presence or absence of conditions (*pratyaya*);
fourth, analyzing the number of preliminary preparations according to the precepts and clarifying their similarities and differences; and fifth, providing a brief classification of the divisions.
First, I shall explain the initial gate. This is analyzed through four sub-sections. First, the enumeration of the seven names. As for these seven names: first, the intensity of the object;

second, a discrepancy in the conditions; third, a discrepancy in the object; fourth, a discrepancy in perception; fifth, doubt; sixth, idle chatter; and seventh, the cessation of wholesome mental states.
These are the seven preliminary practices (*saptaprayoga*).
Second, we shall determine their establishment and exclusion. Regarding the traditional interpretation of the sixth, the "preliminary practice of casual intent" (*pramāda-prayoga*):

it is like a person who, with a casual mind, kills beings of the three lower realms or creates a fire pit; toward all human beings, one incurs the offense of *prayoga-thullaccaya*, while for other realms, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If [it concerns] sentient beings...

Regarding those who die while [the weapon] is still within [the body], they incur the ultimate offense (*ānantarya*). As for discarding the instrument of killing and hoping that others do not die, this is merely a casual utterance;

it lacks the necessary conditions for the preparatory act (*prayoga*). If one were to say that destroying the instrument with a wholesome mind constitutes a cessation of the wholesome intention—as established above—this interpretation is incorrect.
If one relies on the broad scope of obtaining the preparatory act, it may be considered "casual"; however, if the conditions are incomplete, it is fundamentally not so.

Regarding "indeterminate" (*maṇḍa*): if one enters [the act] but does not complete it, it is subsumed under "strong circumstances. If it does not fall under those, or if the instrument of killing is destroyed, it is subsumed under "deficient conditions.

If the intention to kill is abandoned while the instrument remains, the wholesome mind has ceased; since it is only through such "strength" and other factors that the conditions become deficient, it is subsumed under "strong circumstances" and so forth.
How could there be a distinct essence of the indeterminate? It is like the three *karmas*; how could there be something separate from the one hundred and one specific acts?

The third application is as follows: this case is likewise. If there were no other conditions (*pratyaya*), it would simply be a distracted mind proceeding forward. Now, since we are analyzing the deficiency of conditions, there is no separate category for "distracted" [non-discursive] states.

Because the inclusive [category] is set aside, another type is added: namely, the deficiency of the preparatory conditions (*prayoga-pratyaya*). This refers to the deficiency among the two types of conditions—the general and the specific.

Within the deficiency of the general conditions, it includes cases such as a *mahābhikṣu* and the third [type of person], who lacks the condition of a grave illness that impairs the mind, and so forth. These are combined [in this category].

This constitutes the first [condition]: namely, when the act of creating the object has not yet been completed; or when, due to the four types of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and so forth, or the arising of physical infirmity, insanity, and the like, the common conditions are lacking.
This is because [the agent] is a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) and so on. As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, strikes another person, and while that person has not yet died, the bhikṣu becomes insane or renounces the precepts, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. In this case, both the insanity and the renunciation of the precepts lack the common conditions.

Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a bhikṣu incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense for killing himself. Moreover, it is frequently stated that when two people mutually decide to kill one another and die at the same time, there is no offense of violating the precepts, because the reception of the precepts lasts only as long as one's physical life.
Thus, we know that there are preparatory acts (*prayoga*) lacking the final causal condition.

Third, the explanation of the names. Regarding the phrase "deficiency in the conditions for application" (*pratyaya-upāya-vaikalya*): it refers to the deficiency of conditions that produce transgressions;

the mind and its objects diverge from one another; or the intention is obstructed and does not flow forth; or the body is suddenly afflicted by illness and abandoned [to death]. Although these violate the holy teachings, the categories [of such transgressions] have not been fully exhausted. Such are the examples.
The term is called "deficiency of conditions" (*pratyaya-vaikalya*). There are seven types of such deficiencies, namely: first, deficiency of conditions; second, a powerful object;

third, discrepancy in conditions; fourth, discrepancy in the object; fifth, perception and mind; sixth, a doubting mind; and seventh, the cessation of wholesome mind, and so forth. These are what are termed "deficiencies of conditions."
The fourth section analyzes the characteristics. First, regarding "deficiency of conditions" (*pratyaya-vaikalya*): the meaning of "deficiency of conditions" is as discussed above.

If one were to discuss this comprehensively, there would be nothing that does not constitute a deficiency of conditions; however, it is specifically designated as "deficiency of conditions" based on its initial occurrence when the universal conditions (*sāmānya-pratyaya*) are deficient.

Second, regarding "the object being powerful" (*viṣaya-prābalya*): for example, if one intends to kill someone, but the person before one has entered a profound meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), or if they instead turn and harm oneself.

Because that condition is powerful, it displaces this [intention] and obstructs the progression of the volition so that it does not waver; therefore, it is called a "strong object" (*viṣaya-prabalatva*).
Examples include shedding the blood of a Buddha, or attempting to harm one's brothers or striking Śāriputra and others. Third, regarding the displacement of conditions:

while one intends to harm another person through a preliminary effort (*prayoga*), another person suddenly intervenes; fearing that the matter will be discovered, or due to some other circumstance, this mind is displaced. It does not [proceed].

"Ultimately killing the object" refers to the general classification of differences in the conditions (*pratyaya-vaiṣamya*), which includes all seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*). However, because we are now taking up the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), this alone is termed "difference in conditions.

Regarding the four types of differences in the object (*ālambana-vaiṣamya*), examples include when the preparatory stage involves the perception of a human where there is no human, or doubt regarding a non-human, and so forth.

This difference in the object can be explained through three gates: first, the degree of difference in the determined object; second, the preparatory stage of the originally intended object; and third...

Regarding the determination of whether the objects of the various realms exist or not, and the determination of their number according to the first gate: killing encompasses four types of objects: first, the realm of humans; second, the realm of non-humans; and third, the realm of animals.
The fourth is non-sentient objects, such as stumps of wood. These four types of objects all possess the meaning of "difference" (*viśeṣa*). The essential point has not yet been explained in words:
regarding the differences in the objects of the human realm, there are five distinct categories. Regarding the generation of offenses upon these objects, there are two categories:

those that constitute ultimate grave offenses and are not subsumed under preliminary effort (*prayoga*), and the remaining three, which are subsumed under preliminary effort. The five categories of the original objects are all included within the fourth category, the difference of the object. Thus it is said, "five."
Regarding the categories: first, intending to kill a human, where one kills without force when a substitute person arrives; second, intending to kill in another realm with force, which is impossible;
third, intending to kill in another realm with doubt and force; fourth, intending to kill in another realm with doubt and without force. For non-humans and animals, there are likewise five each.

For inanimate objects such as stumps, there are three, excluding the two cases involving force. Thus, they total eighteen variations of the objective field. Question: As for the five variations regarding the human objective field...
In this passage, why is it stated only that the third [type of] wholesome mind ceases due to doubt, without saying that a different object comes to replace its place?

[Why is it not said that] the wholesome mind ceases because a different object arises and produces a conceptualization (*vikalpa*)? Answer: If one says "the wholesome mind ceases," it is because it is the same as the seventh [consciousness].

If that were so, then the second [consciousness], which has a different object, would be stronger; however, among the seven, the object of the seventh is stronger. The explanation of "strength" is based on the preceding object. Since the objects have an original difference, therefore [it is said that] the object...

Regarding the "strong" [attainment] among the seven types, its fundamental object is strong. As for the cessation of the wholesome mind, when compared to my own cessation of mind, although the objects are fundamentally different, because they are not [the same] objects, if one were to say that the wholesome mind ceases through the perception of Zhang, the mind would reside solely in Zhang, which would be identical to the seventh [type].
Therefore, it does not exist. This interpretation is incorrect; as in the case of the "strong" [attainment] confronting a different object, the matter is accomplished.
Because the ultimate [intention] is powerful, the action does not constitute a distinct preliminary effort (*prayoga*) in relation to a different object.

Now, facing a different object, if the mind does not cease, the action will reach its completion. Therefore, if the wholesome mind now ceases while one is still regarding a different object, how could there be no offense?

If the preliminary effort directed toward a different object is powerful, it may be distinguished from those within the seven [categories]; among the five [types of offenses], there are two that are powerful. When the wholesome mind ceases while regarding a different object...
The distinction is also a skillful means; it is not the same as the seventh [case]. Why is it that "non-doubt" and "the cessation of wholesome mind" are not established?

Is it because they are opposed to doubt, such that there are two types of "cessation of wholesome mind"? Furthermore, according to further reasoning, one asks: among the five [cases], the upper two lack the object alone, which refers to the perception of a non-human being as a human being;
the lower three lack both, which refers to the doubt regarding a non-human being. Why is the doubt regarding a non-human being excluded?

There are three conditions for the attainment of the cessation of wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta-vyupaśama*). If only one is missing, it is divided into two cases where the cessation of wholesome mind cannot occur.

If both are missing, what is the reason that these two cases are not the same? This difficulty is hard to resolve; one cannot avoid having to establish that there is no doubt regarding the cessation of wholesome mind.
Since this is the case for the mind, it should apply analogously to the rest, resulting in many permutations—namely, by way of the deficiency of conditions.
When the object is powerful and the conditions differ, the mind ceases; each is paired with its respective [state], whether certain or doubtful, thus forming eight.

There are two further cases for taking life—whether certain or doubtful—making five pairs and ten phrases. This applies equally to the two destinies (*gati*). In the case of a tree stump, there should be eight [phrases], namely excluding the two [cases of] powerful objects.
When the four objects are discussed collectively, they total thirty-eight. Since these thirty-eight are all capable of causing the mind to cease, it is said:
The distinction of objects (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*).

Having completed the definition, next is the explanation of the differentiation of characteristics. First, among the human [offenders], there are five pairs of ten phrases. Regarding the first five: (1) killing when the object is different and the intent is not firm;

(2) the object is different and conditions are lacking; (3) the object is different and the intent is firm; (4) the object is different and the conditions are mistaken; (5) the object is different and the intent is wholesome.
The mind ceases. This is not the perception of a human being; it is divided into five [categories]. Regarding the latter five:

(6) doubt regarding a different object with a wholesome mind ceasing; (7) doubt regarding a different object due to a discrepancy in conditions; (8) doubt regarding a different object due to strength; (9) doubt regarding a different object due to a deficiency in conditions;

(10) doubt regarding a different object that is not strong yet results in killing. These are doubts concerning non-humans, each divided into five. Thus, these ten types of doubt regarding different objects are established. This is the first decade.

This is not subsumed under the preliminary effort (*prayoga*); it is included within the eight intermediate preliminary efforts. The ten phrases of the fundamental object are all subsumed under the category of "difference in the object" (*viṣayāntara*). Regarding the first phrase:

one intends to kill Zhang, but when the King comes to take his place, one takes the King as the object while constantly maintaining the perception that he is Zhang. When the King’s life is severed, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

Because the object was different and there was a difference in the object, the intention to kill Zhang ceased; therefore, it is called a "preliminary effort involving a difference in the object. Question: But if one merely...
Question: Zhang Xīn harbors no intent to harm the king; how can he incur such a grave offense? Answer: Zhang is not the causal condition for the killing; it is the person who is the causal condition.

At the time of killing the king, although there was no intent toward the king, he formed the perception that it was a person. Because the necessary conditions were complete, he incurs the *pārājika* offense. Question:

When one kills a king and incurs *pārājika*, is this accomplished through the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of Zhang, or through the preparatory act of another? Explanation: There are two interpretations. The first interpretation holds that...

The claim that taking [a life] is accomplished through the application of a means (*upāya*) is not like the explanation given for theft. Furthermore, although the human realm is the same, there are distinctions;
how then could one take that [being] and thereby accomplish this [killing]? Since the two objects are distinct, the mental states arising toward them are also different.

Thus, it is known that killing a king involves a distinct application of means: from the moment one encounters the object that is the king, even if the thought of "king" is absent, one perceives him as a human being and proceeds.

When the King’s life has already been severed, one may still inflict injury upon him, which ultimately constitutes a grave offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*); how much more so when his life is not yet severed?
Surely there must be other expedient means by which a grave offense is established that does not parallel the case of theft.

Since they are both the same sovereign, employing the five preliminary preparations (*prayoga*) for taking life results in five grave offenses. If the victims are separate individuals, the remaining nine permutations (*koṭi*) may be understood by analogy with this explanation.
Next is the case of non-human beings (*amanuṣya*). There are five pairs and ten phrases; the numerical categories are the same as above, with the exception that the first five [cases] are omitted.

Regarding non-human beings, there is invariably no offense, because one has no intention toward them as being human beings. This differs from the case of [the names] Zhang and Wang, where they belong to the same category of the human realm (*manuṣyagati*).

Therefore, the text below states: "If one perceives a woman as a man and kills her, the Buddha said it is a *pārājika* offense. Regarding the five cases of the "double omission" (*dvāra-nyūna*), there is an offense even when the object is a non-human being, because of doubt.
The ten phrases concerning the original object (*mūla-viṣaya*) remain within the fourth section. The third section, the ten phrases concerning animals, is identical to that of non-human beings.

The fourth section, the eight phrases concerning a wooden stump, involves no offense regarding the external object, because it is not a sentient being (*asattva-saṃkhyāta*). This also applies to the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) regarding the original object.

The fourth section on "Inclusion. Regarding the second point, the preliminary application (*prayoga*) directed toward the actual object (*maulī bhūmi*): the thirty-eight *dukkaṭa* offenses regarding this actual object are subsumed within the fourth [category].
Specifically, these are the two phrases concerning the perception of the object as being either fourfold or fivefold.

Third, regarding the distinction of objects: there are cases where [the object] exists or does not exist, and cases where it is light or heavy. In the first [category], one commits an offense regardless of whether one distinguishes [the object]. In twenty cases there is an offense;
in two cases of approaching the upper five [realms], and in eight cases within the intermediate realm, these are said to be without offense.

This is because those two realms are without mind, and a stump is not an object of killing, unlike among humans. Although kings and commoners are distinct, they are both nonetheless human. Therefore, in the first five [cases] there is an offense. Second...

Regarding the offenses, there is a distinction between the final completion and the preliminary application (*prayoga*) within the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*). Among the first ten, eight constitute the final completion, while the remaining ten are all preliminary applications.

Within these three types of preliminary applications, there is a distinction between the grave and the light: the eight [offenses] in the human realm are grave because they are *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgressions);
the remaining ten are light because they are *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoings). Regarding the tenth [offense] of the two realms, these two are grave *duṣkṛta*, whereas the other eight are...
[This is] light; thus it may be known. Regarding the question of the tenth *pāyattika* for the two destinies:

why does the text state that doubting [the object to be] a non-human constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*? Answer: This is a *sthūlātyaya* because it refers to the original intended object—namely, the thirty-eight [offenses] and so forth mentioned above.

This means that the offense is determined based on the two objects of doubt. The fourth [category], the inclusion of preparatory acts (*prayoga*), concerns the first ten among humans; these two are not [included here].

The remaining eighteen [minds], when categorized by their stages (*avasthā*), lack the strength of the objective field (*ālambana-viṣaya*). When the conditions differ, the mind subsides; thus, there are four [minds] for each stage, totaling sixteen.
Four are subsumed under the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). As for the two destinies and the two doubts, the doubting mind is included therein. Question:

Regarding the tenth [mind] among the three destinies, which involves doubt, does it possess both the ultimate (*niṣṭhā*) and the preparatory (*prayoga*) stages? Answer: This is because it is viewed from the perspective of the original aspiration (*pūrvābhiprāya*) within the human realm.

It is said that this constitutes "doubt" (*vicikitsā*). Because the conditions for killing are complete, one incurs the offense of *pārājika*. As for the other two [offenses], they are called "doubt" because of hesitation regarding the original intent;
since the mental state is deficient, one only incurs the preparatory offense (*prayoga*). Therefore, people say there is "doubt" rather than "uncertainty," which refers to the tenth among humans.
Regarding the fifth, the preparatory offense of mistaken perception (*saṃjñā-viparyaya*): this applies to all cases where the perception has shifted.
This is the sixth case: the expedient of a doubting mind. One gives rise to the intent to kill a person, yet conceives doubt as to whether it is a human or a non-human (*amanuṣya*).

Although the person has died, because the mind was conditioned by two objects, the killer with a doubting mind incurs the full offense based on both objects. The seventh case, concerning one who ceases [the act] with a wholesome mind, may be understood accordingly.
The second [section] concerns the discrimination of symmetry and asymmetry, explained through six gates: first, symmetry and asymmetry in relation to the object;
second, the pervasive; third, the erroneous; fourth, performing and not performing the task; fifth, the cessation and non-cessation of the mind;
sixth, simultaneous and non-simultaneous. These are called the gates of undiscriminated analysis. These are the seven skillful means.

Regarding the first gate: if the body faces the object before it, and one's various self-performed actions fail to be accomplished due to encountering adverse conditions, one possesses the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*);

these are precisely the aforementioned seven. However, if one employs means such as setting fire pits or using levers, or if the body does not face the object, or if those who provide instruction are not present before one, there are only five preparatory stages—namely, non-conceptualization, doubt, conceptualization, and further doubt. These two [latter cases] take that [object] as their condition; that is, since they...

If there is no object [of perception], how can there be perception (*saṃjñā*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*)? If one instructs another person to manifest [the object] before oneself, it is explained as being the same as acting for oneself.

Regarding the second case, the "deliberate" (*saṃcetanika*), whether the door is directed toward an object or not, if both types of mind are involved—namely, the two deliberate cases and the seven or five non-deliberate cases—the two deliberate cases are equal in being fourfold.
This is because there is no difference in the object regarding perception and doubt. However, if one were to analyze this in detail:
Briefly, there are two gates: first, the contrast between the specific (*krama*) and the general (*amukta*); second, the analysis of the general itself. Regarding the contrast:

if one is exclusively specific, there are seven fives (*pañca-pañca*), meaning the intention is fixed upon a particular object. As for the great general, both types of the general have four, meaning the mental state is not restricted;
therefore, the general has four, and no others exist. Third, with respect to the original intent, it does not depend on the object.
Regarding the object (*viṣaya*) and the relative quality of that object: when the harmful intent is broad and pervasive, lacking a specific focus, it is termed "indiscriminate" (*pārūṣya*).

Because the original mind is indiscriminate, even if one encounters various circumstances and alternately takes this or that as an object, there is no instance where one does not follow the object in terms of whether an offense is committed or not.

Thus, regarding the mental objects—whether they be perceptions or doubts—one is still proceeding toward them rather than being excluded from the scope of the causal conditions; therefore, the other three [types of unwholesome speech] do not apply.

Regarding the specific (*viśeṣa*) and the general (*sāmānya*): there are no objects that are not related by way of proximity, such that one could say, "taking that as the object, one calls it this," or "taking this as the object, one calls it that.

Therefore, both types of mental application (*manasikāra*) are exhaustive and leave nothing remaining. As for the third point, the specific and the general in relation to the extent of their objects: since this is the case for the number of objects, all other instances are likewise similar.

If explained extensively, they would be immeasurable. Second, regarding the distinction between the specific and the general: both the specific and the general consist of seven and five [categories] respectively.
There is only a difference in breadth; however, there are two categories of status. First, let us distinguish them by taking a single realm as a basis.

This refers to cases where one intentionally creates the conditions for an act with the primary intent directed toward human beings, yet regarding other realms, there is a discrepancy in the object, a mistaken perception, or doubt. For this reason, these are combined with the seven [types of killing].

However, within the human realm itself, one does not discriminate between figures such as Zhang or Wang; since the intention encompasses both sides, it remains "indiscriminate" (*maṇḍa*). Since the indiscriminate is itself specific, the indiscriminate also possesses [specificity].

Seventh: This refers to the specific restriction [of the vow] to other realms (*gati*), whereas the general [vow] extends to the human realm; thus it is so called. Although the specific and the general differ in name, they both possess the seven meanings and so forth.

They differ only in their respective objects; being narrower than the former specific [vow], it excludes its own realm. As for perception (*saṃjñā*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), they are identical [to the previous case].
Since this is so for the human realm, it is likewise for the other realms. This should be explained in detail, even unto each of the three realms making their respective original vows.

In both cases of intentional and unintentional [killing], there are seven factors; this is not limited to the specific teaching. In both intentional and unintentional [cases], there are five factors, as previously explained, which should also be discussed in detail.

This applies likewise to each of the three destinies (*gati*). Second, regarding the distinction between sentient and insentient beings, there are also seven factors in both cases, with the meaning as previously stated.

The three [factors] of perception, doubt, and so forth are, in turn, more restricted. This is because, with the exception of the object of the offense, each is finalized only in relation to that specific object of the offense.

As for non-correspondence and instigation, whether the intent is specific or general, both are primary; a discrepancy in the object constitutes one degree of restriction, which is likewise as previously explained.

The third is erroneous discernment (*viparīta-vikalpa*). These seven types all refer to the interval between an unaccomplished act and its completion; they are described as "even if" [the act occurs].

If one lacks the intention regarding the object and the act is completed, it is an error and there is no offense. How much more so for the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), where an error can certainly occur.
Therefore, one cannot discuss "errors" regarding the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*) as a whole.
