If we do discuss their errors, within these seven, considering them by way of their essential nature, there are three—namely, the error of the object (*viṣayaviparyāsa*), the error of perception (*saṃjñāviparyāsa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—all of which involve the delusion and confusion of thought and mind, and are thus collectively termed "errors.

Among these, the single type of "error of the object" consists of taking that [object] to be this; the two types of "error of perception" and "doubt" consist of taking this to be that. The remaining cases are not to be understood otherwise. If...
The errors within the "existence and non-existence" [categories] are explained generally by way of differences in objects; there are five such types, namely the aforementioned differences in objects.

As for the five pairs of ten phrases, these are restricted solely to differences in objects. Question: Why are the two types of error—differences in objects and differences in perception (*saṃjñā*)—not present here?

Answer: Because this is the stage of differences in objects, one cannot say they exist. Regarding differences in perception, they are identical to the five aforementioned [cases], lacking the element of objects.
Therefore, from this point on, the mind of mistaken perception (*saṃjñā*) is severed, and life reaches its ultimate end.

Although the remaining four [factors]—whether severed or not—are skillful means, they are nonetheless subsumed under "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and the like, because they do not arise from perception itself. Consequently, there is no difference regarding the absence of perception.

When it comes to the five types of non-intentional harm toward other realms of existence, regardless of whether perception was severed or not, one does not speak of an offense in terms of gravity or lightness; nor can one speak of a difference in perception.

Therefore, these two types of conventional designations do not apply. Among the five [types of objects], they pertain only to those within one's own sphere of experience; this is done for the purpose of dispelling doubt.

As for the aforementioned points regarding whether an object is "substantially real" (*tattva*) or "existent" (*sat*), all such statements are made from the perspective of the objects created by one’s own [cognition].

If one does not confront [the object] or rely on the conventional designation of "existent objects" as taught [in scripture], because one is not directly perceiving the object, one cannot speak of it being substantially real or existent. This is why it is permissible [to say so].

It is known that these two [the first and second] are not restricted to their own respective objects, because the other five exist [there as well]. Thus, the meaning applies both to the original and the distinct;
this refers to the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*), which are analyzed in terms of their restriction or pervasiveness with respect to the two objects—the original and the distinct.

Furthermore, regarding the various destinies (*gati*), both the single and the dual exclusions are distinguished in terms of existence and non-existence. As for the remaining destinies, they are distinguished solely within the context of the dual exclusion.

Regarding the fourth point, "the accomplishment of the act and the non-accomplishment of the act": among the seven [factors], two intermediate stages lack the conditions of perception (*saṃjñā*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

These three factors are accomplished because, although they lack the conditions, they partially share perception and doubt; since they lack the two specific [conditions], the accomplishment of the act is not precluded.

From the perspective of the time when the offense is incurred, it does not necessarily depend upon the completion of the act. As for the remaining four, with respect to their original objects, the act is invariably unaccomplished, yet they are described as preparatory efforts (*prayoga*).

If one discusses the differences in the objects for incurring offenses: when facing a different object, the remaining three [offenses] do not apply; they do not apply to the five intermediate [objects]. When one [of these five] is established, the four that are not established are to be understood according to the previous explanation.

In the fifth [case], both mind and breath cease; in the seven intermediate positions, four [cases] involve the cessation of both the perception and doubt. In two cases, both minds cease; in one case, the object is missing.
When there is the perception of a person and the intent to kill, both do not cease, yet one attains the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). This is equivalent to the other three strong [cases].

In the case where one stops the intent to kill but the perception of a person does not cease, this is the single case of a discrepancy in the object. If there is a half-doubt regarding each of the four objects, this constitutes a dual deficiency.

Therefore, this is the meaning of "expanding the mind" (*citta-prasāra*) and the mind having "respiration" (*śvāsa*). Upon seeing a king or non-animal beings, one immediately attains the expansion of skillful means (*upāya*).

Since each of the four objects has the first half [of the cycle] and are equally single-deficient objects, both minds are simultaneously non-respiratory as they together proceed toward the upper five.
Because seeing a king is the immediate skillful means, it is said that the mind does not respire; for the other objects, each has its own first half due to the remainder.

There is no offense regarding the object (*viṣaya*), because there is no preliminary effort (*prayoga*). Alternatively, the mind only becomes settled once the act is completed or when factors such as force are present;
this may be understood by analogy with the case of facing a different destination (*gati*), wherein the preliminary effort does not depend on the cessation of the mind.
The sixth [category] does not simultaneously possess all three. Regarding the first pair, there is a lack of both universal and specific conditions;

this clarifies that they do not coexist. If there is a deficiency in the conditions, one is not a bhikṣu; this determines that the other six are absent. If the other six are present, one is indeed a bhikṣu.

This refers to the preceding matter, explained in terms of the mind and its objects. There is no deficiency in the universal [condition]; it clarifies the two deficiencies in the conditions, directly addressing the seven [factors] regarding the fundamental object.
The various skillful means (*upāya*) are not concurrent; they can coexist with two minds, provided there are others that are stronger or equal.

Thirdly, regarding differences in the object (*viṣaya*), when distinguished according to the mind, they are likewise not concurrent. Within this, there are two types: first, those that specifically concern different objects.

This refers to when a person directs their attention toward different objects, such as the two minds of perception (*saṃjñā*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), each having four skillful means; that is, these two minds [coexist] with each of the other four. Each one possesses [them].
Furthermore, although these [other] four types of attraction (*saṃgraha*) exist, these two—single and dual—are mutually exclusive and cannot coexist.

If there are five types of doubting minds regarding other realms, as in the latter five of the aforementioned ten phrases, they constitute a doubting mind; this then pairs with each of the four [types of attraction], making eight.
Second, if one considers both the fundamental and the derivative, it refers to the differences in the objects presented; viewed in relation to the two minds, there are eight, or perhaps five or one.

First, regarding coexistence: among these eight [categories], five and two cannot coexist within themselves. Furthermore, if one speaks of existence and non-existence in relation to different objects, where the presence or absence is heavy or light, then this object-differentiation coexists with each of the thirty-eight [factors] individually, while the thirty-eight factors themselves do not coexist.
The third pair is distinguished by way of the deficiency of conditions (*pratyaya*). First, regarding the deficiency of conditions in relation to the precept against killing:

there is a deficiency of universal conditions, meaning a deficiency in the first three factors—the discrepancy in the object (*viṣaya*), the deficiency in the perception of the object (*saṃjñā*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding it, and a deficiency in the second two factors—the two doubts concerning the two destinies (*gati*). These constitute the "double deficiency. The remaining three [precepts] involve a deficiency in the fifth factor. Question:

What is the distinction between the two types of doubt, such that the deficiencies differ? Answer: Doubt regarding humans extends outward to other objects; because it relates to the primary object, the deficiency differs.

The mind is deficient. Because the mind is deficient, the second [category] lacks the two types of doubt regarding the two destinies (*gati*). Since they turn inward and face different objects, both are lacking.

Thus, regarding the four and five [factors] of the first two phrases, one takes that as this; regarding the second and third phrases, one takes this as that; therefore, their deficiencies differ. Question:

By means of the seven deficiencies, the general and the particular are addressed. However, although the general is one and the particular is two, the deficiencies are not exhaustive. Yet, following...

Explanation of the Precepts. Regarding the categories of "complete," "incomplete," "both," and "entirely incomplete": what is meant by these? Answer: Among the "complete" category, the second type refers to that which is established by the Noble Ones (the Buddha).
In this case, one does not discuss "incompleteness. As for "incomplete but not entirely so," this refers to cases where one has omitted a grave offense within the specific category;

even if there is no actual offense, it is still termed an "incomplete condition. Therefore, one attains the status of being "entirely incomplete. These seven points clarify the transgressions of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). If both the intention (*citta*) and the preparatory action (*prayoga*) are absent, only then...

If one does not proceed to commit the act, then there is no offense regarding the full preparatory effort (*prayoga*); thus, only three factors are lacking. This refers to the deficiency of conditions for the preparatory effort;

it is both the same and different [from the actual offense]. Regarding the fourth point, the application of the precepts to what is open or closed: this may be categorized into two positions regarding the difference in objects. As for the three cases of misapprehension (*saṃjñā*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), [the offenses of] sexual misconduct and drinking alcohol do not apply.

Regarding perception and doubt: these two are present only when the five [factors] are complete; there is no doubt regarding the reception of the precepts, for one who doubts cannot attain the ultimate realization.

Thus, the claim that "the mind does not transgress" is a deluded perception; therefore, if such a perception shifts, a transgression may occur. When understood in this way, there may be six factors, or perhaps there is no discrepancy in the object.
As for the remaining mental and objective constraints, these three should be complete; the other four preparatory stages seem to apply universally, according to...

According to this principle, if one distinguishes by means of the four categories—specified, unspecified, and so forth—the presence or absence of the factors may be understood as in the cases of killing and stealing.
Regarding the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) for false speech, it consists of making a definitive statement; such a factor does not exist in the first precept (killing).

Furthermore, regarding transgressions such as violating [a precept], killing, or causing loss, these are not unmanifested; even if one employs skillful means, the remainder can be known through inference. Question:

How do the object (*viṣaya*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and skillful means (*upāya*) differ from one another? Answer: They possess mutual breadth and narrowness. Because the object and perception encompass both cause and effect, they are broad.

Because they consist only of the preliminary means (*upāya*), they are narrow; having excluded sexual misconduct and intoxicants, the remaining four precepts are narrow regarding the causal stage because the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) applies only to three of the preliminary means.

This is so because they are contrasted with their respective primary objects (*mūla-viṣaya*). If the primary objects were combined and discussed together, their breadth and narrowness would be identical.

As with the four or five propositions regarding the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), there are four differences in the actual object toward which one proceeds, and five differences in the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) toward that object.

Since the preliminary effort may still involve perception or doubt, these constitute the full seven [offenses]. As explained previously in the section on "existence and non-existence," there is therefore no difference in their breadth or narrowness.

Furthermore, it was asked: "Regarding those cases where the verbal expression is not established, are they the same as the seven [offenses]? The answer is: "Their names are narrow, but their substance is broad; they encompass all seven types."

Therefore, since the breadth and narrowness are equal, it may also be argued that [the offense] is not established. This refers to the non-establishment with respect to the *matter* (*vastu*), not with respect to the *offense* (*āpatti*).
It merely subsumes the four factors—non-performance, the object, difference, and so forth; thus, while the seven [factors] are broad, the textual description of non-establishment is narrow.

The fifth [section] is the abbreviated classification of the divisions. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there are only five types of preparatory offenses (*pāyattika*), namely those prohibited based on the object;

these lack the categories of "non-perception" and "doubt. Since the text states that "if one perceives a hermaphrodite or doubts [the gender], or touches a woman, it is also a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*," it follows that the prohibitions should actually comprise seven categories.

This is known from cases such as perceiving a living being as non-living or doubting [the nature of the object], which result in a *duṣkṛta*. Thus, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one does not distinguish between prohibitions and inherent natures; rather, all [offenses] are treated uniformly.

There are six cases where both [factors] are present; this is because there is no doubt. Since doubt always involves two conditions—namely, that it takes the primary mind as its object—one is thereby restrained from the actual offense by virtue of the object.
Therefore, the text states: "If one suspects a woman, suspects water containing insects, or suspects living plants and so forth."

Because [killing] at an improper time or with doubt regarding whether the age is not yet full both incurs a *thullaccaya* offense, and because the investigation of the perception must be thorough, it does not matter whether the object is a natural (*pakati*) or prohibited (*pārājika*) being;

rather, the offense depends on the correspondence between the mind and the object. If there is no such correspondence, the offense is light, namely a *dukkaṭa* or a *pācittiya*. Therefore, killing a human while perceiving them as a non-human incurs a *pācittiya*;
touching a woman while perceiving her as a man or a eunuch incurs a *pācittiya*.
The fourth section concerns upholding and violating the precepts, which is the dharma-gate of following the precepts. This shall now be explained according to the text through a fivefold analysis:
first, explaining the names "upholding" and "violating"; second, clarifying their essential nature, characteristics, fulfillment, accessibility, obstruction, breadth, and narrowness;

third, elucidating the gradual and sudden approaches; fourth, elucidating the sequence of priority and posteriority; and fifth, distinguishing the degrees of increase, decrease, superiority, and inferiority.

The first section has two parts: first, the explanation of the names; second, the derivation of the name. Regarding the explanation of the names: although the *anuçaya* (secondary precepts) are numerous, they do not transcend the categories of observance (*dhāraṇa*) and violation (*atikrama*).

A detailed explanation of their characteristics is as stated in the "Opening of the Doctrine" (*Kai-zong*). Question: Why must these be clarified? Answer: Generally, the meaning of *anuçaya* is explained as "following" because one follows the primary vows (*upasaṃpad*).
If there were no secondary precepts, one would incur the fault of being weak or deficient. The roots were explained previously, and the branches are now discussed. That is to say:
This is because they are directed toward the phenomena (*dharma*) and the objects (*vastu*). Question: Why are there two types of both observance and transgression? Answer:
It is because ordinary beings have long remained in birth and death, drifting and drowning in the four currents; thus, they fail to encounter the path to nirvāṇa.

This is truly because the two types of transgression accord with their worldly passions, allowing them to run wild through body and speech, whereas the two types of observance conform to principle, yet they do not aspire to or cultivate them. Regarding what is called the "two transgressions": [text continues].

One immediately proceeds to extensively create various evils; having acted upon them, one commits an offense, which is called an "active offense" (*kṛta-āpatti*). Regarding wholesome [actions], one fails to practice them and violates them through non-action;
this is called a "cessation offense" (*akṛta-āpatti*). To counter these two faults, two types of observance (*samvara*) are established.

If one does not cultivate the intention to sever all evil, liberation from suffering will not be ultimate. Therefore, in order to achieve the ultimate liberation from suffering, one must clearly understand cessation and observance (*kṛtya-samvara*), so as to bring it forth.
Regarding transgressions: if one does not further cultivate all wholesome states of mind, one will not attain satisfaction in happiness.

To achieve the fulfillment of happiness, one must distinguish between the "active" (kriyā) and the "retentive" (dhāraṇa), so as to eliminate and restrain faults; therefore, both types exist. These points can be understood from the corresponding textual passages. Question:

It is understandable that the retentive [aspect] follows [the precepts], but why does the transgression follow? Answer: It is said that taking up the capacity for repentance constitutes the following of the precepts.

There are, however, two types: first, the fundamental observance (*mūla-dhāraṇa*), which refers to the diligent practice of the two observances; second, the ability to repent after having committed an offense, which refers to the two types of offenses.

This may be understood as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Question: In the act of receiving [the precepts], there is a distinction between the agent and the object, and their respective natures are distinct.

Since there are both observance and violation, why are they treated together? Answer: Although the agent and object within the act of receiving [the precepts] rely upon one another, [they are distinct].

Since their essential natures are distinct, they do not constitute direct opposites; therefore, they must be explained separately. However, in this case, the meanings of "observance" (*dhāraṇa*) and "violation" (*aticāra*) are diametrically opposed, making it convenient to explain them together.
Regarding the second point, concerning how these names are acquired: if one speaks of the "two observances," it refers to being named according to their numerical count and functional capacity.

As for the "two violations," they are designated by counting the transgressions. Alternatively, they may be derived from their function: if one takes up the capacity for repentance, they are established as "subsequent liberation" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

The term "yi" (義) has two aspects: maintaining [the precepts] and violating them. Both are functions of "yi. They are functions because they do not destroy the essence [of the precepts]; they are "yi" because they both accord with the original commitment.
This is because, regarding the name [of the precept], one is single-mindedly diligent in not violating it, and even after a violation, one is able to repent. Thus it is so.

The second section has four parts: first, the essential nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*); second, accomplishment; third, obstruction and penetration; and fourth, breadth and narrowness. Regarding the "essential nature":

the essence of the two types of retention is as explained in the commentary on the precepts (*śīla*). Among the two types of transgressions, errors are excluded because they are not actual offenses and thus do not require confession.
However, within the category of intentional acts, these are what have been prescribed by the Buddha—meaning those which the Buddha did not prohibit, yet which should not be prohibited. If...

Regarding those who act with a light mind, there is no manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) nor non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karman*). However, for those who act with intense purity and a heavy mind, there is both manifest and non-manifest action according to their state of being.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that this manifest and non-manifest action applies to both types of observances (*saṃvara*): according to the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (Mind Treatise), the three aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) are all considered matter (*rūpa*).

According to the *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Treasury), manifest action is matter, while non-manifest action is neither matter nor mind. Moreover, the "matter" mentioned in the *Hṛdaya-śāstra* refers generally to both the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the actual manifestation; it is precisely this [manifestation] that constitutes the manifest action.
It is so. Non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is not a means (*upāya*); the manifestation of the means (*upāya-karman-rūpa*) permeates all three moral natures.

The two types of upholding are virtuous, not the other two; the two types of transgression are unwholesome, not the other two. If one takes [the term] according to its underlying meaning, all four factors are virtuous.

The two kinds of non-manifest action are likewise judged in this way. However, those of former interpretations explained this collectively with respect to the three types of action (*tri-karma*), speaking in terms of their characteristics—that is, reciting...

Reciting [scriptures] and similar activities are termed "active observance" (*kṛta-śīla*). Furthermore, performing acts such as giving alms (*dāna*) to distinguish the essence of observance and transgression is a general explanation, as commonly analyzed.

If one distinguishes the two types of observance and transgression of body and speech according to the prescriptive teachings (*vidhi-śāsana*), then abstaining from killing, sexual misconduct, physical contact, and so forth constitutes "bodily restraint-observance" (*kāya-virati-śīla*).
This includes, for example, welcoming those who arrive, putting away bedding, lighting lamps, and preparing [necessities].
*Śarāva*: Not sitting while receiving food, nor receiving food [in an improper manner], and so forth—these constitute bodily *kṛta-dhāraṇa* (observance through physical action).

To abstain from the four verbal transgressions, such as lying or reviling, and to cease all that constitutes verbal *kṛta-āpatti* (offenses committed by speech)—this is verbal *virati-dhāraṇa* (observance through verbal restraint). For example: receiving and keeping robes and bowls;

performing the formal assignment (*pariṣkāra*) and the declaration of purity (*viśuddhi-kathana*); remaining separated from one's robe for six years; and the staff, the bag, the two-year rule, the six dharmas, and acting as a purifier (*jñapti-viśuddhi*).

Speech. Regarding the two [types of] injury to the earth and destruction of living beings, entering a village, and practicing in accordance with the teachings, these constitute verbal *kṛta-saṃvara* (active restraint).
As for the combination of body and speech, it may be understood by analogy with what has been explained. The two offenses of body and speech are explained as the opposite of the preceding.

What has been analyzed above also refers to the two types of offenses, wherein there is both cessation (*virati*) and action (*kriyā*). When speech constitutes *saṃvara*, citing these two offenses, both are indeed *kṛta-saṃvara*. This is the intention.

Since [the offenses] are established through body and speech, there is no need for a separate explanation. Regarding the mind, there is both observance and violation. As seen in the section on the arising of the six violations below, one must carefully examine the intention by means of body and mind, asking:
"By what state of mind [did you act]? and so forth; all such cases are discussed as auxiliary factors that establish the actions of body and speech.

However, the mind alone does not constitute observance or violation; therefore, the text states only that "the mind does not violate," and likewise within the context of the six violations, it is due to body and speech [that the offense occurs].
"Not thinking" and so forth. Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Ten Unwholesome Paths of Action" in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it is asked:

Why is it that among all types of karma, mental karma is the greatest, yet the Vinaya does not establish offenses for it? This is because the nature of acquiring demerit differs from that of merit, and the methods for establishing the precepts differ accordingly.

Regarding the interpretations held since ancient times, they have focused solely on the gate of breadth and narrowness, explaining them through the dual application of progressive advancement and restrictive regulation; all other gates are treated merely as generalities.
You have advanced and distinguished [the points]. Now, the following sections will explain them based on the two teachings.

Second, regarding accomplishment: according to the *Cittavipāka-śāstra*, for the *vijñapti* (informative) precepts of the *Prātimokṣa*, they are accomplished in the present at the first moment and in the past from the second moment onward.
For the *avijñapti* (non-informative) precepts, they are accomplished in the present at the first moment and in both time periods (present and past) from the second moment onward.
Because form (*rūpa*) is obstructive, there is no accomplishment in the future. This should be explained with reference to feeling (*vedanā*).

If one explains according to the principle of conformity, both manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) should be accomplished in both time periods (*adhvan*), because manifest action within the intermediate state should equally apply to both long and short durations.

If one follows the school of qualities (*guṇa-vāda*), one distinguishes accomplishment based on the four minds and the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). Regarding restraint (*saṃvara*), there are two types: first, that which is not defiled by evil, because of understanding...
Regarding *śīla* as restraint (*saṃvara*): by practicing the three preceding mental states, one possesses the meaning of "restraint.

Since one practices these three preceding mental states in accordance with what was originally received, and no evil comes to defile [the mind], is this not indeed restraint? Both wholesome and neutral natures possess the meaning of restraint;

within the unwholesome nature, there is both general restraint and specific transgression. Question: Since the three preceding mental states are neutral (*avyākṛta*), how can they constitute karma? Answer: By practicing...

Within the first three moments of mind, there exists the essence of the original undertaking (*mūla-śīla*). Because it is luminous, earnest, and without transgression, it is described as "retention" (*dhāraṇā*); however, this is not retention through cultivation (*bhāvanā-dhāraṇā*). Question:

When practicing these first three moments of mind, which of the three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) constitute these three moments? Answer: In terms of the non-destruction of the essence, all three consciousnesses can accomplish these three moments of mind.

If, however, one refers to cultivation, then by clarifying *śamatha-dhāraṇā* (retention through stillness) and *pragraha-dhāraṇā* (retention through application), the practice of the mind is accomplished. As for the first three [moments], they are...

There is none [of the first type] in the wholesome nature; there is [the second type] in the unwholesome. There is none in the unwholesome or neutral natures. Regarding the meaning of the two types of transgressions:

when the mind of action (*karmapatha*) is accomplished, the first three [types of restraint] are also absent; they exist in the unwholesome nature, while the other two natures lack them. This is based on a single moment of mind.

If, however, one considers successive moments of mind or instructing another, then within the other two natures, there can be transgressions of commission (*kṛta-āpatti*), but no transgressions of abstention (*virati-āpatti*). It may also be that both exist. As for this statement: [Question:]...

Regarding "the mind that completes the formation of karma": what kind of mind performs this action? Answer: It is not the mind that operates through the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), because these are entirely incapable of initiating karma.

Only the mind that operates through the five mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*) is able to initiate karma. Therefore, the treatise states: "It must be accomplished by means of the mental consciousness. However, this is not fixed;
it may be accomplished by either the five mental consciousnesses or the sixth mental consciousness. Question: Why is this so?

Regarding "maintaining through cessation" (*zhi-chí*): the first three [types of restraint] possess this quality, whereas "ceasing transgressions" (*zhì-fàn*) does not. Answer: One first possesses the essence of the vow (*śīla-samvara*).

By means of these three mental states, one aligns with what was originally received; because no evil comes to contravene it, it is called "maintaining. As for "ceasing transgressions," this does not exist prior [to the act]; it belongs to oneself [only when it occurs].

Because one performs the first three mental states, one aligns with the evil that was originally received; since no goodness comes to prevent it, it is called "ceasing transgressions. Therefore, one practices...

The mind is not present in the first three [stages]. Question: The original intent was to abandon evil and cultivate good. Because one originally abandoned evil, one does not now commit evil; this is explained as "upholding" (dhāraṇa).
Originally one desired to cultivate good, yet now one does not cultivate good; does this not contradict the original vow? Should this not be considered a transgression? Answer:

Because one does not intentionally cease [the practice], it is not a transgression. If that is so, then because one does not intentionally uphold [the practice], it would likewise not be a transgression.

It should not be "cessation-and-maintenance" (*śīla-samvara*), yet it is called "cessation-and-maintenance. Why is it not an offense? Answer: It is not an offense because one does not perform what is wholesome, thereby contravening the original [vow];

however, this is not "maintenance" (*samvara*) because there is no intention to perform [the wholesome]. Since one merely ceases [unwholesome action], it is not an offense. Furthermore, within "cessation-and-maintenance," because there is also no intentional application of mind, it is not "maintenance through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-samvara*).

Because this is a case of abstention (*virati*), it does not constitute an offense. If one explains it in this way, it accords with both the formal commitment (*samādāna*) and the essence of the undertaking (*pratigraha*), which remains unimpaired.

Regarding the first three mental states, there is both abstention and performance; it is not merely a case of abstention-only (*virati-dhāraṇa*). If one considers the state of intending neither [to act nor to abstain], it is not said that one maintains [the precept].

Since this does not contradict the commitment to cultivate wholesome qualities, how could it be categorized as abstention-only? This is intended so that practicing the first three mental states may likewise possess [the nature of the precept].

This refers to the cessation of transgressions. Furthermore, regarding the previous statement that within the nature of the unwholesome there is both general upholding (*sāmānya-dhāraṇa*) and specific transgression (*viśeṣa-āpatti*):

specific transgression is a transgression of volitional attention (*manasikāra*), whereas general upholding is still explained as receiving [the precepts]; it constitutes upholding by not violating them, rather than upholding through volitional attention. Thus far, two types of upholding have been presented.
Regarding the two offenses, they are called "two offenses" because they are accomplished within a mind of unwholesome conduct. If one repents, they are accomplished as subsequent transgressions;

Third is the penetration and obstruction (*tong-sai*). This refers to whether the maintenance of the posture is present; if the other three [postures] are present, it is called "penetration," and if they are absent, it is termed "obstruction.

The same applies to the mutual relationship between the other three postures regarding penetration and obstruction. To understand this penetration and obstruction, there are four gates, the first of which is the gate of the single mind.
Second, the gate of one mind facing two objects; third, the gate of mutual accomplishment through one’s own karma; fourth, the gate of instructing others.
To distinguish these four gates, they are all explained in reference to the two teachings. First, regarding the gate of one mind: the four modes of conduct are simultaneously obstructed.

This means that when comparing observance with transgression, good and evil are mutually contradictory; since observance and transgression each have their respective prohibitions and prescriptions within their own categories, it causes the four modes of conduct to be [obstructed] in parallel.

It cannot be passed through. For example, when a person gives rise to a thought that is free from killing, stealing, and so forth, they may further take those as objects to cultivate the three [wholesome courses of action] such as generosity;

because the mind does not attend to multiple concerns simultaneously, it is therefore blocked. Just as it is with the observance of prohibitions (*śīla*), so it is with the remaining three. Since one knows that all are blocked, [one understands this principle].

Next, the analysis according to the teachings (*yàojiào*). If one analyzes by means of advancing in the cultivation of the three trainings (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi*), such as maintaining [the precepts] and ceasing transgressions, since these are mutually opposed, they likewise both become obstructed.

If one refers to the prescriptive teachings (*zhìjiào*), regarding the four types of conduct among the five categories of offenses that are obstructed, this is explained in terms of single instances of maintaining or violating the precepts.

Just as there is no sense of "non-action" (akriyā) regarding not killing or stealing, so too, in cases such as listening attentively, the two-year probationary period (*ṣaḍ-dharma*), not requesting instruction when it is not being given, not listening to instruction, not remaining seated, not performing prostrations, and the acceptance of a following—there is no sense of "cessation. The "cessation" (śamatha) and so forth are precisely its stillness. Therefore, within cessation there is activity; within the maintenance of activity, there is also the meaning of cessation.
For example, in sitting meditation or listening to recitations, one must first cease the fault of indolence before one can cultivate goodness—is this not cessation within activity?
If one asks: "If shamatha (calm abiding) and vipashyana (insightful cultivation) are distinct, how are they differentiated? The explanation states: Within shamatha there is cultivation;

by bringing forth cultivation, it becomes shamatha. Within cultivation there is shamatha; by bringing forth shamatha, it becomes cultivation. Although they are subsumed under the general principle [of a single mind], shamatha and cultivation remain distinct.

Furthermore, it is asked: "Since you speak of 'one mind,' how can there be cultivation within shamatha and shamatha within cultivation? The answer is: "One mind" refers to the realization of perfection.

Because cessation (*śamatha*) constitutes the limit of activity, it is "obstructed. If one considers the gate of the two objects, taking the antidote as the referent: within cessation there is activity;
this is the separation from the antidote, while cessation is the separation from the fruit of practice. Within activity there is cessation;

this is the separation from the antidote, while activity is the separation from the fruit of practice. Second, if one considers the gate of a single karma facing two objects in relation to the restrictive teaching, there are two [aspects].
The two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*) are mutually pervasive; the two types of transgression (*āpatti*) are likewise both pervasive.

Regarding the statement that "the two observances are mutually pervasive," this refers to all instances of dual observance, such as the formal procedures for the assignment of a site (*sthāpanā*) and the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*). Regarding the statement that "transgressions are mutually pervasive," this is in reference to the non-assignment [of a site], which is why it is termed "cessation" (*niṣedha*).
The physical act of constructing a dwelling is its "performance" (*kriyā*); thus, while the substance is one, the names are distinct. Is this not cessation?

Within [the category of] "action" (kṛti) there is action; within "action" there is cessation (sthiti). To say that both are applicable means that while one maintains the original [rule], one may conversely incur an offense.

The same applies by analogy. For example, the formal procedure of authorization (*jñapti-cāraṇa-dharma*) is termed "action. By applying this procedure, although one may build a dwelling, there is no offense for the act of building;

conversely, if one were to commit an offense instead, it could not be considered "cessation through maintenance" (*sthiti-śīla*). Although the substance is identical, the names differ. This is not the same as the old interpretation which [asserts] only...

Because the names and their essential natures are distinct, each of the two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*) maintains its own specific application; the same applies to the two types of transgression (*āpatti*). Third is the section on the mutual establishment of individual karmic characteristics.
The former interpretation held that there are two types of abstention (*virati*) but no two types of action (*kriyā*);

this was because while action exists as something previously unestablished that later becomes established, abstention lacks such a principle. The present explanation, however, asserts that both are universally applicable. As it says in the section on the observance of abstention (*virati-dhāraṇa*): "There is..."

Regarding the remaining three types of conduct: as with the previous case of killing and so forth, when an action has not yet been completed but is subsequently completed after returning to a state of mental stillness (*śamatha*), the prior act of killing is then finalized;

this constitutes an "active transgression" (*kṛta-āpatti*) occurring together with the state of stillness. Alternatively, matters such as the use of stūpas, temples, bridges, or boats constitute "active observance" (*kṛta-saṃvara*).
Or, as in the cases of keeping extra robes and bowls or being separated from one's robes, these may also involve a formal commitment (*samaya*); one should not fail to train in this.

Regarding "cessation through non-transgression" (*niṣedha-śīla*), these three [types of non-manifest action] may exist; they coexist with the mind that ceases [unwholesome conduct]. Is it not the case, then, that the other three [types of manifest action] also pertain to "observance through cessation" (*niṣedha-samādāna*)?

Since this is so for observance through cessation, the principle that the other three also pertain to it is likewise as stated before. To know simply that the other three pertain to observance through cessation:

it refers to those instances where one has made a formal vow to abandon evil, and the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) of the middle way coexists with other mental states. Second, if one explains according to the prescriptive teachings (*vidhi-śāsana*), regarding the person...

It is said that there are two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*) and two types of transgression (*āpatti*). There are no two types of transgression without two types of observance. The two types of observance represent restriction (*saṃvara*), while the two types of transgression represent pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Pervasion refers to cases such as killing, burning, and so forth; these are instances where the act of commission (*karmasamutthāna*) is pervasive. Examples include keeping extra robes and bowls or being separated from one’s robes; these are termed instances where the abstention (*virati*) is pervasive.

Through these two matters, each is shown to pervade the remaining three mental states (*citta*); this is how it should be understood. Furthermore, they may also be associated with all four modes of conduct (*carita*).

It applies to the other three [cases]. The offenses are as previously explained. Regarding the two types of "holding" that apply universally: for example, during the month of the *guṇa-cīvara*, one incurs no offense regarding the five benefits;

yet, within the mental states of the two transgressions, there can be both the "active" (*kriyā*) and "cessative" (*nivṛtti*) forms of separation from the robe for nine months, as well as the staff-bag and so forth—how could these not all apply universally?
As for the fourth section, the "instructing others" gate: the ancient interpretation held that the two cessations have two activities, whereas the two activities do not have two cessations.

Because one instructs another to cease, it is "I who am acting"; therefore, there can be no cessation. Question: When instructing another to cease, does the instruction itself constitute the bond (*saṃyojana*), or does the bond occur only after the cessation is completed?
Answer: The meaning depends on the other’s cessation. If that is so, it is known that the statement is made from the perspective of the other’s cessation.

"Cessation" (*thiti*) applies to the other [factors] as well. Furthermore, when the preceding person speaks of "cessation," they refer to cessation in relation to the object; however, because this is an intentional act (*kiriya*), it is termed a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

Since there is already a *dukkaṭa*, why would one instruct another? It cannot be that "cessation" does not apply [to the others]. When interpreted in this way, all four modes of conduct (*cāra*) apply universally.

This is because, although the four modes—cessation and so forth—are distinct, each possesses both the aspect of action (*kiriya*) and the aspect of non-action (*akiriya*). Thus it is established by the formal teaching (*vinaya-śikṣāpada*).
It is likewise so. The four preceding sections all contrast observance (*dhāraṇa*) with transgression (*āpatti*), and thus there is both pervasion and obstruction.

If one takes the perspective of establishing the sense of "conformity" (*anuvartana*), that sense also possesses both pervasion and obstruction. That is to say, regarding the two practices of "exclusive diligence," as previously analyzed, they are pervasive;

however, regarding the two practices of "repentance," they are obstructed within their own respective chapters because the two transgressions collectively constitute observance. They are said to be obstructed across different chapters because the medicinal applications differ. If...

Because one can accomplish the practice of "active maintenance" (kṛtādhāra) through repentance, this active maintenance is now specifically set forth in contrast to the three practices beginning with "cessation" (śamatha).
When instructing those who discern, it should be understood that within this active maintenance, the other three are also universally present.

Fourth, regarding the distinction between narrowness and breadth: first, we shall explain the two types of observance (*dhāraṇī*). Within this, there are further two aspects. First, distinguishing them in terms of "progressing toward" [the goal]:

the observance of restraint (*śīla-dhāraṇī*) is narrow while the observance of performance (*kriyā-dhāraṇī*) is broad. This is because the observance of restraint takes the avoidance of transgressions as its primary principle and is restricted to the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*);

therefore, it is narrow. As for the observance of performance, since its cultivation extends to both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), it is broad. If, however, one distinguishes them by means of the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*) in relation to specific matters, then the observance of restraint is broad.

[The commentary] makes it concise. Question: Why are the five categories [of offenses] called "counter-measures to specific matters" (*pratideśanīya*)? Answer: Merely ceasing from a transgression according to the rules (*śīla*) is not termed an offense;

rather, it is because of specific matters—such as building a dwelling, possessing extra robes, or being separated from one’s robes—that the prohibitive teachings (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) are established. Those that distinguish these are called "counter-measures to specific matters.

This differs from the case of "advancing toward" [an offense], where the mere act of ceasing constitutes an offense. Furthermore, within the prohibitive teachings, there are also cases involving "advancing toward," but because they are not the primary focus, they are not so categorized.

Speaking from the perspective of actual practice, to say that "abstention" (*śīla*) is broad while "action" (*karma*) is narrow means that abstention and maintenance (*śīla-dhāraṇa*) apply to all five categories and are therefore broad, whereas action is restricted to the lower four categories and is thus narrow.
Furthermore, within the category of active deeds, it specifically pertains to the two types of rooms in the second section.

The remaining eleven *śamatha* (cessations) may also apply to both *samāttika* (active observance) and *śamatha*. The thirteen [rules] are restricted to *samāttika* alone. This applies to the first category of dwellings (*āvāsa*) where only a portion is occupied, as well as dwellings with a designated owner;

the same principle applies to the other categories of offenses, with the sole exception of those not included [in this classification]. Among the rules for nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), eighteen specific activities—such as maintaining a retinue, receiving disciples, and providing instruction—are restricted to *samāttika* and do not extend to *śamatha*.
All others beyond these apply to both. Thus, one should know that *śamatha* is broader in scope. Even if a nun performs an act of *samāttika*, [the distinction remains].
It may be applied to the first category of offenses, but it is absent from the second and fourth categories; thus its scope can be known to be narrow.
It may also be applied to the second category, as in the cases of "crossing over thieves" and "resolving a formal act of suspension," because these constitute *kriyā-dhāraṇa* (active observance);

yet even this is narrow, because it does not apply to the remaining fifteen [offenses]. The same applies to the other categories. Next, regarding the explanation of the two types of offenses, when distinguishing them in relation to their objects: *kriyā* (action) is broad, while *virati* (abstinence) is narrow. Action...
These apply to five [offenses]. The "cessation" (niṣedha) is restricted to the lower four. Furthermore, in the second section (*varga*), there are thirteen items where the "cessation" is restricted;

the first dwelling is only partially [included], meaning that which exceeds the proper measure is excluded. The second dwelling is entirely [included]; the others are to be understood by analogy. Based on the eighteen rules such as "listening while being restrained," one should explain them by reversing the previous cases:

where the "construction" (*kārāpana*) is broad, the "cessation" is narrow, which can be known through analogy. As for the cessation of an offense committed by a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), although it may generally apply...
First, the second [category] is likewise absent; thus, it should be understood as narrow when considered in terms of what exists. It may also apply to the second, yet it remains narrow.

Furthermore, because the fourth is absent, if one clarifies the two types of offenses in terms of "progressing toward" [the goal], the ancient interpretation treats them as merely prohibitive offenses (*pratiṣedha-āpatti*).

The object (*viṣaya*) is broad while the essence (*svabhāva*) is narrow; according to the fifth category of offenses, it does not apply to the first four. This is also a case where the act (*kriyā*) is narrow while the offense is broad.

When both object and essence are broad, the transgression encompasses all five groups of offenses (*pañca-nikāya*). Speaking according to the principle of a single characteristic, this is the opposite of the preceding "cessation of offenses" (*virati-karma*);

one should say that the object is narrow while the essence is broad, meaning it pertains solely to the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*). Therefore, I shall now further explain: regarding its nature as an active offense (*kriyā-karma*), both object and essence are narrow.

However, the designation of "offense" (*āpatti*) is broad because, while the object (*viṣaya*) pertains solely to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), the offenses encompass all five groups (*pañca-nikāya*). Regarding the cessation of offenses and the explanation of their meaning:

both the object and the essence are broad, yet the designation of "offense" is narrow because the object extends to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), whereas the name is restricted to the fifth [category]. These explanations of the meanings can thus be understood.
As for the four types of conduct analyzed above regarding their breadth and narrowness, if one considers them according to what constitutes the basis for that breadth or narrowness:

The two *dhāraṇīs* (the prohibitions) are specialized and precise; they are equal to the substance of the precepts themselves, and for this reason they are broad. Among the various forms of repentance for transgressions, the prohibitions (*śīla*) of the two teachings result in everything becoming a transgression of following (*anuvartana*).

Within the prescriptive teachings (*vidhi-śāsana*), there are instances where an action does not constitute a transgression of following, such as when there is no repentance for a violation of the first category (*āpatti-pada*);

thus, these are narrower than the two *dhāraṇīs*. This is said in relation to the *bhikṣu* Sangha: when comparing transgressions to the *dhāraṇīs*, the prohibitions are broad while the actions are narrow. When speaking in relation to the *bhikṣuṇī* Sangha, both the prohibitions and the actions...

Regarding transgressions (*āpatti*), when compared to the two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*), they apply universally to five categories, with the exception of the fourth. That is to say, if one achieves the "conformity" (*anuvartana*) regarding the remaining [offenses] down to the *sthūlātyaya*, all constitute conformity.

However, regarding the first category (the *pārājika*), neither the cessation nor the performance constitutes conformity. Therefore, the performance of transgressions is collectively narrower in scope than the observance.
The various *bhikṣus* differ in that they make what is broad narrow.

Regarding the third point, "gradual and sudden": while the two [aspects of] "interpretation" (*vyākhyā*) have meaning only as gradual and not sudden, when discussing the two types of "stopping" (*śamatha*), both gradual and sudden are encompassed.

As for practicing "stopping through cultivation" (*kṛta-śamatha*), one cultivates it separately according to each matter, achieving it gradually in successive stages; within a single practice, [one cannot]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

One must fully cultivate all practices; even if one possesses a sudden resolve, the actual accomplishment requires gradual development. Therefore, it is said that [enlightenment] is not attained suddenly.

The same applies to the commission of an offense: it is likewise accomplished gradually. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states: "Regarding a single sentient being, one kills due to three conditions: first, one kills out of anger."

Second, killing out of delusion; third, killing out of greed. In contrast to these three roots of evil, at the time one originally received the precepts, one obtained the three precepts against killing with respect to each individual sentient being.
Now, if one kills a single person with a mind of hatred, one violates only one of the three precepts against killing and does not violate the other two.
As for all other sentient beings, the three precepts against killing remain entirely intact.

There is no transgression. Inferring from this principle, one may only attain all the precepts instantaneously at once; it is impossible to transgress them all [at once]. It is clear that this refers to gradualism.

As for the statement that the two types of restraint (the prohibitive and the prescriptive) apply to both the sudden and the gradual: if there is no defilement by evil, then through the understanding of the "restraint-and-maintenance" (*śīla-saṃvara*), one simply ensures that no evils are committed.
Remaining in a state of dignified composure, all two hundred and fifty [precepts] are entirely pure; they are both wholesome and indeterminate in nature.

The sudden differentiation of transgressions and the universal maintenance of precepts are established through the performance of specific acts, thereby manifesting the observance of prohibitions; this too is exclusively gradual.

For example, in order to cease the karma of killing, one cultivates loving-kindness toward specific objects; since there is no further intention to cultivate the remedial practices of other precepts simultaneously, it is likewise accomplished gradually.
Next, in the explanation of the cessation of transgressions (*śamatha-āpatti*), there are four sections: first, defining the names of the cessations of transgression;
second, determining their gradual or sudden nature; third, delimiting the boundaries of the offenses; and fourth, distinguishing between those that can be expiated and those that cannot.

These four sections are all explained in relation to the two teachings (*dvaya-śāsana*). First, regarding the definition of the names of the cessations of transgression: first, we shall explain "progression" (*abhyudgama*), which has two names.

First is the offense of failing to train; therefore, within the *Upasampadā* (full ordination), it is said: "You may study and inquire. Furthermore, in the subsequent text, when the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and the *Karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures) is enjoined, each [monk] says they do not recite them.

Consequently, the rule was established that one must have spent five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) in order to recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and the *Karmavācanā*. If one does not act according to the Dharma, this constitutes an offense.

Second is the offense of ignorance; therefore, the subsequent text states: "Previously I recited it, but now I have forgotten it all. The rule was established stating that one must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that one should not listen to the Dharma with only one ear while distracted; because of ignorance, when questioned regarding the original undertaking, one is made to study.

To cease such study constitutes a transgression. If one accepts the statement that a fruit is attained, yet has not yet attained it now, why is this not a transgression? The answer is: study is based on one's own capacity (*svabhāga*); therefore, it is said that ceasing [study] constitutes a transgression.
As for the attainment of the fruit, one’s power and portion are as yet unready; being similar to ignorance, it is not termed a transgression.

Regarding "cessation-offenses" (*sthāpana-āpatti*): it was further asked, "There are two types of cessation that constitute a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); in this region, these are termed 'misdeeds' (*dukkaṭa*). Since you say they are cessation-offenses, why are they named 'misdeeds'? Answer:

If one were entirely without intention (*citta*), one could not be said to have committed an offense. However, if one gives rise to the thought [to act], yet fails to train oneself or lacks understanding, this is what constitutes a "misdeed.

While the term "cessation" is used in reference to the object (*viṣaya*), furthermore, ignorance does not depend on whether the mind is wholesome or unwholesome; it is simply based on a lack of comprehension.
This constitutes the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*). This is because, due to a prior failure to train, one now fails to comprehend the object of a wholesome mind;

this also constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta*. When understood in this way, there are two layers of offenses incurred: first, the failure to train, which is the non-comprehension based on the condition of not having trained;
second, the subsequent offense of ignorance. This is similar to cases such as silent lying or concealment. Question: Should this be categorized according to body or speech?

Regarding the establishment of an offense: why is it said that one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for failing to understand the limits of the mind? The answer is: this refers to a failure of understanding in the mind, whereas the actual transgression occurs through the body and speech.
It is thus because this defines the boundary for establishing the offense. It is similar to how an offense is established based on the side of a silent lie when questioned.
Second, regarding the prescriptive teaching (*vidhi-śāsana*), "ceasing a transgression" means ceasing a dharma in order to perform an action, or applying a dharma in relation to a specific matter.

...and so forth. These are termed "cessation-offenses" (*nirodha-āpatti*). They apply generally to both monks and nuns and encompass all five categories of offenses (*pañca-nikāya*). Regarding the second pair, the gradual and the sudden:

first, one should understand that "progressing without learning cessation-offenses" implies both the gradual and the sudden. However, "cessation-offenses due to ignorance" are only gradual and not sudden.

This means that at the time of originally receiving the precepts, one makes a formal vow and resolution to cultivate all virtues; by returning to that state, one regains those same virtuous precepts as a defense.

"Not learning. If one now ceases the mind and stops all learning, this violates the original commitment. How could it not be that by following objects of perception, one suddenly commits all offenses of non-learning?
As for what is called "gradual offense," it refers to the arising of a mind that selectively learns; to hope for what is not learned while committing an offense—is this not gradual?
Therefore, the meaning of "not learning" encompasses both the gradual and the sudden. For those who do not understand the gradual, it must necessarily involve the objects of perception as conditions.

One cannot fail to understand [the rule] all at once; rather, it is precisely when one fails to understand that one incurs the offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*). However, within a single moment of mind, it is impossible for all conditions to be simultaneously present such that one would fail to understand everything.

Now, we establish the offense of ignorance based on the specific failure to understand as it arises; thus, it is clearly understood that this constitutes a gradual transgression. Regarding the second point, the gradual and sudden nature of the formulated precepts (*śikṣāpada*):

if one discusses the arising of the intention, it is only gradual and not sudden. For example, if one intends to build a house, one must not harbor the intention to keep extra robes beyond the permitted limit. If...

In terms of the accomplishment of the matter, there is both simultaneity and non-simultaneity; the meaning encompasses both gradual and sudden approaches. This is the third section. Regarding this section, there are two parts:

first, the preliminary advancement (*abhyudgama*). This advancement is further twofold: first, distinguishing it according to the stages of the teaching (*śāsana*). If one discusses its practice (*śikṣā*), it applies throughout from beginning to end;

thus, even those who do not study [formally] all attain what is attained through non-study. As for those who possess such knowledge, it is based on the final stage rather than the initial; therefore, [the text mentions] "five years."

Once [the period] has passed, one formally undertakes the vow of ignorance (*ajñāna*); this is the stage of knowledge (*jñāna*). Because the basis for [the previous status] has been lost, one is permitted to act; because one is performing the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*), [this applies].

Prior to five years, the vow of ignorance has not yet been undertaken; conversely, it can be understood that [the opposite] holds true. Second, this is distinguished according to the actual practice of the ignorant and the wise.

There is no such thing as "not having studied" as a single offense, for it exists in both the foolish and the wise; since everyone must study, there can be no offense of "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) for one who has stopped studying.

Wise persons and others should understand that "not knowing" constitutes the offense of ignorance. A foolish monk who relies [on others] for his entire life and remains unenlightened due to external conditions incurs no offense of ignorance;
this refers to one who has studied but does not yet know. If, however, one knows despite having studied nothing at all, one should calculate it according to the path.

The principle is likewise that there is no knowledge [of the offense]. Second, regarding the boundaries of the prescribed teachings (*śāsana-vinaya*): these boundaries can be understood by reference to the aforementioned matters.

Fourth, concerning what is and is not subject to confession (*deśanā*): according to the ancient interpretation, ignorance is subject to confession because it lacks the sense of a continuous succession (*saṃtati*).

As for that which is not subject to confession due to ignorance: although one may intentionally desire to know, the object is not clearly perceived; thus, because it lacks the sense of a continuous succession, it cannot be confessed.

Regarding confession: if later conditions were fully understood, then that would constitute liberation or the mutual elimination [of faults], and further confession would not be required. This is certainly not the case.

If one were to claim that confession is unnecessary because of liberation or mutual elimination—such that by reversing a delusion through understanding, the principle might indeed allow it—this still fails to account for the limits of the mind.
Once a transgression has already been committed, there is no need for remorse; thus, one knows whether it was intentional or unintentional. However, I shall now further explain this:

even an offense committed through ignorance may involve interruptions and continuities, and therefore it can be confessed. This is because if one originally did not study [the precepts] and furthermore lacked understanding, [the offense is unintentional].
The matter continues in succession. Now, regarding the training of the mind: although one may perceive objects without full clarity, this does not constitute the offense of "ignorance" (*ajñāna*).

Because of this lack of knowledge, one is merely said to be "not fully clear" in relation to the object; even if such lack of clarity persists, the Noble One (*ārya*) does not incur an offense. Since the offense does not continue, it is said that the succession is severed.
Within the *vinaya* (prescriptive teachings), it can be understood whether there is confession or no confession. The above has clarified the meanings of gradual and sudden.

This also concerns the gradual and sudden attainment of the offenses of cessation (*saṃvara*) and action (*kriyā*). If one takes the point of "accomplishing the offense" (*sāpattika*), within the specific category of the rule, there is no distinction between cessation and action regarding the meaning of suddenly accomplishing the offense.
This is like the case of the *śeṣa* (formal meeting) offenses, where categories such as "one name" or "many types" involve advancing toward the accomplishment of the offense;
this is likewise explained in the specific category of the prescriptive teaching (*vidhi-śāsana*).

The fourth sequence: Why does one maintain [the precepts] by placing the later transgressions first? It is because at the time of the original undertaking, when first entering [the path], the intention was earnest and one’s focus was primarily on upholding them;
conversely, regarding the matter of negligence, regret for transgressions occurs later. As it is said in the section on characteristics:

"In all cases, one must not commit sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth"—this first clarifies their maintenance. Then, regarding those who do commit them and so forth, it subsequently clarifies their transgression. This explains the reason why, within the context of maintenance...

First cessation, then action. Regarding the transgression of "action first, then cessation," the answer is: for one who has come to practice, if one does not abandon faults, there is no way to perform what is wholesome.
Therefore, cessation comes first; abandoning faults is the primary principle. Next, action is clarified; cultivating goodness is its meaning. Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* says:

"The characteristics of precepts establish the characteristics of action; cessation comes first, then action, because this is the sequence of their meanings. Furthermore, it may also be [interpreted as] cessation.
The principle of maintaining one's own practice must first be clarified; since one maintains it to perform external transformation, it is explained next.

This is known from the fact that it precedes the text on the precepts (*śīla*) and follows the *Khandhaka*. Regarding the two types of transgressions—first the act and subsequently the cessation—one looks to both the two [types of] transgression and the two [types of] maintenance.

Because they are mutually opposed, both [categories] may also be considered "gross transgressions" (*sthūlātyaya*) and ought logically to be prohibited first. Once the actual transgressions have occurred, they should be explained subsequently.

This is intended so that monks and nuns may abandon both gross and subtle faults, thereby achieving the benefits of the Path. Therefore, the "transgressions" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are presented first, followed by the "prohibitions" (*vāritaka-sāvadya*).

As for explaining them according to the text, this follows the same pattern as the preceding exposition on observance and release. Thus far, we have merely distinguished between observance and transgression, and between prohibition and action.
Subsequently, if one takes "holding" (*dhāraṇa*) to mean "accomplishing," then this cessation and performance would ultimately have no sequence of priority or posteriority.
Regarding the fifth [category], "holding," there are two sections: first, distinguishing it by examining its fundamental meaning;

second, following the textual descriptions of its characteristics, based on the gravity of the matter and the degree of increase or decrease in the offense. First, I shall explain the initial section. Within it—

Within this, there are further two [points]: first, the increase and decrease of the two types of observance; second, the superiority and inferiority of the two types of transgression. Regarding the "two types of observance":

the first is explained in terms of stages (*avasthā*), while the second is distinguished by ease and difficulty. As for "in terms of stages," it refers to the goodness of merely maintaining the precepts, which is cultivated through skillful means (*upāya*).

It begins subtly and culminates in manifestation, with distinct levels and gradations that are difficult to exhaustively describe. Essentially, they can be divided into four: the first is *vīrya* (dignity/majesty).

1. The precept of ritual observance; 2. The precept of guarding the sense faculties; 3. The precept concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*); 4. The precept concomitant with the Path (*mārga*).

The first belongs to the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and is termed the "precept of the nominal Saṃgha. The next two belong to the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) and are the "precept of the harmonious Saṃgha.

The last one belongs to the noble one (*ārya*) and is the "precept of the true Saṃgha. Based on these stages of practice, there are differences in degree of increase or decrease; thus, when designated as belonging to the Saṃgha, they are distinguished into three grades. As for the *Sarvāstivāda* view of the dhyāna-precepts:

This refers to the fundamental four dhyānas and the precepts termed "outflow-free" (anāsrava), which pertain to the first two fruits. These are based on the *anāgāmya* dhyāna when performing outflow-free contemplation;

this is determined by the level (*bhūmi*) upon which they rely, wherein the concentration-inherent (*samādhi-sahaja*) precepts are superior. Furthermore, one may distinguish them by way of ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*), speaking in relation to the five feelings (*vedanā*).

Alternatively, one may distinguish them by way of the Great and Small Vehicles, which is the difference between being complete or incomplete. Moreover, within the category of those who possess [the precepts], there are further distinctions.

First, the scope regarding thieves: observing the precepts for the sake of fame and profit is like being a thief; thus the Sūtra says, "The four kinds [of precept-breaking] do not attain the ten benefits," and so forth.
Second, the scope regarding offenses: as stated in the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one who commits a *pārājika* offense falls into hell for nine hundred twenty-one billion sixty thousand years;
"and so forth" refers to those who observe the precepts with faith in the Buddha’s words. Third, the scope regarding merit: as in the case of the precepts.
This is the beginning, middle, and end. [The practitioner] desires to be born in the heavens; or, if born among humans, to obtain fame and material gain;

and upon death, to be reborn in the heavens and so forth—these are the four boundaries of the paths. As stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: "With pure precepts and wisdom, one attains the foremost path.

The second [path] is distinguished by the contrast between difficulty and ease. If one considers the relative gravity [of offenses], one should cease and distance oneself from grave transgressions; therefore, [it is said]:

It is increased because it involves the abandonment of subtle transgressions; therefore, it is subtle. If distinguished by difficulty and ease: the practice of "stopping" (*śīla*) is subtle because it is easy to accomplish as it merely prevents gross faults;

the practice of "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) is increased because it is difficult to accomplish as it involves the abandonment of subtle transgressions. Furthermore, regarding a single matter, within the categories of stopping and maintaining, there are distinctions of increase and subtlety.

For example, as in the original [text]: "With focused diligence, one remains pure and without deficiency"; or again, "When confronted by an enemy, one is able to restrain one's own mind and does not accept [the provocation]."

Regarding the precepts such as those concerning pleasure and so forth: if one maintains them through such quiescent restraint (*śamatha*), is this not the superior grade? Or, although one does not commit [an offense], because of fear of ill repute, one is constrained by circumstances;

or because the mind lacks internal purity; or because it is permitted by the Noble Ones for the sake of applying an antidote to protect the mind, or due to a mind impaired by illness and the like—although these constitute observance, they are said to be inferior and are considered minor.
Other precepts are likewise of two grades, both superior and inferior, depending on whether they are performed [with full intent] or otherwise.
The sequence of the stages may be inferred by analogy. Verifying this principle, the applications [of the precepts] vary in a thousand ways.

Regarding the second point, the relative gravity of the two types of offenses: first, this concerns the distinction between ordinary persons and sages. For example, an offense committed by a sage is light, whereas for an ordinary person it is heavy.

This is because, when a person of the third fruit encounters conditions, their afflictions arise with little intensity and are therefore considered light; as for a sage who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), [the same applies].

There are no intentional transgressions; there are only accidental transgressions. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in the first three fruits [of the path] possess the sense of intentional transgression.

As for those who are free from attachment (*anāsrava*), they have indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) transgressions. When ordinary persons commit a grave offense, it is because they possess afflictions (*kleśa*) and give rise to the evil of breaking the precepts.

Second, this is analyzed by increasing the number according to the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), distinguishing between action (*kriyā*) and cessation (*virati*). Regarding action, it constitutes a fault.
Coarse [offenses] cease with the transgression being minor; both types of cessation are thus. Yet within the category of cessation itself, there are naturally coarse and subtle distinctions.
If one speaks generally of both commission and cessation in relation to the *pien-chu* (the sections of the Prātimokṣa), each meaning encompasses both the coarse and the subtle.

Although the offenses are numerous, according to the teachings, they range from the upper to the lower levels, beginning with two gates and culminating in eight. Regarding the "two gates," the first is the distinction between intentional and unintentional; the unintentional is entirely non-offensive.
Therefore, it is not discussed. Regarding the statement "because it is not intentional," this means that because one does not act intentionally, it does not violate the intent of the Noble Teaching;

it does not mean that such acts as wearing robes that are neither too high nor too low are non-offenses. Rather, they are offenses, yet they are light. This is because the text states: "Because it was not done intentionally, one directly commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), but there is no violation of the rules of decorum (*aiśārya*).

If, however, one acts intentionally, one further commits a violation of decorum. Thus, within the category of intentional acts, both prohibitive (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) karmas are excluded.

Within the three types of prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), there is a distinction between those that are established and those that are not; thus the text states: "Those that are established are *pārājika*; those that are not are *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Fourth, the four types of prohibitions are subsumed within the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*). Regarding these categories and groups, there is a distinction between the teaching (*śāsana*) and the nature (*svabhāva*).

As for the teaching: in the second category and the first group, the characteristics of the teaching are considered primary; in the third category and the second group, the status [of the offense] is considered secondary. This is because they may pertain to matters of decorum (*īryāpatha*). Thus it is said.

Regarding the classification by nature (*prakṛti-vibhāga*): the Mother [Sūtra] states that the four incurable offenses are designated as grave; this applies to both the higher and lower vehicles. The remaining offenses are considered light.

Alternatively, there is the classification of "with remainder" and "without remainder," or the classification of "confessed" and "unconfessed. Within these, there are two types, namely those that pertain respectively to the teachings and the natures.
Furthermore, there are the twenty-one categories such as the "increased two" and so forth. As for the three gates, they are as stated in the verse. Regarding the four matters, they are not...
"Remediable," etc. Furthermore, it is said in full: five offenses can be confessed; for the sixth, a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is required; one offense cannot be remedied.
Moreover, a verse from the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "Understanding the minor, the non-minor, and the minor precepts accordingly," and so forth. Regarding the four gates:
