as in the verse on the four similes of corpses, they correspond to the four [aspects] within the prohibitive rules (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*), namely: the four fears regarding transgressions, and the four aspects of false speech and the perception of objects within the precept against stealing.

And so forth. Furthermore, the Mother [Sūtra] says: "One may use intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to negate the action (*karman*)," regarding which there are four permutations in relation to retribution (*vipāka*).

First, the offense is grave but the retribution is light; this refers to cases such as acting as a matchmaker, as these are frequent occurrences. Second, the offense is light but the retribution is grave; this refers to cases such as striking the Buddha, as these are rare occurrences.

In these three cases, the methods for establishing the precepts differ: a light offense may be designated by a grave name, and a grave offense may be designated by a light name. While the transgressions and merits differ, the cause and effect remain correspondingly balanced. Third, both are grave, such as in the case of physical contact.

Slander and so forth are examples of these four [offenses] where both factors are light, such as those found in the "Lower Section" (Kṣudraka-vastu). These two subsequent lines conclude that while the method for establishing the precepts does not differ, the method for incurring the offense does.
The five categories refer to the five groups of offenses (*pañca-pārājikādi*) and the five propositions regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*).

The six categories are as when the Buddha explained to Maudgalyāyana that certain offenses are light; that is, combining the sixth and seventh [categories] constitutes the *śaikṣa-dharmas* (rules of training), which are equal in number to the Four Heavenly Kings.

The lifespan of the Sun and Moon [deities] is five hundred years. This continues up to the *yī* (夷) offense; those who commit such a crime fall into the hells with a lifespan equal to that of the Sixth Heaven, which is sixteen thousand years.
The "seven gates" refers to the seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*). As for the "eight gates," Sūrya, taking the case of killing a human as an example:

although the objective condition (*ālambana*) is grave, because the intensity of the mind varies, there are eight degrees of superiority and inferiority, which are categorized into four stages. In the first three cases, both the time and the action are grave. *Note: The term *yī* (夷) likely refers to a specific category of grave offenses within the Vinaya context.*

Two categories: namely, the gravity of the preliminary effort (*upāya*), the gravity of the fundamental act (*mūla*), and the gravity of the completion (*niṣṭhā*). "Gravity" refers to the fact that the murderous intent is particularly harmful.
The second stage consists of two heavy factors and one light factor, forming three permutations: first, the preliminary and fundamental acts are heavy while the completion is light;

next, the preliminary act is light while the latter two are heavy; and finally, the fundamental act is light while the remaining two are heavy. The third stage consists of two light factors and one heavy factor, forming three [permutations].

There are eight phrases: first, the root offense is grave while the other two are light; second, the preparatory effort is grave while the other two are light; third, the completion of the act is grave while the other two are light;

fourth, all three stages are light. "Light" refers to a lack of earnestness and sincerity in the mind. These eight phrases, when viewed according to the Vinaya, take the objective sphere as the basis and define the gravity by way of the mind;
since they equally violate the teachings, these constitute eight levels of grave offenses. If their retribution were to be drawn forth...
There are eight distinct categories. Alternatively, based on the presence or absence of a conscious mind, there may also be eight. To speak briefly by way of the four continents:

in the first three instances, there is a conscious mind throughout—namely, during the preliminary effort (*prayoga*), the fundamental act (*maula*), and its completion (*niṣṭhā*)—wherein all four matters constitute grave offenses (*pārājika*).

Second, regarding the two times when there is a mind and one time when there is no mind, three propositions are formed. First, the first two [moments] have a mind, while the third is already without a mind; thus, all four are equally grave.
Second, the fundamental [moment] is without a mind, while the remaining two have a mind; the first offense is grave, while the remaining three are *thullaccaya* (light offenses).
Third, the preparatory stage (*upakkama*) is without a mind, while the remaining two have a mind; all four constitute a grave offense. The third [category] is that which has a mind at one time.

Regarding the mind, there are three propositions. The first proposition is that the initial precept is grave while the other three are light. The second proposition is that all four are equally grave.
The third proposition is that the initial one is grave while the other three are light. The fourth is that when there was no intention during the three times [of action], none are transgressed.
This should be understood as being based on what is explained in the section on minor false speech.

The second [section] clarifies the distinctions of superiority and inferiority based on the gravity or lightness of the matter and the offense. This is analyzed through two gates: first, a general analysis in contrast to the matters of the teachings;
second, an analysis based on the specific matter and the offense, distinguishing between those who do not study and those who are ignorant, and the categories of definite observance and violation.

Regarding the "general contrast," although the aspects of the teachings are numerous, they consist only of prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) and permissions (*anujñā*). As for "prohibitive teachings" (*pratiṣedha-śāsana*), there are requirements regarding what must be done and what must not be done. If one does what is prohibited...
Thus, by looking upward and following [the precepts], one commits no transgression. Furthermore, there are cases where performing an action constitutes an offense;

such instances are therefore called "prescriptive teachings" (*zhìjiào*). As for what are called "permissive teachings" (*tīngjiào*): whether one performs them or not, there is no fault whatsoever, as the Sage permits both options. Therefore, they are called "permissive teachings."
Therefore, the *Dìchí jīng* (Bodhisattvabhūmi) states: "That which involves transgression is prohibited; that which is without transgression is permitted.

If one refers to this scriptural text, it includes essentials such as the seven formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) for receiving and announcing the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), the determination of the location of offenses, the receiving and maintaining of robes and bowls, and the training in what is to be studied.

One must perform [acts] such as sexual misconduct, theft, and physical contact; one must certainly not perform others. These are all subsumed under the category of prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*).

These are what are called "all offenses committed by simple possession. As for matters such as the demarcation of pure areas (*śuddhasthāna*), the distribution of robes (*kaṭhina*), and various surplus items (*atireka*), these belong to the category of permissive teachings (*anujñā-dvāra*).

This applies to all instances of dual precepts regarding both transgressions and observances. Furthermore, there are cases where both prohibitions and permissions apply, such as the rule concerning staying overnight separated from one’s robes.

As for why women require these two types of instruction: if there were only prohibitions and no permissions, they would be excluded from the subsequent stages and have no means of advancing on the Path;

therefore, the permission is required. Conversely, if there were only permissions and no prohibitions, they would lack self-restraint and fail to achieve excellence in the Path; therefore, the prohibition is likewise required.
These two gates now encompass the three grades [of practitioners], for they are so designed to be beneficial according to their respective faculties.
They comprise all the gates of the teachings regarding prohibitions and permissions, and thus constitute the constant paradigm for the Great Sage’s [Buddha’s] opening and closing [of precepts].

Since they encompass everything, one must rely upon them to distinguish between upholding and violating the precepts. However, the "abiding in cessation" (śīla) and the "active transgression" specifically correspond to what is permissible and impermissible within the two types of teaching.

Regarding the matter of training (*śikṣā-vastu*): although the prohibitive teachings (*prajñapti-śāsana*) constitute only a small portion [of the training], they are termed "exclusions from what may be trained in.

These do not depend upon the formal dharmas; rather, when the dharma is ceased, one commits an offense, and when the dharma is performed, one maintains the precept. Therefore, in the present context, "ceasing" corresponds to maintaining and "performing" corresponds to committing an offense, as these are paired with the formal dharmas.

Conversely, if "performing" corresponds to maintaining and "ceasing" corresponds to committing an offense, this is restricted to those formal dharmas that can be trained in within the two types of teachings. However, the small portion of the prohibitive teachings does not depend upon the specific matters [themselves]; for regarding such matters, if one performs them...

Because it involves transgression, there is also the sense of performing an action (*kriyā*) through formal ritual procedure (*vidhi*). Nevertheless, our primary thesis clarifies that within the context of formal procedures, even the practice of "abstaining" (*saṃvara*) possesses the sense of relying upon the Dharma;

this is because abstaining from specific actions constitutes the core of the thesis. Question: Why is it that the practice of abstaining (*saṃvara*) and so forth does not apply to the Dharma itself? Answer:

Because the Dharma is known only through progressive cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is not an object to be accomplished by the gate of abstention. Since both [the Dharma and abstention] equally eliminate faults, [this principle] encompasses both teachings.
Regarding the matter: it was asked why those things that constitute transgressions when performed but are not transgressions when refrained from are excluded from being "things to be learned.

The answer is: both the phenomena (*dharma*) and the things to be learned are objects for progressive cultivation. Therefore, in the case of the former, performing [the act] constitutes upholding (*dhāraṇa*), while refraining constitutes a transgression (*āpatti*).

These "things not to be learned" are not methods for progressive cultivation; they are thus distinguished and not discussed here. As for the statement that "refraining and upholding" refers to the two teachings, first, taking them literally, one should not...

Training (*śikṣā*). This refers to such things as perceiving what is not a human as a human, and so forth. Regarding the aforementioned prohibitive teachings (*pratiṣedha-vidhi*), one must simply not perform them.

Second is the gate of permission (*anujñā-mukha*), which means that which may be learned; this refers to the aforementioned permitted matters. Whether one performs them or not—such as the measurements for rooms and robes—in these two types of matters, provided one simply does not perform [the prohibited acts], they are all termed "maintaining through cessation" (*virati-dhāraṇa*).
Performing [the permitted acts] serves as the antidote to transgression; however, to perform an act that violates both types of teaching constitutes a transgression.
This is called "transgression. The opposite of what was stated above may be understood accordingly. Regarding "performance and maintenance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) in relation to the two types of teachings:

this refers to those matters within the prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) that are subject to training, such as receiving the precepts, performing the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, receiving robes and bowls, and so forth; and those matters within the permissions (*anujñā*), such as the distribution [of goods], the establishment of pure boundaries (*śuddha-sīmā*), the virtuous robes (*guṇavat-cīvara*), and the various rules concerning surplus robes (*atireka-cīvara*).

Within these two categories, as long as one performs the ritual actions and undertakes the tasks in accordance with the teachings, it is all termed "performance and maintenance. If one speaks of cessation...

The opposite can be understood from this. Thus, while the two teachings each encompass both dual observances and dual transgressions, the prohibitions (the *prātimokṣa*) are restricted to single instances, whereas the permissions (*anujñā*) involve both observance and transgression together.

Regarding the specific analysis of the second dhyāna, there is a threefold classification: first, the sequential explanation of the former interpretation; second, the extensive refutation of its errors;
and third, the elucidation of the correct established doctrine.

First, regarding the analysis of the former meaning: there are nine categories each for the three—observance (*dhāraṇa*), performance (*kriyā*), and transgression (*āpatti*). There are eight phrases for non-performance (*sthiti*) and transgression, which likewise do not distinguish between those who have studied and those who have not.

However, with respect to the first category [of offenses], it is said that there are nine categories for performance and transgression; concerning the second category, there are nine categories for performance and observance.

The observance of prohibitions (*śīla*) and the transgression of prohibitions are explained by way of reference in the first section of the ninety [rules], as previously analyzed in the three sets of nine and the single set of eight.

Furthermore, there are those who say that these are explained collectively here in terms of matters that can be learned and matters that cannot be learned; now, they are explained extensively according to this approach.

This clearly elucidates the preceding meaning. Regarding the categories of "abstaining and maintaining" (*zhi-chí*) and "acting and transgressing" (*zuò-fàn*), because they correspond respectively to matters that can be learned and matters that cannot be learned, each possesses its own instances of maintenance and initiation.

This constitutes four sets of nine propositions. Since "acting and maintaining" (*zuò-chí*) and "abstaining and transgressing" (*zhǐ-fàn*) pertain exclusively to matters that can be learned, there are nine propositions for "acting and maintaining," while "abstaining and transgressing" may consist of eight.
As for the statement that "abstaining and maintaining" lacks distinctions of light or heavy, it may be divided into two sets of nine based on the nature of the matter; first, regarding...
There are nine categories for training in the performance of actions: one for the superior grade, four each for the middle and lower grades.

Regarding the one for the superior grade, it refers to "cognition" (*vijñapti*). This refers to cases where there is cognition regarding the act itself. Regarding the four for the middle grade, two take "cognition" as the primary factor:

the first two cases involve cognition regarding the act while there is doubt or non-cognition regarding the offense; the subsequent two cases involve cognition regarding the offense while there is doubt or non-cognition regarding the act. There are four for the lower grade.

Regarding this, for the most part, two types of "non-recognition" (*asaṃjñā*) are used as the heading. First, there are two phrases: non-recognition regarding the matter itself, and non-recognition regarding doubt concerning the offense.

Next, there are two phrases: doubt regarding the matter, and doubt regarding non-recognition of the offense. In the superior grade, both the matter and the offense are recognized, and there is no offense of non-learning (*aśikṣita*).

In the middle grade, there are four offenses of non-learning; in the inferior grade, there are eight offenses of non-learning. If one is confronted with an offense of ignorance (*ajñāna*), it follows the [inferior] order.

Each of the two categories is explained by doubling [the previous count]. Question: Since there are already twenty-four offenses of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) that constitute "cessation through non-transgression" (*virati-śīla*), how can these be called "observance" (*dhāraṇa*)?

Answer: Because in both cases, the fundamental [offense] is not committed. This "cessation through observance" (*virati-dhāraṇa*) is categorized according to the presence or absence, and the degree, of such non-transgressions;

thus, there are three positions and nine grades. Next, regarding the nine types of "cessation through observance" concerning what is not to be learned (*aśikṣaṇīya-virati-dhāraṇa*): it simply refers to the three mental states based on the object, namely, cognition (*vijñapti*).

If one is doubtful and does not recognize [the offense], the conditions for the transgression are likewise. Therefore, by taking the three mental states regarding the objective conditions and applying each of them to the three mental states regarding the offense, nine [instances] are formed;
this can be understood by counting them. Within each of these three triads, there are two further offenses—namely, "not training" and "unknowing"—which together total twelve offenses.
Although the mental states and objective conditions are thus, as long as one does not commit the fundamental offense, it is termed "cessation."

[The term] *dhāraṇī* (or *dharati*). Next, the commission of offenses (*kṛta-āpatti*) is explained. First, regarding the nine [cases] concerning those who are capable of training, it is as stated in the first set of nine.

Next, regarding the nine [cases] concerning those incapable of training, it is as stated in the latter set of nine. However, because one commits a root offense (*mūlāpatti*), it is termed a "commissioned offense.

Although a root offense has been incurred, if one harbors doubt or fails to recognize [the transgression] regarding matters where one is capable of training, the offense is established in all such cases. As stated above, this excludes only [those cases of] non-...

Regarding the matters that may be learned: although one may have doubts or lack understanding, it should be known that one must never transgress them unilaterally. Next, to distinguish the nine types of "upward-holding" (*āśraya-dhāraṇa*):

if categorized according to the *Abhidharma* (the Dharma of Confrontation) and according to specific matters, there should be two sets of nine; however, since they do not differ in their clarification of the distinctions and stages of progression, they are combined into a single set of nine.

This is distinguished in contrast to the "matters that may be learned," as explained above; thus, the nine types of "superior-holding" (*uttara-uttara-dhāraṇa*) correspond precisely to the "matters that may be learned. It is only [this].

In this context, the distinction lies in performing the preliminary acts in accordance with the Noble Teaching. Next, the discussion concerns the cessation of offenses, which are either nine or eight in number.

Regarding the "nine," these refer to the four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension) that are based on matters subject to training; they primarily take the two types of "lack of awareness" as their basis. As for the "eight," [they refer to] the four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses when applied to the fourfold permutation of superior grades.
The sixteen *duṣkṛta* offenses can be understood [as follows]. In the medium category, there are four permutations; for the most part, two types of consciousness serve as the primary factors.

There are four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and eight *duṣkṛta* offenses, which can be understood [as follows]. In the inferior category, there is one permutation: namely, one who recognizes both the matter and the offense, yet does not request formal authorization (*jñapti*) before constructing a dwelling.
This can be understood [as follows]: because the majority of offenses in this case belong to the superior category, the number "eight" is stated in contrast to the formal teaching (*śāsana*).

Regarding the practice of not learning, the offenses of clear transgression follow the sequence of the preceding nine phrases; specifically, excluding the lower grade, the first eight phrases constitute them.

This can be understood from the detailed explanation. These explanations must be arranged into five sets of nine phrases each, consisting of either nine or eight phrases, totaling six sets of nine and one set of eight.

Second, the refutation of [the opponent's] position. Question: Regarding the nine offenses committed against the *śaikṣadharma*s (trainee rules), how are they distinguished from the nine sentences concerning "cessation-offenses" (*sthāpana-sāvadya*) mentioned below?

Now, as for the cessation-offenses: failing to obtain formal authorization (*jñapti*) is termed a cessation-offense; whereas constructing a dwelling through bodily action is an act-offense (*karaṇa-sāvadya*).
These two share the same essence but differ in name; fundamentally, there are not two distinct offenses. How, then, can there be nine cessation-offenses in addition [to the others]?
To establish the offenses of commission separately as nineteen: is this not merely having the names of relative categories in vain, while lacking actual entities with distinct gradations?

Furthermore, if it were not thus, regarding what matters would one distinguish the "offenses of commission that can be learned" mentioned previously? It too should not exceed the category of dual offenses.
Since they speak of dual offenses yet divide them into two sets of nine, we know it is not so. Moreover, it speaks of "matters that can be learned."

Regarding "clearly committing an offense": this refers to taking up an object that exceeds the permitted measure while maintaining the perception [of it as such]; thus, it constitutes a single act of commission.

If one interprets it in this way, even though it is a single act of commission, the sequence of its grades does not differ from the three higher levels of the perception of the object in the precept against killing.

Why, then, must there be a separate set of nine for the "trainable" (śikṣamāṇā) category? Question: Regarding the nine rules of "abstaining and maintaining" (virati-dhāraṇa) taught in relation to the "trainable" dharma, how do they compare to the nine rules of "actively maintaining" (anuvartana-dhāraṇa)?

What is the distinction between the phrases? That which performs an act of distribution is called "active observance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*), which inherently includes "restraining observance" (*vārita-dhāraṇa*);

these two are inseparable. How, then, can they be established as two separate sets of nine? If one were to argue that "restraining observance" exists as a distinct entity from the name [of the precept], such a position might be acceptable in theory;

however, it still cannot encompass the "restraining observance" that shares the same essence, because the latter is not separate from "active observance. Furthermore, since it is not included therein, it is not clarified.

This is distinguished within the context of the two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*). Therefore, it is said that there are nine instances of "observance through performance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*), while the name "observance through cessation" (*virati-dhāraṇa*) is omitted and not made manifest.

Furthermore, it is said: "If one were to follow the *Abhidharma* in its treatment of individual matters, there should be two sets of nine; however, since the levels of progression are no different, they are combined into a single set of nine.
This makes it clear that because it is a formal rite (*vidhi-karman*), even though the preceding action is performed, there is no offense of non-performance. Is this not indeed "cessation"?

Regarding "maintaining" (dhāraṇa): since there is both "stopping-maintenance" (niṣedha-dhāraṇa) and "practicing-maintenance" (anuṣṭhāna-dhāraṇa), this constitutes "dual maintenance. Why, then, is it said that there are only nine instances of "practicing-maintenance"?

If one argues that the reverse—when one perceives an object as exceeding the prescribed measure—is "single stopping-maintenance," and thus the nine instances of stopping-maintenance are clarified according to what can be learned, this interpretation is incorrect.

When considering their respective stages and categories, they are identical to [the cases of] killing and so forth; the reverse of practicing an offense is used to clarify stopping-maintenance, and is therefore subsumed within those [nine].

What distinct characteristics are there that necessitate a separate ninth category? Question: Regarding the offenses committed through the sequential engagement with objects, on what basis are there nine?

Is it the four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* of the superior grade, the four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* of the middling grade, and one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* of the inferior grade? Furthermore, one must not treat the commission of an offense as something to be learned;

rather, based on the three levels of perception regarding the object (*ālambana*), each of these three being further divided into three, they combine to form nine stages. This is how the cessation of the offense is calculated.

This constitutes an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* due to failure to obtain formal authorization (*an-uddiṣṭa*). It should be understood that this also relies on the three grades of perception regarding the object of the two types of rooms as their hierarchical levels.
If one were to base it solely on the rooms themselves, the meaning would deviate from the sequence of the text, and furthermore, it would seem incorrect. The reason for this is as follows:

regarding the three grades of perception concerning the object, first is "failure to obtain authorization" with the perception of failure to obtain authorization; this refers to a case where the matter is clearly known. Second is "failure to obtain authorization" with doubt [regarding whether authorization was obtained].
That is to say, it is a matter of doubt. Third, the perception of having made a formal disposition where none was made; this is a failure to recognize the matter. The sequence is as follows:
among the nine cases previously established, the four categories of the superior grade seem to subsume the subsequent lower grades because of doubt and non-recognition.

The four categories of the middle grade seem to contain all three [grades] collectively because of recognizing the matter while doubting and failing to recognize it. The single category of the inferior grade is the reverse of the first case. Because...
Because they are cognizant of the matter. For what reason are there three grades? To reverse it in this way, the first [position] is untenable.
Furthermore, according to the text, examining the nine cases: the superior grade should be four *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; the middle grade, two *śeṣa* and two *sthūlātyaya*; and the inferior grade, one *śeṣa*.
Since the text states "saṃghāvaśeṣa" and "sthūlātyaya," why would there be nine? If all nine were to commit *śeṣa*, these two [positions] are untenable. Even if all nine were indeed *śeṣa*...
It is as if the initial phrase were divided into these nine. If this were the case, against what would one identify [the offenses] such as "doubt" and "not knowing"?

Since doubt and the others should be included within the *khaṇḍa* (intermediate) category, why are they listed alongside the *śeṣa* (residual)? These three [interpretations] are untenable. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the nine are established by analogy to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:

the transgressions are established according to the text, while the nine are established by analogy to the matters of consciousness (*vijñapti*). However, those [matters of consciousness] apply to all three [categories], and this [system] likewise...

It should be so. These four [positions] are untenable. If there were no textual basis for them to arise independently, their meaning would be a mere fabrication. If one relies on the "perception of the object" (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), it would further contradict the intent of the text.

Examining the matter from every possible angle, these appear to be forced interpretations. Furthermore, it is asked: why is the superior grade of "possession through performance" (*karmopasthāna*) counted as one, while the subsequent lower grades each have four?

According to what text is this stated? Could it be that it was not said because they are merely prohibitions against offenses? One must therefore employ both the non-offensive and the offensive [distinctions].
To consider the "Lesser" as the superior is likewise incorrect. What is being discussed here concerns only the "restraint from transgression" (śīla-virati).

Since this deviates from the textual sequence, it is evident that the "active observance" (samādāna-śīla) is being treated in a contradictory manner by being ranked as superior or inferior. Since active observance cannot be learned [independently], restraint from transgression fundamentally ought not to exist separately.
This has already been refuted previously; it is clarified within the context of the "twofold observance" (ubhaya-śīla), and the same principle applies here to refute this [misconception].
Third, to clarify the correct meaning: the stages and gradations of observance and transgression may be categorized as five sets of nine or six sets of nine.

If one distinguishes observance and transgression according to specific objects, then "active transgression" (*kṛta-āpatti*) corresponds to "cessation-observance" (*virati-śīla*), while "cessation-transgression" (*virati-āpatti*) corresponds to "active observance" (*kṛta-śīla*).

This is based solely on objects that are subject to training (*śikṣaṇīya*). First, regarding active transgression and cessation-observance, when applied to two types of objects, the former becomes established.

Transgression occurs through action; cessation constitutes observance. Therefore, one must now again distinguish between the commission of transgressions and the maintenance of observances based on these two matters, because they are respectively single instances of transgression and single instances of observance.
Question: What are these? Answer: For example, regarding the precept against killing, the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*);

and regarding the two gross verbal offenses of great falsehood and sexual contact, as well as the perception of the object in cases such as matchmaking and so forth—these are matters that cannot be learned [by mere study]. As for the preceding...
Regarding the offense of exceeding the prescribed dimensions for a dwelling while perceiving it as such: this is a matter that can be trained in. First, the commission of an offense is clarified.

That is to say, among the aforementioned precepts concerning what may and may not be practiced, one takes the objective and the perception for each; with the three superior [categories] combined across the three conditions of the offense and the three mental states, they form a total of nine.

Regarding the observance of restraint (*śīla*), when one acts contrary to it, an offense is committed; this likewise corresponds to two matters, which together form a total of nine. Next, the failure to maintain restraint is clarified.

Regarding the practice of observance (*dhāraṇa*) for those who are capable of training, there are three types: First, there is the dual violation and dual observance in relation to hearing the teachings, such as the instructions on *deśanā* (confession), *śuddhi* (purification), the separation from robes, and the six-year rule.

Second, there is the single violation and single observance according to the prohibitive teachings (*pratikṣepa-śikṣā*), such as the two-year period, the six rules, and the receiving and maintaining of robes and bowls.
Third, there is the observance in relation to progressive cultivation, such as training in what is to be learned, training in the precepts, and recitation.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* and so forth, within these three stages, the meanings are condensed into two categories. The first two are explained together because they both equally involve fundamental transgressions (*mūlāpatti*).

Furthermore, up to this point, the primary tenet is that cessation constitutes transgression while performance constitutes observance (*dhāraṇa*). For this reason, the number of categories for these two is explained in combination.

As for the statement "two transgressions and dual observances," if analyzed according to their meaning, they should be divided into four and nine [sections]. This is truly because the names of the two transgressions...

Although there are distinctions, because their essence is one, they are combined into a single set of nine. Retention (*dhāraṇī*) is likewise; thus, transgressions and retention each constitute a set of nine.
Alternatively, the distinct essence of "cessation-retention" (*śamatha-dhāraṇī*)—referring to the cessation of matters through the aforementioned dharmas—may further be treated as a set of nine.
Thirdly, regarding the progressive cultivation of "cessation-transgression" and "activity-retention," these are collectively treated as a set of nine. Therefore, there are five [sets].

Nine. Or again, it is six times nine. Furthermore, regarding the mention of "nine," this is based on the aforementioned three; it may also be explained by way of reasoning. According to the five phrases concerning the object and perception, these constitute ten and twenty-five.

As for the mention of "twelve," this refers to the fourth case—where there is no person but the perception of a person—which should be stated as two variations: the object being the actual object while the perception of the object is mistaken, and the object being the actual object while there is doubt regarding the perception of the object. These result in two variations each, totaling twelve. Regarding the object and perception, there are five phrases, which immediately become ten and twenty-five. The statement of "twelve" means that by taking the fourth case—non-person with the perception of a person—one should speak of one variation and another; namely, the object is the actual object while the perception of the object is mistaken, and the object is the actual object while there is doubt regarding the perception of the object. These constitute two variations. The object and the perception of the object, along with the doubt, [form the basis for] the calculation.
There are three distinctions regarding offenses. Regarding the object: if one perceives what is not the actual object as the actual object, there is no offense.

As for the statement "fifteen," this refers to the three mental states enumerated above, applied across the various offenses; the count can be understood from this. Since the fixed number is thus established, we shall next proceed with a detailed analysis.

First, regarding the commission of an offense versus the observance of restraint, two factors must be considered. As for "commission of an offense," this refers to acts such as killing and cases involving excessive quantities.

Regarding the thought that takes the three aforementioned objects as its basis: the phrases "a person," "the perception of a person," "excessive," and "perception of the excessive" refer to the object of consciousness (*vijñeya-vastu*).
The phrase "two persons" and "doubt regarding the excessive" refer to the object of doubt (*saṃśaya-vastu*).

The phrase "a non-person," "perception of a non-person," "excessive," and "non-excessive perception" refer to the object of non-consciousness (*avijñeya-vastu*). Furthermore, there are also three types of thoughts that take offenses as their basis; the first is consciousness.

Regarding the offense: among the human dharmas, it refers to one who conceals the intention of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense while claiming it was a *pārājika*. Second is the "doubtful offense," which means doubting whether it is one of the other six [offenses] that do not require formal treatment for concealment.
Third is the "unrecognized offense," such as when one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* but considers it to be one of the other six, and so forth.
By taking these three states of mind and applying them respectively to each of the three types of offenses, nine permutations are formed. First, apply the three states of mind to the offenses.
Regarding the category of "knowing the matter," there are three types: first, knowing the matter and knowing it as an offense; second, knowing the matter but suspecting it to be an offense;

third, knowing the matter but not recognizing it as an offense. Next, regarding the category of "suspecting the matter," there are three types. Next, regarding the category of "not knowing the matter," there are three types. These may be understood by following the same enumeration. These are the three phrases concerning "knowing the matter."

When mind and object correspond, the gravity [of the offense] reaches its ultimate limit; it is therefore judged as "superior" (adhimātra). The next two grades involve objects that are both matters and skillful means;
thus they are judged as "inferior" (mṛdu) to the preceding. This is based on the transformation of perception. If one fundamentally lacks awareness, then there is no offense of the inferior grade.

Question: Regarding the subsequent *kukulan* [offenses], how are they graded? Answer: Because the minds of those who encounter the conditions vary in their duration, there is a corresponding variation in the gravity of the offenses.
Within these three sets of three phrases, if the matter is not something that can be learned, each of the lower two phrases constitutes the two offenses of "not learning" and "lack of knowledge";
thus, there are twelve *duṣkṛta* (minor infractions) in total. If, however, one encounters a matter that can be learned but suspects it or fails to recognize it, and so forth...

Regarding the two sets of three *khandhakas*, there are further twelve *dukkaṭas*. Furthermore, concerning the three types of consciousness regarding an object: if one is conscious of the matter, the offense is grave, because one does not listen to the matter and proceeds to act with a settled mind.

Regarding the three types of consciousness where there is no offense: if one is conscious [of the matter], there is then no offense; this is not due to reasons such as "not having studied" and so forth.

Therefore, there is no offense. Regarding the three doubts and three instances of non-recognition concerning matters superior [to oneself], these are called "expedient means" (*upāya*), because at the time of recognition, there is a heavy fruit toward which one must proceed.

Regarding the three doubts and three instances of non-recognition concerning offenses superior [to oneself], these constitute the ultimate [offense], because at the time of recognition, there is no such fruit.
If there are matters that can be learned, then the three doubts, the three instances of non-recognition, and the twelve forms of delusion (*moha*) are likewise considered ultimate. Next—

Regarding the explanation of the nine phrases of *śīla-dhāraṇa* (maintaining the precepts): as explained in the section on transgressions, these are called *śīla-dhāraṇa* because one does not commit the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).

Depending on whether the gravity is heavy or light, each phrase has its distinct characteristics; furthermore, regarding the commission of offenses due to conditions, it is explained as before, totaling twelve *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoings).
Because these offenses are subject to training, even if the mind harbors doubt or fails to recognize the matter due to the circumstances, [the offense is determined] by the act itself.

Because this cannot be learned [by mere instruction], the Noble Ones do not establish it as a formal offense (*pācittiya*). If one exceeds the prescribed measure, or if there is doubt or lack of recognition regarding the object, one likewise incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
Next, concerning the two teachings of permission and prohibition, the two offenses and two observances, as well as the single offense and single observance—these combined constitute the "two nines.

First, to explain the cessation of offenses: this refers to the precept regarding dwellings (*āvāsa-sikkhāpada*), specifically the three modes of perception regarding the boundary and the act of non-assignment (*appaṭipucchā*) or assignment (*paṭipucchā*).

The mind regarding the object of the formal act (karmavastu) likewise undergoes three stages of transgression, forming nine propositions. The enumeration of these factors is as previously described; in all cases, one does not obtain a formal disposition (viniścaya) and yet performs the aforementioned action.

Following the three types of minds regarding the object of the formal act, there are three *śeṣa* (saṃghāvaśeṣa) offenses for the superior grade, and for each of the subsequent lower grades, there are three *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses).

These differ in name but are identical in substance. The two categories of transgression—cessation (*virati*) and performance (*karaṇa*)—combine to form nine fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*), consisting of two types of offenses regarding the object and the transgression itself.

The mind is in doubt and fails to recognize [the offense]; thus, both the formal act (*saṃvara*) and the transgression (*āpatti*) are incurred. Therefore, one must double the previous two cases, resulting in a total of twenty-four instances of a transgression of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
That is to say: four *duṣkṛtas* for offenses based on superior conditions; ten *duṣkṛtas* each for the two lower grades of offenses based on objective matters;

and ten *duṣkṛtas* each for the two superior grades of offenses based on objective matters. Next, the two types of observance (*dhāraṇī*) are explained: namely, taking the object with the perception [of it], and the non-designation of the portion (*avibhāga*) versus the designation of the portion (*vibhāga*).

Regarding the perception (*saṃjñā*): that which is not an offense is considered "retention" (*dhāraṇa*). As in the rules for the lower robe (*adhovāsaka*), where the division of receiving [the robe] includes both the successful and unsuccessful cases, there are six phrases.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding the perception of the object, there are many instances of the sixth phrase concerning non-offense.

In the present case of the perception of the object, one proceeds directly to the offense and thus omits this text; yet according to principle, it ought to be present. Therefore, this phrase constitutes "retention. Furthermore, conversely...

If one commits an offense while perceiving it as a formal assignment (*pariṇāmanā*), this is because one clearly perceives it as such. Second, regarding the statement in the section on the two dwellings that there is no offense: it refers to a dwelling formally assigned by the Saṃgha;

yet, if one acts with a mind directed toward a specific object, an offense occurs. Third, combining these three cases, there are nine. The ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) are as previously explained and are discussed within the section on the two types of offenses.

However, because one performs the ritual action by means of having obtained the dharma, these constitute two types of "retention" (dhāraṇī). Thus, there is no offense regarding the fundamental basis. Combined, they form the ninth category.

Regarding the offenses within the "non-learning" [category], they are likewise twenty-four. Furthermore, concerning the objects and the state of mind—namely, the distinctions made regarding the ritual procedures and textual formulas—they differ from the three states of mind associated with the objects of the offenses within the "learning" category, which are explained in terms of whether the act is accomplished or not. Consequently, they are merged into the fundamental category.

There are gradations in the offenses. The distinct categories of *zhi-chi* (abstention from transgression) are also nine, as previously stated; they differ only in that one abstains from the dharma and abstains from the matter. Question:

Since *bu-kexue-zhichi* (non-learner’s abstention from transgression) corresponds to the characteristics of the offense by inversion, why does *zuochi* (active observance) correspond to *zhifan* (abstention from transgression) rather than looking toward the offense itself?
Answer: Each phrase is inverted; taking the phrase "regarding the act of disposal with the perception of disposal," it is divided into nine parts. This is because...

"Reversing 'stopping' results in 'offending. Answer: The preceding section clarified 'stopping and maintaining' (*zhi-chi*). However, merely not performing the fundamental act constitutes its maintenance.

Therefore, based on the reversal of offenses—whether grave or light—one establishes the hierarchy of superior and inferior. If one reverses 'maintaining by performance' (*zuo-chi*) to address 'offending by stopping,' one must establish the maintenance through formal ritual action (*zuo-fa*).

This is the essential point: regarding the location of the act and the perception of that location, these constitute nine categories; only then is offending by stopping eliminated. If [one proceeds] directly..."

Regarding the former [category]: as in the statements "cognizing the dharma," "cognizing the matter," or "cognizing the offense," is this a case of cessation (*virati*) or is it a case of action (*kriyā*)?

Therefore, it does not resemble the former. Furthermore, the distinction between "knowing yet doubting" and "not knowing" in relation to an offense is also not like the former, as has already been explained above.

Next, advancing to the cultivation [of practice] to distinguish between offenses and observances: there are eight types of offenses, which are as stated in the traditional teachings; they are the opposites of the minor category.
Regarding the "Upātta" (appropriated) offense as the superior grade of transgression: first, there are two phrases: not recognizing the matter and doubting/not recognizing the offense.
Next, there are two phrases: doubting the matter and doubting/not recognizing the offense. The middle grade has four [phrases]:
the first two phrases refer to recognizing the matter but doubting/not recognizing the offense; the next two phrases refer to recognizing the offense but doubting the matter.
Regarding consciousness: among the four superior grades, there are sixteen *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoings), and in the next grade, eight offenses. These have no separate fundamental [offenses];
one must take the quantity of the offenses as the basis for their ranking as superior or inferior. This principle should be understood thus. Furthermore, this delusion subsumes the preceding five;
among the nine, the first two are matters that cannot be learned, while the remaining three include the superior objects, the mind of offense, and the matters that can be learned.
Regarding the offenses of the mind: these eight may be understood through reflection. Next, the explanation of the "observance through action" (*karmasamādāna*) follows one principle;
that is, the cognition of the rule, the cognition of the matter, and the cognition of the offense. These are the opposites of the aforementioned "offenses through non-study" and so forth. Question:

Since the two preceding types of observance are the opposites of the offenses, and thus form a set of nine versus nine in their correspondence, why is the progression from one to the opposite of eight? Answer: Because the two preceding offenses differ in degree regarding their fundamental nature.
One must necessarily discuss offenses and observances in pairs. In the present case, this refers only to the offense: one *duṣkṛta* (吉羅) for a single category.

Since one recognizes the matter and acts to maintain [the precept], yet fails to do so completely, there are thus eight [instances] for each single [category]. As in the passage below, where many instances of a single [category] correspond to many non-offenses (*anāpatti*), this is also the same.

Regarding the reason why observance and offense each have their respective "cessation" (*sthiti*) and "action" (*kriyā*), they are discussed in pairs; in all cases, the offense is mentioned first, followed by the observance.

What is this? The answer is as explained in the treatise regarding the maintenance of conduct: one cannot distinguish [the antidote] by itself; it is necessary to cite that which is to be guarded against in order to differentiate the capable remedy.

As in the following section, which clarifies only the transgressions of the law—such as the various perceptions of objects, for instance, perceiving a human as a human, or not having made a formal assignment while perceiving it as not having been assigned—one determines the gravity of the offense, light or heavy.
Having recognized the characteristics of the transgression, one ceases the fault and refrains from committing it, or else one practices in accordance with the teachings.
Only then can it constitute "observance" (dhāraṇa). The essential nature and characteristics of this observance are hidden beneath the texts concerning transgressions;

that is to say, by citing the laws regarding transgressions, one gives rise to conduct that avoids them. Therefore, contemporary commentators follow the sacred teachings, first explaining the nine stages of gradation in relation to transgressions.
Conversely, by committing [the offense], one achieves its observance; thus, each subsequent offense is committed to clarify the nine types of observance.

Having completed the general explanation, we shall next provide a detailed, individual commentary according to the eight textual sections. First, we explain the first section: (1) a general analysis, and (2) an explanation based on the text.
This provides a general explanation of the tenfold classification. First, karma does not arise in isolation; it must be incited by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although afflictions are immeasurable, they do not exceed the three poisons. Therefore, the first four [categories] are assigned to the three poisons to establish the characteristics of an offense.

While the incitement arises from afflictions, the full manifestation necessarily requires the instruments. To discuss these instruments, we refer to body and speech. Thus, the second [category] explains how body and speech constitute an offense.

The actions of body and speech do not exceed those performed by oneself or taught to others; therefore, the sequence follows with first performing them oneself and then teaching others. An action does not complete itself; it must depend upon an object (*viṣaya*).

For this reason, the fourth [category] concerns the breadth or narrowness of the object of transgression. Although the objects of transgression are numerous, none exceed the categories of self and other.

Thus, the fifth [category] concerns whether the object is oneself or another. Even when the objective conditions are fully present, an act is not accomplished without intention (*citta*). Intention...

The intentional (*saṃcetanika*) and the unintentional (*asaṃcetanika*) differ in their intended objectives; they differ in the discrepancy of the objects encountered; and they differ in whether an offense is committed or not. Therefore, sixth, the differences between the intentional and the unintentional are distinguished.

Although there may be an intended objective in the mind, due to discrepancies between the intentional and the unintentional, when one proceeds to act, there may be a divergence in the object or an error in the mind, resulting in either an offense or no offense.
Therefore, seventh, the similarities and differences regarding errors are explained. Eighth, the section on minor offenses (*pāyantikā*).
Spontaneous. Ninth, the establishment of the intention. Next, the tenfold sequence of the remedies for transgressions.

Regarding the statement that they arise from the three poisons: the precept against unchaste conduct arises solely because one regards oneself as the object of affliction; the precept against stealing arises through the three poisons because greed is established therein;

the second precept (against taking what is not given) involves affliction that extends to both loss and gain, and thus it arises through all three matters; finally, the precept against false speech is established through the three matters by means of those same three matters.

Regarding the single precept of speech, it is also considered a fault when one acts for one's own benefit. When lust, delusion, and [the act] arise together, sexual misconduct is committed. Concerning the arising of these three factors, *Śraddhākaravarman* states:
"If one personally delights in practicing unchaste conduct, this is called 'arising from greed. If one commits adultery with the relatives of an enemy, this is called 'arising from hatred.
If one practices unchaste conduct with one's own mother, this is called 'arising from delusion. Furthermore, the object must be one that brings pleasure and satisfaction.

Because it arises from volition, it is accomplished through a mind of greed. Regarding the accomplishment of theft through the three factors: it should be understood that when greed arises, it is accomplished by greed. Śāṇakavāsin says:
"Theft involving enmity, burning, burying, and so forth, is accomplished through anger when anger arises. If one steals from a person of low caste, this is called [theft] arising from delusion.

Furthermore, when Jīvaka and Māmātīka misappropriated the property of the Buddha or the Saṃgha, this was also accomplished through delusion arising. The explanation regarding the accomplishment of killing through the three factors may be stated likewise.
[He] knows that lying is intended to gain profit and that anger is contrary to one's feelings; therefore, there is no mind of hatred. When volition (*cetanā*) arises, it constitutes karma.
Since minor lying logically applies to all three [roots], the treatise generally states that lying encompasses both light and heavy offenses, arising from and completing through all three.

Regarding the two [precepts] of body and speech, they occupy three positions. The precept against sexual misconduct is a violation of the body and not of speech; since the matter is determined by physical union, it is because this cannot be accomplished without the body that it is so.

As for the two precepts against stealing and killing, these are fully established as bodily karma: because stealing consists of lifting and moving an object away from its place, and killing consists of severing the continuity of life, they are violations of bodily karma.
However, whether one acts personally or dispatches another, since both parties accomplish the act, there is also a violation of speech—as in the case of using incantations to harm an object.

Instructing others to commit theft, killing, and so forth constitutes false speech; this is a primary transgression of vocal karma. To manifest to oneself that one has attained the state of an *ārya* in order to seek fame and profit is not merely a matter of failing to speak;
thus, it is a primary transgression of vocal karma. However, composing written works or manifesting signs also falls within the limits of transgression;

therefore, bodily action also constitutes a completion [of the offense]. This is based on the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, these four categories consist of two types, the first three of which...

Regarding bodily offenses: the fourth [precept] involves only speech. Among the three that involve bodily offenses, it should be understood that the precept against sexual misconduct is a bodily offense and not one of speech.

As for the two precepts against stealing and killing, they are definitively offenses of bodily action; however, there is also the sense of "creating" [the offense] through speech, such as when instructing others to enchant objects by incantation, which likewise constitutes both types of offenses.
However, this bodily action is spoken of in terms of instructing others; it has not yet reached the point of transgression because it relies upon another's body.

As for the claim that mental discourse is sovereign—that which the sages of old detested as being the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of verbal and mental karma—is incorrect, because the natures of these karmas differ.
Since the matter is not finalized [by the mind alone], false speech is a verbal karma. To claim oneself to be an *arhat* (a sage) is not a case of failing to proclaim what one says.

That is so. However, there are instances where the body performs actions in conjunction with other faculties, such as when writing characters or manifesting signs; these belong solely to verbal offenses. Thus, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states:

"Verbal karma may involve bodily movement or silence, as in the case of the *poṣadha* ceremony. To claim that these possess the nature of bodily or mental karma is incorrect, because their karmic natures are distinct.

Third, regarding the stages of performing an act oneself or instructing another, there are three categories. Regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, acting for oneself is grave while instructing another is light. When one instructs another to commit a transgression, the pleasure resides with the other person;
since it does not personally affect me, the person who can so instruct is not considered grave. For those who have left the household life, they ought to exhort others to cultivate goodness;

yet, instead, they further assist in evil, and thus the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Regarding the two precepts against stealing and killing, the affliction applies equally whether the act results in harm or benefit when performed by oneself.

There is no difference between instructing others to damage the objective sphere (viṣaya) and doing so oneself; the intent is likewise identical. Therefore, whether one acts for oneself or instructs another, both the self and the other are equally guilty.

Regarding false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), acting for oneself constitutes a formal offense (*maulāpatti*). As for instructing another, it may be either the same or different. If one dispatches another to claim for oneself that one has attained holiness (*āryatva*), it is equivalent to acting for oneself because the fame and profit are held by oneself;
thus, one incurs the same offense. However, the person instructed incurs a lighter offense. If one simply instructs another to [act] for themselves...

[The term] "稱" (chēng) [is used]. To attract benefit and protect others [while] providing no moisture for oneself, one merely commits a *duṣkṛta* offense (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*). This is explained specifically regarding the first category of precepts (*ādi-pārājika*). If we discuss this broadly:

when one values oneself and treats the teaching lightly, the first precept involves self-deprecation while the teaching is heavy; the nun’s offense of emission toward a monk involves both self and other being heavy;
stealing, killing, and damaging objects, as well as all cases of joint commission, involve both self and other being light. This is sufficient.
This is the exhortation regarding the feet. If one explains whether an offense has been committed or not, it can likewise be understood through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

If explained according to the agent and the object, two sets of four permutations can also be understood. Question: What is the difference between these meanings of self, other, agent, and object? Answer:

"Self" and "other" do not refer to the actions of the seven classes of disciples who are being instructed; rather, they take up the action of the instructor and distinguish it in relation to the act performed by oneself. If...

Regarding the terms "agent" and "object": by means of the act of teaching (the agent), one compares and evaluates [the offense] in the presence of the fivefold assembly of those being taught who possess the transgression.

There are two stages concerning the breadth or narrowness of the objective sphere (*gocara*) for the four offenses. The precept against sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*) encompasses the objective spheres of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*);

therefore, it is called "broad. The remaining three are restricted to the human realm and are therefore "narrow. This is because the nature of lustful desire flows with the emotions and escapes inwardly; thus, the defiled mind becomes heavy and thick.

In discerning the beauty or foulness of an object, who asks whether it is human or animal? It is sufficient that the right path be followed; thus, there is no distinction in the application of thought.

Therefore, regarding offenses involving the three lower realms, they are governed by the nature of the path itself. Furthermore, since the precepts are not formulated based on the impairment of the object, how could one calculate distinctions of superiority or inferiority among objects?
For what impairment can there be in one who commits an offense against a corpse? As for the last three precepts, their transgressions arise from external factors.

The degree of harm depends on the object before one; as the realms differ, the retribution varies. Whether the increase or decrease is slight or significant, it reflects the gradations of the intention. Thus, when a person commits an offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), it is lighter in other realms.

As for why theft is said to be grave [in the human realm], it is truly because the causes of goodness in the human realm yield superior retribution, and the sentiment of attachment and protection is strong.

When the mind is intensely distressed and heavy, one commits a *pārājika* offense through theft; this is because the retribution is not inferior to that of animals, and the mind lacks awareness of guarding and attachment.

When the mind is subtly distressed and shallow, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Question: The various devas dwelling on earth possess retribution superior to that of humans; therefore, why does stealing from them result only in a *sthūlātyaya* offense? Answer:

Although the retribution of the devas is superior, their realm is distinct and distant, and the scriptural definitions regarding them are sparse. Furthermore, their emotional attachment to material objects is slight.

The harm and affliction are not grave. Furthermore, as for celestial objects, humans have no need for them; for these reasons, they are considered light. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Stealing from the three continents constitutes a grave offense, whereas stealing from the people and things of the northern continent does not constitute a grave offense. This is because the people of that land lack the notion of 'mine' regarding material objects.
Since humans here are different, the precept establishes the commission of a *pārājika* offense. Regarding the precept against killing, humans are grave while others are light."

This person is a vessel for the Path. To kill them now would be to damage a vessel for the Path; therefore, it is grave. Beings in other realms receive inferior retribution, and their forms are not vessels for the Path;
thus, damaging them constitutes a minor offense. Although gods possess superior retribution, they lack the Prātimokṣa and are thus not vessels for the Path;

furthermore, the sense of "killing" is rare among them, so killing a god also constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Question: Since the distinction between realms is rare and the sense of "killing" is rare for gods, [what of killing a god?]

Question: Why is it that committing a sexual transgression with a celestial maiden (devī) is as grave as doing so with a human being? Answer: Although the celestial realm is distinct [from the human], the nature of passionate attachment is no different;

one does not discriminate between the beauty or ugliness of the object. There are instances where a lower being approaches a superior one, and such cases occur more frequently than those involving theft or killing;
therefore, they are treated identically. Regarding lying, humans are grave while other realms are light. Generally speaking, when discussing lying, it refers to falsely proclaiming one's own virtues.
To manifest one's name for the sake of attracting profit and to deceive one's own kind is contrary to the principles of righteousness;

thus, it is rarely in accord with the mind of Heaven or other classes of beings, and even if it were so, such instances would be rare. Therefore, this constitutes only a minor offense. Furthermore, the cultivation and realization of the Path occurs precisely within the human realm.

If one speaks truthful words, there may be gradual stages through which one can achieve their own purpose; however, being deceived now causes that intention to be ruined and disordered, resulting in the loss of benefit.

Because one dwells in a profound state, committing such an act constitutes a *pārājika* offense; for an animal, speaking the truth yields but slight benefit. Now, although deception causes harm, it is not grave; therefore, it is merely a *sthūlātyaya* or *duṣkṛta*.
Although the heavens possess superior retribution, they are not vessels for the Path. Their retributive merit and their knowledge of others' minds are further mixed with other realms of existence;

being rare and lacking in faith, they too incur light offenses. Question: If a celestial being possesses the knowledge of others' minds yet deceives them, lacking integrity and faith, does this constitute an offense?

Regarding those whose offenses are light: what offense does one incur against the Buddha? Answer: Deceiving the Buddha incurs a *pārājika* (defeat) offense. If that is so, then [deceiving] a deva should also be grave. Answer:

A deva lacks trustworthiness (*śraddhā*), and because they belong to a different realm (*gati*), such an act is rare; therefore, a light offense is incurred. Although the Buddha lacks trust, he belongs to the same realm and such acts occur frequently;

since he hears and knows at that very moment, a grave *pārājika* offense is incurred. This is not the same as killing the Buddha, because his life has not yet been severed. Furthermore, it is explained that the Buddha lacks trustworthiness.

If one deceives [the Buddha], one incurs only a light offense. If that is so, since the Buddha is free from fear, it stands to reason that the offense would be light; why then would one fear the Buddha? [Yet] both cases result in the same *pāyattika* offense. Answer:

The Buddha is indeed free from fear, and thus the offense for deception is the same as a light one. However, it is precisely by virtue of fearing the Buddha that this serves as the occasion (*nidāna*) for the establishment of the precept.

Furthermore, it may be feared that the Buddha is equal to ordinary persons in incurring a *pāyattika* offense for the same transgression. Why is this so? Because when the Buddha was traveling, he instead gave rise to anger; this immediately constituted a formal disturbance (*vastu-kleśa*).
Since he incurred the offense based on the frequency of such disturbances, he received a *pāyattika*. Deceiving others out of fear of fame and profit arises from a deliberate state of mind;

moreover, the sense of deceiving the Buddha is rare, and thus a lighter offense is incurred. Question: If the Buddha has no expectations, yet incurs a *pāyattika* even when there is expectation, [how does this differ from] the Noble One?

The Saṃgha cannot be split; even to attempt to split it constitutes a transgression against the Dharma (ānantarya). Answer: The Noble Ones (ārya) cannot be split. Therefore, by attempting to split the Saṃgha of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), one prevents them from attaining the state of a Noble One and incurs the sin of a transgression.
Although the Buddha has no expectations [regarding the laity], he was aware of what was happening at that time; thus, this is likewise classified as a *thullaccaya* offense.

If that is so, since the sphere of a Noble Nun (*āryabhikṣuṇī*) cannot be destroyed, would it not follow that violating her would not be difficult? Answer: Although the objective sphere is not destroyed, the karma of arrogance and contempt is nonetheless established, resulting in defilement and disgrace.
Superficial. Regarding the breaking of the Saṃgha, it is said that this involves taking [others] as followers; since the Noble Ones have no followers, the two cases are not analogous. Question:

Stealing from or deceiving animals both incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, yet why does intentionally killing an animal incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense? Answer: Because the former two [cases] involve those with greater intelligence.

Regarding wealth and life, animals have little understanding; because their attachment to karmic retribution is heavy, they incur a *pāyantika* offense. Because their intent to preserve wealth is slight, stealing from or deceiving them constitutes only a *dukkaṭa*.

According to this principle, when the object is a human, all four matters constitute the stage of a *pārājika* offense; for non-humans, the four matters may result in either a *pārājika* or a *pāyantika* offense.
For animals, there are four stages: namely, *pārājika*, *pāyantika*, *dukkaṭa*, and [the fourth].

Fifth, regarding the two categories of one’s own and another’s state: the precept against impure conduct involves transgression through the objects of both oneself and others, as in the case of those with weak spines and the like.

As for the [remaining] three lower precepts, they necessarily involve the objects of others. Theft is grave because it causes harm to the owner; since there is no separate object to be harmed in self-theft, the Noble Ones did not establish such a rule.
Question: Why does one incur a *duṣkṛta* offense for stealing one's own garment? Answer: Because the other's garment and one's own garment are together in the same place.

In one instance, intending to take another’s robe, one mistakenly obtains one’s own robe. With the expectation focused on the other’s robe, there is a discrepancy in the object (*ālambana*), yet a transgression (*āpatti*) occurs because the act was performed upon one's own robe.

Since the transgression arises despite the discrepancy in the object, it is called "one's own robe as the locus of the transgression" (*svavastra-āpatti*). However, there is no offense regarding one's own robe, for it can be understood that one’s own generosity or stinginess would constitute an obstruction.

Killing another constitutes a violation of the precepts; thus, it becomes a transgressive object. Killing oneself does not constitute a violation of the precepts; therefore, it is not [a transgression].
Regarding the objects of transgression: if one intends to deceive in order to seek profit, why need one deceive oneself?
Sixth, regarding specific versus general distinctions: if viewed in light of the first precept, both specific and general [intentions] constitute a transgression.

For the latter three precepts, according to their broad scope, the gravity of the offense is determined by the object within the three realms of existence. If, however, the intent is specifically directed toward [a particular object], these three precepts are each designated as follows:

If the object constitutes a *pārājika* offense, yet the object is mistaken, the three precepts involve a "mistaken object" (*viṣaya-viparyāsa*). Regarding different objects: if one mistakes a member of the same realm of existence for another, it is an offense of error;
if one mistakes a non-human being for another, it is a simple omission with no offense; if both are omitted, one merely commits a light offense.
If one mistakes an insentient, ownerless thing for another, there is no offense whether one or both are omitted. Since the object is already...

Thus it is. To explain in detail would be immeasurable. If one distinguishes between the specific and the general: this refers to when the intention is directed toward the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*), provided that the identity of the king is not excluded;
this is the case. If viewed from the perspective of the same realm, both the specific and the general constitute a *pārājika* offense.

If non-animals are treated as a different object, the first half [of the verse] lacks the primary factor, and since the object is neither specific nor general, there is no offense. In the second half, both factors are lacking; therefore, both the specific and the general constitute a light offense. If it is not...
When the mind lacks a specific intent and the object is an inanimate thing, there is no offense whether the action is deliberate or accidental.

As it is with one category, so it is with others, including non-human animals. Seventh, regarding "error": generally speaking, "error" refers to that which is mistaken, erroneous, or improper. If one were to follow each specific case...

Investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) are difficult to distinguish from one another. If one attempts to define them by following their names, there may be some confusion; yet, regarding their objects, they differ according to the mind’s delusion or its ordinariness.

When two objects are present before one, their distinct characteristics are clearly apparent; however, when it comes to mental engagement and the accomplishment of an action, a discrepancy may arise. The intermingling of these two objects is termed "borrowing" (*jia*).
If one takes what is perceived as being something else, such that the mental conception is false and erroneous, this is called "mistake" (*wu*).

Since errors have already been categorized, they must be applied to the four precepts, which are thus divided into four positions. First, two cases are paired: the precept against sexual misconduct is committed through both error and intentional transgression.

This is because the affliction arises from internal emotion; provided one follows the correct path, the resulting satisfaction is no different [from the intentional act], and one does not entertain other thoughts.

Therefore, this constitutes an erroneous offense. The text states: "If one doubts it is the path while perceiving it as the path, it is likewise a pārājika offense. Furthermore, this does not distinguish between the three realms of existence.

Even if there is an interaction [with the object], one must simply follow the correct path; even an error constitutes a grave offense. Second, regarding "error" (*viparyāsa*) in relation to the three precepts: in all three precepts, it is grave.
This is because an error cannot be of two kinds simultaneously, and in neither case can it be called "unintentional. Therefore, an error constitutes an offense in both instances. As the text says:

"If one perceives a male and steals from, kills, or deceives a female, the Buddha declared it a *pārājika* offense. Third, regarding "mistake" (*bhrānti*) in relation to the three precepts: in all three precepts, it is...

There is no offense, because one was aiming at another object and had no original intention [to lie]. This is like the case of causing an abortion; thus it is known. Fourth, regarding errors in relation to lying:
when there is an error in what is being designated, neither constitutes an offense. For example, one intends to designate someone as "holy" (ārya) but mistakenly says "ordinary" (pṛthagjana);

or one mistakenly designates a non-object [of praise], such as a person of overweening pride who, being deluded, calls an ordinary person "holy. Because the mind is mistaken and lacks skill, there is no offense.
There is no offense.
Eighth, regarding the lower assembly acting spontaneously: as when one was a śrāmaṇera, one instructed another to kill or steal, or claimed for oneself to be an arhat;

after having given these instructions, that person subsequently carried out the original commands, thereby acquiring wealth or ending a life, and deceived the former [teacher] into believing it had been done. This constitutes the ability to instruct.
Regarding a śrāmaṇera, among the three natures (trividha-svabhāva), he may spontaneously commit the three pārājika offenses.
If he speaks of performing unwholesome acts himself, his nature may be wholesome or neutral, with no fixed sequence; his own karma likewise permeates all three natures.

If the precepts have not yet been fully received when the instructed act is completed, it constitutes a pārājika offense (antimā āpatti), and the category of the precepts does not arise. If the desire for ordination has been accepted and the instructed act is completed, it is an offense.
One incurs both [offenses] simultaneously because the causes for the wholesome [precepts] are fulfilled while the unwholesome karma is accomplished. Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When one has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), taking a person who has not yet received full ordination to a secluded place constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). In the next case, when a person who has not yet received full ordination takes one who has received it to a secluded place, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

In the next case, when one who has received full ordination goes to a secluded place, it is a *pārājika* (defeat). When one employs the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) at the time of receiving full ordination, there are two types of taking."

A single phrase states: "One *pārājika* for stealing after having received full ordination; one *pārājika* for taking [an object] from a non-ordained person who has moved it to another location after having received full ordination.
Based on this text, we know that there is spontaneous transgression (*anābhoga*). Regarding sexual misconduct, there is nothing further to be known.
The ninth section: The sequence of establishing the intent. Question: Although the characteristics of the precepts are numerous, for what reason were four established?
Answer: It is for the sake of severing the three poisons. Ānanda spoke to the Peacock King, saying:
