Regarding the taking of life: if one stands, one must not kill; if the recipient of the instruction stands, then killing at that time is also without fault, because there was no intention to kill toward the person standing.
However, regarding the person who has sat down, if one employs the means [to kill them], it constitutes a grave offense if done with a general intent (*mañcitta*).

As for the instigator, they have not committed a grave offense at the outset, nor do they commit one in the interim, but only a light one. This is because, in regard to the act of killing, they are neither the instructor of the action nor the agent of the action, as they did not personally perform it.
In the case of successive intermediaries, all incur heavy [karmic] results, because both the instructor and the instructed have completed the action. The rest may be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, there are three types of light and heavy [results]: first, the retribution of the person; second, the retribution of those below the rank of deva-sons; and third, the perception of the object. Regarding the perception of the object—

The middle section consists of a fourfold analysis: first, explaining the necessity of the object, perception, and intention; second, a general clarification of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*); third, distinguishing between existence and non-existence;
and fourth, determining their quantity. However, an offense does not arise in isolation; it must necessarily rely upon an object and engage the mind to constitute the karmic act.

Objects possess degrees of excellence or inferiority, and correctness or error; the mind possesses degrees of intensity or weakness, and accuracy or delusion. When the object and the mind correspond, the offense is complete.

In the first category, karma may be either light or heavy. This occurs when the mind does not accord with the object—such as perceiving a human as a non-human or being in doubt—or when the object does not correspond to the mind—such as perceiving a non-human as a human or being in doubt.
Furthermore, there are cases where the object is transgressed while the mind is not, such as perceiving what has an owner as ownerless;

and cases where the mind is transgressed while the object is not, such as perceiving what is ownerless as having an owner. Because of these distinctions, it is clear that both the object and the perception must be examined.
The stages of karmic action are established through the four categories of transgression and so forth; such is the case because of consciousness and perception.

Second, the general clarification of the stages of the objective sphere consists of five aspects: first, internal retribution; second, external objects; third, phenomena (*dharma*); fourth, time; [and fifth, space].

Regarding the five offenses, there is a distinction in their internal retribution, namely that they pertain to humans and devas, but not to animals. If all four conditions are met simultaneously, as in the case of the first precept;

or if they occur individually with varying degrees of gravity, such as in the cases of theft, killing, and so forth. Furthermore, among humans, there is a distinction between the laity and the ordained. For the laity, examples include selling goods or possessing treasure while eating at home;

for the ordained, examples include slandering, concealing, speaking [of others' faults], striking, threatening, harboring doubts, and storing [excess provisions]. These apply to both the ordained and the laity.

As for these, they are like the two cases of sexual contact with two coarse [women], and so forth. However, regarding the internal and external within the path: the external is restricted to food and clothing; the internal is like the two types of disparagement.

Moreover, regarding the retribution of the physical form, one must be careful according to the specific *thullaccaya* (grave offense) rules. This concerns a bhikṣu traveling on the same road, or a bhikṣuṇī traveling by boat, or being preoccupied solely with matters of food and praise.
Regarding the community of nuns, as with the offenses of slander and concealment, the meaning applies to both communities; the rest may be understood accordingly.

Therefore, the original [classification] was based on confusion regarding the four or five cases. If one follows this principle, there are furthermore three positions regarding what constitutes a transgression and what does not, as detailed above in the section on gravity.
Regarding the light [offense], it corresponds to the five [categories] of the fundamental dhyāna; because one has advanced toward non-offense, it thus constitutes four or five.
As for "now, offense or non-offense," this refers to the section on the precept against stealing where it is said to be "four or five.

Now, regarding "receding into offense," when confronting the two objects—human and animal property—if the perception shifts and becomes confused, both cases of five also constitute three positions. Thus, these two pairs are logically equal, yet they are explained elaborately in the text, namely:
Regarding acts such as killing, the gravity depends on the severity [of the offense]; regarding theft, it depends on whether an offense was committed or not, and thus there are variations in degree.

Furthermore, this refers to the existence of light and heavy grades within the category of offenses, as previously discussed. For instance, in cases such as ordering the digging of the earth or encouraging [others] at an improper time, the offenses within this category are immeasurable.

In the case of the light [perception], there are either four or five; the rest may be understood by analogy. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent explanation provided above, these cases can be understood as applying to both the original object (*mūla-viṣaya*) and the different object (*anya-viṣaya*).
Therefore, it is said that they are "definitely five" or "either four or five. If one relies on the original object, the four are equal; this is because the four refer to the original delusion.
As for the five, they are all five, because the perception (*saṃjñā*) has shifted. However, the text is situated in the discussion of their function.
Regarding these offenses and the like, they may be understood by analogy according to the specific object (*ālambana*) and the perception (*saṃjñā*).

The subsequent explanation of the text follows the usual pattern. These five constitute five stages; alternatively, one may possess all four [factors] while another lacks them, forming four pairs in contrast.
In the first case, both the object and the mind are grave; in the next two, the object is grave while the mind is light; in the next, the object is light while the mind is grave; and in the final...

First, both are light. Furthermore, the next four cases involve three combinations: the perception of a human or non-human being, doubt, a discrepancy in the mind, and the preparatory effort regarding the object;

next, one case involves a discrepancy in the object and the preparatory effort regarding the mind; and next, one case involves a discrepancy in both the mind and the object regarding the preparatory effort.
The Fourth Precept: Falsely Claiming to Have Attained Superhuman Qualities.
I. General Explanation of False Speech. II. Specific Explanation of Great Falsehood. There are five general sections: 1. The person who commits false speech.

Second, regarding the false speech of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), there are five successive stages: (1) the object and the mind being either false or true; (2) the limits for the determination of the offense; (3) the presence or absence of one's own admission; (4) [the nature of the offense]; and (5) [the gravity of the offense].

First, I shall explain the initial gate. It is said that the Noble Ones (*ārya*) cultivate the Path and advance in virtue, realizing and attesting to reality, thereby severing all falsehood and delusion.
These are all products of crafty fabrication and superficial exposition. If one speaks according to reality, how could there be any false speech?

As for the Great Sage, his quiescence is constant and active; such matters are beyond the scope of logical discourse. Nevertheless, even the Śrāvaka sages possess rational contemplation prior to meditative concentration.
While in a state of skillful means, he heard the sound of an elephant king entering the pond water and described it to the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus asked: "How could this be?"

While entering the two meditative absorptions of emptiness, Maudgalyāyana heard the sound of an elephant king entering the water. He falsely claimed to have attained the superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma) of those superior practitioners.

The Buddha said: "There was such a state, yet that absorption was not pure. Maudgalyāyana has committed no offense. This refers to the case where one understands through skillful means, conceives the thought [of attainment], yet speaks the truth.
Nor is there the fault of falsehood. This is because ordinary persons lack those two kinds of true speech possessed by such individuals; thus, their utterances constitute falsehood.

However, ordinary persons also possess true speech regarding actual facts. For example, when one experiences suffering or pleasure through bodily sensation and speaks based solely on that reality, it likewise constitutes true speech.

However, this is not an understanding [of the truth]. One has not yet been able to sever that mind of false conceptualization, and because it contradicts one's perception and turns away from the heart, it still constitutes false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), even when there is a basis in fact.
If one perceives something as auspicious and speaks of it as auspicious, there is no fault of falsehood.

Yet, this is not the conceptualization of skillful means through understanding; such [conceptualization] cannot sever falsehood. To speak while contradicting one's perception constitutes false speech. Therefore...
False speech concerns only ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, regarding the question of which of the first three precepts do not necessarily involve an offense for such persons:

the answer is that as for the first three precepts, they concern ordinary persons without doubt, and thus it is unnecessary to specify them definitively. However, the "Dharma" mentioned here refers to the Noble Dharma (*āryadharma*), by means of which an offense is established.

Therefore, it is necessary to specify that these apply to ordinary persons and not to Noble Ones. Moreover, because Maudgalyāyana’s statement was ambiguous, it was necessary to distinguish and define them clearly.

The second section consists of a fourfold analysis. First, the enumeration, the explanation of the names, and the textual basis are presented. Since the meditative concentration relies on the lower stages, there is an increase of four;

however, among the four types of false speech, the *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) for lying is absent. If one includes [cases such as] deceiving non-humans, transforming into an animal, or other deficiencies in the conditions, these are all *sādhika-duṣkṛta* (incomplete offenses).
When fully accounted for, they constitute five distinct categories. If one follows the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the five types of false speech are clearly explained in detail.
Therefore, the tenth is "incomplete pārājika or thullaccaya. This is a *dukkaṭa* (light offense) for lying. According to the text, there are five types;
regarding these five types of lies: first, lying concerning a *pārājika*; second, lying concerning a *saṃghādisesa*; third, a *thullaccaya*; fourth, a *pācittiya*; and fifth, a *dukkaṭa* lie.

These terms, such as "lying concerning a *pārājika*" and so forth, refer to designating the lie by the name of the offense incurred; they do not mean that one is referring to the five categories of offenses, such as the *pārājikas*, themselves.

Regarding "by whom" and "the preceding object": the second [section] distinguishes between noble and ordinary persons based on the dharmas designated; as for the stages, they are divided into three. Regarding the first pārājika, lying:
one incurs an offense by deceiving others using supramundane dharmas. However, since this ordinary person has not yet truly engaged with supramundane dharmas, they falsely claim them as their own.
By deceiving others regarding such objects to scheme for fame and profit, the harm is grave and the transgression is deep. Therefore...
One incurs a *pārājika* offense. The second [offense] is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. These two offenses are identical in that, by means of worldly methods, one deceives others;

though there are in fact no three bases [for the accusation], one falsely fabricates empty appearances. By using such grave matters to deceive the Saṃgha, one seeks to cause them to view the offender as guilty and to expel him, thereby tormenting the other for a lifetime.
Since this transgression is not slight, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Alternatively, one may defame another with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* to damage someone who has committed a minor offense, or violate...
To speak while contradicting what one has seen or heard constitutes a *pācittiya*. The third [offense], a *dukkaṭa*, concerns the two types of falsely claimed dharmas, both mundane and supramundane:
namely, when claiming a lower-grade *mahā-dukkaṭa* (great falsehood), one cites the dharmas of the Noble Ones; whereas for a lower-grade *dukkaṭa*, one cites the dharmas of ordinary persons.
In this context, the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) involves citing the dharmas of the Noble Ones, while the remaining *dukkaṭas* concern ordinary persons; such is the distinction.

Third, regarding the objects deceived, there are two stages concerning the breadth or narrowness of the three realms of existence (*gati*): namely, the *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *sthūlātyaya* offenses all share the same object of deception—the person—but they differ in the specific matter claimed.
Consequently, the three stages descend from *duṣkṛta* to *sthūlātyaya*. Second, false speech generally deceives beings in all three realms, because both the matter claimed and the object differ.
Fourth, regarding the detailed classification of the matter, it is either fully subsumed or not. Question: If it is as previously stated...
Delusion is of many kinds; why then are there only five? The answer is: by subsuming them under their respective categories, delusion is exhausted without exception.
It is like when one speaks of "orchids," all orchids are thereby subsumed; the same applies to "magnolia. Therefore, there are only five types of delusion.
Third, regarding the false and the real, there are likewise three stages. In the *ai-wang* (delusion of the equal) category, both mind and object are false.

In the *can-ti* (delusion of the remainder) category, regardless of whether the object is real or false, only the subjective mind is false. The meaning of the *lan-ji* (delusion of the offense) category is the same as the preceding two. First, to explain the *ai-wang*:

that which must be both [mind and object] false is such that, if the object were real, then even if one skillfully practiced its elimination and severance, there would be no falsity of the mind. If...
The object is false while the mind is real; for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the Noble Ones have opened an allowance so that there is no offense.

If both the object and the mind are real, one does not violate this precept—this refers to one who has truly attained the Path. Therefore, it should be known that it is only when both the object and the mind are false that one commits this offense.

To say "the object is false" means that one has not actually attained the state of a Noble One. To say "the mind is false" means that one knows one has not attained the state of a Noble One. Why is it said to be "false" in terms of expectation?

"Real" means that when one raises up an object, the mind does not correspond to what is spoken with the mouth; these two are considered false. Regarding the two types of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses involving falsehood, the objects are merely matters that pertain to both the internal and external;
it is not the case that they do not exist within the Noble Dharma. Question: Regarding the reality or unreality of an object, if the mind is merely false, does this always constitute lying?
Answer: There are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). When both [the object and the mind] are false, and that person is impure, this constitutes the object.

The sincere mind and the false [mind]: these two constitute an offense. There are cases where one cannot escape [the charge] despite having a non-deceptive mind; this is a case where the object is false but the mind is sincere.
When the three factors—the seeing, the faculty, and so forth—involve both object and mind being real, this constitutes the formal accusation of an offense.

These two [latter cases] do not constitute an offense. This is analyzed according to four permutations; thus, the first two are offenses, while the latter two are not. The principles for *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pāyattika* are the same. Regarding the offenses within the first two permutations, they are further distinguished:

There are six states of mind. Regarding the similarities and differences between minor falsehoods (*mṛṣāvāda*) [and other offenses]: in the first, third, and fifth [of these six] states of mind for minor falsehoods, both the object and the mind are false.

In the second, fourth, and sixth, the object is real while the mind is false. In the case of slander (*paiśunya*), all six states of mind are diminished; this is because both the object and the mind have reached their respective conditions.

Although there may be matters of transgression or non-transgression regarding the object, from my perspective, since the three roots [of greed, hatred, and delusion] are absent, the object is false. Furthermore, because one knows that the three roots are absent, the mind is also false. Thus, it causes [the offense to be classified as such].

This differs from minor false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). Since the two laws of *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* apply to both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*), if one deceives regarding the qualities of a noble one, it is equivalent to a *pārājika* offense;
if one refers to the qualities of an ordinary person, it is equivalent to a *sthūlātyaya*. In these cases, it is solely a matter of mental falsehood.

The fourth section concerns the limits for the determination of offenses. Since lying is fundamentally intended to deceive others so that they may develop faith, an offense is incurred as soon as the person understands the words;
it does not wait for them to actually believe before the offense is established. What is the meaning of this? Answer: The characteristics of faith are difficult to discern.

Furthermore, the limits for determining an offense pertain to the vocal karma (*vākkarman*), which consists of being heard and understood. Faith, however, resides in the mental state of the other party and is not something produced by vocal karma. How, then, could the offense depend upon faith?

Just as with the six types of suspicion and fear, or two-sided slander and disparagement, none of these require the presence of discord, separation, or distress; this case is likewise so, and there is no need for further difficulty.

Fifth, regarding the presence or absence of a self-accusation: speaking in terms of principle, there are cases where a self-accusation exists, such as the *prātimokṣa-vinaya* (the Vinaya of Self-Accusation). Furthermore...
Regarding all precepts, questions are always posed by means of self-accusation (*svavacana*). As for why this particular precept uniquely requires self-accusation, there are many explanations;

here, I shall provide one interpretation based on two reasons. First, it must involve self-accusation because the offense is so grave that it destroys the community (*saṃgha*), and thus the community must administer the disciplinary treatment. Second, [it requires self-accusation] because... [the second reason follows].
This is like the case where the concealment (*paticchādana*) of monks and nuns differs; it is difficult to know whether these two are false or true because they pertain to internal realization.
If one does not speak of it oneself, the matter is likewise difficult to know. Because these two conditions are present, there is "speaking for oneself" (*sabhāvacanīya*).

When the community entrusts the matter to one's own words, the application of disciplinary punishment (*daṇḍa*) becomes easy. The same applies to slander (*ābhyākhyāna*): some cases are difficult to discern yet do not constitute a schism in the Saṃgha, such as minor falsehoods (*mṛṣāvāda*), while others do.

Those who cause schism in the community are not difficult to identify; these are the remaining *pārājika* offenses. Those who are neither difficult to identify nor those who cause schism are the remaining *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and so forth.

Only this [offense] and slander possess both of these two characteristics; therefore, there is the "self-accusation" (*svavacana*). Furthermore, another explanation states that self-accusation is of two kinds:

first, self-accusation upon being questioned, which exists among the various *pārājikas*; second, within this present precept, there is self-accusation of an offense even without being questioned. Thus it is said.

Because it is conditioned by existence (*bhava*), it is cited as the root of the precepts. As with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), there is indeed the actual attainment of the Path through great falsehood.

Question: This and that are not present in the text; even excluding dreams, it is likewise so. It may be different, yet for this reason it is stated again: "If one asks. These are raised because they are relative to one another.
However, these self-accusations are intended to ensure that the community knows how to administer punishment for self-accusation; thus they have come forth.

Regarding the phrase "this text states that there is": this refers to using what follows to overturn what precedes it, thereby directing the focus toward the gravity of the offense. Within the context of slander, one speaks of oneself; in the case of *Spaṭāpā* (Dharmadinnā), one clears [the charge] by means of purity.
In the case of concealment (*paryuṣita*), one acts as the cause for bringing it to light. Because there is such a distinction in meaning, it is necessary to speak of oneself.
The second specific explanation concerns the precept against great falsehood. The untainted True Path is a dharma realized by the noble ones;
it is not something that can be attained by ordinary people through the defilements of their obstructions.

Because they have not yet attained it, those who indulge in empty talk and claim for themselves that they have realized it—whether to disturb the minds of the multitude, to deceive the world, or to seek fame and profit for their own benefit—when they speak of the Dharma, [their words are like] a net [trapping them]. At that time, within [their hearts...]
Because of its gravity, it requires the prohibitions of the Sage. Second, regarding the explanation of the names: speech that does not accord with reality is called "false" (*mṛṣā*).

To falsely proclaim the virtues of a Sage, such that the matter transcends the realm of ordinary beings, is therefore called "a dharma beyond humans" (*uttarimanussadhamma*). This is what is to be guarded against; the precept (*śīla*) is the practice that serves as the remedy.

Since both the object (the false claim) and the subject (the remedial practice) are mentioned together, it is termed "falsely claiming. This term thus encompasses the person, the dharma, and the precept. Question: Why is it not said to encompass [all three] explicitly?

Regarding the "Dharma of the Devas," the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: The Buddha established the precepts among human beings; humans possess the *Prātimokṣa*, and many enter the Path and extensively cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Because they surpass the devas, it is sufficient that those who surpass humans exceed the devas. Furthermore, it says that only those who surpass humans incur grave offenses;
therefore, there is no discussion regarding the devas.
The third [offense] possesses three factors as mentioned above. There are eight distinct conditions: first, the object is a human; second, the marks of a human; third, the object is unreal;
fourth, knowing the object is unreal; fifth, claiming superhuman dharmas; sixth, declaring for oneself that one has attained them; seventh, the speech is articulate and clear.

Regarding the eight [factors] known and understood by the person before, there may be those who further add the intention to deceive others; this interpretation may be acceptable. The preceding eight are sufficient.

Regarding the four factors that lack the sense of conditions: if the first condition is lacking, three *pārājika* offenses may occur, or as some say, six *pārājika* offenses; these may also occur individually.

In both cases, two factors are missing. In each instance, there are nineteen *sthūlātyaya* offenses; since the second and sixth *sthūlātyaya* factors are missing, and there are three instances of doubt regarding the characteristics [of the offense], three factors are thus missing.

Regarding the object: if one treats a non-existent object as existent, there may be a *duṣkṛta* offense, or there may be no offense at all; thus, four factors are missing. For one who acts out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), there is currently no offense; thus, five factors are missing.

If one performs what is not the practice of a universal person (*sarvaga-pudgala*), it is possible that there is no fault, or it is possible that a *sthūlātyaya* is incurred; thus, six factors are missing. If one acts... [incomplete].

If one claims for oneself that one has attained realization, there is either no offense or one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). This excludes seven minor *sthūlātyayas* and excludes eight major *sthūlātyayas*.
Within this, the seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*) are fully present.

Regarding the preceding section on the origin of the precept (*nidāna*), there are two parts: first, the clarification of the arising of the transgression; second, the sixfold reprimand by the other bhikṣus. The former part further divides into two:
first, up to the phrase "not regarding food and drink as a hardship," which concerns the conditions for the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) of an offense;

second, from "At that time, Bhagu... onwards, which concerns false speech according to one's thoughts. The former of these two parts further divides into three: first, the dwelling place of the Tathāgata; second, from "At that time" onwards...

Dispersing from the assembly; false speech distances one from conditions. The text has three parts: First, at the time when those honored by the world [dispersed], this is the condition for the division of the assembly.

Second, at the time when the World-Honored One descended to address the assembly according to conditions, the phrase "those who were like the Upādhyāya" likely reflects the compilers of the collection reversing the order of names from previous events.
The meaning of "abandoning the Upādhyāya," etc., is likewise the same. Third, from the passage beginning "at that time, the bhikṣus... as follows.
The instruction on dispersal: when there are many [people] during the three periods [of time], one reflects and calculates silently.

Regarding the proximate conditions for false speech, there are two parts: first, devising the expedient means; second, from "immediately thinking" onwards, clearly explaining the devising of the plan.

In the second section, the actual text on false speech has four parts: first, manifesting what one has obtained oneself; second, making others' gains obvious; third, being crafty regarding profit and fame; fourth, receiving [the reward].
Benefiting the body, its physical strength becomes full and joyful.
In the second section, the "Reproach," there are two parts: first, up to the phrase "or perhaps no real [person] has come," which explains the cause for the awakening;

second, from "He addressed the bhikṣus" onwards, which formally manifests the reproach. Within the former part, there are two sections: first, the act of paying respects with truthful words, which serves to manifest the awakening. Text.
Three points are to be understood. Second, regarding the monk who spoke falsely, he revealed and made it known. This section has four parts.

First, from "After the rainy season retreat, he paid homage to the World-Honored One" onwards, there are three textual units, each consisting of a question and answer. As for the fourth unit, it concerns the inquiry arising from the statement of renunciation;

it correctly reveals that what was obtained was real and that there is a specific place of refuge. Second, within the formal reprimand, there are two parts: first, the reprimand by contrasting the real with the false regarding his speech.
If even those who actually disparage the Noble Ones are still subject to prohibition and severance, how much more so for one who speaks of the gravity of their nature to others?

To use the light to illustrate the heavy in these two cases—first by citing the number and second by listing the two names—is both a false pretense and a theft of profit; such a person who diminishes the truth is called a thief.

The gravity of such transgressions varies; in principle, they are distinguished as minor or major. To be inwardly a breaker of the precepts, committing every kind of evil while plotting for fame and profit and claiming oneself to be of pure conduct—this is the foremost thief.
Even if one has [theoretical understanding] of the two emptinesses of birth and phenomena (*utpāda-dharma-śūnyatā*), and has moved beyond them, one has not yet actually realized them.
Seeking profit through falsehood and deception is the second thief. Regarding the third comparison: among these, the former two [thieves] act for the sake of food and clothing;

because this [third] steals by deceiving people through worldly means to unlawfully receive food and drink, it is more profound than the first thief and is therefore called the "supreme. Fourth, as for the reason why the former is small and the latter is great:
this is because the former uses supramundane dharmas to falsely steal from and deceive people, whereas the latter’s theft of food and drink is both real and deep.
[This offense is] grave. Because it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) offense for a noble one (*ārya*), it is greater than the previous [offense of] theft.

Regarding the text for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), there are two parts; the first consists of three sections: first, a brief elucidation of the root text of the precept (*śīla-mūla*); second, an expansion upon the preceding section on permissions;

third, citing the past as false and the present as true to establish the object that gives rise to doubt. The untainted noble dharma (*anāsrava-āryadharma*) transcends the characteristics of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*); this is termed "increase" (*vṛddhi*).
[The Buddha said: "It is so. However, this bhikṣu has not attained [realization] yet claims he has; this is called pride (*māna*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
'This person had long dwelt in mountain forests and, having not seen beautiful forms, temporarily suppressed his afflictions and claimed they were forever severed. Thus, pride arose within him.

Later, when he approached a city and saw pure and exquisite forms, lustful defilement arose again. Realizing he was still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), he immediately cultivated the Path and attained Arhatship.'"

"Arhat. Second, regarding those who, having formed this thought, look down upon the realms of sentient beings: the Buddha has taught that such views constitute a fault and an obstacle to the Noble Path.

I too have practiced and attained the Path; judging by my own realization, [those realms] are empty. Thus, I would seem to be in contradiction with the Holy Teaching and should perhaps be considered guilty of an offense.
If I were indeed guilty, I should not have attained the Path; yet since I have now attained it, it seems I am not guilty. Regarding this matter of being guilty or not guilty..."
In the middle, because the mind’s doubts have not yet been resolved, it says, "How is this? Third, the heat of doubt is removed;

if one claims "I am guilty," the punishment is a *nihsargika-pācattika* (exclusion for twenty days), but if one says "I am not guilty," one relies on the pure minds of the assembly to determine whether to proceed or refrain from following the teaching—hence it says, "and so forth, up to practicing accordingly.
Fourth is the formal consultation and resolution; fifth is the praise and opening of the way. Only when the object is empty should one remain within the transgression of the *āpatti*. Because...
This refers to claiming for oneself that one has attained [realization], when in fact the mind lacks such skill.

This opens the way for there being no offense. The third section, the fulfillment of the core precepts (*śīla-sūtra*), consists of seven textual points: first, the person; second, the object being false; third, the act of self-claiming—specifically, claiming to have attained the state of an *ārya* (noble one).

Regarding "self-claiming," this is a general reference to claiming the qualities of a noble one. From "I have entered the state of a noble one" onwards, specific instances are cited; "entering" refers to entering the path.
The Noble One refers to one who has attained the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). One who knows the supreme Dharma attains the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). I know this;

having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and beyond, there are four self-declarations. At another time, when it is not a time of false speech, these are made in view of the previous primary offense.

Fifth, with the exception of cases where an opening condition exists; the sixth and seventh may be understood accordingly. Question: Why is it that although one truly attains the Path, one does not say "except for those with overweening pride" (*adhimāna*)? Answer: There is none.

Because they arise from distinct conditions, the three phrases concerning the [numbers] four, five, seven, and so forth are omitted from the text and not explained. The first [phrase] is understandable upon explanation.

Regarding "not knowing and not seeing," this explains that the object of the second phrase is empty. From "claiming for oneself" onwards, the third phrase is explained. This consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the general statement;
second, the explanation of the specific sub-statements, such as "mindfulness abides in the body. The preceding text further divides into two sections; the first explains "for oneself."

Regarding the terms used: "one who has faith" refers to the faith that understands and realizes [the Dharma]. "One who has precepts" refers to the non-manifest (avijñapti) of concentration and the Path, not merely the non-violation of the five categories of offenses.
If one speaks of upholding the precepts, the dhūtas, and so forth, it is often said that [any lapse] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. "Hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Wisdom" refers to the two types of wisdom: reflection (*cintāmayī*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*). "The stage of eloquence" refers to the teaching of the Dharma.

Regarding the second category, the "Dharma of Persons" (*pudgala-dharma*), the following explains the "Dharma of Superior Persons. First, the Dharma of Persons is explained as referring to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Next, regarding the "Dharma of Superior Persons," this refers collectively to the noble dharmas; therefore, it is said that "all dharmas are untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth. However, these are characterized by detachment and are termed the "essential departure" (*niḥsaraṇa*).

The second [section] concerns the noble qualities that transcend illumination (*vidyā*). First, fourteen categories of gates are enumerated: mindfulness directed toward the body (*kāyagatā smṛti*), which is the foundation of mindfulness of the body;

right mindfulness regarding the other three foundations of mindfulness; speaking for oneself of maintaining the precepts; the right speech and so forth within the Eightfold Path; being one who possesses desire;

the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) as they are spoken of; speaking for oneself of being non-negligent (*apramāda*); the category of non-negligence; being one who is energetic; right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*), up to the tenth.
Fourth. The first section has three parts. The first sentence proceeds from the contemplation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

"Attaining the realization of the emptiness of persons" means that the practitioner possessing mindfulness—namely, the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body—is able to achieve renunciation; that is, they generate the realization of the emptiness of persons and thereby transcend birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, it is called "transcendence. When the mind examines the Dharma and attains the principle to govern the mind, it is termed "thorough cultivation" (*paricaya*).

As one increasingly draws near to the principle and the mind merges with the Dharma, it is said that "one is intimately attached to this Dharma. From the second stage of cultivation onwards, it refers to the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).

One strives to advance what is cultivated, so that understanding and realization increase further; awakening to the emptiness of phenomena surpasses what came before. Therefore, it is said that cultivation increases and expands.

Since the function of contemplation follows the mind, it is said to be like "taming the vehicle. Regarding the third stage, "maintaining the application" (*shou-she*) and below: this refers to giving rise to the true understanding of signlessness (*animitta*).
To record this understanding within the mind is called "maintaining the application. To illuminate the principle with clarity is termed "contemplation" (*guan-cha*).
The mind is darkened by ignorance; when understanding dissolves them, there is no duality. Therefore, it is called "skillfully attained.

When the equal and correct contemplation (*samyak-darśana*) manifests as untainted true liberation, it is firm and non-retrogressive; therefore, it is called "having already attained certainty. Since views are forever shifted, it is called "no further hardship.
It is the ground of spontaneous ease; therefore, it is called "sovereignty. The rest is similar. Based on this, one may interpret the text accordingly. For now, I rely upon this.

Regarding the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), it is explained through traditional transmission. When investigating the underlying principles, the stages (*bhūmi*) ought to be fixed and delimited. If all gates were universally applicable, this [explanation] would also be difficult to employ.

Now, taking the partial meaning—such as in the case of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*)—there is its emergence and departure, up to and including the attainment of the capacity for mastery (*vaśitā*).
Alternatively, because within the various stages they are associated with the applications of mindfulness, it is said "up to mastery. This is the horizontal [classification].
If one were to define them by their respective positions, it would not be thus; all categories are like this. To speak of "attaining concentration" refers to:
the *savitarka-savicāra* samādhi of the first dhyāna; the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) which is *avitarka-vicāramātra*; and from the second dhyāna onwards, which is *avitarka-avicāra*.

As for what is called the "emptiness samādhi" (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), it refers to those meditative states (*samāpatti*) associated with the two aspects of emptiness (*śūnya*) and non-self (*anātman*) within the category of suffering (*duḥkha*). If [it refers to] the cessation [of perception and feeling], there are four...

The meditative concentration associated with the [first] two modes of practice is the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*). The ten modes of practice associated with the four modes each for suffering, origin, and the path are the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).

Regarding "attainment through verbal expression" (*vāg-vijñapti-samāpatti*), this refers to the first two among the eight [liberations]. "Attainment through perception" (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*) refers to all meditative concentrations involving the mind.
It is called "counteracting the distraction within form. "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) refers to the two meditative attainments without mind (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

To eliminate mental distraction, there are next the four right applications. These constitute the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). As for "liberation": first, possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms;
second, not possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms; third, the liberation of the beautiful; fourth, the sphere of infinite space;

fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; eighth, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). The first three abandon greed; the next four...

"Turning away from lower stages" means that the sphere of infinite space turns away from the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite consciousness turns away from the sphere of infinite space, and so on, until the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception turns away from the sphere of nothingness.
The eighth [liberation] turns away from all mental states and their associated factors; therefore, it is called "turning away" (*prātikūlya-vairāgya*). It is also termed the "eight liberations.
Among these eight, the one that follows the Dharma is the eighth, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which refers to following the cessation of twenty-one types of mind.

The numerical factors: one further obtains twenty-one factors that are neither form nor mind to supplement the mental sphere; hence it is called "attainment according to the factors" (*anupadhi-samāpatti*).
Second, the "mental conceptions" refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), which are the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Third, "removing form" refers to the first two liberations, meaning that one removes desire for form by means of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Fourth, "not removing form."
This refers to the third pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*). Next, regarding "the attainment of the eight spheres of mastery" (*abhibhv-āyatana-samāpatti*):

"mastery" (*abhibhū*) means relinquishing (*tyaj*), and "spheres" (*āyatana*) means understanding (*praveśa*). Thus, the preceding three liberations are divided into these eight. The first two each have two:

namely, having the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms, whether many or few; and next, having no perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms, whether many... [or few].

If [the categories] are few, the third [liberation] becomes four—namely, blue, yellow, red, and white. These are also called the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the eight spheres of control (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Next, regarding the meditative attainments of the universal bases (*sarvāyatana-samāpatti*), these are the ten universal bases. Specifically, the third liberation constitutes four bases of mastery;

because one contemplates the original four great elements of form, there are eight; and including the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, there are ten. This is the path with eleven factors.
As for this, people say there are eleven requisites according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*: first, pure observance of the precepts; second, obtaining virtuous friends;
third, guarding the gates of the sense faculties; fourth, moderation in eating and drinking; fifth, diminishing sleep during the first and last watches of the night;
sixth, possessing wholesome awareness; seventh, possessing the factors of practice; eighth, possessing wholesome faith and understanding; ninth, possessing the bases of liberation; tenth...
There is no [separate] vehicle. Eleven are non-attachments. If one explains the eleven branches of the path according to the *Śāriputrābhidharma*, what is the single-branch path?
The foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*); this is called the single-branch path. What is the two-branch path? Concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

What is the path of three factors? It consists of concentration with applied thought and sustained thought, concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

What is the path of four factors? It consists of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four paths of application, the four paths of cultivation, and the four abandonments. What is the path of five factors?

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*), the five powers (*pañcabala*), the five entrances to liberation (*pañca vimuktyāyatanāni*), the five spheres of transcendence (*pañca nissaraṇiyā dhātavaḥ*), the five meditative concentrations on reflection (*pañca paccavekkhaṇā-samādhi*), and the factors for the attainment of liberation (*pañca vimokkha-dhammā*) are such [teachings].

What is the sixfold path (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-mārga*)? It consists of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the six inclinations (*ṣaḍ-abhimukhī*), the six spheres of transcendence (*ṣaḍ nissaraṇiyā dhātavaḥ*), the factors conducive to clear knowledge (*ṣaḍ vidyā-bhāgīyā dharmāḥ*), the factors that cause joy (*ṣaḍ prāmodya-hetavo dharmāḥ*), and the six types of joyful right awakening (*ṣaḍ prāmodya-samyagbodhi*)—these are such [teachings].

What is the sevenfold path (*saptāṅga-mārga*)? It consists of the seven characteristics (*sapta lakṣaṇāni*), the seven meditative absorptions (*sapta samādhayaḥ*), and the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharma*).
These are [the examples]. What is the eightfold path? It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, the Eight Liberations, the Eight Bases of Mastery, and so forth.

What is the ninefold path? It refers to the Nine Ways of Cessation, the Nine Successive Meditative Absorptions, the Nine Similes, and so forth. What is the tenfold path? It refers to the Ten Similes, the Ten Right Dharmas, and so forth.
As for "right" (ṛju), it means right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Mindfulness is right concentration; it is right liberation and right knowledge. As for the "path with eleven factors," these are the eleven liberative entries;

this is called the path with eleven factors. Regarding "cultivation," it refers to cultivating the fivefold Dharma-body, namely: precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Next, regarding the gravity of the offenses as follows: "Vain and unsubstantial" refers to the sixth phrase of the root precept, which explains the gravity of the various forms of transgression.

Within this section, there are four parts: first, the objective basis; second, the person's status, which is twofold—distinguishing between acting oneself and sending another—and within each of these two, there are four methods such as writing, etc., or five methods that constitute the offense. First, verbal expression is cited; the remaining four are combined [with it].
[The section on] "Forming [Karmic Bonds]" (kṣepaṇa). Second, regarding "in a secluded place" and below: this is clarified by comparing the presence or absence of the primary object (*ālambana*).

This is because it refers to speech made in a dark location. Second, regarding "I" in contrast to a different rebirth: for oneself and others, there are four cases each, as above; alternatively, five may also be understood. Third, regarding "if a person has truly attained the Path" and below:
one distinguishes the gravity [of the offense] by classifying the reality or unreality of what was spoken, and by distinguishing between similar and dissimilar types. Fourth...

When two objects are conjoined and one is focused upon both, only the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) is listed, while the perception of the phenomenon (*dharma-saṃjñā*) is omitted for brevity.
Regarding the mention of "speaking in a dream," this refers to excluding those cases occurring within a dream; such doubts frequently arise regarding karma, precepts, and so forth.
● Part Two: The Ninefold Analysis of the Saṃghāvaśeṣa Offenses.
1. Arising from the three poisons; 2. Allocation to body and speech; 3. Personal commission and instruction of others; 4.

Explanation of prohibitions and essential natures; 5. Categories of initial offenses; 6. Methods for maintaining and violating the precepts; 7. Similarities and differences between the two divisions; 8. Contradictions...
The regulations differ. Regarding the nine offenses of the lower assembly that arise spontaneously:
it is said they arise from the three poisons. First, there are seven precepts; these are established through the arising of a mind of greedy attachment due to three matters.

Next, there are two precepts; these are established through the arising of a mind of anger. Next, there are two precepts; these are established through the arising of a mind of delusion and arrogance due to three matters. Next, there are...
Regarding the two precepts: they are accomplished through the arising of hatred and delusion.
As for the second category, the bodily and vocal [precepts], these constitute four positions. The first two are restricted to the body;

the next two consist of harsh speech and the two types of slander—these eight, including the four types of malicious counsel, are primarily offenses of speech, while the body serves as an auxiliary factor in their accomplishment. The next two are the precepts concerning dwellings; here, the body is the primary offender, and speech [is auxiliary].
This is an auxiliary karma. Next is the one precept regarding matchmaking. Regarding the formal offenses of body and speech, there are three categories:

(1) committing it oneself; (2) instructing another; and (3) both. These are divided into three positions. First, regarding the five precepts: if committed by oneself, they constitute a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*);

whether instructing another results in the same or not is as follows—namely, the two coarse verbal offenses and matchmaking are grave for both self-commission and instruction. Regarding the two offenses involving a dwelling (*dvau saṃghāvaśeṣau*), if committed by oneself, they are definitively *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; whether instructing another results in the same or not... [text continues].

The same applies here. If one instructs another to commit the five [offenses] that bring benefit to oneself, one commits the same *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If one generally instructs another where no benefit accrues to oneself, one may only commit a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the two offenses involving both personal action and instruction of others, there is always a commonality in the offense committed; this refers to the two offenses of slander (*paiśunya*).
Whether one acts for oneself or instructs another to act for oneself or not for oneself, the degree of affliction and destruction is equal, as the underlying intention is no different.

Therefore, he and I are equally guilty. Regarding the three categories and six precepts: if one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense oneself, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if one instructs another to do so, it is merely a light offense (*duṣkṛta*). This refers to cases such as emission or touching;

if one commits it oneself, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, but if one instructs another, it is a *sthūlātyaya*, because there is no personal gratification involved. Regarding the precept against plotting [to harm], if one violates it oneself, one also incurs a light offense.
If the Saṃgha has not yet admonished one and one instructs them not to abandon [the misconduct], one incurs only a *dūṣkṛta*, because there is no [formal] Saṃgha [involved].

The formal act of the Saṃgha may be contravened because the transgression is minor. However, if one instructs others not to relinquish [the matter] when the Saṃgha is offering admonition, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense, because the gravity of the transgression lies in defying the Saṃgha’s command.
This applies even if the instruction is given indirectly; if one acts as the instructor, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one does not act according to the instruction, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Why is it that in this case, although the person previously followed my instructions and failed to comply with the admonition, they have already incurred a *sthūlātyaya*?
Answer: That person who received the instruction merely brought about their own ruin and harmed others; there was no violation of the Saṃgha’s command or the communal Dharma.

Since the gravity of the transgression was slight, the matter resulted in a *sthūlātyaya*. Had it not been completed, it would have been merely a *duṣkṛta*. In this context, the person who gave the instruction...

Admonishing [a monk] involves three factors: first, harboring it within oneself; second, causing harm to others; and third, having the collective life of the Saṃgha and the communal Dharma as the basis.
Because the principle applies generally to many cases, the offense is established as a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) even before the matter has been completed. Question:

If Devadatta violates a formal motion (*jñapti*) that has not yet concluded, and the teacher says, "Do not abandon [the course]," does he also incur a *sthūlātyaya*? Answer: He also incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. If that is so, what of the person being instructed who violates the motion before it has concluded?
One incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Why is it that one who has already been instructed can incur a *sthūlātyaya*, which is heavier than the offense for the one being instructed?
What is the meaning of this? The explanation says: Devadatta is precisely the one subject to the offense for violating the dharma of admonition;

since the result is indeed a *sthūlātyaya* when the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is completed, one commits only a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) when the announcement has not yet been completed. Furthermore, there is also the heavy fruit of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [which may follow].
Because it leads toward [a grave state], the intermediate offense is light. As for the person who gave the instruction, this is not a matter that can be remedied by admonition;

there is no method of admonition that could be violated to establish the limits of the offense. Furthermore, because there is no other heavy fruit leading toward [a grave state], for every word of the instruction given, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

Just as there is a formal agreement (*saṃghakappa*) regarding the violation of advice, the determination of the offense likewise precedes the act. If one violates private advice, the offense is determined once the act is completed.

However, when one violates the advice of the Saṃgha and incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it does not depend on the completion of the act; therefore, the current instructor may proceed before the assembly or individually.

This clarifies the preceding point of retreat. Just as with the two cases of physical contact and so forth, which require the completion of the act, if one instructs another to reject a formal admonition, that instruction constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Question: If one instructs another to commit slander and so forth, and I too am guilty of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, then by instructing another to perform confession (*pratideśanā*), should my own offense be extinguished? Answer: This depends on whether the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*) are complete or incomplete.

Regarding the four types of prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*): the two rules concerning matchmaking and the two rules concerning private rooms are prohibitions against misconduct; the remaining ten precepts, however, are unwholesome and are therefore intrinsic evils (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
As for the fifth category, the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* divides them into four levels; the first five precepts are all characterized by attachment. First...

The precept concerning sexual misconduct is of the category of lust. The two precepts concerning dwellings are of the category of theft. The two concerning corrupting families and evil conduct are of the category of killing.
The remaining precepts and so forth are of the category of false speech.

Regarding the six categories of observance and transgression (*dhāraṇa-vilopa*): among these, the two types of rooms possess both observance and transgression. However, because the former type of room lacks the full measure of exclusion (*apavāda*), it does not apply universally.

As for the remaining eleven, they consist of "cessation-observance" (*śamatha-dhāraṇa*) and "action-transgression" (*kriyā-vilopa*), and may also involve "cessation-transgression" (*śamatha-vilopa*) and "action-observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). These apply generally to thirteen precepts.
The partial application to the former type of room and the distinct hierarchical classification of the second type of room have already been explained above.

Regarding the similarities and differences between the seven categories for monks and nuns: the two offenses of matchmaking and the two types of slander, as well as the four offenses of refusing admonition and so forth—these seven are identical in their transgression.

However, while the offense incurred by the four refusals of admonition is equal, the objects of the offense differ; that is, each constitutes a refusal of the specific admonition addressed by the assembly.

Regarding matchmaking and the three types of slander, both the object and the offense are equal for both. As for the remaining six precepts, monks and nuns differ: in the case of emission, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (heavy offense) for a monk, whereas for a nun it is a *pāyattika* (light offense). This is frequently stated.
Women’s afflictions are deep and heavy; they are difficult to restrain and difficult to control.

If one commits the aforementioned grave offenses that afflict sentient beings, and furthermore, because women require private seclusion, involve many conditions and much effort, and their suffering flows forth in abundance, these [offenses] are considered light. Men are not like this;

because they can emerge from such matters according to the situation, theirs are considered heavy. Moreover, there are differences between internal and external susceptibility to defilement, and thus there is lightness and heaviness. [The offense of] a bhikṣu touching...
Regarding physical contact: because the male possesses the power to maintain his own firmness and thus limits it to the preceding stages, he incurs only a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

The nun, however, possesses heavy and thick afflictions; once she has experienced such touching, she fears it may lead to further violation or coercion. Therefore, she strictly guards against it even before that point, and thus the offense is established as a *pārājika*.

There are four points of difference which result in the gradation of the offense: first, whether the person is alive or dead; second, whether the organ is large or small; third, whether there is lustful intent or not; and fourth, whether the part of the body is major or minor. [The case of] the nun...

Because they fear being intimidated or coerced, there must be [the offenses of] *duṣkṛta*, *sthūlātyaya*, and so forth. For the Saṃgha, based on the offense of defilement, there are *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pārājika*, as well as [the grades of] major and minor;

for the Bhikṣuṇīs, there are two types of harsh speech. The Saṃgha [offense] is grave while that of the Bhikṣuṇīs is light because it occurs infrequently. Furthermore, because the Bhikṣuṇīs have a preparatory effort (*prayoga*) that is particularly grave, they incur a *thullaccaya* (Skt.
*sthūlātyaya*). Because the Saṃgha lacks the eight factors that mutually support one another, they incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding the two rules on dwellings, the Great Saṃgha incurs [an offense].

[The previous section is] incomplete. If a nun commits [this offense], she incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If it exceeds the prescribed dimensions, a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) may stay overnight alone;

because a virtuous person might build a room alone, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension from the community) was established [specifically for nuns]. A nun must have a companion for protection. If one builds a room together with another, there is no sense of exceeding the dimensions;

therefore, the Vinaya states that "there is no offense for a house where many people reside. Master Jian says: "If two people build a room together, there is no offense. Even if one were to build it alone, it would result in a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense)."
If that is so, why are both equally guilty when the roof-covering exceeds three [units]? The answer is: this is based on the measurement in *zhǐ* (cubits).

In those two cases, there is no offense. However, one should distinguish [the limit] down to three joints; to break or flatten [the bamboo] would incur public censure regardless of whether it is small or large. Therefore, both constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for the Saṃgha.
Question: Regarding the case where a nun is accompanied by others but falsely claims to be alone—the meaning of which is rare—and yet incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;

since a nun being accompanied while falsely claiming to be alone is a rare occurrence, her offenses in both secluded and non-secluded places should not be identical. Answer: This is based on the impairment of one's karma. When the impairment is slight, the offense is light.

Furthermore, even if she were to act alone, such an instance would be rare and infrequent; therefore, she incurs a light offense. In cases such as sitting, because the gravity of the act is profound, although it may be rare and infrequent, the same retribution is incurred.
When the censure reaches its limit, both monks and nuns commit the same offense. Regarding those who do not take remedial action: for a nun, there is no *pārājika*;

however, if she previously resided in a village and the monks happen to have no quarters, she ought to build them. Even if she does not take remedial action, because her transgression is slight, she incurs only the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
A bhikṣu may dwell in an araṇya, sitting beneath trees or in the open air to settle his body and advance in his practice.
Now that he dwells in a village and constructs a private dwelling for himself, it is necessary to strictly prohibit this, lest he later commit an offense.

Regarding the eight cases where the offense differs from the preceding: in the first nine precepts, one incurs an offense by violating the Buddha’s regulations; in the latter four admonitory precepts, one incurs a transgression by violating the Sangha’s regulations.

"Before the Sangha" here refers to the case where there is only the Sangha in the presence of the Buddha; if the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) is not performed, there is no offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for failing to follow the admonition.
Since the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense arises from violating the Sangha, these four precepts constitute offenses committed before the Sangha.

Regarding the nine cases of spontaneous occurrence (*anābhoga*) or non-occurrence: in seven instances, such as the transgression of the precepts, it is possible for there to be spontaneous occurrence.

In two cases—the two types of *sthūlātyaya* regarding private dwellings—and in two cases of slandering a nun who acts as a matchmaker, one may have another person act on one’s behalf; since the task thus instructed is accomplished, these are included. Among the three natures (*svabhāva*), one commits seven *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; in the remaining cases, because there is no instruction given to another, there is no spontaneous occurrence.
Regarding these thirteen [precepts], the first nine concern the observance of the communal rules of conduct (*saṃgha-kriyā-dharma*); if one violates them, the communal rules of conduct are ruined.

The latter four concern obeying and following the commands of the Saṃgha; by ceasing transgressions and not committing them, the communal rules are shown to be accomplished, which brings benefit at the appropriate time and is called "protecting the communal teachings" (*saṃgha-śāsana-rakṣā*).
If one violates them, the communal teachings are ruined. Within the former [nine], there are again three [subdivisions]; the first five...

The first [case] involves internal defilement; it clarifies the method for destroying the communal practice. The next two involve the affairs of two residences in harmony; they clarify the method for destroying the communal practice.
The following two involve mutual slander in harmony of intent; they clarify the method for destroying the communal practice. Of the preceding five, three are obtained:

the first destroys the community and the practice, but does not destroy the time. The next three destroy the community and the practice, and destroy both the practice and the time. The final one destroys...
The practice of righteousness is subtle. When the assembly is destroyed and the time is ruined—this is why the first [instance of] violating the precepts was not permitted before the Buddha.
Many say it is for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma; furthermore, it is because he wished to stop slander; and furthermore...

It is because one desires to give rise to faith and reverence in the devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits; furthermore, desire is an unwholesome dharma, the very source of birth and death, and the root of craving;
therefore, it ought to be prohibited and severed so that the holy life (*brahmacarya*) may be pure.

Next, the names are explained. Because they involve the movement and shifting of skillful means (*upāya*) while aiming for ultimate realization, they are termed "outflows" (*āsrava*). Furthermore, because they divide and flow forth in abundance, they are called "leakages. Thus, they are so named.

The general conditions for the offense are three, as mentioned above. Regarding the specific conditions, the former interpretation identifies three: first, reaching completion; second, the movement of the preparatory effort;

and third, the violation upon failure. The present explanation identifies five conditions: first, there must be an object consisting of the six types of non-ways (i.e., improper orifices), specifically excluding the anus, because if one lacks this objective condition—such as perceiving a path as a non-path—one incurs a *pārājika* offense. Second, the six types [of persons] and so forth who are non-ways...
It is not the perception of a path. Because one perceives what is not a path as being a path, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Therefore, according to the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*:

if one perceives it as not a path and has no doubt, yet completes the action with the threefold intention and performs the four movements, then upon the fifth failure, an offense is committed. If the first condition is lacking, a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is incurred; if this [first condition] is not met, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is not obtained.
If two conditions are lacking, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses—namely, perceiving what is not a path as a path and doubting whether it is a path. If three or four conditions are lacking...
There is no offense. [If] five factors are missing, there is a heavy or light *duṣkṛta*. The narrative of the origin (*nidāna*) has two parts:

first, the offense; within this, there are two sections: first, the conditions for the offense; second, from "recalling" (*anusmṛtya*) downwards, the actual clarification of the conditions for the offense.

The textual structure is as usual. Second, from "the various faculties are joyful and pleased" (*sarvendriyāṇi prahlāditāni*) downwards, it is a rebuke. Within the rebuke, there are two parts: first, the comparison...

○ The sixth precept concerning the construction of a house of excessive size without the consent of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the opening statement, there are four points. First, the explanation of the term "restriction" (saṃvara). However, as for the retribution of those who practice the higher path, the power of that retribution is strong and robust, capable of enduring [the consequences].

Taking all things as objects of contemplation, one does not abandon right cultivation. For this reason, the Great Sage prescribed robes so that one might cultivate the Way by reducing attachments among graves and under trees, rather than maintaining private dwellings.
As for the two types of "opening" mentioned, those of middling and inferior capacity have weak karmic retribution and physical strength;

they cannot endure cold and hardship. If they were made to follow the same rules as the superior practitioners, it would mutually obstruct their right cultivation; such circumstances would instead become conditions that cause these individuals to ruin the Path. Therefore, [the rules] are established according to their respective capacities.
Regarding the measurement: the keeping of small rooms, stone chambers, and two-room dwellings is permitted; it is said that these belong to this category.

Furthermore, there are three interpretations regarding the reason why rooms were permitted, yet the construction of oversized or unallocated dwellings was not allowed. What is the obstacle? It is because for those who have left the household life...

In principle, there should be no attachments; one should dwell wherever conditions lead, establishing oneself in the practice of the Way. If there are offerings from the faithful, one may accept them as the occasion arises, providing for one's needs so that the body may remain fit for the long path.
Now, however, you have extensively engaged in construction and worldly affairs, which obstructs cultivation and increases your own bonds of greed.

It destroys the practice of contentment. Furthermore, by begging here and there, it troubles and disturbs donors, prevents the arising of reverence and faith, and causes the destruction of the True Dharma;
therefore, excessive amounts are prohibited. Moreover, one who dwells independently without receiving instruction may obstruct and hinder the Sangha, causing much disturbance;

for this reason, dwelling in a place that causes interference is not permitted, nor is it allowed to occupy space without the Sangha’s formal assignment. Additionally, it harms material things and violates the lives of sentient beings.
Maitreya, regarding the violation of the path and its principles, and furthermore not permitting [the raising of] objections, four offenses are established.

Speaking of the Noble Teaching, since it must necessarily be respectfully upheld according to principle, to act in opposition to the Dharma constitutes a transgression; as such, the mental fault is not slight. Therefore, four offenses are established: the Saṃghāvaśeṣa and the Duṣkṛta.

Question: Regarding the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*), if one does not practice them, yet has not previously transgressed before the noble ones (*ārya*), there is a violation within what was permitted;

thus, a prior offense would incur guilt, though the gravity of the offense differs. Answer: If one is unable to practice the four reliances at the level of the highest grade (*adhimātra*), then they should indeed be permitted.

How could it be tolerated that one commits an offense? As for these four permissions, they are granted according to one's capacity; logically, one ought to practice them. That one now willfully violates them makes this clear.
In all these cases, there is an offense; however, because they belong to remote conditions and furthermore involve many transgressions, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

As for the remaining three—robes, food, and medicine—which are requisites for sustaining the body and are essential for urgent needs, and because the emotional attachment is also slight, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in each case.
Next, the explanation of the names: To dwell independently without receiving instructions is called "not being assigned by the Saṃgha"; it is designated as the "Great Reliance on the Aṅguṣṭha."
This is said for the sake of establishing the definitive measure.

Next, the distinctions between separation and combination are analyzed. First, the meaning of "separation" is explained. Question: Why are these two now separated? Answer: Because there is a distinction between that which has a master and that which lacks a master.

Second, the regulated and the unregulated; third, the formal act of assignment (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). Because these matters are contradictory, they are established as two precepts. Next, the combined statement is distinguished.
Regarding the combination of the two precepts within the preceding "present" category, what is the reason? The answer is: the conditions for the arising of the offense are identical.

That is to say, exceeding the proper measure and failing to assign [the robe] both arise from a single dwelling; therefore, they must be combined with the preceding. This is like the *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robe) and the *varṣā-śāṭī* (rainy-season robe). 4.
Regarding the categories such as washing alone, speaking differently, and reviling, the first two are established next. Some interpret this as follows: the previous dwelling was excessive in size;
although the first and last dwellings were not formally authorized (*avippakata*), it is possible for there to be unauthorized [elements] within the previous dwelling.

The second is because the names of the types of non-authorization are not distinct. Our current interpretation is not so; although the name "authorized" (*vippakata*) is the same, [the distinctions remain].

If the method of dividing the dwelling space is applied, both cases likewise have an initial [offense]. In the former case, although the room has no owner, there is an initial offense for failing to assign it;

in the latter case, although the room has an owner, there is an initial offense for failing to assign it. This is just like the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules. Regarding the offenses detected, in both instances one raises the charges of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting) and *pāyattika* (expiation).

Because the private and public settings differ between the two locations, each has its own statement regarding the initial transgression of the precept. Thus, we know that both dwellings also have an initial offense.
First, regarding the offense of building a hut without authorization: the hindrances and difficulties follow the same pattern as for individual cells (*layana*).

The general conditions (*sāmānya-pratyaya*) are as stated above; the specific conditions (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*) are sixfold: first, it has no owner; second, it is for one's own sake; third, one solicits the materials oneself;

fourth, it exceeds the prescribed dimensions and lacks authorization; fifth, there is the perception that it exceeds the dimensions and lacks authorization; sixth, the offense is incurred as soon as the hut is completed. If the first condition is lacking, there is no offense.
Subsequently, there may be three, two, or one offense regarding the precepts. If one constructs a dwelling in accordance with the Dharma such that it is permissible, there will be no offense.

If the second requirement is lacking and one builds for another what is not a proper dwelling, there may be two *sthūlātyaya* and two *duṣkṛta*, or three, two, or one, or there may be no offense at all.
If the third factor is missing—namely, not having personally requested it—then there is no "excessive" amount; thus, while the other three factors may still be present, one incurs no offense.

If the fourth factor is missing—namely, performing an act of distribution that is not excessive—it renders the act free of offense, though one may incur four *sthūlātyaya* offenses: namely, if it is actually not excessive but one perceives it as excessive, this is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one is doubtful [of its excessiveness], it is also a *sthūlātyaya*; and if it is actually a distribution but one performs it as a non-distribution, [it is likewise].

If one perceives it as exceeding [the prescribed size], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if there is doubt, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding the first four [cases], they are established as such even when the [action] is completed. If the fifth is missing, one still incurs four *sthūlātyayas*.

If one actually makes something exceeding [the size] while perceiving it as not exceeding [it], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if there is doubt, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*. If one does not perform the formal authorization (*anujñāpana*) while perceiving that it has been authorized, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if there is doubt, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*. Furthermore, regarding these two cases based on what was stated above, if the fourth is missing, one only incurs [the remaining offenses].
Two *sthūlātyaya* offenses. If the fifth [condition] were missing, there should be six *sthūlātyaya* offenses; for now, we shall follow the traditional explanation of the *Vinayapiṭaka*.

If the sixth condition is missing, even if the final two lumps of clay have not yet been completed, one incurs a full *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one lump of clay remains, it constitutes a heavy *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At first, he cut down the tree himself; this clearly illustrates the arising of his transgression. He then constructed a vast dwelling, which caused distress to two classes of beings.

On both occasions, the deity of that tree descended to rebuke him. Within the rebuke, there are two parts. First is the awakening [of the Buddha]. Within the awakening, there are two parts. First, the tree deity addressed the Buddha:
