Alternatively, it may be understood as words of exhortation for patience addressed to the tree deity. Second, Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: "The reason why [the Buddha] did not reprimand him..."

The Venerable Kaṇṭaka constructed a hut. Because he acted contrary to the teachings, he could not be censured. Furthermore, one must well understand human nature; since many would construct huts, censuring him would have been of no benefit.
It was for the sake of protecting [the Sangha] that he was thus treated. Moreover, because he was subject to reproach, he departed after having made his report.

Second, the World-Honored One censured him with the following passage. First, he asked him about his own words; second, the World-Honored One censured him correctly with the following passage. [End of] Text.

"Chong-qu" (filling the requirements) refers to the formal act of begging.

The instruction for the monks' adjudication is given below.

Within the third section on the determination of offenses, four types of offenses are cited to establish the transgression; specifically, two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings) are established. Therefore, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding these two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the transgression of exceeding the proper measure shall first be explained through three gates: first, the offense regarding the proper measure; second, the offense regarding the unmeasured... [text continues].

1. The offense. 2. Mutual transgressions: whether they are established or not. 3. The relative quantity of mutual offenses. Regarding the first point: Question—If a building measuring two *zhang* and four *chi* is constructed, does one incur an offense immediately, or does one wait for it to exceed [the limit]?
Answer—One incurs the offense only when it exceeds [the limit]. Therefore, this text states: "If one constructs it beyond the prescribed measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If that is so, then in the case of a long [building], if it exceeds eight fingers or four fingers [in width], one should incur an offense even if it is not otherwise compliant. Answer—The dwelling itself is what exceeds [the limit].

The *madhyama-kalpa* (middle rule). This robe is a full *madhyama-kalpa*. Because it exceeds the *madhyama-kalpa*, the *uddhāra* (lifting) has not yet been committed. Since the making of the robe constitutes a full *madhyama-kalpa*, it must be brought out of the state of transgression.

The reason for this is that within the category of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), there is both internal opening (*antara-vivara*) and external opening (*bahiḥ-vivara*). Since the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) pertains to the position of external opening, the transgression must be lifted.
Because opening does not constitute a transgression, this refers to the lifting of the extremely small quantity of a room belonging to the external opening; internally, it is an opening.

Externally it is not opened; there is no formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for it. Regarding "externally opened": this refers to the stage prior to having committed the offense; thus, it constitutes the maximum permissible quantity for internal opening. Question:

Why is it that a dwelling (*vihāra*) does not require a formal ritual and yet may exceed the prescribed measure? Answer: To permit excess would be of no benefit and would only increase greed in general.
Although one may store robes, they first belong to oneself; since there is no collective ownership, this is permitted.

Regarding the two gates: the question is whether one commits an offense through the simultaneous presence of both faults, or whether one also commits an offense through mutual faults. The answer states that in the case of "excess" (atireka) and "medium" (majjhima), it applies to all.

If it exceeds the width, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If it exceeds the length, one likewise commits [the same offense]; if it exceeds both dimensions alternately, one still commits [the offense], let alone if it exceeds both simultaneously.

Furthermore, as stated in the passage below, the same applies to sitting mats, bathing robes, and so forth—offenses are incurred through alternating excesses. Now, the case of exceeding the length or the width is treated as being equivalent to exceeding both.

Regarding the offenses concerning length, medium, and excess: there are three for each of the first three categories, totaling nine when combined (three times three). These are: long-long-excess, medium-long-excess, and medium-medium-excess;

as with the reduction of one from the three, the remaining two are likewise. Among these, five phrases constitute an offense, while the four mutual combinations of the "one-and-all" [category] are without offense.
Regarding the third section: concerning the mutual transgressions from beginning to end, there are two offenses. If both have committed a transgression, are there not two offenses? Answer:
Since they are based on two separate rooms, it is said that there are two fruits for both. Therefore, for the two rooms [involved] in the sequence, one offense is incurred for each;

however, when both have transgressed in a single room, it is the result of a single subsequent action, and thus there is only one offense. If that is so, what about the action of swallowing impure food and the like?
Because they are one, there should also be only one offense. Answer: The formulation of the offenses is not the same; their distinctions can be categorized into four propositions. First:
the karma is either manifold or singular, while the object is either manifold or singular. Second: the object is either manifold or singular, while the karma is either manifold or singular.
Third: both object and karma are identical, being either manifold or singular. Fourth: both object and karma are distinct, being either manifold or singular. If they are mutually...

Regarding "transgressing the boundary" (*sīmātikrānta*): when the conditions (*pratyaya*) are one but the fruits differ, there are two offenses arising from karma; in cases such as impure food, there is one karma and multiple conditions, resulting in many offenses.

IV. The Conclusion by Reciting What Has Been Performed. The Text of the *Jñapti-karman* (Formal Motion) is threefold: I. Announcing to the Assembly and Commanding Them to Listen; II. Properly Discerning the Matter. Within the discernment of the matter, there are two parts.

Now, those who have left the household life and dwell together ought, as a matter of principle, to be harmonious and tolerant. Even when preparing to perform a ritual act, it is permitted not to touch one another; yet now—

Concealing malice and fabricating baseless accusations, they cast heavy charges against others; thus they ruin their own mental conduct, increase the cycle of birth and death, and cause the extinction of the True Dharma.

Because such deceptive acts are so grave, they must be confessed before the Buddha. Therefore, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "This is established for one's own practice, so that the True Dharma may abide for a long time."

What [is the distinction]? Answer: If one bases it on the equality of the location where there is no foundation (*amūlaka*), and the horizontal addition [of the offense] is not differentiated, then logically it should also be subject to restraint.
However, the former case is "without foundation" (*amūlaka*), while the latter is "based on a false foundation" (*mṛṣāmūlaka*); therefore, they must be separated.

If it is consistently "without foundation"—whether it be seeing, hearing, suspecting, and so forth—it is all "without foundation" and is subsumed within the previous precept. If one sees something regarding a different matter, yet falsely claims to have seen this [specific thing], or hears or suspects it... [the same applies].
It is likewise so. This refers to the provisional roots (*prajñapti-mūla*), which are included within the subsequent precepts.
Next, the term "combined" (*samasta*) will be explained. Question: When three roots are used to slander another, each constitutes a separate offense; why then are they combined? Answer:

From the perspective of incurring an offense, they do not necessarily depend upon one another, and thus there should indeed be three [separate offenses]. However, in cases where the basis is absent (*amūlaka*), the degree of the offense is equal, and thus the meaning of the offense is the same. Furthermore...

Later, there may be cases where a single offense is established through common testimony; therefore, they are formulated together. Regarding the degree of the offense: Question: One slanders another and commits a grave offense (*pārājika*), yet in reality lacks the three bases (*trīṇi mūlāni*).
If one deceives the Saṃgha by falsely claiming to have the three bases, does one commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for a false understanding, or a *pāyattika* for lying?

Answer: It is said that there is no separate *pāyattika* offense here. This is because the slander is invariably accomplished through a fabricated falsehood. If, for my own sake or out of a desire to harm the master, I fabricate...

Regarding the killing of animals: one should not inflict damage upon the owner, as this constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). To take life results in a *pāyattika* offense. The answer is that slander is necessarily based on falsehood;

there is no such thing as slander that is not false. One who does not understand this [conflation] therefore holds that the offense of theft is not fixed. There are cases where damage is inflicted upon the owner without resorting to the killing of an animal, such as when stealing silk or cloth.

These are instances where damage is inflicted upon the owner independently. As for those cases requiring the killing of an animal, these do not invariably depend upon one another; they are distinct instances of inflicting damage.

The principal offense is the taking of life. Since the two objects are distinct, one incurs two offenses. If that is so, since the characteristics of slander are dependent [on other factors], it would constitute a single offense;

likewise, regarding the seven-day medicine, as long as it is "excessive," it must necessarily be "at the wrong time," and thus it too should constitute two offenses. The explanation says: this is not a valid analogy.
The reason for this is that what is "excessive" is not necessarily "untimely," and what is "untimely" is not necessarily "excessive. This is the case with pure gifts (*śuddhadāna*):
one may simply lack excess, yet it is impossible to lack something else. Regarding the "untimely," there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, that which is excessive but not untimely.

As for the six types of defiled offenses, they are as follows: first, one is at an improper time while the other is not long-term; second, one is a pure gift while the other is not; third, both are such; fourth, both are not.
Because there are these distinctions, they incur separate offenses. Regarding falsehoods: first, one is a falsehood while the other is not slander; second, both are such; third, both are not.
There are only these two cases, and no instance where it is slander but not a falsehood. Since their characteristics are mutually dependent, they constitute a single offense. Furthermore:

The offenses incurred are not identical in their duration. One becomes guilty when seven [meals] are completed; however, for eating at an improper time, one only becomes guilty when seven [meals] are completed provided there is the condition of receiving food.
This is unlike the cases of slander or false speech, which occur simultaneously; therefore, in this case, there is only a single offense.

Next, the explanation of the complete conditions (*samanvāgata-pratyaya*). There are eight specific conditions: first, a *bhikṣu* or *bhikṣuṇī*; second, the perception of them as such; third, an internal mind of malice;

fourth, the absence of a basis (*amūla*); fifth, the addition of false accusations regarding a grave matter; sixth, down to addressing even a single *bhikṣu*; seventh, the speech being clearly articulated.
Regarding the understanding of the predecessors concerning the initial restriction to the great *saṃgha* of monks and nuns: this was intended to exclude the three lower groups.

First, because the meaning of a general slander is subtle, it does not obstruct formal cultivation. Second, because the offenses for those of the lower groups are minor, how could the person who commits such slander be permitted to incur a heavy penalty?
It is like striking and seizing [an object]: the offense is grave for the great *saṃgha*, yet light for the lower assembly; this case is likewise so.
If that is the case, why would following and complying with the interpretation of the meaning apply equally to the lower assembly? The answer is:

because they equally violate the command of the *saṃgha* and the communal rules (*dharmas*) in the same manner, both incur the offense of *pāyattika*. If that is so, when a *bhikṣuṇī* follows and complies with the five points of the great *saṃgha*, she likewise equally violates them.
Regarding the communal rules (*saṃghadharma*): Why is it that when a monk follows a nun, he incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, whereas when a nun follows a monk, she incurs a *pāyattika*?

Answer: Although these are communal rules, the nuns are dependent on the respect for the teachings; because they follow the numerical categories of the rules, they incur a *pāyattika*. The monks have no such dependence, yet they follow the nuns out of deference; because of this deference, they incur a *duṣkṛta*.

If that were so, when a monk relies on [the testimony of] a nun to bring a formal charge against another nun, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for slandering her; whereas a nun has no one to rely on to bring a charge against a monk, so her slander of a monk should be lighter.
Why is it that slander and the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense are treated as residual (*śeṣa*)? This is because one category is used to infer the other; they follow the same gravity.

One interpretation is that regarding slander, the lightness or heaviness of the offense depends on the object being slandered; thus, while slander itself is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the subordinate group incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

Because they follow [the primary rule] by way of secondary application, and because they occur infrequently among the preceding categories, there are these gradations of severity. Thus, the text of the *Gāthā* XII states: "Is there such a case where this is a *pārājika*? This refers to that very point.
Regarding the offense of *duṣkṛta*: the answer is that there is. That is to say, if a nun follows along with a monk who has not been expelled for refusing to see his fault, she commits a *pārājika*;
if a monk follows along, he commits a *duṣkṛta*. Furthermore, because one may violate two grave injunctions, it is a *pārājika*, whereas violating one grave injunction constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

Since the prevention [of the offense] differs in these cases, there is a distinction between light and heavy offenses. However, as for the great bhikṣus, regardless of whether they are pure or impure, all incur the offense of slander; this is clearly manifested in the Vinaya itself.
Regarding the various rules: within the context of what has been seen or heard, one may perform ritual acts provided they are pure.

Now, to contravene that purity of vision and arbitrarily claim that a transgression was seen—while harboring such a generalization toward others and failing to inquire whether the matter is pure or impure—constitutes the offense of slander in both cases.

As stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: "Because it is impure within the midst of the pure and extensive. If this is so, then there arises a dilemma regarding the objects of nuns, whether pure or impure. The answer is found in the subsequent section of this Vinaya.

To engage in sexual misconduct with one wearing the *kāṣāya*, or to speak of having violated a *bhikṣuṇī*, yields no benefit; these merely constitute the presence of the objective condition (*viṣaya*), and both result in an obstacle that is difficult to overcome.

If it is argued that "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is the meaning of "resolution" (*vyutthāna*), and that impurity (*aśubha*) is likewise a number, the answer is: it is indeed so in terms of fulfilling the count.

However, slander (*abhyākhyāna*) is based on the abandonment of cultivation (*bhāvanā-utsarga*); therefore, they are not the same. If that is the case, then even a person who has committed an offense becomes an object for confession (*pratideśanā-viṣaya*).

Answer: This Vinaya does not require [the confession] to be sought exactly as the text describes. Because one proceeds to the place of purification (*pariśuddhi*), according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, even down to cases where the offenses are different, it still constitutes a valid object for confession.

If that is so, then regarding the method for removing the offense of eating after the proper time (*paryāpta-bhojana*) in the presence of the host, the answer is that the confession allows for offenses that are different to be cleared.
There is no "opening" for the *pāda* (the fourth *niḥsargika-pāyattika*). Furthermore, other food is likewise prevented; the western [rule] does not constitute a violation of the *pāda*.

This is because it is like the prevention of excess through pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*), the prevention of verbal [excess], and the category of "overnight contact" (*rātri-sparśana*) and so forth; therefore, they do not coincide. Regarding the two types of persons possessing the precepts, although the perception of the object (*ālambana*) applies to both, the perception itself is restricted to the pure.
Because one might either commit an accusation (*udghātana*) or fail to establish a slander (*abhyākhyāna*) when facing the two objects with an impure mind, there is no [violation].

The perception of purity. Third, the mind of hatred may be understood according to the text. Question: Regarding the reversal of what has been raised and the slander, why is it that the former possesses five qualities while this consists only of the mind of hatred?
Answer: Within the conditions, the reversals are complete; thus, the third, the mind of hatred, constitutes two [aspects], namely "coarseness" (*pāruṣya*) and "destruction" (*viheṭhanā*).
The phrase "desiring to destroy that pure practitioner" is a term of denigration (*apavāda*). Fourth, there are no three roots.
That would be false and deceptive; adding a sixth item would be redundant, for one must speak of the first category [of offenses], which are the "coarse ores.

To state a seventh would be contrary to the Dharma. When speaking before the assembly, such [an addition] would be untimely; it would merely be called an increase or decrease, though according to principle, all [eight] are present.
As for why only five are cited here while there are eight conditions, those [five] were what was raised by the various Noble Ones.

The offenses enumerated encompass both light and heavy categories; the five virtues (pañca-dharmāḥ) are immeasurably light. Therefore, they are treated as a single category. Now, by reversing the order, we shall distinguish the slanderous acts.

The sin of the one being slandered extends across all levels [of the monastic hierarchy], while the transgression incurred by the slanderer—regardless of whether the offense is removed or mitigated—is established as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Thus, eight conditions are required. The fourth and fifth [conditions] are explained according to the text; the sixth extends down to addressing a single individual, which is based on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Qishi).

It is said: "To revile and slander face-to-face" constitutes five parts. If one slanders another face-to-face and the meaning is understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Now, seeking the meaning according to the principle:
one must confront the Saṃgha to seek disciplinary action. Therefore, the text states that one goes before the Saṃgha as described above; the remaining two cases are easy to understand.

Next, the meaning of the conditions (*pratyaya*) is explained. If the first condition is lacking, and one of the remaining five aggregates is deficient in both respects regarding the object, there are ten *thullaccaya* offenses.

If one is deficient in either of the second two—doubt or misconception—there are five *thullaccaya* offenses each; if anger is lacking, there is no offense of slander at all. If the three roots are present...

However, this is an illegitimate formal accusation (*adhamma-ukkhepanīyakamma*). If one imposes a minor matter upon another, there may be a *thullaccaya* or *dukkaṭa*, depending on whether other conditions are lacking, or whether the offense is light or grave.

In the section concerning the causal conditions of the preceding precept, there are two parts: first, up to the point where it says "as explained above," regarding the imposition of a grave matter; second, from the words "at that time, the Venerable One...

onwards, regarding the discovery and the subsequent reproach. Within the former part, there are again two sections: first, up to the point where it says "one may then do so," regarding the causal conditions for the preliminary stage of slander.
The second section, "At that time, the nun Maitrāyaṇī," clarifies her slander. The preceding text has three parts: first, it clarifies the place where the Tathāgata resided;
second, from "The Venerable One" onwards, it describes her request to manage monastic affairs, which serves as the remote cause for the slander;

third, from "At that time, there was the nun Maitrāyaṇī" onwards, it explains how she obtained a dilapidated room and poor food, and together with her sister, devised a plan, which serves as the proximate cause for the slander.
Regarding the second section, "Requesting the Management of Monastic Affairs," there are four parts: first, the request for food and the petition to manage monastic affairs;

second, from the point where the World-Honored One grants the request, fulfilling that petition by appointing someone to manage the affairs; third, from the point where the Venerable [Upāli] receives the appointment, he attends to the monastic affairs;
fourth, from the point where the World-Honored One [speaks], it accords with the Sage’s mind and is what the Buddha delights in and praises. First:
The text is divided into two parts. The first concerns relying on tranquility to give rise to mindfulness and intending to manage the Saṃgha; herein, there are two sections.
The first describes how Trapuṣa contemplates what he finds pleasing and distasteful, seeking to abandon [worldly ties] and assemble [the community]. The second begins with "He further reflects...

regarding the methods for making [the monastery] firm and secure, noting that these cannot be accomplished without practice, and thus using such management of the Saṃgha as an excellent cause. Fifty [years], plus fourteen [years] of leaving home, and sixteen [years] until completion.
The Arhat replied: "Māra is the name of a king; this is his prince, whose personal name is Dharmapāla.
[The second part, beginning from the time of *pūṣa* (the afternoon), concerns the lifting of the two screens and the request to manage monastic affairs. He asked:

"Since Dharmapāla is already an Arhat, why does he say 'this body is not firm' and request to manage monastic affairs? He answered: "Dharmapāla knows for himself that he possesses residual physical existence and wisdom (*jñāna*)."
However, this [merit] is subject to arising and ceasing; it is not a stable or enduring dharma.

It does not compare to managing monastic affairs so that many people may cultivate the Path, whereby the resulting blessings and benefits conversely provide a foundation for a stable and enduring dharma—this can be accomplished without difficulty. Seeing this benefit, one requests to manage monastic affairs.

Furthermore, even those who worship the Buddha, the Sangha, and the Great Bodhisattvas still practice the management of monastic affairs as Śrāvakas; how could such a principle be considered strange? Many see this and speak thus.

Because of the fulfillment of a former vow, he requested to manage the affairs of the Saṃgha. This differs slightly from what is stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding the "fulfillment of a former vow," which can be understood accordingly.

As for the necessity of appointing [an official], it is because one must act in accordance with the four methods; thus, the appointment is carried out according to the Saṃgha’s legal procedures through a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), as set forth in the text.
The subsequent section on management has two parts: first, the management of resident bhikṣus; second, the management beginning with Rājagṛha.

Regarding the visiting monk (*atithi-bhikṣu*): at the beginning, the persons who manage the practice and the necessary provisions (*sambhāra*) are collectively presented so that one may find suitable companions for the journey and ensure that the provisions are fully prepared.
Among these, first are those who share the same conduct (*caryā-samāna*), followed by those who share the same practice (*karma-samāna*) as clarified below.

As for "sharing the same conduct," this refers to the twelve *dhūta* (ascetic) practices. The *Jian* (Mirror/Commentary) states: "Discerning in the four directions; discerning the afflictions (*kleśa*) to depart from all obstructions."
As for the practitioners, although there are twelve in number, they are divided into two categories. The first is the *prāhāṇika* (one who follows the sitting), who is the most excellent among them;
because he is able to conform to all the other practices, he is called "one who follows the sitting. The remaining eleven are those whose abilities are partial rather than universal.
Within these eleven, they are further divided into two: the *naiṣadyika* (one who always sits) is distinguished by his practice, as he maintains the three postures.

Regarding the ritual protocols: sitting constantly is difficult to maintain. One *dhūta* practice is established as constant; the remaining ten are undertaken according to circumstances. Although these circumstances differ, they may be summarized into three categories:

namely, those concerning food, those concerning place, and those concerning clothing. Within the category of clothing, two *dhūtas* are established: namely, wearing the *naivāsika* (inner robe) and the *tricīvara* (three robes). Within the category of food, four [are established].
This refers to begging for food in a single alms-round and sitting in a single session without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leftover food).

Standing in the middle of a place, staying in an *araṇya* (forest), among graves, or practicing the practice of sitting in the open air and so forth—these are what must be undertaken. The reason they are required is that food and such are the conditions for sustaining the Path; they are of the utmost necessity for maintaining the body.

Therefore, clothing must first be provided for. If one seeks improper methods of using these robes, it will extensively produce karmic burdens and obstruct the path to liberation; thus, such a person is not a dhūta.
Consequently, the Buddha taught the bhikṣus the proper method for receiving and using requisites other than clothing, so that they may obtain what is necessary merely to sustain the body.
Only when one brings an end to long-term travel can one truly accomplish the ascetic practice of contentment (*dhūta*). Therefore, two [categories] are established here.
Regarding "wearing patched robes" (*nāṃsī*), this refers to robes offered by donors and so forth; regarding "the three robes" (*tricīvara*), this refers to keeping extra robes and the like.

Even if one obtains clothing and garments, if they are obstructive and unsightly, or if there is no food to sustain the body, and if one suffers internally from hunger and the like, it will be difficult to practice the path. Thus, [these distinctions are made].
One must approach for food in order to clarify moderation in portioning. To merely satisfy hunger while traveling on the path is not yet true *dhūta* practice.

Regarding those who speak of "begging for food," there are two types of food: that which people call *dāna*, or food intended for the Sangha; because such food has many faults, [one should instead take] the first type: *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (morsel food).

For those who eat excessively, [it is contrasted with] those who eat in a single sitting; for those who eat twice a day, [it is contrasted with] those who do not perform the *khalupaścādbhaktika* practice;

for those who perform the *khalupaścādbhaktika* practice, [it is contrasted with those who do not]. Since clothing already covers the body and food sufficiently fills the frame, and the conditions for cultivating the Path are complete, one must certainly engage in correct cultivation.

For the stage of cultivation, one must rely on a quiet place. Once the clamor of the world is absent, the mind also becomes tranquil; only then can one truly practice the dhūtas. Therefore, this follows next.

Regarding the fields of knowledge: dwelling in an araṇya, among graves, or facing those living in a village; practicing the lower discipline of sitting in the open air while facing those who accept sheltered dwellings;
and as for these robes and other requisites, although there are distinctions of superior and inferior when compared to others, they are collectively termed *dhūta* practices.

These twelve are discussed together as conditions for practice, intended to cause practitioners to intermingle, abandon notions of "self" and "other," and mutually encourage one another in their progress.

The methods for encouragement are systematic; therefore, it is said that they are "common and equal. If one distinguishes between the breadth and narrowness of these [four reliances] and the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), the name of the four reliances is brief yet broad, as it clarifies their medicinal applications and encompasses all three grades [of practitioners]. Herein, the name is broad yet brief, as it contains only a few medicines and is dedicated exclusively to superior practice.
If distinguished according to conditions and conduct, this [latter set] is broad while those [four reliances] are narrow, because those [reliances] lack [the specific application of] impermanence.
Because of sitting.
*Sifen lü shu*, Fascicle 3a; *Sifen lü shu*, Fascicle 3b.

From here below is the third section, concerning the remaining types of practitioners who are equal to others in their conduct, specifically regarding the bhikṣu who manages guests. Why is it that while his virtues are concealed, light issues from his hand?

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "He entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi). The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* answers: "It is because he entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi*. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Because he entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi*. The answer is: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*.

For eight reasons, light issues from his hands. First, to stop slander: to demonstrate that he is free from attachment and aversion, just as when the Buddha was slandered by a Brahmin woman, he declared, "I possess the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses," thereby manifesting his purity.
Second, to quell the contempt and derision that arises in monks who study or practice meditation upon seeing those who manage monastic affairs; thus, light issues from his hands...

1. To eliminate the disparagement of those characterized by lightness; 2. To subdue the mountain-dwelling bhikṣus who were constantly [complacent], for the city-dwelling bhikṣus were always in a state of distracted mind;
therefore, although Trapusa’s affairs were chaotic, he emitted light through his supernormal powers and distributed the monks’ bedding and seating to subdue their arrogant minds;
3. To cause those who see the fruits of diligence to be encouraged, and to cause those who are indolent and arrogant to be stirred.
Because it is done at will. Fifth, for the sake of increasing the donor’s roots of goodness. Sixth, so that the mind does not falter even when currently subjected to slander.

Seventh, because one wishes to manifest to the assembly that the Sangha possesses great majestic power; if even a single bhikṣu has such supernatural power, how much more sublime must the Great Virtuous Ones be!
Eighth, out of love for the right practice, so as not to allow it to be neglected or interrupted. Question: Why?
Question: When affairs are in disorder, how is it that one can attain radiance? Answer: Generally, when performing a task, one first forms a mental intention regarding what is to be done.
Then, from a wholesome mind of the desire realm, one enters a mind of pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*). Next, one enters a mind of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-citta*).

Following that, one enters a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the desire realm and manifests radiance. Returning from the transformative mind, one re-enters the mind of supernormal knowledge, and finally re-enters the mind of pure concentration.

Subsequently, he enters a state of distracted wholesome mind within the desire realm. Having already fulfilled his original intention regarding the extent and distance of the transformative act, because this occurs outside of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) for the sake of accomplishing a task, it is thus.
This is consistent with the principles of logic and the Dharma, pleasing the minds of the multitude, and encouraging their resolve;
since it must be clearly praised, the World-Honored One said: "Even those who are the first and second proximate conditions are capable of transgression."

The exhortation to the people has two parts. First, from the beginning up until the acceptance of the invitation, it explains the cause for the anger and slander resulting from obtaining a dilapidated room and poor food.
Second, from "Luo'ai ni" onwards, it concerns the actual formulation of the plan for slander, which consists of seven sub-sections: first, Cidi respectfully presents his inquiry;
second, he follows the previous discourse by remaining silent as originally instructed; third, he requests forgiveness for his own faults and asks for the reason behind his silence; fourth...
1. Bringing up the matter to confront one another, thereby expressing what was left unsaid. 2. Asking five times about her desires and requesting that she employ skillful means.

3. Showing her the ritual for slander, hoping to fulfill her original intention. 4. Confirming and repeating what she said to demonstrate one’s own capability to act. 5. In the *Jìzhōng* (only in the middle section), it mentions self-slander but does not say she instructed her sister;
in fifteen instances, it is seen that both instruct their sisters to slander, which is consistent with this Vinaya.
The second [section] concerns formal accusation (*sappāṭihāriya*). Below this, the refutation is set forth. The text has two parts: first, the rebuke by the bhikṣus;

second, the rebuke by the Blessed One from "At that time" onwards. Within the rebuke by the bhikṣus, there are three sections: first, the cause for the awakening [of the fault]; second, the rebuke by the bhikṣus;
third, the presentation of the matter to the Buddha. Within the awakening [of the fault], there are two parts: first, Tapassa himself declares his purity, thereby clarifying the awakening; next...
Examining the *Cidi* (Compassionate Ground), he speaks of himself to manifest his own clarity. Within the five sections of the *Tapas*, the first clarifies the Buddha’s inquiry;

the second manifests his own knowledge and requests the Buddha to bear witness; the third is the World-Honored One’s refusal; the fourth is his own declaration of purity; and the fifth is the Sage’s praise, stating: "Never even in a dream...
If one considers the ordinary person in relation to the Sage, this refers to the past being spoken of as the present; if one examines the matter according to its facts...

Discrimination: To explain the difficult by means of the easy. It is asked: Since the Buddha is an omniscient one who thoroughly knows both the pure and the defiled, why did he not certify that Trapusa’s land was pure?
This is a question regarding what constitutes an offense. As for "speaking of oneself" (*svavāda*), many say:

If the Buddha were to certify one as right and another as wrong, it would give rise to public slander. Because this would involve discussing the Buddha’s likes and dislikes, he now does not certify [the land] in order to stop such slander.
Second, if it is proven that Trapusa committed an offense, he would not be considered non-offending in the present;

if it is said he is non-offending, this is because the retribution for past evil fruits has ripened, and furthermore, it would contradict his own later statement regarding the disciplinary method (*vinaya*). Regarding the text on the examination of Maitrībala, there are three parts:
first, the Buddha’s instruction and interrogation, which reveals the grave transgression of the monk who followed the Buddha’s teaching with faith; second, the various monks... [text continues].

The Buddha, having received the instruction, investigated and questioned him. Three times he cleared himself of the offense and expressed his intent to slander, thereby manifesting his own confession. The Elder examined the case;
the junior monk [reported it], followed by the nun Maitrī, then the junior monk’s reprimand, and finally the report to the Buddha. A second time, the Buddha rebuked him.
The text has two parts: first, the censure for having committed transgressions during practice; second, the censure because the retribution received is certain.

Regarding the statement that those who enter hell exclusively [are so defined], this is an exaggerated expression used to highlight their faults. In the other three Vinayas, because Dharmatāpa himself declared his purity, the *smṛtivinaya* (verdict of mindfulness) was granted.

Because the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya involved slandering others through physical action, the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (formal act of reconciliation) was granted via a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motion followed by three proclamations). However, in the [Mūlasarvāstivāda] Vinaya, there are only ten [such cases].
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is not stated that there is an offense; rather, one is subject to the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) solely by virtue of one's own admission.

In the *Pañcavargika*, a monk proclaims: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Because [the accused] asks [the question], and later states 'I have not committed an offense,' his own admission is not established."
Why is it that in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) one is subject to the formal act of *jñapti-cīvara-pratikṣepa* (self-declaration of exclusion)?

The answer is: regarding the statement that "the wording is not established," this refers to one who does not recognize the legal procedure (*dharma*). Because this is an error of insentience (*acetana*), one cannot rely upon them to undergo treatment through self-declaration.

The fifth [section] states: "One is granted exclusion" because they are one who recognizes the legal procedure; since the error of their deceitful slander is not minor, they may be granted exclusion. Furthermore, the two Vinayas may differ on this point. Unfinished.

He attained the supernormal power of clairaudience. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when a nun confesses her own offense, it is considered a genuine offense, and she is therefore subject to formal suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*).
In this case, the nun had committed an offense elsewhere and came to her brother's place. Her brother said to someone, "My sister is wicked;

she is my sister, yet she slanders me with her body. The brother replied, "She is very good; she has troubled me no small amount. You may slander her for me. Consequently, the Sangha granted her formal suspension.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of seven points: 1. The person who commits the offense. 2. A mind of anger (*dveṣa-citta*). 3. The object of the slander, who is a pure person (*pariśuddha-pudgala*).

To explain extensively that one who slanders a pure person as impure commits an offense whether the person is actually defiled or pure, it is stated that both purity and impurity constitute an offense. 4. The absence of the three bases (*trīṇi mūlāni*). 5.

By means of grave matters such as the *pārājika* offenses and below, one expresses caution to manifest one's own state of mind; therefore, it says "desiring to obstruct," and so forth. 6. One’s own admission of the fault.
This refers to the time of slandering; hence it is called "at another time. Because each instance of purity serves to manifest one's own intent to slander, [the text] states:
"If a bhikṣu commits an offense," etc.
The three, six, and two phrases are abbreviated and not explained; the rest are all fully explained. The first phrase can be understood from the commentary. The second...

Regarding "hatred": one who possesses the ten unwholesome dharmas (*daśākuśala-dharma*) gives rise to hatred based on the nine afflictions (*navāghāta-vastūni*) throughout the three periods of time, directed toward both sentient beings and non-sentient objects.
This is called the causal condition for the ten unwholesome dharmas; the detailed explanation may be understood from other sources.

To explain the fourth phrase, "possessing roots" (*sāmūlaka*), one first explains it by way of its opposite, "without roots" (*amūlaka*). If one explains these roots, they are analyzed through four gates: first, enumerating the number and explaining the names; second, defining the roots.
The degrees of falsity and reality are not equal. Regarding the third [point], the designation "existent" or "non-existent" applies to the three concentrations (*samādhi*).

The fourth is identical to minor falsehood. The term "root" (*mūla*) is a designation applied subsequent to its arising; since the meanings of "root" differ, three distinctions are briefly indicated: namely, the root of seeing, the root of hearing, and the root of doubt.
That which observes and displays blue and so forth is termed the "master," called "seeing. That which receives sounds and partakes of them is named "hearing. Thus, the treatise says:
Visual consciousness arises and sees; auditory consciousness arises and hears. Following this seeing and hearing, there is hesitation and indecision, with the mind lacking firm resolve;
this is termed "doubt" (*vicikitsā*). These three [faculties] all give rise to speech; therefore, they are collectively named "roots" (*indriya*).

Question: From what kind of mind does this doubt arise? Answer: It is said that after the five consciousnesses, consciousness gives rise to this doubting mind, because it proceeds from what has been seen and heard.

Furthermore, there are many treatises; those who see them must ensure they are pure, precise, and reliable. One should listen only to the "eye of reality" (*satyacakṣus*), not the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).

The divine eye is subject to error and causes much distraction and confusion. Thus, the *Gāthā* says: "One may cite a bhikṣu by means of the divine eye, but this does not purify him from transgressions, for the divine eye is not a [reliable] matter.
Question: Why is it that doubt arises only after seeing or hearing, and not from [other sources]?
"Seeing. Regarding "doubt arising after hearing," and "hearing arising after doubt," the explanation can be understood accordingly.
As for determining the number [of faculties] in the second section, according to the text there are four: namely, self, others, doubt, and so forth.

Since the two [cases of] non-arising do not involve verbal expression, they can only be categorized under seeing, hearing, and doubt; therefore, they cannot be called "roots. Because this is now stated in a general sense, it says:
There are four [cases]. Regarding the statement that there is both the false and the true: from the perspective of the object (*viṣaya*), these four are all false;
yet from the perspective of one who is pure (*pariśuddha*), it is not precluded that there may be a basis (*mūla*). For the transgressor, there is no basis. Therefore, the text says:
"One who is pure accuses another who is pure-like; one who is impure accuses another who is impure-like. However, among these four, the first two are true.

The latter two [types of] speech are false, because they are characterized by arbitrary imagination and doubt. Within the former two, each consists of what is seen or heard as real, yet accompanied by doubt;

these are also false because the seeing or hearing is not certain. Although there is both the false and the real, if one possesses these three [conditions], all such cases permit the accusation of an offense.
As for the statement that "they do not coexist": if the former two are present, then the latter two cannot be, because the false and the real do not occur simultaneously. If...
If there is a third, then the other three do not exist; if there is a fourth, likewise the other three do not exist.
This means that while the first two may coexist, the latter two cannot coexist with one another; this is how it should be understood. Question: Why does the text state that one relies on others?

If there is only "seeing" or "hearing" and no "doubt," what is the reason? One explanation is that [the former] is strong due to its intimacy, whereas [the latter] is absent because it is weak due to its distance. If that is so—
The remaining three [types of] *tri-vidha* (threefold) exist; from another perspective, there should be only two. When explained in this manner, those below are omitted for brevity.

Within the minor slander (*kṣudra-pāruṣya*), five points are identical to this text. Regarding the statement "raising a charge of whether it is red or not red," there are two types: one's own and that of others. If it exists, it is raised as being "red."

If it were non-existent, one would falsely slander [the teaching]. Regarding the three factors of perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and [volition], they exist; thus, one does not falsely slander them. Because the correct principle (*samyagartha*) is weak, one likewise does not falsely slander [it], for the mind is real. If it were non-existent, one might falsely slander it by raising [a charge];

however, one does not falsely slander it by raising [a charge], for the three factors of perception, mind, and [volition] exist. Even if there is doubt, one does not falsely slander [them]. Regarding the three factors of perception, mind, and [volition], they exist.

If one does not falsely accuse, then there is no accusation; if one falsely accuses, then there is an accusation. To say that one brings forth the actual root of the matter while harboring a hidden, suspicious mind and goes to accuse another of being wrong is a case of "suspicion being false.
This suspicion is not the same as a conceptual perception.

Regarding the third gate, concerning the existence or non-existence of their designations: It is asked, "Since there is no direct apprehension of the object, why is it called the 'seeing faculty' (*cakṣur-indriya*)?

Because it is directed toward hearing, it is called the 'hearing faculty' (*śrotra-indriya*). However, although "seeing" and "hearing" are mentioned separately, the two [faculties] follow from seeing and hearing; subsequently, when one does not reach a definitive conclusion but remains in hesitation, this is called "doubt" (*vicikitsā*).

Question: Is doubt regarding the name not a root based on seeing? Answer: Although the object is indeed existent and real, doubt extends to both seeing and hearing, and furthermore, it extends to both existence and non-existence;
thus, at the time of seeing or hearing, [the object] is not yet determined. If one were to hear of a specific [object] and the doubt were categorized as such, the doubt would not be comprehensive.
Therefore, it is generally termed "doubt. This principle can be understood to apply to all four [roots]. Question: If it is said that it extends to existence and non-existence, etc., then as...
Regarding minor falsehoods (*mṛṣāvāda*): among doubt (*vicikitsā*), seeing (*dṛṣṭi*), and hearing (*śruta*), how can one cite seeing and hearing to distinguish them from doubt?

Furthermore, in the context of the recitation of the precepts (*prātimokṣa*), it is likewise with seeing and doubt, and likewise with hearing and doubt. Answer: If one follows this text, one should likewise be able to cite seeing and hearing to distinguish them from doubt.

For now, we shall proceed according to the general rule. Furthermore, the question is: since perception (*saṃjñā*) pervades the three—seeing and so forth—how are they distinguished by way of these three gates? Three.

The perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and doubts (*vicikitsā*) are also included within the three. Why are the three doubts not distinguished by means of "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, instead of simply stating that there is doubt regarding them?

Answer: Among the faculties (*indriya*), there is no category named "perception," because it lacks the function of investigation (*parīkṣā*). Therefore, one can speak of the three as distinct. However, among the three marks of the faculties, there is the category named "doubt.

If one were to distinguish [the objects] by means of seeing, hearing, and doubting, then two would be distinguished from the three doubts, because one would be investigating the doubt within those three.

The three types of doubt are not distinct from [the three] views and so forth, because they involve the denial or non-denial of what has been seen and heard. Furthermore, there is a difference in their scope. Question:

What is the distinction between their specific characteristics? Answer: Doubt regarding the faculties arises from what has been seen and heard; it does not arise from the first two [types of] faculties.

That is to say, there is a separate category of uncertainty that arises from what has been seen and heard, yet one does not doubt the seeing or hearing itself, but rather doubts whether an action was committed or not. This latter type of doubt arises adventitiously.

It does not arise based on seeing and so forth, yet one doubts whether these three—seeing and so forth—are actually seeing or non-seeing. Furthermore, there is a difference in their breadth and narrowness.

Moreover, fearing that one might slander [the object] as being red when it is not red, because of the doubt regarding the faculty of observation (*indriya*), it simply says "there is doubt. If this is so, what of the triad of perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and [volition]?
This also arises horizontally. Therefore, it is not monitored. Answer: Because one perception shares the same object as the actual faculty, both arise together regarding the offense.
Furthermore, since the three [perceptions] lack the faculty of perception, they are made different. Moreover, that which can be perceived is categorized under the first two faculties;
thus, the name "three" is used to distinguish the three types of doubt. By classifying doubt under the third, the specific is subsumed into the general.

Regarding the fourth section: it is asked, "The minor falsehoods consist of eight phrases; why does this [case of] denial consist of only six? The answer is: because the lower [category] clarifies falsehood, there are eight phrases;

whereas here, the denial is the inverse of the formal accusation (*ukkhepana*). Since the accusation consists of only three [grounds], the denial is likewise. As for why the accusation consists of only three:
when one speaks, one can only testify to an offense based on the three—what was seen, heard, or suspected. If one says...
The four [faculties] beginning with "not seeing" are merely false. If they were presented as a pair, they would simply be praised; thus, there are no other four. Furthermore, regarding the question:
among the four beginning with "seeing," why are only "seeing" and "hearing" mentioned as distinct faculties, while the two factors of "touching" and "knowing" are not?
The answer is: because those two objects produce cognition through separation, whereas the faults committed by the person do not emerge from the body or the mouth. The mouth...
The actions performed are heard by my ears; those committed by the body are seen by my eyes. Because of this seeing and hearing, one is able to give subsequent admonition;
therefore, one commits an offense through distinct faculties based on what is seen and heard. This is because it is not an object known through touch.

Now, since one does not rely on the faculty of touch to know, even if doubt arises from two [faculties], one is still permitted to hear the confession of the offense. Thus, among the faculties, there are only three names. Then...
To further clarify the refutation of slander, the three categories of what is seen, heard, and suspected are taken to demonstrate the non-existence of the object.
To claim existence where there is none is why it is termed "slander. There are only these three cases of non-existence and three instances of slander; no other words can apply here.

If one speaks of minor falsehoods that contradict the facts, yet the mind has shifted, this constitutes "false speech" (mṛṣāvāda). Therefore, while the objects and the words may both exist, among the eight categories [of transgressions], false speech is rooted in the faculty of view.

This refers only to the first three precepts, as there is no false speech [among them]; because it is by means of words and sounds, it does not pertain to what is seen. When it concerns what is heard, it applies to all four [precepts].
From among "seeing" and "doubt," taking the first two precepts—sexual misconduct and killing—as examples: when doubt arises from what is heard, all four are fully present.
Having set this aside, the subsequent section clarifies the absence of a basis (*amūlaka*). The passage beginning "that person is not pure" should be explained in conjunction with what follows.

The method for slandering by means of five, seven, and two phrases consists of two sections. First, the section on the nature of the offense as presented in the text; second, the section on the gravity of the offense from "If a bhikṣu...
onwards. Within the first section, there are seven topical headings. The first is: when there is no basis in reality, one proceeds with a slander based on the three bases (*trivastu*).

This yields six permutations. The second is: when there is no basis, one proceeds with a slander based on two bases—namely, the basis of what was seen combined with either what was heard or what was suspected.
There are six permutations. Three cases lack the faculty of hearing; these form six permutations based on seeing, doubt, and slander. Four cases lack the faculty of doubt;

these form six permutations based on seeing, hearing, and slander. In the subsequent section concerning "affliction" (kleśa), there are three topical headings. The fifth case lacks both the faculties of seeing and hearing.

Based on the single root of doubt (*vicikitsā*), six [denials] are produced. In the sixth, there are two roots: the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*) and doubt. Based on the single root of hearing (*śruta*), six [denials] are produced.

In the seventh, there are two roots: the absence of hearing and doubt. Based on the single root of view (*dṛṣṭi*), six [denials] are produced. Thus, the sixth and seventh [categories] comprise forty-two propositions.
In terms of stages, there are three categories: the first involves slandering by means of all three faculties; the next three involve slandering by means of two faculties;
and the final three involve slandering by means of one faculty. Although the stages are thus, they are here explained according to the seven cases.
The six phrases of the first chapter-gate constitute the correspondence of the six minds. Regarding this text, there are two gates of analysis: first, the explanation of these six minds;
second, the differentiation [of them] in contrast to the minor falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*). However, human interpretations of these six minds are not fixed.

Formerly, it was explained that they possess eight [aspects], and among these eight there are similarities and differences. One type of person explains them as follows: the first is the mind of non-forgetfulness regarding the presence of marks (*sanimitta*); the second is the presence of marks...

[The first case concerns] a mind that forgets the characteristics [of the offense]. In the third and fourth cases, there is doubt as to whether the mind has forgotten or not; in the fifth and sixth cases, there is no doubt as to whether it has forgotten or not. Question:
In the first statement, it simply says "not seeing, hearing, or doubting," yet it speaks of committing an offense through "seeing, hearing, or doubting.

Originally, there was no mention of the term "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa); for what reason, then, is it said that there is a mind with characteristics? Answer: This is because one uses the second mind to verify and testify to the minds of the third and fourth cases; therefore, [the term is used].
[He] knows. [The question is: Why are there no delusive or non-delusive aspects regarding the signless (*animitta*)? Because it is abbreviated, there are only six. To explain it thus:
the first phrase refers to that which possesses signs (*sanimitta*). Regarding the eight minds of non-forgetfulness, all are equally subject to the offense of slander.

Furthermore, according to one person’s explanation, as for why there are six minds, they are spoken of in relation to the faculties (*indriya*); in reality, they do not exceed four minds. The first is called "not giving rise to adventitious signs" (*utpanna-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*).
There is no characteristic (*animitta*). Second, that which has previously given rise to a false characteristic is called "having a characteristic" (*sanimitta*);

these two are relative and constitute two states of mind. First, that which has previously given rise to a false doubt is called "having doubt" (*savimati*); second, that which has not given rise to a false doubt is called "without doubt" (*avimati*);

these also are relative and constitute two states of mind. Thus, there are four states of mind. As for why there are six: "having doubt" is divided into two phrases. First, that which has previously given rise to a false...
Regarding doubt: when it comes to the time of slander, one claims there is no doubt, saying, "I truly saw, heard, and doubted. There are two ways in which a crosswise doubt may arise:
first, having forgotten the doubt, one says, "I saw, heard, and doubted"; second, within the state of being without doubt, this is further divided into two:
first, being without doubt yet claiming there is doubt, saying, "I saw, heard, and doubted"; second, being without doubt and forgetting that one is without doubt, saying, "I saw, heard, and doubted."

The four [types of consciousness] correspond to the preceding [categories]. Including both the non-perceptual (*asaṃjñin*) and the perceptual (*saṃjñin*), there are six states of mind in total. Question: Within the category of "doubtful" (*saṃśaya*), two propositions may be formulated;

likewise, within the second category of "possessing characteristics" (*sanimitta*), there should also be two propositions. Why is it that only "possessing characteristics" is mentioned, while "forgetting" (*vismṛta*) is not mentioned?
Regarding the characteristics of what was seen, heard, or suspected: when it comes time for the accusation, one says, "I have no such characteristics of having seen, heard, or suspected.

Yet, [the offense] actually arose from a transgression committed through seeing, hearing, or suspecting. The response is: "Previously you understood this as a true denial (*abhyākhyāna*), yet you first said there were no characteristics of seeing, hearing, or suspecting, and later said, 'I saw, heard, or suspected the offense.
Because the earlier and later statements contradict each other, the supervisor does not release you. Therefore, there is only this single point. If that is so—
Regarding the third phrase, there was doubt at the time [of the initial statement], yet by the time of the slander, one claimed there was no doubt.
One said, "I truly saw, heard, and doubted," whereas previously one had said there was no doubt; thus, the two statements contradict each other. Why, then, is one released? The answer is:
in the third phrase, the contradiction applies only to the root of doubt itself; it does not apply to the seeing and hearing. Because the contradiction is not complete, one is therefore released.
Now, regarding the three faculties within the [five] marks, because they are fully present and observed both before and after, one cannot escape [the charge]. Question:

If one cannot escape when the observation is complete, then in the fifth chapter below, the "Gate of the Five Doors," where there are no two faculties of seeing and hearing, but only the single faculty of doubt is raised—when one goes to slander based on the third mental state of not having seen or heard another commit an offense, yet possesses doubt therein—and when the time for the slander arrives...
He then says, "I have no doubt. Yet I truly suspect he has committed an offense; furthermore, he is a supervisor. How could he escape [punishment]?

Since we are thus at odds and in breach of our mutual obligations, it is truly difficult to resolve this matter. Moreover, the explanation must indeed exist. Because both gain and loss involve slander, I have omitted them for brevity.

If they were fully detailed, there would be two types of mental states established for those without signs (*animitta*), and two types of mental states established for those with signs (*saṃjñā*). These should consist of eight mental states across the two schools.

Regarding the establishment of the thesis: while it is said that there are eight principles, they are reduced to six for the sake of brevity. In the present correct interpretation, the principles are only six; they do not include the two alternative explanations and so forth.
Among these six, the single [remaining] one accords with the latter explanation; those currently presented as the six are as follows: first, the mind that does not forget despite being signless;
second, the mind that forgets its perceptions despite having signs; third, the mind that claims to be without doubt despite having doubts; fourth, the forgetting of doubt; fifth...

"Doubt" refers to having a doubting mind. There are six types of doubt-free forgetfulness (*asampramoṣa*). Question: Within the state of a mind with perception (*saṃjñin*), there is only forgetful perception;
therefore, there is no such thing as a non-forgetful mind with perception. One should compose the text as follows: "Not seeing, hearing, or doubting his offense.

Within this, there are the aspects of seeing, hearing, and doubting; one then says, "I have seen, heard, or doubted his offense," and thus the [doubt] arises. Answer: Briefly stated, there are five meanings.

It is because coming forward to testify does not constitute slander; therefore, [the rule] does not apply here. First, if one does not forget the three characteristics (the seen, heard, and suspected) yet speaks of having "seen, heard, or suspected," this is merely verbal speech that accords with the mind's reality;
how could this be considered slander? This is because slander involves falsehood, whereas here the mouth [speaks] in accordance with the heart.
It is like a minor lie. Second, when the mind intends to speak but one realizes that what is being said is unnecessary, yet one does not forget the characteristics of what was seen.

In the case where the falsehood contradicts one's own mind, this [case] is likewise. Second, if there is a mind characterized by signs (*nimitta*), then when one slanders another who has committed an offense, one does not rely on a false falsehood;
since it already presupposes a false falsehood, we know that the presence of signs is logically inconsistent with its arising. Third, regarding the judgment upon falsehood:
among the five types of false speech, the latter two do not depend on whether the object is real or unreal; they establish the offense solely by taking the falsity of the mind as the basis. If...

Regarding the "mind with signs" (*sanimitta-citta*), it is logically appropriate that it should exist; thus, the mind indeed incurs an offense. The fourth minor forgetfulness concerns six types of minds.

The second, "with signs," involves neither forgetting nor being stained, yet both violate the [required] phrase. If one perceives a sign and subsequently reports having seen it, this constitutes truthful speech.

Furthermore, there is no deliberate falsehood; therefore, this case is likewise so. How could it constitute slander? Regarding the sixth minor falsehood, the text of the *Kaiwen* states that one speaks based on what has been seen or perceived;
since even a minor falsehood is not considered deliberate, how could it be considered deliberate slander? Based on these five points, it is clear that there is no deliberate slander.
However, to claim there is deliberate falsehood is logically preposterous. Question: If that is so, then speaking of "no doubt" when one actually has doubt would also not be deliberate.
[Question: "Slander. [Answer: To answer without rejecting baseless doubts is to have an open mind. Because you slander me with falsehoods, they come forth. Therefore, the text says:
"If there is doubt within this, one simply says, 'I have no doubt. I truly see, hear, and doubt. If that were so, I too would not reject baseless charges;
I am truly repaying your slander. Your answer arises from an offense against me; your mind is hollow and penetrating, being exclusively full of [malice]. You do not know.

This is a matter of "is" and "is not. Therefore, one cannot do without it. Since [the mind] slanders the true person with such things as the marks of a non-person, how could it be known that this arises adventitiously?
Thus, this case is also like that. Doubt is an adventitious condition based on the sense faculties; furthermore, it is a state of hesitation that extends across both existence and non-existence.

To say, "I saw" or "I did not see," and so forth, is to know that these are not real; thus, one attains non-retrogression. Citing the actual faculties, one slanders them by claiming this attainment exists.

To speak of having doubt or being without doubt—when I have actually seen, heard, or doubted an offense—is like a person who has doubts regarding the mind of another with whom they share a connection;

therefore, it is more significant than the mere characteristics. One asks: in the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), there is only non-conception; is it not the case that the signless (*animitta*) and the forgetting [of signs] are also absent?
What is the mind? Answer: When there is no forgetting of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*), then there is no forgetting of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

Because one does not slander [the truth], this mind of non-conceptualizing and forgetting cannot emerge. If that is so, when there is no forgetting of doubt (*vicikitsā*), then there is no forgetting of doubt;

how then can one emerge? Answer: Although there is no forgetting of non-doubt, there is nonetheless no forgetting of doubt. Because one slanders [the truth] when there is no forgetting of doubt, [one cannot emerge].
In contrast, because there is now a need to prevent cleverness, one asks: "The first phrase is 'non-characteristic and non-forgetful.

Why, then, does the text not mention "non-characteristic" and so forth? Answer: If one does not perceive [characteristics], then it is non-characteristic; why then must one say "non-characteristic"? If that is so, then if one does not perceive, there is no doubt;
what use is there in saying "no doubt"? The explanation says: Within the state of no-doubt, one can utter the words, "I have a doubt."
Therefore, it is said that one first harbors doubt. One cannot claim, "I have the notion [of existence]. Why then would one need to say, "I have the notion of non-existence"?

This is because if one previously possessed the notion [of existence], one might still forget it and falsely slander [the truth]; how much more so when one previously lacked it—why would one need to claim it exists? Thus, one does not respond by affirming existence.

Regarding the statement that there is no "conception" (*saṃjñā*), this differs from the context of doubt; it is for the purpose of preventing the skillful concealment of the distinctions within the mind through false accusations, and thus it is so stated.
Conception cannot be concealed; therefore, they are not of the same category. Furthermore, in the first phrase, it is fundamentally unnecessary to state that there is no conception.

Furthermore, the five subsequent branches, such as "forgetting" and "not forgetting," are distinguished from the preceding ones; thus, "having perception" (*saṃjñin*) and so forth are distinguished from the preceding.

Inferring from this, it is established that there are only six [types of] minds. Since this is the case for the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), the interpretation of the text can be understood accordingly. There are no three instances of exaltation (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) nor three instances of groundless accusation (*apadāna*). The first section is concluded.
Second, there is no single case of the "root of not seeing" (*adṛṣṭamūla*). Regarding [accusations based on] hearing, doubting, or slandering, one also forms six permutations.
First, one does not see that person commit an offense, yet claims to have heard of it or suspects it. One asks: do these instances of hearing and doubting exist or not?

If they do exist, then one could speak of a single "not seeing"; however, one should not then engage in false slander. If they do not exist and one nonetheless engages in false slander, then one should also say that one has neither heard nor suspected it. Why?

Because one instance alone is not seen, the answer is that from this point downward, the six gates are all truly devoid of the three faculties (*indriya*) and are no different from what precedes them.

However, when it comes to the occasion of denial (*apavāda*), the number of faculties cited varies. While the preceding chapter cited three denials and required three sections, citing two denials here constitutes a distinction.

Furthermore, within the subsequent text, there are three variations amidst the complexity; by citing a single faculty alone as the object of denial, a distinction is made. Thus, there are seven gates.

However, when considering the reality of the principle, there are actually no three faculties (*indriya*). The reason the Vinaya text now states that "there is not even one faculty of seeing" is based on the slanderer’s intention:
because they do not wish to bring forward a case based on what was seen, but instead intend to slander using the two faculties of hearing and doubt, they say there is not even one faculty of seeing.

This is intended to manifest their own [reliance on] hearing and doubt as distinct from the expectations of the Saṃgha, thereby generating trust and leading to the formal disciplinary expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) of the person in question. This is...
The Vinaya text explains this from the perspective of the slanderer’s state of mind; therefore, it states that there is no root of "seeing," but it does not say there is no "hearing" or "suspecting.

However, those who have traditionally raised further objections and offered their own interpretations do so not from the standpoint of the initial intention, but rather from the standpoint of a mind that is non-conceptual yet not forgetful.

How could there be perception, mind, hearing, or doubt [regarding such a case]? Therefore, we know it is not so. The same applies to the following sections. Question: In the second phrase, one does not see the offense;
within this, there is a perception of having seen while forgetting the perception of having seen, yet one slanders based on hearing or doubt.

Could there also be no three [factors] in the second mind? Is it for the sake of citing the three types of slander that one does not say "citing the three perceptions" or "forgetting the three perceptions"? The explanation says: "The path."
Within the section on the principles (*li-zhangmen*), there is a state where all three faculties (*trīṇi indriyāṇi*) are absent; therein, one "non-seeing" (*adarśana*) is established.

Now, although the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*) are simultaneously present, if one forgets the three characteristics, how can one not establish one "having-seeing" (*sadarśana*)? If one forgets the characteristic of seeing while maintaining both [the other two], why is it called "one non-seeing"?

Since all three faculties are indeed absent, tell me: when the characteristic of having-seeing exists, one knows that the remaining two exist; yet for now, let us set aside those two. This is why it must be so.

Regarding "forgetting": if one does not forget the two perceptions (*saṃjñā*), it is because one does not falsely deny them. Question: Since both deficiency and simultaneity involve forgetting, why is it said that there is only "one perception of not seeing" (*adṛṣṭasaṃjñā*)?
Answer: Because they are mutually contradictory; since there is no arising [of the former] when the latter is present, it is established as "not seeing."

The perceived object (*nimitta*) and the seeing subject (*darśana*) stand in opposition. Since one cannot hear or doubt a single characteristic, there is no characteristic of hearing or doubting; thus, the characteristics of hearing and doubting are forgotten.

It is as if, when among three [categories] there are not three, one nevertheless speaks of the existence of three characteristics. If this is so, why are the three types of false attribution (*paryāya*) cited, and why does it say there are three characteristics?

Answer: That was stated according to the underlying principle (*yukti*), whereas now the intent of the false attribution is being raised. Therefore, the number [of categories] is established to prevent clever sophistry.

It is for this reason. The subsequent phrases are of the same nature. When interpreted in this way, there are only forty-two phrases; there is no need for further trouble regarding multiple phrases or paired sets.
As for the similarities and differences in the "minor delusions" (*kṣudra-mṛṣā*): the six instances here all involve both object and mind being empty.

By means of the three types of "forgetting the mind," one enters the three types of "not forgetting. These constitute the minor delusions below. Within the first group of six, the first, third, and fifth are narrower than [the others].

Because there is nothing that he does not touch and know, this should be explained in detail in comparison with what follows below. Among the six [types of objects] listed below, the first three and the fifth are reversed in two places;
the second, fourth, and sixth are such that their objects accord with the mind while the seventh opposes it—these differences may be understood accordingly.

The section on the gravity of offenses consists of three parts: first, slandering a bhikṣu; second, slandering a bhikṣuṇī; third, slandering those of lower status. Regarding the text on slandering a bhikṣu, there are three sub-sections. In the first sentence, one slanders a bhikṣu by means of the four pārājika dharmas.
Provided that the internal [accuser] lacks the three roots [of unwholesome intent], it does not matter whether the act was committed personally or through an agent;

in all such cases, it constitutes the offense of false accusation (*abhyākhyāna*). Thus, each of the forty-two items mentioned above, when spoken with clear and distinct words, constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). Is this not so?
*Thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Second, regarding the thirteen grounds for defeat (*pārājika*) according to the rules for bhikkhus: if one lacks the three internal bases [of knowledge] yet slanders a bhikkhu who is truly guilty, it is a *thullaccaya* if the matter is clearly established, and a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) if it is not clearly established.

If one is actually a person guilty of one of the thirteen grounds for defeat, even though they lack the three internal bases, and they suppress the truth and speak of it [falsely], [it is likewise an offense].

Because the bhikṣu harbors such a perception, he incurs only a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), which differs from those who commit the four pārājika offenses through slander; this is because he is a bhikṣu who has defiled the precepts.

If, among the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa] offenses, a bhikṣu slanders one who has committed a *ānantarya* (heinous) or *pārājika* offense, it is also a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, for according to the principle of the teaching, they are equally subject to expulsion.
If the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that for these two—causing blood to flow [from a Tathāgata’s body] and causing a schism in the Saṃgha—one who slanders them incurs a *thullaccaya*.
The remainder constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Because the name [of the offense] is light, this follows that Vinaya;
thus, according to the principle of following the teaching, the third section—excluding the offenses below the category of "defaming a bhikṣu"—is distinguished by its gravity and lightness.

First, I shall explain its meaning through a threefold classification: first, defaming and concealing what is spoken by another; second, self-defamation and concealment; and third, being present during defamation and concealment. This is the first gate.

Question: Why are the two categories of the first and second *pārājika* offenses treated separately as *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pāyattika*, yet both the concealment and the disclosure [of such offenses] result in the same *pāyattika* offense?

Answer: The distinction between the two levels is based on the gravity of the damage to the object of the accusation and the corresponding disciplinary penalty. For example, if one slanders someone regarding the first category (*pārājika*), they are expelled from the community as punishment;

therefore, the slanderer incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If one slanders someone regarding the second category, the person being slandered undergoes the *ābṛhaṇa* (probationary) rite; therefore, the slanderer commits only a *pāyattika*. Thus it is explained in the treatise.

Regarding the concealment (*paticchādana*) and the disclosure (*ārocana*): although the first two categories differ in their gravity, they are alike in that they both involve the destruction of the Saṃgha.
