Concealment is based on internal obstruction; therefore, concealment is always a *thullaccaya*. Disclosure concerns external harm; since even hearing of a gross offense (*sthūlātyaya*) gives rise to deep aversion, the first two [cases] of disclosure are likewise treated as two [types], and both constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Furthermore, they may be distinguished by frequency: the first case of concealment and disclosure is rare, while the second case of concealment and disclosure is frequent; thus, it is concealed.

Having explained the preceding two passages, the question is raised regarding the formal confession of an offense (*pāyattika*). If that is so, why is it that the three lower categories of slander and concealment are all equally declared to incur a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)?
The answer is: while the retributive punishments for slandering the first two categories [of offenses] are unequal, they are both purified through confession.

Although the translations for the three lower categories differ slightly, their retributive punishments are minor; therefore, they are equally declared to incur a *duṣkṛta*. If one slanders the fifth category, one likewise incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

This is because it is an extremely minor offense. Question: Regarding the three stages of the offense of slandering, and the two categories of concealing and speaking [the truth], the formal determination of the offenses differs.

Why is it that [acts such as] disparaging, doubting, and not accepting admonition all pertain to the five types of offenses yet result in only one category—the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation)? What is the reason for this?

Answer: Regarding slander, the basis for punishment is established by explaining the gradations of concealment. These distinctions are made based on the non-destruction of the *dhuta* (ascetic) qualities;

thus, there are differences because they all pertain to offenses. However, disparagement and doubt are general categories. They refer to general objects rather than specific gradations, nor do they focus exclusively on the offense.

For example, regarding the offense within the "Seven Dharmas of Disparagement," if it were only a single category, how could there be a distinction? How could there be a reduction in penalty based solely on that? As for those who do not accept admonition:
This is also because it does not involve formal punishment. Regarding the second point: one only previously slandered others and did not previously slander oneself.

Upon hearing evil, who would willingly slander themselves? The same applies to self-proclamation. If that is so, the meaning of "self-concealment" (*paticchādana*) is manifold; why then are only seven types concealed?

Why is only one category considered a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing)? Answer: This is not based on rarity. The number must be determined according to the *duka* (pairs) [of categories]. There is more and less [in their application].

This concludes the middle section. Because one conceals many *duṣkṛta* offenses while concealing few for oneself, it is so stated. Regarding the third section, there is mutual slander and concealment;

since the text speaks only of one case occurring before the assembly, the subsequent analysis of slandering a nun is also explained in the same manner as before. Among the ten [offenses], this refers to slandering a nun.

One incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if a monk slanders another monk, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if he slanders a nun or any of the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a nun slanders another nun, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if she slanders a monk, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if she slanders any other assembly, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Regarding the principle of having an object and a perception: where the text does not explicitly state this, it is omitted.
Among the cases of non-offense, "speaking the truth" refers to stating the reality of the faculties, such as saying "I saw" when one has actually seen, and so forth.
The Ninth Precept on Groundless Slander: This precept requires a real basis;
that is, there must be a perceived root regarding the matter at hand. One takes that perceived matter and uses it to slander another person.

Although the perception may correspond [to the object], if the actual facts do not correspond, it is termed "groundless" (*amūlaka*). Even if one speaks of having seen, heard, or so forth, if it is based on such [a false perception], it constitutes groundlessness. This differs from the preceding precept.

This is included within the middle [category]. As for the previously mentioned conditions for an offense, they are entirely the same as those of the preceding precept; the only difference lies in using a false basis (*amūlaka*).

Because this occurred before the time of the Venerable Upāli, it is said, "We heard this previously. This statement was made to clarify that whereas the previous case involved slandering with groundless charges, the present case involves grounds that are established (*samūlaka*).

The Prātimokṣa Sūtra consists of seven points: first, the person who has committed an offense; second, the mind of malice; third, falsely attributing a grave offense based on another's conduct; fourth, the purity of the person being slandered;
fifth, the groundless and serious accusation; sixth, the self-accusation; and seventh, the formal determination of the offense.
The middle and upper sections of the extensive explanation may be understood [by the reader]. The fourth and sixth [sections] are omitted and not explained.

Regarding the "diverse categories" (*nānābhāgīya*), the third, fifth, and seventh sections below are explained together. As for the text on the characteristics of slander regarding diverse categories: first, it clarifies the nature of the offense of slander regarding diverse categories;

second, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the gravity of the offense. Within the preceding text, there are five types of divisions. One is "different realms and different categories," as follows:

Explanation of the conditions: First, it is merely a false perception regarding the faculty of sight; briefly, there is no hearing or doubt. Second, if one does not commit a lesser offense, this explains the distinction between different categories.
Third, regarding "impurity," this explains the distinction by means of another person. Fourth, regarding "seeing while originally a householder," this explains the distinction of time.

Fifth, regarding "one's own speech," this explains the four phrases within the category of offenses involving false accusations. First, explaining the first two cases where one does not commit a *pārājika* offense: [accusing someone of] slander.

It is said that [if one] commits a *pārājika* offense; next, two cases involve a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. To falsely accuse [someone] of committing a *pārājika* offense constitutes another case; thus there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Alternatively, the first four and two sentences refer to accusing someone of the six lower offenses while claiming they committed a *pārājika*. The second and third pairs refer to seeing someone commit the six lower offenses and falsely accusing them of a *pārājika*.

This is based on the other six types of views, namely, intentionally stating that it was a different category. One should understand other cases by analogy. Regarding hearing [of an offense], it refers to the six lower offenses.

If one suspects and utters the six types of slanderous speech, one commits a *pārājika* offense. Taken together, there are four sets of six. Those not explicitly mentioned in the text are abbreviated.

Regarding the four permutations among different persons (*pudgala*), the first two involve slandering one who is impure with the superior faculty (*indriya*) of one who is impure; the subsequent two involve [slandering] one who is pure with the superior faculty of one who is pure.
To slander that which is impure as pure; furthermore, the text states directly: "By means of this person's affairs, one slanders based on the principles of another.

Both cases involve the general citation of the three roots of error regarding different categories (*visabhāga*). At other times, only seeing and hearing are cited; when referring to the period before one was ordained as a monk (i.e., while still a householder), doubt is generally not mentioned.

This is because, if we hypothetically assume the case of being situated within a sound, it is restricted to the faculty of hearing, for the other two faculties are not objects of direct confrontation.
The Tenth Precept: The Prohibition Against Schism and Disobeying Admonition.

From here below is the second section concerning the precepts for protecting the teachings of the Saṃgha, beginning with the admonitions. This is analyzed through four gates: first, the distinction between admonishing and not admonishing;
second, the matters for which one is admonished, namely schism and so forth; third, the number of established precepts; and fourth, the clarification of the gravity of disobeying admonitions.
[This section is] weighty. It also explains the meaning of whether [the offense] is raised or not raised.
Within the first gate, there are three sub-gates. First, regarding the number of formal admonitions, both general and specific: there are seven types of bhikṣus.

The nuns have thirteen; together with the [other] twenty rules for formal admonition (*saṃvāsanīya-śikṣāpada*), there are thus twenty admonitions in total. However, regarding these various admonitions:
since the seven admonitions for bhikṣus apply equally to both communities, they constitute fourteen; the nuns have six additional ones, hence the total of twenty.

The second [category] concerns the formal resolution (*jñapti*) in the presence of the Saṃgha. This refers to the precept regarding admonition by the Great Saṃgha. There are five types of "in the presence of the Saṃgha" and two types of "in private.

The two types of "in private" apply to both monks and nuns; the remaining eleven cases concern nuns who violate the admonitions of the Saṃgha. If one wishes to explain this, there are six distinctions between the two types of admonition—formal and in private:

first, the difference in those who offer the admonition; second, the distinction in the legal procedures (*dharma*) employed; third, the difference in the location of the admonition; fourth, the inequality of the matters being admonished; fifth, the attainment... [text truncated].

Regarding the distinctions among offenses, there are six points concerning the extent of the precepts. Within the first category, the status of the person, there are four distinctions: first, the difference between the ordained and the laity;

second, the distinction between those who possess the full precepts and those who do not; third, the difference in gender within those possessing the full precepts—referring to the two assemblies of monks and nuns;

and fourth, the variation in the number of individuals within these two groups—referring to a single person versus a multitude of monks. Second, regarding the category of the dharma, there is only one.
This refers to the formal act of "silencing" (vācanīya-karman). As for this single dharma of karman, it exists only within the context of a formal monastic admonition (saṃgha-vācanīya).

If one considers the act of silencing itself, it applies universally to both the assembly (saṃgha) and private settings (rahasya), as there are two categories of status: first, those established by formal ritual (kriyā-dharma) and those that occur naturally;

second, the distinction between minor and major offenses. These meanings may be understood by analogy. Regarding the fourth point, the difference in the matters being admonished: all matters within a formal monastic admonition consist of committed transgressions. Within private admonitions, however, there are two types.

First, regarding the offense committed upon a single admonition: since the offense is established only when it is completed, "not accepting an admonition" constitutes this [offense]. Second, regarding the offense of ceasing upon a second admonition:

because the offense is incurred once the words are fully understood, "rejecting exhortation to study" constitutes this [offense]. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: the matter of "not accepting an admonition" applies to both the prohibitive (niṣedha) and the prescriptive (vidhi) aspects.
Because the matters of admonition concern the seven groups [of offenses], one may refuse the exhortation to study [the first group] by being intent solely on avoiding transgressions;
for because one is unwilling to study, one may likewise refuse the exhortation to study. Furthermore, such a person treats others with contempt and does not accept instruction;

yet the root of the precepts is not about refusing admonition, as the text itself does not require a sincere mind, but rather establishes the offense based on the actual fact [of refusal]. When interpreted in this way, private admonition applies only to one case, namely, when one does not...

Regarding the acceptance of admonition, the matter pertains to both cessation (*sthiti*) and action (*kriyā*), because the subject of the admonition applies across all seven classes of offenses (*sapta-varga*).
Thus, among the *pārājika* offenses for a bhikṣu, this one is excluded, leaving only six; for a bhikṣuṇī, one is likewise excluded, leaving only twelve.

When the two assemblies discuss the eighteen rules concerning admonition, there are five distinctions regarding the resulting offenses. Among these, there are two [specific points]: first, the distinction between light and heavy, and the number of offenses.
Second, regarding the precedence and sequence of the offenses: first, concerning the number [of offenses]. This refers to the offense of violating advice.
If categorized by their specific names according to the ultimate result (*niṣṭhā*), there are only four: *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *pāyattika*.

If including the preliminary means (*upāya*) and collecting them by name, there are five; adding one *duṣkṛta* makes six. If these five names are further divided by type and by cause and effect, there are ten offenses.

Just as the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses each have four [subdivisions] because they are incomplete when divided into *sthūlātyaya*, so too the two *pāyattika* (saṃghāvaśeṣa) offenses each have four [subdivisions] when divided into *duṣkṛta*.

Because there are the [offenses of] sincere admonition and the violation [of the rule] regarding the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*), there are ten [offenses] in total. Among these sixteen, in the case of the four *sthūlātyaya* within the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, there is one *pāyattika* and three *duṣkṛta*;

in the case of violating the admonition of the Saṃgha, there are two *pārājika*, two *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one *pāyattika*, one *sthūlātyaya*, and one *duṣkṛta*, and so forth. However, regarding the *pāyattika* for violating the Saṃgha’s admonition...

If the mind is truly [guilty], one incurs the actual offense (*pārājika*); in other cases, the determination is made based on whether the mind is insincere (*mṛṣā*). Question: Why is it that when the mind is insincere, there are distinctions of gravity and lightness? Answer:

One explanation is that this is because the deep prevention (*saṃvara*) and the limits of restraint are differentiated accordingly. Furthermore, it may be because one violates one or two admonitions, thereby resulting in *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

*Pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are the "ruination" (*avaśeṣa*) of the precepts; since they are the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for such ruination, they are also considered insincere in intent. Second, regarding "shifting forward or back": the matter is concluded through private deliberation.
This is because there are no individual lives that may be violated. It is like the precept regarding private admonition (*raho-anusāsana*);

it speaks of monastic admonition (*saṃgha-anusāsana*) as a formal delimitation of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), and thus does not concern the specific matter itself. Sixth, regarding the number of established precepts: private admonition applies generally;

wherever such admonition is required, regardless of whether the person is dependent on others or independent, one precept is established in total. Because the scope of the matter is broad, the established precepts are few. Monastic admonition, however, follows the specific matter; therefore, there are many.
"Many matters" refers to the fact that the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* (the section on the establishment of precepts) is extensive. It is divided into six sections above and eleven below;

this corresponds to the attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the two types of breaking [of the vows]. Among these various admonitory precepts (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) listed below, it should be understood that the first three are missing from within the eleven.
Third is the statement regarding formal admonition and non-admonition. If one speaks in private to admonish, this must be done in all cases; therefore, the text describes mutual admonition.
Regarding those who do not accept admonition, if their intent is insincere, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense; if their intent is sincere, it is the fifth [offense].

Furthermore, even in matters of violating admonitions within this context, one must still provide formal admonition; thus the text says: "Do not be censured by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense. Therefore.
It is known that verbal admonition applies to all cases. Regarding the statement that "monastic admonition" possesses four meanings, there are none that do not possess them.

As for the four meanings: first, inherent evil; second, public exposure; third, the collective Sangha; and fourth, collateral injury. The first three meanings can be understood. Regarding "collateral injury":
in the preceding nine precepts, right and wrong are clearly delineated, with no room for dual oversight; thus, it collaterally injures the Sage.

Regarding the teachings: this distinction between right and wrong was not originally established. Since the faults of many who recognize [the truth] have become manifest, why need one provide admonitions and instruction to such individuals?

These four types of precepts and so forth all harbor injuries; their verbal expressions appear similar, yet they indiscriminately conflate the two teachings of principle and practice. Right and wrong are intermingled, making it difficult to distinguish the true from the false.

It is necessary to provide admonitions and instruction so that right and wrong may be clearly understood. Those who harbor views different from these are deluded and ignorant; they must abandon their thoughts and turn toward [the truth].
"Excellent. Since one abandons the heterodox and follows the orthodox, it is necessary to offer admonition, as in the first two rules of admonition.

To 'rely upon and wound' refers to relying on and wounding the Tathāgata’s teaching of the four reliances by proclaiming what is similar [to the Dharma]. Because they cling to the name of practices such as alms-seeking, though the names are identical, it is called 'relying upon and wounding. Regarding those who defile families and slander the Saṃgha:

this refers to the case where six persons act together, yet some are expelled while others are not—this is to be understood according to the fourth rule of training. To 'rely upon and wound' the Śākya clan means to treat them with contempt."

The meaning of "leaning upon" (*niśraya*) as it pertains to the monks must be explained in detail. For such a purpose, the Saṃgha must perform an admonition (*saṃjñapti*); if this is lacking, there is no admonition. Now, the question arises:

why is it that the [first] nine offenses are not subject to the same admonition as the nine *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (requisites) offenses? It is because they share the same causal conditions for the arising of the offense.

Thus, while the offenses of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension from the community) are all generated through the four causes following the admonition, the first nine acts are settled immediately upon their commission. Therefore, these [latter] are concluded in this manner.

That is to say, regarding all matters, if one possesses the four conditions, one must admonish them for their transgression and incur the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. In cases such as "relying on others" or "causing injury," there is no need for formal monastic admonition;

rather, because the gravity of the matter warrants it, one incurs the offense by acting directly. Although these cases may be subject to admonition, failing to do so constitutes a violation identical in status to a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Therefore, they are grouped together in this section.

The second [section] concerns the matters for which one offers admonition (*codanā*). First is the general explanation: Generally speaking, regarding "admonition," there are two factors: first, the person for whose sake the admonition is raised, who possesses the two states of delusion and awakening;

second, the matter for the sake of which the admonition is raised, which consists of what has already occurred and what has not yet occurred—this can be understood from the detailed exposition. Second is the specific explanation of the matters for which [the admonition is given]:

this refers to the formal text (*vibhaṅga*) concerning "schism in the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*), which will be explained when we reach that section. [This also includes] slandering the Saṃgha and evil [actions].
The nature [of these offenses] does not require further elaboration.

Regarding the third point, the establishment of the number of precepts: one asks, "The first two cases involve violating advice, for which two precepts are established; as for the remaining offenses such as slandering the Saṃgha, are they established based on a single principle?

The answer is: "The matter of schism in the Saṃgha is of great magnitude and cannot be established independently; it requires the presence of a principal and its associates, like a shadow following a form, before it can be constituted."

The offense is established. Therefore, when the leader of the admonition does not abandon their contravention—as was the case when the four companions assisted the Sangha by providing counsel and clarifying right from wrong during the initial formal act of admonition—the second [stage] is prescribed because they persist in their refusal despite being exhorted;

the remainder is accomplished alone, and thus there is only one [stage]. Furthermore, the variations in combination and number depend upon the sagely intent; the principle is not uniform in every instance. As it says:

Regarding the recitation of mantras, the rule of having finished eating (*pātra-pūrṇa*), and so forth, these are established as two categories: one's own and that of others. As for the precept against smearing or anointing the body with substances, whether performed by oneself or taught to others, seven rules are established.

For a *bhikṣu*, there are seven; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, there is only one offense of expiation (*pāyattika*). Among the four offenses of censure (*nihsargika-pāyattika*) for a *bhikṣuṇī*, one concerns "fine garments" (*sukumāra*).
Thus, it is known that these are not fixed. In the present case, it is because of the presence or absence of a companion that this is so.

The fourth category: [cases where] one equally defies the Sangha’s admonition. In these matters of communal discipline, these four cases are grave; yet they do not require formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).

Conversely, *thaḷakkhāyika* (defiance through silence) is light, yet it requires formal treatment and censure. One interpretation holds that in the first two instances of breaking the Wheel of Dharma (*cakrabheda*), the objective matter is great and the Sangha’s intention to admonish is grave;
thus, both the matter and the admonition are grave, resulting in a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In the latter two admonitions regarding the precepts, although the matter...
It is not a grave offense, yet one incurs two transgressions. Just as an evil deed defiles a family, one commits a root offense, which may range from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, by slanderously accusing the Saṃgha in an irrational manner, one commits a *dukkaṭa*. As these faults accumulate and increase, the consequences of such actions are not insignificant.
If one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions, one also incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. One of evil character who rejects the Saṃgha may also commit any of the six lower offenses;

furthermore, by violating the private admonition, relying on oneself to insult others, and allowing faults to accumulate and increase, if one does not relinquish them after three admonitions, one likewise incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This is explained as being of minor gravity (*laghu*).

If one intends not to manifest the Way, the matter is not considered grave. Furthermore, it is said that as long as one has not yet committed a root offense (*mūlāpatti*) and there is no further accumulation of such acts, the deed is minor;

therefore, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for violating an admonition. If this were so, then since Devadatta was the leader, his breaking of the Saṃgha would constitute a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, which is truly grave;

thus, it would be logical that violating an admonition in that case results in a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension). However, the four companions [of Devadatta] committed only minor offenses, which are indeed subject to confession. Yet, [if they too violated an admonition,] it would likewise [be a *duṣkṛta*].

The offense for refusing admonition should be light; however, because it does not relinquish [the position], the guilt is equal to that of Devadatta. Furthermore, when a nun stands as an ally, she is like a shadow or an echo that obstructs the Sangha;

she merely accumulates defilement and cannot bring about a final schism. Since this matter is based on the true Sūtra, the offense for refusing admonition should be light; yet, for this reason as well, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Moreover, within the context of a single person’s admonition, there are seven categories (*sapta-nikāya*) of offenses regarding the matters being admonished; therefore, the refusal of admonition constitutes one category of *pāyattika*.

Regarding the offense: based on this textual evidence, it is not necessarily the case that the gravity of the offense is determined by the weight of the action itself; rather, the classification of the offense—whether it is elevated or diminished—is determined by whether the mind [of the offender] is insincere or sincere.

Therefore, in our correct interpretation, the gravity of the offense depends on the reality or unreality of the intention. Regarding these four precepts, the person being admonished clearly understands the nature of their own actions and knows that they are not being admonished by the Saṃgha.
Consequently, they refuse to speak and disobey the command of the Saṃgha; because this involves a transgression of the communal legal spirit, it constitutes a grave violation.
"Admonition" refers to what Khaṇḍadravya said: being deluded by desire and clinging to it as real, one claims that one's own view is [the truth].

This is "admonition by the Saṃgha," because it is not the case that [the offense] was not committed. To violate the admonition of the Saṃgha is a verbal transgression; violating the admonition constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. Furthermore, regarding the object of the admonition...
Evidence from the facts: For instance, in cases such as Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha through unrighteous conduct, the first three offenses are grave while the fourth is light.

How much more so when one disregards admonition—how could one not yield? If the mind is insincere, the offense is grave; if the mind is sincere, it is light. Furthermore, this applies even within the context of a single person offering admonition.
If the mind is insincere, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if the mind is sincere, it is a *duṣkṛta*. How much more so when it concerns the admonition of the Saṃgha?

One does not determine the gravity [of the offense] based on whether the mind is insincere or sincere. Question: How is it known that this is insincere and that is sincere? Answer: This precept specifically states: "After my parinirvāṇa..."
It may be given a name; therefore, one knows that these words regarding the precepts below are truly false, while only this is true, and all else is deceptive.
Thus, one knows they are not the same.

To name "counseling" (*kṣepa*) as "formal accusation" (*utksepa*) is a lenient interpretation of the Vinaya. The subsequent text also states: "Do not be formally accused by the Saṃgha. This applies equally to both parties; originally, there was no need for such questioning.

What is being questioned here refers to the inquiry regarding formal disciplinary action (*daṇḍakarma-utksepa*). The statement that Liṭa (*Liṭa*) spoke of his desire (*chanda*) possesses a meaning that accords with human sentiment.

It is clear that they must also be suspended. Why are they not suspended? The answer is: if one considers whether they are appropriate or inappropriate, it is as explained in the *Dvīsu-vardhana* (Increase by Two); however, if one relies on the actual performance of the rite, [they are not suspended].

Just as with the *codanā* (reproach), this now clarifies the *pratisaṃharaṇīya* (admonition). Why is it raised [as a separate category] next? If that is so, the same applies to the *utkṣepaṇīya* (suspension); why is it raised [separately]? The answer is:

Because there is no basis for a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), one does not proceed with a suspension; this is because both following [the instruction] and refusing a rebuke constitute a *pācittiya* offense.

This is merely explained as a case of "following" (*anuvattana*), which is only a *dukkaṭa* and not a *thullaccaya*; therefore, a suspension is not carried out. This refers to a case where, according to principle, a suspension should be administered; it is not necessary to explain this here.

If that is so, then the rules for censuring those who defile the family (*kuladūṣaka*) should have been explained [here]. Answer: This is because they were intended to clarify the slander occurring at the time of the formal censure;

When it is said here that there is "no raising," this refers to the case of Liṭṭha, meaning that there is no third type of raising; it does not mean that the first two types of raising do not exist. The first two cases involve the schism of the Saṃgha, wherein the group is divided and departs. If one were to subject such a person to formal censure (*ukṣepa*), it would not constitute an effective remedy.

In the four lower *ekottara* cases, one establishes the taking up of the Three Jewels; the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is minorly auspicious. If the third [condition] is lacking, or if no formal admonition is provided, there is no transgression of the admonition;

however, there may be a transgression of the private admonition, constituting a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). Furthermore, if one obtains the first two conditions, one incurs the offense of the preparatory effort for schism (*saṃghabheda-prayoga*).
If the Sangha’s admonition is not successful, and one knows it will not be successful, there is likewise no transgression of the admonition; there is simply the preparatory effort for schism.
Regarding the ultimate offense: if one acts with a mind that conforms to the Dharma, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for rejecting [the admonition], as the fourth condition is lacking.

If one renounces [the course] before the formal announcement (*ñatti*), there is no offense for violating the public admonition, though there is an offense for violating the private admonition. If one renounces after the announcement is completed, one incurs one *pācittiya* (offense of expiation).

Likewise, if one renounces after the second announcement but before the third is finished, one incurs four *pācittiya*s. The absence of the fifth condition may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

From here on, the text is explained. This major section consists of two parts, as in the first precept. Furthermore, the threefold textual structure within the formulation of the precept is likewise identical.

Regarding the narrative of the origin (*nidāna*), there are two parts. From the beginning up to the point where the censure is concluded, it should be understood that this admonition does not arise in isolation; it must necessarily have a specific purpose.
Therefore, the first section correctly clarifies matters such as the schism of the Saṃgha; this is the purpose for which the admonition is intended.

Since there is the matter of a schism, it is necessary to formally admonish the Saṃgha to distinguish right from wrong and reveal what is appropriate and what is not. Thus, the second section—from "The Buddha having spoken" onwards—concerns the formal execution of the admonition according to the Dharma.

Although [the monk] has transgressed, he has not yet committed an offense; he has merely given rise to outflowing faults. This initial text is further divided into two parts: the first extends to "not eating fish."

The preceding section has already clearly demonstrated the breaking of the Saṃgha; this is the subject for which the admonition is intended, as its transgressions are fully evident and must be formally censured.
Therefore, the second section concerning the many bhikṣus distinguishes that censure. The preceding text consists of five parts:

first, from the beginning up to "pure conduct," it identifies the person capable of breaking the Saṃgha; second, from "the Buddha was at Rājagṛha" onwards, it describes the instruction of King Ajātaśatru as the external condition.
Regarding the Buddha’s disciples: third, because the Buddha rebuked him for not handing [the leadership] over, he took this as a pretext to manifest his intent;

from Devadatta, he descended into the grave to seize the position of preeminence, harmed the Buddha, and killed others. Fourth, his evil reputation cut off his gains, and he conspired with those who ate separately;

the Buddha then established prohibitions, forbidding the eating of separate groups. Fifth, he gave rise to these thoughts and established a false Triple Gem below, thereby destroying the wheel of the Saṃgha.

In the first section on the person, there are two parts: first, the circumstances of his renunciation; second, the account of his prior ordination of Upāli and others, followed by his renunciation, reception of the precepts, cultivation of the path, and attainment of realization.
The former section further divides into two: first, the cause for the arising of [the Buddha’s] thought. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When the Father King saw that his son surpassed the thousand disciples of the Brahmin Kaundinya in the Way, yet their outward appearance was not as beautiful, he then ordered one from each of the noble families among the Śākyas..."
People went forth from home to serve and protect him; therefore, it is said that "the Śākyas have gone forth.

In the second period, there were two brothers among the sons of the Śākyas, starting from [the elder] below, who lamented the lack of those who had gone forth and joyfully sought ordination under the Teacher. This section contains four parts:

first, it clarifies how Nanda and Upananda were the first to weary of worldly life; second, it correctly explains the translation of the Śākyas, beginning with Ānanda, as they gathered together in great numbers out of joy.
He was about to approach the various holy ones. Third, after each had bathed and purified themselves, they proceeded forward to pay their respects.
Fourth, from "Having addressed the Buddha" onwards, he formally requests ordination. The preceding text has two parts: first, the account of Nanda’s renunciation as the primary subject;

second, the account of Bhadrika. The text concerning Nanda has three sections: first, it clarifies his life as a layman, enjoying himself according to worldly customs; second, from "Mahānāma" onwards... [text fragment].

Having yielded the position to others so that they might have a place to turn to—Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was the first to do so. He declined three times before departing. There are three parts to the text:

the first three requests and the three suppressions. The text says: "How much more so for those separated while alive? If death—which is most base—still makes one unwilling to part, how much more so for life, which is precious?
How could one permit such separation? Furthermore, even death, which is most difficult to avoid, he still wished to suppress [the desire for].
[The Buddha] accepted. How much more so would he allow you to leave me? The two mothers, reflecting on this, devised means to restrain him.
Having completed their reflections, they spoke words of entreaty to hold him back. Regarding the second section, Udayibhadra, there are two parts:

first, they mutually entreated and exhorted him, revealing that he had left his mother to go forth due to them; second, at the time of Udayibhadra, they requested him to stay and refrain from going forth, concluding with worldly speech.

The preceding passage consists of five sections: first, the three exhortations and three refusals by Bhadrika; second, from "Nanda" onwards, using himself to urge him, which explains the reason for the exhortation;
third, from "He replied" onwards, the reason for the blue lotus as a pledge; fourth, from "Nanda" onwards, expressing his own intent to exhort;
fifth, from "Bhadrika" onwards, accepting the exhortation and taking leave of his mother. The structure of these three [sections] is as before. Second, the Śākyas.
Regarding those who gathered like clouds: Nanda and Upananda made a mutual agreement that it was permissible [to leave the world]. Subsequently, the other six Śākyaputrīyas suddenly also went forth.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, these seven Śākyaputrīyas—namely, Nanda, Upananda, Ānanda, Nandika, Devadatta, Bhadrika, and Kimbila—previously established a covenant, vowing that whatever they did, they would not act contrary to one another. Nanda’s mind was inclined toward [the world], while Upananda...
He did not comply. [The Buddha] spoke again, summarizing the essential points, whereupon he finally gave his consent. The two men entered into an agreement; the six [princes] likewise followed suit.

Thus, all the Śākyas together went forth from the household life. Third, proceeding to the city gate: the first instance of going out of the city and proceeding is described in the text as being like that of the previous day;
comparing the past with the present. Second, the loathing and abandonment of chariots and robes: this refers to the passage beginning with "recompensing Upāli," and so forth.

He abandoned his treasures and followed after him. At all four times of day, the various attendants went together to present offerings. A second time he addressed the Buddha, sincerely seeking ordination. The second section on leaving home has three parts:
first, leaving home and receiving the precepts; [second,] the Buddha ordaining the five men; and third, the remaining three having no karmic affinity.

Therefore, other elders were saved by [the Buddha]. Furthermore, it was to stop slander that [the Buddha] did so. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, eight people—including the Buddha himself—were saved together.

Thus, the text says: "The Buddha first saved the seven persons, and afterwards [he saved] Upaka. In the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, it is said that when the Buddha strongly urged him, he first saved Upatiṣya.
When the sons of the Śākya clan received this exhortation, the earth first shook as they were saved; the mountain of their arrogance collapsed. Therefore...
[The Buddha] dispatched [Ānanda] to clarify the path and achieve realization; next, he dispelled doubts and facilitated universal transformation.

In the second section, "Seeking the External," within the text there are four parts. First, the transformation of the prince, who gave rise to faith and gathered a following; these two parts may be understood as they appear in the text.
Second, from the passage beginning with Kāśyapa down to Maudgalyāyana’s address to the Buddha: that the Buddha was "incapable" serves to manifest [the truth]. This is [the end of the section].

This should not be considered the ultimate truth. The five sections of the text may be understood as follows. Third, from "At that time" onwards, the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) are shown again to increase faith in his benefits.
Within this section, there are four parts: first, manifesting powers to generate faith, which contains five sub-sections: (1) changing the punishment and preaching the Dharma;
(2) the prince’s fear; (3) speaking words to comfort him; (4) requesting the original punishment be deferred; and (5) increasing his practice of reverence. Second, [he] gains a firm [conviction].
Regarding gain and offerings: three bhikṣus addressed the Buddha. Fourth, after the Buddha had finished speaking, he established a rule to examine the mind; there is a teaching with a parable.

Fourth, from "King Māgadha" onwards, [it describes] how jealousy caused him to lose his supernatural powers and seek out the assembly of monks; the fourth section consists of four passages of reproach for not handing over [the teachings].
First, the Buddha’s reproach was grave; he lost his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). A "cauldron" (*bō*) is the name for a vessel; six *dǒu* and four *chǔn* are called a cauldron.

Second, having already acted, he subsequently thought of seeking [reconciliation] from the assembly. Third, the Buddha rebuked him and would not grant it. Fourth, he gave rise to an "unendurable mind" (*akṣānti-citta*).

Previously, he had obtained gains and offerings, which were a heavy matter that accorded with his desires; now, having lost his powers and being rebuked and scolded, this was the ultimate violation of his heart, and thus he gave rise to an unendurable mind.
