onwards, it is shown that having already conquered all enemies, there is no need for protection, thereby clearly revealing the reality; fourth, from "He told the bhikṣus... onwards, five instances where protection is required are cited to clarify what is not [the case].

One must know that by performing evil deeds in the present, one will later receive the retribution of suffering; therefore, it is said, "one shall know this for oneself later. Precepts are based on the substance of what is received;
views and wisdom pertain to understanding; speech manifests the teaching; and livelihood refers to wrong livelihood. Those outside the law and discipline act in ways that deviate from the Dharma.

The five subsequent repetitions can be understood by analogy. This is based on the fact that what cannot be severed is used to distinguish cause and effect. If one takes the original intent, all are skillful means.
Regarding the second [section], Śāriputra and those below were appointed to deliver the discourse;

this explains the second gate within the text. Within this, there are two parts. First, the appointment to deliver the discourse, which consists of four sections: (1) the appointment to deliver the discourse; (2) the doubts of the śrāvakas...
He requested the Buddha to intervene for his removal. Third, he was dispatched to deliver the message;

this was to demonstrate that it was indeed Devadatta who had acted, and not the Buddha or the Saṅgha, thereby exposing his evil reputation and serving as a remote cause for his punishment. The subsequent passage describes the conditions for his eventual liberation.

From the section on the four assemblies onwards, there is a distinction between those who accepted and those who did not. Second, regarding the instruction to harm his father, the text has six parts; the first concerns the instruction to harm the king.
Second, having awakened to the truth, he deliberated on the matter at the gate during three periods and administered punishment.
Fourth, the guards and those below them reported the matter to the king, stating whether it was permissible or not, that all śramaṇas should not be killed, as the king had previously declared.
The fault did not lie with the Buddha or the Saṅgha; they were displeased with the initial statement. Why was this? It was because Devadatta had instructed the king to harm his father.
1. Although they truly deserved death, because it was said that they should not be killed, Devadatta and the others were likewise not to be executed.
When those disciplined by the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are declared as having committed a capital offense, no further punishment is added; therefore, it is said they "should not" [be killed]. 2.
He addressed the ministers and subordinates, issuing an edict to pardon their transgressions. 3. The King spoke words of partiality.
The fourth section concerns eating separately; it consists of four parts: namely, the raising of faults, the reprimand, and the prohibition.
The fifth section concerns Devadatta’s establishment of a schism; it consists of three parts: first, the initial employment of skillful means;
second, from "Devadatta then went" onwards, his plotting with his companions to establish a false Three Jewels; third, at that time, Devadatta [proposed] the five points, which follows below.
Regarding his evil transformations: he entices and deceives those who are newly trained. Initially, there are two mental states in their minds: first, the intent to cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
second, the mind that prizes fame. The text contains four sections: first, the cause for giving rise to such thoughts; next, the actual arousal of the intent to cause a schism;

next, the mind seeking fame; and finally, the cause for obtaining that fame. Within the second section, there are four parts: first, luring them forward with fame and encouraging them to assist oneself.

1. Refutation. 2. Companions at two times. 3. From "Having heard this... onwards, it indicates that fearing the plan might not succeed, he refuses and does not comply. 4. From "Devadatta said... onwards, it correctly clarifies the formulation of the stratagem:
establishing the three false Treasures. 5. From "At that time, Śrutasoma... onwards, it means that [the opponent] will surely be able to refute [the teaching], so he speaks words of compliance.
Within the text of the third section on formulating the stratagem, there are two parts: first, establishing the three false Treasures; second, "When I have spoken... and so forth.

The following section demonstrates the adherence to the correct practice. The preceding text consists of three parts. First, the true Triple Gem is presented. Second, from "I now" onwards, the false Triple Gem is established.
The phrase "I am a false Buddha, and there are also [others]" refers to the five false dharmas. "Those who delight in renunciation" refers to [the followers of the false path].
The three—Kātyāyana and the others—are the Saṃgha; this the Buddha and the Saṃgha already know. As for the false Dharma, it is not yet recognized.

Therefore, the second [point], "for as long as life lasts," and so forth, up to the fifth, concerns the false Dharma. These three are similar in appearance but distinct. The latter two concern false speech;

while the words are the same, their meanings differ, hence they are called "similar. Regarding the Buddha-Jewel, it is not severed, yet it is falsely said to be severed; thus, this is false speech. Furthermore, if the first three...

To state that one has not received [the precepts] is likewise false speech. Because one has stated what was received, it is called "similar. The latter two cases, if one states what was received, are also similar.

If one does not eat meat, one might as well not eat vegetables, fermented medicines, and so forth; because one states that one has not received [the prohibitions against them], it is called false speech.
Since butter and salt impart flavor, they cause one to abandon the harming of living beings through fish and meat; thus, they are treated together.

1. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are five dharmas to be observed for as long as one lives: wearing the patched robe (*pāṃsukūla*), receiving alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), eating only one meal a day (*aikāsanika*), sitting in the open air (*abbhokāsika*), and observing the dharma of abstaining from meat. If a bhikṣu receives these five dharmas, he will quickly attain *nirvāṇa*.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* lists five dharmas: first, begging for food for as long as one lives; second, being naked and sitting in the open air; third, not eating fish or meat; fourth, not eating... [text fragment].
*Sūtra*: Five things for which salt is not consumed. *Vinaya*: Absence of five dharmas. However, this merely amends the characters, phrasing, and order of the Buddhist sūtras and vinayas.
Third, from "I now uphold this" onwards, it forms the conclusion. Now, regarding the refutation of the second [point], one should say to the bhikṣus:

"To demonstrate the correct method of practice and to manifest that one is certainly able to refute [the opponent]. This text has three parts: first, demonstrating the correct method of practice by again citing the preceding text in response to the specific capacity [of the audience].

It is said that there are two types of people: those who oppose and those who comply. From the third point downward, the merits of the three [stages] are concluded. Regarding the two interpretations of "mind" (*citta*) and "name" (*nāman*):
from the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) onward, their understanding is determined and their resolve is firm like a wall, making them difficult to refute; thus they are called "senior" (*sthavira*).

Those below this level may still be refuted by others, and therefore they are called "junior" (*navaka*) who merely accept with faith. Furthermore, according to the latter interpretation, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have attained patience (*kṣānti*) are forever...
That which is indestructible is called "Elder" (*sthavira*). From this point downward, one's own portion is indestructible while the portions of others may be destroyed;

therefore, these are called "Juniors. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, once the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) has been attained, one is an Elder; prior to that wisdom, there is the sense of being obstructed, and thus one is a Junior.
Next, regarding the second section on the reprimand, there are three parts: first, using the transformation of the Dharma to present the matter to the Buddha;

second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, explaining the four true reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) to reveal that the five dharmas are false desires, so as to cause the bhikṣus to recognize and understand the various forms of the correct;

third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, first reprimanding those who lack the precepts to formally manifest the censure, while questioning the many bhikṣus who did not reprimand them.
"What is this? He replied, "It resembles supervision. Alternatively, what he said has not yet been verified as either right or wrong;

therefore, because there was no formal censure (*pratikṣepa*) regarding the existence of the dharma, he raised the matter and informed the Buddha. Next, the third point is explained: today [the opponent] wishes to sever my four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

By teaching the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*), he manifests five dharmas as being false. Since false dharmas obscure the truth, it is said that he "severs the noble lineages. Question: Regarding all the precepts mentioned above...

If one raises an objection, they should be rebuked. Why is it that this precept first explains the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) to reveal the five dharmas as being correct, and only afterwards does it rebuke?
Answer: Regarding those who have committed offenses mentioned above, these all manifest the collective mind; since there is no room for doubt regarding the rebuke, one therefore rebukes them.

This exposition of the five dharmas and the Buddha’s teaching on the four reliances are identical in meaning though different in expression. If one were to rebuke [the former], it would be as if one were rebuking what was spoken by the Buddha. Thus, one should uphold it.
Delusion increases and one no longer knows where to turn; therefore, the five [factors] are first explained to clarify what is right, and only afterwards are they censured.

Regarding the meaning of the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), there is a fivefold analysis: (1) first, the explanation of the various practices; (2) the establishment of the four [lineages] based on the rules of solitary discipline (*vinaya*);

(3) the sequential order of the methods of practice; (4) the permissions and prohibitions regarding the four methods of practice; and (5) the correct elucidation of the lineages through which one can sever [defilements].

Section on Categories. First Gate: Although the dharmas are numerous, they essentially consist only of various practices. What are called "practices as dharmas" (xingfa) refer to that upon which the four reliances and the eightfold right path depend;

because they produce the rules for practice, they are called "practices as dharmas. What are called "various dharmas" (zhongfa) refer to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*).

If one meticulously adheres to principle and collectively honors the non-dual [truth], only then can the various dharmas be accomplished. When the net is cast and the meaning established, the regulations benefit the Sangha;

hence they are called "the dharmas of the assembly. It is for this reason that both of these are required: if the Buddha were to teach only the methods of practice, there would be no dharma upon which to rely.
Without a dharma to rely upon, by what means could practice be regulated? If practice is not regulated, one will fall into delusion within birth and death. How then can one eliminate evil?

Karma ultimately benefits those on the narrow path. Although one may personally practice the "red" (worldly) virtues, if there are no communal laws (*saṃgha-dharma*), how can one distinguish and receive the assembly?

The "red" [virtues] are the benefit of the Jewel of the Saṃgha; therefore, communal laws are necessary to uphold and guide the transformation of beings. Now, Devadatta also studied under the Tathāgata and taught these two dharmas:
first, he established the five rules as the method of practice, yet he instead opposed the Tathāgata’s four reliances and eight [precepts].
Correct. Second, there is the *adharma-karman* (illegal formal act) which is treated as a communal legal procedure (*saṃgha-dharma*).

In contrast to the Tathāgata’s correct communal legal procedures, if a bhikṣu accepts and adheres to it, this constitutes the full possession of false faith and the complete destruction of the true meaning.
Next, the second section has four parts. First, listing the numbers and explaining the names: these refer to clothing, food, bedding, and medicine. "Dependence" (*niśraya*) means to rely upon.

These four are not themselves the objects of dependence; rather, each serves as a support for another. Therefore, they are all termed "dependences. One relies on these four to sustain oneself and carry out one's practice; hence they are called the "Four Dependences" (*catur-niśraya*).
Furthermore, they are the conditions for giving birth to the noble ones (*ārya*), and later they are all referred to by the term "seed. Second, defining their essential nature.
If distinguished by way of phenomena (*vastu*), it consists of the four objects (*viṣaya*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

If distinguished by way of practice (*caryā*), both the manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) that accord with the fundamental essentials within these conditions are the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). According to the *Cittaviveka-śāstra*, only the unmanifest is taken;
this is stated in view of the formal undertaking (*samādāna*), referring to the unmanifest taught within a mind induced by the wholesome state of non-greed (*alobha*). This is non-greed.
It is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*). Furthermore, there are two types of non-attachment (*alobha*): namely, having few desires (*alpecchatā*) and being content (*saṃtuṣṭi*).

Here, contentment is taken as the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), not having few desires. This is because contentment arises with respect to present objects; thus, one who does not take even a single coin in the present cannot be said to have failed to become a Cakravartin king, for contentment is superior.
Contentment is established as the noble lineage. Thirdly, regarding the establishment of the four [noble lineages]: practice depends upon...
The requisites are provided by the laity; these must be supplemented. Although the conditions for sustenance are many, they are briefly categorized as internal and external matters.

Each requires two types of internal provisions: alms-food and medicine; these two fulfill the internal needs. Clothing and bedding are the two external requisites. The body must be covered with coarse garments, and the path of enlightenment relies upon study;
therefore, the two categories of clothing and bedding are distinguished externally. Furthermore, because the four great elements are subject to illness, there is the matter of sickness.

Because they differ, the internal requisites—food and medicine—are distinct; however, these are combined and discussed collectively as internal and external. Thus, they are called the "Four Reliances.
Furthermore, because they serve as antidotes to the four types of offerings, one cultivates the practice of contentment regarding these four. For this reason, there are only four.
The distinction between the fourth [reliance] and the dhūtas can be understood through comparison.
Next is the third gate. As for what is called "reliance," it is necessary at all times; therefore, it is explained first. For this reason, first one relies on rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*);
clothing manifests the physical form, yet even if one lacks food to sustain the body, one may still practice the Way.

Next, because one must rely on alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*) to provide the conditions for nourishing the Way, one should rely on a dwelling place to practice the Way. Thus, next is the third reliance: relying on those of lower status (*niśraya-adhastāt*). One must also rely on medicine.

The meaning is rarefied; therefore, the four successive sections follow the practice. Although the sequence differs and the dhūtas appear in a disordered order, the arrangement of these four gates is truly due to the Tathāgata’s skillful mastery of the faculties and natures of beings, administering the medicine according to their capacity. This constitutes the supreme practice of contentment.
Retribution serves as a support for strength. Regarding the aforementioned practice of wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), this is intended for those capable of enduring hardship;

it is not prescribed as a universal rule. This is because maintaining the body while remaining free from attachment brings benefit to the long path [of cultivation]. Why, then, is the wearing of robes offered by donors (*dānapati*) permitted? It is because those of lower capacity possess weak retributive power.
If they were restricted to the same practice as those above, it would not accord with their faculties (*indriya*), and thus there would be no merit for the long path. For this reason, the Sage...

The permission to wear robes offered as gifts provides for the sustenance and enjoyment of the body, bringing the benefit of long-term progress on the Path. Because the Buddha permitted this, all three types of persons may receive them;

by relying upon them to cultivate the Path, they all attain union with the Sages. Thus, they are called "Noble Lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*). The remaining three regulations—both prohibitions and permissions—may be understood by analogy.

The fifth section in sequence concerns that which the Tathāgata has taught, which is correct for four reasons: first, it is spoken with a compassionate mind, originally intended to benefit sentient beings;

second, he possesses excellent knowledge of their faculties and natures, providing the path according to their capacities to bring them to maturity; third, because he knows their faculties and natures, he is skilled in understanding what is permitted and what is prohibited.

It is not only for those of middle and inferior capacities; even for those of superior practice who do not possess rag-robes (pāṃsukūla), they are permitted to accept and wear robes offered by others.

Through these permissions and prohibitions, the three grades of practitioners can all proceed toward and realize the state of the Sage. The permissions and prohibitions for the [remaining] three lower categories may be understood by analogy.

Fourth, the Buddha taught that the four practices such as alms-gathering can give rise to the Eightfold Noble Path; therefore, he said that these conditions serve as the seeds for the path to Nirvāṇa and its remote cause.
The Eightfold Noble Path is the lineage of the sages; however, as it is the proximate cause for proceeding toward Nirvana, it is called "Right" when discussed according to the Dharma.

Devadatta is termed "Wrong" because he does not possess these four meanings: first, he was possessed by an evil mind; second, he caused a schism in the Sangha; third, he sought fame; and fourth, [he acted] contrary to the Dharma. Thus, he is designated as "Wicked."

Taking this as the seed [of practice], there are four faults: first, one takes it as the primary cause; second, failing to recognize the nature of one's faculties, one lacks the benefit of cultivating the Path;

third, being restricted by prohibitions alone without opening for progress, it is difficult for those of superior capacity to advance, let alone those of middling or inferior capacity—how could their spiritual potential not be severed?

Fourth, the *Mahā-śāstra* states that when Devadatta taught the Eightfold Noble Path as a proximate cause for Nirvāṇa, it was actually taught as a remote cause; thus, his approach to the Path was contrary and difficult, for he clung to practices such as begging for alms.

That which is a remote cause for *nirvāṇa* is here spoken of as a proximate cause, because it surpasses the entry into the Path via the Eightfold Noble Path and is the most rapid method for overturning false teachings.
For this reason, these seeds are established and brought forth; at the time of practicing transformation, the dharma of death arises and becomes manifest, and thus the True Dharma must be discussed.

Therefore, it is said that the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are severed. What are the four noble lineages from which the noble ones emerge? Through countless skillful means, [the Buddha] has explained them.
Regarding the "approach to contentment with clothing": this refers to praising the superior practice of wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*).
This has two benefits: first, one discards what is like refuse, which is a lowly substance; second, by rejecting fine and soft fabrics, one abandons attachment to one's own body.

Thus, it is called the "approach to contentment. Second, one cannot be plundered by kings, thieves, or greed; it sustains the body for the sake of the Path. Possessing these two benefits, it is praised by the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "I also praise and speak of [these] as equal," this means that even for those of middling or inferior capacity who are attached to robes given by donors, there are likewise two benefits:

first, they sustain the body so that the Path may be cultivated; second, they bring merit and benefit to the donor. Since both the permitted and the prohibited practices lead to the same realization of the sages, the Buddha praised them both equally.
The following three are explained together. By "innumerable skillful means," it is said that "food" refers to begging for alms;
"bedding and requisites" refers to the collection of lower items for sustaining the body; and "medicine" refers to medicinal decoctions. These three are practiced in the higher lands.

Nevertheless, because they give rise to contentment and together lead one to meet the Sages, they are praised by the Buddha. I too have innumerable ways of explaining "food," which refers to opening [the gates of generosity].
The middle and lower classes of monks, as well as those invited for meals; "bedding and seating" refers to the furnishings and requisites within the rooms and stone caves;

"medicine" refers to substances such as ghee and oil that possess the power to treat illness. Because one relies on these four dharmas to ultimately meet with the Noble Ones, they are called the "Noble Lineages" (āryavaṃśa).

The third section, the Text of Reproach, has two parts. First, the text of the inquiry regarding the self-accusation, which may be understood as it stands. Second, from "At that time" onwards, the reproach. Within the reproach, there are three sections: first, the general presentation of the reproach;
second, the specific enumeration of the words of reproach; and third, the general application of the reproach. Within the second [the specific enumeration], there are three sub-sections.
The beginning consists of four phrases. These rebuke his conduct and that which he has abandoned, and exhort him to cultivate relinquishment. Within this section, there are two parts;
the first two phrases rebuke his conduct and that which he has abandoned. Therefore, the text says: "How can you, with these five things, instruct the bhikṣus as described above?"
This is the censure of what has been practiced. Next, from "Devadatta" onwards, is the censure of what has been abandoned;

thus it says, "Do not abandon," and so forth, as above. The second section consists of two phrases: first, it cites the previous practice that was abandoned; second, it exhorts and encourages the cultivation of relinquishment.

Regarding the phrase "Do not employ expedients" and so forth, this cites the previous conduct and exhorts one not to perform it, which is precisely the abandonment of the previous conduct. Furthermore, it says, "You should be in harmony with the Sangha."
Regarding the phrase "the combination and so forth": this refers back to what was previously severed, exhorting one to practice accordingly and to jointly honor [the teaching] like water and milk.
This refers to what the practitioner previously severed. Second, the subsequent words of reproach and exhortation are as follows:

first, the reproach is directed at you for being one who, through non-practitioner-like conduct, has destroyed the harmony of the Sangha; this constitutes the first three phrases. Second, it is you who have severed my four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
The principle of being like water and milk is not the same; therefore, this constitutes the second and fourth alternatives of the tetralemma. For this reason, you would otherwise fall into hell.
Furthermore, if I were to reprove you and instead offer encouragement, it would mean that you have severed those five wrongs and have not broken the harmony of the Saṃgha;

this is precisely the reverse of the first three alternatives mentioned above. It means that you practice the four reliances together in mutual veneration, according to the principle of being like water and milk.
Conversely, by avoiding the first two sets of four lines, one does not fall into hell and attains great merit; therefore, I exhort you. The text is abbreviated where there is nothing to be said.
Thirdly, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, [the text describes] the benefits of reprimanding and admonishing him.

The second major section concerns the administration of the formal act of admonition (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Within the discussion of transgressions for those who disobey, there are again three parts:

first, the Buddha’s instruction that bhikṣus perform the formal act of admonition consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*); second, the Sangha’s execution of the command to carry out the specific admonition, which serves as the basis for the offense of *sthūlātyaya*;

this should be explained in detail in its place, as the application of the method of admonition and exhortation is clearly presented in the "Analysis of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*) for the sake of establishing the gravity of the offense; third, at that time...
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who thereupon explained it in detail. The method of admonition applies universally to all cases of illicit marriage.

As for the question of why the bhikṣus did not rebuke Devadatta when they saw him disobeying their admonitions, there are several interpretations: either there were obstacles above and below [in the narrative], or it is simply a case of textual abbreviation.
From here below is the second section: the detailed formulation that supplements the brief. Question: Why is there no mention of "many kinds of outflows" for those with little delusion?

Answer: This is because the method of admonition is clarified; furthermore, the momentum of the discourse is also briefly indicated. The preceding section on the characteristics of the formulated precepts is concluded.

From here below, the exposition of the *Poṣadha* begins with the first section, which clarifies the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. The second section provides a detailed analysis of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, consisting of five parts:
first, the clarification of the matter for which the admonition is intended; second, the admonition and exhortation by other virtuous bhikṣus in private;

third, that bhikṣu’s stubborn adherence to his own mind and refusal to follow the exhortation; fourth, the monks’ formal admonition to that bhikṣu to induce him to relinquish [his position]; and fifth...
"Does not relinquish" means that [the monk] below disregards the admonition. The first phrase consists of two parts. "If a bhikṣu" identifies the offender, who is the one being admonished.

From "desiring to divide the Saṃgha" onwards, it correctly clarifies the act for which he is being admonished—the division of the Saṃgha. "Desiring to obstruct" restates his initial intention and preparatory effort (*upāya*).
From "having made the effort" onwards, it restates his prior establishment of the Three Jewels as dead and his stubborn persistence in not relinquishing [his position].
That person first approaches and provides a private admonition. This section has two parts. First, citing the initial three phrases from the formal reprimand, it exhorts him to desist;
thus it says, "That bhikṣu should be admonished and must not employ such means," and so forth. Second, from "Venerable sirs, you should grant [him]...

onwards, it cites the second and fourth points from the formal reprimand to exhort them to be as harmonious as water and milk. Although the conduct of the various venerable ones differs, that which they have received...
The teacher is the same; the training in the Dharma is non-dual. In principle, they should be harmonious and without discord, just as water and milk blend together in mutual accord.

Therefore, it is said that they study under the same teacher, like the blending of water and milk. Furthermore, it is said that they are like the blending of water and milk because one does not criticize water for joining with water, nor milk for joining with milk. The third phrase, "those who are bhikṣus," refers to all virtuous bhikṣus.

Regarding such admonition: when various virtuous bhikṣus offer private counsel, if [the offender] persists and does not relinquish [his position], this refers to the bhikṣu Devadatta, who maintains his resolve and resists exhortation.
As for the fourth case, if he relinquishes [his position] after the third admonition, it is well; having heard [the advice], he then complies.

If he stops, he does not cause a schism in the Saṃgha. First, there is no offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for refusing to heed admonition; second, there is no offense of *sthūlātyaya* for causing a schism. Since these two [offenses] are avoided, it is said that "it is good if he relinquishes [the position].

Question: In reality, this is a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Why then is it said that "it is good if he relinquishes it after three admonitions up to the third admonition"?

Answer: This refers to taking the initial motion (*jñapti*) together with the two subsequent proclamations (*karman*). Therefore, it is called "three," excluding the fourth proclamation. That is why it is so stated.

Regarding this, there are two points: first, the distinction between the stages of having committed and not having committed an offense. In the first three cases, the *śeṣa* (residual offense) has not yet been committed; when the third case is concluded, the *śeṣa* is committed. Second, the distinction between light and heavy offenses.

In the first three cases, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*; in the third case, one incurs a *śeṣa*. Therefore, it is said that it is well if one relinquishes [the offense] after the three admonitions, because although the grave offense has not yet been committed, the *śeṣa* has been incurred.

According to the underlying principle, this is actually a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Furthermore, the specific text of the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states: "One commits three dharmas."
Regarding "that which should be relinquished": this refers to the fact that if one does not relinquish these three matters, one enters the state of having committed a grave offense;

therefore, the fifth phrase concludes the determination of the offense. Below this, the root text of the precept is explained in detail. Within the section on the characteristics of a bhikṣu’s transgression, the preceding five points are fully explained:

first, the explanation of the matter for which the admonition is given; second, if a bhikṣu [does not comply], the explanation of the method of private admonition mentioned above; third, if he still does not heed the words, the explanation of what follows above.
1. Refusing to heed admonitions and exhortations. 2. The fourfold formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for resolving the aforementioned monastic admonitions. 3.

From the conclusion of the third proclamation (*karmavācanā*), the resolution of the gravity of the offense incurred. Regarding the first section, the monks may be understood [from the text]. Second, the matter for which the admonition is performed.

I shall now address only the single phrase "the initial mind. Regarding the two characters *yù* (欲) and *zhě* (者), which have not yet been explained, I will first analyze the term "harmonious Saṃgha" (*sāmagrī-saṃgha*).

This is explained by means of two principles: first, using four or more individuals to explain the meaning of the "assembly" (*gaṇa*); second, explaining the term "Saṃgha" itself. As for the term "Saṃgha," it is translated as "assembly" (*zhòng*).

Thus, it is said that "Saṃgha" refers to a harmonious group of four bhikṣus, or ten, or even up to an infinite number. Once this [definition] has been established, the term "Saṃgha" is then analyzed through its constituent members.
The following explains the preceding character "怡" (yi). First, it cites the number of schismatic utterances; thus, it says "eighteen. Second, it lists the names and provides explanations.

Third, "is for" serves as a conclusion. Fourth, regarding "one who dwells in causing a schism," this refers to one who is capable of causing a schism; they will inevitably undergo the legal penalty for death.
In the second explanation, regarding "those who take what is not the Dharma as the Dharma": the Eightfold Right Path is truly upright;
yet, those who cling to it while generating a false understanding are near-cause for *nirvāṇa*—this is called the Dharma of Devadatta, which is taught as non-Dharma.

Those who cannot die five times [in succession] and who generate true understanding through what is non-Dharma, taking that which is non-Dharma to be the law and discipline—those who lack understanding are likewise so in their teaching. Regarding "offenses and non-offenses": as for the term...

Regarding the pulling of hair: the Buddha ordained that it be shaved using a razor. Yet now Devadatta claims that pulling hair constitutes taking life; he asserts that if one does not shave it first, it is not an offense.
This is like harboring evil thoughts in the mind: although it logically contradicts the Dharma, because ordinary persons have not yet been subject to the formal precepts, it is termed "non-offense."

Devadatta taught that transgressions were minor; he claimed that only those acts which obstruct [the path] were grave. Devadatta saw a leaf fall from a *nyagrodha* tree and was reborn among the *dīrghāyuṣka* nāgas;

he then declared, "The sin of killing all grasses and trees is the most serious. Because the karma of the first category (the *pārājika* offenses) is heavy, it results in permanent obstruction for the duration of one's life.

Seeing that Sūtiputra committed his initial act and did not incur a grave offense, Devadatta then asserted that all instances of theft and sexual misconduct are entirely minor offenses involving residual defilement (*sāvaśeṣa*).

One who commits the offenses of the lower four categories does not constitute a permanent obstruction; these are offenses with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*). To speak of them as "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) is incorrect.

Those "without remainder" refer to the commission of the first category [pārājika], which permanently destroys the sprout of the Path; thus it is termed "without remainder. To speak of it as "with remainder" is incorrect. The Mother [Sūtra] says:

"Gross and evil" refers to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the first two categories. If one commits them through body or speech with a mind devoid of shame and dread, one incurs a grave *sthūlātyaya*; this is called "without remainder."
What is grave is said to be non-grave; offenses from the *pāyattika* downward, as well as other *sthūlātyaya* and so forth, are all non-grave yet are said to be grave.

Regarding those practices performed constantly, the "Eightfold Right Path and Five Dharmas" mentioned in the mutual expositions and regulations refers to the prohibitions of the five categories of offenses (*pañca-pārājikādi*).

That which is proclaimed from the golden mouth [of the Buddha] is called a "prohibition" (prajñapti). To say that something is not a prohibition when it is a prohibition, or to say that something is a prohibition when it is not a prohibition, constitutes a misrepresentation.

Regarding those who claim that the five dharmas were not spoken by the golden mouth of the Buddha and thus are not prohibitions: this is the teaching of those who speak erroneously. Those who claim they are prohibitions argue that the four prohibitions are grave while the rest are light;

this is the correct teaching and is therefore called "what was spoken. To claim that the Buddha did not speak these [grave rules], or to speak of their gravity and lightness in reverse, is not the Buddha's teaching.

It is called "non-explanation," yet it is explained as an explanation. If one consults the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā) regarding the explanation of the Vinaya, the Buddha stated there are fourteen [factors].

However, regarding the schism of the Saṃgha, that which is non-dharma (*adharma*) therein consists of five factors of the wrong path (*mithyāmārgāṅga*), while the dharma consists of five factors of the right path (*samyagmārgāṅga*).

The *vinaya* consists of the three branches of the right path; that which is not *vinaya* consists of the three branches of the wrong path. "Offenses" (*āpatti*) are those established by the Tathāgata;
"prior non-offenses" (*pubba-āpatti*) follow what was established by the Tathāgata. Regarding the gravity of the regulations, there are two types: first, gravity of the field (*khetta-garuka*);

second, gravity of the preceding circumstances (*pubba-garuka*). The same applies to minor offenses. One should understand the relative gravity within each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*). As for what is called "with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣa*):
Those [offenses] include the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and so forth. Those without remainder (*avaśeṣa*) are the four *pārājika* offenses. Those that cannot be remedied are the four precepts.
Among the thirteen [other *saṃghāvaśeṣa*], each one individually—if both sides have already been transgressed—cannot be known; the *saṃgha* establishes what is most grave.

The *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (settlement of disputes) *karmavācanā* and so forth are the reverse of these, and are thus called "remediable. There are two kinds of "coarse" [offenses]: one arises from the intention to transgress, and one arises from the offense itself.
Reversing this is called "not coarse. The *Śāstra* says: "That which is not spoken by the Tathāgata and not taught by the Tathāgata, he claims is spoken by the Tathāgata and taught by the Tathāgata;
that which is spoken by the Tathāgata and taught by the Tathāgata, he claims is not spoken by the Tathāgata and not taught by the Tathāgata.
The Tripiṭaka master explains: "The Tathāgata spoke of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)."
The eighty thousand dharma-gates, such as the twenty-two faculties arising through conditions, serve as antidotes to the afflictive conduct of sentient beings.
By means of these dharma-gates, one now contemplates the twelvefold scriptures of the Tathāgata’s teaching. Such phrases were spoken by the Tathāgata;
yet he [the opponent] speaks to the contrary. The treatise states: "That which was produced and practiced by the Tathāgata, he [the opponent] says is not."
"That which is performed and practiced by the Tathāgata is not that which is performed and practiced by the Tathāgata;
yet it is said to be what is performed and practiced by the Tathāgata. The commentary explains: activities that benefit sentient beings are what is performed by the Tathāgata;

entering meditative absorption to experience the bliss of the Dharma and maintaining constant dignified deportment are what is practiced by the Tathāgata. This is stated in reverse as well. These constitute the two pairs below.
The four-line [formula] is derived from the Vinaya. In the Abhidharma and throughout the Vinaya, there are fourteen [sections], totaling nine pairs.

According to those texts, using this Vinaya to expel [the offense], it seems that the Tathāgata’s teaching—what the Tathāgata spoke—is equivalent to this ninth discourse on "speaking" and "not speaking."
That which is performed and practiced by the Tathāgata is what should be constantly practiced and not what is practiced only occasionally.
Since these two are absent among the aforementioned fourteen, people speak of eighteen; this also seems to be a combined enumeration.

Next, regarding the second section on the text for private admonition (*raho-vādanīya*), it mentions the four assemblies; logically, it should apply to all seven [assemblies]. This is because the legal procedure (*dharmakarma*) is not performed separately for each. Regarding the third point:

"If they do not heed the words," what offense is incurred by one who thus rejects the private admonition? Answer: This is merely a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), because there is no formal communal procedure (*saṃghakarma*).

Furthermore, since the matter to be corrected by the person being admonished has not yet been accomplished, and the period for refusing the admonition has not yet expired, one must wait until the matter is finalized.

Lanjiti Chengti asked: "If one violates [the rule] regarding the private admonition by nuns and others, what offense is incurred? He replied: "Although this is not explicitly mentioned in the text, by principle it should be a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Within this context, there are four successive causes and effects: first, schism in the Saṃgha; second, violating the private admonition of a bhikṣu;
third, violating the private admonition of the group of six monks; and fourth, violating the admonition of the Saṃgha. Although these four offenses arise in a sequence, they are four..."
The causes are fully explained, while the results are merely summarized as the remainder. The remaining three groups are not included in this text.

If one considers the cause in relation to the result, the single type of "remainder" refers to the latter of the four causes and the former of the four results; it pertains to the four causes such as *lāntika* and so forth.

Among the four preceding fruits, the latter is distinguished by its reliance on the Dharma, as their specific applications differ. Thus, the sequence of the four causes and their respective stages remains fourfold.

Furthermore, regarding the stages of attaining the fruits, only two—namely, the *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses and so forth—attain the three fruits simultaneously. Therefore, the cause and effect of slandering the Saṃgha and so forth are to be understood by analogy with the fourth [fruit], following the procedure for communal admonition (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) as described in the text.

Fifth, regarding the section on the final determination of the offense for one who does not relinquish [the position], there are two parts. First, the gravity of the offense for personally acting in violation of the admonition;
second, the gravity of the offense for instructing others. This latter part has two sections: first, the determination of the offense for violating the admonition;

second, the matters to be admonished prior to the formal act, beginning with "if one has not yet performed the *jñapti*. Prior to performing the admonition, there is only the *duṣkṛta* (transgression) of preparatory contrariness. Within the preceding text, there are two [sections]; the third is the *karman*...

Regarding "the remainder after the *mardana* (rubbing/grinding) is finished": the conditions are fully present and the gravity [of the offense] is redoubled. If one abandons [the intention] after the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (one motion and one proclamation) is finished, it constitutes three *sthūlātyaya*s (grave offenses), though the specific meaning of the lower limit is missing.

This applies similarly to all admonitions. Question: At the conclusion of the third [proclamation], one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting offense). Is this because the cause and the result are conjoined? It is not so;

as in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is merely by relying on the preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*), the mental application (*cetana*), and the momentum (*vega*), which assist one another to bring about the karma of the subsequent mind.
They increase sequentially. When one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, there are still *sthūlātyaya* offenses remaining that must first be confessed.
This is because the fruits they induce differ according to the varying weight of their karmic intentions; therefore, they do not cancel one another out.

What this Vinaya clarifies is simply that if one commits evil, one incurs guilt in every lifetime, as evidenced by the passage on generating merit. Furthermore, one obtains merit at every step, as stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*: "If one desires..."
Regarding the offense of theft (*steya*), at every step there is a *sthūlātyaya*. This Vinaya also states that once the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) is concluded, three *sthūlātyayas* are incurred;

this clarifies that the offense is committed during the causal process. However, when the result is attained, one observes that the fruit corresponds to its cause. Therefore, in the subsequent Vinaya text, before the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is finished, there is a *duṣkṛta*;
once the announcement is completed, one is directly charged with a *sthūlātyaya*. It does not say that there is a separate *duṣkṛta* to be confessed, even up until the third *karmavācanā*.

[The procedure] concludes. At the time of the *śukra-saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it is not stated that there is a separate *sthūlātyaya* to be confessed; therefore, we know that although there is an offense due to the cause, it is subsumed by the fruit.
Furthermore, the *Jñānaprasthāna* states: "All *sthūlātyayas* are subsumed by the *śukra-saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Also, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

"The preceding *duṣkṛta* is transformed and extinguished, thereby forming the subsequent fruit. Thus, we know that once the three *karmavācanās* are concluded, the four [instances of] *sthūlātyaya* are subsumed.
*Thullaccaya*. Together with the preceding *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the text of the inquiry states only: "After two *karmavācanās* are completed, three *thullaccayas*.

Why, then, does it consolidate four [cases] to come together as an offense? Answer: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "Consolidating four cases is likewise according to this principle. Question: Regarding the first three *thullaccayas*, they must constitute a violation of the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) before they become *thullaccaya*;
if the motion is not yet completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is analogous to the previous text; thus, in the third case, if the motion is not yet completed, it should be a *duṣkṛta*.
It is not a *sthūlātyaya*. Answer: When the *jñapti* (formal motion) for a *sthūlātyaya* has been completed, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;

since the cause is heavy, one obtains [the full offense]. Therefore, when the *jñapti* has not yet been completed, one only incurs a *duṣkṛta*. At the conclusion of the third [announcement], it is indeed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; since the cause is light, one would obtain [only] a light [offense].
Furthermore, because it subsequently borders upon a heavy state, the karma becomes increasingly grave through mutual reinforcement; thus, while the third [announcement] has not yet been completed—

One incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). This is not the same as the previous case. Furthermore, because one wishes to employ the term "favorable" (*śubha*), the cause and effect share the same name; however, because this is a transgression, it is a *duṣkṛta*. One employs "favorable" (*śubha*) [as the name for the result], whereas "faulty" (*aśubha*) is not the same as "favorable.

Because it is an extremely minor offense, one instead uses "favorable" (*śubha*). There are cases where the cause itself is a "faulty" (*aśubha*) *duṣkṛta*: namely, the *duṣkṛta* resulting from the completion of the "white" (*śukla*) *pācittiya*, and the *duṣkṛta* resulting from the completion of the "white" (*śukla*) *pratideśanīya*. There are also cases where the cause itself is a "faulty" (*aśubha*) *duṣkṛta*:

namely, the *duṣkṛta* resulting from the completion of the "white" (*śukla*) *sthūlātyaya*, and the *duṣkṛta* resulting from the completion of the "white" (*śukla*) *pratideśanīya*. There are also cases where the cause itself is a "faulty" (*aśubha*) *duṣkṛta*.

If one does not recite the *pāṭimokkha* at the end, it is a *duṣkṛta*; as with the white [robe], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not recite the first *karmavācanā*, it is a *duṣkṛta* because of the intervention by the formal procedure (*dharma*).
Furthermore, it is because both subsequent acts constitute the cause for a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding the text's mention of "abandoning," this refers to the three *sthūlātyaya*s;

it is not a matter of abandoning the intention. There is indeed this *sthūlātyaya* offense. Having applied the preliminary means, one acts in violation of the exhortation; by virtue of that subsequent mind, it is designated as the preceding mind.

It is an offense. Therefore it is said: "If one abandons [the intention], it is a *sthūlātyaya* (*thullaccaya*). All instances where one has not yet formally announced (*jñapti*) through expedient means, such as desiring to block [the path] and so forth, up until the point of not abandoning [the intention], are all *duṣkṛta* (*dukkaṭa*).

This means that from the initial thought through the performance of the transformation and so on, they are all [offenses]; hence it says "all. Furthermore, they may vary in duration according to the time;

thus, up until before the formal ritual (*karman*) is performed, it is called "all. This is because it is included within the text of the [Vinaya] sections; therefore, one should know that it is subsumed therein.

The *Vinayavibhaṅga* (Commentary on the Monastic Code) explains the three types of instruction for persons: first, instruction for bhikṣus; second, instruction for bhikṣuṇīs; and third, instruction for the lower assemblies (*avarāḥ saṃghāḥ*).

There should be an admonition, and the formal procedure for performing the admonition consists of five phrases, as in the text of the *Cīvaravastu*. While there are various other categories of admonitions, those not explicitly mentioned in the text are omitted. The explanations for the remaining categories of assemblies may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the non-offenses, they are relinquished at the first utterance; this generally allows for three types, namely, the non-offenses of the *pāyattika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and so forth.

Therefore, the subsequent five cases—such as "unlawful and separate" (*adharma-vinirbhoga*) and so on—and "unlawful and contrary to the Vinaya" (*adharmam avinayam*), are like the first of the seven [cases] and the first of the six "non-[offenses]" (*na-ṣaṭka*) respectively.

Regarding the method of admonition (*codanā*), it is not permitted to leave it open-ended. There is no *sthūlātyaya* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense [in failing to admonish]; alternatively, three [offenses] may be permitted.

If those evil associates act for the sake of benefit, there is no offense of causing schism (*bhedaka-śikṣāpada*), and thus there is no violation of the admonition. Furthermore, regarding the six cases where it is not permitted to leave it open:

because the offenses of various admonitions pertain to individuals, the formal act of the Saṃgha (*saṃghakarma*) is employed; since the individual case differs from the general rule, it is merely reduced in the subsequent instances.
The precepts for those who deliver others belong to the Saṃgha; therefore, separate matters are used to open the way for the Saṃgha as prescribed in the text.
One should have faith in one's parents, the various emperors, great ministers, and so forth.
The eleventh precept: Assisting in the schism by defying admonition.
When the Saṃgha was performing the formal ritual to admonish Devadatta, his four companions sided with him and assisted in the schism. The Saṃgha immediately issued an admonition.
He refuses and does not accept it; therefore, it is called "assisting in the breaking [of the Sangha] and violating the precept against admonition.
There are six specific conditions: first, Devadatta commits an act that breaks the Sangha; second, the Sangha offers formal admonition according to the Dharma;

third, he obstructs the Sangha’s formal admonition and assists in the breaking of the Sangha; fourth, the monastic community acts according to the Dharma and addresses this assistance; fifth, he refuses and does not comply; sixth, [he persists in his refusal].

The three *karmavācanās* are concluded. These six conditions must be understood through mental reflection; if a condition is missing, the explanation may be inferred accordingly. The division of the text is as before.

Now, within the section on the origin of the event (*nidāna*), there are two parts: first, up until the point of reproaching [the monk], which concerns assisting in the schism of the Saṃgha and admonishing the act committed;

second, from "informing the bhikṣus" onwards, which concerns the formal administration of the law and the offering of admonition—this constitutes a transgression of the rule without yet being an offense. The preceding text further...
Two. First, from "When he first arrived" up to "Devadatta assisted in coming to break the Saṃgha," this clearly explains the four companions and their shadow-like influence.
Second, from "When the bhikṣus heard" onwards, it rebukes what was improper. Since this precept is thus, all subsequent exhortations are identical;

they will not be further categorized below. The first section has three parts: first, citing Devadatta’s act of breaking the Saṃgha; second, from "At that time, the bhikṣus" onwards, citing the preceding assembly.
The Saṃgha exhorted and admonished Devadatta. At three times, Devadatta’s followers—like shadows following their forms—assisted him in accomplishing his schismatic aims.

When they were formally admonished regarding their actions, they questioned why the monks who had previously observed the precepts did not reprove them. This was the reason for the reproach. The answer is that because those previously observing the precepts had not yet discerned right from wrong, they lacked the opportunity to reprove him.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*). Once the admonition to Devadatta was concluded and right and wrong were thus distinguished, the reproach was finally issued.

How could there be any discrepancy? Regarding the violation of advice, there are likewise three [cases] as before. Question: How is it that after the stage of the *saṃgha* (the monastic community), when there are four or more companions assisting, one is advised later?
Answer: It is like an individual seeking the *saṃgha*; the *saṃgha* deliberates upon it. Because it is performed separately, there are eight difficulties.

However, it stops at three people and does not extend to the full assembly (*gaṇa*). Furthermore, the principle for the assembly performing disciplinary measures, such as the seven types of *karmavācanā*, is also the same.
It is a separate proceeding. Therefore, the text below states: "The Saṃgha’s raising [of the issue] is un-Dharmic. These cases must be distinguished.

Furthermore, there is room for it to be performed by the Saṃgha, as in the case of the settling of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), where right and wrong are determined directly according to the sacred teaching, and the assembly likewise has no such [authority].

Moreover, this admonition is not a disciplinary punishment (*daṇḍakarma*). Furthermore, it is a separate matter that does not seek the Saṃgha; it is simply an act of schism (*saṃghabheda*) within the Great Assembly.

In detail, one should encourage [the monks] to focus primarily on the practice of restraint (*saṃvara*). Even if others offer admonitions, they may be tolerated; it might be appropriate to act in this way.

Furthermore, this is a method for putting forth a proposal that does not differentiate between individuals within the assembly. However, according to the underlying principle, it is essential that there be individual admonitions.

This is as stated in the *Pravāraṇā* text regarding the appointment of persons from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: "Such-and-such monk, such-and-such monk"—how could it be appropriate to appoint them all at once? This case is likewise.
This is according to what resides in one's own mind.
The root of the precepts consists of five sections: first, the matter for which the admonition is made; second, the method of private admonition by that bhikṣu and others;

third, the refusal of the admonition by the bhikṣu and others; fourth, the formal admonition by the Saṃgha; fifth, the offense incurred by one who does not relinquish [the position]. First, the matter for which the admonition is made.

The matter consists of three parts: first, a general explanation of those who assist in the schism of the Saṃgha; second, the number of their factions; third, a formal explanation of the assistance in the schism.
This third part has two sections: first, exhorting the Saṃgha not to admonish Devadatta; second, from the words "these bhikṣus" onwards, an explanation of that exhortation to the Saṃgha.
Therefore, when I now advise the Saṃgha not to offer admonition, it is because the person acts in accordance with the Dharma; thus, the first two phrases refer to the person being such as this.
Devadatta’s speech follows a proper course, and is therefore called "Dharma-speech. Furthermore, because it can extinguish evil and give rise to good, it is called "Vinaya-speech.
The next two phrases refer to the Dharma. Consequently, we now joyfully encounter what we have heard; hence, it is called "delightful."
This accords with reason and brings peace of mind through compliance; therefore, one should accept it. Regarding the four-part text on the private admonition:

first, acknowledging the previous words of admonition to preclude their support; second, from "However, this... onwards, showing that both person and dharma are improper, thereby demonstrating that such support is irrational.

From "The three Great Virtuous Ones, do not desire [this]" onwards, the text presents a series of opposing viewpoints on right and wrong, urging their abandonment; this constitutes the actual words of admonition.

This is what is meant by "admonishing to abandon and assisting what is compliant," and "urging the cultivation of water-and-milk harmony. The section following "The four Great Virtuous Ones" clarifies that harmony is beneficial, thereby explaining the preceding exhortation.

A detailed explanation is provided throughout the full text. Within the first sentence, there are three parts: first, the individual; second, the preliminary explanation; and third, the assistance for compliance, and so forth.
There is the sense of "conformity. Therefore, Devadatta was approved [as a follower]. Is it not the case that, because of these two kinds of conformity, admonitions must be offered to both?

Regarding the phrase "the three companions and their faction" (*trayaḥ pāriṣadyāḥ*) below, this explains the second point: the number of those in the faction. Those who do not join in plotting together are called a "faction."
Is it necessary that four or more persons constitute a *saṃgha*? If they form a group, they are called "associates" (*sahāya-pakṣa*).
Whether there be one, two, three, or many, these two types of associates must all be admonished. Regarding the four cases in the *Cīvara-vastu*:

"seeing differently but speaking the same," and "seeing and speaking the same"—these two require admonition. "Seeing the same but speaking differently," and "seeing and speaking differently"—these do not require it.
Admonition. The remaining text is identical [to the previous rule].

○ The twelfth precept concerning the admonition against slandering the Saṃgha contains six points in its formulation of the rule. First, the purpose for permitting reliance on a village has two intentions. First, there is...
The punishment for such [behavior] is as follows: To borrow resources is to establish one's standing; clothing is required to conceal the form, and food is used to fill the body.
To sustain the person on the path is for the sake of one’s own benefit, and secondly, to benefit the donor. When the Sangha-field practices giving, one obtains the merit of a reciprocal reward.

Second, regarding those who do not permit themselves to defile the household or engage in evil conduct: they must rely upon the monastic community and refrain from extensively committing various transgressions. If one’s person lacks dignified decorum, then one is not [a true practitioner].

It is for one's own benefit. There are four ways of defiling the household; when one obstructs others at that time, even a mind of pure goodness is not beneficial to others, and therefore its transgression is defined.
Third, those who must be expelled do so because their faults are deep-seated and they obstruct both internally and externally; if they were not punished, [the community would suffer].
There would be no lasting benefit in entering the Path by reforming one's faults; furthermore, it would increase the tendency among worldly people to mistake wrong for right.
Therefore, they must be disciplined and expelled. This involves removing two walls and resolving four types of slander. The Sangha’s words rely upon [the Vinaya], and six persons act together.
As stated in the *Jì*: "Sudatta and Mahīsāsaka Sudatta ran to the village of Rājagṛha; Kāliya and Channa met them on the road and offered their repentance."

[The offense of] *kaukṛtya* (remorse). These four are not subject to formal disciplinary action (*adharma*) because they involve the increase of attachment (*rāga*). Fifth, there must be words of admonition (*codanā-vākya*). Since there are both those who are disciplined and those who are not, it appears as though there is an increase of attachment;
because their mutual observations are difficult to distinguish, the Saṃgha must rely on principle to admonish the other and clarify itself, ensuring that no words of fear or anger arise within.

Sixth, the resolution of the offense through the lifting of the bond (*saṃvara-vimokṣa*). This refers to when the assembly of monks settles the matter for themselves and admonishes the other; once right and wrong have been distinguished, yet the person remains stubbornly attached and rejects the exhortation.
Because he did not desist despite three admonitions, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* was established. The explanation of the name may be understood [from the commentary].

There are seven specific conditions: first, committing acts that defile the family; second, having no intention of repentance or reform; third, being subjected to legal disciplinary measures and expulsion.
Fourth, groundless slander of the Saṃgha; fifth, offering admonition in accordance with the Dharma; sixth, refusing to comply; seventh, the completion of the three *karmavācanas*.

Regarding the intent of the opening section: if discussed generally, all five categories of disciplinary rules (*pañcāpattinikāya*) that serve as remedies for transgressions prevent wrongdoing and are collectively termed "precepts" (*śīla*).

The categories are divided into two. The first two prevent what is coarse, and thus their antidotes are termed *śīla* (precepts). The latter three involve subtle transgressions, and their antidotes are *īryāpatha* (dignified conduct).

Śāriputra asked whether one who has committed the four grades of offenses from the "light" category downward could be disciplined within the *aniyata* (undetermined) class.

The Buddha replied, "Yes. Second, the explanation of the name. There are three parts to this explanation: first, explaining the meaning of the name *aniyata*; second, demonstrating that it applies to those who have committed many offenses.

Therefore, it is established as indeterminate (*aniyata*). Regarding its inclusion within the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* categories, it is exhaustive or non-exhaustive. As for the explanation of the name:

since it is not fixed, it is designated according to the specific facts of the case, and thus remains undetermined. As for the third, "self-accusation is undetermined," since the number of factors raised varies, it is likewise undetermined.

Regarding "confessing one's own offenses" (*svayaṃ-vāda*), how could it possibly be treated according to a single standard? Alternatively, one might confess that one has not committed an offense; thus, the four methods of treating offenses are not fixed.

Even if one does not confess and instead brings forward the offense, the offense is still treated according to its specific category. Therefore, it is said that "the treatment of the offense is not fixed. Now, I shall explain these two [categories of] non-offenses.

The "triangular" [classification] refers to the path that is both determinate and indeterminate, resembling those of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) among the three groups.
Therefore, the treatise states: "For example, like the indeterminate group. Second, it establishes the indeterminate nature by means of possessing many offenses. The treatise says:

"Subsequently, these two are indeterminate because they are the causes of all offenses; thus, all offenses are manifested. This is explained as the arising of offenses based on the conditions of the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination)."
All [the factors] are fully present therein; therefore, these two indeterminate offenses (*aniyata*) are explained again. For what reason are these two cases indeterminate?
Because they involve both secluded and public settings, which together give rise to many offenses. Since they admit of many offenses, when one is raised, there are four points lacking certainty.
As the lower two categories have not yet been definitively determined, how could a fixed conclusion be reached? Therefore, they are called "indeterminate. Regarding the category of offenses:

As for the "five classes of offenses" (*pañca-varga-apatti*), "sections" (*varga*) refers to the exposition of the seven groups (*sapta-varga*). "Expositions" (*bhāṣya*) refers to the five types of recitations of the *Prātimokṣa*.

Regarding the "origins of the offenses to be prevented," this refers to the various offenses arising from the eight origins (*aṣṭa-nidāna*), such as those arising from the body rather than from speech or mind.
These offenses are fully produced within two locations. Since they are produced in this manner, it is therefore permissible...
It is indeterminate.

Regarding the third section: it is asked, since these three pairs of categories involve the commission of many offenses, how do they compare in terms of breadth or narrowness relative to the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* groups?
It is answered: although there are seven and five offenses respectively, these numbers are not exhaustive, because they do not encompass all two hundred and fifty precepts.

This refers to cases involving sexual desire, such as making a formal accusation against a woman, or being subject to public censure for such acts. These are included within the "undetermined" (*aniyata*) category.

Excluding matters such as those involving a refusal to heed admonition, the possession of extra robes, bowls, or medicine, eating separately from the community, teaching the Dharma without prior permission, listening to the recitation without having been selected, or conferring full ordination upon one who is under age—matters that do not overlap with these specific cases—are not included here.

Within the indeterminate offenses (*aniyata*), there is no such thing as a "sufficient number of transgressions" (*pāpasaṃpad*) rather than a "sufficient number of counts" (*saṃkhyāsaṃpad*). Therefore, the Śāstra states:

"Other masters say that these two [categories] are indeterminate and resemble the original meaning of the Vinaya. Because the number is insufficient, they do not obtain [the full offense]. According to the original meaning of the Vinaya, this is a brief version while that is an extensive one.
If one can lead the brief into the extensive—namely, by correlating it with the specific clusters of offenses (*skandhaka*) within the category of indeterminate transgressions—or..."

"Admonishing the extensive by means of the concise" refers to when, within the exposition of the meaning of the *piṇḍa* (aggregates) and *varga* (sections), one introduces them in connection with the *aniyata* (undetermined) offenses.
If one can thus cite the concise from the extensive and select the concise over the extensive, such a person is proficient in the Vinaya.
Third, the analysis of the indeterminate (*aniyata*). As for the statement that "that which is prevented is thus," the ancient interpretation cites the *pārājika* offenses and records three [cases].

First, regarding the essence of the indeterminate: if one discusses the offense based on the location, the offense is determinate; if one discusses the location based on the offense, the location is also determinate.
When citing the location to record the offense, one may speak of an "indeterminate citation. Recording two offenses while exposed constitutes the second indeterminate offense; this is the meaning.

It is also as before. The reason for knowing that three offenses and two offenses are employed is that they are sought through three locations. Furthermore, it says: "According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātr̥kā*, it is also thus;

the three offenses are raised together with the intention (*cetanā*), though their lightness or heaviness differs. How can three be brought together to form one precept, or two be combined to form one?
If that were so, would it not be necessary to wait until an offense of *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or *pāyattika* has been committed before the first precept is established? [End of passage]

Regarding the *śaikṣa* rules, one first violates the subsequent precepts; if one commits even a single instance, one has already violated them—why wait for all three? Furthermore, the later [text] states that they "govern the precepts and dignified deportment.
Therefore, these are established here to manifest what is trustworthy; thus, one may cite the five categories of offenses, as their underlying principle applies to all five.

How can it be that you do not state that, in general, the five offenses constitute the *pārājika* (definitive) indeterminate [offenses], while the following four offenses constitute the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (exposed) indeterminate [offenses]?
Why do you speak only of three or two? Furthermore, regarding the citation from the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, its meaning is not as you claim later on. The text of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he had already determined the five categories [of offenses]. Regarding the gravity or lightness, the pervasiveness or non-pervasiveness, and the openness or closure of the precepts, there was no dharma that was not definitively established; therefore, it is said 'not'."

Regarding the "indeterminate" (aniyata): it is simply because [the case] is credible, yet one does not recognize the gravity of the offense's characteristics, nor does one know the name of the transgression.

One merely sees that [the monk] was sitting in the same place as a woman, but does not know whether he committed an act of sexual intercourse, an act of touching, an act of coarse speech, or perhaps five or six such acts;
therefore, it is called "indeterminate. Examining the intent of this passage, it also does not exclusively take the three offenses as its object.
The *Míng* (Explanatory Notes) provides a direct interpretation of the meaning of "not reaching a definitive conclusion" (*adhyavasāya*), which is identical to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Furthermore, some say that what is clarified is the self-accusation of having committed an illegal act, and that the Saṃgha then inflicts punishment for it; others say it refers to cases of suspicion or doubt.

Since all such points have already been addressed in the *Śīlaskandha-vibhaṅga*, and since these are merely the words of those who do not perceive the correct principle, I shall not trouble myself with refuting them. Now, I shall distinguish the correct meaning.

The treatise states that in two instances—namely, when a trustworthy woman reports a case involving one of the four modes of deportment to the Saṃgha—the monastic community, having heard it, must investigate thoroughly whether the twenty-eight offenses in private or the twenty-four offenses in public have been proven. If the truth has not yet been established, [the matter remains unresolved].

These are the transgressions to be guarded against; they do not constitute separate names for offenses. To be free from defilement and pure, such that one does not engage in walking, standing, sitting, or staying in either of the two [unwholesome] places, is the practice of the remedy. If this is so, then would the three or two types of offenses not be names of offenses?

Answer: These are matters to be examined. If the reality has not yet been attained, they are subsumed under the "indeterminate" (aniyata); once determined, they belong to the formal categories (pārājika or saṃghāvaśeṣa), and are not included here. Now...
This is what is being clarified: it is established that one must conduct a thorough examination. Since it is said to be "indeterminate," how could there be a formal offense?

If this is so, what then constitutes a precept? Answer: There are two types of the *Śīla-sūtra* (Precept Scripture). First, those established according to specific matters; for this reason, they are called "precepts" (*śīla*).

As for the treatises on the *Skandhaka*, *Varga*, and so forth, these are indeterminate and not yet fixed, and thus they are not established within those *Skandhaka* or *Varga* precepts. Therefore, regarding the question of right and wrong, there are not two [distinct categories].

Regarding the *niyata* (fixed) rules: because they are established according to specific offenses to distinguish whether one’s own statement is true or false, the two types of *aniyata* (undetermined) rules in the world—which involve prohibitions and restrictions based on particular circumstances rather than fixed names for offenses—are also termed "precepts" (*śīla*).
Furthermore, the two types of *aniyata* discussed in the treatise are likewise subsumed within the category of precepts. The question is: why are these considered precepts?

Why is it that there is no designation of an offense? The answer is: since one has already proceeded to the point of investigation, yet has not yet reached a definitive conclusion, how can one establish a fixed name for this state of indeterminacy?

For a name implies a fixed definition. Nevertheless, because of the nature of the precepts, they are expanded or abbreviated into fifteen, and both types of *aniyata* (undetermined offenses) are fully present.
Furthermore, it is said: "Regarding the initial transgression of the precepts, from now on the rules shall be established; this brings ten benefits. Thus, two more [offenses] are added.

Regarding the benefits of formulating the precepts, there are two types of *aniyata* (undetermined offenses). Furthermore, as with the five or ten precepts, before their specific names were established as offenses, were they not nonetheless precepts?
Now, these *aniyata* rules are considered precepts because they are capable of providing restraint and protection; one must examine the underlying facts to determine whether an offense has occurred.
Therefore, they are established as precepts.

Next, regarding the fourth gate, the distinction between the general and the specific concerning locations and persons: there are only four types of locations, namely, the places of monks, nuns, and laypeople, as well as those other than these three.

These refer to secluded places where one is out of sight and hearing, and so forth. However, having discussed the case of lay locations based on the specific conditions, it remains unknown how to determine the principle for the other locations.
By analogy, they should be treated similarly. Within the discussion of the residences of monks and nuns, one may rely on the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*).

[The offense of] *āpatti* should also be treated as falling within the category of the *aniyata* (undetermined) offenses. Now, regarding the restriction to the literal text: when it concerns a layperson (*gṛhastha*) and is distinguished by the person [involved], the text mentions only a layperson;

therefore, it is classified as *aniyata*. Because a bhikṣu understands names and categories, there is no *aniyata* [offense] for him. This is also stated according to our own school’s doctrine. As for the matter of quantity, it also falls under the *aniyata*;

that is to say, it is "either present or absent. This meaning is not... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Vinaya rules, likely concerning the application of the *aniyata* offenses. The final phrase "此義不" suggests the sentence was cut off.)*
That is so. If one were to claim that [the *aniyata* offenses] are indeterminate because they arise according to the quantity of the object, this too is actually determinate;

for they follow the preceding object: if it is many, one incurs many [offenses], and if it is few, one incurs few. Therefore, they are not indeterminate. One must not rely on this to explain the six types of persons who are indeterminate (*aniyata-pudgala*).
The commentary states: "Indeterminate" refers to the fact that there is no fixed standard regarding the number of transgressions or their relative gravity.

Since one has not yet reached an understanding of the specific names and categories within the indeterminate offenses, it is impossible to definitively determine which specific offense has been committed; hence they are called "indeterminate.
This applies to both nuns and laymen, and while it may not necessarily refer exclusively to laywomen, this is stated here based on the specific circumstances of the case.
The second section clarifies the distinctions. Regarding the first two [categories], one is the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* in private and the other is the *pāyattika* in public.
