First, because they would otherwise conflict; second, because the two would not support one another; third, because of the difference between the determinate and the indeterminate. As for robes, their size is indeterminate depending on the person upon whom they rely; the Saṃgha...

Because the *dhātu* (boundary) is fixed, it cannot be mutually agreed upon (*saṃmata*). Regarding the presence or absence of the four spheres of influence (*pradeśa*), there are two types of ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*).

Because they possess four characteristics, they are mutually agreeable. First, because the ritual procedure for the robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) is intended for those who delight in tranquility, it permits haste while being slow [in its application];

thus, it may be bound upon a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). Second, it requires dependence on a great boundary for its binding to be accomplished. Third, both are fixed. Fourth, neither lacks [these characteristics].
Because they share a common boundary (*sīmā*), their mutual recognition is permissible.
Regarding the third case, the presence or absence of the boundary is treated as two relative conditions, both of which lack a formal boundary; these two types are natural occurrences.

As for the robe being present while the Sangha is absent, the reason is that these all constitute permissions granted for urgent matters to be fulfilled at leisure; this is why it is so. The robe is defined by its distance.

Because [the robe] is lax, it possesses a zone of influence (*sīmā*); because the Saṃgha is proximate, it lacks a zone of influence. If the Saṃgha were dependent upon the robe, it would conversely become difficult to protect;
if the robe were compliant with the Saṃgha, the robe would become excessively urgent. Thus, these two possess a distinction between reason and lack of reason.

Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, even a village has a zone of influence. If that is so, the reason why [the Saṃgha] exists is that the Saṃgha is broad, whereas the robe is narrow.

Regarding the question of why it is narrow: the answer is that although the robe was originally tight and is now tight as well, it must be worn with ample space; though the robe was originally tight and is now tight as well, it is nonetheless narrow. Question:
Since the ritual procedure for the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) is the same, why is there no *pradeśa* (territorial extension)? Answer: Because what has already been opened cannot be opened again.
Next, I shall explain the text. Regarding the first section within the ten realms:

as for "one realm or several realms within a single monastery," if one’s body and robes are situated within the same monastery enclosure (*sīmā*), this is called "one realm. If the body and the robes are in separate monastery enclosures, it is therefore called "several realms."

Furthermore, when the boundaries of a monastery (*ārāma*) encompass the entire area such that their functional spheres (*pradeśa*) meet, this is called a single boundary (*ekasīman*). Alternatively, if there are no large trees or obstructions and the individual rooms are distinct, each has its own functional sphere;
if one’s body and robes are separated [from these spheres], staying overnight results in a loss [of the protective boundary]. Therefore, it is called "various" (*nānā*).

Moreover, although the monastery's boundaries may be all-encompassing, if no laypeople come and only renunciants are present, the entire monastery is without distinction; this is called [a single boundary].

One boundary (*ekasīma*). If a man or woman enters a monastery (*ārāma*) and stays there, their robes—which had arisen within the village boundary (*grāmamaryādā*)—are lost if they stay overnight while separated from one another;
thus the robes become numerous. Therefore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Muli*) says:

"If a king enters the interior of a boundary and stays there, all places where his attendants of high and low rank come and go in his vicinity are not robe-boundaries. Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "As for 'one boundary,' within it..."
In the center, one attains mastery; it is because of coming and going that this is so. Regarding "several realms" (*nānā-sīmā*): within them, one does not attain mastery over coming and going.
When there is "one realm" (*eka-sīmā*) for a tree, it means the body and the robe are together beneath the same tree; this is called one realm.
If the body and the robe are under separate trees, it is called several realms. Or, if no other worldly women have come and they remain together under the tree, this is [also one realm].
It is called a single boundary (*ekadhātu*). If laymen or laywomen come [there], it is called a manifold boundary (*nānādhātu*), such as a threshing floor or even a granary.
The seven boundaries are explained by analogy with trees.
Next is the explanation of the text concerning village boundaries (*grāma-sīman*). To say that "a village has one boundary" means, for example, when the Zhang family invites me to receive offerings;
because there is no obstruction to their intention, throughout the entire household, one does not lose one's robe. This is called "one boundary.

Alternatively, if another royal family comes to reside there, and they are separated by mutual obstruction, it is called "several boundaries. Therefore, the *Cīvara-vastu* states: "If within a single household..."

Regarding the boundaries between elder and younger brothers: if their feelings are estranged such that they do not permit one another to come and go, and their bodies and robes are situated on opposite sides [of the boundary], this is called a "conflict of boundaries" (*khandasīma*).

If the brothers are harmonious and allow the teacher to reside there as he pleases, coming and going at will, and their bodies and robes are situated on opposite sides within the brothers' boundary, then they do not lose their robes; this is called a "single boundary. Therefore, it is the same now as well, throughout...

"To call all those whose feelings are unobstructed by one another 'one boundary' (*ekasīma*) is not correct. Why is this so? Because it refers specifically to emotional obstruction, as was explained above.
According to this Vinaya, insofar as it concerns the acquisition of defilement, censure, and transgression, it differs from that [other system].
Therefore, the text below states: 'If one’s clothes are removed and the body is exposed,' the Buddha said, 'except for the external boundary of a village. Now, we rely on this."

In principle, even if the sentiments between members of the same family are very close—such as when one’s own kinswoman’s robe is in the possession of her mother, daughter, or sister—and one must go to fetch or deliver it during cold or hot weather or at night, there is a fear of physical contact.
If such a situation arises, the mind immediately becomes distanced. If there are such obstacles, it indicates that the robe should not be given; this is the correct principle.
If even those who have become somewhat acquainted [with one another] do not constitute a single boundary (*sīmā*), how much less so for other distant persons, such as men and women;

these are termed the "household sphere" (*grāma-sīman*). This, moreover, becomes a partitioned space (*vyavahita*). How could it then be possible for the entire household to be called a single boundary?

Therefore, we shall now further explain that what constitutes a single boundary for a village is the area delimited by the residence of the bhikṣus; this is called a single boundary. As for the area outside the delimitation of the bhikṣus' residence, it follows...
Regarding the number of rooms: this constitutes a certain number of boundaries (*sīmā*). When asked why this differs from the single boundary within a monastery (*ārāma*), the answer is:

it is called a "single boundary" because no laypeople come to pervade the interior of that monastery. The response is: since a monastery is the dwelling place of bhikṣus, if there are no laypeople present, it can be designated as a single boundary.
A house, however, is not our [monastic] domain; therefore, it does not resemble a monastery. Pervading this entire household is what is termed a "single [boundary]."
Regarding the boundary (*sīmā*): it must necessarily be within the designated limits of a bhikṣu’s residence to be called a single boundary;
that which is outside the scope of the residence constitutes multiple boundaries.
The essential characteristics of the second realm are each as stated in the text.
Third, the explanation of the meaning of "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to such statements as "this bowl is not that bowl," which involve the conceptualization of existence;

these are extensively analyzed as thirty [categories], and the other categories should be understood by analogy. If one does not understand the meaning of such passages, the common understanding would be to think that "this bowl holds the robe, while the other bowls do not."
"Overnight stay. One should not commit an offense [by staying overnight], because although they share the same name "vihāra," the locations for each side are distinct;
therefore, this text is required. The same applies to the other cases as well.

The four areas of influence (*pradeśa*) are as stated in the text. Regarding the term "middle person" (*madhyama-puruṣa*): it refers to one who is neither strong nor weak; regarding the "thrower": it refers to one who does not throw too close.

The fifth section concerns the formalization of the offense (*āpatti-prajñapti*), which is also composed of one hundred statements. There are twenty textual units, but they correspond to the first ten; within these, there are five [sections]: (1) the mutual presence of the body and the robe;
(2) the clarification of the boundaries (*sīmā*) and below, which teaches the methods for non-offense; (3) "if not... and below, which concerns non-performance.

One must relinquish [the robe]. From the passage "Once the signs of dawn have appeared" onwards, there is a *thullaccaya* for being separated from the three robes, and a *dukkaṭa* for being separated from other robes.

Regarding the sequence of exemptions within the second category of non-offenses (*anāpatti*), one should state that first one takes hold of it with the hand, next one reaches a place with stones, and finally one should relinquish the robe.
Because the text explains the sequence [of actions], it first clarifies the relinquishing of robes. Regarding the phrase "holding with the hand":

because there are various boundaries (*sīmā*), one must hold [the robe] with the hand in order not to commit an offense. As for "reaching a place of stone," this refers to entering a single boundary where there is no force [of the previous boundary], and thus there is no offense;
this applies equally across all boundaries. This explanation regarding the relinquishing of robes is incomplete; one must immediately relinquish the robe. How could it be otherwise?
If one is without robes, one obtains merit; there is no offense of *thullaccaya*. Because one is taking away what is light for what is heavy, the *Cīvaravastu* states:

"This saṃghāṭī is among my three robes; having previously received and maintained it, I now relinquish it. The relinquishment of the two lower robes is likewise. For nuns, the relinquishment of the four lower robes is also the same.

Regarding the text on relinquishment in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "I have accepted this saṃghāṭī of such-and-such strips; I now relinquish it," recited three times. The two lower robes are treated similarly.

Next, ten phrases regarding trees are established; all others are omitted. Furthermore, among these twenty [phrases], following the third [case] above, when this *ārāma* is not that *ārāma*, one should say that one is staying in another *ārāma*.
Because it is omitted in the text, there are only nine [phrases] for this single category.

Regarding the five phrases on the *araṇya*: the first clarifies the nature of the boundary (*sīmā*). As for "between eight trees," this refers to forty-nine *dhanus* (bows), as seven times seven equals forty-nine. A *dhanus*...
The length is four *zhǔ*, which calculates to seven chi and two cun. Between them, there are seven *gōng*, which is fifty chi and four cun. This totals three hundred fifty-two chi and eight cun.
Altogether, this amounts to fifty-eight paces and one chi and eight cun.

Including the stones and the site, these constitute the distinct boundaries of the monastic territory (*sīmā*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, a *gōng* consists of five *zhǔ*; thus, the monastic boundary is seventy-three [units].
Half a step [apart]. The two robes remain intermingled. Third, if one does not go to relinquish them but holds them with both hands, the case of a stone location is explained as before.

Next, if one ties them together, it is a heavy offense; next, if one obtains them, it is a light *duṣkṛta*. The relinquishment and confession are as above. Among those that do not constitute an offense, five specific exemptions are opened:

first, because the *karmavācanā* was performed and the *māṣaka* was not lost, there is no offense; second, because they were assembled, there is no offense; third, because they were relinquished... there is no offense.

1. An offense. 2. Regarding the four cases of mistaken perception (*caturvidha-saṃjñā*), because the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) is lost, there is no offense. 3. If there are difficulties regarding water or other obstacles, the undertaking is not lost and thus there is no offense.
The wording of the text is not yet clear; the following four allowances must all occur before the boundary markers (*sīmā*) have appeared.

Only when these four conditions exist can one avoid an offense. Regarding the non-loss of the undertaking due to various difficulties of water or land: the mind must know that the robe remains within the constant [boundary], and one merely maintains it.

Regarding the meaning of "receiving": it is so called because one does not lose [the precept]. It is like receiving the *kāmacchanda* (desire) vow; even when encountering difficult conditions that lead one out of the boundary, one does not lose the dharma of the desire-vow.
This case is likewise identical to those two; it can be understood through this general principle.
The third precept concerning the one-month robe:

The intention behind this regulation is that robes serve as requisites for sustaining the body and are to be used according to the seasons. Although one may already possess robes, if they are old, tattered, and worn out, one may continue to maintain them even if they are no longer fit for wear.
Now, having obtained some wealth, one may use it to make three robes (tricīvara) in exchange for those old ones. However—

A small amount is insufficient to wait for it to become full; therefore, the Sage permitted keeping [extra robes] for one month beyond that limit. To harbor excessive greed and violate the teaching obstructs the Path, and thus he established the rule regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*).
If the robes are not fit for use and require replacement, if the materials for the new robes differ from the old, one may keep them for one month each.
If the materials are the same, they must be combined into a single robe. Should one act otherwise, one commits an offense as soon as the time limit has passed. For this reason:

The scriptural text states: "If one has sufficient robes of the same kind, one must cut them [into patches]; otherwise, there is an offense. This applies regardless of whether one expects more or not, and whether the cutting is completed or not.
However, if one has sufficient robes of the same kind, an offense is incurred; if insufficient, it is permitted accordingly. This is not the same as other Vinayas."
There are six distinct conditions [for opening a new robe]: First, if it is a new robe that is currently fit for use, other wealth is not permitted [to be acquired], whereas robes are permitted;
thus, due to this first condition, one may discard the three robes. Even if the robes are old and worn out, if one obtains sufficient wealth, it is still not permitted to acquire more.
Second, if one obtains little wealth that is insufficient [to make a robe], and does not intend to make it into the three robes, one incurs only the initial offense.

One must not keep [the robe] for even one month; it is clear that the third [condition] is required for making the three robes (*tricīvara*). Regarding the phrase "because of shaving": (1) not declaring it as pure (*apariśuddha*) while making the three robes;

(2) having no valid cause or condition; (3) exceeding the time limit, which constitutes an offense. The narrative of the origin (*nidāna*) has two parts: first, up to the point where wandering gives rise to the fault of outflows (*āsrava*);
second, from "at that time, having received a deposit" onwards, the discovery and the reproach. The preceding text further has two sections: first, the allowance...
Regarding the sufficiency of robes: during the two periods [of the rainy season], the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks went out. Because of this, the rule against going out was established.

Among those who possess rag-robes (pāṃśukūla), those who possess other types of ownerless cloth, or those for whom the robes offered by donors (dānapati) are insufficient—it is said that among these kinds of robes, there may be cases where one has not yet obtained enough.
To say "to take from among them" means to take from between those two types of rag-robes, to prepare and purify them, in order to prevent the offense of *kṣudrāpatti* (minor transgression).
Having kept these robes and entrusted them to a relative or friend, if a long period passes, such a lapse is improper. Yet, if one possesses sufficient *kāṭhina* cloth, why not make robes?
It may be said that the Buddha permitted [the robe] to be completed; could it be that this was further extended for a longer duration?
Consequently, the root precept was established to allow a maximum of one month. If one exceeds this limit, one incurs an offense according to the transgression.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra contains six sections: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the exclusion of the opening conditions and the duration of the offense;

third, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the robes obtained by cutting hair; fourth, from "Having received them, quickly... onwards, which does not permit an exception; fifth, from "If they are insufficient...
onwards, which permits a full month if they are insufficient; sixth, from "If it exceeds... onwards, which defines the offense according to the transgression. These are distinct.

The explanation of the first three [periods] is clear and easy to understand. Regarding the passage beginning with "If within ten days one has sufficient cloth," the following three [periods] are explained together.
Within the span of one month, the period is divided into three parts. During the first ten days, by following the usual practice, one does not incur an offense.
From the subsequent ten days onward, if one does not make the robe, an offense is incurred by the thirtieth day. How is the offense incurred?

It is an offense. Once thirty days have passed, it is invariably an offense. Within the categories of "offense" and "non-offense," there are two divisions. From the beginning up to the twenty-ninth day, it is likewise:
if the full period is reached, there is no exemption; if it is not yet reached, there is an exemption. Second, regarding those with the same robe who have not yet completed thirty days:
regardless of whether the period is complete or not, once the limit is reached, there is no exemption. This concerns the first [category], specifically the tenth [day].

The midday is divided into two parts. From the beginning until the point of *pāyattika*, the [robe] will not open if it is sufficient. This explains the fourth and sixth lines of the four-part couplet. Within this section, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the instruction to perform five methods to avoid the offense of excess, which explains the fourth line;
second, "if one does not cut or trim," which refers to the violation of the rule and constitutes an offense, explaining the sixth line. Second, "if the same robe is insufficient."
Regarding "until the eleventh day," this explains the fifth phrase. It is not permissible to grant a temporary exemption. Question:

If all three robes are insufficient and each requires a one-month extension, yet the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) is sufficient and incurs the offense of dyeing, while the two lower robes do not—[is it so]? Answer:

Regarding the material for the two lower robes, if there is no surplus, they originally receive a one-month extension; now, because they are being dyed for another's sake, both parties incur the offense together. Question:

The substance of the three robes (tricīvara) itself does not inherently possess excess. How, then, can one incur an offense? Answer: Because there are already existing robes, these [additional ones] remain outside the limit of the three;

it is only when they fulfill the characteristics of a robe that one incurs no offense. This is because they do not differ from those [existing robes]. The text states that according to the number of robes, there is *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If other materials are dyed, the dyer incurs no offense, whereas the one who has the materials dyed may incur an offense if they live together [in community]. Next, the eleven [rules].
The procedure for the twelve cases is the same as before. From this point onward, the various phrases are included because the status of the offense is identical.

It says, "up to and including the twenty-ninth day, it is also like this. If the shared robe is not sufficient until the thirtieth day, there is no offense; however, if it is sufficient, one is definitely guilty of an offense.
Regarding the "shared robe," among the ten types of robes, those that belong to the same category are considered shared, whereas those that differ in type are not. This may also be the case.

"Same cloth" refers to the material for the three robes (*tricīvara*); "different cloth" refers to other surplus materials. When these reach the prescribed limit, there is no exception and no offense.
In the section on specific exceptions, there are two parts: first, citing the fourth phrase of the *Śikṣāpada*, which states that if the requirements are met, there is no exception;
furthermore, among the twenty cases of "sufficient cloth" detailed in the *Vistara*, twenty cases of "insufficient cloth" are provisionally permitted as exceptions to clarify this point.

There is no offense. Second, regarding the section from "if one has the perception that it has been cut" downwards, which cites the four and six lines of the *Śīla-mūla* (the core precept), as well as the detailed explanation from "once the ten-day period for shared robes is fulfilled" downwards—concerning the twenty cases where fulfillment is not permitted and so forth—even if the robe is not yet completed, there are nine circumstances:
the four perceptions, the four such as the "seizing of robes," and the nine such as "receiving a deposit and dying. In these various conditions...
Each [case] is an offense. By passing through twenty distinct stages, one is opened to non-offense.
○ Regarding the fourth precept on taking a nun’s robe:
the reason it was established is that there are three kinds of faults. First, generally, when the inferior shows respect to the superior, they should offer their devotion with sincere emotion. So...

There are those who possess wealth and, desiring to give it away in charity, grant their permission without hesitation. Yet, as the Great Saṃgha is not their relative, they often fail to deliberate carefully;

they accept whatever is offered, causing the other’s wealth to be exhausted and leading them to the distress of poverty. Furthermore, the forms of men and women are distinct by principle and should have no mutual involvement.

Once their property has been interchanged, their thoughts become biased toward one another as relatives. Because of this exchange, defilement arises, which may cause the destruction of the pure conduct (brahmacarya). When facing...
Perilous matters and steep precipices are most terrifying; the three traces involve the world and invite censure, leading to slander and defamation.
When one’s purity and integrity are difficult to distinguish, it is impossible to extricate oneself from these various faults. For this reason, the Sage established the prohibitions.

There are five distinct conditions: first, a bhikṣuṇī excludes the two lower groups [of the saṃgha], because according to the *Cīvara-vastu*, there is no offense regarding the robes of the two lower groups;
now, this case should likewise be the same. According to the *Mahā-sāṃghika-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), the two lower groups incur the same offense as a bhikṣuṇī.

Second, one who is not a relative excludes those who are relatives, for there is no offense in such cases. Third, it refers to the five robes of proper measure. According to the *Mahā-sāṃghika-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, "robes" refers specifically to robes of proper measure, excluding those that are not.

One should measure the robe-cloth. Taking it with a key, a chest, or similar means constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, if one sends it with a pure intention—meaning that having obtained it through begging, one intends to trade for something else—one does not incur an offense.

If many bhikṣus take a single robe from a bhikṣuṇī, all those many bhikṣus incur the offense. If one takes a single robe from many bhikṣuṇīs, the offense is calculated as being incurred by each individual bhikṣuṇī.

Fifth, once one has accepted it and it has come under one's possession, the offense is incurred. Question: Why is it prescribed that taking a bhikṣuṇī’s robe is an offense, while taking [a layperson’s robe] is not?
Regarding the bowl: the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that there are five types of robes offered to nuns with joyful intent, which are subject to the principle of being accepted as frequent gifts;

therefore, the Noble One prescribed the bowl. Since there is only one instance where a nun relinquishes [her bowl], such acceptance is rare and not considered frequent. Even if one were to accept it, one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).

There is a textual passage in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* stating that taking a nun’s bowl does not constitute an offense. However, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, taking a bowl also constitutes an offense of forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). There are two textual sources for this: the first...

This leads to the offense of taking a nun’s robe and wearing it. Second, at a later time, there is the censure found in the passage beginning with "at another time. The preceding text is further divided into two parts.

First, the section explaining the conditions for the offense (*āpatti-pratyaya*), which has two sub-sections. The first raises the setting of the residence and the person who gave the robe—one who had left the household life and attained the Way.

The second, beginning with "at that time there were many nuns in a secluded place," distinguishes the specific conditions for the offense. Within the text on the conditions for the offense, there are three parts. The first is the cause (*hetu*).

Sending food is its remote condition (*dūre-pratyaya*). The passage beginning with "At that time, there was a bhikṣu wearing tattered and old [robes]" and continuing through "the one who could take the robe" refers to the person who committed the offense;

the passage beginning with "having seen the two lotuses" and so forth constitutes its proximate condition (*āsanne-pratyaya*). The second section, beginning with "he immediately took them off," constitutes the actual offense (*maulāpatti*).
When he rebuked him, saying, "You should not act in this way," it refers to the Buddha’s regulation permitting the possession of five robes, originally intended for the sustenance of the body. Now...
By giving it to another person, one incurs the offense of being "unclothed. To practice *dāna* while violating the precepts is contrary to the Dharma; therefore, it is said to be "inappropriate.

As for the statement that "other robes may be given to others as one pleases," this refers to the fact that outside of the five robes, one may give them to the three assemblies (*trīṇi saṃghāni*). It is not permitted to give them to the *saṃgha*;

to do so would constitute an offense for both the giver and the receiver. Furthermore, according to another interpretation, "if one gives" refers to the fact that surplus wealth outside of the five robes may be given to a fellow practitioner.
Ānanda, when the Saṃgha receives a gift from a nun, one should interrogate the donor beforehand. If it is known that she is not possessed of the five robes, then [the gift] must not be accepted;

if she is possessed of the five robes, it may be accepted without offense. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if there was a prior invitation, or if she gives because she is staying in a separate room, or if she gives for the sake of hearing the Dharma, there is no offense.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if she has no intention of seeking [anything in return] and gives of her own accord, there is no offense.
If one knows that the other person possesses [the robe], and takes it accordingly, there is no offense.
This constitutes five phrases in the core text of the precepts: first, the person; second, a nun who is not a relative; third, taking the robe; fourth, excluding trade.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun): "If trade is permitted, it is because by being free from that [attachment] and seeking [the robe] with diligence, one attains peace and happiness, and furthermore, one is freed from suffering and affliction."

The fifth section distinguishes the characteristics of the transgressions of the five fetters (*pañca-saṃyojana*). One should fully understand the aforementioned five. Regarding "two types of relatives" (*dvi-jñāti*):

these refer to parents and blood relations within seven generations. According to the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, four types of relatives should be understood: first, paternal uncles; second, maternal uncles; third, paternal aunts; and fourth, maternal aunts.

Regarding the four types of mothers and the mother’s mother: if these four close nuns take [the robes], there is no offense. The other texts explaining "close relatives" all follow this principle. Question:

Why is it that when a nun takes robes from the *saṃgha*, she incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (light) offense? Answer: Because the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* are superior and venerable, it is rare for a nun to receive [their property] without censure;

furthermore, the meaning of the prohibition against taking after midday involves deep implications regarding the arising of afflictions. Therefore, she incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave) offense. This is the explanation. Second.
Regarding the comparison between the meaning of the offenses and the absence of censure: the two types of "taking" (ādāna) are discussed separately because their frequency differs.

Consequently, for the great monks (bhikṣus), the number of instances of taking coincides with the offense of censure (pātayantika). For the bhikṣuṇīs, however, because such acts are rare and lack censure, both taking and the act itself constitute a simple offense (duṣkṛta).
Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya, Fascicle Four, Part One.

Written by the bhikṣu Zhàoshān Huáng on the final day of the seventh month of the Year of Yín in the seventh year of the Bǎoyǒng era (1680), at the quarters of Tiān'ān Lùsì during the reconstruction of the Tripitaka. (Lay age: fifty-five.)
The Fourth Fascicle, Part Two of the *Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*.
The Fifth Precept: On Sending a Nun to Wash Soiled Garments.

As for the reason this rule was established: when those of high status employ those of lower rank, the tasks are numerous and burdensome; yet those of lower status feel reverence toward their superiors, making it difficult to restrain themselves.
Failing to exercise due deliberation, they neglect their duties regardless of whether there is space or not; the resulting harm is not slight.

They give rise to afflictions of passion and incur worldly censure, no different from what was stated before. For these reasons, the rule was established. Question: Why are washing, dyeing, and beating combined into a single regulation?
Answer: First, because the location for the *śrāmaṇerī* is the same; second, because both involve old garments; and third, because a single garment may be involved, leading to mutual complications.
If one commits [this offense], it must be washed because of stains and sweat;

it must be dyed if the color has faded; and it must be beaten if it is stiff. There are six distinct conditions: first, the person is a bhikṣuṇī; second, she is not a relative; third, it is an old garment; fourth, one causes her to wash, dye, or beat it.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duolun), if one causes her to write, seal, or send a message, it is a *duṣkṛta* (吉羅). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four permutations: giving it oneself and receiving it oneself, giving it oneself and having another receive it, and so forth.

If both parties wash [the robes] and so forth together, they both commit an offense. This point is not explicitly stated in the text; however, because there is no underlying cause [for the prohibition], the subsequent section on allowances states:
"If one washes, dyes, or beats [a robe] due to illness, or if one borrows another's robe and washes, dyes, or beats it, there is no offense.

Apart from such circumstances, [the rule applies]. Sixth, having finished washing, dyeing, and beating [the robes]. Question: Why is it not prohibited to have a nun polish a bowl? Explanation: Old robes give rise to affliction, as [stated] below.

Regarding the teaching on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): furthermore, the meanings of washing and dyeing are easy to understand, and nuns are frequently proficient in them; because they repeatedly commit violations regarding these, the regulations were established. As for the bowl, it does not give rise to afflictions;
moreover, the matter of its polishing and treatment is difficult, and nuns are generally unskilled in it; because such instances are rare, no regulation was established.

The *Śīlaskandha* (Precept Text) contains five points: first, the person; second, a nun who is not a relative; third, the old garment to be washed; fourth, causing her to wash, dye, and beat it; fifth, the determination of the offense.
The first three are explained individually, while the fourth and fifth are interpreted together. According to its eight constituent acts, there should be eight points:

the first three *pārājika*-like offenses (*thullaccaya*) are combined into one point; the next two *pārājika*-like offenses and one *dukkaṭa* form three points. Thus, there should be three [separate] points.

One [offense] is a *pāyattika* (提) and two are *śaikṣa-dharmas* (吉). These three are abbreviated. Next, there is one sentence concerning the three *śaikṣa-dharmas*. Regarding the "lower two groups" (the *śrāmaṇera*s and *śrāmaṇerī*s): they are not full disciples; because their transgressions are rare, the offense is light.

Furthermore, as they do not possess the full precepts (*upasampadā*), their failure does not obstruct their primary cultivation. According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the lower two groups commit a *pāyattika* when they offend, similar to the *bhikṣuṇī*s.
Because new clothes are rarely washed and there is no risk of discoloration, it is likewise a light offense.
The Sixth Precept: Begging for Robes from a Householder Who Is Not a Relative.
In general, those who have left the household life should be content with what they have.

Now that the three robes are complete and the requirements for travel are sufficient, to further seek out garments would increase greed and distress others, inviting public censure and causing no small harm. For this reason, the rule was established. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
First, to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish; second, to bring an end to disputes and litigation; third, to extinguish the unwholesome minds of others;
and fourth, to inspire faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma among sentient beings.
There are six conditions for the offense: first, the possession of the three robes; second, the absence of a valid reason;

third, the donor being a householder who is not a relative; fourth, requesting a robe of standard measure for oneself; fifth, the donor giving it; and sixth, receiving and taking possession of it. Furthermore, there are two circumstances of transgression:
first, the fault arising from the act of removing the robe and giving it to Upananda; second, the verbal reproach following the speech. These are explained in detail in the text.
He possesses wisdom and is skilled at preaching the Dharma; he specifically understands the meaning of the rewards for the merit of giving within the Sūtras, and thus he is said to possess wisdom.
However, regarding the forfeiture of robes in the Vinaya, he does not comprehend the gravity or lightness of the disciplinary teachings, and therefore it is said that he abandons what he knows not.
The text of the precept has three parts: first, the brief formulation of the precept; second, the section reiterating the formulation and providing exceptions, which has two sub-sections:

first, excluding relatives; second, excluding the four exceptional circumstances. Third, the fulfillment of the five phrases of the precept text: first, the person; second, a non-relative householder;

third, begging for robes; fourth, excluding the exceptional circumstances; fifth, the conclusion regarding the offense. The phrase "at other times" and below recites the aforementioned fourth phrase. Below.
In the commentary, only the four phrases are explained; the remaining conditions are omitted for brevity.
○ Regarding the seventh precept on receiving robes beyond what is sufficient:
the reason this rule was established and receiving robes beyond one’s needs is not permitted is that a renunciant may lose [their status] upon encountering four causes and conditions.
If someone were to take away one's three robes, a person of sincere faith who hears of this would exhaust their poverty to give them as an offering.
It is only right that one should accept such a gift in accordance with its nature, thereby manifesting within oneself a mind of integrity and moderation while outwardly not troubling others.

Now, since the three robes are already sufficient, to accept more than that is to increase the fetters of greed within and to contradict the donor’s intention without; this is most improper. Therefore, the Sage established this regulation.
There are six distinct conditions: first, a bhikṣu loses or has his three robes stolen; second, a householder who is not a relative;

third, giving specifically because of the loss—if it were not for the loss, receiving them at any other time would be no offense; fourth, knowing that the gift was made because of the loss; fifth, taking more than the standard measure of cloth beyond what is sufficient;
sixth, the offense being incurred when the cloth is received and taken into one's possession. Question: Regarding the offense of exceeding the sufficient measure of cloth, what...
"One should not take more than one's need; one should receive only what fills the bowl. The answer is: "There are three types of robes. If they are lost, the amount [one may receive] is not fixed.

If one loses one robe, one may receive two; even if one loses all three, one may receive four. Furthermore, as people often receive more than necessary, it was therefore necessary for the Noble One to establish this regulation."
There is only one bowl; losing the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) of one [bowl] was originally not a transgression. Why, then, was it necessary for the Noble One to establish this rule?
Furthermore, since there is no fault in having many bowls, and because the meaning of "acceptance" is rare, the rule against excessive acceptance was not established.

Regarding the phrase in the text, "taking from or giving to the group of six," since the previous precept did not first involve a personal violation, one does not commit an offense for another. Now, this donor has lost the certainty of the *kaṭhina* robe; it is sufficient.

If one receives [the precepts] again and transfers them to another person, this likewise contradicts one's original intention; to do so for the sake of another constitutes an offense as well. Question: Since they have been transferred to another person, what is there left to relinquish? Answer: This refers to the circumstances under which the rule was established. If it is already a transgression to act for the sake of another, how much more so when acting for oneself?

As the *Śāstra* correctly explains: The original vow was made with the thought: "I shall uphold the precepts for my own sake. Now, having received them again and transferred them to another, one has abandoned the original intent. Furthermore, if one acts for the sake of another, one violates the precepts even more severely than if one had acted for oneself. Therefore, it is said that one commits an offense. This is the principle of the correct reasoning of the treatise.
One must personally accept [the robe] before it may be relinquished.
The root text of the precept consists of six points: first, the offender; second, encountering four causes and conditions—this refers to the occasion of giving robes;

third, a householder who is not a relative acting as the donor of the robe; fourth, giving out of a spontaneous invitation for fear of falling into loss; fifth, [the case of] a bhikṣu... [and so forth].
The instruction is to accept with contentment. Sixth, if one exceeds the lower limit or accepts excessively, one commits an offense of formal transgression (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).

Among these six, the second is omitted and not explained; the first and third are clear in their wording. From the words "As for 'clothing'" (*cīvara*) onwards, the fourth and fifth [clauses] are explained together.

From the words "If a bhikṣu" onwards, the sixth clause is explained. Within the section explaining the fourth and fifth clauses together, there are two parts. The first explains the character "clothing" (*cīvara*); the second...
The combined explanation of the text has four parts. First, clarifying what should be accepted and what should not be accepted. This refers to the two cases where one should not accept [robes]:

when the three robes are entirely lost, one should accept them with contentment. Second, regarding contentment, there are two types: the lower limit of the portion and that which was previously mentioned as "accepting with contentment.
First, the enumeration; second, the listing of names; third, the explanation. As for the householder’s contentment, it follows the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Regarding the recipient who accepts the garment being given: this refers to a layperson (*avadātavasana*) who gives because they have incurred a loss; originally, it was for the purpose of alleviating insufficiency.

If the recipient has not yet reached sufficiency, they should accept three times and then forfeit them three times. This follows the principle that when a layperson lacks the intention to give further, one must be content with what has been received.
However, this contentment accords with the way of householders; therefore, it is called "the householder's contentment. Regarding the three types of contentment for renunciants:
as for clothing, it means that originally one had lost the three robes and thus was insufficient; now, by receiving those three again, one attains contentment.
This contentment accords with the rules of renunciation; therefore, it is called "the three robes. This refers to having lost the three and then receiving them again.

There are two [types of] contentment with what is received in accordance with the rule. Regarding the third [case], from "if a householder has already invited one to accept as much as desired" onwards, it is permitted to take more because the robes are thin and coarse;

for the sake of completing the three robes, this is not an excessive acceptance. Regarding the fourth [case], from "if there are leftovers" onwards, since there is no fault in losing them, one may accept whatever is offered.
From "if a bhikṣu... onwards is the explanation of the sixth phrase: excessive acceptance constitutes an offense, resulting in the loss of one [robe].
Losing two, and so on up to losing three and receiving four—these are all cases of receiving more than one's full measure.
Because they violate the two forms of contentment, they are called "receiving in excess of contentment."
Precept Eight: Exhorting and Praising a Lay Devotee to Increase the Price of Robes.
When a lay devotee of profound faith resolves to give a gift and has already fixed the price, it is proper to accept the offering as given so as not to violate the Dharma.
Yet now, [the monk] instead complains that it is too little and seeks more than his share, thereby increasing his own greed and destroying the other’s faith and respect. For this reason...

The Noble Regulation: There are six distinct conditions. First, a non-relative householder sincerely provides the price for a robe. Second, the intention is restricted to that specific amount. Third, one knows the donor’s mind is limited to that amount.
Fourth, one disparages the small amount and urges an increase. Fifth, the donor increases the price or the thread-count. Sixth, one accepts [the robe].
This constitutes an offense. Question: Why is it that there is an exhortation to increase [the number of] robes, but none for the alms-bowl? Answer: The purpose of robes as requisites is broad;

people are prone to encouraging their increase, and therefore a precept must be established to regulate this. The bowl has but a single function; the sense of "increasing" it is rare, and for this reason no such regulation is established.

If that is so, why does one beg for a bowl? It is the same as begging for robes. Answer: In truth, there is no great need for many bowls; however, even if one is permitted to beg for only one, it still causes harm.
The affliction is not slight; therefore, it constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Within this context, there are two sections:
first, up to the point "what is the use of this," which concerns the fault arising from encouraging an increase [in the number of robes]; second, from "at that time, he...
onwards, which concerns the reproach.
This completes the four phrases of the *Śīla-mūla* (Sūtra on Precepts). First, the person who commits the offense; second, the limitation regarding the gift of robes;
third, the monk’s dissatisfaction with the small amount and his exhortation for an increase; fourth, if robes are obtained, the offense is incurred upon receiving them below that point.

These four points are fully explained. The first two are already known. From "the seeker" (*yācaka*) onwards, the third point is explained. Although the word "seeker" (*yāca*) is not explicitly present, because its meaning is implied, it is cited and then explained. "Seeking" (*yāca*).
Regarding "price": this refers to making a silk robe. Now, it is explained that one commits an offense by encouraging [the donor] to purchase fine [material].

Only when the original value is increased upon the essential substance does one fall under this precept. It is the same for seeking robes. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, encouraging an increase in color also constitutes an offense. Question:

If encouraging an increase of even a single thread constitutes an offense, why is it that in the case of seeking robes, one only commits an offense upon obtaining a single strip? Answer: When initially seeking, there was no such intention; it was only at the time of actually seeking that [the intention arose].
Leave it to them to deliberate; the meaning of "disturbance" here is subtle, such that one must violate the rule only when a single strand [of thread] is involved.

In this case, the donor initially possessed sincere intentions and had already fixed the limit of the gift. To fail to appreciate that kindness and, out of resentment over what was considered too little, to demand more—this constitutes a deep-seated disturbance, and thus the violation occurs with even a single strand.
○ The Ninth Precept on Exhorting Two Laymen to Increase the Price:
The Intention and Conditions for the Offense are no different from those previously stated; the only distinction is that two laymen act together. Question:

If one exhorts them to act together, whether there is an increase in the price or not, what offense is committed? Answer: Although an offense is committed if there is an increase, there is no offense if there is no increase. It is as follows:
These two persons act in concert; therefore, they are subsumed under this precept. Question: Why is there no exhortation regarding the three householders? Answer:

Exhorting two may cause harm, whereas exhorting three causes only slight vexation. If that is so, when one exhorts a householder to discard cotton cloth and instead produce silk, does this not carry the sense of causing harm?

Answer: This case is governed by the precept on begging for robes. In the present instance of exhorting an increase, an offense is committed only when the increase is made upon the original substance itself.
Because of the precepts, there is no transgression.
○ The tenth precept: Regarding the soliciting of robes through three times and six silent gestures.

Now, jewels, pearls, and refined essences are highly valued by worldly sentiment; they increase greed and obstruct the Path, giving rise to afflictions in profound measure. This is not comparable [to other matters].

"What the Master ought to possess has now been offered by a donor with sincere faith as the price for robes. Fearing that I might commit the offense of hoarding precious objects, it is not appropriate for me to accept them myself;
therefore, I have entrusted them to a layperson to exchange for pure goods. My search for such items has been urgent and pressing, leaving no room for hesitation."

They alternately urge and compel one another, harassing the person before them; thus they establish a restriction of "three requests and six silences. However, if one now exceeds these requests, the offense is incurred based on the state of the victim's distress.

There are five distinct conditions: first, one [monk] is the recipient and the other is a donor who sends precious goods; second, for the purpose of trading to obtain clothing for use; third, entrusting them to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a steward) to trade for clothing and requisites;

fourth, requesting more than the prescribed limit; and fifth, committing a *thullaccaya* offense upon obtaining the clothing. Question: If there is a fault regarding the clothing, why is there no such fault regarding the begging bowl? Answer: The primary function of the bowl is for eating food.

Obtaining one is sufficient; there is no need for multiple ones. Why? Because it serves its purpose with a single vessel. Furthermore, the bowl is not subject to the same rules as clothing regarding the accumulation of property or the necessity of a steward (*kappiya-kāraka*) for its acquisition. Thus, while exceeding the limit for clothing incurs an offense, there is no corresponding fault for the bowl.

One must be granted permission to ask. Regarding the three requests and six silences: if there is no prior permission to ask, how could there be any fault? If one has no bowl at all, there is no fault in asking many times.
If one already possesses a bowl, even a single request constitutes an offense. Since this falls within the category of begging for a bowl, there is no fault in the request itself. Question:

Does this precept harm the owner of the precious object, or does it harm the *pariṣkāra* (steward) owner? Answer: It is because the king or minister’s mind was moved that they requested an excessive amount, thereby resulting in the offense.

The donor of the pure [offering] incurs an offense. Regarding the textual basis, there are two parts: first, the master imposes a fine of five hundred coins for the fault of rising after having been asked;
second, at that time, the elder rebukes him with reproach.
The main text of the precept has two parts. First, the offense of seeking and binding [the robe]; second, from "If one does not obtain the robe" onwards, clarifying whether to proceed or refrain.

The preceding section has six points: first, the offender; second, from "If a king" onwards, correctly identifying the donor who dispatches a messenger to offer precious goods as the price for making the robe;
third, from "The bhikṣu should say" onwards, where, fearing the offense of possessing precious goods, he does not dare to accept them himself; fourth...
The messenger speaks to the bhikṣu [at the bottom]. This clarifies the subject of the messenger sending jewels and entrusting a layperson to purchase pure [cloth]. Five:

[starting from] "the bhikṣu who requires robes" at the bottom, this correctly opens the three verbal and six silent methods for requesting robes. Six: [starting from] "if one does not obtain the robe" at the bottom, this concerns the limit of excessive requests, the offense incurred upon obtaining the robe, and so forth.
However, these six textual sections are grouped into three: first, the offender; second, the four [conditions]; [and third, the specific acts].

The Text. The Noble One established the rule: namely, the method of sending the robe-cloth while not accepting it oneself, having entrusted it to a *viśuddhika* (pure person), and then requesting it back; third, the offense incurred upon obtaining the robe;
fourth, the procedure for entrusting it to a *viśuddhika*. There are four parts: first, questioning the *viśuddhika*; second, the monk who requires the robe.

1. Informing the *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person). 2. Sending [the item] to him. 3. Delivering it to him. 4. Reporting back to the bhikṣu. 5. Requesting the dharma. According to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing):

If one goes to request using only pure speech, there is no offense up to the sixth [step]; beyond the sixth, one commits an offense. If one uses only silence, there is no offense up to the twelfth [step]; at the thirteenth, one commits an offense.
Speech and silence alternate. After nine repetitions, there is no offense; at the tenth repetition, one commits an offense. Know that similar cases follow this pattern:
five speeches and two silences—seven repetitions, no offense; four silences and eight repetitions, no offense; three speeches and six silences—nine repetitions, no offense;
two speeches and eight silences—ten repetitions, no offense; one speech and ten silences—eleven repetitions, no offense. Once the full cycle is complete, one returns to the first silence.

Up to the sixth [case], this differs from the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the second [section], "Not Obtaining," there are three points in the Chinese text: first, going in person or sending a messenger to the donor's location;

second, stating that one will not cause them distress; third, returning to the original donor. In the detailed explanation, only the obtaining of the robe is analyzed; within that analysis of obtaining the robe, only the first two [points] are explained.
The two middle phrases of the latter two [sections] are omitted and not explained. As for "recollection" (*smṛti*):

The fifth section below explains the method for requesting [an item]. First, three words; next, six moments of silence; then, the relative strength of speech and silence. Regarding how long one may remain silent when asking:

the *Cīvara-vastu* states that it is like a person entering a storehouse to take goods and remaining for the duration of placing them on the counter, or like the time it takes to wrap up a bundle of goods.

Within this interval, there is no offense. One should immediately offer the item in exchange; since the owner of the treasure has relinquished it forever and does not fear its loss, one may request it with composure and deliberation.
He takes it. He does not commit an offense. Why does he not commit an offense regarding the possession of precious objects?

Because the precious object is not present before him, and he constantly maintains the intention that it is a purified object. It is given for the sake of *pārikkāra* (miscellaneous requisites), meaning items such as small odds and ends;
since the matter of gain and loss is trivial, even if the original owner’s mind changes and demands it back, there is no offense.
The eleventh precept concerning the making of bedding from mixed wild silk cotton.

The reason it was established is that because this material is precious and difficult to obtain, its production involves the destruction of life and invites public censure; furthermore, it fosters greed and obstructs the Path, representing a most grave transgression.

Therefore, the Sage established this rule. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, "Because this cotton is precious, and because many insects are killed for it. (From the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*).
It is said: There are four reasons why bhikṣus establish the precepts: first, to stop slander; second, to increase faith and respect;
third, so that those practicing the Path may attain peace and happiness; and fourth, to avoid harming sentient beings.

There are five conditions: first, *koseyya* (silk); second, begging for it oneself; third, making it into bedding; fourth, for one's own sake; and fifth, the act being completed constitutes an offense.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, *koseyya* is a name for cotton. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, *koseyya* here refers to a cocoon. Thus the Vinaya says:
"If one is given *koseyya*, and the water has already been heated, one may place the cocoons [into it]"; that is, one takes the cocoons and puts them inside a cauldron.
It makes a "jiu jiu" sound. However, this does not necessarily mean that *kṣauma* is translated as "silk cocoon"; rather, it is simply a name for cotton. It may be so.
Furthermore, using pure black wool together with *kṣauma*, they further create five types of warp and weft threads;

these may be used interchangeably to make robes or borders, or used purely to make the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsaka*. In the two Vinayas, [the term] *uruvūka* is called "bedding."
The characteristics [of this offense] are also difficult to discern.

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* contains three phrases: first, the person; second, the three types of mixed bedding; and third, the commission of the offense. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, one may either stuff it with cloth according to the rules for making cushions, or weave it from threads;
in both cases, one commits the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). This is because it involves taking life and, furthermore, consists of precious materials.

Therefore, it must be cut down and destroyed to prevent future transgressions. As for other [offenses] that do not involve harming living beings, one should completely relinquish them; however, these involve only the relinquishment of material wealth and lack a formal ritual for the confession of guilt.
The Twelfth Precept: Regarding Bedding Made of Black Sheep’s Wool.
This wool is a precious material and should not be used for such lowly purposes. To do so would waste the offerings of donors and incur useless expenses;
furthermore, the labor involved hinders the Path and invites public censure. Therefore, this rule must be established.
There are four conditions: first, pure black wool; this wool is precious and fine, produced in the four great kingdoms, being both costly and difficult to obtain.

Second, making it into bedding. Third, for one's own sake. Fourth, having completed it. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duōlùn), there are two methods: either sewing and storing it according to the rules for [patched] robes, or weaving it from yarn to complete it.
In both cases, one commits an offense. Regarding non-offenses, the two phrases concerning "cutting" and "damaging" refer to the original intention.
This is to avoid the fault of redundancy. At the time of its completion, there is no offense. If one has already made items such as bedding and so forth, these are not articles for wearing;
therefore, they are permitted without fault.
The Tenth Precept on Woolen Bedding: According to the *Triṃśaloka-vinaya*, this does not refer to pure white wool;
rather, it is not an offense if the bedding is made from a mixture of three types of wool. Among the three types of black wool, [the rule applies].

If one adds one *liang* of black fur, one commits a *pāyattika* offense because it is precious. If one adds one *liang* of white fur, one commits a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*) because it is base. Adding brindled fur does not constitute an offense.
If one removes one *liang*, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

There are five conditions: first, the three types of hair must be interwoven; second, it must be made into bedding; third, it must be for one's own use; fourth, one *liang* of high-quality hair must be added;

fifth, it must be manifested as white within the context of its completion. Because these conditions serve as the basis, and because according to this Vinaya it appears that only pure white [wool] constitutes an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), the Buddha taught that the fault of using pure white [wool] is committed when the three types of hair are interwoven. Thus, the offense is established through four conditions: first, pure white [wool].

[The rule concerns] hair. Second, making it into bedding; third, for oneself; fourth, the offense is incurred as soon as it is completed. Question: Both black [wool] and white [wool] constitute an offense when combined.

Why is it that the white [wool] rule prohibits mixing, whereas the black [wool] rule does not? Answer: Provided that the mixing is done correctly, there is no fault in either case. One should follow the prohibition regarding white wool.

As for the category of "mixing," it is clarified in the preceding precept that if the mixing is done properly, there is no offense. Question: When three types of hair are mixed together, why is it [an offense] in the case of black [wool]?

Regarding "many": The answer is that although black wool is expensive, it is used in large quantities because the robes of those who have left the household life are identical. White [wool] is used sparingly because it is a garment of the laity;
its length would breed arrogance and invite derision. Therefore, it must be limited.

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of three sections: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the instruction for the bhikṣu regarding the ritual of the three hairs; and third, from the words "If a bhikṣu...
onwards, which does not participate in the formal determination of the offense. This will be explained in detail below. Regarding the "three *pala*": this is translated as four *liang*.

Since it is included within the category of non-offenses, there is no fault. As for "cutting and destroying," if the original intention was to cut [the cloth], yet it is destroyed [in color], it is because its color is not pure white.

There is no offense if one intends to cut, detail, or destroy [the material] but does not complete the act; furthermore, there is no offense if it has already been made into items such as pillows and the like, because these are not articles of clothing.
Thus, they are permitted without fault.
The Fourteenth Precept: Regarding the Making of Bedding Before Six Years Have Passed.

If one already possesses old bedding that has not yet reached six years of use, yet is sufficient to support the body and cultivate the Path, and one nevertheless discards it without relinquishing the old to instead create something new, this increases craving and obstructs the Path while inviting the reproach of the world. For this reason, the Sage established this precept.

The offense is established through six conditions: first, there is an existing bedding or furniture that has not been used for six years; second, one does not relinquish the old item; third, the Saṃgha grants permission;
fourth, one makes a new item; fifth, it is for one’s own sake; sixth, upon its completion, the offense is incurred.

The text of the *Prātimokṣa* has three parts: first, a brief explanation of the *Prātimokṣa* itself; second, the section on prohibitions and subsequent permissions, which consists of five parts. Regarding the fifth point above concerning the procedure for granting permission: Question:
If a person provides bedding and furniture, and they mutually fail to act according to the Dharma, does the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) succeed? Answer:

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, it should be understood by analogy with the previous case of being separated from one's robes (*cīvara-vipravāsa*); thus, it should likewise be successful. However, it may also not be successful, as in the case where instruction is given to one who lacks virtue, and the ritual does not succeed.

Regarding the gradations: Question—Once the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) has been completed, one then makes the distinction between "black" and "white. Does this constitute a violation of the rule concerning the reduction of the six-year period?

Answer—There is no violation of the reduction of the six years, because the dharma has been obtained. Regarding the making of the black and white boundaries, there are separate violations for the two preceding cases:

for example, as when one constructs a dwelling exceeding the prescribed measure after having been subject to formal disciplinary action (*pravāsanīya-karman*), there is a separate offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, yet the original disciplinary action remains intact; there is no offense of "not being subject to disciplinary action. This case is also like that. [End of] Precept.
This text has three parts: first, the offender; second, the six-year limit; and third, the offense incurred if one makes a new mat after reducing the old one below the prescribed size.

In the detailed explanation below, only the first and third points are explained, while the second sentence is omitted. Question: Why is a time limit established for bedding so that it does not become worn out, whereas no such limit is set for [other items]?

Why are they treated differently? Answer: Bedding is intended to absorb moisture and odors. Therefore, a limit is set to prevent it from becoming excessively worn. As for other items, since they do not have this function, no such limit is established.
Regarding the requisites for sustaining the body: if they have been used for six years or more and have become old, worn out, and dilapidated, their utility for sustaining the body is diminished;

therefore, a limit is established. However, there is no need to establish a limit for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). This is only because one fears it might soil the monastic bedding and obstruct the use of the body;

as long as the material remains, there is no limit on its age. If one already possesses a sitting mat but, out of greed, makes another, it must be regulated by requiring it to be patched, thereby putting an end to attachment to fine things.
It is because of such a mind that it is so.
○ Precept Fifteen: Regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).

Since one already possesses an old sitting mat, it is sufficient for shielding the body; now, to loathe the old and create a new one is to wastefully squander the offerings of the faithful and to increase greed.
It obstructs the Path; therefore, the *jie* (undergarment) was prescribed so as to cause [the practitioner] to rest and to lengthen the Path. There is benefit in the use of existing items;
now, to create something new and not use the old *jie* violates the holy teaching, and thus the offense of *thullaccaya* is prescribed.
There are five conditions for a separate offense: first, possessing a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat); second, making a new one; third, making it for oneself; fourth, not patching it with an old one;

and fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as it is completed. Question: If one makes a *niṣīdana* that is not patched and exceeds the prescribed dimensions, does one incur one offense or two? Answer: One incurs two offenses.
When relinquishing it, one must first cut away the portion exceeding the proper measure, and only then perform the confession (*pratideśanā*). If this is so...
Regarding "not mending": if one has already mended it and then repented, why must it be relinquished? Answer: If a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is not mended, there is a fault throughout its entire body;

even if it is mended again now, the original fault still remains. Therefore, it must be relinquished. Regarding "measuring the fault": if there is a fault outside the measured limit, and once that portion is cut away there is no longer a fault within the measured limit, why must it be relinquished?
Furthermore, since it is to be returned to the owner, there is no sense of personal use [in keeping it]. Therefore.
It must be cut. If it is made from an old garment, there is only the fault of exceeding the prescribed dimensions; there is no transgression of not patching it. Question:

Why is there no rule for cutting down an oversized bowl to be used as one’s personal possession, as is done with a sitting mat? Answer: A sitting mat may be cut and still remain according to the Dharma, but if a bowl were cut down, it would no longer resemble a bowl.
Therefore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, bowls have neither extension nor reduction, whereas robes involve cutting and joining.

The text on the causal narrative consists of two parts: first, up to the point where the fault of not discoloring [the robes] is raised; second, the fact that the bhikṣus did not reprimand him. The first part further consists of two sections:
first, up to the point where discolored [robes] are prescribed so that new ones may be worn; second, from the group of six down to the point where the fault of not discoloring them is raised.
The preceding text has three parts. First, the disorderliness of sitting mats constitutes a fault regarding their use. There are five conditions for one who does not accept an invitation:

first, for the sake of entering into meditative seclusion; second, for the sake of preaching the Dharma to the devas; third, for the sake of tending to the sick; fourth, for the sake of establishing the precepts.

1. Inspecting the rooms, dwellings, and bedding; 2. From "The Buddha, having seen this," below, he conceived the intention to establish the rule for wearing the inner robe (*saṃkakṣikā*); 3. From "After the meal was finished," below, he informed the assembly and established the rule for wearing the inner robe.

The Prātimokṣa Sūtra contains three sections: first, the person; second, the threefold regulation of the method of preparation; and third, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the determination of the offense.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one *vitasti* of the Sugata is two feet. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika*, it should be made with an old rug all around, because the color of the Sugata’s *vitasti* has been altered.
The Sixteenth Precept on Carrying Wool for More Than Three Yojanas:

Now, when one who has left the household life carries wool while traveling along the road, their conduct becomes indistinguishable from that of worldly people, thereby violating the rules of dignified demeanor.

This would invite public censure and damage the Way; therefore, it was prohibited. As for why the distance of three *yojanas* was later permitted: those with bodies dependent on material sustenance have no other means to survive.
Thus, the limit was later expanded to three *yojanas*; however, if one exceeds this limit, one incurs an offense of transgression.
There are four conditions: first, noble wool; second, one's own property; third, carrying it oneself; fourth, exceeding three *yojanas*. The *Prātimokṣa* has three clauses: first, the person;
second, the allowance for three *yojanas*; third, the offense incurred by carrying it beyond that limit.
In the extensive explanation, the first phrase is self-evident. Next, the second phrase is explained from "If one upholds it oneself" through to the third [phrase].
From "If there is someone who has upheld it" onwards, the third section explains the offense; herein, the five phrases are divided into three parts. First is "if there is someone who upholds it."
One must not assist in carrying it; to carry it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, because one is not carrying it entirely oneself and exceeds the limit of three [yojanas].

The next two phrases refer to causing the other four assemblies to carry it beyond the limit, which incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Following the exclusion of wool, the next two phrases concern other inferior or base items;
to carry them oneself beyond the limit incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Briefly stated, if one improperly understands high-value wool and carries it oneself beyond the limit, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
The seventeenth precept concerning causing a *bhikṣuṇī* to wash and card wool:

The intent and the conditions for the offense are the same as those for washing old robes. However, this offense applies to both new and old wool, because it was established as a prohibition against wasting labor and neglecting one's duties.
The Eighteenth Precept: Regarding the Possession of Precious Objects.
First, a general summary; second, a detailed explanation. As for these "precious objects," they constitute one of the eight types of impure wealth.
Therefore, I shall now provide a general explanation of the meaning of the eight types of impurity, analyzing them through four sections: first, enumerating the items and explaining their names;

second, what is permitted and what is prohibited to possess; third, the gravity of the offenses incurred by possessing them; and fourth, the gravity of the offenses incurred when exchanging them with one another.
Regarding the first gate: first, fields and dwellings; second, planting roots and sprouts; third, storing and accumulating grain, salt, and seeking profit therefrom;
fourth, male and female slaves and dependents; fifth, raising herds of livestock; sixth, gold, silver, coins, and treasures;
seventh, keeping ivory, and large beds carved with gold and silver, along with cotton mattresses and woolen carpets; eighth, all copper and iron cauldrons and pots, excluding sixteen.
Vessels are not included in this restriction. If one keeps these eight items, they increase a person's greed and defile their holy life (brahmacarya); therefore, they are called "impure.

This is from the *Sujāta-sūtra*. Although there are textual references to these in two places within this Vinaya—the section on robes (*cīvara*) and the section on miscellaneous matters (*kṣudraka*)—they are not arranged in sequence.

Regarding the second section: among the first category of fields and the second category of root-plants, these increase greed and obstruct the Path; thus, there is no principle permitting their possession.

Regarding the first category of houses and dwellings, there are cases where possession is permitted and cases where it is not. If one extensively possesses manors and residences, this is not permitted.

However, even though a single small room is a heavy object, because it serves the purpose of supporting the Path, the Noble Ones have permitted its possession; it does not require the ritual of *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (purification by declaration). The second...

Regarding the three types of impure [grain], the *Śāriputra-vinaya* records this reflection: "I fear that at that time grain will be expensive. Now, with this surplus grain, I shall rely upon it to recite the sūtras, sit in meditation, cultivate merit, and practice the Way.

When the time comes and grain becomes very dear, if he sells the remainder—whether for his own consumption, to give to his upādhyāya or ācārya, or to perform meritorious deeds—and profits from the sale, there is no offense. The same applies to the purchase of medicinal herbs. This is...

It is not permitted to keep or trade [these items]; otherwise, it is not allowed. If one is ill, it is permitted to keep medicinal salt for as long as one lives; if one is not ill, it is not permitted.
Regarding the fourth and fifth [categories], if one is not ill, all are prohibited. If one is old or ill, keeping them is permitted.
As for the sixth—gold, silver, money, jewels, and so forth—it is not opened for use whether one is ill or not, because the harm is grave. Nevertheless, they serve as provisions...

One must perform the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification). One may keep [an item] by entrusting it to a layperson for the purpose of purification, always maintaining the intention that it is a purified object received through formal acceptance.

Among the seven or eight [categories], regardless of whether one is ill or not, there are cases where exceptions are granted and cases where they are not, such as with bedding, quilts, and woolen rugs.

These may be kept through the three or five periods of purification by means of a gift of purity (*śuddhika-dāna*), as well as the sixteen [types of items] and so forth; such are the explanations for this class of objects.

The third category consists of two types: those that are precious in substance and those that are deeply conducive to the growth of greed. Regarding the former, there exists the method of "pure giving" (*viśuddha-dāna*);

to possess them without such purification violates the teachings and constitutes an offense of transgression (*thullaccaya*). As for the latter, since their substance is not precious and the affliction they produce is slight, and furthermore, because there is no method of pure giving, there is no fault of failing to declare what should be declared; possessing them is merely a minor offense.
The Fourth Gate: Trading the eight kinds of impure goods for the ten kinds of robes constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Trading the ten kinds of robes for two of the eight kinds of impure goods—the sixth and seventh—constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the remaining six kinds of impure goods, one incurs only a *dukkaṭa*.
