If one trades the sixth or seventh for the eighth, there is both a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*; likewise, trading the remaining six for the eighth also entails both a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*. This concludes the separate explanation of the precept regarding precious objects.

The substance of jewels is of great value and weight; it fosters greed and obstructs the Path, giving rise to contention and inviting the world’s reproach and suspicion. Therefore, the Sage established a precept prohibiting their acceptance and possession.

Nevertheless, because they are essential requisites, he made an exception: one may accept them after entrusting them to a layperson to exchange for pure goods. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-āloka* (Manyi-lun) states:
The reason for establishing the precept for bhikṣus is that it serves three benefits: first, to stop slander; second, to extinguish strife and contention;
and third, to fulfill the practice of the noble lineage of contentment. To store and use items for one's own sake is called "possessing" (畜);

to cherish what one prizes and plays with is termed "treasure" (寶). Therefore, it is called the "precept against possessing treasures. Regarding the three categories of treasures, robes, and medicine, they are designated as "possessing" and "trading."

One may possess an alms bowl when one lacks it, and trade for food when one lacks it; the meaning of these cases is different. Answer: Precious objects carry heavy consequences, while medicine can prolong life;

clothing and requisites have a broader scope of utility, yet all violate the rules regarding contentious matters. Therefore, possessing them constitutes an offense. Since they invite public censure from laypeople, trading for them is likewise an offense.
Thus, the texts mention trading for precious objects as well as *pārikkhāra* (miscellaneous requisites), exchanging a seven-day period for another seven-day period.

[The text continues with] "and so forth. Because there is the fault of storing food that has become raw, one must not keep food [overnight]. Because it is exchanged with the laity, the offense of trading is established.

Therefore, the text says: "exchanging time for time," and so forth. Since the bowl is something kept, trading it would also constitute an offense. That it is not mentioned in the text is due to brevity;

it is like the case where, within the rules regarding an extra bowl, if one does not relinquish it and instead trades it for another bowl—since the phrase "trading again" is used, we know that trading a bowl is likewise [an offense].

Regarding the transgression of limits: if one clearly establishes the number of precepts, the categories of robes, jewels, and so forth are distinct, and the conditions for their possession likewise differ.

From beginning to end, there are six types of possessions; that is to say, there are three types of robes, as well as bowls, medicine, jewels, and so on. However, there are only two types of exchange. Which are they?
Just as jewels constitute a distinct substance, they are established as one type of "hoarding" (*nikṣepa*). If one trades in them, all seven classes of monastics incur an offense simultaneously;

because this trading differs from other forms of trade, a separate rule is established for trading in jewels. As for the remaining items such as robes and so forth, their substances are distinct and the conditions for their possession differ; thus, five types of hoarding must be established.
Regarding the same two types of laypeople, in cases such as those that give rise to public censure, the prohibition against trading is established as a single rule;

this refers to buying and selling. There are four distinct conditions: first, it must be money or precious gems; second, one must know it to be money or precious gems; third, it must be for one's own sake; fourth, upon receiving it, one commits the offense.

Regarding the first condition, "precious gems," this refers to gold, silver, and coins, which are further divided into seven types as in the text; the remainder are counterfeit gems. Possessing them [constitutes an offense].

Committing a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*): the value of the money is also not fixed. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if there are inscriptions or images on it, and it is used in the country as currency capable of generating interest and profit—this being a place where greed grows deep—it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If there are inscriptions or images on it, but it is not used in the country, it is a minor offense.

If there are no inscriptions or images on it and it is used in the country, although there is no explicit text in the Vinaya regarding its origin, since it is not used [as currency], there is no offense. This *vinaya* merely states "on top... [and so forth].
There are inscribed images; these are likely what the country regards as "forfeiture through transgression" (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), while others would not constitute a transgression.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, all seven treasures constitute a downfall (*pāyattika*), whereas copper coins constitute a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). Regarding the fourth condition for committing an offense by receiving [precious objects]: if one intends to keep them as wealth, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Wǔfēnlù*), one commits an offense in five ways of receiving:
first, taking them with the hand; second, taking them from another; third, taking them from another using a vessel.
Fourth, if one becomes attached to this; fifth, answering by saying, "I have given it to this *śuddhika-puruṣa*," both constitute the acceptance of precious objects.
The textual basis for this has two parts: first, up to the marketplace, where the transgression arises; second, from "the various householders" onwards, where three people reprimand him.

The Worldly Censure of the Text, Part Three: 1. Monastics and laypeople express derision and reproach. 2. At that time, the king, ministers, and those below them deliberate upon the right and wrong of the matter, report it to the Buddha, and present their case.
3. The Buddha addresses the ministers and others to manifest the Great Sage’s praise and his discourse on the transgressions.

Regarding the Chinese text, there are three parts. First, an exaltation of this teaching. Second, from "I have such words" onwards, it explains that [the Buddha] permitted [the use of] dwellings and the like, as well as the acceptance of precious objects, while other matters were not permitted.
Third, from "The ministers should know" onwards, it enumerates four transgressions to demonstrate that he is not a son of the Śākya, thereby clarifying the intent of the preceding censure.
By speaking of these faults through words, one knows for certain that he is not a śramaṇa.
"Disciples of the Śākya" is a term used to highlight a transgression. [The Buddha] said, "I am your teacher; I do not permit you to take precious objects.
This opens up the wording regarding acceptance: "I have such a statement: if one seeks timber, bamboo, grass, or tree bark for the purpose of building a house, it may be accepted."

These are essential requisites; because they are without fault, one may accept them as treasures. One should not, however, receive them for one's own personal use, for to do otherwise would constitute a transgression.

Regarding the four afflictions of the sun and moon: first, the asuras; second, smoke and clouds; third, dust; and fourth, mist. Regarding the four afflictions of the śramaṇa: alcohol is the root of heedlessness;
sexual desire is the source of birth and death; gold and silver give rise to heavy afflictions; and false views destroy goodness.

Just as the sun and moon lack the power to illuminate because they are subject to four afflictions, so too does the Dharma lack the reputation for radiant manifestation because the śramaṇas commit four transgressions.
Now, this person’s possession of treasure is one of those four afflictions; therefore, he is not a son of the Śākya.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra has three points: first, the person; second, the treasure that was seized; and third, the commissioning of the offense through the dual action of both oneself and another.
Below this, the method for relinquishing [the object] is distinguished. While there should be four major sections, only three are presented here;

this is because confessing the offense is not appropriate before laypeople, and it is omitted for fear of confusion. First, the text for relinquishing the treasure has three parts. Since these items were not permitted by the Buddha, it says:
This is not what I should do. Second, regarding the passage beginning with "If that person, having taken it... and continuing down to the end of the legal text, there are two parts.

First, if the steward who purifies the object does not understand the matter, and the one returning what resembles a jewel accepts it because he intends to do so, he may further transfer it as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) and, having obtained the robe, keep it.
Second, if that *upāsaka* [and so forth]—meaning the steward who knows the law—obtains the robe, he may keep it. Third, if he has taken it and not...

Regarding "returning," this refers to returning to seek whether one has progressed or not; it is a brief way of saying there is no abandonment of the offense, as already explained above. This differs from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which speaks of permanent abandonment.
As for the statement that "observing [the rule] is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing)," this refers to the fault of losing the Dharma through formal resolution.
The Nineteenth Precept on Trading Jewels:
Using precious objects to trade with one another for the sake of profit and interest increases greed, obstructs the Path, and invites worldly reproach and transgression.

Therefore, the Noble One’s regulations must be followed regarding the similarities and differences between this [monastic offense] and that of trading with laypeople. There are eight points of difference: 1. **The breadth of the object of the offense:** This offense applies to all seven classes of monastics;

the latter [offense] applies only to two types of laypeople. 2. **The nature of the traded goods:** Here, it concerns only money and the like; in the latter case, there are five items or three items. 3.

**Distinctions regarding the action:** In this case, both oneself and others commit the offense; in the case of selling, only oneself commits the offense. The text states that one should cause it to be purified.
1. Human trade. 2. Among the four types of relinquishing wealth, there are distinctions regarding the object of the wealth (*dharma*) and the legal procedure (*vidhi*). 3.

Regarding the five methods for removing offenses, this refers to trading that involves six, five, or four [categories of goods], as it corresponds to three types of objects. Furthermore, one must not handle precious gems; there are only four legal procedures, along with the specific confession (*pratideśanā*). 4.
The different ways of returning the object—namely, whether it is transferred or not—and the distinctions between the objects and the legal procedures. 5. Not...

They are not the same; there are distinctions among these eight types of openings. The opening for jewels pertains to the utilization of merit, while the opening for trade pertains to external necessities. These eight positions fall into three categories:

the first three concern the time of transgression, the next four concern the time of relinquishment, and the final one concerns the opening itself. Such are their distinct characteristics regarding the two types of prohibitions and exchanges.

There are five distinct conditions: first, precious objects; second, mutual trade; third, fixing the price; fourth, for one's own sake; and fifth, receiving. The three phrases of the root precept are:
first, the person; second, mutual trade; and third, the completion of the offense. The first phrase is self-evident. [The term] *vividha* (various)...
Below this, the explanation of the second phrase consists of two parts. First, the explanation of the various kinds of gold and silver, each having three types, while coins have only one;
together there are seven types. These are exchanged with one another, forming seven sets of seven phrases. Second, coins alone are singled out as eight types because they generate much profit;
even coins that are not precious metals are included under the category of "treasure. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards is the explanation of the third part, which defines the offense.
The method for relinquishing [the offense] is the same as for the previous rule on keeping precious objects. **The Twentieth Precept:

On Buying and Selling** In principle, those who have left the household life should cease worldly affairs and sit in stillness to cultivate the Way. How could one personally engage in trade or commerce, rushing about in pursuit of profit?

Running through the marketplaces and streets, they violate dignified decorum and incur the reproach and shame of the world. Once wealth and goods are exchanged, there is even the possibility of committing a grave offense;

when facing perilous and dangerous situations, their conduct lacks noble integrity. Because of these various faults, the Sage prohibited such behavior based on the four principles of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*.
First, for the sake of increasing the Buddha-dharma; second, for the sake of ceasing strife and contention; third, for the sake of establishing the noble lineage;
fourth, for the sake of increasing faith and reverence so as not to slander [the Dharma]. A merchant is not like a butcher; the mind of a butcher is [not so].

Desiring that all others do not perform [certain acts] while he alone does them—just as a merchant, regardless of the quantity of goods he possesses, intends for the world to become extremely expensive and plagued by famine and blockades—so too, such extensive explanations used to deceive both the noble and the ordinary are full of faults.
Therefore, it is improper to use these items of trade to construct stūpas or images; one must not dwell in such rooms, and so forth. There are [scriptural prohibitions] to this effect.

Because there are many transgressions, there are six distinct conditions: first, being at home; second, among the assembly (which includes non-Buddhists as well); third, mutual trade; fourth, fixing the price; fifth, for one's own sake;
sixth, personal bartering; and seventh, receiving. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, these are distinguished by pure speech and impure speech.

Regarding the analysis of the four permutations (*catuskoṭi*) concerning equal value and mutual exchange: while the *Mahīśāsaka* (Daoshi) school establishes four permutations based on whether there is an offense at the time of the cause but not at the time of the fruit, and so forth, this Vinaya [the Dharmaguptaka] considers it an offense even when using pure speech (*viśuddhavāda*). It cannot be equated with the *Mahāsāṃghika* (Ji).
However, as long as buying and selling take place, each act of buying and selling constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; thus, it differs from the *Mahīśāsaka*.
The introductory narrative consists of two parts: first, the exchange with householders and the resulting transgression;

second, the criticism from the non-Buddhists after they obtained the robes. The former part further divides into two: first, the exchange of ginger for food, which refers to exchanging that which lasts for a lifetime for that which is temporary;
second, the section beginning with Śrāvastī, which concerns external material exchanges, referring to exchanging *pārikāra* for *pārikāra*. Having already...

The inferior is easily surpassed by the superior; it may even involve the commission of a grave offense (*pārājika*), though that is not what is clarified here. It may also be considered doubly urgent because it involves repaying a price, yet it is not said to be a grave offense.

This may indeed be so, for there is no censure from fellow practitioners; thus, the five assemblies (*pañca-nikāya*) are permitted [to trade]. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, only laypeople commit an offense through trade.

Although non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are heterodox, because they are renunciants, they do not commit an offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, only non-Buddhists commit an offense through trade.

[This constitutes] an offense. Because their wrong views differ, laypeople commit a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, all seven classes of followers commit the offense;

here, however, it refers specifically to the two types of laypeople and the limit of the non-Buddhist laity, and thus they also commit the offense. Because the discourse on reality is straightforward, it is said that [the teaching] is "thoroughly determined" and so forth.
One must not engage in trade with these two types of laypeople or non-Buddhists; therefore, it says, "one must not trade with others. Since trading is not permitted:
One should employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant). Furthermore, it is already known that one may not trade for oneself, nor may one do so for another bhikṣu;

therefore, it is said that one must not trade with others. One should have a *kappiya-kāraka* perform the trade. Moreover, the essence of the monastic discipline (*pravrajyā-dharma*) is such that one does not violate the sentiments of others;
if there is regret, the item must be returned. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the limit is within seven days for its return.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra consists of three sections: first, the person; second, the explanation of buying and selling;

third, the conclusion regarding the offense. The detailed explanation likewise consists of these three parts. The first section is self-evident. Regarding the explanation of the second section: first, there is a general restatement of the heading;

second, under the phrase "exchanging time for time," there is the specific commentary. Within this commentary, there are two parts. First, the explanation of the various types [of exchange] in relation to the five kinds of objects, which comprises five phrases.

This can be understood from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. A bowl is similar to a bowl; likewise, robes, bathing basins, fans, medicines for the time, medicines for the night, medicines for seven days, and medicines for life—all these are "similar" when they are of their own respective kind.
If one uses a bowl to purchase a robe, this is "dissimilar," and so on up to using [a bowl] to purchase a bowl for life;
all such acts constitute the offense of trading. According to this text, other miscellaneous cases are to be judged by analogy.

Items of this kind should all be subsumed under the *pāṭidesanīya* (offenses requiring confession). Second, from "the seller" onwards, there is the explanation of the preceding section on buying and selling.

First, the explanation of the text concerning selling has three parts: first, a general statement that "higher and lower" refers to selling; second, the increased sale; third, the further increased sale—these two refer to the higher price.
Following this is the explanation of the section on buying, which should likewise have three points: first, a general statement that the value is five *kārsāpaṇas*; [second, the calculation...]
Regarding "counting up and down": this refers to a reduction in the purchase price. Next, giving three *kārsāpaṇas* refers to an increase or decrease in the purchase price.

Next, giving one *kārsāpaṇa* refers to a further increase or decrease in the purchase price. These three correctly explain the lower price; therefore it is said, "the purchase is also like this. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*:
if an object is worth fifty [coins], yet the price demanded is a hundred coins, and one now gives fifty, this is not called a "lower price. This explains the third point.

The offenses may be understood [from the preceding]. Among those that do not constitute an offense, this is permitted for the sake of external use so that there is no transgression. Furthermore, while previously it was for one's own use, this permission allows for the offering of lamps and light.
The Twenty-first Precept: Regarding the Keeping of an Extra Alms Bowl.

Now, the alms bowl is the vessel for receiving offerings; it is sufficient for the sustenance of the body. To now store and keep an extra one beyond necessity obstructs the Path, invites reproach and disgrace, and the damage caused by its loss is no small matter.
For this reason, the Sage established this rule. However, as material things are subject to constant change, there may be occasions of loss or theft.

The essential requirements for the body must not be neglected. Since one cannot accept [extra bowls] at the time of giving, and they will later be difficult to obtain, the Buddha permitted the practice of declaring them "pure" (*śuddha*) for ten days and keeping them.
To contravene the holy teaching carries the fault of an offense (*āpatti*). According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu who obtained two bowls;
because the Buddha did not permit the keeping of surplus items, he gave one away. Later, his bowl broke. The Buddha asked, "After how many days did it break? He replied, "Ten days. Because of this...
The ten-day period is opened. Because this Vinaya was requested [on that occasion], it likewise opens for ten days; hence it is called the precept regarding keeping a bowl beyond ten days.
There are five specific conditions: first, one already possesses a bowl that has been formally accepted; second, one further obtains another bowl;

third, it must be a bowl that is *dharmya* (in accordance with the Dharma)—if it is not *dharmya*, there is no offense—meaning it must possess three kinds of conformity: first, conformity of substance, meaning it is made only of clay or iron; second, conformity of measure... [the text continues with "three"].

Less than one *dǒu* [of capacity] and more than one and a half *dǒu*—these three are considered "proper color" (*sèrú*), according to the *Jiàn lùn* (Treatise on Seeing). Regarding the bowl, it must be fired and fumigated five times;

for earthenware bowls, it must be fired and fumigated three times or more before they are considered "proper color. Question: If a layperson commits the offense of "excess" (*cháng*) regarding robes, does this not also apply to a white (unfired) bowl?

Answer: The *Duō lùn* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra) states: "Clothing can be dyed to suit one's wishes, yet even so, it constitutes an offense. If a bowl is fired or fumigated, it may become damaged or ruined; thus, it is difficult [to maintain]."
It may be as you wish; therefore, there is no offense. Question: If a robe is either oversized or undersized, it still constitutes valid possession (*parigraha*).

Why is it not so for the alms bowl (*pātra*), which must necessarily be of the correct measure? Answer: A robe can be cut and joined, whereas an alms bowl cannot be extended or shortened. Therefore, if it is oversized or undersized, it does not constitute valid possession.

Fourth, regarding the failure to declare purity (*apariśuddhi-ākhyāpana*); fifth, the offense of exceeding ten days. Based on the four types of perception (*saṃjñā*) discussed below, one should add an additional condition; [however, in this case] there is none.
Because the causes and conditions are conflated with those of the one-month and five-month [periods], they are omitted here and not discussed.

If one obtains a bowl on the fifth day and it has been subject to three formal acts of suspension (*ukkhepana*), even if many days have passed, there is no offense of prolongation (*atireka-āpatti*). If, after the suspension is lifted, one obtains another bowl on the fifth day...
This fulfills the four points of the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*: first, the person; second, the extra bowl that may be kept; third, the allowance to keep it for ten days;

and fourth, the offense incurred by violating the time limit. Question: When the *kaṭhina* robe has already been removed, why is there no such provision for the bowl? Answer: The substance of the robe and the bowl are distinct.

Because the [extra] does not exceed the bowl, one cannot say that the robe has already been "taken out" (distributed). [Question: It may be so regarding the principle that the robe does not exceed the bowl;

why then is the *kaṭhina* not accepted for the bowl? [Answer: There are three types of robes; because the *saṃghāṭī* is heavy, the acceptance of the *guṇa-kaṭhina* (merit-robe) is permitted, and there is no offense in being separated from it overnight.

Furthermore, the *guṇa-kaṭhina* is not merely an extra item, as it also serves to supplement other long robes. However, as for the bowl, one possesses only a single one, which must accompany the person.
Regarding the use [of the bowl]: how could one receive the *kaṭhina* bowl? Since its reception is not permitted, it is clear that it does not provide for an increase [in possessions];

therefore, it does not exist [as a separate category]. Question: For what reason is the month of *kārttika* not opened as a period for making bowls? Answer: Because the bowl has not yet been completed, one has not yet committed the offense of "excess" (*atireka*).

What need is there for a further month? Once his bowl is completed, ten days have already elapsed; since he has performed the ritual of pure donation (*śuddhaka-dāna*) by giving it to another, there is no need to open the period of use.

A detailed explanation of the four propositions follows. The first two are explained individually. Regarding the second section on the bowl, there are four parts: (1) a general enumeration of the six types of bowls—namely, substance, location, and color;

(2) a detailed determination of the substance, which consists of only two types; (3) the determination of the measurements and limits; and (4) the possession of the three characteristics of conformity.

The Vinaya regulations mandate that one must accept and maintain [the bowl] and perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one accepts the bowl because this *pātra* is of the proper measure for long-term use.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one accepts and maintains this *pātra* as a vessel for alms-round, reciting the formula three times.
If a bhikṣu violates these rules, the analysis of the offense, its relinquishment, and the cases where there is no offense is identical to that regarding "extra robes" (*atireka-cīvara*). Its...
The method for returning the bowl (*pātra*) also requires an overnight stay; otherwise, it is returned immediately. The only difference is that the bowl itself is used [as the object].

Regarding the eight sections explaining the characteristics of the offenses concerning long robes, bowls, medicine, and so forth, when they all state "neither robe, nor bowl, nor medicine," this means that the substance itself is fundamentally not what it purports to be, and thus no offense is committed.
When each section below, under the heading of "not returning," states "having made it into something other than a robe, bowl, or medicine," this means...
Having accepted and relinquished [the previous rules], one transforms the three preceding entities into "non-existence.
The Twenty-second Precept on Begging for Alms Bowls:

Now, if a bowl has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, it is fit for use as a support for the body. Yet, one now goes about begging for them from non-relatives in various places, thereby increasing [one's possessions].
Greed obstructs the Path and causes distress to the donor; this is contrary to principle and therefore must be prohibited by the Noble Ones.

There are six specific conditions [for this offense]: first, one already possesses a bowl that has been formally accepted; second, it has fewer than five patches and does not leak; third, one repeatedly solicits from a householder who is not a relative;
fourth, it is for one's own sake; fifth, one solicits a bowl in accordance with the Dharma; and sixth, one accepts it, thereby committing the offense.

The two phrases of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* are divided into three parts in the first section explaining the text of the precept itself: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the old bowl that has not yet leaked;

third, the renewed seeking and the resulting offense. Second, from "That bhikṣu... onwards, is the procedure for relinquishing and returning [the bowl], which differs from other precepts. Within this section, there are two parts.
First, the recitation for relinquishing the bowl; second, from "having passed it on" onwards, these are combined into a single phrase for the collective recitation of returning the bowl.

Regarding the phrase "this is the proper time," it refers to the period when one uses the old bowl to hold the new one, until it breaks and is no longer held. However, the four sections concerning the return [of the bowl] below should all follow this same text.

Since there are no distinct characteristics regarding the confession or the non-returning [of the bowl], they are omitted here and not discussed. This concludes the explanation of the *Śīlaskandha* (Fundamental Precepts).

This may be understood. Next, the explanation of the text for relinquishing and confessing has four parts: first, the relinquishing of the bowl; second, having relinquished it, one should confess—this is the confession of the offense;

third, "The bowl of this bhikṣu... and below is the returning of the bowl; fourth, "In the midst of the Saṃgha... and below is the formal determination of the offense for not returning it. First, the explanation of the initial relinquishing involves four methods.

The same as above. First, regarding this *niḥsargika* (offense involving forfeiture): 1) it concerns the bowl that has been relinquished; 2) it involves the middle or lower grades of objects; 3) one should remain in a humble posture;

and 4) there are the formal words for the act of relinquishment. Second, the phrase "in the midst" (*antaḥ*) and below serves to distinguish this from other precepts. The term "residence" (*āvāsa*) excludes three types:

namely, the *śīma-kaṭhina* (formal boundary), the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), and the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*), because these are not considered "residences. Furthermore, it excludes those who have no fixed residence.

Because there is no monastic storehouse (*saṃghakośa*), the phrase "discarding within the Saṃgha" excludes cases involving three or fewer individuals; the remaining two textual passages can be understood accordingly.

As for the reason why it must be [deposited] in the residence and so forth, the answer is that an alms bowl has little utility; one returns the inferior one while keeping the superior one to enter the monastic storehouse.
If that is so, then even if one receives many extra robes, it both troubles the donor and damages the monastery; why not return one robe to the donor and take the rest for the Saṃgha?
Answer: The purpose of robes is broad and extensive; therefore, they should all be returned to the donor. As for alms bowls, there is no great need for many;
obtaining one is sufficient, and any more would be of no use, so they must be entered into the Saṃgha. Objection: If that is so, an extra bowl is likewise of little use; why then take them all?
If one obtains an extra bowl to return to its owner, or acquires it by trading one's own property, or if the donor personally delivers it, there is no harm or affliction involved;
although it is not of much use, it must nevertheless be returned to the owner. To beg for bowls is a source of many troubles: first, it increases excessive greed; second, it afflicts the donor.
Since three alms bowls are not of much use, only one is returned. This corresponds to the text for relinquishing [the bowl] recited in the *Śīla-sūtra* (Precept Manual).
Second, the confession of transgressions is as explained in the usual procedures.
The third section, "The Text on Returning the Alms Bowl," consists of four parts. It includes the text concerning how one should successively take down the lower bowl and have it held, etc.
Within this, there are four sub-sections: 1. When a person of high status seizes and retains [the bowl], the lower bowl should be returned. 2.

Regarding the text beginning with "That bhikṣu’s bowl should be formally announced (*jñapti*)," even if [the current holder] considers himself superior, he must successively take down the lower bowl. 3. Regarding the text beginning with "If one has taken this bhikṣu’s bowl," he is to be punished.

"Take the new one; use the old one for the lower bowl. Regarding these four passages: after that bhikṣu has taken charge of this bowl, he uses the new one for fear of damaging it, while protecting the old one as the lower bowl.
These four texts all concern taking down the lower bowl and having it held. The first passage is divided into two parts.

There are two ways of returning [the bowl]: first, returning it after setting it aside; second, returning it through the performance of formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), such as the announcement (*jñapti*). Regarding the previous rule on the "extra bowl" (*atireka-pātra*):

if one discards it alone, there are two possibilities for its return—returning it immediately when there is a reason for its transfer, or returning it directly after having spent a night [without it] when there is no reason.

Since the text relies on the latter meaning, it refers simply to direct return. Now, this "begging for a bowl" refers to its transfer upon being discarded, or its exchange for robes, medicine, and so forth.
Therefore, within the text, one returns directly from the seat of the *karmavācanā*.

Because the remaining extra bowls and so forth do not obstruct one another, or if the extra bowl is discarded simultaneously with the others, even if there is a reason for keeping the extra bowl, one may not carry this begging bowl. One must immediately transfer it while seated;
specifically, one must perform a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to take down the bowl, and then punish [the offender] by making them hold the new bowl while using the old one.

He sets down the bowl. For this reason, it cannot be understood through mere transfer; one must necessarily receive it from another for a full night, and only then perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and so forth.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "If it is of great value, one should take the price of ten bowls;

the price of nine bowls shall enter the Sangha’s pure kitchen, and the price of one bowl shall be returned to the owner. If one obtains the price of two bowls, one bowl shall enter the Sangha, and one bowl [shall be returned]."
Return the value to the owner. In this manner, according to how much has been obtained, one should directly return that amount to the owner;

the remainder shall all enter the monastic kitchen. Second, regarding the taking down of the bowls: first, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made, and next, the bowls are distributed. In the other three Vinayas, a person specifically appointed to distribute the bowls is selected.

[The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*] states: "Possessing five qualities, one shall not receive [the bowl], etc., as well as those who should and should not be appointed. A formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) shall appoint a person to distribute the bowls.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "This bhikṣu should proclaim: 'Let all the bhikṣus each take their bowls and come forth. He shall ask the elders in order: 'Do you require this bowl?
If they say they do, he should take the elder's bowl and examine it; if there is no bowl, or if it is too large or too small..."
If a bowl has holes, cracks, or is crooked, it should not be given. However, if it lacks these five defects, it should be given, even to one who has newly received the precepts.

According to the *Jìzhù* (Commentary on the Vinaya): "The bhikṣus filled their bowls to the brim with water and passed them around. According to this Vinaya, when distributing bowls, one should follow the method of the three other Vinayas:

calculate the appropriate number of people to distribute the bowls, proceeding from the seniors down to the juniors according to the needs of the Saṃgha; alternatively, one may take a new bowl or an old one.

It is said that one should take the bowl from the senior monk and give it to the next in rank, or it is also permissible to give it directly; therefore, it says, "If you give this bowl to that bhikṣu.

Furthermore, it means that one should not disregard the intentions of the monks seated below the next in rank; these are words of respectful deference, hence it says, "one should not disregard them," and so forth.
Moreover, one should not take away the good and give the bad because of causes for anger or resentment; rather, one must simply take [the bowl].

It is called "lowering the bowl" (*pātra-nyasana*) for this reason. Regarding the three penalties that require one to hold a new bowl while using an old one: the first two items are listed because they involve the indefinite offense (*aniyata*) of "lowering.
Second, after the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), the penalty is imposed to hold a new bowl while using an old one; the ancient interpretation calls this "protecting the bowl.
As for the "two-fold proclamation" (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), this does not refer to the two-fold proclamation for dispatching someone to carry two bowls; rather, the text says "give to [Name]."
When it is said that a bhikṣu "receives and maintains [the bowl] until it breaks," this does not mean that a formal ritual for receiving it is added;

rather, it is simply a disciplinary measure requiring him to accept and practice its use. Because he must maintain these two bowls, it is said that he "receives and maintains them until they break. This refers to the period during which he uses the old one while holding the new.
Once the old bowl has broken, he holds both simultaneously. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, he is required to always hold them at the time of eating. First, he receives the bowl.

He then begged for two bowls and ascended the hall; he continued in this manner for the rest of his life to demonstrate the fault of excessive greed and to sever the causes and conditions for future unwholesome dharmas.
Regarding the four protections for the old lower bowl: they used a new one because they feared the old one would be damaged.

One must not hold two bowls with one hand, and those who do so shall be punished; others are likewise prohibited from doing so. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, [this applies to] the Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
By means of holding and washing two bowls, one employs a stratagem to destroy the old ones before being permitted to use new ones.
○ The twenty-third precept: Begging for thread and having a non-relative weave it.
Now, although the three robes are complete and sufficient to sustain the body, one nevertheless begs for thread and silk, relying on the influence of the powerful and noble to compel them.

[If one] compels [a weaver] to weave the three robes, it increases greed and excessive desire, harms the weaver, and conversely invites censure and slander. Therefore, the Noble One established the rule.
There are four distinct conditions: first, personally begging for thread; second, [employing] a weaver who is a layperson not related by kinship; third, relying upon...
If one sends a weaver to weave [cloth] and does not pay the price, an offense is committed once four parts are completed. Question:

Why is it that there are only householders who are non-relatives who weave, and no instruction for nuns to weave? Answer: Nuns are not permitted to weave themselves. Since the Great Sangha (monks) know the Dharma, the principle of employing them is rare.
A layperson’s involvement is merely light; therefore, there is only the offense of causing a laywoman to weave. If that were so, one might as well simply cause a laywoman to wash clothes.
Answer: The holy teaching permits a nun to wash her own clothes without fault. However, for a monk to employ a nun [for such tasks] is grave, as it obstructs her cultivation.
Laypeople are not those who cultivate the Path. Furthermore, washing and dyeing are simple matters that cause no further significant harm; therefore, washing does not constitute an offense.
Weaving, however, involves extensive labor and expense, and because the transgression is profound, washing and weaving are treated differently. This is the point of the matter.

The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* state: (1) [the recipient]; (2) one must personally beg for the thread; if one uses thread provided by a layperson, one commits the subsequent offense, and therefore it is necessary to beg for it oneself.

Even if one does not beg, using thread that belongs to oneself should be considered a minor offense. (3) One must not coerce a weaver by relying on one's power; if one obtains it through reasoned persuasion, there is no offense.
If one provides the price [for the cloth], there is no offense.

There are four formulated offenses (*pācittiya*). A detailed explanation follows. The first two [offenses] may be understood as above. Regarding the third phrase, "the weaver is not a relative," the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*) explains it as follows:

"The weaver being a non-relative consists of three phrases; this constitutes the formal substance of the precept. If one causes actual harm to the weaver, one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If one begs for thread from a non-relative, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). [If one causes] the weaving..."
Regarding the weaver being either a relative or a non-relative, there should be three permutations; however, there are two permutations when the weaver is a relative from one's own village.

The third permutation—where both parties are relatives—is omitted as it carries no offense. Thus, there are only eight permutations in total. If the act primarily harms the weaver, one commits a *thullaccaya* (offense of wrong-doing); if it simultaneously harms the owner of the yarn, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrongdoing).

I shall cite one offense as an example to encompass both grave and minor transgressions; therefore, I simply say "offense. The explanation below, beginning with "If a bhikṣu," clarifies the fourth section on the demarcation of offenses and the procedures for relinquishing them through confession, which may be understood from the text itself.
24. The Precept on Exhorting and Praising the Weaver to Increase the Weaving of Robes:
A devout layperson, with sincere intent, prepares thread for the sake of a bhikṣu and weaves three robes; it is appropriate that he be commended for his offering.
By accepting [the cloth], one manifests within oneself a mind of integrity and moderation, while externally not causing distress to the donor.

Now, however, by encouraging and praising the weaver and personally paying the price, one harms the owner of the thread and ruins one’s own mental conduct; this brings no benefit to either self or other. For this reason, the rule was established.
There are six distinct conditions: first, a householder prepares the thread himself and sends a weaver to weave it; second, there is a limited expectation; third, one knows it is limited;
fourth, one gives payment and encourages the weaving; fifth, the weaver adds extra thread; sixth, upon receiving it, one commits the offense. Question:

What is the difference between this case of damaging a householder and the case of encouraging a single householder? In the former, one encourages the owner of the thread to increase [the amount]; in this case...
In the middle section [of the Vinaya], it is advised that the weaver increase the threads and strands. A question is raised: "In the previous precept, there was advice given to one or two [weavers];

why is there no mention here of advising two weavers? The answer is: In the previous case, it was directed toward the owner of the thread, and since they could collaborate, it was necessary to establish a rule.
In this case, if there are two lay devotees (gṛhapati), each with their own weaver, and a bhikṣu secretly advises the two weavers to join together to weave a single robe, [the rule applies].
Since he is not the owner of the thread, it is logically inconsistent; therefore, there is no exhortation of two weavers.

If the owner of the thread were one and there were two weavers, then while the exhortation to weave well would constitute one [factor], the damaging of the thread would be the other; thus, they are not established separately.

If the owner of the thread were two and there were one weaver, then since the damage to the thread is caused by the weaver and the weaver is only one, one could not say that there is an exhortation of two weavers; therefore, they are not [established separately].
The same as before. If one exhorts the owner of the thread, it falls entirely under the preceding precept; if one exhorts [the owner] in private, it is subsumed under this precept. Question:

What is the difference between this and the previous precept concerning the weaver? Answer: Four points of distinction are clarified. First, in the previous case, the owner of the thread is harmed because [the weaver] obtained [the cloth] by begging;
in this case, the owner of the thread is harmed, but the weaver is not. Second, the previous precept arises from harming the weaver by not paying him his wage.

Regarding the offense: this constitutes an offense because the owner of the thread was deprived of its value. Third, the previous case involved an offense when the person was not a relative; here, it is an offense when the person is a relative.

Fourth, in the previous case, the offense occurred as soon as the thread was woven into cloth; here, the offense occurs only upon receiving the garment made from another's thread. There are two parts to the textual account:
first, up to the point where the transgression arises when [the robe] is sent to the householder’s wife; second, the householder returns from elsewhere at that time and utters words of reproach.
There are three types of *Prātimokṣa* (precept texts): first, the abbreviated; second, the expanded; and third, the complete *Prātimokṣa* consisting of four sections.

First, the person who commits the offense. Second, the owner of the thread sends a weaver to weave a robe. Third, from "that bhikṣu" onwards, up to the point where he encourages and praises the weaver to hire laborers at his own expense.
Fourth, from "if he obtains" onwards, the conclusion of the offense. Below, these four points are explained in detail.
The Twenty-fifth Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Forcibly Taking Back a Robe Previously Given to Another.
If one has previously given a robe to another with the intention of traveling together, and that person does not go, it is only right to request its return with a conciliatory and gentle manner;

originally, there is no fault in this. However, to forcibly seize it out of anger and to mutually oppress and harass the other is improper conduct. Therefore, this precept was established as a prohibition.
There are five distinct conditions. First, a *śrāmaṇera* who is a *mahābhikṣu* does not commit an offense. Question:

If a *śrāmaṇera* says he does not commit an offense, why is it that by following along, he is expelled and commits the same offense as the *mahāsaṃgha*? Answer: A *śrāmaṇera* who shares robes and travels together is of a different category [from a regular *śrāmaṇera*].

Giving [the robe] is rare; taking it away is not frequent. To follow and interpret the meaning [of the rule] while simultaneously violating the Saṃgha’s Dharma results in no difference in the damage caused;

thus, they constitute an identical offense. Second, one first gives the robe with the intention of traveling together. Third, one gives it to a person without certainty but takes it back with certainty.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are four permutations: first, giving with certainty and taking with certainty; second, giving with certainty and taking without certainty.

In these two cases of taking back what was [previously] given, one does not commit this offense. If one takes what was given indistinctly or takes it when it was not yet given, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

If one takes what was given indistinctly but then takes it with certainty, one delights in the dispute at the time of taking; therefore, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Fifth, when one seizes property with a mind of anger and claims it as one's own, if one does not know the recitation of the precepts (*śikṣāpada*), the first two [cases] prevent the offense from arising; it is not that one who does not know the recitation of the precepts is exempt from the offense.
Not knowing how to personally practice the prevention of unarisen [faults] is not the same as not knowing the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

If one does not understand the communal rules or the ritual for reciting them, then the next two [cases] exclude those who have already committed offenses. Not knowing the *poṣadha* ceremony means not knowing how to personally practice it; [in such cases, one must perform] confession before another person (*pratideśanā*).

Those who do not understand the *poṣadha* ritual, who do not conform to the communal rules, and who lack the methods for repentance—regarding these four dharmas, they are like those facing a blank wall;
therefore, it is said that they are ignorant and know nothing.

The Prātimokṣa Sūtra contains three points: first, the person who commits the offense; second, having previously given the robe; third, subsequently seizing it with a mind of anger and thereby incurring the offense.

In the detailed commentary (*vibhaṅga*), regarding "seizing and concealing," this refers to seizing it in the presence of the person. If it has not yet been concealed, the matter is not yet finalized, and thus the offense is not yet complete.
Only upon concealment does the offense become established. As for the phrase "if placed on a tree or the like" below, this refers to cases where the person is not present.

If one seizes [an item] and it leaves its place, an offense is committed; because there is no one with whom to dispute it, there is no fault in subsequently concealing it. This is not a repeated offense.

Regarding the opening passage below, from "if one borrows another's robe" up to "until it is lost or destroyed," the text cites this case: because it is a borrowed robe, there is no fault in seizing it.

There is no offense for one who seizes and suspends [a monk]. This differs from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. One commits an offense regarding all four types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*), such as separate residence (*pārājika*) and so forth.

Seizing and expelling one who has committed a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) is a minor offense. If it is asked: "What is the difference between one who has broken the precepts and one who is subject to expulsion?

Furthermore, since breaking the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*) falls under the lower three categories of offenses, how could one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, or one who has committed the lower three categories, be free from offense when seizing them? Herein lies my explanation of this matter.

Regarding the "three types of schisms" (*tīṇi bhedāni*): these refer to cases where the entire household is subject to formal disciplinary action (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). It does not mean that one commits no offense by seizing all three [of the requisites]. Rather, it means that [the act] is permitted as an exception for those undergoing formal procedures such as suspension (*ukkhepa*), and thus constitutes no offense.
○ Precept on Storing Medicine Beyond Seven Days, Twenty-sixth.

Explanation of the Meaning in Seven Sections: First, enumeration, definition of names, and determination of the essence; second, the similarities and differences between the two modes of receiving—by hand and by mouth;
third, the ritual procedure for preparing medicine by mouth and the principles regarding its distribution to other bhikṣus; fourth, explanation of the storage of the four kinds [of medicine].

1. Regarding medicinal substances, the gravity of the offense incurred; 2. Explaining that on the first day one may store medicine, but after seven days one commits an offense, with the subsequent six days being subject to defilement—whether the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is lost or not;
3. Regarding the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) involving medicine, whether it is exchanged for other medicine and whether such exchange is subject to defilement or not;
4. Regarding the consumption of impure medicine, the extent of the offense incurred.

The first section has three parts: first, enumerating the categories and explaining the names; second, identifying the substance of the medicine; third, the principle of administering the four medicines in combination according to their relative strength.
They are called "medicines" because they all possess the capacity to treat ailments. Although the meanings of "medicine" differ, there are briefly four types discussed here.
This refers to "timely" and "untimely," such as for a period of seven days or for the duration of one's life. Regarding what is called "timely medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*):

according to the ancient interpretation, that which accords with the Dharma and does not give rise to the burden of transgression is termed "timely. This meaning applies universally; provided it is without fault and conforms to the Dharma, everything is "timely.
If one explains it in this way, all four types of medicine are "timely," as they all accord with the Dharma. Just as there is no fault during the [permitted] time, there is none after midday either.

It is an offense; this is precisely what is called "improper time" (*akāla*). Taking [medicine] after seven days have passed, or taking it for the remainder of one's life without illness—categories such as these are termed "improper time.
The term "proper time" (*kāla*) is explained by its opposite. Thus, we know that the four types of medicine all possess the meanings of both "proper time" and "improper time.

Now, to explain according to the twelve periods of the day: the period before noon is called "proper time"; once it has passed, it is "improper time," as explained in the rules regarding the precept on improper time. Question: Why is it before noon?

When it is the proper time to speak, it is not the improper time; yet, regarding this medicine, it is analyzed by means of its application. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains "proper time" and "improper time" through four meanings.
Furthermore, in the *Vīra-samādhi-sūtra*, the World-Honored One spoke to the Bodhisattva Hui-fa (Wisdom-Dharma) concerning food, clarifying four types:
morning is the time for devas' food, noon is the time for the Dharma's food, evening is the time for animals' food, and night is the time for ghosts' food. As for the latter two...

Eating [at improper times] gives rise to many illnesses. For those who have left the household life, there is the "food at the proper time" (*kālabhojana*), which refers to the time for celestial food or dharma-food;

hence it is called "timely food" (*kālabhojana*). After midday, it is no longer the time for the aforementioned two types of food; hence it is called "improper time" (*akāla*). In contrast to this time, medicinal substances are of only two kinds:
first, timely medicine (*kālabhaiṣajya*); second, medicine for improper times (*akālabhaiṣajya*). Timely medicine is established as one category based on its essential nature; the following three...

Medicines are generally "non-timely" (vikāla). What is now referred to as the "four [medicines]" refers to those among non-timely items that—like non-timely drinks—are permitted for consumption at non-timely hours when one is in the presence of a family who observes the proper time;
thus they are called "non-timely. As for the other two medicines, they originate from families who observe the proper time, yet they are rounded out by the non-timely category.
Therefore, their duration is determined by the length of the period from the day they were received; thus, two must be established. Following this distinction, the classification becomes clear.
The four medicines. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, there are five measures of medicine: first, the measure of time; second, the measure based on a watch (*yāma*);

third, the measure based on seven days; fourth, the measure based on a single lifetime; and fifth, the measure based on a great opening. These five encompass all medicinal substances without exception.

However, these four names are designated in relation to "proper time" (*kāla*) and "improper time" (*akāla*). As for the latter two types, they are designated based on the nature of the dharma received.

Second, regarding the analysis of their essence (*svabhāva*): first, analyzed generally according to the three aggregates (*triskandha*), their essence is material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), which does not exceed the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the eight subtle particles (*aṇu*) as its essence.

Among the three types of matter, it is subsumed under the first two; among the four nutriments (*āhāra*), if it is exclusively the nutriment of physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), then [it consists of] the eight...

In the *Mikkyō* (Esoteric) tradition, "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is taken strictly in the sense of that which sustains life. Regarding the substance of medicine, it consists only of the three [objects] of odor, flavor, and tangibility;
those such as visible form are not. Second, when distinguished by way of their physical entities, there are fifteen kinds of food: five *pūjāni*, five *khādaniya*, and five *śayyāni*.

These three groups of five medicines, when setting aside their ritual functions to consider their essential nature, still fall into two categories. The first two groups of five consist exclusively of "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*), namely beans.
Regarding fermented milk, curd, and so forth: the third category consists of five types of non-time medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*).

Here, they are treated as four by way of their method of administration; in meaning, they are "non-time," and thus they are to be consumed at non-time. Thus the text says: "If one obtains sweet molasses, it is permitted to eat it at the proper time.

This refers to the eight kinds of syrups and the like. Butter, oil, and the five kinds of fats are seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*). All pungent, salty, and similar substances [are medicinal decoctions].
Because the substance of life-long medicine (*yāvajjīvikam*) is [included], although there are two categories, they constitute four types of medicine.

Third, regarding "blending": the four types of medicine may be blended; one should take them according to their potency, such that those for a specific time or for life-long use assist those for seven days.
For example, if meat is boiled with ghee (*sarpis*), this broth is taken as a seven-day medicine; or, medicine for a specific time or for life-long use may assist [the seven-day medicine].

It constitutes a lifelong medicine. For example, like a mixture of ghee and milk, or a *tiṅ-li* fruit; or sometimes for seven days. These assist in forming a "timely medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*) for consumption.
If their potency and so forth are equal, they are determined according to their names. For instance, because of its name, a stone-honey pill (*śarkarā-guḍa*) is made a seven-day medicine;
whereas the Five-Stone Powder (*pañca-śilājatu-cūrṇa*) is made a lifelong medicine. Question: Is the resultant substance a timely medicine, or is the juice a non-timely one?

[Question: Then rice and the like should also be "medicines for the proper time" (*kālabhaiṣajya*), while fermented drinks (*mantha*) would be "medicines for the improper time" (*akālabhaiṣajya*). [Answer: Because fruits possess the quality of being liquid, they are made into medicines for the improper time;
however, because fermented drinks are mixed with substances that are medicines for the proper time, they are not [exclusively] medicines for the improper time.

The second section concerns the similarities and differences between the two types of formal acceptance (*pratigraha*). There are three parts: first, the explanation of the names of the two acceptances; second, the distinctions between the two acceptances;

and third, an analysis of their breadth, narrowness, length, and brevity. Regarding the explanation of the names: because the four types of medicine are gathered and received using items such as robes or vessels, it is called "hand acceptance" (*pāṇigraha*);
because one receives them orally in accordance with the sacred teachings and maintains them in compliance with the Dharma, it is termed "oral acceptance" (*mukhagraha*).

Second, the analysis of distinctions. There are six gates of distinction. First, the necessity of receiving with the intention. Regarding why one must receive with the hand: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there are five reasons why food must be received.

Why is it that receiving with the mouth is also required? It is to prevent the fault of "receiving without formal acceptance" (*pratigraha*). Question: How is it known that there is such a thing as receiving with the mouth?

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that when Upāli asked whether non-timely medicine, seven-day medicine, or lifetime medicine could be consumed without offense if kept overnight, [the Buddha] declared it to be an offense. Thus, we know that receiving with the mouth is required.
"Is it permissible to receive food with the hands? The Buddha said, "It is permissible. "If one is not ill, is it permissible to consume it?

He replied, "It is not permissible. "If one is ill, is it permissible to consume it? The Buddha said, "It is permissible. Based on this textual evidence, it is clearly understood that for those who employ the *adhikāra* (formal authorization), there must be both purity and illness.

Furthermore, if one were to receive food directly with the hands, who would inquire whether one is ill? Moreover, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "With the exception of the five types of persons, such as those living alone, one may receive food with the mind (*cittena*)."

Regarding the "mindful acceptance" (*cetanā-paribhoga*) of seven-day medicines and so forth—these seven types of matters involving mindful acceptance—no other person may perform them through mere mental intention.

For this reason, if there were no need to apply formal procedures such as addressing another person, what would be the use of those words? It is precisely because of these seven matters that one obtains the right to accept them through mental intention.

One must not harbor such thoughts. Furthermore, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) and it is difficult to find one through request, one may receive it directly from the hand of another.
Having received it orally from a *bhikṣu*, one may keep it in a single place and consume it oneself within seven days.

This refers to cases where there is no *kappiya-kāraka* and the medicine must be taken over a long period. If a *kappiya-kāraka* is available, one may receive it by hand as the occasion arises; it is not strictly required [to follow the former procedure].

The Dharma of the Mouth. Second, the objects to be confronted. Third, the classification of the three destinies (*gati*). Receiving with the hands applies to all three. This is for the purpose of preventing theft.
For example, the tree deity of the *harītakī* tree received [food] from a non-human (*amanuṣya*). Śāriputra’s lotus root was received from an animal. The human realm may be understood accordingly.
As in other Vinayas, when Mahākāśyapa accepted food from a poor woman, the Buddha said it was food from Devadatta.

This constitutes formal acceptance (*pratigraha*). Oral acceptance is restricted to human beings. Furthermore, distinctions can be understood regarding whether one is a monastic or a layperson, and whether one possesses or lacks a physical form and karmic retribution (*vipāka*), and so forth.
Regarding the third type of accepted medicine: although there are four kinds of medicine, all four must be accepted by hand; therefore, they do not constitute the taking of precepts.

When it is said that food for the time being (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) is not accepted, if the medicine has already entered the mouth, then the other three types of medicine—excluding water and the like—are also included, as are the two types of water: salty and turbid.

One must receive [the food] with the hand. If it is naturally salty or white, it need not be received. For the seven-day medicine and lifetime medicine, it is clear that no words need be spoken; therefore, for the latter three types of medicine, the verbal ritual must always be performed to prevent their loss.
Because of receiving [the medicine]. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Upāliparipṛcchā* raises the three lower types of medicine and asks whether their reception is valid or not.
Furthermore, the oral ritual (*vākkarma*) serves to prevent the loss of the reception; this is because [if one does not perform it], one might set it down on the ground.

Even if it is during a time when [eating] is prohibited, as long as one continues to hold it in the hand, the reception is not lost—this is like one's own medicine. However, since this cannot always be done, one must perform the oral ritual. Fourth.

Regarding the undertaking of mental actions, there are ten ways of undertaking them by hand, as explained in the precept on not accepting food. The distinctions of undertaking them by speech can be understood through the three [precepts].

why is only 'non-time' mentioned here? The answer is: because there are other offenses that do not arise from verbal action (*vāg-dharma*), they are not mentioned despite the existence of seven offenses.

The time is long, and the use [of the mouth-rule] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; throughout one's life, there is no occasion for it to be otherwise.
Because the mouth-rule is extremely narrow at its lower end, it is wide; because the hand is precisely one finger-width thick, it is narrow.

The reason the mouth-rule prevents what is wide from becoming narrow is that prior to applying the mouth-rule, the hand’s reception [of food] would also constitute a transgression. It is necessary to apply the mouth-rule to prevent such prior faults; therefore, it serves as a broad safeguard.

However, because the ritual for the oral [confession] has a fixed temporal limit, violating this standard now results in a different offense. If one were to generate it directly from the oral ritual itself, it would be minimal;

thus, it is generated narrowly. This is why the offenses generated differ: when the hand [is used], the *śeṣa* (residual) offense is generated; when the mouth [is used], the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* is generated.
If there were no two-fold acceptance regarding the improper time, then this fault would not exist. Therefore, the conditions for generating the offense are distinct. This...

The state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) can be understood from the cited text. Regarding the second point, the long and short [periods] correspond to the two types of feeling; this can be understood through their mutual explanation.

Regarding the third point, the strong and weak are also explained in relation to the two types of feeling. There are two strengths of the hand: first, the distinction between the conventional and the non-conventional;

second, the distinction between the root and the branches. There are two strengths of the mouth: first, the length or brevity of the duration; second, the extent of the prevention of transgressions. Each has two weaknesses, which are the reverse [of the strengths].
This can be explained as follows.
In the third gate, the explanation of medicinal flavors is general; receiving [the medicine] with the hands is also general.

Because it is a rule of the mouth, when one adds another general flavor-medicine, this rule of the mouth is likewise general. Therefore, once one person has finished receiving it, when giving it to others, the method of receiving applies.
It is not lost. There is no fault in the person before eating it. Therefore, the text states that on the seventh day, the medicine is relinquished and given to the bhikṣus to eat;

thus we know that for the donor, the method of receiving [the medicine] is not lost. If it were lost, it would be impure. Why, then, is eating permitted? Furthermore, this concerns the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (the rule regarding leftover food).

This also applies to other persons; therefore, the same holds true for medicinal substances. If this is so, why does the *Jñānaprasthāna* state that giving [medicine] to another person results in the loss of the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*)?

The answer is: it refers to giving to novices (*śrāmaṇera*) or laypeople (*gṛhapati*), and thus it says "loss of acceptance. This does not refer to those of the same class [of monastics]. This interpretation is subject to many difficulties:

first, it conflicts with the principle that what arises simultaneously with the superior [precepts] is not a shared offense (*asaṃvāsa-āpatti*). Furthermore, it lacks three necessary conditions and conflicts with the rule regarding the forfeiture of what has been acquired. Moreover, it relies on artificial conditions.

Regarding the ritual procedure (*vidhi*): if it were universally applicable, there would be no need for the pretext of illness. Furthermore, since items such as robes and bowls are designated by calling out their names, they cannot be considered non-specific.

Now, this [act] is performed under the pretext of illness; how then could it be universally applicable? Therefore, it is not necessarily so. Moreover, regarding the method of "washing hands" to prevent theft:
once one person has completed the reception, it may extend to other persons. As for the oral ritual, it involves the pretext of illness and the calling of names.

Regarding the expectation that one possesses a specific portion of medicine: before it has been given to another, as long as it remains within one's own possession, it may be considered permissible without offense.
However, once the resolve to relinquish it is made, it is lost the moment another receives it by mouth; it perishes immediately upon being received by hand. It is not permitted to consume it again.

In this case, neither party commits the offense of "excess" (*atireka*), because the legal status of the medicine does not transfer through the mouth and the intention of possession is distinct. Therefore, according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Observation), medicine received by mouth, when relinquished and given to another person, [is no longer subject to the rules of excess].
In that case, the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*) of the food would be lost; it would not be like other food, where once it has become "leftover" (*vighasa*), the matter is concluded.

Since the original [acceptance] was not performed by mentioning the name [of the recipient], it can apply to others as well—just as in the case of a patient’s leftover food, how could there be a specific rule? Therefore, they are not of the same category. If this is so, why does the text say:
"All seven-day medicines, having been relinquished, may be given to the bhikṣus for them to eat"? If the formal acceptance were lost, how could they eat it? However...

The Buddha permitted the eating [of food]. Regarding the *mukhādhāraṇa* (oral-authorization) rule, it is generally understood as being non-transferable. However, although it may not be transferable, when one relinquishes it to the Saṃgha, the original acceptance is not lost.

This is because the relinquishment was originally made for the purpose of disposing of an excess; the formal act (*karmavācanā*) was not intended to be permanent. Since the *mukhādhāraṇa* was not fundamentally relinquished and its time limit had not yet expired, it remains valid.
Furthermore, even if the acceptance were lost due to encountering certain circumstances, in this case it is not lost. Because it is not lost, the following five...

Regarding daily medicine, it is permitted to return it to its owner; however, regarding seven-day medicine, it may be given to the Saṃgha for consumption. Furthermore, once one has accepted another's relinquishment [of medicine], it is auspicious to consume it repeatedly.
If there were relinquishment without acceptance, how could one obtain food from it? Therefore, we know that it is not lost.
Regarding the fourth section on the gravity of storing medicines: the seven-day medicine is grave, while the other three are merely *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses).
The reason for this is twofold: first, the seven-day medicine serves as sustenance for physical strength; second, its substance remains constantly present, such that its continuity persists.

The mind of hoarding is earnest; the defiled mind is heavy and thick. This is because [the substance] is present in its physical form and constantly exists, leading to a persistent and earnest mind of hoarding.

To prevent the fault of hoarding, one must listen to and understand the rules for purification (*śuddhi*). Now, impure giving (*aśuddha-dāna*) contradicts the holy teachings; therefore, it incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.

Although seasonal medicine (*kālika-bhesajja*) may serve as a support for the body while it is present, it is exhausted upon completion and cannot be extended in storage for long. Thus, the defiled mind is slight; furthermore, because the mind is thin, [it does not constitute hoarding].

One must perform the *viśuddhi* (declaration of purity). If one were to keep [medicines] now, there would be no fault of either performing or not performing the declaration. Therefore, it is merely light;

because they are stored for a long time beyond the proper time, they readily turn into wine, and there is no continuous accumulation. Because the intention to keep them is slight and shallow, it does not contradict the rule of *viśuddhi*.

As for medicines to be taken for life (*yāvajjīvika*), they are the most minimal support for the body, and the intention [to keep them] is not weighty. Because the intention to keep them is thin, there is no violation of the teaching regarding the declaration of purity.
Therefore, it is auspicious to keep all three types of medicine mentioned below.
The fifth and sixth [cases] are explained by correlating them with the text.

Regarding the seventh category, the consumption of impure medicine: the degree of the offense incurred is as follows—if one has already set aside the seven-day limit and resumes taking it, even a single swallow constitutes an offense.

There are seven offenses and three *pācittiyas* (offenses requiring expiation), along with four *dukkaṭas* (wrongdoings). These are: eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*), consuming food that has not been formally accepted (*apratigrāhita*), consuming food kept overnight (*sannidhikāraka*), internal storage (*antarāvāsika*), impure contact (*duṣṭasparśa*), cooking within [the monastery] (*antargrha-pākya*), and the forfeiture offense (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) regarding food and medicines, among others.
Each of these is distinct because their karmic actions are identical while their conditions differ. A single swallow incurs seven offenses.

There are also cases where there is "residue" (*sannidhi*) but no "impure contact" (*duṣṭasparśa*), such as when one encounters circumstances where the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is lost due to contact; this refers to medicine taken at an improper time. For lifetime-medicine (*yāvajjīvika*), there is no offense, and the rule for receiving it for life is not lost.

If there is no occasion of illness, one incurs only a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) and no further blame. If one does not perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), there is no fault except for taking it at an improper time.
[The offense is incurred. All other [aspects] are the same as those for [the seven-day medicine]. Regarding the four gates of the separate interpretation of the seven-day medicine:

the intention behind the formulation of this precept is that ordinary persons are defiled by impurities and take the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their physical bodies. At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, when the seasonal energies contend with one another, the four great elements undergo transformation, and various illnesses arise.

Since such afflictions exist, they hinder the cultivation of the path and its practices. Out of compassion, the Great Sage, employing skillful means, permitted the storage and consumption of these [medicines].
Medicine is used to treat the suffering of illness, intended solely to bring peace to the body so that one may advance in the practice of the Path.

Although the Noble One permitted its broad storage, to do so out of greed and thereby ruin one's conduct violates the teachings and invites censure; such a fault is not slight. Therefore, the offense of *thullaccaya* (grave transgression) was established.

To store it for one’s own use is termed "possessing" (*parikkhāra*). That which treats affliction is called "medicine. To exceed the prescribed limit is termed "exceeding seven days. Hence, it is called "possessing."

The second, from "At that time, the Venerable One... onwards, permits even healthy bhikṣus to take medicine at appropriate times. The preceding text has three parts: first, the permission to take the five medicines;
