Previously, there was no fault of being subject to reproach or censure; therefore, eating was permitted. This is not the same as the case of Tiṣya. Within the *bhikṣuṇī* saṃgha, when instructions are given before the assembly, one must act with careful mindfulness.
To tolerate concealment and remain silent while refusing to accept censure constitutes a transgression of the collective sentiment; all such individuals commit an offense subject to reproach.
As for the words of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, "So-and-so has heard much from the assembly and is diligent," this is a request that must be granted; it is a praise. If one says, "The assembly..."
The master, who was preeminent in learning, acted as the host for this bhikṣu. He invited twenty people in total; one person was a "praiseworthy" guest (*praśasta*), while the others were not.
If there is such a praiseworthy guest, when it is time to eat, they may exchange food with one another, but the food may not be taken away.

If the person sitting beside him is impure and does not wish to exchange food, he should reflect: "This food in the bowl is permitted to me by such-and-such a person; there is no offense. This is why.

There is no exemption for those who are ill. In all cases, one must simply ensure that they do not praise either illness or health; if they obtain food in this manner, there is no offense. Why then would an exemption for the ill be necessary?

If one were to allow the ill, those of high virtue would surely disparage those who are healthy, and even so, it would still constitute a transgression. What need is there for an exemption for the ill?
Therefore, the seven conditions for the separate meal (*pṛthak-bhakta*) are not permitted. Generally, when sages establish precepts, they permit what is beneficial and prohibit what leads to fault.
Since that [other] person’s intention to give was intended to benefit the recipient, the various conditions were permitted. Here, however, there is no intention to give;

rather, one praises [the food] and seeks it, thereby distressing others and inviting censure—thus, the seven conditions are not permitted. Furthermore, because it has never been established as sufficient, the rule against "remaining food" (*atireka-bhakti*) does not apply.

Regarding the Dharma-opening: furthermore, because opening leads to loss, there are two aspects to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). First, from the beginning up until the arrival at the dragon, he disparaged [the practice] and sought food, thereby giving rise to the fault of outflows (*sāsrava*).
Second, from the section on the lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) onwards, he rebuked him.

This completes the six sections of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: first, the offender; second, the knowledge [of the offense]; third, the praise and exhortation; fourth, the obtaining of food; fifth, the exclusion of exceptions; and sixth, the determination of the offense.
Among these six sections, the fifth—the exclusion of exceptions—is omitted and not explained here. The first, third, and fourth sections are explained individually.
From the words "That bhikṣu... onwards, the second and sixth sections are interpreted together. This text has three parts: first, the formal explanation of the offense.

First, the external application of the offense is minor. Second, regarding the four permutations of the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), the reason why the robe is minor is that material wealth and profit are of great importance, and attachment to them makes them difficult to relinquish;

furthermore, as they belong to specific individuals, there is no principle for their common use, and thus the sense of "encouraging relinquishment" is rare, leading to infrequent instances of receiving [the gift].
For this reason, the offense is minor. As for food, there is no eating alone; the sense of "encouraging the preparation" is easy, and the sense of "leading to receiving" is frequent. Therefore—

The gravity of the offense is determined by the external application of the lamp oil; since such exhortations are rare, the offense is considered light. Regarding the principle that the *bhikṣuṇīs* receive the exhortation from the *bhikṣus*, because they do not receive it frequently, the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is light.
The thirtieth precept: The prohibition against traveling together with a woman by appointment.
The intent of the regulation is the same as before; the only difference is that it concerns a laywoman.
The specific conditions consist of six factors: first, she must be a human female; second, there must be a mutual agreement; third, they travel along the same path; fourth, they do not part ways.

Regarding the practice of traveling while being seen or heard: there are five conditions that constitute no offense, such as the absence of obstacles and so forth; sixth, one may transform [the situation] according to the boundaries of the realm crossed, provided there is a mutual agreement.

As for the question of how many third persons constitute an offense, it applies to all, because they do not share the same dharma and are not comparable to the bhikṣuṇīs; thus, traveling with multiple companions is permitted.
The former interpretation that permits a third person is unfounded, as there is no such basis in the subsequent text. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one travels with the king’s consort..."

And so forth. Having agreed not to commit an offense, when traveling with one’s mother or sisters, at the time of setting out or departing, if one calls out, "Come here! Do not [go]," and fails to keep pace with the companion, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
If one says, "Go; do not [wait for] the companion," there is no offense. This completes the five phrases of the basic rule (*sikkhāpada*). First is the person who commits the offense.

2. The object of common practice; 3. The mutual agreement; 4. Traveling together on the same path; 5. The determination of the offense. To distinguish the characteristics, all five of the above must be present.
*Śikṣāpada* 31: Receiving More Than One Meal [from the Same Person].
A lay devotee of profound faith relinquished his household treasures to establish a dwelling place and vowed to provide only one meal a day, awaiting the arrival of other monks.

One should measure one's own portion and accept according to what is appropriate. This demonstrates that within, one possesses a mind of integrity and moderation, while without, one does not overstep the bounds of the donor.

Now, if one remains for a long time without justification and accepts food from others in excess, it will increase greed for collective property, ruin what is wholesome, and augment what is unwholesome.
Such excessive harm is no small matter; therefore, this rule was established.

The separate conditions for [accepting] food consist of five factors: first, it is a non-relative householder; second, the donor restricts the gift to a single meal; third, one knows the restriction to a single meal;

fourth, there is no reason to accept the food other than being invited to stay; fifth, if one eats, one commits an offense. Regarding the seven conditions for eating separately, only the sick are exempted.
However, if a sick person suffers, their departure would cause harm while their staying would be beneficial. When a donor understands this, they do not give rise to criticism;
therefore, the Noble One permitted it. Among the exceptions for eating separately from the community, the invitation by a donor is permitted, as it is one of the six exceptions that cause no harm.

Regarding this precept on eating once, if there is no intention to give after the meal, yet one partakes under the six conditions of exception, it would constitute harm and distress; therefore, there are no other six [exceptions]. As previously stated.
One meal: no further eating is permitted thereafter; other matters are not governed by this rule, and thus it is not removed [from the list].

This fulfills the five clauses of the basic precept (*śīla-mūla*): first, the place where one meal is given; second, the condition of being free from illness (the contrary case being cited as an opening for exceptions);

third, the person who commits the offense, namely a *bhikṣu*; fourth, that which should be eaten as a single meal, which is the limit of the portion; fifth, if one exceeds this, the offense is established at the conclusion.
Within the analysis of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), first the third person is explained; next, the "one eating place" from the first phrase is explained;

next, the section beginning with "the eater" explains the fourth clause within the first phrase. "Eating" refers to timely food (*kālabhojana*), as the three medicines are excluded due to their light nature.

Next, the section beginning with "the sick person" provides an exegesis of the permitted conditions (*anujñāta-pratyaya*). Next, the section beginning with "if a bhikṣu who is not ill" explains the fifth point, the formal offense (*sāpattika*). This is because...
Food is heavy and clothing is light. Answer: Food is the most urgent necessity for sustaining life; yet people delight in receiving it in excess.

Furthermore, by using it, one harbors within oneself the potential to cause harm or distress to the donor. Therefore, out of respect for the donor, one establishes a merit-house (*puṇya-śālā*) and provides bedding and clothing, permitting their use for only one night, but not allowing them to be taken away.
While receiving in excess is rare, even if one does use more than permitted, [the fault remains].
The substance of the robe is not destroyed and still belongs to the donor; because the sense of causing harm is slight, it is therefore minor.
Although lamp oil, foot-unguent, and so forth are entirely consumed, they are used externally on the body, and since the transgression of receiving them improperly is rare, the offense is minor.
Precept 32: On Eating Successively.

Now, when a devout layperson has prepared excellent food and invited the community of monks, fearing that they might not accept it, he first grants his permission and later goes back on his word, causing the food and drink provided for others to be set in vain and depriving the Sangha of the benefit of the offering. This brings distress and harm to the donor.

The fault of this is not slight; therefore, the Sage established a rule. Having already accepted a prior invitation, to then accept a subsequent invitation while turning one's back on the former and the latter is called "successive" (or "turning over").
Hence, it is termed the precept against successive meals (*paryuṣitaparibhoga-śikṣāpada*).
The secondary conditions consist of five factors: first, having previously accepted an invitation for the five kinds of formal food from another household;

second, being physically pure and capable of eating to satiety; third, accepting an invitation for the five kinds of formal food at a different location; fourth, the absence of a valid cause—meaning that except in cases of illness or during the time of distributing robes, if one relinquishes the cause of the invitation, there is no offense;
fifth, the offense is incurred immediately upon eating. By means of the first two conditions, the previous invitation is contrasted with [the subsequent one].

Third: Subsequently, there may be three sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, both the preceding and succeeding [factors] are correct, which constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Second, five [factors] are deficient; next, one is incorrect while the other three are below it, which constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Next, regarding whether the requirements are fulfilled or not, this forms four [propositions]: first, both preceding and succeeding factors are fulfilled, yet because one has turned away from the practice, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Next, the three [remaining cases] involve mutual discrepancies and so forth, all of which result in a *duṣkṛta* offense. Next, regarding purity and impurity, this forms four [propositions]; in all cases, they are pure.
Regarding the previous purification, these two cases constitute *pāyattika* offenses for eating against an invitation; the remaining two are *duṣkṛta* offenses. The textual source has two parts.

The first, up to "to be dealt with according to the Dharma," concerns Anāpindada, who ate thick gruel and thus violated the prohibition against accepting invitations. The second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, concerns Rājagṛha, where he ate the five types of formal meals and thus violated the prohibition against accepting invitations.
The text on the preceding offense has two parts: the first explains the causal conditions for permitting the consumption of gruel due to the request of Śroṇa.
Second, there was a minister of slight faith who, having already eaten thick gruel, declined the invitation. In the preceding text, there are three sections:

first, from the beginning up to "having informed the Honored One," which clarifies the circumstances for the distribution of gruel; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, which describes hearing and permitting the eating of gruel, and subsequently accepting three kinds of medicinal gruels:

first, *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the day), namely sesame and milk; second, *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for seven days), namely ghee and oil; third, [the *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for life)].

Regarding the acceptance of medicinal substances in the form of food: this refers to ginger, pepper, and *pippalī*. The Buddha praised the consumption of rice gruel; the five benefits are as stated in the text.

There are specifically ten benefits, as the verse says: "One who maintains pure precepts is honored by others," and so forth. At the three times after [the meal], the various lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) and others rejoiced at having gained the opportunity to cultivate merit.
Second, regarding the rejection of invitations, there are three sections in the text concerning the arising of faults: first, the citation; second, the invitation; and third, the prohibition.

The conditions for the offense consist of two parts. First, accepting a prior invitation, which refers to that which is being transgressed. Second, after the time for *aṇā* [food] has passed, when thick gruel is being served, one again accepts a subsequent invitation.
Regarding the second point, the various bhikṣus first accept the lower grade of food and then clearly consume the thick gruel, thereby committing the offense.

Third, from "the minister of slight faith" onwards, there is the censure. Within this section, there are three parts: first, up to "do not [allow it]," which reveals the cause of the discovery; second...

A junior monk, having lost faith and felt resentment toward this, rebuked him and reported the matter to the Buddha. [The Buddha] praised the preaching of the Dharma, and through this specific cause and condition, he attained realization of the Path.

Thirdly, because of these circumstances, [the Buddha] issued a reprimand and established a formal rule: "If one writes [a text] that is not in accordance with the Dharma, one shall not eat; if one eats, one shall be dealt with according to the law.
If there was no prior invitation, or if one does not eat again, there is no offense at all. What is now referred to as "dealt with according to the law" refers to this.

If one has previously accepted an invitation, one immediately commits the offense of "rejecting an invitation" (*paccācāra*). Or, if one eats again later, it merely constitutes the condition for being "sufficiently satiated," as the specific types [of food] have not yet been categorized.
One intends to conclude the prior rejection of the sufficient meal with a single item, stating simply that it is "as if treated. Question:

Having already accepted another's invitation, if one eats thick gruel at dawn, or does not go at the midday meal, or eats what has been offered after declaring one’s own food, or eats from the communal monastic food (*saṃgha-bhaktaka*), does one commit an offense?

Regarding "backing out of an invitation" (*paccācāra*): one commits an offense simply by not attending when one has accepted to go; it is not a minor offense to back out of an invitation that is not a formal *pavāraṇā*.

Because it is not a [formal] invitation at all, it is not termed "acceptance. Since backing out later causes distress to the former host, it is a minor offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one eats monastic food or private food, there is no offense.
Regarding the second of the five [types of] eating, in the main text on "backing out," there are three parts: first, the conditions for the offense, namely the sequence of before and after.
2. From "At that time, the bhikṣus... downwards, it explicitly demonstrates the refusal of the invitation. 3. From "At that time, the musician...
onwards, [the text] is as above, repeated three times.

This fulfills the four clauses of the *Śīla-mūla* (Precept Root): first, the person; second, eating in succession (*paryāya-bhojana*); third, the non-offense when an opening condition (*anujñāta-pratyaya*) exists;

and fourth, the determination of the offense (*āpatti-vinirṇaya*). From the words "at that time" (*tasmin samaye*) onwards, one recites the third clause. As for the reason for reciting the *Śīla-mūla*, it does not state "the robes are finished," and so forth.
The answer regarding "except at other times" is as follows: In this text, first the offense is set forth, and subsequently the non-offense is excluded.

Regarding the "extra robes" and so forth mentioned previously, the non-offenses were first excluded while taking up the occasions of offense; this was because of whether one was focused or not focused on the matter, which is why the phrasing differs.
Furthermore, since these three precepts coincide with the occasion for the distribution of robes, they are treated in contrast to the subsequent explanation of their application.
The terminology differs.

Within the "Discernment of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇavibhāga*), the first [point] can be understood. From "From successive transmission... downward, the second is explained. From "From the sick person...

downward, the third is interpreted. From "If on this day... downward, the fourth—the determination of the gravity of the offense—is explained. The reason for permitting [the action] in cases of illness is as follows:
As for the sick person’s suffering: if what is appropriate were not permitted, their life would be difficult to sustain.

Furthermore, because the donor understands this and does not criticize or cause distress, there is no offense in disregarding [the restrictions]. This is not something that sentient beings delight in; therefore, it is always permitted during the twelve months without being restricted by specific time limits.
Regarding the permission to give robes, there are two reasons: first, to benefit the dependent physical form of the bhikṣu, providing robes as a means of sustenance.

If one practices giving, one will not suffer the hardships of seeking what is difficult to obtain in future lives; for fear that seeking through improper means would give rise to much affliction. Second, it is for the benefit of future generations:
by providing the two gifts of food and clothing, the donor enables [the recipient] to obtain these two kinds of things, and thus the merit of this reciprocal response serves as a benefit for both.
Therefore, the Sage granted permission. Since the benefit of robes is significant, yet they might increase the fetters of greed, he permitted them for a specific time rather than at all times;

thus the text mentions "one month" or "five months. Furthermore, regarding other gifts of food or robes, the prior mention of "one month" or "five months" refers to the period during which one may accept or expect food and robes.
Food and robes are the surplus from such households during that time. [End of] section.
At that time, there was no opening [for acceptance]. It must depend upon the giving of food and robes; therefore it is said: "If there should be further giving of food and robes.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one proceeds according to the timing, when there is an invitation for a meal from the former house, the first three cases are as follows: 1. An invitation for a meal from the former house and an invitation for food and robes from the latter house;
if one accepts, there is no offense. 2. An invitation for a meal from the former house and an invitation for robes from the latter house; if one takes the robes, there is no offense.
If one eats at the previous host’s house, and having taken the robes, does not eat for the entire day, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for violating the agreement.

If there is an invitation to eat at the previous host’s house and another invitation to eat later, to turn away from them constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). Furthermore, if one uses the food and clothing of the previous host as the primary basis, there are three cases.

First, if there is an invitation to the food and clothing of the previous host, and the subsequent invitation likewise concerns food and clothing, to turn away from them constitutes a *thullaccaya*. Furthermore, if by means of the food and clothing of the previous host...
Regarding clothing and food for one's household, there are three cases for the head of the work: 1. One first requests clothing and food, and later also requests clothing and food;

it is permitted to turn away [the latter request] without offense, because the subsequent clothing will be sufficient and the feet will be well-provided for. 2. One first requests clothing and food, and later requests clothing alone;

as before, it is permitted to turn away [the latter request] without offense. 3. One first requests clothing and food, and later requests food alone; this constitutes an offense. This is based on the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the third precept.

The original statement says: "If a bhikṣu eats more than once [a day], except for specific causes, it is a pāyattika offense. As for the 'causes,' they are: when one is ill, when [food] is given according to the proper time, and when robes are being given.
According to this, it appears that at all times when robes are being given, the time for robes is permitted. Regarding the time for robes:

during the month or the five months, when one is alone and without robes, it is also permitted to be without a back [to the robe]. This is not the same as those other times; it is merely the time when robes and food are provided alone."

It is not permitted; there is likewise no permission from outside. This may be understood in the same way as that [previous case]. A detailed explanation will be provided below in the section on the "separate assembly. Question:

Among the seven instances where separate food is permitted, why are two allowed while the others are not? Answer: Making robes, traveling on a journey, traveling by boat, and attending a great assembly.
He raised the difficulty regarding food and drink: "If a bhikṣu receives an invitation to a meal from a donor, it is beneficial for him and does not trouble the donor;

therefore, this [rule] must be relaxed. In this case, since there are two families [inviting], the meal invitations will be abundant. How could one, on that basis, take four items such as robes and so forth, and then—by violating the rule—take them later?
This would give rise to the fetter of greed, trouble the previous host, and result in harm rather than benefit; therefore, this is not permitted.
The śramaṇas provide food. Their precepts are intended for minimal benefit, and furthermore, there are no externalists (tīrthika) to trouble as donors;

for these reasons, it is permitted. In this context, if one were to allow [the consumption of] food from śramaṇas by turning one's back on the Buddha’s disciples, it would harm the Buddha’s disciples and result in profound loss of merit.
Such an allowance would cause great detriment; therefore, even the practice of restricting other foods is not a remedial measure.
Next, the explanation of the fourth section has two parts: first, the instruction on how to relinquish an invitation so as not to incur an offense;

second, the formal definition of "turning away from an invitation" (paccācikkhaṇa-pācittiya), beginning with the passage "If a bhikṣu does not relinquish a previous invitation... First, I shall explain the preceding text: if one receives many invitations, one may accept one for oneself and give the remainder to others;
there is no offense of turning away from an invitation provided that one truly relinquishes it, thereby ensuring that the other person actually gains the benefit of receiving food. Furthermore...

One should reflect upon the donor so that there is no pointlessly induced distress; this principle is indeed so. This is consistent with the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which state that by performing the mental reflection (*manasikāra*) at the time of relinquishing [the food], one gains the opportunity for the preparatory rite (*upāya*) and thereby succeeds in preventing the offense of transgression (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). However, if there was no actual benefit beforehand, the meal remains as stale as dust. Thus says the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
Ānanda, having accepted the food from the householder, forgot it. While he was about to eat the meal he had previously accepted, the householder reminded him, saying, "Please take this food;
I have already made an invitation. The householder spoke with resentment, saying, "How can you accept an offering and then later regret it?

Ānanda hurried back and said to the Buddha, "If such a circumstance arises, one should first form a mental intention. One should perform this thought: 'I shall give my portion to such-and-such a bhikṣu. Thus it should be done.

One may eat [the food] afterwards. Because of this, one is thereby liberated. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there is an explanation of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) in four sections: first, enumerating the items and explaining their names and functions;
second, the method of recollection; third, distinguishing the antidotes and what they prevent; and fourth, resolving obstacles and difficulties.

Regarding the listing of names at the beginning of the section: A bhikṣu should know the number of days [since ordination]; he should know the number of years since his upasaṃpadā when offering food; he should remember the robes he has received and kept;
and he should distinguish between being in a separate assembly and being ill or not ill. Regarding these six dharmas, binding the mind so as not to forget them is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
The essence of mindfulness is not sixfold; it is differentiated according to conditions. It is the arising of mindfulness with respect to these six that constitutes its function.
Regarding the second section: first, one should recollect those words. If someone asks, "How many days until today? one must not answer perversely. If asked, "What day was yesterday?
one should say, "It was the first day," or "the second day," and so on up to the fourteenth day and the fifteenth day, as well as whether the month is large or small;
since all of this must be known, one must mentally calculate and verbally state the number of days according to whether the month is large or the specific day is large or small.
First recitation. On the second thought, the bhikṣu should be pure and clear; he should form the thought of giving food: "Today I have obtained food to give to such-and-such a person.
Such-and-such a person does not calculate me as 'I' when I eat; this is the third recitation. Regarding the words of the third thought:

one should daily remember for oneself the number of years since ordination (*varṣa*), the year of the celestial stem (*tai-sui*), the day, month, season, and the summer retreat. One should reflect upon these after having received the precepts.

The first recitation concerns the amount [of food]. The fourth recitation states: "One should remember to maintain the three robes (*tricīvara*), as well as those not formally accepted or purified (*apariśuddha*).
One should reflect: "I maintain my three robes; the extra robes (*atireka*) have already been declared, and the purpose of declaring them pure has been stated.

At that time, the declaration of purity (*pariśuddhi*) is made once. The fifth recitation concerns not eating separately from the assembly; this is the one recitation. The sixth recitation states: "If one is ill..."

Regarding the ritual for those who are not ill: one should say that although there is illness, it shall be treated. Or, if one is not ill, one should silently reflect upon following the path in reliance upon the community; this is stated once.

The third section, which clarifies the remedies (*pratipakṣa*), refers specifically to the application of mindfulness (*smṛti*) as the remedy for phenomena. Furthermore, the function of mindfulness is twofold:

first, to give rise to practice; second, to prevent transgressions. Regarding the giving rise to practice: although there are six types of mindfulness, in terms of their meaning they are reduced to two.

As for the first type of mindfulness: it consists of knowing the size of the months and days in order to recognize the timing for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), and it involves mindfulness in accordance with cultivation.
Regarding the dharma of pure conduct: once the characteristics of the precepts have been recognized, one must next proceed to practice them. This practice is divided into two parts.

The first three moments of mindfulness clarify the cultivation of one's own practice (*svacaryā*), while the subsequent two moments of mindfulness establish the communal practice (*saṃghacaryā*). Within the practice of oneself, there are further two divisions: the second and fourth moments of mindfulness.

Regarding the practice of moderation in internal and external requisites, although the principle of cultivation is the same, because the internal states differ, one must distinguish two moments of thought.

In the third moment of thought, if arrogance remains in the mind, the water of the Dharma will not abide; therefore, one must correctly reflect upon one's seniority in years and abandon the conduct of pride.

Among the various practices of the Dharma, the first—consisting of physical food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra)—does not conflict with the practice of harmonious cultivation. Furthermore, it signifies that there is no separation from the sustenance of the Dharma.

Next, the practice of advancing toward the Path through prosperity is clarified. Regarding the phrase "preventing transgressions," this refers to the five categories of offenses (pañcāpatti-skandha), as can be understood according to the explanations provided.
Regarding the fourth section: as for why the second mindfulness must specifically be recited three times while the other five are only once, the explanation states:

the first mindfulness prevents the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) regarding the thought of not performing [the service]; the second mindfulness prevents the offense of *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) regarding the rejection of the invitation.

Because it prevents these two offenses, it must be recited three times. As for the remaining five mindfullnesses, they only prevent the *dukkaṭa* of the thought of not performing [the service]; they do not fundamentally prevent the root offense itself, and thus this [second mindfulness] is required.

Because they share a single purpose, only one recitation is required. Question: Why does the fourth mindfulness not prevent the offense of *pāyattika* for failing to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) regarding an extra robe?
Answer: Since the robe originally belongs to another and cannot be kept [by oneself], it must immediately be purified; therefore, there is no prevention [of the offense].
The taste of food is a commonality; therefore, it can be guarded against. If that were so, eating in a separate group would likewise be a commonality of taste.

Once the mental resolve has been made, one ought to guard against the offense of *pācittiya* for eating in a separate group. If you claim this is permissible, it leads to the present contradiction and fracture; thus, these two cases are not analogous.

The reason for performing this as described above—specifically reciting it three times—is to prevent two types of offenses. According to the *Cīvara-vastu*, one must confess both the *thullaccaya* and the *pācittiya* together;

by forming a mental resolve (*manasikāra*) to guard against them, one also eliminates the *pācittiya*. Therefore, it is necessary to recite it three times. Alternatively, another interpretation holds that this is not the case.

Just as when one forms a mental resolve during the fourth [recitation], even though the formal act is completed, the fundamental offense (*mūla-āpatti*) still remains outside of that. Thus, it is possible for there to be a separate "non-performance" outside of the fundamental offense.
Regarding the mindfulness of the offense: this is the second mindfulness, which correctly prevents the root [offense]. When the mindfulness is completed, there is no separate root [offense];
how then could there be a distinct offense for failing to maintain mindfulness when one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation)?

Just as with the formal ritual (*kamma*), which primarily prevents staying overnight apart from one's robes—if there is no such separation, and one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), there is no offense for failing to maintain mindfulness beyond the forfeiture itself.

There is no separate offense for failing to perform the ritual; this case is the same as that. Furthermore, it is like the six-year period for declaring the *sthūlātyaya* (grave concealment) and the *viśuddhi* (purification) procedures;

the two categories of upholding and violating are likewise similar in all respects. This is the second defense against the root offense. There is no separate offense for failing to maintain mindfulness. Question:
It may be acceptable in principle that [the precept] merely defends against the root offense. Why, then, are three [defenses] required? Answer: To defend against the root offense.

Therefore, regarding the root *pārājika* offenses, since one has already performed the threefold confession for those that have arisen, one must now likewise perform the threefold [confession] to prevent future transgressions.

As for the remaining five types of mindfulness, because they primarily involve the mindfulness of "not doing," one performs a single recitation to express remorse for what has already occurred; now, to prevent future transgressions, one likewise performs a single recitation.

If this is so, then within the sections concerning the theft of jewels, digging the earth, destroying living beings, and communal recitation, if these were not mentioned, it would be understood [that the same principle applies].

Regarding these cases where one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing): is it not the case that, apart from the fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*), there are distinct offenses for the failure to perform prescribed actions? Answer: This is not the same.

Since this refers specifically to [the transgression of] facing toward or away from [a person], there is only the fundamental offense; there is no separate offense for failing to perform the action, as is the case with categories such as handling precious objects.
Furthermore, speaking according to the teachings for those within the community, this causes there to be a distinct offense of violating the Dharma.

There are indeed cases where one acts with "pure speech" (*jñapticaturtha-karman*) regarding the destruction of a dwelling or the handling of stored treasures and the like; because these are not done intentionally, they are categorized as non-offenses.

Since the three [categories] are thus known, if one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika* school, regardless of whether an invitation has been received or not, it is necessary to perform the formal announcement three times to prevent the offense of *sthūlātyaya*. This is because that school designates it as a specific location.
Regarding the precept on eating at an improper place: how could one possibly be entirely without a designated place for a meal for even a single day?

It is because if one merely directs the mind toward a fixed location while turning one's back [to others], there is still an offense. In this *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is called the "precept on turning away from an invitation. Furthermore, there remains a subsequent explanation concerning the three recitations:
if there is no invitation, this second mindfulness renders it unnecessary; however, if there is an invitation, or if one fails to perform the mindfulness, or perhaps...
It is stated once or three times. This is because it corresponds to what arises from oneself; alternatively, it may be so because the two preceding requests are mutually opposed.
The reason for specifically prohibiting the root [offense] alone is that its flavor is pervasive. Other meanings are as explained previously.

From here below, the correct interpretation of the offense for declining an invitation is established. Suppose one accepts ten invitations on a single day: if one eats at the last one, one commits one *pārājika* and eight *duṣkṛta* offenses.
This is because the first is considered "prior" and the remaining eight are "subsequent. If one declines the latter nine, one incurs nine *pārājikas*.

If one eats at the middle ones, the principle can be understood by analogy. According to the *Vinaya-śāstra*: if one has accepted a prior invitation and goes to the house of the host, one must sit [there].
If one has not yet eaten when food is sent from another household, and one eats that later food, one commits the offense of "contravening an invitation" (*pratijñā-viparyaya*).

If, however, one has already finished eating the first meal and then sits down to eat the food from the later household, there is no offense. According to the explanatory text (*vyākhyāna*), if one is invited to one place but receives food at a non-invited location, there is no offense regardless of what is eaten.
Or, if after having eaten one receives more food, one may accept it provided that one has already accepted the food from the first household and then accepts this further portion.

Regarding eating at home: it may involve the offense of *pātra-pūrṇa* (filling the bowl) but not the offense of *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (refusal of an invitation). Or, regarding eating before or after [the meal] at a single location:

this refers to when a single donor provides five types of formal food (*bhojana*). Even if there are two donors, because it is still a single instance, there is no offense of *pratikṣepaṇa*. It may, however, involve the offense of *pātra-pūrṇa*.
○ The Thirty-third Precept on Eating in a Separate Group:
The prohibition against eating in a separate group has two purposes. First, it is out of compassion for lay families.

Since the quantity of food portions is limited, it is difficult to provide for everyone universally; if a small amount were used to supply many, the resources would be exhausted and the overall benefit would be shallow.

Therefore, the reason for this regulation was twofold: first, to restrain those who are difficult to discipline; and second, out of fear that they might perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act of the fourfold proclamation) as a separate group while excluding the rest of the Saṃgha.
For these two reasons, it was prohibited to eat separately with like-minded individuals.

Next, the second [section] explains the meaning of the names and provides an interpretation, along with the *karmavācanā* for separate assemblies (*pṛthaggaṇa*), as well as their similarities and differences.

Regarding "separate assembly food" (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*): it refers to the person who separates [the group], where the place of eating constitutes a formal assembly (*saṃgha*). Because this assembly distinguishes itself from others, one incurs an offense by not sharing the same meal;
therefore, it is called "separate assembly food. As for the place being separated, how could there not be an assembly there? However, the subsequent Vinaya text [speaks of] "separate assembly..."

Regarding "eating": this refers to four people or more. Thus, it is known that the name is applied from the perspective of those who receive [the food]. This is because within the category of those being distinguished, even a single person commits an offense.
If the name were applied from the perspective of the group [receiving], it would erroneously include those who commit the offense individually. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:

"If, within a group, one specifically invites four or more people, this is called 'a separate invitation for a group meal. It is the same for nuns. If one first accepts such a separate invitation for a group meal, once..."

If one goes and separately accepts different invitations, the community is no longer constituted, yet there is no offense; to say that this constitutes "breaking the Sangha" refers specifically to those three individuals who, in such a case, commit no offense.

Next, the similarities and differences are distinguished. There are seven points of difference. First, the names used in dispute differ. Thus, within the context of eating separately from the assembly (*pṛthag-bhukti*), one does not speak of "separating from the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*);

and within the context of breaking the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha, one does not speak of "breaking [the Saṃgha]. This is because although there are four types of persons, they do not exercise formal authority (*dharmakarma*).

It is simply said that "separating the community" (*saṃghabheda*) refers to a distinct group; both sides consist of four persons, and as they both exercise the communal rites (*saṃghakarma*), they are given the name "Saṃgha.

If one were to apply the name [of the other] indiscriminately, then this side and that side would each become confused. If this side is called "Saṃgha," it implies they are awaiting the performance of the Dharma-rites;

if that side is called "the assembly" (*gaṇa*), it implies they do not perform the rites and thus commit an offense. Therefore, according to the *Gāthā-vyākhyāna*, when these four persons of this assembly perform the *karmavācanā* (formal motion), they are those who are separated.

Even in cases numbering up to hundreds or thousands, if they do not uphold the Dharma, they are all termed a "separate assembly" (pṛthaggaṇa) and are not termed a "schism in the Saṃgha" (saṃghabheda).
Thus we know that those who do not uphold the Dharma are merely called an "assembly" (gaṇa); this shows that the name "Saṃgha" is restrictive, whereas the name "assembly" is universal.

If this is so, since the Western [Sanskrit] term *saṃgha* is translated here as "assembly," how can it be that the Western term is restrictive while the Chinese term is universal? Therefore, we know [the distinction].
It is not so. Now, regarding the distinction between the terms *saṃgha* and *gaṇa*, these are respectively the Sanskrit and Chinese names;

their mutual clarification poses no contradiction. This [term] cites the name, while that [term] follows the Sanskrit original. A detailed explanation is as set forth in the section on "Schism" (*saṃghabheda*) within the "Contravention of Admonition.

Regarding the two types of distinct groups (*bhedaka*), they differ: the group for separate meals (*pṛthag-bhojana*) requires four or more persons to constitute an offense; with three persons, there is no offense. Thus says the text.
It is said that only three persons are invited; the reason for this is that from four persons downward, there are two faults. First, regarding the limited quantity of alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*):

if the number of people is small, it is easy to provide for them, but if they are many, it is difficult to sustain them all. Fearing that this might trouble the donor, the rule against four [or more] was established as an offense.
Second, when four or more arrive, they may act with a common intent to eat separately, fearing that they might conspire together to cause a breach.

When monastic affairs arise, these two [faults] must be prevented; therefore, the offense is established by the rule. With three or fewer people, the aforementioned two harms do not exist, so it is permitted without fault.
There is no limit to the *dharma* or the food; in principle, one should follow this in detail. The more there are, the more excellent it becomes;

thus, one may separate into different locations. It is not restricted by the number of people; provided that the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is performed, all should assemble. To separate otherwise constitutes an offense. Section Three.

The distinctions are as follows. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Manyūlun*), in places where food is difficult to obtain, if one separates from four or more persons, it is permitted and does not constitute an offense, because there is no surplus food to provide for others.
If one separates from three or fewer persons, it constitutes an offense, because [the food] can still suffice for all.

However, in places where food is easily obtained, regardless of the number of people, being able to provide for others constitutes an offense of *pṛthak-bhojana* (separate eating). If one follows this Vinaya, since the village is small...

Furthermore, food is difficult to obtain; it is restricted by those who give and those who receive, such that they do not communicate with one another. In cases where such restrictions apply, regardless of the quantity, it is entirely permissible to eat without offense.
The rule of the Dharma is not like this: in cases of such restriction, it applies from a single person up to hundreds or thousands.

All of these constitute offenses. Since there are no limits to the food provided by the Dharma, it is logically appropriate to follow the rules with meticulous care; indeed, doing more is considered excellent. To do otherwise constitutes an offense.

Fourth, the nature of the transgression differs. Furthermore, regarding the food itself—whether one distinguishes between what is to be eaten and what is not, or between what is proper and what is improper—at the point where such distinctions are made, there is one grade of *pāyattika* (offense).
Within the Dharma, the quantity is irrelevant; it is simply a matter of whether one maintains [the proper conduct].
Regarding the Dharma: one may commit only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) by merely transgressing; even if one presides over a face-to-face (*pratimukha*) procedure, it is likewise only a *duṣkṛta*.

Only when four or more persons preside over a formal assembly (*sabhya-dharma*) does it constitute a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). This is because food is the sustenance for these matters, and thus the affliction of the mind is particularly heavy; therefore, all such violations constitute a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

The Dharma is distinguished by what is correct and what is not; this is why there are hierarchical gradations. Furthermore, regarding these two, it can be understood through reflection that the agent and the object are each either determinate or indeterminate.
Fifth, they differ in terms of time. For example, in the case of eating separately from the assembly, the separation is established during the mealtime;

therefore, the requisite conditions are stipulated as needing to exist within that specific time. The Dharma, however, is not like this; rather, one takes up the performance of the rite precisely to demarcate the time. Below...
Regarding the formal expression (*vācana*): when performing a *karmavācanā* within the same boundary (*sīmā*), if there are those who do not attend, there are six cases where the location differs.
During the meal, because the formal procedure cannot be performed in their absence, the two locations naturally constitute separate legal assemblies (*dharmasaṃgha*).
This applies equally to three or more persons. Regarding the meal, for four or more persons, it is exclusively a formal procedure; however, this excludes [the case of]...

Regarding the establishment of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), there are seven exceptions (*anvaya*) that differ [from the general rule]. As for the exception regarding food, it follows the order of the *saṃgha* because the individuals involved are not fixed;

this demonstrates the absence of shared intent (*samāna-citta*). Furthermore, it serves to additionally benefit the donor; therefore, the order of the *saṃgha* is required. Since food only becomes beneficial as sustenance when actually consumed, there is no [need for] the formal transmission of consent (*chanda*).
Even if consent were transmitted, one would still expect the *saṃgha* to lack merit. Since there is no order of the *saṃgha*, one cannot avoid having shared intent. Therefore...
There is no opening for [selecting] by desire. The food of the Dharma is limitless; the more there are, the more wondrous it becomes. How could there be any difficulty in providing for all?

The method for opening the assembly is that if one were to be dispatched individually, it would inevitably lead to separation. It is only logical that everyone should gather together; therefore, there is no "monastic order" (sequential selection).

This is like the assembly of seven hundred [monks], where the multitude was screened and the *chanda* (consent) was taken; this too was not a matter of monastic order. The principle of the Dharma-food supports those who are far away through the mind; outwardly, it manifests harmony between this and that.
Harmony. Because both this [person] and that [person] obtain benefit, the granting of consent (*chanda*) is permitted.

Next, regarding the explanation of the complete conditions: the general conditions are as stated above; the specific conditions are sevenfold. First, there must be a donor. Second, there must be a separate invitation and separate begging.

Third, the substance of the three kinds of formal food must be pure and within the proper time. Fourth, the place of eating must constitute a *saṃgha*. Fifth, one must know [the location] to be within the boundary (*sīmā*).
It is not fully assembled. Sixth, there is no causal condition. Seventh, one commits an offense immediately upon eating.

First, I shall explain the initial condition. The reason a donor must be present is that it excludes food belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions, as there would otherwise be no offense of eating separately from the assembly.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣikā* (Manyūlun), if one obstructs or guards the food of the Saṃgha, one commits the offense of stealing property belonging to the Saṃgha. As stated in the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness): "Know [this]..."
For ninety billion *kalpas*, one will be born among excrement and urine. One’s form will resemble that of a human, possessing many hands and feet.

If the *saṃgha* present before one each brings forth food and eats together in one place, even though it is separate from others, there is no offense because one does not give [to them] and they do not take [from one], as each member of the separate group eats their own food.
Regarding the term "donor" (*dānapati*), the commentaries provide different explanations; according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*...
First interpretation: This must refer to a layperson acting as a donor; in such a case, there is the offense of "separating from the assembly" (*pṛthag-varga-doṣa*).

Because householders and white-robed laypeople store food and provisions, they may be capable of receiving separate invitations and offerings of the heart; however, fearing that many people might find it difficult to provide for them, one would cause distress to the donor.
This is a sacred regulation: one is not permitted to accept invitations from a separate group. Therefore, the Vinaya states:

"Out of compassion for the families of laypeople, those who have left the household life should abide in few desires and sustain themselves by begging for alms; how could there be the principle of acting as a patron through a separate invitation?

It is clear that for a renunciant, acting as a patron does not constitute an offense. Thus, the Śāstra says: "A śramaṇa does not commit an offense when providing food, provided it is for those of the same Dharma."
Whether they be śramaṇas or non-Buddhist śramaṇas, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, both monastics and lay donors commit the offense of eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

Therefore, the treatise states: "If one bhikṣu goes out for food while three remain without food, and they eat together in one place, the other three commit the offense of *thullaccaya* (saṃghāvaśeṣa)."
There is no offense for one who eats as the host, because they are eating their own food and thus cause no harm or affliction. Furthermore, this Vinaya states:

"Regarding those who give food to śramaṇas, it refers here to śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākya, other renunciants outside [the Buddhist fold], and those who have gone forth from among non-Buddhist paths."

Therefore, it should be known that even among those within our own tradition, śramaṇas likewise violate their limits. As for the previous statement regarding compassion for laypeople, this was spoken merely from a worldly perspective.
Regarding the second condition: although there may be a donor, if the invitation is made according to the sequence of the saṃgha, the mind should have no discrimination; fundamentally, there is none.

[This is] an error. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the distinction between individual invitations (*pṛthak-nimantraṇa*) and invitations by monastic order (*saṃgha-paṅkti*). Regarding individual invitations, there are two true [types].

As for "invitations by monastic order," this can be understood. Alternatively, if one says "in order" (*anupūrva*), such as "the *sthavira* and so many others," this is also subsumed under invitations by monastic order.
Because persons are not fixed, as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If there is no one at the head, that person is the *upādhyāya* (preceptor). Thus, one knows they are not fixed.

There are also two ways to make a specific invitation (*pṛthak-nimantraṇa*): first, if one specifies a name, it is appropriate to make a specific invitation because of that specification; second, to take a person by means of their dharma [or role].
This is also a separate invitation (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*). For example, if one says "ten meditation masters" (*dhyāna-ācāryas*), it does not include the Dharma teachers (*dharma-bhāṇakas*).
There is a distinction of selection between [these] and the Vinaya masters (*vinaya-dhara*s). This clarifies that it is not according to the regular monastic order (*saṃgha-krama*).

Thus, in the Vinaya, when Mṛgāramātṛ addressed the Buddha regarding a separate invitation for five hundred arhats for the meal on the following day, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent. On the following day, Ānanda brought his portion of the meal for the Buddha. May it be so.
The mother and son first called for Ānanda; once he had entered the house, they closed the door.

When the time arrived for the five hundred [monks], each used their supernatural power to emerge from their seats, after which the food was served. Ānanda first ate his own portion and then delivered the Buddha’s share.
Having arrived and offered the food, Ānanda said to the Buddha, "Today, the mother and son have invited us separately."
The five hundred arhats were eating. The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked: "Did you invite a single bhikṣu from among the Saṃgha? She replied: "No. The Buddha said: "Daughter of a concubine!
You invited five hundred arhats separately, yet you did not invite a single bhikṣu from among the Saṃgha. The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked again:

"Did you invite a single bhikṣu from among the Saṃgha? She replied: "No. The Buddha said: "Daughter of a concubine! You are ignorant and unskilled; you did not invite even one person from among the Saṃgha."
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If one invites a single person from within the Saṃgha, by reason of this, one will attain great merit in future lives, obtain a great reward, and gain great benefit.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If one invites a single person from within the Saṃgha, the great merit obtained is superior to that of inviting five hundred arhats individually;
the latter's merit is very slight. According to the explanation in this text, one thus knows that one should invite according to the Dharma.

This person clarifies that it is not a case of following the regular monastic order (*saṃgha-krama*). Even if one has made a separate invitation, if there is someone in the monastic order within the boundary (*sīmā*), there is likewise no offense.

Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duolun) states: "If within a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) there is a donor who separately invites four persons to a meal but does not invite the monks within the boundary, and does not send even a single portion of food;
even if a monk from outside the boundary comes in the regular order, he still commits the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthag-jana-bhakta*). One must [properly] invite..."
If there is one person in the sequence of the monastic assembly within the boundary, it is not an offense to send a portion of food to them.
However, if the distance to the monastery is too great to send this portion of food, one should instead take that portion of food and distribute it according to the sequence of the assembly;

this constitutes the sequence of the assembly, and eating in this manner is likewise faultless. Since it is stated that one must necessarily follow the sequence of the assembly within the boundary, any separate invitation [given outside of this] constitutes a violation of the sequence of the assembly.

Regarding the relative [classification], there is a fourfold analysis: either the prior [invitation] is in the order of the Saṃgha while the subsequent [invitation] is restricted to that specific location, which constitutes a separate invitation (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*);

or both the prior and subsequent are separate—these two cases constitute a *thullaccaya* offense; or the prior is a separate invitation while the subsequent is not restricted to that location, thereby becoming part of the order of the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, if both the preceding and succeeding [monks] are in the proper order of seniority, there is no offense in either case. If there is another monk at the place where the meal is being served, one should not obstruct him from teaching or exhorting [the laity].
If one is unable to refrain from obstructing him, one should instruct the donor to announce the seniority [of the monks] in order of their *varṣa*.
If one enters [the meal] even for a single person, once having entered, there is no further fault even if others are subsequently barred.
If an invitation for food is made for a long duration—having been announced during the first month, it need not be announced again until the ninety-day period of offerings concludes.

If it was not announced on the first day, it must be announced every day; only then will there be no separate offense. If, within a village, there is no monastery where monks previously resided and someone offers alms...
If the host separately invites four people for a meal, one should strike the *gandī* (wooden gong) to manifest that there is no discord among sentient beings;

it does not matter whether or not there are other monks present. There is no fault whatsoever. Regarding "separate begging," it may mean that the four beg at the same time, or that they are made to beg separately so that they do not know of one another, yet share the same host. It simply requires that the assembly be complete at the place of eating, and that they eat together.

This constitutes an offense of acting as a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*). Thus, the Vinaya text states: "Devadatta took four others with him, making five including himself, and went from house to house to beg for alms.
The Buddha immediately rebuked and prohibited this for two reasons. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Daolun) says: "If the four individuals were to beg for alms separately..."

Eating at a single location also does not constitute a separate offense. Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the *Vibhajyavāda*, it is plausible that the first and fourth [propositions] constitute an offense.
As for the second proposition—where one receives food at different times but eats at different locations—an offense would occur because the receiving of the food occurs simultaneously;
this point is somewhat difficult. How could one commit an offense at the moment of receiving the food? For it is not based on the act of swallowing. These two [cases] are like two tubes.
The fourfold categorization need not be discussed here. Regarding the third condition:
if it were not a formal meal (*bhojana*), it would lack the capacity to sustain the body; because of the principle of traveling on a long journey, five types of formal meals are required.
Therefore, the text states: "As for 'meals,' these are rice, gruel, and so forth. As for the question regarding the offense of a formal meal: within the context of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

Furthermore, one may commit an offense against a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*) through a formal act (*dharma*). Answer: Within a formal act, there is no *saṃgha*; it refers instead to those facing one another and so forth. How could a formal act be devoid of a *saṃgha*?
When the assembly is not constituted, the eating alone is improper; therefore, it is not of the same category. If the food is impure, it is not permissible.
If one eats with the bhikṣus as part of the same meal, one does not commit the offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthaggaṇa*). It must be stated that they are pure;

if it were otherwise, it would be an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*) and could not be followed collectively, thus one should not commit the offense of eating separately. Answer: This is an illegal assembly (*adharma-saṃnipāta*), which can be rectified by overturning the illegality.

As for the established rule regarding eating separately: if the food has already been consumed and is impure, even if one goes [to the assembly], one cannot turn them back to make it pure; going there is of no avail.

It is beneficial because one does not commit an offense. As the text says, it concerns an "unlawful separate assembly" (*adharma-vinīta*). If that is so, why is there no offense for the precept against causing disturbance?

Within the opening [provisions] for the precept regarding granting consent (*chanda*), if it is an unlawful formal act (*adharma-karman*), whether one is summoned and does not come or not, or whether one grants consent or not, there is no offense.

Answer: That case is different; it refers to matters such as schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*) or causing its decline. Therefore, an exception was made. This present statement, however, concerns what is "unlawful."

This refers to the seven "non-cases" (*asādhāraṇa*); thus, there is also a distinction. Although the food may be pure, if it is consumed at an improper time (*akāla*), it likewise lacks the same flavor [of communal sharing].

Since there is no fault in being distinct under such conditions, it must occur within the proper time (*kāla*). Although the food may consist of the five types of solid food (*bhojana*), if the place of eating is not a communal assembly, there is likewise no offense.
Therefore, the fourth condition is required: the place of eating must constitute a community (*gaṇa*), meaning four or more bhikṣus of the same class who are harmonious.

The above constitutes a single meal-time reception; there is a specific doctrinal interpretation according to which one only commits the offense of *pṛthaggaṇa* (eating separately) when these conditions are met.

Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* states: three bhikṣus and one bhikṣuṇī; three bhikṣus and one śrāmaṇera; three bhikṣus and one who regards [the fourth] as a pillar; three bhikṣus and one who has been expelled (*pravāsanīya*); three on the ground and one in the air;
three within the boundary (*sīmā*) and one outside the boundary; or cases where the bhikṣuṇī and others are insane or have been suspended (*utkṣepanīya*). These do not constitute an offense.
Regarding the number of monks: if they are outside the boundary of the empty space (ākāśa-dhātu) and furthermore belong to a different boundary, they do not count toward the required quorum;

in all such cases, there is no offense. Furthermore, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If among four persons, one person covers their bowl and does not eat, it likewise does not constitute an offense. Therefore, it is essential [to ensure the presence of the full number].
This refers to bhikṣus of the same class who eat together in one place within the same boundary; only then does the assembly become constituted for the purpose of eating.

This excludes those of a different class, such as a single person whose bowl has been turned upside down (*pātra-nyubja*). Regarding this, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* presents four cases: First, when the host of the meal is one, all have assembled, and they eat in one place—this is most excellent and faultless.
Second, when the food and the place are the same but [the participants] are distinct; although they are separate from one another, because the flavor of the food is the same, [they may eat together].
This is also not an offense. If there are other people within the boundary, both groups commit the offense. Third, regarding eating separately in different places:
for example, when the entire Saṃgha has assembled in one location and has not yet eaten the food of the Saṃgha, a donor comes and invites four bhikṣus to their seats in succession, giving them food.

These four bhikṣus commit the offense of eating separately, because there is Saṃgha food available that they could have eaten [together], and thus it does not fall [under the category of separate eating].
A major offense. Regarding the opening of the conditions for the assembly: the four types of food must be kept separate in different locations.

If these two assemblies do not mutually invite one person from each other, nor send a portion of food, both parties commit an offense. Although the meal may constitute a formal assembly, if it is gathered within the same boundary (*sīmā*), there is likewise no offense;

therefore, a fifth person is required. If they are not fully assembled within the boundary, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two kinds of boundaries: namely, the natural (*prakṛti*)...
Furthermore, there are two types: the *araṇya* (wilderness) *krośa* and the village boundary, which is naturally seventy-three *yojanas* less than half.
Within these natural boundaries and for the *poṣadha*, if they are separate and even one person does not assemble, it constitutes an offense for those who perceive themselves as monks (*bhikṣu*).

If one harbors doubt, the offense is light; if there is no intention to think about it, there is no transgression. If one is separately expelled for insanity, or if it concerns a śrāmaṇera, there is no fault in not assembling.
The sixth and seventh [cases] are explained in the main text. Omissions in the conditions are to be understood by analogy.

This fulfills the four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra: first, [the rule regarding] a single person; second, eating in a group apart from others; third, excluding the permitted circumstances; and fourth, concluding with the offenses below.
As for the phrase "at other times," it refers to the third [clause] recited previously and does not belong to the fourth.

In the explanation of the conditions for opening [the precepts], there is a sixfold analysis: first, the conditions for opening and the explanation of the names; second, their length and brevity; third, their commonality and distinctness;
fourth, their breadth and narrowness; fifth, the relative strength of their mutual inclusion; and sixth, their similarities and differences in comparison with others.
First, I shall explain the initial section by interpreting the names and correlating them with the text. Regarding the phrase "fixed conditions" (*niyata-paccaya*):

within these permitted conditions, the illness [condition] and the following four [conditions] are here treated as five types of robes offered as alms. These two meanings include the time for making robes, namely one month or five months;
because seeking food for the purpose of making robes might make the task difficult to accomplish, the Buddha permitted separate invitations for communal meals. Thus it is said.

Regarding the "time for making robes": this refers to the periods of one month or five months, as these are times when merit is abundant; thus, one may obtain separate food. Regarding the "giver of robes":
this refers to the general giving of food, and it is also permitted for those who give both food and robes to form a separate assembly.

This can be categorized into three [types]: first, the time for making robes; second, the time for the gift of robes; third, the inclusion of the aforementioned five [cases], totaling eight grounds for exemption. As for how this is known, the answer is as follows:

The fifth rule regarding the precept on eating frequently: the first section concerning the exception for those who are ill. If a bhikṣu eats frequently, except when there is a specific cause, it is a pāyattika offense.
A "specific cause" refers to the time of illness. Second, at that time, the World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to accept *kaṭhina* robes;
they do not commit an offense in five matters. The bhikṣus thought: "Is this the time for the robe, such that one does not commit an offense by eating frequently?"

If one has finished eating and clothing [has been provided], there is no offense in taking [more]. The Buddha said to the monks: "There is no offense during the time for clothing; it is an offense after the time for clothing.
If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, except when there is a cause, it is a pāyattika. A "cause" refers to the time of illness or the time for clothing.
Third, there were some laypeople who knew that bhikṣus were not permitted to eat more than once a day.

They thought to themselves, "I shall employ a skillful means to provide robes for the bhikṣus so that they will come to receive them, and I may also make offerings. They then had robes made and went to invite the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus said, "We are not permitted to eat; we only ask for robes. The laypeople replied, "If you eat our food, then we shall give it to you."
The bhikṣu thought to himself: "If the Buddha permits me to eat repeatedly for the sake of receiving robes, I shall not lack clothing.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "I permit you to eat repeatedly for the sake of receiving robes. It should be stated thus: 'If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly...'"

Regarding the exceptions to the rule: there is the time of illness and the time of [receiving] robes. Next comes the precept concerning eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhojana*). Within the section on the promulgation of the rule and its subsequent allowances, first is the exception for illness;

next, it mentions the time of robes and the time of receiving robes, as explained in the precept on frequent eating (*abhīkṣṇa-bhojana*). Next are the times for making robes and so forth, which are permitted before the formal conclusion of the robe-making season.

To complete the core of the precept (*śikṣāpada*), it says that the "exceptional circumstances" (*nidāna*) are: the time of illness, the time of robes, the time of receiving robes, the time of making robes, and the time of traveling.

The eight occasions are: when traveling on land, when traveling by boat, during a great assembly, and when giving food to śramaṇas. These eight are listed in full. In this Vinaya, they are collectively referred to as "the time for giving robes.
In the detailed explanation that follows, it states: "The time for giving robes refers to one month or five months, as well as other instances of giving food and various types of clothing.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, these may likewise be categorized as eight.

Regarding the two cases of "long" and "short": there are six [cases] when the two illnesses and the four [occasions] such as the distribution of robes (*cīvara*) and traveling on a journey are combined;

there are five when illness and traveling on a journey are excluded. Since the preceding conditions serve as the time-limit, and those conditions lack a fixed standard, how could the time be determined?

If the twelve months are present, then the one occasion of the distribution of robes is opened. Although it is an object of craving, because the benefit of the robe is weighty, it provides a single advantage.

The donor receives two kinds of rewards. Furthermore, it benefits the bhikṣu; for if he does not accept when the gift is offered, later it will be difficult to obtain, and he may fear that unreasonable solicitation would hinder and obstruct his cultivation of the Path.
Because he accepts and listens according to what is given, it also serves as a long-term provision of robes for one interval.

Since the time of receiving the benefit is fixed, it is limited to one month or five months, regardless of whether he already possesses robes or not. Even if they are separate, there is no offense in making robes [from them].

At that time, [the period] was only one month or five months. Therefore, the Vinaya text itself fears that if one makes robes during the *kārttika* month, the bhikṣus might lack food and suffer from exhaustion;
thus it requests the bhikṣus [to accept the robe-material]. The Buddha said, "I permit you to receive it," as stated in the text. It does not mention "and other times.
Because it concerns making robes, it does not apply [to other occasions]. Question: Since one may naturally form a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*) within that very time, why is it necessary to say...?
"Making robes" (kathina): one interpretation explains the literal meaning as follows: even down to making a single "horse-tooth" stitch upon a robe, it is called "making robes.
Furthermore, this can be understood as "making robes" because, within the month, this refers to the time of receiving the robe-material;

since there is no fixed limit for the duration of the project, the period extends at most to one month or five months from the time of receiving the material, and at its minimum, it is even as short as making a single patched robe (*saṃdhika-cīvara*). This is also the case when resources are abundant.
Therefore it is said: "down to even a single thread.
Third, regarding what is common and what is distinct: giving robes to the great assembly and to śramaṇas—these three share the commonality of the gift of robes.

This is because they refer to the same objective field and are mutually dependent for the sake of the great assembly; thus, these three are opened [for use] only when there is necessarily a common sharing. As for the remaining five...
It is indeterminate; it is not that there is no common purpose.

Regarding the four distinctions of breadth and narrowness: these eight [precepts] are distinguished by their scope when compared to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. The scope of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* conditions is broad, because they benefit both oneself and others.

Furthermore, because it benefits the donor, the remaining [types of giving] are merely permitted under specific conditions; they lack the benefit of the "field of the Sangha" (saṅgha-kṣetra), and for this reason, they are narrow.

Regarding the eight [types of giving], when viewed in relation to one another, the first three share common conditions but do not distinguish between benefits, as they involve both self and others through their shared nature. The remaining five are all narrow.

It can only benefit oneself and cannot moisten others; therefore, the text below states: "Those without a connection. This means that even though they appear white, other things with which he has a connection do not benefit him.

Regarding the relative strength of inclusion among the five characteristics: if one is among a great assembly of śramaṇas receiving robes, even if there were other exceptions among these three allowances, they would be subsumed solely within the three conditions pertaining to the great assembly and so forth. This is because the allowance is not granted on account of any other conditions, and since there is no offense even in the absence of those other conditions.

As for the mutual relationship of the remaining five, even if they are separated from their specific conditions, such as the case of food for individuals, each is subsumed under its own respective condition. Or...

The same may be understood for the others. Regarding the sixth point, "sameness and difference": while [the rules for] the seventh and eighth [categories] are restricted, these two—[those for] water and land—are common. Regarding bathing, there are both commonalities and differences.

As for the three cases such as the time for wearing robes and so forth, they generally pertain to the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit), the *lābha-śīla* (benefit of the precepts), and the occasion of illness; however, there are distinctions among them, which follow what has been stated previously.

What has been explained follows the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben) to clarify its underlying intent. If the sick were not granted this exemption when suffering from affliction, they would have no means of survival;
furthermore, there would be no reason for them to cause distress to the Saṃgha. For these reasons, it is permitted. Regarding the delay in making robes:
fearing that the primary practice might be neglected, the donor of the robe benefits both the monastics and the laity. Thus, the time for receiving the robe is either one month or five months.
Because it concerns the time of receiving benefits; because these two—traveling by land and traveling by boat—are frequently paired;

and furthermore, because food is difficult to obtain, when a large assembly gathers, many people would find it difficult to be provided for, which is why this was permitted. Regarding the Śramaṇas offering food, it is for the sake of providing some small benefit to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Question: If [the non-Buddhists] have no intention [to benefit others] when they invite [monks], how can it be said that it is "for the benefit of the non-Buddhists" to allow separate invitations?
