Regarding the benefit of food: this passage is not clear. For example, in the *Pañcavargika*, it is said that King Bimbisāra’s younger brother was named Kāla.

He practiced a certain path and every year held a great assembly where ninety-six types of śramaṇas were invited to recite [scriptures] together; however, the sons of Śākya did not accept [this invitation].

He had invited the assembly for a separate meal, but his resources were insufficient to extend it to the entire Sangha. Because of this deficiency regarding the śramaṇas of the Buddha’s path, he was distressed and unhappy.
He thought to himself, "How can I bring the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya here? I must entrust this matter to the King; only then can it be accomplished.
He then respectfully informed the Buddha of his intention. The Buddha consequently granted permission. When the time came for the assembly of śramaṇas, he accepted the separate invitation.
Regarding the invitation to a communal meal (*saṃghabhojana*), this is to be understood by analogy with other cases; in all instances, it is because the food is not exhausted.

To say that one should only invite three people is intended to clarify that there is a specific distinction. Furthermore, some claim that when the inviter acts with the intention of a separate invitation and the recipient accepts with the same intent, an offense is committed if four people eat;

however, this does not require a specific distinction. Such a view deeply contradicts the sūtras and śāstras. The five exceptional circumstances mentioned above, such as illness and so forth, apply only to...
One can benefit oneself, but cannot moisten others. If it reaches others, it causes three people not to commit offenses.

As for why there is no formal act of confession (*jñapti*), if that were so, why does the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* state that for a sick person, the four [categories] are sufficient for all to be free from offense? The explanation is this:

when that text speaks of a "sick person," it does not refer to those who are insane or deranged. It means that by virtue of being ill, the four [categories] are sufficient for there to be no fault at all. In this context, the "sick person" refers to...

Because it is light, it benefits oneself but cannot extend to others. That treatise states that there are five instances where the four [prohibitions] are not violated: first, when not invited; second, regarding alms-food;
third, regarding śrāmaṇeras; fourth, regarding the alms bowl; and fifth, regarding the sick person. Thus, one knows that the illness in that context is not the same as this "light" case.

In the section below that clarifies the characteristics, the first two are understandable. Regarding the passage beginning with "the sick," this explains the third allowance for exceptions. The rest is as previously stated.

As for "the assembly of the great multitude," according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is the constant law of all Buddhas to hold two great assemblies each year: in the sixth month of spring and the sixth month of summer.
Because there were so many people visiting from all directions to offer greetings, invitations for meals became very infrequent and it was difficult to obtain food through begging.

A bhikṣu thought to himself, "If the Buddha would allow us to accept separate invitations for communal meals during large assemblies, we would not suffer such hardship. He informed the Buddha, who then granted permission.
Regarding the phrase "when the great assembly gathers," there are two interpretations. First, "the great assembly" refers to eight or more persons.

This is called a "large assembly. Since they consume offerings from those lacking faith, and because it is difficult to permit them to do so without committing an offense, [the rule] is not relaxed for them. An assembly of seven or fewer people is called a "small assembly.
Although food may be difficult to obtain for them, it is possible for them to share it; therefore, [the rule] is likewise not relaxed for them. Thus, the Vinaya text states:
There is no offense when a large assembly is about to gather; conversely, it is an offense when one instead explains it as a small group.

Therefore, it is said that "when food is sufficient for four people, a fifth person is a trouble. Because the permission [to eat together] is not granted, this one person causes the other four to incur an offense;
thus, he is called a "trouble. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: a "large assembly" refers to four or more persons; hence, below...
The Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states: "Without informing the *saṃgha*, one causes them to understand [the offense] extensively. Regarding the phrase "the *saṃgha*," it refers to four persons or more.
Based on this textual evidence, it is known that four persons or above are termed the *saṃgha*. Furthermore, regarding this same text, "when the *saṃgha* has assembled":
if there are four persons sufficient for a meal, adding one more constitutes a "disturbance" (*ābādha*). This concerns two households in a village; the eastern household...

The eastern family restricted [the alms] to four people; the western family restricted it to one person. Because the charitable intentions of these two families were limited and mutually exclusive, it was difficult to obtain food by begging elsewhere.
If this restriction were not lifted, the single person from the western family would become a source of trouble for the four people of the eastern family.
Due to this trouble, the rule was relaxed so that they would not commit an offense; this is called "raising a concern" (ādīnava) to grant an exemption.

There is no offense. This applies even up to a group of one hundred; if only one person among them falls ill, provided that food is difficult to obtain, it is permitted for all to eat together without fault.
This is called "when a great assembly has gathered."

Next, the explanation of the fourth section on the offense of transgression has two parts: first, the preliminary instruction on the proper procedure for a bhikṣu to eat; second, the formulation of the offense for violating [the rules], beginning with "If a bhikṣu...
The preceding text consists of four phrases. The first pair of four phrases concerns the first phrase: when there is no cause, one is permitted to leave after making a formal announcement (*jñapti*);

the fourth phrase concerns when there is a cause, one is permitted to enter after making a formal announcement. The middle two phrases concern the first pair: eating at will when there are few people; when there are many people, dividing [the food].

Regarding the communal meal (*saṃghabhojana*): the first four points concern the formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding entry and departure. This refers to cases where there is a valid reason (*sanimitta*) or no valid reason (*animitta*).

In the miscellaneous explanation for resolving doubts concerning the announcement of entry and departure: the first phrase concerns those without a valid reason who must announce their departure. This indicates that others are not part of the monastic succession;

because they have a valid reason [to leave], their presence would not benefit me through the meal, and thus they must announce their departure. Outsiders who lack a valid reason may not enter. This is intended to dispel the doubts of the assembly regarding those outside.

Thus, regarding the fourth case, there is a *pratyaya* (circumstance). One who must announce their entry does so to show that they are not entering according to the sequence of the *saṃgha*, but rather because they have a specific circumstance;
otherwise, their food would not benefit others. If one has no such circumstance, they must exit; this is done to remove doubts from within the assembly.

These two instances of announcing entry and exit refer to speaking in relation to the other five [categories], and do not concern the three cases where entry and exit are announced based on a common *pratyaya*. [End of middle section]
Regarding the two cases: in the first case, the community is small and they eat according to their own will; in the second case, the food is divided between two groups.

Since these two situations are purely without cause for concern or doubt, it is not necessary to announce one's entry or departure. Provided that the quorum of the assembly is not completed, it is permitted to eat according to one's will.
Regarding "not clearly understanding those with purely objective conditions": this refers to the three common conditions and the other five, such as the common meaning (*sādhāraṇārtha*) and so forth.
This also does not require a formal announcement (*jñapti*). Second, the offense of violating the teaching: one incurs a *pāyattika* for eating in a separate group (*gaṇabhojana*). Question:

Why is it said that one commits an offense for every swallow, regardless of the quantity of food? Answer: The Buddha’s original intention in establishing this rule was out of compassion for the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Regarding robes: fearing they might disturb the community of monks, it was established that one must not eat separately. This is not intended solely to prevent harm; why then focus exclusively on the one eating separately? One incurs the offense according to the object [of the act].
Furthermore, since the offense is committed only through reliance upon the assembly, and because one eats out of a greedy mind, one incurs the karmic fault simply by following that action.

Question: Why is it that only those with a connection [to the assembly] incur the offense for failing to announce their intention (*an-ārocana*), while those without such a connection do not? One interpretation is as follows: [The text continues...]
This is because it is improper to eat food that has been set aside; furthermore, the text may be abbreviated here.
○ Regarding the thirty-fourth precept on taking more than three bowls of the price for a bride returning home or provisions for travelers on the road:

now, as for the price for a bride returning home or provisions for travelers, they have abandoned their own travel rations and bestowed them upon the bhikṣus; one ought to protect these and accept them according to the limit.

[The rule for] taking [food]: Now, to take more than three bowls, causing the food to be completely exhausted, increases greed and violates the teachings; because the resulting harm and affliction are not slight, this is established as a prohibition.

There are five specific conditions [for an exception]: first, food provided by a woman returning home, or provisions for a traveler on a journey; second, knowing it to be such; third, having no other cause or condition—excluding [the following cases].

There is no offense if there is a reason related to illness. Regarding taking more than three bowls: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, if one uses a large bowl, taking one bowl is without offense;
taking two bowls constitutes an offense. If one uses a medium bowl, taking two is without offense; taking three constitutes an offense. If one uses a small bowl, taking three is without offense.
One incurs an offense only upon taking the fourth bowl. Regarding the scriptural statement "exceeding three bowls," this refers to the counting from the bottom bowl.
If one person takes one bowl, the first three persons do not incur an offense because they have not exceeded the limit. The last person incurs an offense;

since the previous three said, "Do not bring it," yet he intentionally went to take it, the fault lies with the last person. Furthermore, it is "exceeding three," and thus it is the last person who incurs the offense. (5)

As soon as she went out, she committed an offense. Regarding the two individuals involved, there were two [cases]: first, taking the food of a woman returning from her husband’s home, which gave rise to the fault of *āsrava* (outflow).

In the *Kṣudraka-vastu*, one who deviates from this is called "blind" (*andha*). The tenth is called "squinting" (*kaṭākṣa*). As stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "I no longer need you, blind woman.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is said that this woman was so beautiful that the king might have forcibly taken her; therefore, he intended to give her an inauspicious name. Indeed, the king wished to take her.
Because the name was inauspicious, he went instead to another person. The second [case] concerns the offense of taking a portion of food from a traveler who has stopped at Vārāṇasī;

this fulfills three phrases of the core precept (*śikṣāpada*). First, the offender. Second, the method for receiving and consuming a portion [of food] once one has reached a layperson’s home, which is explained below.
The text has three parts: first, the provision of travel provisions; second, "If a bhikṣu... and so forth, which teaches the limits for receiving [food]; and the reason why.
The opening of these three [sections] is for the purpose of enabling the donor to obtain the merit of a reciprocal reward, and also to enable the bhikṣu to nourish and grow in the Path.

Third, regarding the method of teaching on the distribution of food from the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules: the third section, beginning with "If a bhikṣu is not ill," etc., clearly explains the transgression of taking more than permitted and violating the teaching;

this concludes the offense by contrasting it with the preceding text. The second section, beginning with "The allowance to receive," etc., explains the offense of departing [from the proper conduct]. It is not [an offense of] *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

The minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*) are categorized separately because the text is not explicit regarding them. Thus, among the eight conditions for being in a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), only the case of illness is permitted.

This is because a sick person suffers from affliction; if such an exemption were not granted, they would have no means to sustain their life. Furthermore, the donor understands this and does not give rise to reproach or distress.

Therefore, the other conditions are not permitted, as their allowance might cause harm or distress. Since one commits an offense the moment one steps out [of the boundary], why rely on the formal procedure of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?

The first section, "Discerning the Characteristics," is fully explained. From the second section, "Laypeople," onwards, up to the point where three bowls have arrived, this correctly explains the method for receiving and dividing food according to the second teaching. Within this, there are three parts: first, explaining the giving of food by laypeople;
second, regarding the precept for the sick, the root text is abbreviated and not explained here, whereas the present explanation excludes those who are ill; third, if a bhikṣu...
Below: The method for receiving [food] by opening the bundle; the ritual for eating, including the text on bringing it forth and announcing it—these four sections may be understood.
Third, from "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the explanation of the root precept (śīla-mūla). Third, regarding the determination of the gravity of the offense, there are four points:

one [offense] is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), three are *pācittiya* (requiring expiation), and according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, both over-receiving and not distributing food to other bhikṣus constitute a *pācittiya* offense. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*...
The same applies to the middle [period]. Furthermore, it is said that if a woman or a visiting monk departs and one eats afterward, there is no offense.
○ The thirty-fifth precept, the Rule Against Eating After Having Sufficient Food:

Generally, food is for the purpose of sustaining the body; to exceed this is to increase greed, while too little is insufficient. Therefore, one must exercise moderation and measure. However, [the text continues:]

The physical strength of the four great elements varies in its karmic retribution, being sometimes strong and sometimes weak. Consequently, there are four distinct grades for those who are about to attain sainthood (*ārya*).

Beginning with a single morsel and culminating in the ritual for leftover food (*vighasa-vidhi*), all these are methods for moderation according to one's faculties. This ensures that the fourth person does not perform the ritual for leftovers;
to eat the five types of staple foods again would increase craving and obstruct the Path. Such an act violates the teachings and incurs a profound transgression; therefore, this rule was established.
The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, having finished eating; second, the perception that one has finished eating; third, abandoning the formal posture;

fourth, being without a valid cause—except in cases of illness or when performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (post-midday) ritual, where such causes do not constitute an offense; fifth, each swallow of further food constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*.
Regarding the conditions, there are two parts. First, from "attaining [the food]" down to "eating," it clarifies that if one does not perform other prescribed methods, a transgression arises.
Second is the reprimand. The preceding text further has two sections: first, up to "Dharma-food," it permits the performance of other methods;

second, from "Śrāvastī" onwards, it explains that failing to perform them constitutes an offense. The first section has four parts: for those of superior practice, it teaches (1) the method of eating, (2) the time, (3) various illnesses, and (4) comparisons.

Although the Buddha had already permitted those who were ill to eat several times before noon without fault, he further allowed that if sick bhikṣus of the three periods of the day should obtain the leftover food of those who were ill—even if its substance is loathsome—they need not perform any further ritual purification;

it is permitted for them to eat it without fault. Fourth, regarding the permission to eat, this specifically clarifies that what is not the leftover food of the ill is pure food (*śuddha-bhakṣa*). It is permissible to eat.

Regarding the practice of eating after having performed other [prescribed] rites, the first section has three parts: (1) the exposition of the one-meal rule; (2) from "At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard it...
onwards, the exposition of being satisfied at a single sitting, which precedes the restriction of the one-meal rule; and (3) from "The bhikṣus...

onwards, the instruction on being satisfied before the previous [meal]. As for the initial exposition of the one-meal rule, it refers to the exposition of the one-meal rule in relation to the aforementioned practice.
This praises and extols the practice of eating a single meal (*ekāsanika*). It extols the efficacy of this practice: reducing external conditions and being content.
It may also praise those capable of practicing it, so that by relying on this sacred teaching, one accomplishes the conduct of contentment. The second section has four parts:

first, relying on the aforementioned sacred teaching, one consumes improper food, resulting in physical emaciation; second, at that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion, inquired after him; third, Ānanda and others... [text continues].
He reported all of this to the Buddha. The four Buddhas having finished speaking, [the meal] was concluded; thus it is said that "he ate to full satisfaction while remaining on a single seat.
Regarding the third section, there are four points: first, although he relied on eating until full, because this included both proper and improper food, he remained emaciated.

The subsequent questions and so forth may be understood accordingly; this refers to concluding the previous state of fullness, hence it says, "regarding each of the five kinds of food, he caused himself to be satisfied."
[The section on] the full [meal]. Second, the opening for the sick has four parts; as with the third, it also has four. The fourth is the opening for performing other practices.

Because of the rule restricting one to a single meal, the remaining [food] was discarded by the Noble Ones. To benefit the donors and because there is no harm to the bhikṣus, the practice of "leftovers" (vighasa) was permitted. Within this:

The text consists of two parts. First, the ritual for designating food as "leftover" (*kṛtapiṇḍapāta*) when it is monastic food; second, the ritual for designating clothing as "leftover" given by a donor, following the passage beginning with "Furthermore, there was an elder...
who had received alms-food. In each of these two sections, four points can be discerned. Regarding the traditional interpretation:

whenever the ritual for leftover food (*atiriktabhojana-vidhi*) is performed, one should first receive the food from a lay attendant (*upāsaka*). Having thus received the food, one should then arrange it before a monk who has not yet finished his meal. (From the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*).

It is established only when five conditions are fulfilled, namely, the five non-separations, as stated in that text. There are five improper ways which do not constitute the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) rite:

first, if a *bhikṣu* who has left the place is walking while another remains standing, sitting, or lying down and speaks of the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite to him, this is not called performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite;
the same applies to the other three postures, as also explained in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Furthermore, if a *bhikṣu* is washing his mouth while walking, and there is...

When a donor offers the five kinds of food, a bhikṣu may eat them and walk about after having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of accepting leftover food). He must not remain standing, sitting, or lying down.

If he remains standing, sitting, or lying down, it should be known that his deportment is impaired and it does not count as having accepted [the food]. If one considers this to be the acceptance of food, it is a *pāyattika*. Second, regarding the separation from food:
if the food is not given, yet one chews it and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* ritual, and then says, "I give it," this is called improper. Third.

1. Regarding "separation from the boundary": if one places the food on the ground to perform the *kuṭi-kāra* (leftover) rite, it is not within hand's reach; this is not called performing the *kuṭi-kāra* rite. 2. Fourth, "separation by extending the hand":

performing the *kuṭi-kāra* outside the reach of the extended hand is improper; performing it inside the reach of the extended hand is not called the *kuṭi-kāra* rite. 3. Fifth, "separation by speech":
if one does not speak these words—"The food in my hands and in my bowl, all of it, is for me; you have no need for this as leftover food"—this is not called *kuṭi-kāra*.

Regarding food, first we shall distinguish what is contrary to the Dharma within the Dharma, so that one may recognize the five types of "non-separation" (*anapatti*). These are the formal procedures for the *atireka-śeṣa* (leftover) food, which consist of the five reversals of the aforementioned separations:
1. **Non-separation of place**: Receiving food at this location and returning to this same location to receive food and perform the formal act of distribution.

2. **Non-separation of food**: Consuming a small amount of food [before the formal act]. 3. **Non-separation of the objective sphere** (*viṣaya*): [The remaining three are as follows:]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends with the third category; the full list of five typically includes non-separation of the assembly, non-separation of the substance, and non-separation of the boundary.)

1. This refers to taking food with one's own hand and giving it to another. 2. "Not departing from within arm's reach" means that the act is completed while remaining within the range of an outstretched hand.

3. "Not departing from speech" means saying, "Venerable sir, I have already finished my meal. If the other person understands this, then even though that person has already eaten, they may say again, "I have already eaten everything in my hands and bowl;
there is no need to perform the *khalupaṭiggaha-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food). This constitutes the aforementioned rule.

This is merely the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), yet it is not yet complete. According to this Vinaya, it must possess four "factors of conformity" (*yathādharma*) to constitute a formal offense of residual transgression (*śeṣasaṃghāvaśeṣa*).

First, there must be one person who acts according to the Dharma; second, there must be two persons as the accused; third, there must be three persons capable of performing the rite—namely, monks, excluding other assemblies;

and fourth, there must be five conditions fulfilled, including the person being free from illness. To act contrary to these is termed "non-conformity" (*ayathādharma*). Second, the person addressed...

"Person" refers to a bhikṣu and not to other assemblies. Furthermore, because the five requirements have not yet been fulfilled, the text states "having finished eating" (*paryāpta-bhukta*) so that the remaining formalities may be performed;

otherwise, it does not constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense. These five factors constitute a person who acts in accordance with the Dharma, as do the two times [of eating] when acting in accordance with the Dharma.
This means that abundance is not considered frugality, for frugality opens the door to insatiability. Furthermore, during this [proper] time, one must exclude improper times;
if one eats at an improper time, it causes one to incur a transgression from the previous meal, as one's own fault would then exist. Regarding the three types of food that accord with the Dharma:

first, "timely food" (kālabhojana), which excludes *sukhallikānuyoga* (indulgence in luxury) and items such as bitter, sour, pungent, or salty foods; second, "fresh food," excluding the leftovers of a sick person.

Third, the food must be pure and not "leftover" (ucchista), nor tainted by touch, sight, hearing, or suspicion; according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, food that is stale, previously stored, poorly handled, or impure is not called "the rite for receiving leftover food.
Fourth, one’s deportment (*īryāpatha*) must be in accordance with the Dharma. This further has two aspects: first, regarding the deportment itself, one must receive the food with palms joined;
second, it must be in plain view, meaning it should not be poorly concealed, as what is improperly hidden does not constitute [proper] practice. Third, one must use one's own hand.

[The food] must be held; it must not be sent by a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) nor placed on the ground. Fourth, it must be within hand-reach. Fifth, there must be a formal declaration (*ārocana*), saying: "I have already finished eating; Venerable One, look at this and know that I [have done so].

This constitutes the *khalupaṭiggahaṇa-vidhi* (the procedure for leftover food). If one speaks contrary to this, it is not accomplished. It must be performed in the presence of one who possesses the proper deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Second, the person addressed must possess six qualities: first, they must not be separated from their place while eating; third, they must not be separated from their range, meaning [the food] must be within the reach of one's own hand.

1. Seizing; 2. Not leaving the reach of the hand (meaning it must remain within the range of one’s outstretched hand); 3. Not leaving the verbal instruction (meaning one must say, "Stop! Take this food"); 4.
Returning it to its original owner (meaning it must not be taken away entirely). If these conditions are fully met, it is called the "completed remainder" (*pariśeṣa-dharma*).

If any one of these is mutually lacking, one either incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (or *pāyattika*), or merely loses the [merit] of the dharma, but does not incur the offense. Or, there is merely a loss of the dharma, and no [offense].

The fundamental transgressions can only be known through explanation. Thus, regarding the rules for "sufficient" (*pūrta*) and "having sufficient" (*pūrtavat*), there are the remaining twelve precepts concerning the ritual for leftover food (*vighasa-dharma*).
Why is the ritual for leftover food not permitted for the other [precepts]? Answer: These two precepts involve eating again with a greedy mind after one has already become "sufficient.

One must perform the ritual for leftovers (*atirikta-dharma*) to pacify that greedy disposition; this serves as the specific remedy (*pratipakṣa*). It is a case of the medicine corresponding to the illness. This...
There are two that allow for exceptions; the remaining twelve are as follows: praising the two types of food; accepting invitations while turning away from others or eating in a separate group;
taking more than three bowls of fine medicine; accepting invitations for food at improper times or leftover food kept overnight; drinking alcohol; and drinking water containing insects.

Regarding the first seven precepts—excluding the one concerning the three bowls—the remaining six have never been fully established [as having exceptions]; they are committed immediately upon transgression and do not serve as antidotes to those [faults], and therefore they are not included.

It must be permitted. The five cases such as "at an improper time" (*akāla*) and so forth have not yet reached completion; furthermore, these are faults such as being at an improper time, and their substance is impure.

If other rules were permitted, it would cause one to incur the aforementioned offense and bring calamity upon oneself; since there is no formal confrontation [of the fault], there is no taking [of the food].

Once three bowls have been carried out of the door, one commits an offense. Other rules do not serve as a remedy. Regarding the eight conditions for a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), illness is the reason for permission; if there were no other [conditions], it would likewise not be permitted.

Regarding eating apart from the community (*pṛthag-bhakta*), since it has never been established as sufficient for one’s needs, it is permitted through seven conditions so that the body may be sustained and one’s practice may progress.

If this were already sufficient previously, it would be capable of sustaining the body and nourishing the Path for a single day. However, if it were permitted under the same seven conditions and so forth, it would cause greed to increase further; therefore, it does not serve as an antidote.

Next is the second fault that arises. The text states: "Not knowing what constitutes sufficient food and what does not. This means they do not know which items are considered *pratyaya-bhojana* (proper food) that constitute sufficiency, and which are not *pratyaya-bhojana* and thus do not constitute sufficiency.

Furthermore, they do not know how many conditions must be fulfilled for the *kṛta-śeṣa-karma* (the ritual of making food "leftover") to be valid, nor how many conditions must be lacking for it to be invalid;
therefore, it is said they do not know what is "leftover" (*śeṣa*) and what is "not leftover" (*aśeṣa*).

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of three sections: first, the person; second, the explicit clarification of having completed the meal; and third, the violation incurred by failing to perform the *kṛta-kṛtya-vidhi* (the ritual for declaring the meal finished).
Regarding the second section, "having finished eating," this refers to eating either private food or food belonging to the Saṃgha, wherein the meal is considered complete at five points.

Alternatively, regarding "one who has accepted an invitation," this refers to eating the alms-food of a donor, wherein the meal is complete at five points according to the rules. Once these two types of completion have occurred—

In all cases, the *kṛtāvadāna* (the ritual of declaring what has been set aside) must be performed; if it is not done, one commits a *pāyattika*. This does not mean that the *kṛtāvadāna* is the only factor that permits one to accept an invitation without returning.

Below, in the section defining the characteristics, there are two parts: first, up to the *pāyattika*, a brief explanation of the three phrases of the precept’s basis regarding the characteristics of the offense;

second, from "The Venerable One was concerned for him... onwards, a detailed explanation of the three phrases of the precept’s basis regarding the characteristics of how the offense is established. In the following text, the monk knows...

When walking, is this not indeed the first [point] of non-understanding? Regarding the phrase "if a bhikṣu," the three [points] are explained extensively; the first phrase of the middle [section] on the brief [explanation] may be understood.

From the words "one who has eaten" (*bhuktavant*) onwards, the second phrase is explained. From "having finished eating and abandoned the deportment" (*bhuktavān vihāraṃ tyaktvā*) onwards, the third is explained.

Regarding the explanation of the second, it only explains "having finished eating," which is the same as explaining "accepting an invitation. Within the section on "having finished eating," the text...
Three points: First, explaining the character for "food" (*āhāra*). Second, from "among the five kinds of food" onwards, the explanation of the character for "completed" (*pūrṇa*) is finished.
Third, from "there are five kinds of sufficiency" onwards, the conditions that constitute sufficiency are distinguished. Regarding the "five foods," the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states:

when rice, millet, sorghum, wheat, and so forth are made into gruel, if at the moment they first emerge from the cauldron they cannot yet be formed into a mass, they are categorized as "rice"; if they coalesce by the following day, they are categorized as "gruel."

Dried [grains] are called "dry rice. If made from beans as dry flour (*cūrṇa*), they are not classified as "proper food" (*bhojana*); however, flour made from other grains such as millet is included among proper foods.
As for fish and meat, if they are intended to be made into porridge and appear in the form of mustard seeds, they are termed "proper food."

Because they serve as the basis for sustaining life, they differ from rice gruel; thus, it is not appropriate to record them [as such]. These five essentials are powerful and are called the "five types of formal food" (*pañca bhojanāni*).
Next, regarding the explanation of "having finished eating": among these five kinds of food, if one eats even one of them to the point of satiety, there are two kinds of satiety:

first, satiety of self-indulgence (*paryāpti*), meaning being fully satisfied according to one's desire; second, satiety of the objective field (*viṣaya-paryāpti*), which refers to when the food before one is sufficient to satisfy one's capacity.
"Satiation. Even if one eats but a single mouthful to fill the body for a day, once one has relinquished the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*), it is also called "being satiated.

Therefore, the textual passage regarding the general opening [of the rule] states that even if the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of leftover food) is not performed, if one does not rise [from the seat], there is no offense. Thus, we know that when the quantity of the object is large, this also constitutes "satiation.

Next, the conditions for satiation are explained as being fivefold. First, "knowing it is rice": this refers to knowing well that the five types of primary foods constitute the offense of satiation; it is not otherwise.

Regarding "not violating the limit when eating properly": there are two ways of understanding "as it is brought. First, one understands that which is brought; if it is much, it constitutes a full meal (*paryāpta*), whereas if it is little, it does not constitute a full meal.
Therefore, it is called "knowing what is brought. Alternatively, it means that at the time another brings it, one's own mind clearly recognizes it.

Regarding rice, forming the perception of it as rice is called "knowing its reception. As for "knowing the prohibitions," there are five types of formal meals (*bhojana*) prescribed by the Noble Teaching that must not be consumed at improper times:

(1) eating at the wrong time, and (2) eating to satiety. Therefore, "knowing the prohibitions" means knowing that eating while already seated is a significant obstacle to being able to eat to one's fill.

Because one eats little at midday and does not display [excessive greed], it is called "knowing the prohibitions" (*jñāna-pratikṣepa*). Among the eight prohibitions for the *pravāraṇā*, this single point may be understood as being equivalent to this;
the others need not be guarded against and are thus omitted without discussion. Fourth is "knowing the deportment" (*īryāpatha*), which refers to walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

Fifth is "knowing the relinquishing of deportment," which refers to ceasing from walking until reaching the state of standing, and so forth; hence it is called "relinquishing the deportment. It is also said:
"Completing" refers to possessing the five preceding conditions, which together constitute the causal conditions for completion; this subsequently precludes further [eating].

The third point, "the formal act of committing the offense," constitutes the causal conditions for the offense itself. Regarding the phrase "having finished eating": first, the two conditions of having finished eating and the perception that one has finished eating;
second, abandoning the formal deportment; third, not performing the remaining ritual acts; fourth, the offense incurred with every swallow of food; fifth, [the rule] applies from the point below...

Detailed Explanation. Because the brief characteristics are difficult to understand, there are two sections within this text. First, it clarifies the characteristics of committing an offense by eating a full meal at five locations.
Second, from "Having finished eating for oneself" onwards, it correctly explains the characteristics of whether a ritual procedure is valid or invalid, and its gravity or lightness.

The first section is further divided into two parts. From the beginning up to "is also thus," it correctly clarifies the five locations where a full meal is completed and one must relinquish the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Having already eaten the five kinds of *maṇḍala-bhojana* (solid foods), one commits an offense. Second, regarding the *yavāgū* (gruel) and so forth: after first eating the five kinds of solid foods and having finished at the five designated places, one then eats the *yavāgū*.
The preceding text further contains two parts: first, a detailed explanation of the characteristics concerning the deportment of movement;

second, a brief explanation of the remaining three [categories]. Within the first part, there is a question posed by Upāli. The reason for his questioning is that, within the aforementioned summary, it was stated only as follows:

One knows the deportment and one knows the relinquishing of deportment; however, because the characteristics [of these] have not yet been fully understood, one relies upon the practice of deportment to inquire about the completion of the meal.
Second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, there is a general response. There are five points regarding the completion of the meal.

What is meant by "point" (*sthāna*) refers to the aforementioned locations where rice and other foods constitute the completion of the meal; these are designated as "points. Third, the single phrase "What is it? serves as a repeated inquiry.
Fourth, Upāli extensively clarifies their characteristics; fifth, Upāli provides the concluding summary.

Within the fourth section on the extensive explanation, there are five parts corresponding to the five types of formal meals (*bhojana*). First, regarding rice as the primary meal, there are two statements. First, concerning eating rice:

once one has finished eating at the five permissible locations, if one abandons the formal posture (*īryāpatha*) and eats again, one commits an offense. This further explains the preceding three [meals]. As for the term "bhikṣu":

This person next explains the section on "knowing the time" (*kāla-vijñāna*). Below this, five points are established as the basis for the offense. This corresponds to the second case, "having finished eating.

Next, from the phrase "once the meal is finished," the text explains the formation of the offense by tying together the conditions for the transgression. Since this one sentence is thus explained, the remaining cases should be understood analogously.

Second, regarding eating mixed foods while remaining in a single sitting posture: the other four or five points establish the basis for the offense. Once the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*) has been relinquished, eating again constitutes an offense; this applies to each of the four subsequent cases of eating. Each of these is likewise explained.
This constitutes five pairs of ten phrases. The remaining three modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) likewise each have ten, totaling forty phrases, which serve to clarify the characteristics of offenses;
thus, the principle is complete. However, some commentators explain that taking rice as the primary example requires sixteen phrases:
one for eating rice alone, four phrases for mixing rice with each of the other four types of food individually, and another four phrases for mixing rice with two of the other four foods at a time.
There are six [categories]. Two pairs combined to form three; with four, they distinguish one harmonious [category]; below, with *khajjaka* (solid food), they form another one.

Altogether there are sixteen phrases. The remaining four are each likewise, totaling eighty. The other three modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) are also each eighty, totaling three hundred and twenty phrases.
While it may be possible to proceed in this manner, for now we shall follow the initial explanation. By means of the two types of *khajjaka*, the offense is manifested.
Among these, the ninth is *khādaniya* that has not been ground, such as flour and the like. The tenth is ground rice, barley, and so forth.

The reason these must be clearly defined is that if one eats these five types of *khādaniya* before having eaten [the other foods], they do not properly constitute a sufficient meal; therefore, eating them at will carries no offense.
If one has already eaten the five types of *maulabhakta* (solid foods) to satiety and, having abandoned that formal posture (*īryāpatha*), wishes to eat again, this also constitutes a transgression.

Because substances such as oil and honey are mixed with food to be consumed during the proper time (*kālabhojana*), one must perform the appropriate ritual procedure (*vidhi*). If one eats them alone, they are considered "medicine at improper times" (*vikālabhaiṣajya*), and thus there is no fault in consuming them accordingly.
The reason for knowing this is as follows: among the ten matters of the practice of giving (*dāna*), it is asked, "How are they mixed? and the answer is given: [as described above].

This means that once one has finished eating and abandoned the formal posture (*īryāpatha*), if one obtains ghee, honey, oil, fresh butter, or rock-salt mixed with curd in a single place, one may eat them without violating the *pātra* rule;
however, it is not permitted to speak at length. When asked, "Where was this prohibited? the answer is: "In Śrāvastī.

This prohibition is established within the context of not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food). Therefore, one should know that in this case, the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta-vidhi* must be performed, because it is a time of mixture.

If this were not a mixture, how could it be subject to the *pāyattika* rule? Yet some say that if these substances, such as oil or honey, are consecrated with the ritual of "mouth-usage" (*mukha-dharmatā*), they may be consumed for seven days;
if they are consumed without such a ritual, they may only be consumed during the proper time (*kāla-bhojana*).

Therefore, the claim that this text does not constitute a *thullaccaya* offense because it is not a mixture is incorrect. This is why it is treated identically to the case of mixing [substances] with one's finger. In this regard—
The second section on light and heavy offenses consists of two parts. First, up to the point concerning whether the ritual procedure for a *pācittiya* offense is established or not;

second, from "eating with the thought that one has eaten enough" onwards, regarding the gravity of the offense based on the perception of the object (*ālambana*) and the perception of the situation (*saṃjñā*). Within the former, there are eight phrases, which can be categorized into four pairs: the first two concern the contrast between the ignorant and the learned (*ajña*);

the next two concern respect and arrogance; the next two concern the laity and the ordained; and the final two concern the contrast between stinginess and greed. Whether an offense is established or not established can be determined solely by these.

There are two cases. In the sixth case, when one is with a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) and performs the *vighāsa-dharma* (the ritual for leftover food) in the presence of a *mahābhikṣu*, it is accomplished but incurs an offense;

because one did not face a layperson, a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) is incurred. In the remaining seven cases, it is not accomplished and incurs an offense; because the ritual was lost, it is merely a fault (*sthūlātyaya*).
Because it is not established, it is a *pāyattika*. Regarding the four permutations of the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) concerning the primary food (*bhojana*):

in the first permutation, where the mind and the object correspond, it is a *pāyattika* because of the gravity of the transgression. In the second permutation, at the time of beginning to eat, one actually has thick gruel but the mind harbors doubt;

during the meal, eating further constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), because the intention was slight. Therefore, there is no third permutation. [The same applies to] having eaten enough while perceiving that one has not eaten enough.

This is because, in one interpretation, there is no offense due to confusion of the mind. This is precisely what the subsequent explanatory text clarifies: "If one eats what is considered non-food, there is no violation. Furthermore, there may also be a shift in perception;

for example, as previously mentioned, if one initially perceives it as a formal meal (*bhojana*), but at the time of eating shifts the perception to that of non-food, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

It is not explicitly stated here because it is [already] implied. The third case is indeed real: thin gruel is not a formal meal, yet because it becomes thick after a period of time, it is treated as such.

Regarding the perception of it being a formal meal (*bhojana-saṃjñā*): if one further commits an offense regarding food while in the midst of eating, because the transgression arises from the mind, it constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Since it is not actually a formal meal, one does not commit a *pāyattika*. The fourth case concerns the doubt that it is something other than food; this is the distinction.

According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, for a *bhikṣuṇī* who has eaten her fill, committing an offense constitutes a minor transgression, which differs from that of a *bhikṣu*. The reason for this is that she is not permitted by the rule of "remaining food" (*atiritta-bhojana*).

Because this [offense] is light, this text is also light. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it states that for each mouthful of food not treated as "leftover food" (*atiriktapiṇḍapāta*), there is a *pāyattika*.

For the *bhikṣuṇīs* as well, one should observe the precepts in the same way; it also says, "The *bhikṣuṇīs* are also like this. Question: Since the *bhikṣuṇīs* commit the same offense, why is it only a *duṣkṛta*? Answer:
Because the combination and separation differ, it is established as a minor offense to manifest a distinct meaning. Regarding the non-offenses: eating what has been made into non-food.

Regarding the perception: if one perceives thick gruel as thin gruel while eating, one does not incur an offense if one does not accept more food and performs the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* (the ritual of leftover food).

This permits the aforementioned "sufficient food" (*paryāpta-bhojana*). There is no offense in the two cases of perception and doubt. As for non-food, if one does not perform the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā*, there is likewise no offense.
The two phrases "opening [the meal]" and "not being satisfied" refer to the perception of having had enough. Furthermore, one may perceive what is edible as inedible;

for example, when eating thick gruel in the morning, one might resolve upon the perception of thin gruel as it leaves the pot. Or, while eating, if one cannot endure the hunger because the previous portion was insufficient, it is said that one has not received [the food].
This clarifies that one does not eat at all. To perform the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) rite means to make [the food] into a remainder...

Regarding the phrase "because of the dharma; one who has not performed the *kṛtānna* (remaining-food) rite does not perform it for another": this refers to the previous case where thin gruel was eaten.
Taking it with one's own hand, one performs the *kṛtānna* rite, which permits the fifth [case]—the sentence concerning having a pure person (*pariśuddha*) carry the food.

If one places it on the ground to perform the *kṛtānna* rite, the word "not" (*a-*) is omitted. Conversely, regarding placing it on the ground: because two people suffering from wind-disease (*vāta-roga*) are not permitted to hold the food, placing it on the ground is authorized. To perform...

Regarding other dharmas: this refers to the opening of the preceding preparatory stage (*pūrvakṛta*). Because that [stage] is free from illness, it does not constitute the performance of other dharmas, up to and including the hand and the location.
In total, the five factors such as "not being separated from the object" (*aviyukta-viṣaya*) must be complete for success; conversely, the seven factors result in failure.
If one reverses the third [factor] previously mentioned—whereby one takes for oneself what was given by another—the eighth factor is reversed, resulting in the failure of taking everything away.
Within each individual opening, only the four [cases] that are the reverse are briefly mentioned; the other four phrases do not exist.
○ Regarding the thirty-sixth precept on "Exhorting [a monk] to eat more than enough," there are three intentions for its formulation:

first, the intention of not permitting exhortation; second, the intention of explaining the commonality of the offense; third, the intention of interpreting the combination and separation [of factors]. As for...

Regarding "not listening" and "encouraging another to be satisfied": one who has left the household life ought, by principle, to benefit others—welcoming them, guiding them, and encouraging the cultivation of all manner of wholesome deeds.
Now, to instead encourage another with an evil intent, causing them to incur guilt while bringing blame upon oneself, results in mutual harm for both self and others;

this is what reason deems improper, and it is for this reason that the rule was established. Next, regarding those who share the same intention of the offense: [it concerns] the question of the various precepts concerning food.

By means of this precept, one exhorts those who have committed the same offense. The answer is: it is precisely because this precept allows for the *kṛtānna* (leftover food) ritual that one might avoid committing an offense;

yet now, one neither avoids the offense nor performs the ritual. With an evil mind, one exhorts another, causing them to take pleasure in the act. Furthermore, out of a sense of intimacy, one conceals the matter; such conduct is identical to that [of the offender].
By failing to provide full protection, one causes the other to commit the offense; the internal deception is a grave transgression, which is why they are considered co-offenders.

In other cases where there is no opening condition (*an-āpatti-pratyaya*), people do not take pleasure in performing [the act], and for this reason it is considered light. For example, when a *bhikṣuṇī* lacks other [offenses] and merely encourages someone [to commit one], it is considered light;

this case is likewise. If that is so, then even when encouraging someone who does not accept [the teaching], there is still the factor of acceptance, and since there is an opening condition where people take pleasure in performing it, the encouragement should entail the same offense.
Why, then, is it considered light? The answer is: since the encouragement itself could potentially avoid the offense, it is therefore treated as the same offense.

It is not accepted because it violates the regulations and because it constitutes an opening [for transgression]. Since there is no case where one does not commit an offense, the exhortation is not considered a shared offense.

If that is so, would not the method of acceptance itself be a condition for an opening? Answer: If one accepts and does not refuse, there are cases where, despite the exhortation, one does not commit an offense. Because of the exhortation, the cases are rendered dissimilar.

If that is so, then regarding food and clothing obtained with a mind of leakage (defilement), there would likewise be no case of non-offense; why then are they considered offenses in the same way? Answer: That—

Regarding these words: one who slanders the Buddha will inevitably suffer the consequences of their assault. Therefore, this is consistent with the principle that those who commit the same offense share the same status;

such cases are numerous, and for the most part, they converge on a single meaning, rendering it unnecessary to resolve them through mutual comparison. Next, regarding the intent of combining and separating [the categories]: this is because the "sufficient" (paryāpta) and the "inciting to sufficiency" (anuprayoga) are identical.

There are four distinctions between these two [acts of eating to satiety and encouraging another to eat to satiety]: first, the difference in the motivating karma; that is, the act of eating to satiety arises from a mind of greed, whereas encouraging another to eat to satiety arises from a mind of anger.

Second, there is a difference in the nature of the karma: eating to satiety involves both verbal restraint and physical transgression, while encouraging another to eat to satiety involves verbal restraint and the performance of an action dependent on another’s body.

Third, there is a difference in the conditions for exemption: eating to satiety is permitted under the condition of illness, whereas encouraging another to eat to satiety is not. Fourth, the distinction regarding the food itself.

They are not different. [In one case,] there is an offense for eating when one has already finished a sufficient meal; [in the other,] there is an offense for urging another to eat until they have had enough while one does not eat oneself.

There is this distinct difference, so they cannot be combined. The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, the other person has already finished eating a sufficient meal; second, one knows that they have eaten; third, one urges them with an evil intention; fourth, one desires to combine [the food] with theirs; [fifth, the other person eats].

The offense consists of four points: (1) not performing the remaining formalities; (2) the offense regarding the food of the person before one; (3) the narrative of the origin (*nidāna*) in two parts: first, up to the phrase "eating it," which concerns the transgression arising from encouraging [the recipient] to eat until full;
second, from the phrase "having eaten the delicacies" onwards, which is the censure.

This fulfills the four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra: first, the person capable of inciting the offense; second, the knowledge [of the situation]; third, the understanding that the other’s consumption of the two kinds of food fulfills one’s own intention;
and fourth, the formal act of urging [the recipient] to fulfill [the meal] followed by the incurrence of the offense. "By this cause and condition" refers to these factors.

Regarding "the bond that can incite": it refers to the intention to cause another to commit an offense. "Not others" means it does not refer to non-offenses, nor to intentions such as making offerings.

In the subsequent commentary, there are two parts: first, the separate explanation of one and three; second, the combined explanation of two and four. First, the eight phrases concerning lightness and heaviness are presented.

In the first case, both the intention and the object are grave; both constitute a *pāyattika* offense. In the following seven cases, all are *dukkaṭa*, because the person [involved] does not commit an offense;

thus, they are light. Regarding the second section on the four permutations of perception concerning the object, the first is grave and the other three are light. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, there is no other rule [that would apply].

The meaning of exhorting others is rare; people accept it infrequently. Even if such cases were to exist, why would there be a need for a repeated prohibition? Therefore, an offense constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The lower section provides an opening while omitting the middle; this does not apply to the previous case concerning the sick person. All other phrases are the reverse of this.
The Thirty-Seventh Precept: Against Eating at Improper Times.
In general, eating without regard for the proper seasons leads to illness; therefore, it is necessary to impose limits and establish fixed rules.

Thus, from the dawn of the *yin* hour until midday, one acts in accordance with the Dharma; this period is designated as "the proper time" (*kāla*). To eat beyond this is improper. Long... [text fragment]
Greed obstructs the Path and invites worldly faults; such actions do not accord with the Dharma and extensively produce karmic burdens.
This is termed "inopportune," and for this reason it was prohibited. There are four meanings to this: first, from sunrise until midday, the time becomes increasingly intense.

This is called "the proper time. To eat when there is no transgression is permitted; from after midday until the final watch of the night, that period has ceased to exist, and is therefore called "improper time.
Second, from dawn until midday is the season for preparing food; begging at such times causes no distress, and this is called "the proper time.
From midday until the final watch of the night, laypeople engage in banquets and amusements; if one enters the village to beg for alms during these hours, it will cause much [disturbance].
It is called "untimely" because it causes provocation and distress. Third, from dawn until midday, laypeople are occupied with various affairs;
thus, sexual provocations do not arise, and begging does not give rise to slander. Therefore, this is called "timely. From midday onwards, affairs have ceased, yet sexual games and idle talk persist.
If one enters the village to beg for food at such a time, one may be subjected to defamation, suffering various insults and humiliations; therefore, this is called "untimely. Fourth, from dawn...

"Midday" refers to the time for begging food. Because this is done to sustain the body so that one may cultivate the Way, and because the activity accords with and conforms to the Dharma, it is called "the proper time.
After midday, one should appropriately cultivate the Way by sitting upright in meditation; it is no longer the occasion for traveling or begging for food, and is therefore called "the improper time.
Furthermore, according to the *Vīrarāja-sūtra*, there is the time for celestial food at dawn, the time for Dharma-food at midday, and [the time for] food after noon.

The time for consuming stored food and the time for the consumption of nocturnal spirits—these two types of food consumed by those who have left the household life are termed "timely" (*kāla*) according to the celestial law.

Once the sun has passed its meridian, it is no longer the time for these two aforementioned foods; this period is termed "untimely" (*akāla*). Therefore, it is called the precept against untimely eating.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this refers to the period from after midday until the end of the day.

There are four conditions for this separate offense: first, the improper time; second, the perception that it is not the proper time; third, eating at the proper time; and fourth, the occasion of eating.
Among those who violated the conditions for transformation, Upananda watched performances and music, ate at an improper time, and did not return until late evening.
Kālodāyin went on a nightly round of begging from households, terrifying the masters and thereby manifesting his transgression.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of four sections: first, the person; second, the improper time; third, food;

and fourth, the determination of the offense. These characteristics are fully explained. Regarding the first section, it is already understood. As for the general explanation and resolution of the texts of the following three sections, there are two parts:

first, explaining the three [sections] by contrast with the meal at the proper time; second, explaining the lower three [sections] by contrast with the three medicinal substances other than the improper time. This refers to: [The text continues with the specific analysis of each section.]
Based on the two types of formal acceptance (*paribhoga*), they are divided; thus, they may also be categorized as three: first, by way of time, one understands what is not the proper time (*akāla*);

second, by way of the loss of the two medicines through acceptance, one understands what is not the proper time; third, from the end of one’s life onwards, in the absence of the condition of illness, one understands what is not the proper time.
Because illness constitutes a [permissible] time, it may alternatively be fourfold; that is, with respect to the four types of medicine, there are four.

As for the text’s reference to the latter three, these three explanations all apply to "residual" (saṃsṛṣṭa) and "overnight" (paryuṣita) food, as well as to what is not formally accepted (apratigrāhita).

Regarding these three methods of textual analysis, while there is reason for confusion and divergence, for now we shall retain the second [explanation], dividing it into three parts as being superior. First, explaining the three in terms of "timely medicine" (kālabhojya): first, the explanation.

[This concerns] the improper time (*akāla*). First, having explained [the term] "time" in reverse, it is now explained in its proper sequence. Regarding the passage "The two meals," etc., this distinguishes the third meal; that is, the aforementioned five [meals].

Third, regarding the passage "If a bhikṣu," etc., this explains the formation of the offense. The second [point], concerning the loss of the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*), explains the three phrases:
that is, when the eight kinds of water have passed through the dawn (*aruṇodgama*), one loses the two acceptances, as they have exceeded the permitted time limit. Thus...

This is "improper time" (*akāla*). The same applies for seven days. Regarding the third category, medicines for life-long use (*yāvajjīvika*), they cannot be obtained because there is no lapse of time;

this is explained in terms of the loss of the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*). Simply put, it is called "improper time" because there is no [valid] occasion. Next, regarding the five propositions concerning the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*): according to the *Pañcavargika*, both the perception and the doubt constitute a *pāyattika*.

The text permits drinking the juice of parched barley when the husks have not been broken and the liquid has been strained. According to the *Pañcavargika*, if a sick person is unable to [reach the medicine in time], [it may be taken].
Having eaten, one feels empty and stifled in the stomach. One may be permitted to apply [food] to the body, yet it does not improve. Applying flour paste to the body likewise does not improve it.

Applying parched rice flour mixed with ghee also does not improve it. Washing with warm water does not improve it either. Sitting amidst such things as meat broth contained in a jar until dawn—none of these are permitted.
One must eat only at the proper time. If one sees food being brought out and swallows it again, there is no offense.
[Opening the section on] eating at improper times: swallowing mouthful by mouthful does not constitute an offense.
The 38th Precept: Regarding Food Stored Overnight.

Generally, food and drink are filthy and impure; to consume them frequently increases greed and prevents one from practicing moderation. Furthermore, as they are physically digested and exhausted, there is no further meaning [in hoarding them].
Because these are stored for later use, they ought to be kept in a separate place; it is logically impossible for them to remain overnight together.

Therefore, the Sage established a rule with three specific conditions: first, the food must be leftover from a previous night; second, one must know it is leftover; third, eating it constitutes an offense. What is eaten today is the remainder of yesterday;
having passed through the night, it is "overnight" (rātriśeṣa). The term "overnight" has five meanings. "Leftover" (śeṣa) refers to food that has already been accepted.

He kept it for an overnight stay. Regarding "storing overnight" (*uṣita*) according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: when a *mahābhikḥu* takes food in hand on one day and stores it until the next day. Within this, there are four permutations: 1.

It is both "leftover" (*vighasa*) and "stored overnight. This incurs one *pāyattika* offense; internally storing and improper contact (*duṣṭasparśa*) are two further faults. 2. It is "leftover" but not "stored overnight.
This means taking this remaining food and placing it outside the boundary so that it does not stay overnight; thus, there is no internal storage.

There are two other types of offenses. First, those that are not "leftovers" (*vighasa*) but involve staying overnight; these constitute only a *duṣkṛta* offense. Second, those that are neither "leftovers" nor involving staying overnight;

this refers to pure food which one knows to be leftover or food kept overnight, where the offense is incurred immediately without waiting for the night to pass—specifically, within a single day and night, which consists of thirty *muhūrtas*.

Thus, even if the food is set aside only after midday, the offense is incurred as soon as a *muhūrta* has passed. Therefore, it is said that one incurs the offense by eating food that has been set aside.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra consists of three phrases: first, the person; second, the overnight food; and third, the offense incurred by the formal act of eating.

To distinguish their characteristics, one first provides a general explanation of the initial phrase, followed by a combined interpretation of the latter two. This text also has three parts: first, explaining the formation of "leftover" (vighasa) through timely eating;
second, from the words "as for overnight food" (*paryuṣita-bhakta*) down to "and meat," explaining the second phrase; and finally, listing [the remaining points].

25. There should be a brief text on the *śayanāsana* (lodgings). Next, the determination of offenses (*āpatti*) is explained. Next, the two medicines [that] lose their status as received [medicines] are used to explain the remainder.

Third, regarding medicines for life, one only incurs an offense of lack of basis (*anālambana*). Regarding the four permutations of the perception of the lower object, the *Daśabhāṇaka-vibhaṅga* says:

"When traveling on a road and food is difficult to obtain, it is permitted to carry provisions oneself; giving them to another in exchange, it is permitted to eat them. Having washed the bowl clean according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, it is not permitted to use the hand [to eat]."
And regarding objects: when a bhikṣu wipes [his face] with his hand after eating, he should protect the cleanliness of that hand.

If he touches his head, grasps his three robes, or any miscellaneous items such as the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment), he must wash it again with water. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: if a śrāmaṇera holds an impure bowl and gives it to his teacher, the teacher informs the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Unless there is an urgent matter, one should not have him hold the bowl. If one has him hold it, one should receive it from him. *Gāthā*.
Treatise: If food remains in a broken bowl, one should place it in another vessel and wash it with extreme care three times before using it for food when it is no longer greasy.
This concludes the thirty-ninth precept on not eating food that has not been formally received.
As for why this was established, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states it was established for five reasons: first, to sever the causes and conditions for theft; second, to... [text continues]
5. For the sake of establishing proof: receiving food from a non-human may result in it being considered either properly received or improperly received; this would fail to establish proof.

This means that such an allowance was made for cases in desolate wildernesses where no humans are present. However, if among humans there are those who are non-human-like, ignorant, or small children, in all such cases the reception is not valid.
6. To stop slander. 7. To establish fewness of desires and contentment. 5. [End of section].
This is for the sake of inspiring faith and respect in others, and to ensure that non-Buddhists may obtain benefit.
There are four specific conditions: first, it must be food; second, one has not accepted it; third, one knows it has not been accepted; and fourth, eating it constitutes an offense.

This fulfills the five phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra: first, the person; second, the fact that [the food] was not formally received; third, the substance of the food; fourth, the exclusion of water and so forth;
fifth, the commission of the offense upon eating it.

In analyzing the characteristics, first there is a general explanation. The first phrase is self-evident. Regarding the second section, "those who do not accept," and so forth, the explanation of the following four phrases consists of three parts:

first, an explanation of the four phrases with respect to the *kālāhāra* (timely medicine); second, an individual explanation of the first two; and third, a combined interpretation of the latter two. Within the individual explanation:
First, regarding the two points on not formally accepting food: the first is the direct explanation of not accepting; the second, from "one who accepts" onwards, is the reverse explanation.
Second, the five methods of formal acceptance clarify the preceding [case of] not accepting. Regarding the general method for accepting food: one must lift the vessel and move it away from its place;

this constitutes the intention of formal acceptance, and if done otherwise, it is not accomplished. Placing it on the ground is permitted as an exception. Next, from "khajjaka" (solid food) onwards, the third point—the substance of the food—is explained in full detail.

Regarding the "five or three" types of food substances, the *Śīla* [text] states: if water is turbid, one must accept it; if its natural color is yellow, one may drink it without fault. Snow and hail are also accepted.

If there is no *pariṣkāra-puruṣa* (attendant), it is permitted to eat. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: if the water is salty and does not adhere [to the vessel], it is permitted to drink it without accepting it.

Next, from "if a bhikṣu... onwards, this explains the four or five phrases combined. Second, regarding the lower two, these concern the loss of the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) for the two medicines. Because...

[The Buddha] declared it not accepted. Third, "as long as life lasts" and below, this concludes the offense of being without a formal invitation (*an-ālambana*). Next are the four propositions regarding the perception of the object.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one may taste food prepared for others, but must not swallow it. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If a bhikṣu eats what has not been formally offered, placing it in his mouth—except for tasting food, chewing sticks, water, or rinsing the mouth—he commits a *pāyattika* offense."
The Fortieth Precept: Seeking Delicate Food.

Those who have left the household life should especially be pure and incorruptible. Now, to indulge in exquisite flavors and seek out fine food increases one’s own fetters of greed, disturbs the donors, and invites the reproach of the world; therefore, this rule must be established.
The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, it is fine food; second, it is requested from a householder who is not a relative; third, it is requested for one's own sake;
fourth, there is no valid reason; and fifth, upon eating it, one commits an offense.
This fulfills the four clauses of the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*: first, the production of the four kinds of fine foods; second, if a bhikṣu produces them for one who commits the offense;
third, such fine [foods] being obtained without illness; fourth, seeking them for oneself and thereby incurring the offense.
In the section on the analysis of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*), first the second [clause]—beginning with "one who commits the offense" and "one who eats"—is explained;
then the first clause—beginning with "the sick person"—is explained in reverse; and finally, the fourth clause—beginning with "if a bhikṣu"—is correctly interpreted.

As for why the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is a *duṣkṛta* (light offense): because the *bhikṣuṇī* is female and weak, seeking fine food is something women generally avoid; since such behavior is rare, the offense is minor.

This may be censured as a *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing), constituting a preliminary offense (*prayoga*). A senior monk (*sthavira*) possesses great physical strength and frequently solicits choice food;
because he repeatedly takes what benefits his own body, the offense is grave.
Precept 41: Giving Food to Non-Buddhists.

There are three kinds of faults in giving food to non-Buddhists: First, those of heterodox learning harbor resentment; they constantly maintain a sense of alienation and find it difficult to become intimate through reason.

Even if one bestows gifts upon them during the summer retreat, they do not appreciate the kindness and instead give rise to slander. Second, their false views deviate from the fundamental tenets; they are not true [to the Dharma].
Regarding the field of merit: if one now gives the food of a donor to a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), one harms that donor and fails to obtain the superior field [of merit];

instead, one gains only the karmic fruit of a contrary retribution. Thirdly, if one personally carries food and gives it to a non-Buddhist, there may arise the misconception or inversion of thinking that the non-Buddhist is superior and the bhikṣu is inferior. Because such faults are manifold, it was prohibited and not permitted.
The distinct conditions consist of six factors. First, the person is a renunciant non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), which excludes laypeople; this is because lay non-Buddhists commit only light offenses.

The reason for this is that since renunciants share the same name [as Buddhist monks], it is difficult to distinguish between the genuine and the false, and they may give rise to confusion; therefore, the offense is established as grave.

As for laypeople, their status as householders is distinct from that of the monastic community, and they do not cause such public confusion; thus, their offense is light. Second, knowing [the person to be a non-Buddhist].

Regarding those who have left home to become non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas): three types are excluded because they do not accord with the principles of kinship; however, those who are non-Buddhists but have parents are permitted [to receive robes] because their debt of gratitude is heavy.

Fourth, food is excluded: while the violation regarding clothing is a minor offense, the error regarding the taste of food is grave. This rule was established because it concerns the principle of providing what is appropriate.

First, because heavy robes are fundamentally attached to one’s own person and are difficult to relinquish due to such craving, they are considered light [in terms of the gravity of the offense]. Fifth, giving with one's own hand constitutes an offense; however, placing food on the ground and sending someone else to give it does not constitute an offense.

Since the flavor of food is common to all, there is no principle for eating alone; furthermore, as this does not give rise to delusion or inversion, the rule is relaxed so that one may do so without committing an offense.

Sixth, if the recipient accepts it, it is immediately an offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one should take one's own portion of food, form it into a single morsel, set it aside separately, and have [another] give it.
One must not take [food] for oneself. One should give food from the Sangha’s store to beggars, dogs, birds, and the like;

one should first assess one's own portion and then reduce it to give, never giving away what exceeds one's share. Within this context, the text clarifies the fault arising from giving food to a female non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
Next is the offense of giving food with one's own hands to a male non-Buddhist. The reason there is no formal reprimand is that there is no fault of the mind; thus, the reprimand is omitted.
This completes the four clauses of the fundamental precept: first, the person; second, the male and female non-Buddhists; third, giving food with one's own hand; and fourth, the resulting offense.

The details of the characteristics and the full explanation may be understood [from the Vinaya]. A nun also commits a *thullaccaya* offense; however, while the nature of the offense is the same, the conditions differ because it concerns a specific precept. The preparatory effort (*prayoga*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. 42.
The Precept concerning going to another's house before or after a meal when one has previously accepted an invitation.
It was established as a precept due to three faults: First, the secular village is full of many affairs, making it difficult to perform virtuous deeds;

if one exhausts oneself with household duties yet devotes oneself exclusively to auspicious assemblies, and having already accepted an invitation, goes to another's house, should the matter go awry, the resulting distress would not be slight.
