Second, since there is already a place where food is provided, one ought to cease worldly distractions to cultivate the Way; wandering about aimlessly without purpose hinders and abandons what one has practiced. Third, [the fault of] receiving [offerings] together with the assembly.
He intentionally turned his back and entered the village so that other donors would see that the Saṃgha had not assembled; consequently, he failed to provide food.
He detained the great assembly, preventing them from being fully satiated, thereby causing them profound distress. Because of this transgression, it was thus forbidden by the Sage.
The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, having previously accepted an invitation from another; second, not being under the authority of a donor;

third, going to the house of a layperson—this is because there is no offense in going to a monastery; fourth, lacking a valid reason, except in cases of illness or when there is a reason such as making robes or receiving robes;
fifth, entering the gate constitutes an offense immediately.

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of three parts. First, the brief summary of the preceding meal regulations. Second, the explanation of the subsequent rules (*anupaññatti*). Regarding these subsequent rules, there are two types.

The first restates the prohibitions and establishes further regulations; that is, it restates the prohibition against eating after the proper time. Next, there are four sections that restate the prohibitions and provide exceptions (*anujñā*).

The first is the exception for entrusting one's bowl (*patta-pariṇāmana*), which applies where there is already an invitation or where one may be summoned for other important matters; therefore, entrusting is permitted. Next...
The opening of the illness; next, the opening for making robes; next, the opening for the distribution of robes. These three complete five clauses of the *Śīlaskandha* (Precept Text):

first, it correctly clarifies that this bhikṣu has previously accepted an invitation from another; second, he goes to another's house before or after the meal; third, he does not inform [another monk];
fourth, except in cases where there is a permissible condition; fifth, the conclusion regarding the offense. The section beginning with "at other times" recites the fourth clause mentioned above.

The detailed explanation of the characteristics is complete; the first [point] may be understood. The section beginning with "As for those who have already eaten" explains the second. The section beginning with "other bhikṣus" explains the third, the entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇa*).

It must be entrusted within the boundary (*sīmā*) to those who have accepted the invitation together; there is the possibility that they might not see one another. Those who do not share the same meal-time [restriction] may receive it through mutual transmission.
The section beginning with "having informed the sick person" explains the fourth, the opening of the conditions (*anujñāta-pratyaya*): first, illness; second, performing...
Regarding robes: during the three-month period for robes, if it coincides with the time for receiving donated robes—namely, the one-month or five-month periods—it is permitted as an exception.

Apart from these times, regarding those who encourage others to give, this means that because it is a donation of robes outside of the prescribed season, it is permitted; this has already been explained in the context of the rule on eating in a group.

This constitutes a mutual exception, meaning it is inclusive of the previous requirement for formal entrustment (*anujñāpana*). If the donor has previously had the intention [to give], [it is likewise permitted].

Regarding the distribution of food and the offering of robes: if one has been invited, one may depart at will. However, if the donor originally had no intention [to invite], yet a bhikṣu who was already residing in that house encourages them to prepare food and offers robes as well—because such an act brings great benefit and merit—it is also permitted to depart. Therefore, it says "encouraging [the preparation of] food," and so forth.
If a bhikṣu does not understand this, the second part of the fifth section concerns the first loss of the boundary of the entrustment; within this, there is the returning to the center.
1. It is lost while going to another house. 2. It is lost while going to yet another house. 3. It is lost while going to places such as a storehouse; these being:

(a) a storehouse, (b) a village, and (c) a peripheral dwelling. A "peripheral dwelling" refers to the edge of the boundary where nuns who have strayed to a distance reside. 4. It is lost while going to a nunnery.
The fifth case concerns departing from one’s original lay residence; this refers to the period before midday when time is short.

For the sake of protecting the Saṃgha, if one proceeds directly to the place where the announcement was made and passes through other paths, the formal entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇā*) is not lost. This differs from the case of entering a village at an improper time, where the senior monks might cause disturbance.
Therefore, once the announcement has been made, even if one passes through other locations, the entrustment is not lost, because there is no fault according to the Vinaya text.
The same may be applied here as well. Regarding the second section, "If a bhikṣu... and so forth, it concerns the offense of sitting in many households.

"Sitting in many households" means that several families have gathered together for a single assembly; each household spreads out a seat in anticipation. Whichever house the Saṃgha happens to visit is considered the place of invitation.
Therefore, there is no offense.
○ The forty-third precept: Regarding sitting firmly in a householder’s home where valuables are present.

Generally, when laypeople hold wedding feasts, they do so at irregular times. To sit for a long time and refuse to leave may obstruct their deviant intentions and lead them to commit offenses. Thus, [the Buddha] established this rule.

To force oneself into an improper union is contrary to reason. Furthermore, for one who has left the household life, having departed from the place of defilement and passionate attachment, it is necessary to guard against transgressions.
To harbor such thoughts within one's heart and engage in conduct that is loathsome is why this rule was established.

There are four distinct conditions [for this offense]. First is the case of a household where food is being consumed. This excludes households that have renounced sexual desire, as well as those where both husband and wife have received the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts and do not commit an offense.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "Whether one has renounced sexual desire, or whether both have received the *upavāsa* and do not commit an offense—these two phrases apply to each other. If it is merely the case that they have not received [the precepts], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If a husband and wife have received the eight precepts, there is no offense. Second is a household where a husband and wife constantly reside together."
In a secluded place where there are three people but no fourth; and in a place where one cannot reach the door by stretching out the arms—sitting down constitutes an offense.

The *Prātimokṣa* has three phrases: first, a person; second, the householder has treasure; third, sitting down forcibly constitutes the offense. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, for every instance of rising and sitting, there is a corresponding *pāyattika* (offense).
The definitions of these characteristics are easy to understand.
○ The forty-fourth precept concerning sitting in a secluded place with a laywoman:
The intent of the regulation is the same as before; the only difference is that the offense is established by the absence of a third person.

First, there is a laywoman; second, a secluded place; third, the absence of a third person; fourth, sitting at a distance where one’s hand cannot reach the door. The precept text consists of four clauses, the first being: [as above].
[The offense occurs when there is] a person; second, a house containing valuables; third, a secluded place; fourth, the commission of the transgression.
○ The forty-fifth precept regarding sitting exposed with a secular woman:

the intent of its enactment is the same as before. It is completed as an offense through four conditions: first, it must be a secular woman; second, it must be an exposed place; third, there must be no third person present.

This refers to a place secluded from sight and hearing, yet it is not a heavy object; because it is an obstruction, it is called "exposed. Therefore, as with the preceding precept, the third person is permitted.
Fourth, if [the distance] is within arm’s reach, or if outside of arm’s reach, one commits a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). If the distance is more than one *vyāma* (fathom), there is no offense.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: if the distance is one *zhang*, one commits a *thullaccaya*; if five *chi*, one commits a *duṣkṛta*; at two *zhang*, there is no offense. Furthermore...

Regarding the origin (*nidāna*) within these precepts: the *Śīlaskandha* (the body of the precepts) refers to what is manifest (*prakāśa*), while the detailed commentary (*vyākhyā*) refers to what is concealed (*rahasya*).

This "concealed" truly refers to being secluded from sight and hearing; it is named in contrast to the "manifest. Thus, concealment and manifestation are established as a combined regulation. Furthermore, two cases are established for those without property (*niṣkiñcana*) and two cases are established for those with property (*sakiñcana*).

Moreover, among these three precepts, the first two concern the manifest and the concealed; although the third involves being seen or heard, because it is categorized alongside the two indeterminate offenses (*aniyata-dharma*), it is subsumed under the first precept. This is why.
The three precepts concern sitting in a secluded place.
The root text consists of four phrases: first, a man; second, a woman; third, an exposed place; and fourth, the definition of the offense. The characteristics are distinguished and fully explained.
The Forty-sixth Precept: Expelling Others from the Settlement.
Generally speaking, those who have left the household life ought to dwell in sincerity, loyalty, and faithfulness.

To first promise another food and then ultimately fail to give it, expelling them with an evil intent after the time limit has passed, thereby causing another to go a full day without food to sustain their body—this constitutes a state of extreme affliction.
This is grave; therefore, it is regulated by six conditions for the commission of the offense: first, being a *mahābhikṣu*; second, having previously given consent; third, not providing food;

fourth, being without a valid cause—meaning that there is no offense if there are difficulties such as formal censure (*ukkhepana*), expulsion (*pabbājana*), life-threatening danger, or obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*); fifth, expelling [the person] with a malicious mind;
and sixth, although one has seen or heard [of the act], or because the person has already departed.

The Prātimokṣa Sūtra contains three sections: first, the person; second, the speech and the remainder, up to "I shall give you food," which clearly indicates that one is about to enter a village and intends to give food to the other;
third, from "that bhikṣu [having finished... onwards, it concerns not giving him food, sending him away, and the resulting offense.
"By this cause and condition" refers to the cause and condition of causing vexation; "not otherwise" means that there is no offense in cases other than this.
The Conditions: As with the lack of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), the characteristics are explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga*.
The Forty-seventh Precept: Regarding the Acceptance of Medicinal Invitations for a Period of Four Months.
Now, when a devout lay devotee prepares excellent medicines and extends an invitation to the Saṃgha to receive this mental offering, if the intention to give...

There are limits. One should protect oneself by receiving only what is offered. To accept more than necessary from others' medicine causes greed and distress to arise, ruins what is wholesome, increases evil, and harms those who provide it;
therefore, the Sage has now established this regulation.
The separate conditions consist of six: first, an invitation for medicine; second, the limitation of the intention to give; third, the knowledge of the limitation of time;

fourth, receiving it after the time limit has passed; fifth, the absence of a valid cause or condition; and sixth, the offense incurred with every swallow of food. To first explain the initial condition regarding the invitation for medicine:

among the four types of medicine, if one receives more than three types, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in each case. According to the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, receiving solid food (*kavalikāra-āhāra*) beyond the permitted time also constitutes an offense.

[This constitutes] a *pāyattika* offense. [The duration is] seven days or for as long as one lives. Since this Vinaya text later states that one may take medicine as prescribed by a physician, we know that [taking it beyond the limit] is an offense.

Just as receiving more than one meal [as an offering] constitutes an upper-grade offense (*sthūlātyaya*), how much more so would receiving [medicine] beyond four months? How could one not commit a *pāyattika* offense?

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, after the four months have passed, if one requests substances such as ghee (or *susa*)—which are seven-day medicines—as well as black pepper, *pippalī*, ginger, salt, and so forth, which are for life-long use, [it is an offense].

One commits a *thullaccaya* offense. If one requests *vibhītaka* and the other two [of the three myrobalans], it is a *duṣkṛta*. Because non-timely medicine is of low value, because its therapeutic purpose is slight, and because the sense of "receiving beyond the limit" is rare, one incurs a minor offense.
Question: Within the context of the "one-meal" rule (*ekāsanika*), receiving butter or oil beyond the limit constitutes a light offense;

why, then, is this receiving of butter and oil considered heavy? Answer: That case refers to external use—applying them to the feet or lighting lamps. Since these are external uses, [the offense is lighter].
The meaning of "receiving more than permitted" is rare; therefore, that offense is light. This [present case] involves the meaning of "receiving more than permitted" within the context of giving;

therefore, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If a donor provides oil for four months, yet [the monk] requests *sugandha-taila* (fragrant oil), one knows that the offense for requesting medicine is light."
Receiving [medicine] beyond the limit is grave. Why is this so? It is because one understands that the donor initially gave medicine out of a virtuous heart for a period of four months.
Once the term has expired, the intention to provide offerings has ceased; yet, by receiving it beyond the limit, one causes distress and brings about deep ruin and corruption.

Furthermore, because one takes advantage of the previous act of offering and receives it excessively, receiving it beyond the limit is grave. If one asks for medicine, it is because the layperson had no prior intention to give.
Regarding the mind: since the intent to cause harm or distress is minimal, and because the donor initially had no such intention, the act is minor due to the petitioner’s hope.

This differs from the case of giving robes; for while robes serve as a broad basis of support, both the giving and the receiving beyond what was requested constitute a formal count, and thus the offense is equal to a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
As for the mention of the fault of "seeking medicine" within the causal context, this serves as the occasion for the prohibition against accepting medicine for more than four months.

The offense; other conditions may be inferred. This completes the six clauses of the root text of the precept: first, the person; second, the request for medicine for four months; third, the instruction on the limit for those who are not ill;

fourth, clarifying the acceptance after the four months have passed; fifth, excluding cases where there is no offense due to specific allowances; sixth, the formal commission of the offense upon accepting beyond that time.
In the section below that clarifies the characteristics [of the rules], it can be understood that the two [sections] are explained out of sequence.

From the passage beginning with "from the patient" onwards, the fifth [rule], which concerns the method of receiving [the medicine] for up to four months, is first explained. From the passage beginning with "the requester has four [types]" onwards, the third [rule] is instead explained.

From the passage beginning with "that bhikṣu" onwards, the fourth and sixth phrases are explained together: the offense incurred by receiving [the medicine] beyond the limit. This concludes the explanation of the fifth [rule].

The fifth section concerns the conditions for opening [the precept]. Regarding the phrase "may always invite": since there is no fixed limit as to whether the teacher may come at all times, this opening is without fault.

Regarding the phrase "throughout one's life": it is because of the lifelong commitment of these two individuals. The explanation of the third chapter has four parts. The first is the enumeration of the number.

The second section lists the names of the four invitations (*pravāraṇā*). The third section, beginning with "How so," provides a detailed explanation of the four invitations, each being introduced, interpreted, and concluded.

The fourth section, beginning with "Among these," distinguishes the four invitations; specifically, the first two invitations should be accepted for four months, while the second and fourth invitations...

One should accept offerings according to what is given, except for those cases where there is an exception. Regarding the inclusion of medicines, if there is a fixed limit, it refers to a specific invitation;
if there is no fixed limit, it refers to a lifelong invitation.
Chapter 48: On Viewing Military Arrays and Precautions.

In general, military formations are perilous and treacherous; when weapons clash and compete, actual defeat can occur in an instant. To view such spectacles for amusement merely provides the mind with fleeting distraction, inviting censure and damaging the Path.
The transgression is profound and the fault is extreme, as it directly contravenes the spirit of compassion. Therefore, viewing them is not permitted. (From the *Samantapāsādikā*, fascicle 3)

Regarding the meaning: first, it is for the sake of honoring the Buddha-dharma; second, for the sake of extinguishing slander; third, for the sake of extinguishing all evils and increasing wholesome dharmas;
fourth, regarding the conditions that constitute an offense: first, there is the military array; second, intentionally going to observe it;

third, the absence of a valid cause—meaning that if one has been invited, or if the military array is followed by urgent distress on land or water, there is no offense; fourth, the act of going to see it.
Thus he committed an offense. Regarding the "six armies" mentioned in the context: the Son of Heaven has six armies; the lords of the great states have three armies.
*Zheng* (征) means to go forth [on campaign]; *tao* (討) means to punish.
This fulfills the four sections of the *Śīla-sūtra*: first, the person; second, observing military arrays; third, excluding the conditions for exemption; and fourth, concluding the offense.

The following is omitted without further explanation. Regarding the section on excluding the conditions: the first phrase is self-evident. Second, explaining the seven groups (*saptaka*) of military vehicles, tents, and enclosures that are to be observed.

The term "military formation" (*vyūha*) refers to an arrayed line of troops facing an opponent; within this, there are two parts: first, an explanation of the formation itself, and second, an explanation of the army.
Regarding the army, there are two sections: first, the four armies are enumerated based on their original number, hence the reference to "one, two, and four armies.
Second, they are explained sequentially in four segments. Within the section on a single army, there are two parts: first, the presentation of one army, referring here to a single army. Only...
The power of the written word is greatest; four people following it constitute the strength of an elephant army.
Next weaker, eight people following it constitute a cavalry or chariot army. Next weaker still, sixteen people following it constitute a chariot army.
Thirty-two people, including those with musical instruments, constitute a foot soldier. Second, to explain its pure meaning: because it is unmixed, the two lower armies [are so designated].

Within these [categories], there are both pure and mixed [units]. However, the meaning of "pure" is not understood. To investigate the number of armies: in the first army, there are four pure [units];
in the second army, there are four pure [units]; the mixed [units] are six, totaling ten. In the third army, there are four pure and three mixed, totaling seven.
In the fourth army, there are four pure and one mixed, totaling five. Combining the divisions, there are twenty-six armies. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, the second [section] is explained.
The three fetters. Regarding the transgressions of light and heavy offenses, the expedient means for observing [the path] from one stage to another.
The forty-ninth precept: The rule against staying overnight with an army for more than three nights when there is a reason to do so.

The intent of the regulation is the same as before. An offense is established through five conditions: first, having a reason to stay overnight within an army; second, having already stayed for two [nights]; [and so forth].

[The first] three [factors]: (3) not being out of sight or hearing; (4) having no cause or condition—meaning that if one does not leave during the two periods of the day when life is at risk or during difficulties such as those involving a Brahmin, there is no offense;
(5) exceeding three nights until the appearance of the dawn light constitutes an offense. The three phrases of the precept text are as follows; the explanation below is clear.
Fifty: The Precept Regarding Staying Two Nights in an Army to Observe Battle Formations. This offense is no different from the preceding one.
Since there may be a valid reason, it is permitted to go into the army; however, one should remain seated and instead employ skillful means to observe from a distance.
Because the fault is identical to the first case, this rule was established.
Five conditions constitute an offense: first, arriving at the military camp and staying overnight; second, the army engaging in battle; third, intentionally going to observe;

fourth, lacking a valid reason—meaning that one has not been invited for some announcement, nor summoned by the two paths [of the army], nor is there any other such difficulty, as these would not constitute an offense; fifth, upon seeing them, the offense is incurred.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* contains five sections: first, the person; second, the circumstance of being previously among an army; third, the observation, which clarifies the act of observing;
fourth, the four objects of observation within the military array: (1) the army, (2) the battle formation, (3) the combat, and (4) the military force;
and fifth, the determination of the offense.
Broad Explanation. Among the five [categories], the second is not explained in detail here, as it is considered an exception to the preceding precept regarding staying overnight within an army.

The remaining four are fully explained. The first is self-evident. Regarding the second, "those who fight," the following explains what is observed in the fourth [category]. This section contains four parts; though slightly out of order, they are as follows:
first, an explanation of "fighting"; second, an explanation of "army"; third, a clarification of "force"; and fourth, an explanation of the formations and characteristics of the ranks.
That bhikṣu [is] below. [This concludes] the combined explanation of the three or five [sections on] the gravity of the offenses incurred by the precepts.
○ The Fifty-first Precept: Against Drinking Alcohol.

Alcohol is a poisonous water; to drink it brings about affliction. It causes one’s will and nature to become deranged and gives rise extensively to all manner of evils, obstructing spiritual cultivation.
Neglecting one's duties, it harms the Path and invites censure; as it is the root of all afflictions, how could it be permitted without restraint?

Therefore, the Sage established the rule: the specific conditions for an offense consist of three factors: first, alcohol; second, the absence of a serious illness; and third, drinking it. Within these conditions, there are two parts:
first, the arising of transgressions from drinking until full satiation; second, the case of *Sakṛdāgata*, who rose from his seat and descended, whereupon [the Buddha] became aware and rebuked him.

Reproach. The preceding text further divides into two parts. First, from the beginning up to "having circumambulated, he departed," which concerns the subduing of the dragon through supernatural power and the causal conditions for bestowing wine.

Second, from "The next day, when it was clear" onwards, which correctly clarifies the text concerning the Buddha’s reproach for the offense of drinking: (1) the reproach for losing the fundamental mind of awakening, hence the statement, "How much more so for a great dragon";
(2) from "He addressed Ānanda" onwards, the reproach regarding the many faults of alcohol; (3) from "He addressed Ānanda" onwards...
Those who are not restrained or rebuked by the assembly of disciples are like the venomous dragons of the world;

they harm only others and their impermanence causes only slight damage to body and life, and are thus called "small dragons. The afflictions of the three poisons can destroy the merit, virtuous wealth, Dharma-body, and wisdom-life of others;
as the most poisonous of poisons, they are called "great dragons. They cause ignorant people to become intoxicated by the wine of delusion, losing their clarity.

He understood the mind [of the dragon], yet he could not enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He was unable to exercise supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to subdue this small dragon, let alone exercise the knowledge (*jñāna*) to subdue that great dragon of the three poisons and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, because he was intoxicated by liquor, he could not even subdue the small dragon that was a toad. Thirdly, he was unable to subdue the small dragon that was a toad.

How much more so could he subdue the great dragon of the stone cave? According to this Vinaya, it is merely a *pāyattika* offense; the *Mahīśāsaka* school considers the various birds to be minor dragons.
The *Pañcavargika* states: "Previously you were able to subdue the evil dragon; can you now subdue a frog? He replied, "I cannot. The *Daśabhāṇavāra* has five sections;
the first three constitute offenses that damage the faculties (*indriya*), while the subsequent four constitute offenses where anger increases and retribution is deficient, thereby causing neglect.

Regarding the precept on fermented liquors: first, one currently incurs a foul reputation; second, one is deluded regarding the principle and manifests a lack of understanding; third, one incurs a grave retribution for the transgression.
The three phrases of the root text are: first, the person; second, the liquor to be drunk; and third, the drinking itself which constitutes the offense.
In the detailed explanation, the first phrase is self-evident. Regarding the section beginning with "As for *madya* (alcohol)," this explains the second [category], alcohol.

This section contains two parts: first, the listing of the five types of alcohol, which may be understood from the text; second, the specific discussion of wooden alcohol (*kāṣṭhamadya*), which begins with "As for wooden alcohol.
This part consists of two sub-sections: the first, from the beginning up to "one should not drink," establishes that because it is alcohol, its consumption is prohibited by precept.
Regarding "drinking": the second section, beginning from "that which is not wine, yet has the color, fragrance, and taste of wine," explains that it should be drunk because it is not [actual] wine.
The preceding text has three parts: first, the listing of wooden wines, of which there are six varieties;

second, from "wine made from pear juice" onwards, the methods for various fermentations, which explain the meaning of how the aforementioned six types constitute wine; third, from "mixed wine" onwards, four lines [of verse]. Because...
If there is no admixture of fermenting agents, its substance is not wine; or if it has undergone transformation for only a short duration, it is not subsumed under the category of wine.

Since it lacks the color and fragrance of what resembles wine, it should not be drunk. Regarding the second set of four propositions concerning what may be drunk: because these tree juices were originally not mixed with fermenting agents, their substance is not wine;
furthermore, as the time [of fermentation] is brief, they have not yet undergone transformation. Even if they possess color, aroma, and flavor, [they are not wine].
There is a similarity to the excess of liquor; however, since it is subsumed under "non-timely drinks" (*akālika-pāna*), it is stated that one may drink both.

This is because the juice of the tree possesses this quality of excess. Therefore, among the remaining four types, these are not liquor and lack such excess, so there is no need for further discrimination.

Third, from "that bhikṣu" onwards, the section explains the formation of the offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, each swallow constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This rule text is abbreviated.

It does not say "swallowing each mouthful. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding sweet wine, sour wine, and so forth made from wine dregs, drinking them constitutes a *pāyattika* for every swallow.

In this *vinaya*, consuming yeast is a *duṣkṛta*. "Duṣkṛta" refers to the perception of the object as being within the category of alcohol. For the three [types of wine] mentioned above, it is a definitive *pāyattika*; for the two below, it is a preliminary offense (*prayoga*).

Regarding the four types of wine listed below, one phrase corresponds to the first, the wood-wine; however, because there is ambiguity and confusion regarding the actual substance, [the rule is applied differently].

This constitutes the fifth [section]. It is divided into five parts. If those who were previously accustomed to drinking alcohol do not obtain it, they will lose consciousness and be on the verge of death;

their food and drink will not be digested. Even if they merely smell the contents of a wine vessel and do not recover, one should place wine within cakes or porridge and have them eat it; if they still do not recover, [further measures must be taken].
Give them wine to drink and gradually cause them to abstain from it.
○ The Fifty-second Precept on Sporting in Water:

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, this was established for four reasons. First, the Buddha-dharma is revered; it is only fitting that one should show it respect. To cause [monastics] to enter the water to play is contrary to this.
The damage [caused] is not slight. Second, one ought to maintain dignified decorum so as to foster faith and respect externally;
to enter the water for play violates such decorum and invites worldly reproach and fault. Third, one ought to cease worldly conditions and cultivate the Path;

entering the water for play obstructs and abandons one’s primary practice. Fourth, one ought to cultivate right mindfulness; entering the water for play causes the mind to lose its right mindfulness. For these reasons, [it is forbidden].
According to the noble prohibitions, an offense is established through three conditions: first, water; second, the absence of a valid cause or necessity;
and third, entering it to play, which constitutes an offense. The *Mahāmegha Sūtra* states that when the King saw them playing, he spoke a verse to his consort, saying:
"I have heard that these bhikṣus have long since abandoned the bonds of worldly dust; how can they act as teachers of men by sporting in the muddy waters? The bhikṣus were thus playing.
Having finished their play, they immediately entered meditative concentration and knew the king's mind. Thereupon, by means of their supernatural power, they departed in a single file like geese.

When the lady saw this, she spoke a verse to the king: "The bhikṣus of our house have long since been free from the bonds of dust; if even the śrāmaṇeras are thus, how much more so is the Teacher Śākyamuni!
Because of this, the king gave rise to faith.
The fifty-third precept concerning striking or tickling another bhikṣu:
Although this matter is minor, its transgression can be grave. Since people are prone to such behavior, it must be strictly prohibited; therefore, this rule was established.
Five conditions constitute an offense: first, it must be a *bhikṣu*; second, one must have the intention to cause disturbance; third, it must involve the ten fingers of the hands and feet;

fourth, there must be no valid reason—since if one touches them while giving medicine or clothing, or if one touches them by mistake while seeing someone coming or going, there is no offense; fifth, the moment contact occurs, the offense is committed.
The Fifty-Fourth Precept: Refusing Counsel.
Generally, those who have left the household life ought to take the abandonment of evil as their fundamental principle.

Yet, when one’s own deluded mind is about to commit a transgression and another offers reasoned counsel, if one does not comply and instead persistently acts wrongly, thereby causing harm and loss, it is for this reason that the Sage established this regulation.
There are five conditions for this separate offense: first, one has committed an unrighteous act oneself; second, another person offers a formal admonition in accordance with the Dharma;

third, one recognizes that the act was one's own doing and that it was not the other person who initiated the admonition; fourth, one does not accept the admonition; and fifth, one proceeds to commit the root offense. To fail to comply with the words [of the admonisher] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of three parts: first, the person; second, not accepting admonition;

and third, the formal determination of the offense (*pārājika*). The details of these characteristics are explained below for the sake of thorough understanding. However, it is because one acts contrary to the admonisher out of a lack of awareness that the violation of the heart is grave;

therefore, this constitutes a *thullaccaya* (heavy offense). If, however, one claims that what was done was by the previous admonisher and thus it was not an intentional transgression, the fault is slight; therefore, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
[The term] *la* [refers to] the side of whatever action has been performed. Because one recognizes the matter, one acts with knowledge rather than ignorance;

thus, one incurs a root offense (*mūlāpatti*). This constitutes a violation of the admonition of a single person. Regarding the gravity of the offense incurred when not following the previous matter, it is distinguished solely by way of the mind:

because the mind is false, the offense is heavy; because the mind is true, it is light. In the text, first the auspiciousness of a true mind is established, followed by the *thullaccaya* for a false mind. Question: What constitutes a violation?
Regarding the admonition by the Saṃgha: in the case of the former, one commits the offense immediately upon the conclusion of the admonition, without waiting for the act to be carried out.

Why is it that in this [latter] case, one does not commit the offense until the conclusion of the admonition, but rather commits the offense of "defying the admonition" only after waiting for the act to be performed? The explanation states: during the Saṃgha’s admonition, there are certain commands of the Saṃgha or communal rules (*sāṃghika-dharma*) that may be transgressed;
because the gravity of the emotional transgression is so great, one commits the offense immediately upon the conclusion of the admonition, without waiting for the act. In this case, however, since...

This is the case of a single individual. In the instance where one offers counsel but there is no communal decree (*saṃgha-ājñā*) that may be transgressed, the communal rule (*saṃghadharma*) can be violated;

therefore, although the counsel has been completed, no offense has yet been committed. It is only when one awaits the performance of the act that the meaning of "transgressing the counsel" is fulfilled. Because this is dissimilar [to other cases], if it were so, then in the case of the lower offense of "refusing instruction," which also involves a single individual, there would likewise be no communal decree to be transgressed.

Why, then, is an offense committed immediately upon the completion of the counsel? How could this not be contradictory? To explain: [The commentary] says:... (The text continues with the resolution of the contradiction.)

That person who has committed an offense is being admonished to cease it. Previously, they did not train; this person who has committed an offense speaks to reject the admonition, saying, "I have already ceased training.

This constitutes a *thitāpatti* (an offense of persistence), because by expressing such opposition, the offense is established. This is an offense of action (*kiccāpatti*). Although they speak of rejecting the admonition and say, "I am the one who acts," they have not yet actually performed the act;
thus, while there is still no formal expression of opposition (*viññatti*), the meaning of opposing the admonition is nonetheless fulfilled through the intent to persist in the matter. It is also...
This is not of one kind; there is yet another meaning, as will be explained below.
○ Chapter Fifty-five: On Fear and Dread.
All who have left the household life ought to protect themselves and not provoke or offend others, so that they may [avoid] mutual conflict regarding the six sense objects and other such matters.

To cause fear is to make another tremble with terror, thereby causing them to neglect their practice of the right dharma; because such affliction is extremely profound, it must be restrained and abandoned.
There are five distinct conditions: first, a great bhikṣu; second, the intention to terrify that person; third, the objects of the six sense-fields and so forth.

Each point is explained as follows: Fourth, the words must be clearly articulated; fifth, the person before one must see or hear them and thereby perceive them, at which point the offense is incurred.
This does not depend on whether the person feels fear or not, because fear is difficult to discern and because this matter pertains to the limits of vocal karma.

The text concerning the origin of the rule has two parts: first, up to the words "I am a ghost," where [the monk] inverted his robes and used color and sound to frighten the Buddha, thereby giving rise to a transgression. Second...
From "The World-Honored One [spoke] below" onwards, this clearly explains the reprimand. Since he was confronted by the Buddha and felt terror, his transgression was made manifest to all;

therefore, there is no separate mention of another person, nor is there any questioning of his own words. Previously, he wore his upper robe backward and assumed a malevolent expression—this is unwholesome bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
To say, "I am a śramaṇa, yet I am a ghost," is unwholesome verbal action (*vākkarman*). It is not merely these two types of action; his evil mind (*citta*) is likewise unwholesome.
"Excellent. Because [the fault] resides in body and speech, it is said that the mind is likewise evil; this precisely demonstrates that all three karmas are equally transgressions.

Śakra constantly believed that the Saṃgha was purely virtuous, yet suddenly encountering such a transformation, he was therefore struck with astonishment. Such individuals also exist within the assembly."

"Is this person such? The Buddha said, "This person is one who receives retribution in the present life. Because their realization accords with the Way and they are free from attachment, it is said that in this very life they have attained the pure Dharma.
Śakra praised the Buddha, saying: "Their inner mind is pure; they are detached from the eight worldly dharmas. When encountering gain, fame, praise, or pleasure, they do not take joy in them;
when encountering loss, defamation, blame, or suffering, they do not become distressed by them. They do not allow these eight things to cause them to deviate from their careful vigilance."
Because he was thus transformed, it is said that he remained unmoved by praise or blame, and so forth. When the Buddha spoke these verses, it was in response to the original intention of Śakra;
others had constantly claimed that the Buddha experienced fear, and for this reason, the Buddha subsequently assembled the Saṃgha to reprimand and regulate them.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of three sections: first, the person; second, the fear;

and third, the formal conclusion of the offense (*āpatti*). Regarding the analysis of their characteristics: the first section is self-evident. From the words "If by means of form... and below, the second and third sections are explained together; this passage has three parts:

first, the enumeration of the six sense objects as topical headings; second, from the words "How [does one... and below, the method by which each individual instance constitutes a fearful offense; third, the comparison.

Below the section on "Hills" (Kū), regarding the demarcation of the gravity of offenses and the method for instilling fear: one must first inform [the offender] with words, and only thereafter employ the six matters such as physical appearance and so forth.

If any one of these is not done, it constitutes an offense. By citing the preceding words, the characteristics of the offense are explained; thus it says: "If one speaks and makes it clear, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
There are three parts to the text concerning non-offenses: first, citing the matter of color and sound; second, showing that there was no lack of intent; third, the demonstration.

Therefore, there is no offense. Second, if one uses physical form as a pretext, this distinguishes and enumerates the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); since there is no intention to cause fear, there is no offense.
Third, if such a situation occurs, it is not merely a matter of citing the mental object (*dharma-viṣaya*); it is stated that there is no intention to cause fear.
The Fifty-sixth Precept: Bathing Beyond Half a Month.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are five benefits to bathing: first, it removes impurities; second, it purifies the body; third, it serves as a cleansing agent for the physical form; fourth, it makes the body radiant and lustrous;

and fifth, by causing one to become attached to the physical body, it leads to a lack of revulsion toward it, which directly contradicts the goal of renunciation. Therefore, [the rule was established].
One must establish a limit: wash once every half-month; if one exceeds this, it constitutes an offense.
This requires five conditions: (1) having previously bathed; (2) less than half a month having passed; (3) bathing again; (4) being without a valid reason;
and (5) pouring water over half the body constitutes an offense.

This fulfills the four clauses of the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*: first, the person; second, the clarification that one must wash once every half-month and may not exceed this; third, the exception for special circumstances;
and fourth, the conclusion regarding the offense.

Regarding the phrase "at other times," it refers back to the third clause recited above. This statement that "one may not exceed" does not mean that one is forbidden from washing more than once every half-month.
"Rinsing" refers to the fact that one must not rinse [the robes] during the half-month; therefore it says "one must not exceed [this period]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"One should follow the number of days until the full fifteen days are reached, at which point one may rinse them again. This is briefly explained in the section on defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The second [point], "at the time of the seasonal momentum," and so forth, explains the third [point]. There is no offense if there are extenuating circumstances. Because the seasons in India are early, [the period begins] from the first day of the third month.
Until the fifteenth day of the fifth month—during these two and a half months—one is permitted to wash without fault. Likewise, one may also use cooling agents during these two and a half months.
When this period of time is complete, it is sufficient; this is called the "hot season. Regarding the "time for work," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

This extends even to sweeping the interior floors of the monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma*). According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it is five chi; according to the *Mahā-saṃghika-vinaya*, it is five or six chi. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that this includes even sweeping the floors inside the buildings.
If a bhikṣu unties [the belt] at the lower part [of the waist], and if it exceeds the washing [limit], he incurs an offense.
○ Regarding the prohibition against lighting fires without necessity, rule fifty-seven:
Generally, the nature of fire is fiercely burning and its transformations are unstable; there is the possibility that it may cause damage or destruction, so it must be restrained.

Furthermore, when fire is lit for communal gatherings, it mostly serves worldly livelihoods and causes one to neglect the cultivation of the correct practice. For this reason, the Sage established this regulation.

There are four other points. First, regarding the absence of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*): one does not commit an offense by avoiding the causes and conditions [that would otherwise constitute one].

Even in the absence of causes and conditions, if one is in a concealed place, the sense of causing harm is slight, and thus it is also not an offense; therefore, the second point requires being in the open air. Third, regarding grass, wood, and the like:
since the sense of causing harm from producing charcoal is slight, one merely commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*); however, if one burns them, one commits an offense. In this context, only...

The regulation: There is no offense for lighting a fire when there is no purpose. It does not mention the offense of damaging the earth or harming the five types of living seeds; this is because those [regulations] have already been established above.
The precept text consists of three phrases: first, the person; second, clarifying that there is no cause or condition of illness—there is no offense if one has an illness; third, for oneself.
The offense of burning [a robe] has already been established.
○ The fifty-eighth precept: Regarding the concealment of another’s robes and bowl.

The reason this must be enacted is as follows: first, to restrain frivolous behavior and eliminate disturbances. Listing the causal circumstances: one who, out of vexation, conceals another’s robes and bowl and searches for them.

It is not the proper time. Now, he is filled with panic and his state of distress is no light matter. First, it may give rise to thoughts of theft; second, facing such peril, the situation is fraught with danger and is most terrifying;
third, even if one lacks the intent to steal, one may incur verbal slander from him, making it difficult to distinguish one's own innocence and impossible to extricate oneself.
Because of these various faults, it is in accordance with the holy regulations.
The separate conditions consist of four factors: first, being a *bhikṣu* who possesses robes, a bowl, and other such items; second, causing alarm or agitation to that person’s mind;

third, lacking a valid reason—either because the owner stores the items out of pride, for the sake of a formal admonition regarding the precepts, or because the items were borrowed from another; or fourth, on account of these very objects.
There are cases where one does not commit an offense regarding the two difficulties, etc., but commits an offense as soon as one takes and conceals [the items].
The root text of the precept has three phrases: first, the person; second, taking out the robes and bowl that were concealed; third, "if one conceals them oneself," and so forth.

This clearly explains the concealment by oneself or by another and establishes the offense. Since it is an offense even for such acts as intentionally harassing, taking [by force], or playing [with the items], how much more so for the purpose of intentional harassment? Therefore...
It is said: "Down to the case of joking. In the middle section of the *Xiàbiàn* (Lower Analysis), the second phrase is not explained in detail, while the other two are fully explained.
