The seventy-fourth precept: After the Sangha has collectively performed the *karmavācanā* and bestowed communal property upon an administrator, if one subsequently regrets it and slanders the Sangha for having distributed the goods according to favoritism, thereby provoking the community, giving rise to strife and competition, and causing mutual suffering. Explanation: The property of the Sangha is held in common; the sentiments of the multitude are not uniform.

Once the formal procedure of reconciliation has been completed and the administrator has been rewarded, if one should suddenly regret this and slander the Sangha, claiming they gave the items out of partiality, this will be verified as stirring up the collective sentiment. This gives rise to disputes and rivalry, leading to mutual affliction and distress.
One cannot dwell in peace and happiness while practicing the Way; therefore, this precept was established.

The specific conditions for its violation consist of four factors: first, it must be monastic property—meaning items acquired as offerings to the Saṃgha that are not permanent endowments of the Saṃgha.

Regarding such permanent endowments of the Saṃgha, including clothing, furs, silk, fields, lands, gardens, and groves, one must not bestow them upon administrative officers (*karmadāna*). If one were to give them...

[In such a case], one incurs an offense simultaneously with the act of receiving. Regarding "monastic property" in the *Qilu* (Sīla-vinaya): if items such as the *saṃghāṭī* robe are to be distributed among the assembly, all such things must be divided.

According to the *Shi-lü* (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya), there are four [offenses] regarding monastic property that should be divided: first, when the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed by two [people]; second, after the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* (steward) has been rewarded;
third, when one suddenly regrets [the distribution] and acts contrary to the assembly’s wishes out of favoritism; fourth, when the words are clearly articulated, one commits the offense.
As for those who do not offer admonition: since they have already acted together with the Saṃgha according to the prescribed ritual, if the Saṃgha has favoritism, they likewise have favoritism;
there is no further confusion here, so why should one provide admonition?
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* contains three phrases: first, the individual; second, performing the *karmavācanā* together with the administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*);

third, subsequently speaking as follows: "He slanders the Saṃgha according to his partiality. The text for the formal determination of the offense (*āpatti*) has three parts: first, following a personal friend; second, giving property belonging to the Saṃgha [to that person]; third, the determination of the offense.

In the section on the analysis of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*), the second phrase is omitted and not explained, while the other two are fully interpreted. Regarding offenses committed by the lower three assemblies:
when there is vocal chanting in agreement, one incurs an offense upon subsequent regret; there is no offense of "concordant formal act" (*sabhāga-karman*).
Precept 75: Departing Without Having Granted Consent Regarding Dharma-Compliant Sangha Affairs.

Sangha affairs conducted in accordance with the Dharma ought to be meticulously observed and followed, allowing for no discord or separation. Now, while the Sangha is performing formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), you have abruptly abandoned the assembly and departed.
Your mind is not in harmony, thereby obstructing the Sangha’s business; such disturbance to the community is no small matter. For this reason, the Sage established this precept.

The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, it must be a monastic matter (*saṃghakaraṇīya*) that is in accordance with the Dharma; this excludes matters that do not constitute an offense, as can be understood from the context.

Second, one must know that the matter is in accordance with the Dharma. Third, one must not have granted one’s consent (*chanda*). Fourth, one must depart abruptly. However, if it is for the purpose of answering the calls of nature, returning after a brief moment does not invalidate the monastic business and is without fault.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one goes for defecation or urination, provided one does not leave the range of sight or hearing, there is no offense. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one rises to answer the calls of nature..."
Minor offenses: not relinquishing the place where one has seen or heard [the formal act], it is not called "leaving the assembly.

Relinquishing the place where one has seen or heard and leaving the assembly—according to this text—if one is performing the formal act correctly and may not come or go, whether the act is finished or not yet finished, for one who temporarily comes and goes in the interim, it may be as stated above.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if five pairs of feet cross the threshold, one commits an offense; if one leaves while the formal act is being performed under a roof, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If it is in the open air...

Regarding the location: if one goes beyond the distance of one *xun* (fathom) from the assembly, it constitutes a *duo-duo-yi-ti* (sthūlātyaya). If one uses supernatural powers to go four *ti* (yojanas) away, it is a full offense according to the three clauses of the *Śīla-mūla*.
These are: first, the individual; second, the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha; and third, departing without having granted one’s consent (*chanda*).
Thus the offense is established.

This provides a detailed explanation of the characteristics. The first phrase is self-evident. The section beginning with "The Sangha" explains the second phrase. This has two parts: first, an explanation of the Sangha; second, an explanation of the matter, namely the eighteen dharmas.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, these are performed through three *karmavācanās*. If the formal procedure (*karma*) is not performed, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu... [The third phrase is explained below].
○ Precept Seventy-six: Having Given Consent and Then Regretting It.

Generally, in matters concerning the Saṃgha that accord with the Dharma, one ought to comply. Having first given consent, if one sees that the disciplinary action follows the same principle, yet acts out of partiality or private bias...

Out of such feelings, they immediately repent and turn back, claiming that [the act] was not accomplished; they join together to disparage the Dharma and disturb the assembly without regard for its gravity.

For this reason, it is thus regulated. The specific conditions consist of four factors: first, a formal *karmavācanā* performed according to the Dharma; second, the granting of consent (*chanda*) according to the Dharma; third, the immediate subsequent regret.
It is stated that [the act] is not accomplished. Regarding the four-word phrase, if it is clearly articulated, one commits an offense. The *Nidāna* (Explanatory Narrative) consists of two parts:

first, up to the point where it says "do not come with this person's *chanda*," which correctly clarifies the formal granting of *chanda* and states that the words of regret are not accomplished; second, from "When the bhikṣus heard this" onwards, it is the censure.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of three points: first, the individual; second, having formally granted consent (*chanda*) in accordance with the Dharma;

and third, repenting and then concluding the offense. The characteristics [of these] are fully explained in the commentary. The three lower assemblies (śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, and śikṣamāṇā) are not permitted to grant formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*). However, they may still repent after granting their consent.
Regarding other matters, if the community was harmonious and one later repents the offense, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The Seventy-Seventh Precept: Regarding Listening in Secret During the Four Kinds of Disputes.

Generally, when matters are discussed openly, the principles are made manifest; however, in private conversation, people tend to follow their own inclinations. Now, to walk stealthily and listen surreptitiously to another's words is a transgression.

To transmit [this] from one to another with the intent to cause strife and disorder—this transgression is not light. Therefore, the Sage established the rule that five conditions must be present for this offense:
first, the prior occurrence of one of the four types of disputes; second, the person’s assessment [of the situation]; third, the intention to incite strife and disorder in the other;
fourth, going to eavesdrop on the secret deliberations without being detected; and fifth, committing the offense upon hearing the words. Question: If one commits the offense upon hearing the words...
Question: For what reason is it said that if one listens to these words in secret and then reports them to another, it is a *pāyattika* offense? Answer:

This refers to the listener whose intention was originally to listen in secret with the intent to report those words to another for the purpose of inciting strife. One incurs the offense at the moment of listening; it does not depend upon actually reporting it to the other person.
If the offense were incurred only upon reporting it to the other, it would fall under the precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*) and would not be included here. Question.

Why is it that this precept is committed at the very moment one listens, whereas the previous precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*) is committed only after one has transmitted [the words] from one side to the other?

The explanation states: Regarding the former precept, there was previously no dispute; when one first listens, a dispute is not necessarily produced. It is only upon speaking that one commits the offense.
Regarding this precept, there was previously a matter of dispute. If one goes to listen, that dispute will inevitably arise; the transgression is profound and grave.
Therefore, one incurs an offense at the time of listening.

The root text of the precept consists of three points: first, the person; second, having previously engaged in mutual quarreling and dispute; third, having listened to this [dispute] and so forth, secretly eavesdropping, which constitutes the formal offense.
Discriminating the characteristics, one fully understands the three [preceding] points above.
○ Precept 78: Striking a Bhikṣu with an Angry Mind.

Generally, those who have left the household life ought by principle to abide in patience and be capable of enduring provocative conditions. Now, however, harboring internal anger and resentment, one...
Striking another person destroys one's own mental conduct; if one suddenly assails the object before them, the transgression and damage are not slight.

Therefore, it must be restrained. The specific conditions for this offense consist of four factors: first, the victim must be a *bhikṣu*; second, there must be a mind of anger; third, one must have the intention to strike them—meaning there is no offense if there are extenuating circumstances such as illness;
fourth, the offense is incurred the moment the blow lands.
The Seventy-ninth Precept: Striking Another Bhikṣu with the Hand.

Within the scope of the preceding precept, striking [another] was established as the point at which an offense is incurred. In this precept, which provides a deeper protection, the mere raising of the hand to strike is established as an offense, without waiting for the blow to land. This is subsumed under the preceding precept.
The Eightieth Precept: Slandering Without Basis.

Regarding the intent behind its formulation, the conditions for its transgression, and the number of factors involved, it is identical to the four grave offenses of slandering; it differs only in being classified as a lighter offense. The core text of the precept consists of five phrases.

First, the offender; second, the mind of anger; third, groundlessness; fourth, accusing another with a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*); and fifth, the formal conclusion of the offense.

In the following section on the analysis of characteristics, the second point will not be explained in detail, while the others will all be explained. Of these, the first two are explained separately, while the fourth and fifth are analyzed together.

It may also be explained in full. That is to say, the two, four, and five phrases are combined and explained extensively. Following the above, one should likewise fully apply this to the six states of mind to prevent clever rationalizations.
Furthermore, matters such as the weight of letters, messengers, or hand gestures are not discussed here because they are easily understood.

Also, regarding the fourfold assembly of those who slander, the text is likewise abbreviated. False accusations based on grounds that do not exist also constitute an offense; all such cases are treated briefly.
The 81st Precept on Entering the Royal Palace:

Generally, kings possess sovereign power and their passions are often excessive; they disregard propriety and lack restraint, allowing themselves to be intrusive and offensive. Such conduct causes mutual shame and is fundamentally inappropriate.
Furthermore, the palace ladies possess such radiant beauty that they agitate the hearts of men. It is not permissible to enter the royal palace [for improper purposes].
This gives rise to defiled attachment and ruins one's own mental conduct; the fault is no small matter. Therefore, the Sage established this rule:

it requires five specific conditions. First, the person must be a Kṣatriya king. Second, the king and his consort must be together in one place. Third, the king has not yet departed and the royal treasures have not yet been concealed.

Fourth, there must be no extenuating circumstances—meaning that if there is a formal petition, an invitation, or other such difficulties, there is no offense. Fifth, [the fifth condition is] the absence of these aforementioned exceptions.

Fifth, entering the palace gate constitutes an offense immediately; according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if both feet have crossed the threshold, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. For every further step taken deeper inside, there is a *sthūlātyaya* for each.

There are two parts to the narrative of the origin (*nidāna*): first, up to this point, there is no suffering [yet], which correctly clarifies that the offense arises from the act of rashly entering; second, regarding Kāla... [the text continues].

The following section provides an awakening and reprimand. The preceding text further divides into two parts. First, up until the phrase "there were no obstructions," it describes how the King and Queen, out of faith and reverence, permitted the bhikṣus to enter the palace;
this constitutes the causal origin (*nidāna*) for the sudden entry. Second, from "Kāliya" onwards, it describes the transgression of entering and then departing.
The preceding text [of this second part] has three sections. First, up until the phrase "the first queen, Mallikā," it describes her offering food to the Buddha and manifesting [her devotion].

First, since the two ladies had already received visible rewards, their sense of gratitude was profound; thus, they descended from the high tower to pay their respects and inquire after his well-being.
Second, having returned to the palace, they transformed those born there so that all gained faith, permitting the bhikṣus to enter and exit without hindrance.
Third, regarding the text for the second inquiry, there are three parts: first, repaying kindness and paying respect; then, the inquiry.
I. The fourfold doubt regarding the cause and effect of the Buddha; II. From "At that time, the Buddha having spoken" onwards, there is a detailed explanation to engender faith and understanding;
III. From "Thus, Mālikā" onwards, each point is summarized and shown; IV.

From "At that time, Mālikā again addressed [the Buddha]" onwards, it correctly clarifies how Mālikā received the teaching in her heart, made vows, entered the Way, and obtained benefits. Although Queen Mālikā was...

Regarding the second point: one may receive the five precepts for a third time in order to increase one's wholesome mind; it need not be received again beyond that, as it remains identical to what was originally received.

This is the explanation in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Shat-samukta-vinaya-śāstra*). Furthermore, as stated in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Citta-viśeṣa-śāstra*, the precepts are entirely received anew. These points have already been explained above.
The four phrases of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra are as follows: First, [the subject] is a person; second, he is a Kṣatriya king—excluding all other minor kings, who do not incur the offense;

third, "while the king has not yet emerged" [indicates that] it clearly explains the king being in the same place as a woman; fourth, "and having entered" and so forth, refers to the act of forcing one's way in, which constitutes the offense.

This provides a detailed analysis of the characteristics and a comprehensive explanation. The first phrase may be understood directly. From "the king of the kṣatriya caste" down to "the ābhīra caste," the second phrase is explained.
From "one who has not yet gone forth," the third phrase is interpreted. From "if a bhikṣu," the fourth phrase—concerning the gravity of the offense—is explained.
The Eighty-second Precept on Taking Lost Treasure:
Treasure is of great value and stirs deep greed in the human heart. Once it has fallen upon the ground, it is difficult to approach;

yet though one may pick it up with good intentions, desiring only to return it to its owner, one may incur false accusations from others. It is difficult to distinguish between purity and impurity, and one cannot extricate oneself from the situation. Furthermore, once...
To take these objects may give rise to a mind of theft; when facing perilous circumstances, such conduct is not of high integrity. The resulting damage is no small matter;
therefore, this rule was established. If the items were not left behind, to seize them constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, it must be a lost article; second, it must be a jewel or an ornament made of jewels; third, it must not be within a monastery or a place where one is temporarily lodging;

fourth, there must be no intent to steal, but rather the desire to return it to its owner—this excludes cases where there is an intent to steal, as one does not violate this precept in such instances;
fifth, the offense is incurred the moment one takes hold of it. This is why taking [items] within a monastery or from a temporary lodging is permitted.

Regarding the taking of lodging without offense: the explanation states that if one does not take it, there may be another person who carries it away, and thus one would still not escape censure and slander.
For this reason, taking it is permitted, provided one waits for the owner and consults with them before returning it; this is because of the fault of internal censure.
This satisfies the five phrases of the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya-sūtra*: first, the person; second, the lost treasure that was seized; third, the act of seizing it oneself (the agent of the seizure);
fourth, the exemption from offense in places such as monasteries (*ārāma*); and fifth, the determination of the offense. In the recitation of the fourth phrase—beginning with "If a bhikṣu...

and including the clause "excluding [places such as] monasteries"—the commentary on the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) briefly omits the explanation of the third phrase (the act) and the fifth phrase (the determination of the offense). The remaining three...

This is fully explained. The first two phrases may be understood as they stand. If a bhikṣu is in a saṃghārāma and clearly identifies two locations where [gold or other valuables] were seized, he shall wait for the owner to return.
If the owner does not come for a long time, it is simply said that no one has come to take the gold and so forth.

Upon reaching three years, it is permitted that within the portion belonging to the Three Jewels, the item may be used according to the distribution of that specific boundary. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this exceeds the five or six precepts.

Regarding the use for the Saṃgha of the four directions: according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if [an item] has not been taken for twelve years, the assembly of monks shall convene to appraise its value and designate it as property for the use of the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Should anyone later come to claim it, they shall be compensated from the monastic funds.
83. Entering a Village at an Improper Time:

Generally, for one who has left the household life to cultivate the Way, wandering about and dissipating the mind is contrary to principle. However, for the sake of sustaining one's life, it is necessary to go back and forth.

Since this is an improper time, there is no cause for entering; to do so would obstruct and ruin the cultivation of the Way, invite reproach and disgrace, and the resulting harm is not slight. Therefore, [it must be avoided].

The regulation: The separate conditions consist of five factors. First, it is not the proper time. Second, one is heading toward a village of laypeople. Third, there is no cause or condition such as having made a formal announcement or being summoned by others.
Fourth, one has not entrusted the matter to another. Fifth, upon entering the gate, one commits the offense. This applies even if there are no bhikṣus residing in that dwelling place.

It may be entrusted. There is a circumstance involving the Three Jewels; if one enters [a village] for this purpose, there is no offense. If one travels until nightfall and wishes to enter a village to stay overnight, according to the *Śāriputra-vinaya*, one should inform each other in succession;
there is no offense, and failing to announce it does not constitute a transgression. According to this Vinaya, it may be permissible to enter without announcement and remain free of offense.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if one passes through a village while traveling, or goes there to stay at dusk, or if the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) arise, there is no offense. Entering a village outside of the proper time is [otherwise considered an offense].
In this Vinaya, regarding what constitutes non-offense: passing through a village by way of a path does not constitute an offense. This completes the five phrases of the core precept (*śikṣāpada*):

first, a person; second, at an improper time; third, entering a village; fourth, failing to inform [another monk], which means not practicing the permitted method; and fifth, the formal determination of the offense. The characteristics are distinguished and fully explained.
The Eighty-fourth Precept on Exceeding the Allowable Size for Beds:
High beds foster arrogance and conceit; such is logically inappropriate. Matters must accord with the Dharma and not exceed prescribed limits. To exceed them fosters excessive greed.
This violates the sacred teachings; therefore, it is prohibited and shall not be heard.

The distinct conditions consist of five factors: first, it must be a bed; second, it must be made for oneself; third, it must exceed the prescribed dimensions; fourth, one must either make it oneself or cause another to make it.
The five acts constitute an immediate offense (*sadyaḥpācattika*). The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* contains three points: first, the person; second, the establishment of the limit of the rule;

and third, the determination of the offense once the cutting is finished. For a detailed explanation of the characteristics, see the full commentary. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, regarding the precept on high beds, it states that one should first cut and destroy [the bedding] and only then perform the confession (*deśanā*).
The Eighty-fifth Precept on Cotton and Linen Beds:
Because these beds harbor many minute insects, their use results in the destruction of living beings and violates the path of compassion; therefore, they are not permitted.
This offense is also established through five conditions: first, *tūla* cotton; second, a wooden bedstead; third, for one's own sake; fourth, making it oneself or instructing another to make it;

fifth, the completion of the act constitutes the offense. The core text of the precept consists of three phrases: first, the person; second, the wooden bedstead; third, the determination of the offense.

The characteristics [of these precepts] are explained in detail. Regarding the two aforementioned precepts, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, sitting upon [a seat] with another constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*.
The eighty-sixth precept, concerning the making of needle-cases from bone, ivory, or horn:
because these are small objects for which the labor expended is great, yet the benefit is slight, such toil is excessive and frequent, leading to the neglect and ruin of one's household affairs.
This leads to censure and fault; therefore, a sacred regulation (śāsana) is required.

The conditions for this precept are specifically fivefold: first, it must be made of ivory or horn; second, it must be made as a needle case; third, it must be for one's own use; fourth, one must either make it oneself or have another make it;

fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as it is completed. For nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), the rule generally applies equally; however, since they do not delight in wandering about, the purpose of making [the case] is the same, though there are differences in the details.
Committing a minor offense.
○ Precept 87: On the Oversized *niṣīdana* (Sitting Mat).

The four precepts from here on down all prohibit exceeding the prescribed measurements. As objects offered out of faith, they ought to accord with the Dharma; one should not merely seek to obtain them [at any cost].

It serves as a barrier to protect the body; once that purpose is fulfilled, it is sufficient. Now, to make it in excessive proportions increases one's own greed and covetousness, externally wastes the offerings of the faithful, and incurs useless expenditure.

It causes the pursuit of the Way to be neglected, and the resulting afflictions and entanglements are profound. For this reason, the Sage established the rule: [the size of] the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is as follows.
This rule is called the "Covering Cloth for Lying Down. It refers to covering and shielding the place where one sleeps in order to protect the bedding.

There are five specific conditions for its transgression: first, it must be used as a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat); second, it must be for one's own use; third, it must be made by oneself or caused to be made by another;

fourth, it must exceed the prescribed dimensions; and fifth, the offense is incurred upon its completion. The three subsequent precepts share these same conditions for transgression; they differ only in their physical substance.

The introductory narrative consists of two parts. First, up to the point where the offense of exceeding the prescribed measurements for the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) arises; second, the time when the various bhikṣus rebuked [the offenders].

The former section further divides into two: first, the prohibition against possessing a sitting mat that obstructs the body’s use [of the bedding]; second, the fact that from the group of six onwards, they exceeded the measurements even though the Noble Ones had permitted its manufacture.

This fulfills the three points of the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*: first, the person; second, the method for determining the measurements of width, breadth, length, and height; and third, the offense incurred by exceeding these limits.
A *buddha-vitasti* (a Buddha’s span) according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is two feet long; the longest of the medium lengths is five feet, and the medium width is four feet.

This is called "measured"; to exceed this is an offense. If one commits an offense even with five [fingers], how much more so when adding incantations? The measurement by the *cubit* (hasta) is the most important; the principle should indeed be thus.
However, because of Kātyāyana, each added a span (*vitasti*); the root text of the precepts separately increased it, leading to the existence of these various [versions].
Some claim that [the robe] must necessarily be continuous; this interpretation is not correct. ○ Precept 88:
The Rule on Garments for Covering Wounds Exceeding the Proper Measure. Precept 89: The Rule on Rain-Bathing Garments Exceeding the Proper Measure.
The meaning of these two precepts is identical; therefore, there is no need for further explanation. Question: Why are the two upper [sections] and the lower [section] presented here?

First: Why is it that while a bhikṣuṇī incurs only a light offense for making an over-sized rain-cloak, she incurs the same offense as a bhikṣu? The explanation states: Rain-cloaks are used externally;
because women have exposed bodies, they fear their unseemly forms will be revealed, and thus they tend to prefer making them wide and long. Therefore, they incur the same offense of *pāyattika*.
As for the remaining three precepts, they are to be worn on the body. Nuns prefer to make them small, as it is rare for them to exceed [the standard].
Regarding the ninety-first precept on exceeding the size of the three robes:

while the Buddha established the measurement limits for the aforementioned three precepts using his own *vitasti* (span), the reason this precept concerning the three robes exists is so that they may be worn on the body.
Regarding the question of why the measurements are not fixed, the explanation states: the other three precepts concerning robes are not the specific monastic attire for the path of a śramaṇa;

they may be used according to their size, whether large or small, and thus no fixed measurements are prescribed for them. These three robes, however, are the symbols of the monastic attire for the path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
If one were to rely on the Buddha’s own hand to determine the fixed limits of their dimensions, then regardless of whether a person is small or large in stature, [the robes would not fit].
It conforms to the body. Because his deportment was ugly and coarse, it was thus because he measured according to the size of his own body;

since his robes were not fixed in measure, he obtained the precept of being equal in size to the Buddha. As for the other three [robes], their measurements are fixed, and therefore there is no possibility of exceeding them. This is the origin of the rule.

It was necessary to restrict Nanda from wearing black robes. The explanation is as follows: Nanda’s physical form resembled that of the Buddha so closely that when the bhikṣus saw him, they took him for the Buddha;
both parties felt ashamed. Therefore, it was decreed that he wear black robes, distinct from the color of the Buddha’s robes.
Consequently, the color of the bhikṣus’ robes was made identical to that of the Buddha’s. When the group of six bhikṣus saw that the color of their own robes...

It is the same as for the Buddha; that is to say, the measurements should also be equal. Consequently, one might act in a way that exceeds what is equal to the Buddha; therefore, it is necessary to clarify this. Question:

Regarding the precept on robes exceeding the prescribed measure, why is it not the same for the alms bowl? Answer: If a robe exceeds the prescribed measure, it may be cut down and used. Because people delight in making things excessive, it was thus prohibited.
If a bowl were to exceed the prescribed measure, there would be no purpose in cutting it down, and people do not delight in excess; therefore, [the rule is different].

There is no need to establish a rule for this. Furthermore, the substance of the robe is the same as that of the Buddha; that is to say, its dimensions are also equal. Because [the monks] took pleasure in the fault of equality with him, this precept was established.
The substance of the bowl, however, differs from that of the Buddha; they did not take pleasure in the fault of equality with him, and therefore there is no need to establish a rule.

Question: Why is it that the robes and bowls of the Buddha are sometimes the same and sometimes different? Answer: All Buddhas of the past have used stone bowls. For this reason, the Tathāgata abandoned [using one] among humans.

The stone bowl: [He] took a celestial, fine-grained stone bowl and donned human clothing to manifest himself as a teacher of both humans and devas—a field of merit that is truly excellent and profound.
Because he wore human clothing, his physical form was identical to that of a bhikṣu; however, since his bowl was not a human bowl, it was made different.
As for the reason why a bhikṣu does not keep a stone bowl: a bhikṣu’s merit is shallow and cannot thus move material objects. Furthermore...
This is difficult to obtain; it is feared that it would hinder correct cultivation. Furthermore, because it is heavy to carry, stones found among humans are likewise not fit for use.
Therefore, the rule was established that one is not permitted to keep them; to keep them constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
● The Sevenfold Analysis of the Four *Pātideśanīya* Dharmas: 1.

Explaining the purpose of their introduction and the interpretation of their names. 2. Explaining the reasons for establishing four categories. 3. The characteristics of their sequential order. 4. Differences regarding violations of the regulations. 5.
The proper methods for maintaining and transgressing the precepts. 6. Self-maintenance and superior progress. 7. Commonalities between the two divisions [of the Vinaya].
This is different.

Regarding the intent of the first section: although the preceding volume clarifies majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), if one avoids censure and suspicion, there would be no means to advance on the Path.
Therefore, the subsequent section clarifies avoiding conduct that incurs censure; this is the meaning of the title in the Western language.
*Pratideśanīya* (to be confessed): this is named "confessing toward another. Therefore, the text below says: "I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones.
This is called the *pratideśanā-dharma* (the method of confession). It may also be called the *nigarhaṇīya-dharma* (the method of reproach), because the text states:
"I have committed a reproachable dharma, which ought not to have been done."
Regarding the second category: whenever one incurs reproach or fault, it is based on two types of retinues: first, the internal retinue; second, the external retinue.
Within the internal retinue, there are two [subdivisions]: namely, in private seclusion and in the midst of a crowd. Regarding the first precept, the offense arises in private seclusion.

While the bhikṣu and the bhikṣuṇī share the same black robes, they are distinguished by gender. To manifest this in a village, [the rule concerns] taking food with one's own hand. It is permissible...
It gives rise to defilement and impurity, inviting censure and damaging the Path. To eliminate these faults, the first precept was established.

If one shows partiality in assigning tasks within the community, acting with private favoritism, and accepts it in silence without rebuking it—thus failing to manifest the fault before the assembly—the second precept was established to dispel this transgression.
Furthermore, regarding external relatives, faults and censure arise in two locations: the village and the forest hermitage (araṇya). This refers to training...

Regarding the third [precept]: to accept food from a household excessively causes others to exhaust their resources and invites public reproach; to avoid this fault, the third was established. Regarding the fourth:

for those dwelling in an araṇya (wilderness), to remain seated indolently while receiving food may lead to harassment by thieves, and to cause the women who deliver the food to incur no small amount of reproach;
to avoid these faults, the fourth was established. From beginning to end, these distinctions provide these four benefits.

Regarding the third category: because those within the monastic community share close personal ties and stand in the relationship of teacher and disciple, they are prone to giving rise to such transgressions;

therefore, this is explained first. As for laypeople who constitute the external community, the likelihood of committing such offenses is rare; therefore, they are discussed later. Within the internal community, private and secluded settings are the most frequent context for such occurrences.

Among the assembly, such instances are rare; hence there is a distinction between earlier and later occurrences. In the external world, those in villages are prone to transgressions, whereas those in forest hermitages do so infrequently.
It is both appropriate and logical that this should be so.
Regarding the fourth section: among these four, the third concerns the offense incurred by violating the monastic regulations (*saṃgha-śikṣāpada*).
This *kula-karma* (formal act concerning a family) is indeed performed by the various bhikṣus following the Buddha’s teaching; however, the Buddha himself does not personally preside over it.
If the bhikṣus have not yet performed the *kula-karma* for that family, there is no monastic regulation to violate, and thus receiving food is without fault. This is because of the Saṃgha.

These are established and arise from formal regulations; therefore, it is said that violating the monastic regulations constitutes an offense. These regulations do not differ from the Buddha’s regulations, as they vary according to the individuals involved.
As for the remaining three precepts, they all violate the Buddha’s regulations, as there are no monastic regulations to be violated in their case.
Regarding the fifth section: among these four precepts, two pairs of precepts possess both aspects of observance and transgression. As for the "two observances":
if, upon seeing a nun point out food, one does not eat it because of the mind [of the nun], this constitutes the superior observance.

Furthermore, when witnessing such an occurrence, one should comply with the holy teaching and reprimand her according to the ritual procedure, saying: "Sister, please stop! When eating with the body, no fault is incurred. This is called performing the action.

These two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*) differ both in name and in essence. Regarding the two types of offenses: if one observes a transgression but does not reprove it, and then eats, one incurs an offense.

Because this arises from "refraining" (*sthāpana*), it is called an offense of refraining (*sthāpanāpatti*). Although one refrains from reproving, if the bodily action (*kāyakarman*) of eating does not occur, there is no such offense of refraining.

Furthermore, because it arises from the bodily action of eating, it is termed an offense of commission (*kriyāpatti*). In relation to the former, it is called "refraining"; in relation to the latter...
Regarding "performing" (kṛta): the substance of this offense is one, though its names differ. Furthermore, the two types of observance (*dhāraṇa*) are also one in substance but distinct in name.

For example, as in the ritual procedure of formal censure (*pravrājana*): it is called "observance by performance" because through that censure, although one eats, there is no transgression; conversely, the opposite of this constitutes an offense.

Is this not the practice of *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (observance)? The fourth [type of] forest-dweller (*araṇyaka*) practices restraint by not eating; this is called "restraint-observance" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
If one follows the holy teaching and says to the donor, "Do not send food," yet the donor, knowing [the intention], sends it anyway, there is no fault in eating it.
This is called "active observance" (*kriyā-śīla*). Regarding the two types of transgressions: if one does not inform the donor, it is called a "transgression of abstention" (*virati-āpatti*);
yet to accept and eat the food constitutes an "active transgression. As for the remaining two precepts, abstention constitutes observance, whereas activity constitutes a transgression.
The sixth gate: Of the preceding three precepts, one avoids censure within the stage of self-maintenance;
of the fourth single precept, one avoids censure within the stage of superior progress.

The Seventh Section: Similarities and Differences Between the Two Divisions. For nuns, it is always a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), as this is generally rare; these matters will be discussed according to the specific cases and explained within the text itself.
○ The First Precept: Receiving Food with One’s Own Hands from a Nun Who Is Not a Relative While in a Layperson’s House.

The great monks are the most venerable seniors, while the nuns are of the lower assembly. Out of a sincere heart of reverence for their superiors, they would give away all their food and drink as alms;

having done so, they would not consider the consequences, accepting [the offerings] as soon as they were received. This led to the nuns falling into hunger and exhaustion, causing them to neglect their cultivation of the Path.

Furthermore, if they were not related by blood, there was the potential for the arising of defilement and affliction, inviting public censure and disgrace. Such damage is no light matter; therefore, it was necessary to establish this regulation.
The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, being in a layperson’s house; second, it being a nun who is not a relative;
third, there being no valid cause—excluding the circumstance of illness; fourth, taking with one's own hand; and fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as the food is consumed.

The reason for excluding relatives is that, as explained above regarding sitting together or traveling in the same boat, their outward appearance is indistinguishable, and the resulting censure and harm are no different; therefore, [taking from] a relative also constitutes an offense. In this context, "layperson" refers to...

Within the household, matters are entrusted to one another; as they are truly close and beyond reproach, it is for this reason that [the rule] is relaxed. For a sick person suffering in affliction, it is not permissible to allow distress to arise;
therefore, for the sake of preserving life, it is likewise permitted without offense. Furthermore, by sending someone directly to the four quarters, the expression of respect remains uninterrupted.
He listens because there is no censure.
This completes the four phrases of the root precept (*śikṣāpada*): first, the person; second, clarifying that there is a nun who is not a relative within a village;

third, "if one is not ill" and below, correctly clarifying the act of taking food with one's own hand and eating it; fourth, "if a bhikṣu" and below, the formal establishment of the offense for violating the instruction. [The term] *yin* (hidden/obscured) [refers to the concealment of the fault].
Regarding its Sanskrit name, it is termed *jiezui* (binding the offense) in Chinese; thus, it is called the "Dharma of Repentance.

Its characteristics and full interpretation may be understood from the detailed exegesis. As for a nun receiving a minor offense: since she is of lower status than the senior monks (*bhikṣu*), if they were to personally hand her food, it would contradict the principle of giving to a nun;
therefore, her acceptance does not count as a formal act, and she incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The Second Precept on Assigning Food with Partiality in the House of a Layperson:

Generally, a multitude values purity and excellence, and cannot tolerate impure traces. Yet, this nun, out of partiality and favoritism, publicly assigns food among the assembly by bypassing the proper order;
this appears to constitute a reversal of private interests for public gain, a profound defilement. Since the great assembly has witnessed her transgression...
If one accepts [the food] in silence without rebuking [the donor], this indicates that the assembly’s mind is impure and that it harbors and conceals wicked people;
therefore, the rule was established that the entire assembly shall not eat. Question: Why are relatives and the sick not exempted from this? Answer:

Since the food is being distributed with partiality within the assembly, the resulting transgression is no different. Thus, both relatives and the sick are equally subject to censure. Now, because they accepted it in silence without rebuke, the matter is raised.
It was not disclosed because of the transgression of public sentiment.

The specific conditions require four factors: first, it must be in the house of a layperson; second, one must intentionally bypass the order of seating to receive food; third, the assembly must accept it in silence without protest;
and fourth, the offense is incurred immediately upon eating it.

The four clauses of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra: 1. A single person; 2. A white-robed female lay follower (*śrāmaṇerī*) who, being clearly aware, bypasses the order and points out food for distribution; 3.

The bhikṣus should speak to her, saying, "The Buddha has taught that bhikṣus must stop this by means of formal ritual action"; 4. If there is not even one bhikṣu [who does so], the offense is incurred without the formal act of censure.

The details of the characteristics and their full interpretation can be understood from the [relevant] treatises. As for a nun receiving a light offense: since the instruction given by a *bhikṣu* (monk) to a nun is equivalent in meaning, it does not count as a formal reception [of the precept].
Furthermore, it is difficult for those of lower status to reprimand those of higher status; since the transgression of intent is slight, the offense is therefore light.
The Third Precept on Receiving Food from a Family:
In general, when receiving offerings, one should exercise self-restraint and not exceed moderation.

Now, these members of a family who are disciples having realized the Truths do not spare even their own flesh for the sake of the Triple Gem; yet this bhikṣu fails to take account of the situation beforehand.
People have needs, yet they seek and take without moderation, exhausting the resources of others until those fall into distress despite their merit, thereby engendering external disbelief.

Furthermore, there are those who receive offerings who take excessively out of greed, lacking any heart of compassion. Therefore, the Sangha has established regulations to provide protection; should one knowingly and intentionally accept [such things], it is a transgression.
Such a matter is unreasonable; therefore, it was thus regulated. There are five distinct conditions [for this]:
first, both the husband and wife have attained the vision of the Truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*). Second, the Saṃgha has performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the rite of granting training) for them;

this excludes those who have not yet performed it. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if the husband and wife are of differing statuses—one being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the other an *ārya*—the *karman* may not be performed for them. If...

Regarding husbands and wives within the context of the three fruits [of the path]: whether they are both [qualified], or each is [qualified] individually, one may perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for them;
the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is likewise. Third, there are three causes that exempt one from offense: excluding cases of illness, invitations, and so forth.

Fourth, taking with one's own hand is prohibited except when placing it on the ground or having someone else give it, as this serves to manifest uninterrupted signs of respect. Fifth, eating it constitutes an offense at every swallow.

The introductory narrative consists of three parts: first, from the beginning up to the end of the section, it correctly clarifies the arising of the transgression; second, from "Those people living nearby...

onwards, it correctly distinguishes the reprimand; third, from "He addressed the bhikṣus... onwards, it shows his compassionate concern for the family under training and instructs the Saṃgha to establish regulations and strictly restrain the four quarters.
One must not accept food [from such a household]. This *karmavācanā* is a rule corresponding to the person, meaning it corresponds to the *bhikṣu*.

It is a regulation established by the Saṃgha of the four quarters; therefore, "requesting the lifting of the restriction for a family of declining wealth" means requesting the lifting of the Saṃgha’s regulation.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if that family's wealth and property are completely exhausted, the Saṃgha should grant them their gardens and fields so that they may fulfill their regular obligations, while using the remainder for their own support. If...
When there is no Saṃgha present but there is a special offering, one should have it prepared at that person's home so that they may receive the leftovers.
If there is still none, when one has obtained food through alms, one should eat at that person's home and give them what remains.

If this is not done, then having placed the father and son in a monastery for bhikṣus and the women in a nunnery for bhikṣuṇīs, and having provided them with rooms, dwellings, and bedding, only then may one distribute the robes and belongings; in all such cases, [the procedure must be followed].
Give it to him. However, this present Vinaya shall now establish the monastic regulations.

To fulfill the four lines of the core precept (*śīla-mūla*), first it clarifies that the Saṃgha performs the *karmavācanā* for a family under investigation; second, it identifies the monk who is the offender;
third, from "having done thus" onwards, it correctly clarifies the case of receiving food with one's own hands when there is no [allowable] reason; fourth, [it concerns] eating.
This bhikṣu’s offense is established by violating the instruction below.

In the section below that analyzes the characteristics [of the offense], first the second type of person who can commit the offense is explained, followed by the explanation of the first phrase regarding the objective conditions for committing the offense against a family of practitioners (*śaikṣakula*).

The remainder of the text is self-evident. A *bhikṣuṇī* belongs to the lower assembly; her feelings toward such [a household] are thin, and thus there will certainly be no distress involving the depletion [of their resources].
Therefore, it is for this reason that [the offense] is considered light. Regarding the request for release from begging from a family under training (*śaikṣa-kula*):

this text merely states that if the wealth and goods have increased again, one may request release from the monastic rule (*saṃgha-vidhi*), and the Buddha immediately permits such release. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if the wealth and goods of a family under training have decreased and do not increase, [one must remain bound by the restriction].

If, whether asked for or not, the wealth does not decrease—or if it increases—then in either case, whether asked for or not, one must relinquish the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act regarding a family under training).
If the wealth neither increases nor decreases, then it should be relinquished if asked for, but should not be relinquished if not asked for.

If the ritual procedure has been completed, none of the five groups of monastics may take [the food]. If the *karmavācanā* for relinquishing it has been completed, the five groups may take it as they please.
○ The Fourth Precept on Sitting to Receive Food in an Āraṇya:
Whenever one is in an *āraṇya*, one must be diligent in one's practice; only then may one sit at ease to receive food. Otherwise, it is not conducive to the advancement of the Path. Furthermore—

Furthermore, in remote and perilous places where there are many dangers from bandits, the coming and going for food delivery may lead to exhaustion, humiliation, and mental distress, inviting worldly censure and reproach.

Therefore, the Noble One established the rule in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: if food is given while an army is passing through, or if a thief comes and one personally offers and receives it, there is no offense.
If a person delivering food suddenly arrives at a monastery and the bhikṣus do not know [the situation], the Buddha said:
It is permitted for one person to receive [food] directly from [a donor] and set aside one portion for themselves, while giving the remainder to the Saṃgha.

Using one's own portion of food to exchange for food with someone within the Saṃgha does not constitute an offense. If food is being sent and a thief sees it and prevents its departure, one should give them a *kāṣāya* robe to wear.
If they still cannot depart, one should have their hair shaved, provide them with the Dharma robes, and send them away.
The separate conditions consist of five factors: first, it is a forest hermitage or a place of danger; second, one has not previously informed the donor;

third, there is no cause or condition such as illness or hardship; fourth, one eats with one's own hands—this does not constitute an offense if the food is placed on the ground and given by another; fifth, each swallow of the food constitutes an offense.
This fulfills the four phrases of the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*: first, the person; second, being in a secluded forest or a place of danger;

third, having not previously spoken [to the donor] and so forth, sitting down in a place of danger to receive and eat food; fourth, "should turn toward" and so forth, which concerns the offense incurred for violating the instruction.

Regarding the third sentence: "First, one does not inform the donor" means that if one has informed them, saying "do not come," yet they come and one accepts [the food], it is therefore said "first, one does not inform.

Although one did not first inform them, because one may accept food outside the monastery grounds (*ārāma*), it is said "one does not receive food outside the grounds"; yet here, one receives food within the grounds.
Although it is permissible to receive food within the grounds due to the circumstance of illness, it is stated "without illness. Placing [food] on the ground is likewise permitted.
Therefore it is said: "One eats food received with one's own hand. When explained in this way, the offense occurs only within the *ārāma* (monastery grounds);

receiving [food] outside the *ārāma*, on the road, or in a village, does not constitute an offense in any case. This interpretation seems to accord with the original text of the first precept. Furthermore, there is another explanation.
If there are difficult places on the roads outside the blue boundary, one must not receive [alms] there either; one may receive them only within a village without offense.
Therefore, the *Nidāna* (Origin Story) states that women should not go out onto the roads because of the fear of bandits.

If they have already left the city, one should tell them not to go to the monastery (*saṃghārāma*), as there is the fear of bandits along the way. Since offenses would be incurred at both locations, this is explained.

Regarding the textual passage: "If one has not previously informed the donor, or if one has informed the donor, 'Do not send food,' yet receives it both at the monastery and on the road, there is no offense in either case because there was no prior restriction.
However, if one receives it at both places, an offense is committed. Nevertheless, the text reverses this; one should study it but not practice it as written."
In the *Vinaya-saṃvara-vibhaṅga*, it is stated that when informing a donor (*dānapati*), one does not mention non-acceptance in two places;

rather, one mentions only non-acceptance outside the monastery grounds (*ārāma*) while omitting non-acceptance within the grounds. Therefore, it says: "First, one does not inform the donor," and so on, up to "not accepting food.

Next, regarding the actual offense of acceptance due to failing to inform, although there are offenses for acceptance in both places, it only mentions the offense of acceptance within the grounds while omitting the path.
Receiving this constitutes a *kiccha* (intermingled offense). Regarding the absence of illness and other such conditions, they may be understood from the remaining [rules].

If, among those established as "timely" conditions, one were to speak of an *araṇya* (wilderness) or a road with dangerous obstacles, their characteristics could be distinguished. However, for a *bhikṣuṇī*, there is no wilderness; even if one were hypothetically present, it would be considered light.
● The Seventh Section: The Rules of the Saṃvara-śikṣāpada-dharma.

This statement, "one should train [in them]," refers directly to the collection [of rules] without enumerating their specific number. The explanation states that the violations of the dignified conduct (īryāpatha) contained within this section are immeasurable;
because they cannot be encompassed by a fixed count, it simply says "the collection. If one considers what is being guarded against...

To clarify the meaning: it should be called the "Section on Various Duṣkṛtas. Here, what is being prohibited is concealed, and because one trains in conduct to receive [the designation], it is called "śikṣā" (training).
*Śikṣā* means training; *kāraṇī* means "should. This is established by analogy with the terminology used. As for this training, it is discussed as follows:
In reality, this applies to all four preceding categories. However, the reason it is specifically highlighted here is that the *vinaya* (dignified conduct) in this section is subtle and minute;
unless one studies it with exclusive devotion and maintains it with diligent care in the mind, its practice will be difficult to perfect. Therefore, it is designated as "Encouragement to Study.

Furthermore, if one can maintain it fully and without deficiency, the connection between study and practice will be manifest, and the significance of the merit of such study will be evident; thus, it alone receives the title of "Study."
Regarding the enumeration of their majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), the matters are indeed numerous. For now, we shall extract the essential hundred precepts;

those that are grave yet prone to negligence, or light yet easily transgressed, are compiled here for clarification. The remainder will be distinguished within the miscellaneous rules of deportment. Within these, there is a distinction between bodily and vocal actions.
There are twenty precepts that are committed through verbal action by employing another’s body, such as a person wielding a weapon while preaching the Dharma and so forth;
the others are committed through bodily action, their characteristics being readily discernible.
Next is the analysis of observance and transgression (*śīla-āpatti-vibhāga*). If distinguished according to what should be practiced, both types of observance and transgression are included:

namely, the arousal of the mind to engage in cultivation is called "observance through action" (*kriyā-samvara*); looking toward not performing such acts as dressing with high or low [edges] is "observance through restraint" (*virati-samvara*).

The absence of the intent to cultivate [virtue] is called "transgression through restraint," while performing such acts as dressing with high or low [edges] is called "transgression through action. If one says "action"...

Regarding the statement that "the Dharma can constitute the preceding category [of offenses] and is thus called 'possession' (dhāraṇa)," only the single precept concerning the staff and pouch allows for both possession and violation;

all others consist solely of non-possession as maintenance and action as violation. If one explains it according to the previous interpretation, then the four preceding categories of offenses should likewise all involve both types of maintenance and violation.

Why then is this restricted to this case alone? The answer is: in principle, it should indeed be so. However, not violating these [specific rules] is termed "training" (śikṣamāṇa); therefore, the others are not analogous.
This is explained as follows for now. The text is divided into four parts: first, fifty-one precepts concerning the conduct of revering the Sangha;
second, eight precepts below "one who does not respect others shall not preach the Dharma to them" concerning the conduct of revering the Dharma;
third, twenty-six precepts below "one shall not stay overnight in a Buddha-stūpa" concerning the conduct of revering the Buddha; fourth, [the section on] persons.
Having sat down, there are fifteen precepts for those who wish to show reverence while standing. These clarify the precepts for honoring the Triple Gem across the four modes of deportment.
First, regarding the honoring of the Saṃgha, this is because the Saṃgha is the sustainer of the Triple Gem. Thus, it is necessary to clarify the practice of honoring the Saṃgha;
for whether it be clothing and adornment, walking, sitting, advancing, or retreating, eating, drinking, or entering and exiting—all these pertain to the Saṃgha.

One's deportment should be orderly, dignified, and majestic; one's movements should accord with the rules, manifesting within oneself the mind of the Dharma and inspiring faith and respect in those who observe from without.
This fosters worldly goodness and brings glory to the Buddha-dharma, benefiting the Sangha. To act contrary to this is to ruin one’s own mental conduct.
Externally, they cultivate hatred toward others; regarding that Jewel of the Sangha, they harbor feelings of contempt and bring no small amount of disgrace upon it.

Therefore, it is necessary to restrain them. Reverence for the Sangha’s dignified deportment does not arise spontaneously; its accomplishment depends upon the Dharma. Thus, one must revere the Dharma.
The Dharma is the excellent medicine that cures birth and death, and the eye that unfolds the Path. If one reveres it and acts in accordance with it, one will transcend all burdens and attain purity.
Those who ascend to the other shore may do so; yet those who are arrogant and disparage others will sink forever into birth and death, long remaining submerged in the ocean of suffering.

The gravity of such calamity is profound; therefore, one must maintain reverence. The Dharma does not propagate itself; its proclamation depends upon the Master of the Way. Thus, it is necessary to revere the Buddha, for the Buddha is the honored guide.

Standing alone and transcending all burdens, his realization surpasses that of all sages. With myriads of virtues perfected and his great compassion manifesting transformation, he benefits all classes of beings;

his grace is profound and deep. One must therefore revere him to seek deliverance from the world. For this reason, regulations must be established for honoring stupas and sacred temples, ensuring they are kept pure and in peaceful locations, and that one performs rituals of devout reverence morning and night.
Since the preceding section has not yet exhausted the matter, it is further necessary to include miscellaneous matters.

Because it is improper, one violates the holy teaching; thus, not only does one commit a fundamental offense, but one also incurs the fault of losing proper decorum due to performing what is inappropriate.
This also involves the offense of *pratideśanīya* (confession). All violations of the precepts involve two types of offenses; it is not as in this section [where there is only one].

For example, it is improper to intentionally cut down a fine tree; by cutting it, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for destroying a living seed, and furthermore, it is a violation of decorum (*ābhisamācārikā*).

Just as speaking to someone while they are sitting above one’s own bed, lifting up bedding, or leaving the door, constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta* for violating decorum—one should understand all such cases in this manner. If not...
