they are applied thought, sustained thought, joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*), inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), equanimity, mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), bliss, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*).

This is because they are experienced separately according to their respective stages (*bhūmi*). That is to say, the aforementioned nine factors, when combined with these, result in eighteen factors within the nine dharmas.

In the middle [category], the four factors—vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), śraddhā (faith), and prajñā (wisdom)—are not divided; each is counted as one. The remaining five are divided, thus forming fourteen. There are four each for concentration (*samādhi*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
That is to say, the four dhyānas and the single mind constitute the category of concentration. In the first and second dhyānas there is joy (*prīti*); in the third dhyāna there is pleasure (*sukha*);

in the fourth dhyāna there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*). These together constitute the category of feeling. Thus, concentration and feeling together make eight. The remaining three [factors] are each...

The second [set] consists of six [factors]. That is to say, *praśrabdhi* (tranquility) is common to the first two dhyānas because it is the pleasure (*sukha*) of *praśrabdhi*. *Upekṣā* (equanimity) and *smṛti* (mindfulness) are common to the third and fourth [dhyānas].

By assigning these six to the eight [factors], there are fourteen. The remaining four are not subdivided. The first three [dhyānas] have five [factors] each, while the latter two are uniform with four each; thus, there are eighteen factors (*aṅga*).
If one relies on the *Tattva-śāstra* (Real Discourse), the pleasure of the first and second dhyānas is the pleasure of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*); their meanings are distinct, namely:

Applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) exist in the first dhyāna; internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) exists only in the second; tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are restricted to the third;

and the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*) exists only in the fourth. The limb of joy (*prīti*) is present in the first two; equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are common to the third and fourth;

and the limb of pleasure (*sukha*) pervades the three preceding mental states and other stages. For now, we shall follow the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* as previously stated. The text on the first dhyāna has three parts: first, the elimination [of hindrances] and the manifestation of the attainment of dhyāna; second, the practice...

Having finished the playful [preliminary] practices, one attains mastery through accomplishment. This is concluded by way of numerical sequence. Third, the section beginning with "For what reason" explains the cause for this attainment.
"Removing desire and love" refers to the five sensory desires: form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. "Evil and unwholesome" refers to the five hindrances:
greed, anger, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt. These desires and hindrances are obstacles to the first dhyāna; therefore, they must be abandoned. Next...

The attainment of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) through initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*) constitutes the antidote to practice; joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) constitute the benefit of practice.
One-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon which those two depend; that is to say, both the antidote and the benefit rely upon one-pointedness of mind.

As for the five factors (*pañca-aṅga*): coarse mental activity is called initial application, while subtle mental activity is called sustained investigation—meaning the gathering of the mind upon its object and the initial examination of phenomena.

Vitality (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*): Re-examining this dharma is called "observation" (*vipaśyanā*). Internal joy is termed "rapture" (*prīti*). The subsiding of [mental] agitation is termed "bliss" (*sukha*). Because it is concentrated and unchanging, it is called "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*).

Because vitality and observation are present, there is no "internal purity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*). Because rapture is present, there is no equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, or the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
The latter two passages may be understood accordingly. Regarding the three factors of the second *dhyāna*: first, attaining the *dhyāna* by removing obstacles. As for "removing obstacles":

That is to say, excluding applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Having attained internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), that which is obtained below it—namely, internal purity—is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Joy and bliss (*prītisukha*) are the benefit (*anuśaṃsa*). One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon which those two depend.

Applied and sustained thought disturb the second dhyāna; just as one sees nothing in clear water when it is disturbed by waves, because there is internal purity, applied and sustained thought are eliminated through their antidote.
The remainder is as previously explained; the following two passages may be understood accordingly. Regarding the three types of the third dhyāna: first, attaining dhyāna by removing hindrances.

As for the bodhisattva’s removal of joy (*prīti*): they perceive that joy has many faults because it is separated from the hindrances. It is like a poor person who, having obtained wealth, rejoices; yet once it is lost...
Because that anxiety is intense and profound, joy is eliminated. From the phrase "having experienced [this] with the body" (*kāyena*) onwards, the five factors (*pañca-aṅga*) are manifested.
"The body experiences bliss" first clarifies the benefit. Next, "noble wisdom is the protector" refers to equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*);

these three are the remedies (*pratipakṣa*). Mindfulness is the retrospective knowledge of the faults of joy; wisdom discriminates joy; and equanimity is the state of impartiality because it abandons joy. This is a brief summary.
There is no single mind; yet, that which can be delighted in is also the single mind. The following two passages are understandable. Regarding the three [aspects] of the fourth dhyāna:

first, attaining dhyāna by removing obstacles. Since the Bodhisattva has already abandoned pleasure, this refers to the fourth dhyāna because it is free from the pleasure of the third dhyāna. Suffering is contrasted with the second dhyāna.

In the second dhyāna, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is extinguished. As for the statement "previously, grief and joy have already been eliminated," this refers to the first three [dhyānas]:

in the first dhyāna, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is extinguished; in the third dhyāna, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is extinguished. Since these are stated together with the first dhyāna, it says "previously already eliminated.

Because the fourth dhyāna is severed from the four types of feeling (*vedanā*), one attains the two [subsequent] dhyānas. That which is neither painful nor pleasant is called "beneficial" (*upakāra*). "Guarded mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti*) refers to equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti*); this is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

"Purity" refers to single-mindedness (*ekacitta*). The remaining two passages can be understood accordingly. The first three [sections] each contain five [factors], because they correspond to the beginnings of the two types of distraction.
The second four [sections] each contain four [factors], because they correspond to the ends of the two types of distraction.

From here below is the third section: Severing Doubts or Attaining Buddhahood. When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all the gateways of his meritorious qualities were perfectly bright and penetratingly clear.

To briefly distinguish the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*): first, knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*); second, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); and third, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). That which illuminates the past is called knowledge of past lives.
Illuminating the good and evil of the future is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*). Illuminating present affairs is called the "knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).

When an affair has passed away, it is termed "past" (*atīta*); when it turns away from the present, it is termed "gone" (*gata*). Having once traversed days and nights, the past—both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—is known;

since life is the master of retribution, this is therefore simply called the "knowledge of past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), deriving its name from its object. When an affair is yet to come, it is termed "future" (*anāgata*).

That which necessarily moves toward the present is designated as "coming. To illuminate the future—its virtues and evils, its suffering and joy—is like the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); the name is established based on this analogy.

Alternatively, it may be named according to its retribution (*vipāka*), or named according to its faculty (*indriya*); thus it is called the "divine eye. Its characteristics manifest in the present, and by virtue of this, it is termed "present.

Abiding within these present characteristics, it is referred to as "being present. The afflictions of the five stages of dwelling silently defile the pure mind; this is what is called [the state of being stained].

The outflows (*āsrava*) are extinguished; the state where the outflows have perished is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). Thus it is named "the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*). As for the essence of its clarity, it is solely the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Because it illuminates everything within the realms of the three periods of time, it is called the "threefold clarity" (*traividyā*).

The first section clarifies the three meanings. First, the preceding [text] is cited to introduce what follows. Second, from "Realizing past lives" (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) onwards, the objects are presented to manifest the wisdom.
Third, from "Why is this? (*tat kasya hetoḥ*) onwards, the reasons for attaining it are explained. As for the bodhisattva who attains this meditative state of mind:

This refers to the four dhyānas. For those who have exhausted all fetters (*saṃyojana*), they have abandoned faulty conduct and achieved its fulfillment; because their minds follow [reality] without grasping, it is called "supple" (*mṛdu*). Regarding "abiding in a firm state":
this is because one is exempt from the three calamities and has severed the four types of sensation (*vedanā*).

As for the fourth dhyāna, it is because the Tathāgata frequently dwells therein. The second [point] cites the object to manifest the essence of wisdom; the third concerns the temporal period when bodhisattvas and those below them attain it.
This forms the Wisdom of Illumination (*jñānāloka*). Within the second [section], there are five parts: first, wisdom is manifested by summarizing it according to the number of births;

second, from "after the kalpa was formed" onwards, wisdom is manifested by reference to time; third, from "I have previously been born" onwards, it is revealed by means of specific retributions, namely, knowing eight kinds of matters and six kinds of common characteristics.
Regarding the eight matters mentioned in the *Bhūmivastu*, they are as follows: such a name, such a birth, such a...
Lineage; likewise food, likewise suffering and pleasure, likewise long life, likewise duration of stay, and likewise the limit of lifespan.
There are six types of commonalities: secular clan, name, caste such as Kṣatriya and so forth, physical appearance, parents, food and drink, and good or bad fortune regarding lifespan.
Among these, the two categories of lifespan and so forth should be combined; thus there are six and eight types. As for the six types, they consist of those of others and oneself.
The body speaks thus: "This is my name; I am a kṣatriya and so forth; these are my parents; I ate such food;
I performed such good and evil deeds; whether I was young, middle-aged, or old"—thus one knows the six commonalities of past lives.
In this present passage, only eight matters are cited: "I was once born in such-and-such a place," and so on, summarizing them all together.
First, the place of birth is cited. Next, after the phrase "his name was [so-and-so]," his eight matters are listed; the six types of companions are omitted.
Fourth, from the phrase "at the end of that" onwards, it is explained by way of location. Fifth, from the phrase "such were his characteristics" onwards, the scope of wisdom is summarized.

The third [section] concerns the timing of attainment. "Ignorance is exhausted and clarity arises" refers to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*). "Darkness is exhausted and light arises" refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Furthermore, "the exhaustion of ignorance" and so forth refer to the removal of the obscuration of hindrances (*āvaraṇa-āvaraṇa*); "the exhaustion of darkness" and so forth refer to the removal of the obscuration of nature (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*).

The phrase "that which is called... and below is the summary of the names. As for the section beginning with "For what reason is the third...", the underlying cause for this can be understood from the explanation that follows.

Next is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Its textual structure is as above. The citation of the preceding section follows the text. Regarding the second point, "knowing sentient beings" and so forth, this raises the object to manifest the knowledge;
it also has three parts. First is the wisdom that is able to illuminate. Second, from "observing and seeing those who are born, age, and die" onwards, this raises the object to manifest the wisdom;
it also has three parts. First, it generally cites cause and effect. Second, from "furthermore, within oneself" onwards, it specifically cites them.

The object. Third, from "Thus it has been" below, there is the summary. Regarding the first two [categories], "wholesome form" refers to the subtle, soft, and pure forms among those of merit, which are like the light of the bright moon;
therefore, they are called wholesome form. The intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) of those with little merit is coarse and stiff, like a coarse woolen cloth;
this is called unwholesome form. The happy realms are the fruit of merit; the miserable realms are the fruit of demerit. As for...
Regarding the performance of karmic actions: it is said that one "knows all" because both the causes of good and evil can be thoroughly understood.

Next, in the section on individual illumination following the self-examination, one first knows the cause and subsequently knows the distinct nature of the fruit. This differs from the previous general overview which presented the fruit first and the cause later.

Here, the causes and fruits of the unwholesome are listed first; this is an expansion upon the aforementioned points concerning death, an ugly appearance, and rebirth in the miserable destinies as a lowly being. Following this, one further contemplates...

Sentient beings, having already understood below [in the preceding section] the good causes and effects, are thus extensively explained above as being born with virtuous form, in fortunate realms, in noble positions, and so forth.

In this way, the preceding general and specific points are concluded. Third, the timing and the naming of the conclusion are as stated in the text; the third explanation of "attainment" can be understood accordingly.

Next is the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). This also has three parts. Within the second [section], there are three: first, the wisdom that is capable of illumination; second, the raising of the object to manifest it.

Within this, there are four sections. First, taking the Four Truths as the object: the first is the initial engagement with the Truths; the second, from "having attained" onwards, is the repeated and careful examination.

It may also be that the Truths are abandoned sequentially, or that the views of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) are abandoned. Next, through repeated careful examination, the Peak of Existence is abandoned.
The first [stage] is cultivation of exertion. The second is knowing the outflows (*āsrava*) as they truly are; because one has subsequently seen the truths (*satya*), the outflows are abandoned.
The third is that, having known thus, one attains liberation by abandoning the outflows. He forms this knowledge, restating the previously conditioned truths.

Thus observing and directing himself toward the abandonment of the outflows, regarding the "outflow of desire" (*kāmāsrava*) and so forth: the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), are called the outflow of desire. Above [that],...

The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the two realms (*dhātu*), excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), are called the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*). Ignorance of the three realms is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Because it is not "leaked" by these three outflows, it is called liberation. This is stated generally as "attaining liberation from the three outflows.

However, according to the underlying principle, when a Bodhisattva reaches these thirty-four moments of mind—namely, the four patiences (*kṣānti*) and four cognitions (*jñāna*) regarding the subsequent realization (*anvaya*) within the vision of the truths (*satya-darśana*)—and in the [subsequent] non-...

In the cultivation of the eighteen mental states of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one eliminates only the outflows of the view-taint (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)—both pertaining to the path of vision and the path of cultivation—belonging to that single stage.

Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my roots of goodness"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's kuśalamūla. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my merit"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's puṇya. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my virtue"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's śīla. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my patience"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's kṣānti. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my vigor"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's vīrya. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my meditation"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's dhyāna. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my wisdom"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's prajñā. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my skillful means"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's upāya. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my vows"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's praṇidhāna. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my power"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's bala. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my fearlessness"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's vaiśāradya. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my unique qualities"—this means that if one preaches the Dharma for those who do not believe, one will lose one's āveṇika-buddhadharma. Furthermore, "if I were to preach the Dharma for them, they would not believe me, and I would lose my dharmas"—this means that

Second. First, the profundity and excellence of the medicine are established by way of its essence (*tattva*). Second, from "The wise person" onwards, the profundity and excellence of the medicine are established in relation to persons.

To clarify the principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), its essence is simply that which has existed from the beginning; how could there be any distinction between attaining or abandoning, or defilement and purity?
Speaking figuratively by way of signs (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not that birth-and-death does not exist here, nor that nirvāṇa is manifest there. [He] sat...
At the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), [ignorance] is either resolved or exhausted; therefore, it is said: "I have now attained this Dharma.
The principle realized therein is the fundamental limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and the ultimate purport of exhausting the source; therefore, it is called "profound" (*gambhīra*).

This principle transcends names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) and cannot be understood through the investigation of scriptural authority or the sphere of cognitive objects; therefore, it is called "difficult to understand" (*durvigāhya*). Its essence is non-discriminative and is free from mental factors (*caitta*).

Because it is conditioned by such causes, it is said to be "difficult to know. Its own essence is without marks; though the cycle of birth and death is turbulent, it cannot defile it, and thus it is said to be "eternally tranquil.
Realizing its essence through perfect study, one reaches the unconditioned fruit, and thus it is said to be "rest. The principle that exhausts the source is refined, supreme, and peerless;

nothing can surpass it, and thus it is said to be "subtle, wondrous, and most excellent. This explanation clarifies its profundity. Next, it is distinguished according to persons. As for the principle...
Although it is extremely profound, it is not the case that it cannot be realized by anyone; those who possess the vessel of the Mahāyāna will certainly be able to realize and witness it.
Therefore, it is said that "the wise are able to know it. It is not the sphere of the two vehicles' lineage, and thus it is said that "it is not what the ignorant practice.
This concludes the explanation that the principle is deep and the medicine is subtle.
The second [section] clarifies the gravity of the affliction (*ādīnava*). First is the gravity of the affliction regarding the cause; next is the gravity of the affliction regarding the fruit.

Now, these sentient beings are entangled by the darkness of ignorance and are deluded regarding the true principle. Their minds follow forgetful thoughts, grasping at appearances as being manifest—such as [the practice of] indigo-dyeing and the like—or their minds grasp at what is not to be used, such as self-starvation and the like;
these are called "heterodox views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Contemplating this, one settles the mind and accepts it, meaning that the mind finds peace therein.
The use of equality is called "different patience" (*vītarāga-viśeṣa*). The longing for non-equality is called "different desire.

By means of these afflictions, one initiates and completes karma, sustaining oneself through wrong livelihood; hence it is called "different livelihood" (*mithyājīva*). Next, the suffering of the fruit is grave. Relying on causes, there is the retribution of the fruit, namely the karmic results of the three realms.

As for the statement "relying on different views," this refers to being deludedly attached to prior causes and aspiring to be born within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), thereby remaining forever stagnant.

Because there are two kinds of existence (*bhava*), it is said that they "delight in nests and caves. Human and celestial realms are like nests, while the three miserable destinies (*durgati*) are like caves;
this is because those with divergent views and the like are bound to the retributive fruits of the three existences.

The second section in the Chinese text has two parts. The first, extending to "difficult to understand," raises the gravity of the previous affliction: being deluded regarding the cause of the One Vehicle.
The second, from "furthermore, there is that which is profound" onwards, raises the gravity of the previous affliction: being deluded regarding the fruit of the One Vehicle.

The phrase "sentient beings who delight in these nests and caves" briefly cites the afflictions regarding the fruit. The true principle of the *dharmatā* gives rise to the root of both defilement and purity; therefore, it is called the *pratītyasamutpāda-dharma*.

However, these sentient beings cling to self-starvation and the like, thereby remaining bound within the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). They are unable to discern the true nature (*tattva*) of these various conditions;

that is, they cannot establish the habitual cultivation of the pure portion (*śukla-bhāga*). Therefore, it is said to be "profound and difficult to understand. The preceding section clarified the profundity of the cause.

Now, proceeding from the essence to its manifestation, we further clarify the profundity of the fruit; hence it is said: "Furthermore, there is a point of profound depth that is difficult to understand.

Because one is detached from the afflictions of the four abodes, it is called "extinguishing all desires. Because ignorance is forever eliminated, it is named "the exhaustion of craving. Because it is ultimate quiescence, it is termed "nirvāṇa.
Even regarding this state of fruition, people cannot comprehend it, for they grasp at the two kinds of emptiness as being nirvāṇa itself. Therefore—
It is said: "This state is likewise difficult to perceive.
Next, the four knots are successively resolved into emptiness and transformation. That which I now wish to explain refers to the two dharmas of cause and effect within the Mahāyāna.

Those who practice the Two Vehicles become confused and distressed upon hearing [this teaching]; therefore, it is said that "other people do not know. In contrast to those of great capacity, those of small capacity are referred to as "others.
Since they cannot understand it, empty exhortations provide no benefit; hence, it is said that it is "in vain laborious and exhausting."
"Arranging them from below and placing them in the mouth" refers to reciting two verses; that is, the latter two verses were not previously heard.
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (Great Ornament Treatise) dispels doubt by stating that these were not heard in the past from [the Buddha] at Rājagṛha and other locations.

"Nor have they been spoken before" means that since their realization, they have not yet been taught; as they are now about to be taught for the first time, it is said, "nor have they been spoken before. Next, [the text] clarifies...

The Verse Recitation (*geya*). Having completed the first verse recitation, [the Buddha] intended to gather and transform sentient beings through the causal vehicle (*hetu-yāna*), the fundamental purpose for appearing in the world.

However, because their delusions were so heavy that it would have been of no benefit, he spoke the second verse concerning the fruition vehicle (*phala-yāna*). Since they still could not attain awakening, he remained silent and ceased his teaching for others.

The fault lies with the sentient beings; the blame does not rest with me. This clearly demonstrates the Tathāgata’s faultlessness in being without parsimony regarding the Dharma. This is the *geya* sūtra. I...

The realization of the Way is extremely difficult. Recite the preceding passage: "I have now attained this Dharma... until 'rest. This was spoken while dwelling in a cave. Recite the preceding passage:
"I now wish to preach the Dharma to those who are greedy and deluded. Recite the preceding passage: "Sentient beings with divergent views suffer from heavy afflictions regarding cause and effect;
they cannot enter this Dharma. Recite the preceding passage: "It is not something practiced by the foolish" regarding the Dharma of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
It is difficult to understand, and others do not know it either. Regarding the two lines on "going against the stream," the recitation is profound from beginning to end, up to the point of *nirvāṇa*.
The subsequent two lines are likewise difficult to perceive; therefore, they are recited in this manner.

Regarding the third concluding passage: these sentient beings have no great faculties and their present afflictions are moreover grave. Upon hearing the teaching, they would only become further deluded;
it would be better to remain silent and let them follow other paths. Therefore, it is said that having reflected thus, he remained silent and did not preach the Dharma.
The second section, the text of the request, has three parts. First, it clarifies that the Brahma King makes his request out of compassion for the world.

Second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One, having accepted the Brahma’s request," onwards, it shows how he observes the faculties [of beings] to accept the request and grants permission to preach.

Third, from "At that time, the Brahma [King]" onwards, it describes how he subsequently requests to return to his palace. The preceding text is divided into two: first, the introductory sequence of the request; second, his address to the Buddha.
The following is the formal request. In the introduction, there are three parts. First, Brahmā knows the Buddha’s thoughts from afar because the Buddha has entered into the mundane mind;

thus, Brahmā is able to perceive them. Second, from "He then thought of the world" onwards, he laments the loss of the benefits of the Dharma, based on the principle that [the Dharma] was gradually being established.
Therefore it is said: "Is it that you have not even heard [of this]? Next, it clarifies my thought of going in person to pay my respects.
This consists of three parts in the formal petition: first, the petition based on the fundamental cause; second, from "At that time, Brahmā again addressed [the Buddha]" onwards, the urging petition.
Following the third statement, what follows is the "Difficult Request," also known as the "Mockery Request. The initial request consists of two parts: first, the direct request;
second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, the Tathāgata’s recounting of his refusal. Within the request addressed to the Buddha, the phrase "I only pray...
briefly cites two titles for the direct request. Subsequently, from "In this world... onwards, it cites those sentient beings who possess the three vehicles.

Regarding their faculties: because they possess the capacity to extinguish evil and give rise to good, they have the quality of being transformable; thus, I vow to preach the Dharma for them. Because their fetters and compulsions are slight, they are said to have "thin defilements.
Because they are not ignorant regarding principles, they are called "wise. Because they are swift and nimble in practical affairs, they are called "clever.

Because they can understand upon hearing [the teaching], they are termed "easily delivered. They are able to extinguish unwholesome dharmas—this refers to the accomplishment of the virtue of severing [evil] and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

Wisdom is fully perfected, and there is a sense in which [beings] can be transformed; why, then, was it not taught? Following the Buddha’s account of the refusal, the first part describes the words of the request.
Therefore, he says, "As you have said," and so forth. If there were a valid reason for the request, the reason it was not taught is that I had a different intention.
Thus, from the second section beginning with "The one who came before" and so on, he explains his own reasons for not teaching.
The meaning is as stated in the text, up to the point where it asks, "Why do you not preach the Dharma? The Tathāgata answers this intention:
"Indeed, in my quiet contemplation, I desire to transform all sentient beings by means of that Mahāyāna Dharma; I do not wish to deliver them by means of the Hīnayāna.
However, because those sentient beings have heavy afflictions and are deluded and inverted, I remain silent. Why do you now request that I preach the Hīnayāna? This is logically impossible."
Regarding the matter:

next, in the section on the exhortation to invite [the Buddha], it is further stated that while there is arising, there is also cessation; why is it that evil is made to cease and good is made to arise?

Why is this not taught so that the world might hear it? As for the statement "it is utterly ruined," these sentient beings have previously attained the conceptual understanding of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), yet they have long wandered through birth and death.
This becomes a minor delusion, termed a "minor ruin. Now, one ought to hear the teaching of the Small [Vehicle], which can extinguish evil and give rise to goodness.

If the Buddha does not preach it for them, they will again lose the opportunity for the minor realization and sink forever into birth and death, failing to hear the True Dharma; this is a "great ruin.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will at this time expound the True Dharma, so that they may first understand the Small and ultimately enter the Great, lest they suffer such ruin. Furthermore—

One should request [the teaching] with earnest and persistent entreaty; if the Buddha does not speak, there would be a great loss. Therefore, it is said that "it will be utterly ruined," just as people in the world say of something extraordinary, "this is a great matter."

The third [verse] concerns the request for instruction. The first half establishes a challenge by means of a counter-argument; the second half returns to the fundamental principle to comply with the request.
If there were no beings in Magadha who could be transformed, the Buddha would not have fulfilled his vow to attain enlightenment here.

Since he was born among them, it is clear that these beings possess the capacity for transformation. If they are indeed transformable, may you open the gate of the ambrosia for the sake of all sentient beings.
He preached the Dharma. The intention of this request is as follows. Next, I shall explain the text. Among the beings of Magadha, both purity and defilement coexist;

therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is "free from defilement. That the Buddha was born therein refers to the place where the Dharma-body arises through the cultivation of the path and the perfection of merit through mindfulness.
I pray that you will unfold and expound the True Dharma so that its principles may be made brilliantly clear, and that those who hear of it may attain the truth and nourish their minds.

Harmonizing with the divine and suiting one’s own will, its meaning is identical to ambrosia (*amṛta*), and its principle penetrates spiritual understanding. It is taught as the gateway; thus it is said, "I pray you open [the gate] equally," and so forth.
He addressed the Buddha five times, saying: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on sentient beings and preach the Dharma for them at this time.
There are sentient beings who are able to receive the Buddha's teaching; if they do not hear it, they will surely fall away. Thus he repeated this three times, and again with these words...

[He] spoke a verse to request the Buddha: "Previously, in this realm of Magadha, only defiled and impure teachings were ever preached. I pray that you shall open the gate of nectar and expound the meaning of pure truth.
Since I was in the celestial palaces, I have constantly seen the ancient Buddhas preach; I only pray that the All-Seeing One [will do so now]."
Furthermore, the teachings of the Dharma-hall are being destroyed; sentient beings are submerged in grief and affliction, unable to escape birth, aging, and death.
Yet, as many are fond of what is wholesome, I pray that you will preach the Dharma of victory. The World-Honored One accepted this by remaining silent.

The second section, "Observing the Faculties and Accepting the Invitation," contains two parts. First, up until the point where it says "accomplishing wholesome dharmas," he silently accepts the invitation in his mind and observes the recipient's faculties.
Second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, he expresses his acceptance verbally and agrees to preach the Dharma.

The preceding passage consists of three parts: the teaching (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*). Regarding the phrase "having accepted the invitation of Brahmā," this refers to his silent reflection and acceptance.
He then surveyed sentient beings to see who possessed the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) to be transformed. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"For example, when a great dragon emerges from the great ocean, wishing to spread dense clouds and pour down heavy rain, it first observes which country should receive the rain."
Only then does it send down rain. The Buddha is also like this. From the ocean of the four immeasurables, he brings forth the clouds of compassion;
wishing to rain down the Dharma-rain, he first observes the faculties [of beings] to see who is capable of receiving transformation. Only then does he preach the Dharma.

He observes those sentient beings and finds they possess the faculties for the three vehicles—namely, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—each of which has superior, middling, and inferior levels. Thus, combined, there are nine. It is as follows:

Those born in the world with dull faculties fear the retribution of future lives. Among the śrāvakas, there are superior, middling, and inferior types; those with few defilements and those with many defilements are difficult to deliver.

Among the pratyekabuddhas, there are superior, middling, and inferior types; those with long-standing sharp faculties are easy to deliver. Among the bodhisattvas, there are also superior, middling, and inferior types.

Furthermore, although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess both sharp and dull faculties, they equally receive the Lesser Dharma (Hīnayāna) and are thus grouped together as "those who are born. The Great Beings, the Bodhisattvas, are said to be... [the text ends here].
Long. These two types of contemplation differ according to the capacity of individuals, whether great or small.

The reason they are categorized as great or small is truly because defilements vary in thickness, faculties vary in sharpness or dullness, and the reception of the Way varies in difficulty or ease. Those with few defilements and sharp faculties are easily delivered;

these three constitute the vessel for the Mahāyāna. Those with many defilements and dull faculties are difficult to deliver; these three are termed the vessel for the Hīnayāna. [They] fear future lives...

From the point of transgression downward, although there may be differences in capacity—whether sharp or dull, easy or difficult—all without exception fear evil and incline toward the good; therefore, it is said, "down to the wholesome dharmas.

What follows is an illustration by means of a parable. It does not take the four types of activity as the metaphor, but directly takes the pond, the flowers, and the water as the metaphors. The pond represents the responsive capacity of the sentient being.

The flower is a metaphor for the mind of understanding; the water is a metaphor for the teaching. If one pours the water of the teaching on the Four Truths into the pool of the śrāvaka’s responsive capacity, the flower of the śrāvaka’s mind of understanding will grow therein.

Because the śrāvaka’s faculties are soft, they rely initially upon the teaching as a condition; therefore, it is said that "having first emerged from the ground, they have not yet emerged from the water.
This metaphor illustrates those of dull faculties who are born into higher realms and fear the sins of future lives. Third, if one uses the teaching of causes and conditions...

Regarding the "water of the teaching": when this water is poured into the pool of those whose faculties are receptive to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, it causes the flowers of the mind of understanding for Pratyekabuddhas to grow. At the time of their conclusion, they are said to have attained understanding through the teaching;
thus, it is said that "the water and [the flowers] are level. This metaphor refers to those with few defilements above and many defilements below, who are difficult to deliver.

Third, if the water of the teaching of the six perfections is poured into the pool of those whose faculties are receptive to the Mahāyāna, it can cause the flowers of the mind of understanding for Bodhisattvas to grow.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the ultimate meaning and abandons the conventional expressions; thus, he is not constrained by the characteristics of the teachings. Therefore it is said: "Having already emerged from the water and dust, the water does not adhere to him.

This metaphor illustrates those of superior, long-standing, and sharp faculties who are easily delivered. Thirdly, according to the later interpretation, this refers to the lotus flower that has first emerged from the pond.
When the flower is level with the water, it serves as a metaphor for the four types of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have been reborn above [the world] yet possess many defilements,

dull faculties, and are difficult to deliver. When the flower has emerged from the water and dust does not adhere to it, this serves as a metaphor for the four types of Mahāyāna roots who have grown further above [the world], possess few defilements, sharp faculties, and are easy to deliver.

From here below, the analogy is applied. "The Tathāgata is also like this" means that the Tathāgata observes the faculties of those of the three vehicles with perfect clarity, just as a man with sight in the world distinguishes the three different kinds of lotuses in a pond; therefore, it is said, "he is also like this.

In the analogy, there is a man with sight, and since he exists within the application [of the analogy], there are two ways of explaining the application text. This may be inferred according to the principle.
[The Buddha] knows. He speaks for a second time in response to the invitation; because he addresses the one who invited him, he is called "Brahmā.

I tell you: now I shall expound the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Thus it is said, "Now I open the gate of ambrosia. Regarding the faculties and capacities observed, the Three Vehicles are not one. It is said:
All [disciples] have received instruction and gained benefit; they resolutely accept it, and thus it is said that "those who hear it believe and receive it.

The following three lines explain the intention behind teaching the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). If I were to teach only the Lesser Vehicle, I would remain fixed within the Lesser and would not enable them to attain the Great Vehicle’s ultimate and eternal peace;
this would be the fault of being stingy with the Dharma, which is equivalent in meaning to causing affliction. My present teaching... begins.
At that time, they understood the small; in the end, they attained the great. Because they share in the subtle and wondrous Dharma I have realized, it is said:

"It is not for the sake of vexation that I speak. This extends even to the Dharma realized by the Muni. Furthermore, the latter two lines may also resolve doubts. The Buddha first reflected [upon this].
The medicine is subtle and the afflictions are grave; therefore, he remained silent and did not preach the Dharma. Now that the request has been made, he permits the preaching.

One might think this is not the Dharma attained by the Buddha, and thus it is necessary to provide an explanation: "O Brahmā, among what I have attained, I have preached three [vehicles] as skillful means;

therefore, I say these are the subtle and wondrous Dharmas of Brahmā, which are precisely the Dharmas attained by the Muni. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Fearing that [the listeners] would merely exhaust themselves in vain, he did not preach the profound [Dharma]."
The profound meaning and the nectar shall now be opened; all should hear it.
Third, he takes his leave and returns to the palace. Having accepted the invitation for the third time, he proceeds to the sense-faculties to preach the Dharma. This section has two parts.

First, from the beginning up to the passage on the practice leading to *nirvāṇa*, it is to demonstrate that although the five men had adhered to heterodoxy for a long time, they currently lacked the capacity to receive the Way.

Vessel. Therefore, one must first exhort [the disciples] to abandon the two extremes, thereby establishing them as suitable vessels. Once they possess the vessel of faith, they are capable of receiving the medicine of the Dharma.
For this reason, from the second section on the Four Noble Truths onwards, the teaching of the Dharma is clearly elucidated to immerse those vessels of faith.

The preceding text is further divided into two parts: first, the thought that the two false teachers had not heard the supreme Dharma, which dispels the doubts of the assembly; second, at that time, the World-Honored One...
Having further formed this thought, he below exhorted the five bhikṣus to become vessels of faith. First, let us explain the preceding text.
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "If those people were destined to enter the Path, they should not have died before hearing the Dharma;
if they were not destined to enter the Path, for what reason did the Buddha intend to deliver them? The answer is that there are two reasons. First, the Buddha wished to...

Sentient beings do not forget a debt of gratitude. This was a minor kindness [previously received], yet the Buddha remembered it and desired to deliver them, fearing that such great kindness might go unrequited.
Second, there were the various teachers of heterodox paths whom people of the time venerated and looked up to, all of whom claimed to have attained the Way.

The Buddha thought of delivering them in order to extinguish all their deluded conceptualizations (*vitarka-vicāra*). Thus, he came to explain away their doubts based on the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*. That treatise asks:
You claim that the Buddha is an omniscient one (*sarvajña*). Yet, when the Buddha was mindful of Kāla, the latter had already passed away seven days prior;
the Buddha did not even know that Kāla was dead. How, then, can he be called omniscient? The commentary explains:

When our World-Honored One first left the household life, he once stayed overnight with Kāla and practiced the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*) together with him. The devas...

If the people should harbor doubts, thinking that the Buddha received the Dharma from him and attained enlightenment elsewhere, and that what he now teaches is merely the Dharma learned at the edge of the grove—asking where there could be any superior Dharma—the Buddha, knowing that Kālāma had passed away seven days prior, made this statement in order to sever their doubts.
Kālāma possessed sharp faculties; it was for his sake that I first taught [the Dharma], and he immediately...
He reflected that seven days had already passed; "How bitter it is! How is it that such a sublime Dharma was not heard?
At that moment, the doubts of the devas and humans were completely dispelled, as they knew that the Buddha possessed even more excellent teachings than those obtained at Āḷavī.
Therefore, the World-Honored One is omniscient. Those of sharp faculties understood that the Buddha’s Dharma was not merely what was obtained at Āḷavī, while those of dull faculties further thought:
"If the Tathāgata were to teach the Dharma of Udraka Rāmaputra now, it would mostly consist of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Where else could there be a superior Dharma?
To sever this doubt, he again thought of Māluṅkyaputra, knowing that Māluṅkyaputra had passed away that very day; therefore, he made this statement.
He first preached the Dharma to them, whereupon they thought to themselves: "How bitter it is! We have not heard the sublime Dharma.
For this reason, the World-Honored One is the All-Knowing One; based on this principle, the matter of the five bhikṣus can likewise be understood. This is done to dispel all doubts.

Regarding the section on establishing the spiritual capacity (*indriya*), there are three parts to the text. First, from the beginning up to "Did he preach the Dharma? [it shows] that the five bhikṣus possessed the karmic conditions for a response.
Second, from "Then the World-Honored One again had this thought" onwards, it describes how he observed the five bhikṣus and knew their location.

Third, from "Having seen them" onwards, it describes how he followed those with whom he had a connection, exhorted them to abandon the two extremes, and caused them to give rise to faith and understanding. Within this section:
Second: The first section, from the beginning up to "no longer receiving further existence," addresses those who cling to the past while harboring doubts about the present;

it establishes their resolve and rejects their discouragement by citing the Tathāgata’s testimony, exhorting them in terms of the fruit (*phala*). The second section, beginning with "Bhikṣus who have gone forth," exhorts them to abandon the two extremes and establish the vessel of the faculties (*indriya*), exhorting them in terms of the cause (*hetu*).
If one were to explain this exhaustively, it would involve both cause and fruit; the intent of the exhortation can thus be understood as a refutation [of opposing views].

This is because the cause and effect he clings to are such. The preceding passage further consists of two parts. First, up to "bewildered and lost in purpose," [the Buddha] establishes his resolve and rejects their exhortations.
Second, from "The Buddha addressed the five men" onwards, he cites past words regarding non-duality to demonstrate that the present is the reality, using his own fourfold wisdom.

Exhorting them to practice and study: within the preceding text, there are four pairs of eight phrases. First, the initial establishment of the rule; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One gradually...
downwards, the breaking of the rule; third, from "I would now rather... downwards, the Buddha’s sitting and addressing you;
fourth, from "At that time, the Buddha told the five bhikṣus... downwards, the exhortation not to [yield], your establishing of resolve to resist.
Exhortation. At the beginning, when he was traveling toward Vārāṇasī, he encountered Udraka Rāmaputra on the road.

This demonstrated that his Wheel of Dharma is applied to those with whom there is a karmic affinity, and not to those without such affinity. The two former teachers were entirely without such affinity, whereas Udraka Rāmaputra [possessed it].
There were those who had met the Buddha but lacked the vessel for attaining the Way. As for the five men of lower status, they were entirely moved by external conditions.

The Brahmin Udraka was refined and elegant by nature; having seen the Tathāgata, his faculties became tranquil and his countenance was serene and joyful, indicating that he must have encountered an excellent teacher and sublime Dharma.
He posed three questions: first, he asked who his teacher for leaving the household life was; second, he asked who his teacher for receiving instruction was.

The three questions concern what Dharma he had studied; [the fifth part] concerns his appearance. Seeing that the World-Honored One’s countenance was exceptionally distinguished, his faculties serene, and his halo extending one fathom like a mountain of gold, he immediately asked: "Under whom did you formerly study? What path and Dharma did you practice to attain such supreme honor?
The Buddha answered with a verse. According to the Āgamas, this appears as four questions, namely: "Where do you go? and so forth, followed by "Now..."
Furthermore, based on this text, there are only three questions. Within the Buddha’s response, there are four verses. The first three verses answer the aforementioned three questions;
the fourth verse is spoken to dispel doubts. The first verse answers the second question, the next verse answers the first question, and the third verse answers the third question.
First, I shall explain the initial verse to address the intent of the second question. You previously asked me from whom I have learned;

however, my delusions are exhausted and my understanding is full, with all virtues universally complete. What deficiency could there be such that I would need to learn from a teacher? This response conveys the meaning of having no teacher from whom to receive instruction.
As for what wisdom illuminates—both emptiness and existence—the myriad objects are not one; therefore, it is said that "all is clearly perceived. This...
To fully comprehend names is called wisdom (*jñāna*). When wisdom’s illumination reaches ultimate perfection, there is nothing further to surpass it;

thus it is designated as "supreme. As understanding arises and delusion perishes, the myriad burdens are thereby diminished; hence it is said that "all desires and anxieties are resolved. This clarifies the exhaustion of delusion.

Regarding the third phrase, one does not rely on the consultation of a teacher but attains sudden, solitary penetration; hence it is said that "one naturally attains realization and awakening. This clarifies that once wisdom is fulfilled, delusion [is exhausted].
Having fully understood and perfected [the teachings], he does not rely on the instructions of a teacher. Therefore it is said:
"How could one learn from another? Next, the second verse is explained to answer the intent of the first question: "Whose teacher did you have when you went forth?"
"If my wisdom and virtue were not perfected and my afflictions not yet exhausted, I might rely upon teachers and monks to inquire about and receive their instructions on the Dharma.

However, since my own virtue is already perfected and I do not require the instruction of a teacher, what need is there for a teacher? This response shows that he has no intention of having an ordination teacher.

Next, the text explains: "Not only is there no teacher of the Unlearned (aśaikṣa), but there is also no teacher of the renunciant (pravrajyā). Therefore, it says, "I likewise have no teacher. Furthermore—

"Furthermore, having no equal companion" explains the meaning of "having no teacher" by means of having no equal companion; if even an equal companion does not exist, how much less could there be a teacher?
"The world has but one Buddha" explains the meaning of "having no equal," for in a single world-system, only one Buddha appears in the world.
No second Buddha shall ever appear in the world; therefore, there is none equal to him. Thus it is said that in the world there is but one Buddha.
Having exhausted all delusions and realized the coolness of the Dharma, he is free from the afflictions of distress and oppression; hence he is called "cool and eternally tranquil."
Next, I shall explain the meaning of the third response. You previously asked me, "What dharma do you study? However, my essence of wisdom is perfect and complete;

all delusions have been exhausted, and both emptiness and existence have subsided into oneness. There is no further dharma to be studied; therefore, I am called the "World’s Unattached One," even to the point of being "without equal.
To explain this state of non-attachment, one must first understand attachment. Ordinary beings lack wisdom and remain within the cycle of birth.

To be defiled by death is called "attachment to existence. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles lack great compassion, they realize the realization of emptiness; this is called "attachment to non-existence. The Tathāgata himself has said:
"Because he possesses wisdom, he conditions existence without being defiled by it, unlike ordinary beings who are attached to existence.

Because he possesses great compassion, he does not take the realization of emptiness as a final attainment, unlike the followers of the Two Vehicles who are attached to non-existence. Since both existence and non-existence have been extinguished, it is so called."

He is without attachment. Since he is inwardly without attachment, his Way surpasses that of humans and devas; he alone is supreme and foremost. Therefore it is said, "I am the most excellent in the world.
It may also be said that I am the one without attachment in the world. Having destroyed the causes of birth and death, I am the most excellent in the world.

Being free from the fruits of birth and death, and since I possess neither the cause nor the fruit of birth and death, no one among humans or devas exceeds me. Therefore it is said: "Among all devas and worldly people..."
"There is none equal to me; my own virtues are perfected, and there is no dharma left to be learned.
This fourth verse explains a doubt: when the brahmin heard the Buddha say that his own virtuous conduct was fully perfected, he immediately conceived a doubt.
"If his virtue were full, he should be a teacher for others and one to whom others turn for refuge.
Why, then, does he today travel along the road as if he had some deficiency and were seeking it out? The Buddha, knowing his mind, spoke thus to dispel this doubt:
"I wish to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī to be a teacher for others; I do not seek the Dharma for myself. The first phrase refers to following [the path].
Following those with whom one has a karmic affinity, one bestows transformative teachings upon their respective locations and transmits what one has personally realized; this is called "turning.
Because nothing is more profound than this, it is called the "Unsurpassed Dharma. Because it crushes and grinds away the fetters and delusions, it is termed a "wheel.

Since the sentient beings of the world are shrouded by the thick gloom of ignorance and are obscured regarding their objects of perception, they are said to be all "blind and dark. It is for the sake of these blind and dark sentient beings that [the Buddha] intends to manifest and proclaim [this teaching].
The True Dharma is called "Appropriate" (*dang*); when its teachings set forth the principles of its intent, it is called "Striking" (*ji*).

When these principles manifest and moisten the spirit, they cause birth and death to be forever severed and the life of wisdom to endure long, like ambrosia (*amṛta*). When the principle is revealed externally, those with the karmic affinity to encounter it shall hear it.
The meaning is the same as that of a drum; therefore, it is said: "One should beat the drum of ambrosia. The Brahmin again raised a third response and inquired further regarding its meaning.

The Buddha replied: "I have conquered all fetters (*saṃyojana*). "Conquered" means brought to rest. Because the causes of affliction are exhausted, one attains the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Since suffering has nothing that does not perish and cause and effect are utterly extinguished, it is said: "I have conquered all unwholesome dharmas."
It may also mean "to surpass," referring to transcending all evils; thus it is called "surpassing unwholesome dharmas. Since no humans or devas surpass him, he says, "I am the most supreme.

The answer accords with the fundamental tenet, yet the Brahmin, failing to grasp the profound words beyond the literal, refused to accept the five-fold division [of the teachings] and departed, slapping his thigh.
A tutelary deity from that Brahmin’s past lives immediately spoke a verse from mid-air as the Buddha first began [his teaching].
"He has transcended the world; he is the most honored one above and below the heavens. How can you pass him by and instead abandon him?
Although the brahmin heard this verse, he still departed without looking back. This was the fourth time he was exhorted not to reject the Buddha’s resolve.
Holding onto past doubts regarding the present, you claim that the Tathāgata abandoned his own true path of self-restraint through fasting to instead practice eating food;

you say that the path he follows is not a path of reality, and thus you state, "This is what you yourself originally created," even going so far as to say, "How much more so now that he is lost in confusion and delusion."

The second section refutes the former claim of non-duality and clarifies that within the present reality there are three aspects. First, by using the past as a parallel to the present, it demonstrates that the Buddha’s words are non-dual.
Second, from the passage "The Buddha said, 'Come, you all'" onwards, it shows that he originally spoke words of non-duality;

now that [the disciples] have realized and attained the ultimate four wisdoms, it is clear that this is real and not false. He says: "If you are able to receive and uphold this, before long you shall likewise attain it."

Third, from the passage "therefore, O son of noble family" onwards, he correctly cites his own past seeking and his present attainment of the four wisdoms to clarify that you, having received and practiced [the teachings], will surely attain what was obtained by him;
the fruit is not in vain, for it is acquired through its cause.
Therefore, from this point downward, he proceeds by means of exhortation. Within this section, there are two parts: first, the exhortation to abandon the two extremes;
second, the instruction for the bhikṣus and others to establish the Middle Way. In the former part, there are four sentences. The first enumerates the number of the two extremes.
Regarding the two types of attachment to practice mentioned below, the names of the two extremes are listed. An ancient interpretation states:

"Those who delight in the practice of sensual desire" refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which is called an extreme of phenomena; or "those who practice self-mortification," which is called an extreme of asceticism. This may not be correct.

If these five classes of people do not study such things as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, why would it be necessary to urge them to abandon them? Therefore, the correct interpretation is simply that sentient beings who hold views of annihilationism...

Regarding the practice of pleasure and the asceticism of those with eternalist views: here, the phrase "practicing the enjoyment of sensual desires" refers to the extreme of excessive pleasure held by those with nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Alternatively, the phrase "those who practice self-mortification" refers to the extreme of excessive suffering held by those with eternalist views (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).

Because these two deviate from the Middle Way, they are called "extremes. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* is likewise: first, those who are greedily attached to sensual desires claim that there is no fault in desire; second, those with false views [practice] asceticism.

Form. Since there are no traces of the Path [in form], we know that sensual desire is not without its function. Furthermore, in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-ṭīkā*, it is explained within the commentary on the *Vinaya*:
"The *Vinaya* is established in order to counteract the two extremes of enjoyment. The *Vinaya* is established because the Buddha prohibited the enjoyment of what is blameworthy;
this establishes the *Vinaya* as a counteragent to the extreme of indulgence in pleasure. Because the Buddha rejoiced in the enjoyment of what is blameless, he established..."
The *Vinaya* serves as the antidote to the extreme of asceticism (*duṣkaracaryā*). It is to remain free from both pleasure and suffering, cultivating the Middle Way with the mind.

Question: If one is addressing five people, it is sufficient merely to leave suffering behind; why then is pleasure also dismissed? Answer: If one were to speak only of leaving suffering behind, there would be the fear that they might become attached to pleasure;
therefore, both are exhorted to be relinquished.
Third, from "not the dharma of the noble ones" onwards, it reveals the faults of the two extremes. Indulgence is not the dharma of the noble ones;
asceticism and strenuous toil are merely exhausting labor that yields no benefit. Therefore, it says "exhaustion and fatigue," and so forth.

The fourth section, "Incapability of Discernment," concludes the two preceding faults via the Middle Way. This passage consists of four parts: first, distinguishing the non-existent to reveal the existent, thereby manifesting the essence of the Middle Way;
the text states, "Excluding these... and so forth, up to "the practices leading to nirvāṇa," which constitutes the causal essence of the Middle Way.
Second, from "How then... onwards to "the practices leading to nirvāṇa," which poses subtle questions regarding the Middle Way. Third, this... [text continues].

The "Noble Eightfold Path" below [the preceding section] correctly brings forth the Middle Way. The fourth [section], from "is called" onwards, up to "the practice leading to Nirvāṇa," defines its middle way.
First, I shall explain the initial passage. The phrase "excluding this" serves to distinguish what is not [the path];

that is, it excludes the two extremes of pleasure and suffering. As for the text stating "furthermore, there is a middle way," this refers to the practice of the tranquil conduct of Nirvāṇa and so forth.

The Middle Way. "Clarity of the eye" refers to the clarity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). "Clarity of wisdom" refers to the clarity of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*). "Eternal tranquility" refers to the clarity of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
"Accomplishing supernormal powers" refers to the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). "Attaining equal enlightenment" refers to the perfection of wisdom.
"Becoming a śramaṇa" refers to the perfection of abandonment. "Nirvāṇa" refers to the two types of nirvāṇa. Thus far, the results have been cited to indicate their causes. As for the practitioner:
This is the Middle Way. Regarding the third [section], the emergence of the Middle Way, there are two parts to the text. First, the general presentation of these Eightfold Noble Path of the Sages;

second, the specific enumeration of its eight components beginning with Right View. As for the definitive nature of these eight: speech, action, and livelihood—these three are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*);
the remaining five are mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*). Right View is wisdom (*prajñā*). Right Action refers to right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), which is...

The factor of awakening called right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) refers to vigor (*vīrya*). Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the factor of mindfulness. Concentration (*samādhi*) refers to the factor of concentration.

This concludes the analysis of their essential natures (*svabhāva*). Next, their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) will be explained. Regarding "right view" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), it refers to the wisdom-mind of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Regarding the three factors beginning with right action (*samyak-karmānta*), as stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*: "Physical action (*kāya-karman*) initiated by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is right action; verbal action initiated [by such wisdom] is right speech..."
Regarding speech: abstaining from the five types of wrong livelihood constitutes right livelihood, as stated in the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra*.
There are four kinds of bodily action: first, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct; and fourth, abstaining from improper conduct.

There are four kinds of vocal action: first, abstaining from false speech; second, abstaining from divisive speech; third, abstaining from harsh speech; and fourth, abstaining from frivolous speech. These are the four kinds of bodily [action].

Regarding wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*): if one abstains from it through the wholesome roots of non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and non-delusion (*amoha*), these eight [factors] are called right action (*samyakkarmānta*).

Regarding the four wrong actions of speech (*vāc*): if one abstains from them through non-hatred and non-delusion, these eight [factors] are called right speech (*samyagvāc*). Regarding the eight wrong actions of body and speech:

if one abstains from them through the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*), these eight factors of body and speech are called right livelihood (*samyagājīva*). This is right conduct (*samyakpratipatti*).
This refers to right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). Now, because it takes an object as its condition, it is called "practice" (*saṃskāra*); because it is not a deviant mind, it is termed "right.

Because the mind of training does not fall [into error], it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Expedient means is neither deviant nor [merely] right. Mindfulness and concentration can be understood [as before]. The fourth concluding passage can be understood.
From here below, the text correctly clarifies the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, casting [the teaching] into the vessel of faith. Within this section, there are two parts:

first, the individual turnings that exhort one to practice; second, from "If I do not practice" onwards, which correctly clarifies the general presentation of the three turnings and twelve aspects, exhorting one to train therein.
The text for the individual turnings has four parts: first, stating the number; second, "What is meant by... and so forth, which is a provisional...

A brief enumeration of the names. Third, "What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? and so forth constitutes the actual exposition of the characteristics. Fourth, "This is called... and so forth constitutes the conclusion.
Although the truths are four in number, they are divided into two categories: the two truths of suffering and its origin, which are the worldly cause and effect;

and the two truths of cessation and the path, which are the supramundane cause and effect. Suffering and its origin are defiled; their faults and conditions are extensively revealed in order to engender world-weariness. Therefore—

The Truths of Cessation and the Path involve ascending toward purity; because one wishes to inspire joy, they should appropriately be distinguished later. When the feelings of weariness and joy reside within the mind, there will necessarily be that which is accomplished.

Furthermore, Suffering and its Origin have existed since beginningless time; therefore, they are explained first. The two truths of Cessation and the Path exist only when one encounters the Sage; therefore, they are spoken of next.
As for the reason why Suffering is mentioned first and Origin second, it is because of the sequence of cause and effect. It must be so.

The origin (*samudaya*) must necessarily precede suffering (*duḥkha*). Here, however, according to the sequence of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), one proceeds from the coarse to the subtle; therefore, suffering comes first and origin follows.

As for the fact that even within the supramundane cause and effect (*lokottara-hetu-phala*) the fruit is mentioned first, this is also a matter of the sequence of contemplative practice: the path (*mārga*) comes first and cessation (*nirodha*) follows.
This is done so as to first indicate the fruit of cessation, thereby inspiring aspiration in sentient beings; such is the reason it is so.
Next, regarding the explanation of the names: "Suffering" (duḥkha) has the meaning of oppression; "Origin" (samudaya) means accumulation; "Cessation" (nirodha) means tranquility;

and "Path" (mārga) refers to that which leads universally. Since the names are thus, their essential natures must now be set forth. As for the essence of the Truth of Suffering, it refers to the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ).

While form (rūpa) is not itself of the nature of affliction, it is judged to be an instrument of suffering. The mind (citta), being characterized by deliberation and cognition, is the actual essence of suffering. Taken collectively, these constitute the general definition of its essence.
The Truth of Suffering. As for the essence of the Truth of Origination: it refers to karma and afflictions. Karma is the primary seed, while afflictions act as the auxiliary conditions.

Although the primary cause and the conditions differ, they together construct the future fruit; thus, this is designated as "origination. As for the essence of the Truth of Cessation: cessation has no distinct characteristics.

Regarding the treatise on phenomena, there are three [types of mental cessation]: namely, the cessation of the mind of conventional designations, the mind of real dharmas, and the mind of emptiness. First, through the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, one ceases the mind of conventional designations.

Second, through the wisdom of cultivation, such as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, one ceases the mind of real dharmas. Third, the cessation of meditative concentration is temporary, whereas *nirvāṇa* is permanent; this is the cessation of the mind of emptiness that dispels signs.

Although the three minds differ, their cessation is identical in principle. Therefore, the point at which these three minds are exhausted is taken as the true essence of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

As for what is called the essence of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is the essence of the path; ethical discipline and meditative concentration are the requisites for the path.

Since both the provisional path and the ultimate path can lead one to liberation and effect cessation, they are both termed the Truth of the Path. These four types [of truths] are all thoroughly examined and unerring. All...

These are called the Truths (satya). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Suffering cannot be made into pleasure," and so forth, up to: "The path that leads to the cessation of suffering is truly the authentic path; there is no other path.
This is unlike ordinary people who falsely conceive of suffering as pleasure, or who take atoms, primordial matter (prakṛti), or Īśvara to be its cause;
or who take the two kinds of emptiness to be its cessation; or who reckon the vows of the crow and the cock to be the path. This...

This is not [the ultimate] truth. Next, the text is explained. The passage beginning with "What are called the noble truths? is a provisional inquiry that enumerates their names, namely: the noble truth of suffering, and so forth.

One who loathes suffering and cultivates the path, attaining realization of the truths and giving rise to understanding, is called "noble" (*ārya*); therefore, it is named the "noble truth of suffering. The meaning of "truth" (*satya*) does not differ from what was stated previously.

Explanation: Suffering is obtained through causes, namely the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Because it is the origination that gives rise to suffering, yet when one eliminates it and produces understanding, it is called "Noble" (*ārya*);
thus, it is termed the "Noble Truth of the Origination of Suffering. Because one realizes its cessation and produces understanding, it is called "Noble";

since this is the actual state where the other three truths are absent, it is named from the perspective of its initial function as the "Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering" (*nirodha-satya*). Cessation does not exist inherently; it must necessarily arise through causes. Its cause is...
What is it? It is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). The Eightfold Noble Right Path and its constituent factors are able to remove obstructions and allow for passage;
they are supreme among those leading to transcendence. Therefore, it is called the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
The third section distinguishes the characteristics [of the teaching]. This passage consists of two parts. First, it clarifies the three turnings of the twelvefold wheel of Dharma.
Second, from the phrase "This noble truth of suffering, a dharma never heard before" onwards, it cites the upper and lower turnings;

each turning is capable of accomplishing six kinds of merit, thereby exhorting others to practice and study, though they have not yet actually realized the benefits. Since there are three turnings for each of the Four Noble Truths, they total twelve turnings. Thus, it is called "the three."

There are three [turnings]: first, the turning that demonstrates characteristics; second, the turning that exhorts practice; third, the turning that cites evidence. Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of Suffering:

first, citing the eight sufferings to demonstrate them to others is called "demonstrating characteristics. Second, from the phrase "Furthermore" (*dvitīyaṃ khalu punaḥ*) onwards, it is the exhortation to know.
Third, from the phrase "I have already known" (*mayā jñātam*) onwards, it is citing one's own realization as evidence. As for the preceding demonstration of characteristics, its text is as follows:
There are three [sections]: namely, the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. The remaining truths (*satya*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are likewise presented in this manner.

Now, the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is explained; that is to say, the eight types of suffering (*aṣṭa-duḥkha*). This is analyzed through two gates: first, distinguishing their characteristics and how they receive their names; second, the inclusion of these within the three characteristics. The eight sufferings are categorized into three positions.

The four sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death are designated by name according to time. The three sufferings of separation from the beloved and so forth are received based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

It is called the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). The name is established by enumerating their faults: because there is suffering at the time of birth, it is called the suffering of birth. Regarding the suffering of old age:
