when the hair turns white, the face wrinkles, and the physical form decays and changes, this is called old age; because there is suffering at the time of old age, it is called the suffering of old age.

When the wind element increases in relation to the others and one of the elements becomes unbalanced, the hundred and one diseases arise; because there is suffering at the time of illness, it is called the suffering of illness.
Regarding "the suffering of death": "death" means exhaustion. At the time of death there is suffering; therefore, it is called the suffering of death.

The subsequent three [types of suffering] receive their names based on causes and conditions. The "cause" refers to the internal mind, namely craving, increased seeking, and so forth. The "condition" refers to external objects, namely those that are adverse or favorable.

There are two types of favorable conditions (*anuloma-viṣaya*). If one has already experienced a favorable condition and it is separated from them, it gives rise to suffering; this is subsumed under the suffering of parting from what is loved (*priya-viprayoga-duḥkha*).

If one has not yet experienced a favorable condition and seeks it but does not obtain it, it is included within the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks (*yad-apicchatā-duḥkha*). Unfavorable conditions (*pratikūla-viṣaya*) are also of two types. If one has not yet experienced unwholesome phenomena...

Due to the convergence of conditions and events, there is the suffering of association with the hated. If one has already received unwholesome dharmas and cannot abandon them, this constitutes the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

Next, regarding the explanation of the names: when one has already received favorable conditions and ordinary sentiment delights in and clings to them, it is called "love" (*tṛṣṇā*). Because that which was originally united is now divided, it is so named.

Separation: Because it arises entirely from being separated from those one loves, it is called the suffering of separation from the beloved (*priya-viprayoga-duḥkha*). Adverse conditions that harm oneself are termed resentment (*āghāta*); when the mind aligns with such evil, it is called intensification (*āghāta-vṛddhi*).

The convergence of conditions and the meeting of events are termed encounter (*samnipāta*); because it arises entirely from the intensification and encounter of resentment, it is called the suffering of the intensification and encounter of resentment (*āghāta-vṛddhi-samnipāta-duḥkha*).

The longing of the heart for favorable conditions is termed seeking (*prārthana*); when there is a discrepancy between what was originally sought and what is obtained, it is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks (*yad-icchan na labhate tad-duḥkha*). These are the [eight] sufferings.

Because it cannot be obtained, suffering arises. This is the suffering of not yet having attained wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*): the mind feels aversion toward unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*) and yearns to abandon them; this is also called "seeking.

Because one seeks but cannot avoid separation [from what is desired], it is called "non-attainment," and suffering arises from this. This is the suffering of not yet being free from unwholesome dharmas.
When these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and seven sufferings converge together, and all sufferings blaze intensely, they are called the "five aggregates of clinging" (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Suffering.

Regarding the subsequent mutual inclusion: birth, aging, sickness, death, and encountering those one dislikes are subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Separation from what one loves is included within the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
As the treatise states: "At the time of separation from what one loves, whatever suffering arises—referring to such things as wives and children—is called the suffering of change."

Suffering. The suffering of not obtaining what one desires and seeks. There are two types [of suffering]: that which has not yet abandoned unwholesome dharmas is subsumed under *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of suffering); that which has not yet attained wholesome dharmas is gathered under *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of change).

The suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) subsumes all three types of suffering. By explaining the characteristics of these eight sufferings, one causes others to know them and develop revulsion;

this is called the "turning through the manifestation of characteristics. The other two [turnings] may be understood accordingly. Once one knows that suffering is to be reviled, it is essential to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path; only then can one overturn suffering.

[The text] is collected again. Therefore, beneath each of the Truths (satya), one must invariably exhort the cultivation of the Middle Way in order to turn back from the two extremes mentioned previously.
The meaning of the Eightfold Noble Path has already been explained.

Next, regarding the three aspects of the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya): first, the listing of karma and afflictions (kleśa) clarifies origination; this is termed "manifesting the characteristics through transformation. [This refers to] the ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
That which can assist karma in drawing forth rebirth is not the primary seed itself; it is designated as a "condition" (*pratyaya*). To cite one example briefly:

when greed becomes defiled attachment toward an object, it can give rise to volition (*cetanā*) that initiates karma; this is termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Volitions of body and speech are the primary seeds that draw forth rebirth; therefore, they are called "the karma produced from the root.
When these correspond with the deluded craving at the moment of death, they can moisten the karma and produce rebirth; therefore, it is said that they "correspond with desire."
One should, regarding the place of future rebirth, form the perception of it as a lotus pond and so forth, falsely accepting it as pleasant; therefore, it is called "experiencing pleasure.

This is the affliction that moistens karma. From the second section, "Furthermore," onwards, there is the exhortation to extinguish it. From the third section, "I have already extinguished it," onwards, there is the citation of its extinction.

Next, regarding the three aspects of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): first, from "the exhaustion of suffering" up to "the Noble Truth of Right Cessation," it is shown that the other three truths have no place [therein], being tranquil, still, and unconditioned;
this is the essence of the Truth of Cessation. To cite those characteristics of cessation and thereby inspire joy in them is called the "turning through the indication of characteristics.

Second, from "furthermore" onwards is the "turning through the exhortation to realize. Third, from "I have already realized" onwards is the "turning through the citation of realization. First, I shall explain the initial turning. Regarding that:
Craving is forever exhausted; afflictions have no place. Without desire, karma is extinguished and has no place; this is the non-existence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Abandonment, renunciation, and liberation—the empty mind has no place. Once forever exhausted, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) has no place.

To take up this cessation and gather it in, thereby showing that [cessation] to inspire joy in birth, is called "turning by way of indicating characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-parivarta*). The latter two turnings may be understood according to the text.

Next, regarding the three aspects of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*): first, from the beginning up to "this is called the noble truth of the escape from suffering," the eightfold right path is presented and shown to them for cultivation;

this is termed the "turning that reveals the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapravartana*). Second, from "furthermore, one should cultivate it" onwards, it is the "turning that exhorts cultivation" (*anuśāsanapravartana*).

Third, from "I have already cultivated it" onwards, it is the "turning that leads to and exhorts cultivation. What is revealed as the characteristic is itself the path; there is no separate path to be cultivated.
In the second section on the successive increase [of benefits], each successive stage below is shown to possess six kinds of merit, encouraging one to practice and study.

Regarding the first turning of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there are six [benefits]: if one can cultivate the Path with revulsion toward suffering, one will certainly obtain these six benefits.

Why, then, would one not practice? "The arising of knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). "The arising of the eye" (*cakṣus*) refers to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). "The arising of clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
"Exhaustion" refers to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). "Arising through supernormal power" refers to the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).
"Arising through wisdom" refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-jñāna*). These are still the fruits of the middle way of the causal stage. Other categories are likewise so.

However, in this text, while both Suffering and its Origin are concluded, there is no concluding text for Cessation and the Path. "The Four" refers to the summary conclusion after the Four Noble Truths have been explained. Above.
The detailed explanation of the fourfold transformation is now complete.
Second, the general transformation consists of four parts. From the beginning up to "without doubt or obstruction," it establishes the unsurpassed path by citing oneself as proof.

"Why do you not cultivate that which I have realized?"—this second section, beginning with "The Tathāgata," cites those among the assembly who are suitable vessels for instruction and exhorts them to practice and study.
The third section, beginning with "Śramaṇas," clearly demonstrates that which worldly people cannot turn, but only a Buddha can turn;
it reveals the profound excellence of the Dharma and exhorts them to practice and study. The fourth section, beginning with "Therefore," is the actual...

This clearly enumerates the three preceding benefits and exhorts the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths. The phrase "for this reason" (*tasmāt*) reiterates the three preceding statements to conclude the exhortation to study.
Regarding the first "for this reason": it is because I have, through the three turnings of the twelvefold wheel of Dharma, known things as they truly are and thereby realized the Unsurpassed Way.

Regarding the second "for this reason": it is because the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma is fundamentally not turned in vain; whenever it is turned, it necessarily accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
Therefore, the third point, "therefore," means that this wheel of Dharma cannot be turned by those of the world; only a Buddha can turn it, for it is a profound and supreme wheel.
Why, then, do you not diligently practice in accordance with these three preceding meanings? Fourth, regarding the attainment of benefit and the realization of the Way:
because the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma, among the five bhikṣus, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to realize it. Therefore, the Buddha praised him, saying: "Without..."
Regarding Kauṇḍinya: "A" means "non-" (or "not"), and "yu" means "like. Because he was uniquely eminent among the five, he is called Aniruddha-Kauṇḍinya.

The fifth [section] concerns the successive proclamations that resounded throughout the invitation to the King; thus it says, "even as far as the Brahma Heaven. This concludes the preceding account of the causal origin (*nidāna*).
From here below is the second section, "Converting People through the 'Welcome' (Svāgata) [formula]. This major section contains six parts:
first, the conversion of the five bhikṣus; second, from Vārāṇasī onwards, the conversion of Yaśas;
third, from Vārāṇasī onwards, the conversion of Yaśas’s four companions; fourth, from Vārāṇasī onwards, the conversion of Yaśas’s fifty companions.
Fifth, from "At Vārāṇasī" onwards, the householder is addressed. Sixth, from "At Vārāṇasī" onwards, because of the Nāga King, Nalada is converted.
The initial section has three parts: first, it clarifies how the five persons received the precepts;

second, from "The World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the three persons" onwards, it properly clarifies how the Tathāgata preached the Dharma to transform and teach them, increasing their practice and understanding; third, the world... [text continues].

When the World-Honored One preached this Dharma, [Kauṇḍinya] immediately attained liberation, his afflictions were exhausted, and he realized the Way, becoming an Arhat free from attachment. The preceding text is further divided into three parts:

first, the conversion of Kauṇḍinya; second, the conversion of Aśvajit and Mahānāman; and third, the conversion of Bāṣpa. Regarding the section on Kauṇḍinya, there are three parts: first, his request for ordination;
second, from the Buddha’s words downward, the formal conferral of the precepts, up until the exhaustion of the source of suffering.

This refers to the power of the precepts; thus, it is designated as the first [stage]. In the third period, the Venerable One and those below him practiced this conduct and the aforementioned self-starvation;
the others may likewise be understood through these three categories. However, for the sake of others, he spoke by changing the terminology.

Regarding "generosity" (*dāna*): it refers to uplifting the wholesome and causing it to be cultivated; this is "active observance" (*vidhi-śīla*). Regarding "precept-keeping" (*śīla*): it refers to being able to abandon unwholesome dharmas; this is "restraint observance" (*saṃvara-śīla*).

Since one has already cultivated the wholesome and abandoned the unwholesome, one will necessarily be able to attain a superior retribution in the near future; therefore, it is called "the dharma for rebirth in heaven. To censure sensual desire as impure refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
To refer to the fetters of outflows (*āsrava*) as bondage refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). To praise renunciation as bliss [refers to the Truth of Cessation].
This refers to the two truths of Cessation (Nirodha) and the Path (Mārga).
Next, regarding the second discourse on the Dharma, in the text concerning the teaching given before the morning meal for three people:

as for the two who went begging for alms and so forth, each having different companions and differing in their going and staying, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (*Duolun*) offers one interpretation, stating that these three people were the father of the Buddha.

Because [the Buddha] was affectionate toward them and showed much love, and because these two were the Buddha’s mother and had seen him frequently, for these reasons the three and the two differed in their going and staying.

Furthermore, it is explained that he wished to demonstrate that the Dharma is not empty; since alms-gathering was successfully accomplished, he caused the three and the two to differ in their going and staying.
Following the meal, he preached to shatter their attachment to a self (*ātman*). Within this section, there are four parts: first, shattering their attachment to a self. Second...

The second section, beginning with "How so," examines the understanding of the bhikṣus. The third section, beginning with "Therefore, O bhikṣus," extensively employs analogies to refute [their views].
The fourth section, beginning with "The noble disciple, O bhikṣus," cultivates the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).

First, let us explain the initial passage. These five types of persons have all realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). For a *srotāpanna*, there is in reality no view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to be destroyed;

yet, what is here called "destruction" refers to the case where the mind perceives a self. Logically, such an attachment does not exist [in the realized one], yet there still remains a sense of "I" rooted in pride (*māna*).
Therefore, it is said that in the refutation within the text, one first addresses the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). This section contains three parts:
first, the monk [states] that form is not-self, establishing the thesis of non-self; second, two topical headings are established to explain the aforementioned non-self:
(1) because it is the suffering of suffering, it is not-self. Thus the text says: "If form were self, form would not be subject to increase, yet I experience [such increase]."

It is suffering, and it increases the experience of suffering; therefore, one knows there is no self. Second, if form were the self, [it would follow that] one lacks sovereignty; thus, there is no self.
Generally speaking, that which is called "self" must be something characterized by pleasure and sovereignty; yet, when we examine form now...
One does not attain mastery; one clearly knows there is no self. Third, because form is non-self, the following explains the two preceding gates.
From the beginning up to "suffering," this explains the first gate of suffering. From "nor can one obtain it at will" onwards, this explains the second gate of lack of mastery.
"Obtaining it whenever one desires" refers to the physical form of youth and vigor. "Not obtaining it even when one does not desire it" refers to [the onset of] old age and so forth.

This refers to the physical form that undergoes decay in old age; since it does not conform to one's desires, it is clearly understood to be without self (*anātman*). When observing the remaining four aggregates (*skandha*), the meaning of their being without self is the same.
The composition of this refutation of attachment does not differ from what preceded; therefore, it says, "it is also thus."

Next, within the assembly of bhikṣus, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is examined in detail: first, by inquiring whether it is permanent or impermanent; second, by inquiring whether it is suffering or pleasure; and third, by inquiring regarding the grasping at a self.
Once it is known to be an impermanent phenomenon subject to suffering and change, one asks: "Is this the self? If one says "it is," does one mean the self as an inherent nature of one's own person?
Or if one says "it is not," does one mean the self as an inherent nature of another person? Or does one mean "it is mine"? [If so, is it the self as an inherent nature of what belongs to oneself?]
These are the remaining four aggregates (*skandhas*). If form (*rūpa*) were the self, then feeling (*vedanā*) would be its servant, and so forth—these three combined make twelve propositions.

Within these, the notions "this is mine" and "that belongs to that" refer to the view of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*). Because the five bhikṣus each addressed the Buddha with their own understanding, he said "no.
Since the analytical meaning is identical regarding the remaining four aggregates, he stated that feeling, perception, and the others are likewise [not the self].

Thus it is. In the third section, "Extensive Classification and Refutation," the extensive [categories] are distinguished in contrast to form (*rūpa*). By citing all types of form, it is shown that they are all without self (*anātman*). Therefore, it says:
"All forms and so forth—whether internal, meaning the form of one's own body, or external, meaning the form of another's body."
If coarse, it refers to the four great elements and the five sense-faculties; if subtle, it refers to the form of the formless realm and the four objects of the senses.

If beautiful, it refers to pure and exquisite forms; if ugly, it refers to base and loathsome forms. If distant, it refers to forms outside of one's own body; if near, it refers to forms within one's own body.
That they are "not-self" is as you understand them: they are truly not of a fixed nature. That "I am not that" means that I am certainly not another person.
"Nature. "I am not that which belongs to them" means that one does not view the other four aggregates as "mine. "Not mine" means that one does not view the other four aggregates as "my self.
Regarding these four propositions, the first two—"not I" and "not that which belongs to them"—refute the view that the aggregates themselves are the self.
"Not that which belongs to them" and "not mine" refute the view of a self existing apart from the aggregates. Furthermore, the first two...
It is not that after the view of self, the two subsequent [views] are what is seen. One should practice such true and correct contemplation with wisdom;
this refers to cultivating the correct contemplation of non-self. This applies equally to the remaining aggregates (skandhas). Therefore, it says, "it is also thus."
Fourth is the correct cultivation of the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*). First, one discerns the faults of grasping at form (*rūpa*) by means of the middle way.

Therefore, it is called "disgust" (*nibbidā*). Because the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) abandons grasping, one is not attached; because one is no longer bound by the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), it is called "liberation.

When the four knowledges (*jñāna*) reach their culmination, one attains the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*). The same applies to the remaining four aggregates; therefore, it is said, "it is also thus. [This applies to] all five bhikṣus.

Regarding "liberation of the mind with outflows": this refers to liberation of the mind, meaning that one has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Regarding "one who has attained the knowledge of unimpeded liberation":

this refers to liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*), meaning such a person is one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). The four subsequent passages below can be understood accordingly.
The sixth reason is that a dragon king had previously heard this verse from the Buddha. Valuing the Dharma, he sought an explanation, but a brahmin who heard it was unable to understand it.
He slandered the Buddha until the verse was finally explained. Later, for the sake of the dragon king, [the Buddha] further expounded and interpreted it.

The dragon king immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling, heard the Dharma, and attained benefit. Having welcomed him, he received the precepts; thus, this verse is clarified. First, the original text of the sutra is set forth in two parts.
The verse consists of three stanzas by the Buddha as an explanation. The first stanza and a half sequentially explain the first six lines.
The next stanza explains the seventh line. The final two lines explain the eighth line. The six consciousnesses act as guides and all serve as kings;
yet the sixth is the strongest, capable of generating the roots of both good and evil, and is thus called "superior. Therefore, it is said: "The sixth king is superior."

This answers the first phrase. "The defiled one is equal to the defilement," etc., is explained according to the text. Karma and afflictions are, by their very nature, defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*);

they are termed "defilements. That which is produced by these defilements is called the "defiled one" (*rakta*). Since the "one" is not distinct from the "defilement," it is said to be "equal to the defilement.
This answers the second phrase. Because the active mind is free from afflictions such as greed, it is said to be "undefiled. Since it is... [text ends]
Because afflictions (*kleśa*) and the fetters of karma do not arise, it is called "stainless" (*vimala*). Thus, it is said that being unstained means being stainless; this answers the third phrase.

When one gives rise to the afflictions of karma and is entangled by defilements, one is called a "stained person. Because one is intoxicated by afflictions and is obscured regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*), one is termed "deluded.
Thus, it is said that a stained person is called deluded; this answers the fourth phrase. [The term] "ordinary" (*pṛthagjana*)...
Lacking wisdom, one is drifted away by the four currents; thus it is said that "the fool is drifted by the currents. This answers the fifth phrase.

Because understanding brings about the arising [of wisdom] while delusion leads to ruin, it is said that "one who can extinguish [them] possesses wisdom. This answers the sixth phrase. The four currents are not singular.

Therefore, it is said "all. Because they cause one to drift and drown, they are called "flows" (*ogha*). Once wisdom and understanding arise, these four flows are abandoned; thus it is said "one is able to relinquish.
This clarifies that because the causal flows are exhausted, the retributions of humans and devas cease; hence it says "devas and the world. This clarifies that the resultant flows are lost.
Being no longer associated with the flows, it refers back to the point where the causal flows were exhausted: one is not deluded by death. This refers back to the result.

At the place where the outflows are exhausted, cause and effect no longer exist; this clearly demonstrates the perfection of cessation. This answers the seventh phrase: "How is it that there are outflows and no outflows?

Wisdom arises from concentration; therefore, it is said that one can take mindfulness as the master. When samādhi is tranquil and still, it can give rise to the wisdom of contemplation according to reality (*yathābhūta*).
When wisdom arises, delusions perish, and one is no longer bound by the four outflows; therefore, it is called "liberation."
This half-verse answers the eighth point. Previously, the Dragon King, with a mind of negligence, damaged the leaves; among the long-lived dragons, this was not a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
One who holds a wrong view falls into hell. It is traditionally said that this is called the "Tree Leaf": a tree grows upon the head of the Dragon King, causing him great suffering.
Regarding the loss of those two extremes: it arose during the time of a previous Buddha and ceased after the subsequent Buddha had passed away. Later...
To escape this body, one must pass directly through two Buddhas; otherwise, emptiness provides no benefit. Therefore it is said:

"From here below, the second section concerns the person who attains ordination through the Three Refuges. This has three parts: first, the ritual for receiving the precepts through the Three Refuges; second, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One...

onwards, it again clarifies the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikṣu) ordination, which is named according to its original practice; hence it is called "the method of receiving [ordination] through the Three Refuges. Alternatively, it may also be understood thus.

From this point onward, the ritual of the Three Refuges arises; it is presented alongside the "Come hither" (ehi-bhikkhu) ordination. Thirdly, at that time, the World-Honored One cleared away the public censure.
The preceding section consists of four parts:
first, the Buddha praised his disciples as being capable of serving as teachers and guides; second, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus.

The section beginning with "Having already issued the command to travel and transform" concerns the third period, wherein the bhikṣus, having lost faith and understanding, provide the conditions for the Three Refuges.
The section beginning with "The Buddha said" correctly explains the ritual for receiving the Three Refuges. The first half-verse praises the perfection of his own virtues;

the second half-verse praises the disciples whose virtues are equal to what he himself has realized: "I have already been liberated from all causes of suffering, and [my afflictions] are exhausted. O Deva!
Furthermore, regarding the loss of the fruits and sufferings in the world: the second half [of the verse] is the same as above, differing only in that it specifically laments the disciples.

As for the "difficulties posed by Māra," these refer to the obstacles of heterodox persons and the obstacles of envy. [The opponent argues: "Since the Buddha and his disciples lack the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), how can they transform others?

The first half of the verse challenges [the claim] that the Buddha lacks the field of merit; the second half challenges [the claim] that the disciples are incomplete. "You are bound by all fetters" refers to the cause of suffering.

Not yet exhausted. As long as the afflictions of the fruit remain unextinguished for both gods and those in the world, and all the bonds that bind them persist, my disciples cannot escape these two afflictions of cause and fruit;
thus, the śramaṇa cannot attain liberation. In summary, both types of persons fail to escape these faults. I am liberated from all bonds;
conditions cannot restrain me, and the afflictions of the cause are exhausted. Thus, the afflictions of the fruit for both gods and those in the world are extinguished, and all bonds are severed.
"You have attained liberation; you have demonstrated that for a disciple, both cause and effect have perished. I am now superior to you. Thus he concluded his victory in general.

The Māra King could not distinguish [the truth] and again raised an objection: "The external person's conceptual calculation holds that the nature of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) is that which binds.

Internally, there are the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), which are likewise of the nature of bondage. If you do not perceive them, then it is as it may; but if you perceive them, you are bound. You possess internal fetters and bonds within."

This means that the nature of the five consciousnesses is the essence of bondage. Because the minds of the five consciousnesses take the five sense objects as their conditions, it is said that "the mind moves within [them].
When conditioned, one is bound; one is pursued and fettered by evil karma. Therefore, it is said: "By this, you are pursued. This difficult cause of affliction has not yet been extinguished.
Since the cause of accumulation exists, future suffering will inevitably be summoned. It entangles and binds the śramaṇa; therefore, it is said: "No."
[They] have attained liberation. This difficult fruit of suffering has not yet perished. The intention behind the Tathāgata’s reply was this:
the mental calculations of outsiders know only the five consciousnesses and do not perceive the sixth, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, the Tathāgata said:

"If even the sixth mental consciousness of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not defiled by the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), how much more so for me, whose desires are severed and exhausted, whose inner mind is pure—though it may take the five sense objects as its conditions, what [defilement could there be]?"
Because there can still be defilement, he says: "There are five desires in the world, yet I have no desire for them.

When these two afflictions are exhausted, one transcends your realm; therefore he says: "I have now surpassed you. His eloquence is difficult to withstand, and the heretics, though haughty, are subdued.
Feeling unhappy in his heart, he vanished from sight as if departing. Once Yana had been sent away, the entire clan addressed him again with the remaining three [precepts] as written in the text.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), the brothers of the cow-chewing bhikṣu led seventy thousand people to the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon them all by means of the "three-fold proclamation."
Next, the section on the *ehibhikṣu* (Come, monk) formula is explained in three parts: first, the ordination of fifty companions; second, the ordination of one thousand people from Uruvilvā;
and third, the ordination of Śāriputra and others, numbering two hundred and fifty. Regarding the section on the ordination of Kāśyapa, there are also three parts:

first, arriving at the reception of full ordination through the *ehibhikṣu* formula for himself and the ordination of one thousand people; second, the time when the Buddha ordained one thousand brahmins.
Thereafter, he went down to Mount Elephant Head (*Gajaśīrṣa*) and taught them three matters. At that time, the thousand bhikṣus, having received these three matters, practiced as instructed.

They attained the Way and became free from attachment. They extensively manifested supernatural transformations and converted Kāśyapa, causing him to abandon his former heterodoxy and follow the truth. [They said:
"Those like us who have attained arhatship do not falsely cling to the notion that we have personally realized the fruit of sainthood."
Śreṇika wished to subdue his mind, yet he abandoned the fruit while clinging to the cause, claiming that his own path was great and that it was the true road leading to Nirvāṇa;
thus he said, "Your Way is not as true as mine. Knowing that he was about to be subdued, the Buddha simultaneously negated both of these views, stating that he was not an Arhat.

This is not the fruit of sainthood; it does not lead toward the path of an Arhat. Since the "Great Matter" (大事) is not the cause for proceeding toward sainthood, and having heard that both the cause and the fruit are non-existent, he abandoned the Great Matter and fully undertook the renunciation and reception of the precepts. He then ordained his two younger brothers and subsequently went to Mount Elephant Head (Gajaśīrṣa).
Regarding these three matters of instruction, they demonstrate how these bhikṣus obtained [realization] by relying upon the appropriate time, place, and companions.

Because of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). First, teaching through the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhipāda*) means using the power of physical transformation to inspire widespread faith.

Second, teaching through the supernormal power of recollection (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) means knowing the mental inclinations of sentient beings through the power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and bestowing the appropriate remedy according to their capacity.

Third, teaching through the exposition of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*) means using the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) to correctly instruct others to initiate practice and sever the outflows. This was first explained in detail with respect to the faculty of the eye.
The first part of the middle section provides a general summary of the blazing; thus it says, "all are ablaze. From the question "What are they?
onwards, there is a detailed enumeration of the blazing. Within this, there are two sections: the first clarifies the blazing of the causes, and from "Furthermore, how...
onwards, it clarifies the blazing of the results. Within the causes, there are four parts. First, it presents the three conditions for the blazing, beginning with the eye.

Regarding "blazing": this refers to the arising of blazing through the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Regarding "the blazing of form": this refers to the arising of blazing within the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding "the blazing of eye-consciousness": this refers to the arising of blazing within the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Regarding "the second, the blazing of eye-contact":

one explanation states that this refers to the arising of blazing through conjunction (*sāmagrī*), which is categorized solely as contact (*sparśa*). Furthermore, according to the *Tattva-śāstra* (The Treatise on Reality):
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the beginning of the provisional; it is termed "contact" (*sparśa*). Because the three poisons arise from the three perceptions, it is said that "eye-contact is ablaze.

Third, regarding the passage beginning with "If again... and so forth: the nature of the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) as karmic retribution is neutral (*avyākṛta*), yet it is not that the three afflictions do not arise based on these three feelings;
therefore, they are also called "ablaze. Fourth, regarding the passage beginning with "What is... and so forth:

The three fires of affliction: this refers to the arising of three types of afflictions within the active mind, which burn away a person’s roots of goodness; these constitute the essence of the blazing fire.
Next is the blazing of the fruit, which clearly explains how the eight sufferings incinerate pleasant sensations; therefore, it is called the blazing of the fruit. This is what I have taught.
Regarding "the place where suffering arises": the preceding causes are ablaze; this is the place where the eight types of suffering originate.
To bring about the cessation of the cause, since the fruit is naturally lost when the cause perishes, it is said: "I declare this to be the place where suffering arises.

If compared with the other five [sense organs], they do not differ from the eye faculty. They are explained in relation to one another to clarify the blazing of cause and effect; therefore, it is said that "up to the mind, it is also like this."
This is so. The third passage may be understood.
Next, regarding the passage on the conversion of Śāriputra and others, there are two parts. First, concerning the location where he accepted the Bamboo Grove and the conditions for his conversion:

although the King had originally invited the Buddha, saying, "If you have attained the Way, please first accept my invitation," the Buddha did not go to the King's invitation immediately; rather, he delayed in order to convert the thousand [monks].
When the people had already departed, he then considered accepting the invitation. There are two reasons for this: first, because the faculties of sentient beings were not yet mature;

furthermore, because they proceed concurrently with the *tri-vācika-karman*, and moreover, because in this initial case, there has been no instruction, examination, or supervision.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics [of the formal act], only the *jñapti-caturtha* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is cited;

this does not mean that other elements are omitted. In the section concerning the second party—the officiating person—there are two parts. The first, up to the point where it says "the preceptor and the two teachers share the same conduct," explains the conduct of the two teachers.

The second, beginning with "there are five qualities," clarifies the virtues of the two teachers. Question: What is the distinction between conduct (*caryā*) and virtue (*guṇa*)? Answer: Conduct refers to...

One first cultivates skillful means; when virtue is established and perfected to fulfillment, and both essential practice and virtue are fully prepared, only then may one be permitted to deliver others.

Furthermore, "virtue" may refer to liberative wisdom—the understanding that penetrates the characteristics of phenomena—but this does not necessarily entail [extensive] practice, nor is such a person permitted to deliver others.

Alternatively, one might be able to cultivate practice according to the teachings, yet not necessarily possess the understanding that penetrates the characteristics of phenomena; such a person is likewise not permitted to deliver others. It is essential to possess both understanding and practice; thus we know.

The practice of virtue has distinctions. The preceding text consists of three parts. The first, up to the point where it says "the texts are the same and not different," refers to the method of gathering disciples by means of seven types of conduct, wherein they mutually look after and support one another.
The second part, from "at that time the disciples were no longer respectful" onwards, correctly clarifies how the disciples did not honor the teacher's commands and did not accept his instruction;
the teacher then rebuked them, and despite their transgressions, he continued to gather them in. The third...

In the section beginning with "The third, the teacher Jìng-bhikṣu," the text clearly explains which persons are subject to censure and which are not. This preceding passage is further divided into two parts:

first, up to the point where it says "governing according to the Dharma," it concerns the methods for conducting oneself in harmony; second, from there on, it concerns the preceptor’s careful supervision of lapses and omissions.

If there is no fault of intention, one should employ skillful means to enlighten them and instruct them to perform repentance and purification, as in the previous seven methods. This concludes the first five.
Regarding those who are difficult to speak with: this refers to when a teacher’s instruction is met with total refusal and rejection, such that they do not accept the teaching;

or when, having received the teacher’s words, they do not act according to what was said; or when they associate with evil people, or take pleasure in visiting the houses of courtesans, the houses of women, or the homes of young maidens.

Regarding "households," "eunuch households," "nuns' monasteries," "śikṣamāṇās," and so forth: because [the Buddha] feared that such places might give rise to censure or obstruct the cultivation of the right practice, he would reprimand each instance as it occurred.
Only then can one abandon evil conduct and achieve the benefit of progress in cultivation;
it does not require waiting until the full term is completed. Among these fifteen faults, when speaking in contrast to nuns, one should say "great male novice" (mahā-śrāmaṇera).
The monasteries for bhikṣus and the monasteries for śrāmaṇeras are collectively criticized. The remainder applies to both communities. Regarding the third criticism concerning transgressions:
having been reprimanded, if one commits an offense by providing services [to the reprimander], this refers to the original third period.

Since one has not yet offered [the reprimander] joy, to suddenly perform tasks for him only serves to increase his irritation and vexation; therefore, it is stated below that one incurs an offense if one does not perform duties for the upādhyāya.

This refers to one who originally committed the second *āpatti* of *utkṣepaṇīya-karman*, yet out of resentment refused to perform the duties required of a servant; for this reason, he incurs an offense.

As for "this disciple is not in the proper order, yet receives provisions": because the *upādhyāya* is not in the proper order, the *niśraya-śiṣya* (dependent disciple) is also not in the proper order.
To provide *niśraya* to one who is not in the proper order is improper for an *ācārya*. "Lowering one's mind to comply and seeking skillful means to resolve the transgression" refers to:

From the section "Initially Receiving the Preceptor" downward, during the four occasions of reprimand, one is absolutely not permitted to offer self-justification or exculpation; one may only perform repentance three times daily.
Only thereafter may one speak with gentle words to personally clear away one's transgression; thus it is said that one employs skillful means to resolve what has been committed.
If one diligently seeks to resolve a transgression, the preceptor should instruct them on how to remit the offense; otherwise, the preceptor incurs a fault.
The third section, concerning those who are or are not subject to censure, consists of two parts. First, a general explanation of the loss and non-loss of dependence (*niśraya*).
Second, from "The World-Honored One traveled to Rājagṛha" onwards, the formal explanation of the rules regarding the loss of dependence. The preceding section contains seven points:

first, two types of persons—those who delight in solitude and so forth—are permitted to remain without dependence, as they establish themselves through their own practice. Second, the monk’s firm resolve...
The two sets of four propositions following "having gone outside the boundary" concern whether the mind temporarily or permanently loses or does not lose [the precepts].

The third set of four propositions, beginning with "the one about to receive the precepts having gone outside the boundary," clarifies that one must rely on a person who is fit to provide formal instruction (*niśraya*) and who is subject to censure.

The fourth set, beginning with "he dispatches a messenger to receive the *niśraya*," concerns the faults of both teacher and disciple. The fifth [set] concerns the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) going outside the boundary.

The following two lines state that although one has not gone away permanently, because the intention was to go for at least one night, the precepts are lost even upon crossing the boundary; this also distinguishes the characteristics [of the offense].

The sixth section, beginning with "the sick bhikṣu," consists of two lines concerning the permission to be without a formal mentor (*niśraya*). The seventh section, beginning with "that preceptor having been subjected to the *karmavācanā*," consists of five pairs concerning the forfeiture and non-forfeiture through remedial punishments.

The second [point] concerns the temporary and permanent [nature of the departure] from the mind. Regarding the first two phrases: one resolves to leave the boundary with the intention of not returning;
even if one returns on that very day, at the moment of leaving the boundary, the basis of dependence (*niśraya*) has already been lost. As for the two phrases in the fifth section, the text says:
"If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or instructor (*ācārya*) departs and will return before long, I shall remain in dependence upon them. In such a case, one remains without a formal basis of dependence.

The Buddha said: "If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the instructor (*ācārya*) goes beyond the boundary on a journey, one must immediately seek another person to rely upon; failing to do so is contrary to the Dharma and constitutes an offense.

Furthermore, if a junior disciple goes far beyond the boundary on a journey and thinks, 'I shall return before long,' he may continue to dwell under the reliance of his current preceptor and instructor.
The Buddha declared that a newly ordained person who requires reliance must not first drink water or perform other such acts [without having formally established reliance]."
"Even until one has first received formal dependence (*niśraya*). These two phrases refer to cases where, although one does not return for long, one nevertheless intends to stay overnight on the way;

this is the same as the previous two phrases regarding the firm intention to go beyond the boundary. However, because one stays overnight while away from the boundary, at the time of departing the boundary, one must still maintain formal dependence.
These four phrases all constitute a loss of dependence due to a separation of mind, because there is only a single [person] upon whom dependence is placed, and thus it is deficient.

There is no taking up [of the precepts]. When two parties mutually relinquish their feelings, the separation does not depend on a physical distance; therefore, a mental separation constitutes a loss of the boundary [of the vow].

If there is no intention to temporarily depart, yet an unexpected overnight stay occurs, it is lost only if there is no *kṣaṇika* (exceptional circumstance); if there is such a *kṣaṇika*, it is not lost. If there is no *kṣaṇika*, it is lost immediately.
There is no fault of being separated by an intervening night, because one who intends to go away for good does not wait for the passing of the night.
If one temporarily leaves the boundary, this likewise does not constitute a loss [of the robe]. These last two lines of the present text concern the two matters of the robe and the summer retreat.
Only the fault of being separated by both [factors] applies. The fault of being separated by distance is as previously explained regarding the basis of reliance (*niśraya*). Question:

If one loses the basis of reliance on the very same day, what kind of dharma is lost when it is said that one has "lost the basis of reliance"? Answer: There are three types of reliance: first, the dharma of requesting a teacher for reliance;
second, the dharma of dwelling in mutual dependence; and third, the dharma of requesting instruction and reporting matters. This is according to the formal ritual procedure (*vidhi*).
Regarding the request to become a teacher: the former request constitutes the *balotpādana* (generation of power), while the latter constitutes the *niśraya* (dependence).

If one instructs according to the rules and procedures of the latter two dharmas, it is termed "dependence"; thus, both the generation of power and the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*) are termed "dependence. Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"If the Upādhyāya and Ācārya intentionally go outside the boundary, the Buddha declared that the dependence is lost; this establishes the grounds for the loss [of dependence]."

"Loss" refers to the loss of the two lower dharmas; it does not mean the loss of the dharma of requesting a teacher. For example, if one loses [the status of] an upādhyāya, how could one truly lose the upādhyāya himself?

Furthermore, it may be said that one "loses" [the status of dependence] because, being deficient in the two lower dharmas, the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) does not arise in continuous succession; thus, one is said to have lost reliance.

Later, if one returns, there is no need to perform the formal act (*karma*) of requesting a teacher again; one simply makes the mental resolve to rely and abide, and makes the formal declaration (*jñapti*).

Regarding the equality of these matters, there is still a basis for reliance upon which unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) continues to arise. If one considers the four permutations regarding robes and the summer retreat, the cases where the mind and the object are both separated constitute a loss [of the vow].
This differs from the case of relying on a physical support, where the loss occurs when the mind is separated but not both; in those two latter cases, there is no loss.
The third case involves the distinction between loss and non-loss due to an intervening night; this is difficult to explain in response to objections. Question:

Why is it that an intervening night causes the loss of the *niśraya* (dependence), whereas the same does not apply to the robes? Answer: The *niśraya* pertains to the mental path; since both parties mutually effect its relinquishment, it is lost as soon as one departs.

If one does not form the intention to relinquish both [the robe and the dwelling], the loss of the "separation from the robe" (*nissaggiya*) occurs only after an overnight stay; this is appropriate for the *vassa* (rainy season retreat).

This is because I have the intention to relinquish him, while he lacks the intention to relinquish me; thus, it is necessary that both the mind and the night be separated for the loss to occur. Question:

If there is no offense when one is separated from a *niśraya* (place of dependence), why is there an offense for being separated from a robe during the summer retreat? Answer: The permission to be separated from a *niśraya* applies when one has gone to another location.
The Buddha has prescribed that one may seek a new formal reliance (*niśraya*). If one departs in accordance with this instruction, there is no offense even if the robes are lost.

However, the Buddha does not permit departing from one's robes or breaking the summer retreat (*varṣā*); therefore, if these are lost or broken, there is an offense. Question: Why is the offense for losing the robes heavy, while the offense for breaking the summer retreat is light?

Answer: The three robes are monastic vestments that specifically provide for the sustenance of the body; because they are essential and urgent, they are treated with gravity. Although the summer retreat may be broken, the cultivation of practice can still be maintained;
therefore, the offense for breaking it is light.

The third and fourth lines clarify that there is no formal instruction from a teacher; for those who are unacquainted with the characteristics of the Dharma, it is mandated that they rely upon others to inquire about and receive the teachings on the Dharma.
According to the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*, when one preceptor and three *karmavācanā* masters confer full ordination upon three individuals simultaneously, they all attain the precepts at the same time.
Regarding the seniority of precepts, there is no distinction of great or small. Ānanda, if there is one Preceptor and one Precept-Master, two or three people may receive the precepts simultaneously;

this is not said to be difficult. However, because Upāli had two śrāmaṇeras, he feared that if they received them at different times, one might harbor resentment toward the other and not know how to attain [the precepts].
[Upāli asked: "May two people from a single assembly receive the precepts simultaneously under one Preceptor and one Precept-Master? The Buddha [permitted it].

It is said that it is permissible. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* also states: When the two śrāmaṇeras Upasena—one named Datta and the other Pāla—were about to receive the precepts, Datta said, "First, you must accept my offerings of whatever you require," and the other did likewise.

Upasena asked the Buddha, "Is it permissible to receive the precepts for two śrāmaṇeras simultaneously? The Buddha replied, "It is permissible," and immediately issued the *karmavācanā*. This is recorded in the eighth fascicle of this Vinaya.

[Question: Difficult. [Answer: Other circumstances permit two or three people to perform a *karmavācanā* simultaneously, but it must not exceed that number. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if there is one *upādhyāya* and one *śīla-ācārya* for a group, even those who have received the precepts imperfectly may attain them;
other similar cases are all valid. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* records that Upāli asked whether a *karmavācanā* could be performed by three people when asking about other matters.
The Buddha said: "It is permitted. This is because it is not the same as the formal act of conveying a proxy vote (*chanda*) or commissioning someone on a mission. Therefore, [it is permitted].
The first three cases have been explained; the fourth may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the fifth, the rule for relying on a teacher (*niśraya*) is established to clarify the distinctions between what is permissible and what is prohibited. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one lacks a teacher to rely upon, one is not permitted even to drink water or wear the inner robes within the monastery;
such an act incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Later, due to various difficulties, the Buddha said: "From now on, I permit [the practice] without receiving formal reliance."
The dependence lasts for up to six nights; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is the same. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states that the seventh teacher refutes the seven formal acts (*karmas*).

Regarding the treatment of one who has not lost their dependence: this means they have not lost the two aforementioned types of dharmas, but they should lose the dharma of requesting instruction and admonition.

If the teacher has committed an offense and is undergoing disciplinary treatment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), yet the practice of the Dharma remains within himself and the disciple is pure, then if he requests instruction, it would cause the teacher to incur further fault.
Among the thirty-five [cases] below, those in whom one may not receive dependence (*niśraya*) mean that one may not request instruction from them;

they may also be undergoing disciplinary treatment and thus may not accept the request to serve as a teacher of dependence. If the disciple is the one undergoing disciplinary treatment, all three [parties] lose nothing.

One must seek the teacher’s instruction and admonition, act in accordance with the monastic laws, and seek swift resolution from the Saṃgha; thus, when two persons observe one another, there is no fault of "following the suspension" (anuvartana).

Whether the formal act of banishment has been performed or not, both lose their status as a *niśraya* (reliance). The reason for mentioning only those who have already been suspended is that this serves as an antidote to the previous formal procedure, so as not to lose public confidence.
The underlying intention is that even if the act of banishment were performed, it would still not constitute a loss [of reliance]; it is for the sake of dispelling such doubts that this is stated.

It is necessary to cite specifically the formal procedures (*vidhi*) in order to clarify the transgressions. As for those who may be subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya*), once their misconduct has been made manifest, there is no longer the principle of mutual reliance or instruction;

therefore, the text speaks of "loss" [of the precepts]. Although one may have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), as long as it has not been made public, they still maintain mutual reliance, and thus there is no loss.
*Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Fascicle Seven, Part One;
*Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Fascicle Seven, Part Two.

Second, the explicit explanation of losing one’s *niśraya* (dependence). This section has two parts: from the beginning up to "he reported the circumstances to the World-Honored One" constitutes the first part. The second part...

After the World-Honored One had finished speaking, the following section correctly establishes the limits of the transgressions. Regarding "one who is five years old and possesses wisdom," this refers to one who has just entered their fifth summer retreat;
such a person must rely on a preceptor who is ten years senior. If one is foolish and lacks wisdom, they must rely [on a preceptor] for as long as life lasts.
In the text, the number is increased to eight and five; if the specific cases are distinguished, there are nine or eight. First, the aforementioned passage states that...
1. Expulsion; 2. Death; 3. Departure; 4. Cessation of the path; 5. Reprimand by the teacher; 6. Injury to the precepts; 7.
Being more than five years [of standing]; 8. Seeing one’s original *upādhyāya*; 9. Returning to dwell under the supervision of the *upādhyāya*.

Now, regarding these eight, the five distinct characteristics are actually only eight, because the first [category] includes expulsion, making nine. As for the statement that there are eight: among the first five, the fourth is excluded.

Because it is not granted [as a formal support], it is identical to the first [case]. Next, within the five [periods], there are two [types]: namely, death during the fifth year. Within the third set of five, there is one;
within the eighth set of five, there are four intermediate [periods] out of the five, which are entirely identical and without difference.

Regarding the nine [cases], in the upper four, if both master and disciple possess [the fault], they both lose [their status]; in the lower five, it concerns only the disciple. The master reprimands [him].
This refers to the five types of non-reproach by the Saṃgha. Sixth is the loss [of status] upon entering the boundary of the precept-platform (*sīmā*).

Since this is a place where separate disciplinary procedures (*pṛthag-dharma*) are performed, those who are young and ignorant may be easily misled by others; thus, the status is lost immediately upon entry, without waiting for the completion of a night’s stay.

This is because it differs from being outside the boundary, which is not a place where separate disciplinary procedures are performed. If that is so, then temporarily going out to another major boundary (*mahāsīmā*) would likewise constitute a separate disciplinary procedure.

Regarding the location: why is it not stated that one loses [the status] by entering another boundary? One explanation is that its meaning is the same as that of the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept platform), and thus it is not discussed separately.

Furthermore, another great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is also a place where the Saṃgha permanently resides; since the sense of "ruining" is rare there, one does not lose [the status]. It is like how a *karmavastu* (work site) requires a formal summons;
how could it be that within another great boundary one is restricted by saying a summons is required? Therefore, we know they are not analogous. Seven.
Regarding those aged five years or older: because they possess self-awareness, they do not require formal instruction. For this reason, there is a discrepancy in the wording. Question:
Why does the text state that a bhikṣu of five years' standing should seek a wise bhikṣu of ten years' standing as his preceptor (niśraya)? Answer:

This statement regarding the need for a preceptor refers to one who has just entered his fifth summer retreat (*pañca-varṣa*), not to one who has completed five years without losing [the status]. If this were not stated, it would imply...

Upon entering the fifth summer retreat, one is immediately exempt from dependence on a teacher; this refers, therefore, to those who possess wisdom. As for a person of dull intellect, they must remain dependent for as long as they live.

If one sees that their original *upādhyāya* (preceptor) has passed away, and there is no vacancy to fill in the position of the original *upādhyāya*, then because the fundamental source is lost, there is no vacancy to be filled, and thus [the status] is lost.

Regarding those who reside under the direct supervision of a *upādhyāya*: if they first relinquish their status as a teacher of others (*saṃgraha*), they do not lose [their own status] even if [the preceptor] passes away.
Now, he returns to receive [the precepts], thereby rectifying his current state of loss. This may also be seen as the restoration of the conduct of one's original Upādhyāya.
Regarding the "current state": when a disciple returns from another realm, he initially forms a temporary intention, but upon arriving at the teacher’s place, he adopts it as a permanent resolve.

Therefore, the dwelling [of the preceptor] is lost. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, in a time of famine when one is about to die of hunger, what is the use of relying [on a preceptor]? The Buddha said:
"If one cannot see the upādhyāya day by day, if that is not possible, it is permitted for five days. If one cannot see him after five days, it is permitted to come at the time of the *poṣadha*.
If one still cannot see him upon arriving at the time of the *poṣadha*, then [one may go] as far as two and a half *yojanas*."
Upon arriving at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he came to see his preceptor (*upādhyāya*).

Next, the second section clarifies the virtues of the two masters. These are presented in pairs of opposites, each consisting of eight sets of five. The first ten apply exclusively to the noble ones (*ārya*);
the subsequent thirty apply to both the noble and the ordinary (*pṛthagjana*). When their actual substance is examined, there are only thirty-nine [qualities], as the sixth...
Because one [factor] is missing.

Third, from this point downward, is the section on those who are the objects of the instruction. Within this, there are two parts: first, up to the section on "price," which generally clarifies the prohibitions and difficulties;

second, from "darkness" and below, which specifically clarifies the prohibitions and difficulties. Alternatively, the preceding text provides a brief clarification of the prohibitions and difficulties.

The section following "Darkness" provides an extensive analysis of the refutations (*dūṣaṇa*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*). Because it is all-encompassing, there are seventeen matters within the preceding text;
the first and seventh are refutations, while the remainder are collectively termed prohibitions. First, I shall explain the first [refutation], which refutes the internal and external paths.

Within this, there are four parts: first, clarifying that after the *poṣadha* and ordination (*pravrajyā*), one performs actions that subvert the internal [teachings], and reporting this to the Buddha.
The second section, beginning with "The Buddha spoke," teaches the method for ordaining [monks] according to the rules for testing their fitness.

The third section, beginning with "At the time of the *poṣadha*," records his returning again to inform the Buddha. The fourth section, beginning with "The Buddha spoke," demonstrates the accomplishment of difficult deeds. The first of these sections further contains four parts.

First, regarding the mind that subdues through debate, the essence of the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is solely wisdom (*prajñā*). To be skillfully proficient and unimpeded regarding all phenomena of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called "analytical eloquence of Dharma" (*dharma-pratibhāna*).
To be profoundly in accord with the meaning of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called "analytical eloquence of meaning" (*artha-pratibhāna*).

Alternatively, being skilled in knowing the conventional truth is called "analytical eloquence of meaning," while penetrating the ultimate truth is "analytical eloquence of Dharma. Having thus recognized these two...

One must bestow [the teaching] in accordance with the capacity of the recipient; having deeply mastered the medicines for the various faculties without obstruction, this is called "clarity of discernment" (*pratibhāna*), also called "appropriate discernment," and also called "joyful eloquence. Being skilled in local dialects, one’s speech flows with grace, remaining entirely unimpeded.

This is called eloquence. One who possesses these four types of eloquence cannot be refuted by outsiders; since there is no such principle [that they could], it is said that "there is no such possibility.
In the *Pañcavargika*, Śāriputra debated with non-Buddhists, beginning on the first day and continuing until the sixth day.
He discussed other matters until all were rendered speechless; they remained silent for seven days.
Śāriputra then said, "All worldly desires fundamentally arise from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Dwelling upon the basis of worldly desire, one develops a mind of attachment.
A non-Buddhist challenged him, saying, "If desire arises from conceptualization and results in attachment, then the evil thoughts and reflections of a bhikṣu would already constitute [desire]."
[He] lost his brahmacarya. Śāriputra countered, saying: "Desire does not arise from mere thought; it arises from sensory opposition.
When your teacher beholds various forms, why does he not experience pleasure? Upasīva did not understand; he abandoned [his life] and went forth as a renunciant.
These words were a pressing challenge because they were logically compelling. At that second moment, he immediately gave rise to a thought, and thereafter, out of faith, he went forth. Third...
Below the section "At a later time," the internal karma of schism is established. From the fourth section, "The bhikṣus," onwards, having raised the matter, they inform the Venerable One.

Second, the method for testing through the *jñapti* (motion) is explained; herein there are four parts: first, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) for testing; second, the preliminary...

He did not grant them full ordination because he wished to provide the śrāmaṇeras with something upon which they could rely, and because he feared that if he were to grant it prematurely, their practice might regress and become difficult.

Thirdly, he tested them for four months through correct practice. This was intended to demonstrate that these outsiders had long adhered to heterodox views and that their faith was not yet firmly established;

had he granted them full ordination immediately, they certainly would not have been able to deeply accord with the profound essence of the school. To examine their faith, it was necessary to subject them to this trial.
This refers to requesting a four-month period of co-residence (*sārdha-vihāra*) because one remains within the boundary (*sīmā*).

As for the other three Vinayas and both the *Mātṛkā* treatises, they all state that this is a separate residence (*pārivaśa*). The *Mahāsāṃghika* and *Dharmaguptaka* Vinayas speak of requesting separate residence and granting separate residence;
the *Daśabhāṇavāra* Vinaya speaks of requesting *pārivāsa* and granting *pārivāsa*. This is because one must not dwell together with those [monks] in the same location. The *Mātṛkā*...
Treatise: A follower of an external path (*tīrthika*) should undergo a four-month period of separate residence (*parivāsa*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "What is meant by 'separate residence'?

If a follower of an external path wishes to leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they must reside with a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) for four months. Only after the fourth month has been verified as a time when their mind is found to be joyful may they proceed to receive full ordination.
If they have already attained the Path in its entirety, they do not need to wait for the four months to be completed; they are immediately ordained. Those who are not like this [are different]."
One must wait for four months; this can be understood from the two texts [of the *Mahīśāsaka* and *Dharmaguptaka* Vinayas] regarding the third and fourth cases. Second, regarding slaves:

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya*, there are five kinds of slaves—those purchased, those captured, and those born in the household. These three types are not permitted here, nor are they permitted elsewhere.

The other two—those given by others and those who come of their own accord—are permitted elsewhere. Third, regarding thieves; fourth, regarding those with debts; fifth, regarding those whose age has been reduced; sixth, the five [categories].

Sickness. Seven *pārājika* offenses. The text has four parts: first, committing a *pārājika* and not concealing it; second, granting training (*śikṣamāṇā*) or probation (*parivāsa*); third, the forfeiture of thirty-five [robes];

fourth, removing doubts regarding advancement or regression. Eighth, parents do not permit [ordination]. Ninth, restricting physical form as in the two types of *jñapti*. Tenth, ordaining those under twelve years of age;

this was opened up because one capable of driving away crows could be ordained. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, a *kākavācaka-śrāmaṇera* (crow-driving novice) is eight years old; according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the maximum age is eighty.
Seventy years. The minimum age is seven years; if one exceeds or falls short of this, one may not be granted ordination.
From seven to thirteen years of age, one is a *kākavāṇa-śrāmaṇera* (crow-driving novice). From fourteen to nineteen, one is a *dharmika-śrāmaṇera* (dharma-compliant novice).

From twenty to seventy, one is a *nāmamātra-śrāmaṇera* (nominal novice). According to the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*, [the minimum] is seven years. Eleventh, it is not permitted to maintain two novices [simultaneously]. Hereafter...

Second, regarding the opening for ordination: In the twelfth [case], having received [the precepts], one may harbor doubts; therefore, it is permitted to count the number of those in the womb and so forth to demonstrate that the precepts have been obtained.

If one has attained Arhatship, they are called a "fully ordained" (upasampadā) person; this refers to the "higher dharma" method of receiving [ordination]. Next, the small boundary (sīmā) is demarcated; in the procedure for receiving the precepts, the specific number of persons is not stated.
It is simply because the assembly of monks has gathered that the size of the boundary (*sīmā*) is not known; in principle, it would also be difficult to know.
Furthermore, there is no preceptor (*upādhyāya*), for [an ordination] with two, three, many, or more [preceptors] is not valid.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a bhikṣu might take one person as a preceptor, or two, three, four, five, or even ten people as preceptors. The Buddha said: "One person shall be the preceptor; one should not have two."

Up to ten people. According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing), one may not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) without a preceptor (*upādhyāya*). If one does confer it, the Saṃgha commits a *duṣkṛta* offense, though the person receives the precepts.

The same applies when there are more than ten. According to the *Shi duolun* (Daśottara-vibhāṣā-śāstra), if one receives full ordination through *karmavācanā* and the preceptor is not present, the precepts are not obtained because the number of the Saṃgha is incomplete; if the number is complete, they are obtained. This Vinaya, however, is not so.
Next, the four reliances are explained. Previously, there were four instances of ordaining [persons], and now there are five parts. The King established a regulation:

if anyone should ordain another again, the preceptor’s ribs shall be broken, the ācārya’s tongue shall be cut out, and the remaining monks shall be whipped with raw leather lashes eight times and driven out of the country.
Ji had three of his ribs broken by the Upādhyāya, and his tongue was pulled out by the Preceptor. Each member of the ten-member assembly struck him eight times with a whip.

The judicial official administered this punishment and brought him before King Bimbisāra. The King asked, "Who is the king? He replied, "The king is the king. The King said, "Release him; let him go forth into the religious life as he pleases.
Because they had punished him arbitrarily without informing the King, their offices and wealth were confiscated. This is what is meant by "office" (guan).

Regarding persons: there are those who have a name but no official rank (lu), and those who have both a name and an official rank. In this country and other countries, neither of these two categories is permitted to receive ordination.
As for the remaining two [categories], this country does not permit it, but other countries do permit ordination. Next, regarding receiving the precepts by borrowing the three robes:

in principle, it is possible to obtain the precepts. This is because the disciple knows that borrowing is improper; however, if they do not know that they cannot obtain the precepts, yet maintain the intention that they can obtain them, then they do obtain the precepts. This is to be judged accordingly.
Upādhyāya, as for the first three phrases, these constitute five parts. One should ask whether the disciple’s robes and bowl are complete.

If he says they are complete, one should ask whether they are his own or borrowed from another. If he says they were borrowed from someone, one should tell him that he may have the owner relinquish them.
The second section, "Avoiding and Clarifying Obstacles," consists of two parts. The first, extending up to the point of "expulsion" (*pārājika*), specifically clarifies the obstacles.

The second, beginning from "At that time, the one about to receive the precepts does not state their own name," separately clarifies the various obstacles, including the obstacle of being a non-human being, which falls under the subsequent category of obstacles.
Regarding the meaning of the thirteen obstacles, there is a fivefold analytical examination. First, the explanation of names and the definition of the meaning of the obstacles, etc.

The second [topic] concerns the names of disputes and their establishment or abandonment; the third, the inclusion of difficulties that are either exhaustive or inexhaustible; the fourth, the meaning of the mutual inclusion of the three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*);
and the fifth, the difficulty of attaining the precepts, the arising of the precepts, and whether the precepts are lost or not lost.

The first section has five parts: 1. Explaining the name and resolving difficult points; 2. Distinguishing the characteristics of the obstacles; 3. Revealing the essence of the obstacles; 4. Explaining how the name is derived; 5.
Resolving the points of penetration and obstruction. Now, the dharma of the precepts is pure and ethereal, a sublime ladder for exiting the mundane world.

Since the dharma is so refined and subtle, its reception is not easily achieved. Regarding this reception: it cannot be accomplished unless the body is pure. Thus, the body is the vessel for receiving the Way.
The body is the vessel; the mind is the master that attains the Dharma. When body and mind are perfectly pure, one attains the precepts beyond words.

If there are internal defects or obstacles within, and the bodily vessel is impure, then even if all other conditions are complete, it is merely laborious and of no benefit. One's prospects for this life are severed, manifesting that the precepts have not been generated.

This is termed "difficult. On one hand, the transformation [of sentient beings] should be characterized by thirteen categories; beginning from the "extreme offenses" (*pārājika*) and ending with the "two sexual organs," these are their names.

Regarding what is called an "extreme offense": although one has previously received and attained the precepts and ought logically to advance toward them, one merely fails to maintain a firm grasp of the mind.

To violate the four prohibitions is a grave karmic act that lies beyond the bounds of ordinary conduct; hence it is called a "limiting offense" (*pārājika*). Because it severs one's connection to the precepts, it is termed a "difficulty.

Thus, it is called the "difficulty of the limiting offenses. Second, regarding the objects of the pure requisites: these are fields of merit for generating goodness, and it is only right to treat them with reverent devotion and plant blessings therein.
Now, to instead defile and insult them, thereby destroying their holy life (*brahmacarya*), constitutes the accomplishment of an arrogant karma that acts as an obstruction.

To dwell in such depth, though one receives no benefit, is called a "difficulty. This difficulty arises from the corruption of *bhikṣuṇīs*; therefore, it is called the "difficulty of violating a *bhikṣuṇī*. Third, as for *śrāmaṇeras* and laypeople:
their persons are not those to whom [the precepts] should apply, and the Dharma is not their rightful portion. Yet, they assume the outward deportment and falsely claim to possess full ordination.
They plunder the wealth of the Dharma and are thus termed "thieves. Because their karma is heavy and obstructs the precepts, it is called the "difficulty of the thieving mind."

Fourth: Previously, this person was a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who, with a mind of faith in the Buddha-dharma, abandoned the heterodox for the orthodox, left the household life, and received full ordination.

Although they dwelt within the monastic discipline, their faith had not yet become firm; they subsequently abandoned the true path and returned to receiving heterodox teachings. Even down to the point of plucking out a single hair [in a ritual of renunciation], this is called "the difficulty of refuting both internal and external paths.
