This distinguishes them from other non-Buddhists, as it is not difficult to convert those who have already returned to the orthodox. Therefore, it says: "You are not one who has refuted the internal [path]."
The non-Buddhists [do not] [accept them]. Fifth, as for the eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*): although they possess the human form, their physical constitution lacks the vessel for the Path;

their nature is full of afflictions, and they do not manifest the attainment of the noble stages. Because this defiled mind is so heavy and thick, even if they were to receive [the precepts], they could not attain them;

therefore, it is said that the eunuch is a "difficulty. Sixth and seventh, as for the two difficulties: humans are not of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*); their karma is entrusted to a womb-retribution, relying upon the physical remains of their parents to serve as [their basis].

One's own body is the source of profound and deep kindness; by principle, it should be revered and honored. Yet, one instead violates that kindness and turns one's back on that upbringing, giving rise to rebellious harm.

Since the karma created is so grave, even if one were to receive [the fruit of merit], it could not be attained; therefore, it is said that killing one’s parents is difficult [to overcome]. Eighth, as for killing an Arhat:

although this person’s retribution in the present life has not yet shifted, their merit has advanced further, and their fruition transcends the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). They serve as a fertile field for the world. By principle...
One should respectfully serve [the Sangha] and seek instruction to cultivate merit. Yet, by harboring anger, one destroys their noble body and suffers the loss of benefit to an extreme degree.

Such heavy karma obstructs the precepts; therefore, it is said that killing an Arhat is a grave transgression. Ninthly, when the community is harmonious and the Dharma is unified, this is the way to enter the Path.

Now, if one alters the True Dharma with false teachings, dividing the assembly into divergent tracks, the radiance of the Orthodox Teaching will be obscured and false teachings will flourish in the world. One should realize that such a deviation from the fundamental principle is a cause for awakening.
One loses their understanding; the karma is extremely grave. It obstructs the arising of the precepts; therefore, it is said that "breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha" is a difficult transgression.

Tenth, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, internally cultivates the four immeasurables and guides the various classes of beings, enabling those who are drowning in saṃsāra to rely upon him to transcend the world.

This benevolence and compassion are supreme, and it is only right that one should follow and honor them. Yet, to violate this kindness and commit harm—specifically, shedding blood—constitutes an immediate offense. This...
The karma is particularly profound; it obstructs one from receiving the precepts. Therefore, it is said that shedding the Buddha’s blood with an evil mind is a grave difficulty.

[Cases] eleven and twelve involve non-humans and animals; their retributive states are lowly, and both their physical forms and minds lack the capacity to receive the Way. Their bodies are beset by the obstruction of retribution.

One will never obtain the precepts; therefore, it is called "difficult. Thirteen, regarding those of "both genders" (*ubhayavyañjana*): generally, for one to be a vessel for the Path, it is essential that male and female characteristics be distinct.

Now, since their physical form is ambiguous and they cause disturbance to both assemblies, even if they had previously received and obtained the precepts, they are still subject to expulsion and banishment.

How much more so for one who has only now first resolved to attain enlightenment—how could such a person possibly obtain the precepts? Therefore, it is termed "difficult. Question: Regarding these ten...

All three cases involve the difficulty of receiving the precepts. As for why the third case alone is designated as "the difficulty of receiving the precepts with a thievish mind" (*caura-citta*), the answer is:
this does not actually refer to the present act of receiving them as being difficult; rather, it is called "the difficulty of receiving the precepts" because it is a hindrance.

Therefore, there is no need to treat all three as identical. It is simply said that such a thievish mind is absent [in the other two]. This deceptive reception of the precepts constitutes a hindrance to the present [act], and thus it is singled out and specifically labeled.

Because other [cases] are not of this category. Question: Why is it that regarding the shedding of blood, one speaks specifically of "an evil mind"? Answer: This is to distinguish it from a "good mind," for [with a good mind] there is no offense; thus it is so.
However, as these are merely the "liminal" (sīmāntika) offenses and the like, who would inquire about the goodness or evil of the mind? Therefore, no distinction is made.

Second, regarding the clarification of the characteristics: this term "one who has previously transgressed" (*pūrvāpattika*) does not have its characteristics clearly defined. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it refers to one who has previously committed an offense against the precepts.

Regarding those who have committed offenses against the precepts, according to both the *Mahīśāsaka-śāstra* and the *Dharmaguptaka-śāstra*, offenses encompassing either five or eight [categories] are all termed "having previously transgressed. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-śāstra* states:
If one violates the five precepts, they are not permitted to receive the latter three [bodhisattva] precepts. The same applies to the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*).

According to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, if an upāsaka violates even one of his precepts, or if one violates even one of the eight precepts, such persons, even if they later go forth as monastics, will neither obtain the precepts nor be permitted to act as an upādhyāya.

The same applies to the twelve types of individuals, including those who have defiled a nun (*dūṣita-bhikṣuṇī*) and so forth. Based on this, the rule is extremely strict; I have now extracted and explained it here.

Regarding the ten precepts for householders (*gṛhastha*), once they have been transgressed, they constitute an obstacle (*āpatti*). This is because they are termed "borderline offenses" (*antāpatti*); that is, they are defined as "borderline" in relation to the internal [monastic] discipline, since the five and eight precepts do not pertain to the internal [monastic] sphere.
As for the statement that "transgressing against a *bhikṣuṇī* constitutes an obstacle," this refers specifically to the case where the object is a fully ordained nun.

According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, one who violates a *bhikṣuṇī*’s pure conduct is permanently barred from leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*). This does not apply as an obstacle for the two lower assemblies [of *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs*]. In this Vinaya, it is stated simply as "transgressing against a *bhikṣuṇī*."
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, regarding one who violates a bhikṣuṇī’s brahmacarya, the Buddha said: "A bhikṣu who engages in sexual intercourse with a bhikṣuṇī shall be expelled.

Furthermore, this refers specifically to sexual intercourse and not to mere physical contact and so forth. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "If a single person defiles a bhikṣuṇī through eight acts, the bhikṣuṇī is considered 'defiled,' but that person is not considered 'defiled' and may receive the precepts.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "One must select a pure bhikṣuṇī. Now, this present Vinaya (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*) alone possesses [this rule], which is identical to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding purity and impurity.

Both [cases] are established as offenses, differing from the *Cīvaravastu* (only-seeing). This is because the subsequent text merely states that one commits sexual misconduct with one who wears the *kāṣāya*, without distinguishing whether the person is of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

Regarding the phrase "with a thieving mind," this is explained according to the text. There are five types of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs/impotent persons); all five constitute an obstacle (*antarāyika-dharma*). [This is stated in] the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
One should not ordain eunuchs. One must first ask: "Are you a man? Based on this, an eunuch refers to one who is incapable of performing the functions of a man;

by their very nature, they possess abundant afflictions (*kleśa*). Only one's biological parents constitute an obstacle [to ordination], not foster parents and the like, as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
"One who causes a schism in the Saṃgha refers to the leader of the Dharma-wheel, not the leader of the followers. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*...

Regarding the two statements, it refers to the six *pārājika* offenses; the remaining characteristics may be understood accordingly. Question: Why are the *pārājikas* grouped together while the *ānantaryas* (immediate transgressions) are treated separately? Answer:

The *pārājikas* follow the *ānantaryas* because they share the commonality of having a "limit" (*anta*)—that is, they involve a definitive exclusion from the community. If the *ānantaryas* were instead grouped with the *pārājikas*, they would be confused with those who merely break the rules of the community.

Therefore, they are not of the same category. Furthermore, regarding the question: why are the *ānantaryas* divided into five, whereas only one is established for the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch/impotent)? Answer: "Reversal" (*ānantarya*) refers specifically to the five immediate transgressions.

Because they are distinguished by their respective objects and activities, eunuchs (paṇḍaka) are not included among those who face objects and so forth; therefore, they are combined into one category.

Regarding the third difficulty concerning the essence [of the categories], there are three possible positions. First, if one distinguishes according to the three aggregates (triskandha), the essence consists of the dharmas of all three aggregates.

If categorized by position, there are two types: eunuchs, animals, and those with dual sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) take the three aggregates as their collective essence, while the remaining nine [categories] [take them individually].

Only matter (*rūpa*). Regarding the second [type], if it were to be distinguished separately, its substance would not be the retribution of an animal; it obstructs the physical form and is not a vessel for the Path, because the mind does not receive the Path.

Generally, it takes the four characteristics—retributive matter, mind, life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth—as its substance. The other two [types] are also like this, as they are explained according to their predominant strength.

For the eunuch (*pandaka*), the latent tendency of greed (*lobha-anuśaya*) alone acts as the primary obstacle. If one considers the deficiency of the physical form, it means that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is incomplete.

Because these factors are incomplete, greed consequently increases. Second, those with a dual-gendered body have an excessive development of the physical faculty (*kāyendriya*), and thus they are not vessels for the Path.

As for the remaining nine obstacles, they are distinguished by body and speech: the schism of the Saṃgha is an oral karma; the violation of a nun and the violation of one's own inner [preceptor] pertain to the body. These two are restricted to the body.
The remaining [karmas] pertain to both body and speech. Within body and speech, there are both manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actions.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-śāstra*, if the essence of unmanifest action is definitively form (*rūpa*), it consists only of unwholesome form and sound; its unmanifest aspect is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, the manifest is form, while the unmanifest is neither form nor mind. Since it states that karma has form as its essence, even when a bhikṣu commits the four pārājika offenses, they are [only]...

To commit an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense is difficult; its nature is neither that of a *pārājika* nor a *sthūlātyaya*. Since it is committed by a layperson, it is also difficult to subsume under those categories.

Just as with the schism of the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*), it may be considered an *ānantarya* or a *sthūlātyaya*, yet it generally constitutes a grave obstacle. This is because a layperson cannot commit the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

Thirdly, if these are distinguished according to their respective dharma-gates, these thirteen [offenses] likewise take the thirteen matters such as the "border regions" (*pratyantaka*) as their essential substance.
Regarding the fourth point, "receiving the name": this directly clarifies the general designation for the obstacles (*antarāya*). They receive their titles based on their functional meaning;

it is because these thirteen matters and so forth are all capable of obstructing the meaning of the precepts that they are so named. As for how the thirteen [obstacles], such as the "grave offenses" (*pārājika*), receive their names:

if one refers to the first two [categories] regarding the definition of their essence, they are all named according to their specific meanings. There are five different types of these specific meanings. First is the grave offense (*pārājika*).
Names are derived from their meaning. Because committing this offense is logically beyond the bounds of propriety, it is named according to its meaning.
Second, the seven offenses involving nuns and so forth—namely, violating a nun and committing the five internal heinous crimes—are named after their objective conditions (*ālambana*).

That is to say, offenses such as killing and so forth are named by using these conditions, because nuns, parents, and so on constitute their objective conditions. Third, the single difficulty regarding the "thieving mind" is designated based on its remote cause.

Regarding the four non-human [beings], they receive their names based on having no other [distinctive] characteristics. Regarding the fifth, the three types of eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and so forth, the causes are established based on their physical retribution (*vipāka*).
If one follows the third [method] for defining their essential nature (*svabhāva*), these thirteen matters all receive their names according to their respective natures.

Fifth, the discernment of the open and the obstructed. There are three aspects to this: first, the distinction by physical form; second, the distinction by location; and third, the distinction by time.
Regarding the first, the distinction by physical form, there are two parts: first, the distinction among the three realms of existence;
second, the distinction among the seven assemblies within the human realm. As for the "three realms," these refer to one each for the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. Regarding humans...
Eleventh: Since this and that [category] are collectively included, there are thirteen [types]. Because humans create karma, there are nine types of karma;

other realms of existence do not create these nine types of karma, and thus they are omitted and not discussed. Furthermore, because humans receive the Path, those who are not vessels for the Path are described as obstacles.
This includes those with the two sexual organs (*paṇḍaka*) and those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*). As for non-humans and animals, since they lack the capacity to receive the Path...
In principle, the self-nature [of these two] is an obstruction. Even if these two exist, they cannot obstruct the precepts by virtue of their own nature;

therefore, they are not described as "difficulties. This is like the seven-day medicine: although it involves many transgressions, because they arise from the ritual of the mouth, only two faults are produced.
This is because the remaining [offenses] do not arise through verbal means. Second, regarding the explanation according to the seven classes of practitioners:

for the *saṃgha*, there are only eleven, excluding two—namely, because the three types of misconduct have already been divided—and for the *bhikṣuṇī*, there are further excluded, leaving only ten. For each of the three lower classes, there are nine; for the two lay groups, there are only eight.
These are all general descriptions. If one were to specify them individually: for a *bhikṣu*, in terms of actual acts, there are only ten, namely, excluding...

Because of the intent of a thief (*caura-citta*), there are six "actual" [offenses]. This means that three offenses involving a nun and the three involving killing are excluded, as these four are subsumed within the category of "borderline offenses" (*pārājika*).
For a nun, there are only nine; the intent of a thief is the same as before. Furthermore, excluding the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, it should be understood that there are five.

Regarding the three matters of *śikṣamāṇā* and so forth, there are nine; this means that because the two types of schisms are excluded when the intent of a thief is present, it should be understood that there are five. For laypeople, there are two.

Regarding the eight categories of both conventional matters (*vastu*) and names (*nāman*): excluding the two extreme offenses (*antya-āpatti*), because there is no collective "extreme" category, both the matters and the names are eightfold.

The three cases of shedding blood, being a *paṇḍaka*, and having both sexual organs—these three are said to apply universally across the seven classes of practitioners (*saptasaṃgha*). The remaining eight meanings are restricted; when subsumed by stage (*avasthā*), they constitute five categories.

The extreme offenses (*antya-āpatti*) apply to the upper five classes but do not reach the one class of laypeople. The offense of a thief’s mind applies to the lower five classes but does not extend to the upper two. The offense of breaking the inner [refuges] applies to the upper two. The [offense of]... [does not apply].

The five offenses listed below, including those involving nuns, are restricted to the four [grave offenses] and two [intermediate offenses] for laypeople; they are not included among the aforementioned five.

The offense of schism (*saṃghabheda*) is restricted solely to the great monks (*bhikṣu*) and does not extend to the six groups of novices. Such distinctions regarding the scope and number of these offenses are explained according to their names.

Since it is difficult to establish this definitively, one must further examine where they can occur based on the accessibility of karmic retribution (*vipāka*). Thus, a second time, we shall distinguish them by location; except for the northern region, there is no attainment [of these offenses].

Because this concerns the meaning of the precepts (*śīla*), it is unnecessary to distinguish the obstacles that hinder the precepts. Among the other three continents, Jambudvīpa in the south lacks them;
in the other two continents, there are only eleven, excluding the shedding of blood and the schism of the Saṃgha, because they do not exist during those times. Next, thirdly, regarding time:
even if we provisionally take Jambudvīpa in the south as an example, if a Buddha is currently present, all thirteen obstacles exist; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are likewise only [eleven].

Eleven. Excluding two as previously stated. Although the above cases of pervasion and obstruction may be categorized according to retribution (*vipāka*), they are thus [treated] because of the increase or decrease and presence or absence relative to the locus, the time, and the essential substance.
This is because at the time of posing the question, although there may be pervasion or obstruction, presence or absence, one asks about what is absent and does not ask about what is present;
thus, the holy teaching establishes a single rule: regarding retribution, for both male and female, and for other directions or future lives, one asks about all ten.
Third. Regarding the second point, the dispute over names: since ancient times, the established doctrine has been questioned as to its basis.

First, it is difficult to maintain that only one receives the name of a "border-dweller" (*pratyantaka*), while the other twelve who receive the precepts are excluded from this category and thus cannot be called border-dwellers. This must be explained by providing the full meaning of the principle.
This "difficult-to-understand non-duality" need not be listed in detail. Now, regarding the explanation of the "difficulties":

these are the general names for obstacles to the precepts, such as *pārājika* offenses and so forth. These are precisely the specific designations for the "difficulties. For what reason would one take the periphery of another's specific name?
It also causes [the meaning] to penetrate through all twelve [categories], which is similar to the objection raised. All dharmas possess both specific names and general names.
For instance, regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the six *pāramitās*, they share the general name "pāramitā," which can be applied to all six.
Furthermore, the term *dāna* (generosity) extends to the [other] five below it; this case is likewise. Therefore, one should know that it is not as [the opponent] claims. Thus, at the beginning...
Difficult. Regarding the term "extreme" (*anta*) used alone: as in the first objection, this is a specific case among the thirteen [offenses].

If one has previously received the precepts and then violates a grave prohibition (*pārājika*), it logically falls outside the bounds [of the discipline]; therefore, it is called an "extreme. This is considered an "extreme" in contrast to what was previously explained. Such a person who has committed an extreme offense—

Later, regarding the obstacles to the precepts (*śīlāntarāya*), they were termed "obstacles" (*antarāya*). Since these obstacles refer to what lies beyond, how can one rely on them? These obstacles that look toward what follows encompass all thirteen [grounds for defeat].

Even when looking toward the side of the person [who commits them], they likewise encompass all thirteen. For example, the obstacle of violating a nun (*bhikṣuṇī-antarāya*) occurs at the time of being a layperson;
it is not called an obstacle because of having violated the Buddha's precepts. How could it then be designated as a "ground" (*pārājika*)? This applies even unto...
Those who possess both sexual organs and so forth do not constitute an offense against the precepts; therefore, it is said only that those with both sexual organs and so forth are "difficult cases.

If one were to designate all such instances as "extremes," then by citing the twelve lower [categories], the counter-objection can be understood. Thus, regarding this dispute over names, there was originally nothing to dispute.
The Third Gate: These thirteen difficulties encompass all obstacles to the precepts.

Regarding the resolution of these difficulties, those who intentionally leave the household life, seek the precepts from the Saṃgha, and undergo the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) yet fail to obtain the precepts are included within these difficulties.
However, among the other eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), only a small portion of non-humans and animals—such as dragon kings (*nāgarāja*) and the like—are included within these thirteen;

the remaining six are not. The reason for this is that those in the hells, long-lived gods, those with worldly cleverness and eloquence, those in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, those born before or after a Buddha, and those with impaired faculties, all lack the capacity to seek [refuge] or perform the ritual procedure.

[This] meaning [is not included here], and therefore it is not subsumed under this [category]. As for a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled: according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*, once he has left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he is granted release from expulsion;
furthermore, it is not difficult [to exclude him]. Thus, the inclusion of these thirteen [offenses] is exhaustive in its meaning.

Question: Why is there no mention of the offense of killing a pratyekabuddha? Answer: Because killing a pratyekabuddha is not included among the five ānantarya (immediate) offenses. As stated in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*: "Killing a pratyekabuddha..."
The Buddha. Because committing a root offense is not a *ānantarya* (heinous) crime.

The fourth category: the single obstacle of being a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*). Because their desire is so excessive that they harbor such thoughts, this is subsumed under the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

It is not included among the three [obstacles] of possessing two sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), which are categorized as the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). As for the remaining nine, they are all obstacles of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) because they hinder the precepts. If one considers them in terms of hindering the hearing [of the Dharma]:

Regarding the boundaries of cultivation through reflection, only the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) constitute such obstacles; the others do not. If one distinguishes between their breadth and narrowness: among these thirteen [types of karma], the karma is the broadest, the retribution is intermediate, and the afflictions (*kleśa*) are the narrowest.
If one discusses the breadth and narrowness of obstructions to retribution in a general sense, they are said to be broad within the context of the five destinies (*gati*).
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are narrower than that; the karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*) are the narrowest.
Fifth gate: if one permanently transforms into a non-human or an animal, or becomes a hermaphrodite (*ubhayavyañjana*), these three cases constitute the loss of the precepts.

Furthermore, if one breaks the internal or external paths due to wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), this is logically a loss of the precepts. Also, if after having received the precepts, one becomes one of the five types of eunuchs (*pañca-paṇḍaka*), it likewise [constitutes a loss].

One does not lose the precepts; there is only the distinction between being expelled or not expelled. Regarding all other matters that arise after receiving the precepts, they diminish but do not cause the loss of the precepts.
Question: Why is it that while thirteen factors constitute obstacles to loss, only four actually result in loss? Answer: This means that not all contrary conditions necessarily lead to loss.
The reason for this is as follows: for example, the arising of both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) results in loss, yet the removal of one organ results in its recovery.
The precepts [for other categories] may be understood by analogy.
Next, regarding the explanation of the text: it simply states that there was once a layperson who committed sexual misconduct with one wearing the *kāṣāya*.
This appears not to distinguish between those who are pure or impure, which differs from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The text on "those who dwell as thieves" consists of three sections. First, the circumstances are raised to inform the Buddha, followed by a general judgment regarding expulsion.

Second, within this section, those who enter the Path with a thieving mind are categorized under two heavy and four light offenses, which serve as the topical headings. Third, within this section, the distinctions between light and heavy offenses are determined;
first, the four light offenses are explained, followed by the explanation of the two heavy ones. These six points were previously stated merely as...
The Dharma is upheld by persons; therefore, there are one, two, three, four, and six [categories] such as the *karmavācanā*, which clarify the descending grades of a thief.

Since the communal rule (*saṃghadharma*) is equivalent to five *kārsāpaṇas* and the individual rule (*pudgaladharma*) resembles the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), stealing an individual rule does not constitute a state of being a thief (*steyasaṃvāsa*).

Regarding these four preceding phrases, they apply to cases where one has passed through one, two, three, or four *uposatha* periods. It is not that the Dharma was not administered; the Buddha judged such individuals not to be thieves. Thus, the *Gāthā-śāstra* states:
"One who has passed through two or three *uposathas* may not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*); one who has passed through one *uposatha*, or has not passed through any at all, may receive it."

Furthermore, Jīvaka, regarding eavesdropping: one may not receive [the formal acts] if they hear them clearly and distinctly from the beginning, middle, and end; however, if the beginning, middle, and end are not recorded in their entirety, they may be received.

Thus it is known that the legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) are only established when one is present as a "thief-dweller" (*corāvāsa*). Now, this interpretation is incorrect. Inferior assemblies are not appropriate;

since the Dharma is not their portion, how could an inferior assembly be the one authorized to perform [the rites], such as the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) and so forth, which are performed before a counterpart? How could an inferior assembly be the proper agent for these?

Furthermore, regarding the two cases of five or six [monks] approaching one monk, two monks, or three monks, or reaching the Saṃgha, or the four boundaries for performing a collective *karmavācanā* and so forth—the Buddha ruled these as *pravāsanīya-karman* (expulsion) because they had obtained the Dharma. This constitutes two types of theft.

As for the previous four cases where the Buddha ruled that the full ordination was validly received, this is because they completely failed to obtain the Dharma and merely stole the outward form. Thus it is.
The four points above all refer to *asādhāraṇa-karman* (exclusive formal acts) and so forth. Furthermore, according to the ancient interpretation:

regarding the first phrase, "exclusive formal act" (*asādhāraṇa-karman*), it means that it is not shared with the [other] three lower categories, yet it is not the case that it is not shared at all; for even when a single person performs the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), they are said to obtain the dharma.
For example, if one goes to the place of one or two people, the method of stealing by direct confrontation cannot constitute the offense of theft.
However, upon reaching the place of three or four people—and indeed from four people upward—one must employ the method of stealing from a group (*saṃgha*). Why would one accept [the contrary]?

Therefore, we know that the phrase "not performing the ritual together" refers to not being with the persons present at the location. Furthermore, the first three phrases are contrasted with the subsequent ones to clarify this point.
It is not shared. From the fourth [case] up to the point of facing the Saṃgha, why is it called "not shared"? Therefore, we know that in all these cases one does not obtain the Dharma;

this clarifies that by stealing the individual [monastic] rules, one universally becomes a *corāvasatha* (one who dwells as a thief). Furthermore, from the fifth and sixth cases onward, one merely steals from the person facing them;
one cannot judge this to be the theft of the mind’s recollection of the Dharma. Since going to the place of one bhikṣu makes two when including oneself, how could it be considered "shared"?

"Maintaining the mind to be mindful of the Dharma. *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views). Regarding the three types of theft, they are distinguished as usual. According to this Vinaya, all five types [of persons] should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*).

As for the "eunuch born of jealousy" (*dveṣa-paṇḍaka*), because his condition is triggered by another and ceases when that other person is removed, it is said that he is initially described as being [excluded] for half a month;

this refers to the fact that there are specific temporal conditions involved. The *Zengyi ahan jing* (Ekottarika Āgama) states: "The five types of eunuchs should not be granted the precepts. Therefore, none of them are eligible.

Furthermore, there are six types of eunuchs: first, those born so; second, those castrated; third, those whose [genitals] were severed; fourth, those who became so because of another; fifth, those who encountered [a situation]; and sixth, those who are so for half a month.

Of these, the first three are not permitted to leave the household life. Regarding the latter three, if they have not yet left the household life, it is improper; however, if they have already left the household life, they are permitted.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* lists five types of impotent persons (*paṇḍaka*): first, those born so; second, the *kliba*; third, those who are so for half a month; fourth, those whose semen is [deficient]; and fifth, those so due to illness.

Of these, the first four are not permitted to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*), whereas the fifth is permitted to do so. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* simply refers to them as "eunuchs" (*pandaka*) without distinguishing between their various subtypes or whether they are capable of sexual intercourse.
The *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra* states that the five characteristics of a dragon king do not depart from his original form; first, when he engages in sexual intercourse with his own kind, if he...

Humans engage in sexual intercourse, transform into humans, undergo two types of rebirth, shed their bones, sleep, and die at the time of death; the present Vinaya, however, manifests only two of these.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, because of the ordination of a dragon, from now on, when bestowing the precepts, one who is not personally known should be tested for seven days.
As for those like Devadatta, this refers to each of the other six *pārājika* offenses where one acts as the leader of a schism in the Saṃgha. Upon seeing [this],...
Treatise: There are three types of those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*). First, those who can conceive by themselves and can cause others to conceive;

second, those who can conceive by themselves but cannot cause others to conceive; third, those who cannot conceive by themselves but can cause others to conceive. All of these are difficult to categorize;
the intent here is to clarify the nature of those with both sexual organs.

Based on this, the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parivṛtti*) is analyzed through six gates: first, that which can prevent the arising of what has not yet arisen; second, whether offenses already committed are extinguished or not;
third, whether the same offense requires the performance of the *ānulomika-dharma* again; fourth, whether the disciplinary methods for those who violate their vows are resolved through ritual action;
fifth, the meaning of loss or non-loss regarding the purification of robes, medicine, and other dharmas; and sixth, the reception of the precepts.

Whether the establishment of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is successful or not depends on the indeterminate nature of the accumulated karma of sentient beings; thus, there is transformation. This principle is plausible.

As for the case where a monk immediately becomes a nun, or a nun transforms into a monk: one interpretation holds that monks and nuns differ in their possession or lack thereof regarding certain precepts.

For instance, if one’s gender organ were to transform into that of a woman, the monk would still possess the original vows he received, which prevent him from suddenly providing instruction [to nuns] and so forth.
The precepts are immediately diminished. Precepts such as those regarding excessive washing arise anew. Why is this so?

It is because the primary vow—to sever all that is evil—serves as the cause, and the transformation of the faculties serves as the requisite condition; thus, the precepts arise. The same applies to the transformation of a *bhikṣuṇī*. Question:

If the arising of the precepts were not identical [to their previous state], it would mean one obtains them without having formally received them, and there would be the fault of receiving them gradually. Furthermore, regarding the transformation of the faculties...

This karma is not a condition for the arousal of the precepts. Furthermore, beyond the five types of ordination (*pañca-upasampadā*), there is also the ordination through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
Based on this reasoning, it is clearly known that [the precepts] are not produced [again]. Moreover, if they were not distinct from the loss of the precepts, then:

first, they would not be relinquished at the time of relinquishment, and thus the restraint (*saṃvara*) would undergo increase or decrease; second, there would be the fault of gradual relinquishment; and third, the two subsequent transformations of faculties would not be conditions for relinquishment. If...

Regarding the abandonment of the precepts, there should be five ways of abandoning them. However, since this is not the case, we know that [the precepts] are not lost. Now, to explain the essence of what is received, which is capable of acting as a defense:

it neither arises nor perishes. Thus, even when one changes status from monk to nun or vice versa, one cannot claim that because the original object of transgression no longer exists, the capacity to prevent such transgressions must likewise be abandoned.
Furthermore, one cannot claim that because the object of prevention—the evil—arises again, the capacity to prevent it must likewise arise again.

The reason for this is that, based on one's original vow—that whatever evil arises in a single movement must be severed—one is able to bring about the non-manifesting restraint (*avijñapti*) through prevention.

Consequently, even when encountering transgressive objects, although the capacity for prevention may fluctuate between arising and ceasing, it never follows along with the conditions to undergo birth and extinction.

Since one has fulfilled the original vow and completely severed the intention toward evil, the non-manifesting wholesome restraint is thereby attained. This is why it differs from the case of a *bhikṣuṇī*; thus, the great [vow] is established.

When a monk undergoes a transformation of his faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), he immediately becomes a nun; thus, the substance of his restraint remains capable of preventing transgression, without further arising or ceasing. This is like a weapon:

it may simply be put to use or not used, but it cannot be said that the weapon itself has ceased to exist. This is also like the case of the non-virtuous discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*): one must have the intention to kill a sheep;
[this applies] from the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) above down to the hells below—toward all sentient beings—one fully brings forth this non-virtue.

Regarding the restraint (*saṃvara*): while non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) may potentially involve manifest action (*vijñapti*), the same principle applies here to the category of wholesome restraints as well.

Because karma is not fixed, it is possible for it to undergo transformation; there is the sense that one might commit an offense through excessive purification. For this reason, the *bhikṣuṇī* does not differ from the [other] precepts;
they are all acquired collectively, and they likewise neither arise nor cease.
Question: If one has received precepts that are not identical to those of a *bhikṣuṇī*, why is such a person not called a *bhikṣuṇī*? Answer:

Although the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) is indeed no different, there are distinctions based on physical form. Because this person currently possesses a male retribution (*puruṣa-vipāka*), they have not yet been granted that name.

If one examines the precepts according to the teachings, the conditions for transgression (*āpatti-pratyaya*) are either identical or different. However, as long as the transgressions are the same—such as theft, killing, and so forth—the teaching remains applicable. Furthermore, as in...
The same applies to the long bowl, the separation from one’s robes, and the oversized bathing robe; they share the same transgression, yet differ in their specific matters.

For example, regarding the various precepts on admonition, staying for three nights, double-tongued speech, disparagement, abuse, striking, threatening, and [the treatment of] laywomen in public or private—these also constitute the same course of action, and the instruction remains unchanged.
Alternatively, while the prohibited matter may be the same, there are differences in gravity, such as in the case of emission.

Regarding the seven types of offenses such as touching a woman with lust and so forth, within these various teachings there are instances of abolition and instances of restoration; they differ in their presence or absence, with some being abolished entirely.
Since this is the case for the transformation of the Saṃgha, it is likewise for the transformation of the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha.
The second section: Provided that the offense is the same and has already been committed, even if one undergoes a change of gender (*indriya-parivṛtti*), the transgression does not cease.

This is because the object to be guarded against remains present, and there is still the sense of continuity in its commission. However, if the offense involves a different object (*ālambana*) or differs in terms of gravity, presence, or absence, the previously committed offense ceases.
Since the evil object to be guarded against no longer exists, the continuity of the offense is severed; therefore, it is invariably extinguished. This is because [the conditions] are complete.

This is due to three reasons. First, the transformation of karma and its retribution differ; they are not the same as those who have abandoned the Way, because their own minds turn away from the Path.

Second, there is no continuity [of the offense], which serves to distinguish them from those who commit the same transgression [but do not abandon the precepts]. Third, although the retribution for monks and nuns may differ, both are fully ordained practitioners of the Path;
this differs from the case of death, for even at death there is no continuity [of the offense], and thus it is not extinguished. Therefore, it must be stated...

They are vessels for the Path. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "Is it possible for a bhikṣu to commit four kinds of offenses, yet neither repent nor confess them, and yet not be considered an offender?
The Buddha said: "It is possible; this refers to one who has undergone a change of gender (*vyañjana-parivṛtti*). Is it possible for a bhikṣuṇī to commit five kinds of offenses..."

[The question was: "Is there one who does not feel regret, does not confess, yet has not committed an offense? The Buddha said: "There is; namely, one who has undergone a change of gender (*vyañjana-parivṛtti*). He further asked:
"Is there a case where a non-monk commits an offense, yet the monk is released [from it]? Is there a case where a monk commits an offense, yet the non-monk is released?
The Buddha said: "There is; namely, one who has undergone a change of gender. Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When a monk's sexual organ ceases and he becomes a woman..."
The Buddha said: "One receives the precepts by this very [method]; one requests a teacher by this very [method]; and one follows the rules regarding age by this very [method].

One goes to the nuns' residence and dwells according to the nuns' rules. If one commits an offense shared with the nuns, one confesses it among the nuns; as for offenses not shared [with them], one confesses them first."
There is no further regret. It is the same for a *bhikṣuṇī* who undergoes a change of gender (*vyañjana-parivṛtti*).

Third section: The method of disciplinary treatment for identical offenses. Regarding those whose methods of practice differ—meaning this is explained in reference to the confession of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and so forth—it concerns only the difference in the commission of the offense.
Whether the practice of the rules is sufficient or insufficient, whether it is complete or incomplete, in all such cases of mutual transformation, [the procedure remains the same].
Because they are pure persons, it is not necessary for them to have mutual continuity of action.

Since the fundamental offense has already been extinguished, even if one changes while the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*) is not yet completed, or changes while the *parivāsa* is not yet completed, both remain in a state of purity.
The same applies to a nun who changes. If they have committed the offense together, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, up to ten..."
Regarding concealment for a year, there is one type where the individual subsequently changes into a *bhikṣuṇī*; in this case, the offense is removed after fifteen days.

If one changes into a *bhikṣuṇī* before having completed the six-night penance, they are further granted the half-month procedure (*ardhamāsa-vidhi*). If one changes into a *bhikṣuṇī* after the six nights have been completed, the offense is immediately expiated.

Next, the case of a *bhikṣuṇī* changing into a *bhikṣu* is distinguished: if she changes before having ever obtained the formal procedures, she is given a six-night treatment; if she had obtained the half-month procedure, she [performs] it...
If the offense changes before six nights have passed, one should grant another six nights. If it changes after the six days have concluded, it is logically unnecessary to grant another six nights;
rather, one should immediately grant the absolution from the offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). This is stated with reference to those who were previously without concealment (*anāvṛta*).

If a *bhikṣuṇī* was previously in a state of concealment, she should be granted the disciplinary treatment for concealment (*āvṛta-prāyaścitta*). Thus, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and does not conceal it for even a single thought, up until..."
Confessing: While practicing the fifteen-day rite, if on the first or second day one transforms into a bhikṣu, one should simply undergo the six-night *parivāsa* discipline.
If one has previously committed an offense and there were days of concealment, upon transforming into a bhikṣu, one must perform *pārivāsika* according to the original number of concealed days.

According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, even if a bhikṣuṇī had previously concealed her offenses, once she transforms into a bhikṣu, she does not continue the period of concealment, as it was [the nun's] transgression.

Because the discussion of the principles is not yet complete, there is the fourth section. This refers to the treatment by means of the seven types of *karmavācanā*. Regarding offenses that are dissimilar, there are seven types of emotional transgressions (*saptavidha-kaṣāya*).

For both monks and nuns, there are five changes of status. If the offense has not yet been treated, there is no need for treatment. If it has already been treated, one need not inquire further; since the matter is settled and no longer troublesome, there is no need to perform the ritual procedure again. Although...

The subduing is finished; there is no need for a formal release (*visarjana*). This is because the fundamental matter is different, and since it will not arise again subsequently, [a release is unnecessary].

If explained according to the meaning, this excludes the case of "not reaching one. Although the offense has been extinguished, one must still offer an apology (*kṣamāpanā*). This is because a layperson (*avadātavasana*) does not achieve resolution merely by that.

Regarding the disciplinary procedure (*dharma-vinaya*) where no apology is required, it means that a release is still necessary. Or, in the case of those who have committed the same offense and possess the seven faults... [the text continues].
One who should be disciplined must be disciplined. Once disciplined, she is transformed into a bhikṣuṇī and subsequently conducts herself in accordance with the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
If she is to be tamed, the community of bhikṣuṇīs shall release her; the transformation into a bhikṣuṇī is likewise.
Fifth Gate: On the Treatise on Views. When a bhikṣu transforms into a bhikṣuṇī, the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) of the three robes and medicinal substances is lost;
the *śuddhi* (purification) is also lost. This is because the bhikṣu’s acceptance of robes involves the offense of exceeding six nights, whereas for a bhikṣuṇī this rule does not apply;

since the two cases are dissimilar, [the former] is lost. Furthermore, the method for a bhikṣu to accept medicine does not apply to a bhikṣuṇī, so that too is lost. As for the *śuddhi* rite, it is performed by addressing a person differently [in each case], and therefore the purification is lost.

Regarding the Dharma: furthermore, this [rule] does not result in loss. Why is this so? It is because, as in the case of the initial *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), although it is spoken of differently in relation to the person, why then would one say that it depends on the original year of ordination?
When going among the community of nuns, the transformation into a nun is likewise the same as the previous case of receiving the precepts:

by not sitting [in the assembly], the monk-status is extinguished and the nun-status is established. Since the nun-status is established, why do you alone claim that the robes and other requisites are lost?

According to the Dharma, because the transformation of the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) does not involve the conditions for losing robes overnight, nor does it involve the conditions for losing purity, the subsequent medicine transformed [by this] should likewise remain valid even when encountering such conditions.
When this explanation is made, that which was previously established according to the Dharma remains mutually transformed without being lost.

If one undergoes a transformation while the ritual action has not yet been completed, it is possible that it will not be accomplished. However, if one undergoes a transformation with respect to the objective force (*vastu-śakti*) such that the transformation is about to be accomplished, it should also be considered accomplished.
This is like the discussion regarding whether the reception of precepts and the establishment of a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) are accomplished or not.

Yet, the *Vibhāṣā* (Jielun) states that one must be sent to again undertake the practice of the *viśuddhi-dharma*. This appears to be a discussion based on the premise that the ritual action has not yet been completed; this interpretation may be acceptable.

Thus it is. Regarding the sixth section, as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: if a bhikṣu confers the precepts upon a śrāmaṇera, and the Sangha suddenly transforms into nuns, [the candidate] departs and the boundary of influence (*śakti*) becomes distant;
in such a case, the precepts are not obtained. This is because there is no principle for a nun to confer the precepts upon a man. Furthermore, this is also the rule.

If [the candidate] becomes a nun just as the ceremony is concluding, the śrāmaṇera obtains the bhikṣu precepts. Next, if a disciple changes [gender], it is like a bhikṣu conferring the precepts upon another:
this śrāmaṇera who has changed into a woman does not obtain the precepts, because the original basis [of the ritual] was deficient.
Furthermore, there is the method for when the number is incomplete. If, as the ceremony is nearing completion, the status changes, one obtains the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts.

If ten *bhikṣus* confer the precepts upon a *śrāmaṇerikā*, and the teacher and disciple mutually change status, the case is to be understood by analogy with what preceded. Again, if ten *bhikṣuṇīs* act as the formal preceptors (*upādhyāyī*) for a *śikṣamāṇā*.
Regarding whether the transformation of the preceptor constitutes a valid ordination or not, it is the same as explained above.

As for the transformation of the disciple, it is invariably invalid, because the male body does not at all rely upon the original dharma. Therefore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Upāli asked concerning the *karmavācanā* for the reception of the śrāmaṇera precepts.
When undergoing the *karmavācanā* for receiving the full precepts, if a male organ transforms into a female organ, is he called a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī*? The Buddha replied:

"He is a *bhikṣu*. When undergoing the *karmavācanā* for the *śikṣamāṇā* and the full ordination, if a female transforms into a male, even if he has squinting eyes, one arm is disproportionately long and the other is disproportionately short, if he is left-handed, mute, deaf, blind, afflicted with consumption, insane, extremely old, or lacks dignity..."
[The one who is] of extremely ugly appearance and who brings disgrace upon the Saṃgha—such a bhikṣu should not be ordained.

If he has already been ordained, it is said that he is considered to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), as explained above. This Vinaya may be understood according to the text. Regarding the sixth [section], there are three [points].
As for those who dwell in the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*), they might perhaps be seen or heard; however, because the space and the realm of existence are distinct, [they do not interact].

The seventh [category] has three [cases], because they do not see one another, though it is possible for them to hear [one another]. The eighth [category] has three [cases], because they are mutually beyond both seeing and hearing.
The ninth [category] has three [cases], because they reside outside the realm (*dhātu*). The tenth does not receive the *śrāmaṇera* precepts;

if one were to obtain the precepts, there would be an offense, because it would constitute a loss of the sequential order of entering the Dharma. Below this, in the state of emptiness (*ākāśa*), the four [categories] do not obtain the precepts and incur an offense. As for the preceding...
Or it may be indeterminate; there may also be cases where one receives or does not receive the precepts even when cutting off a hand or similar limb.

Regarding the tenth [case], one who does not accept the status of a *śrāmaṇera* invariably receives the precepts, whereas all others do not. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the preceptor recites the *karmavācanā*, and the person receiving full ordination also recites the *karmavācanā*.
The *bhikṣuṇī* recites the *karmavācanā*, but this is not called "receiving full ordination.

From here below is the fourth section, the procedure for receiving the precepts. This text has two parts: first, the method for receiving the precepts; second, clearing away doubts regarding those who have been suspended within the assembly.
The former part has three sections: first, [the procedure] up to "thus one maintains the dharma of correctly receiving the precepts."
After the second bhikṣu has received the precepts and the assembly of monks has departed, the characteristics of maintaining the precepts are explained below.

After "Third, you have completed receiving full ordination," and so forth, the exhortation to receive and maintain them is concluded. Within this section on receiving [the precepts], there are two parts:
