According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: because of Baddhananda acting as a senior monk, he proclaimed: "The Sangha is now performing the fifteenth-day *poṣadha*.
Those monks who have not come must announce their consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pāriśuddhi*). What shall the Sangha do now? What matter do the monks wish to address?"
The bhikṣus replied, "A certain bhikṣu should be subjected to the seven disciplinary measures, such as censure (tarjanīya) and so forth;
another should be subjected to parivāsa, mānāpya, mūlāpakarṣa, and āvarhaṇa. Upāli said, "I do not know the formal procedures (karmavācanā).
The bhikṣus asked, "If you do not know the formal procedures, why did you question the Saṃgha and the bhikṣus?"

"What should be done? They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "The *upādhyāya* (preceptor) should recite the precepts (*śīla*), and the one who maintains the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) should perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
Furthermore, on the day of the *poṣadha*, when the monk Upananda was the *upādhyāya* and the community of monks requested him to recite the precepts, he replied, 'I have forgotten. The bhikṣus said:

If one forgets [the procedure], why does one sit in the place of the *upasthāyaka*? [They] asked the Buddha. The Buddha said: "The *upasthāyaka* should recite the precepts (*poṣadha*). If not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, they did not know up to what point one is considered an *upasthāyaka*. They asked the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If there is no one above them, all are called *upasthāyakas*.
Regarding the sixth question of the layperson concerning how many people there are below [him], this is the origin story (*nidāna*) for the distribution of voting tickets (*śalākā*).

The second section, the text on the *sīmā-bandhana* (demarcation of boundaries), has two parts. First, from the beginning up to "Thus, one should maintain the natural boundary," it concerns the accumulation of obstacles and difficulties within the sphere of activity;

it describes how the Great Sage, knowing the proper time, opened the field and established the formal procedure for the *sīmā-bandhana*. Second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, it correctly clarifies the *sīmā-bandhana* itself.
Within this, there are three sections. First, up to "Thus, one should maintain the method for binding large and small boundaries," it concerns the gathering of people together through a common [vow].

The Dharma. Second, from the passage concerning the bhikṣu who has become weary [of worldly things] down to the bridge, the method for establishing the *acīvāra-sīmā* (the boundary where robes need not be kept with one) and the inclusion of robes as belonging to a person.
Third, from the passage "At that time there were two residences" onwards, the method for opening and establishing the boundaries of large and small areas.
The initial section further divides into two parts. The first part, extending up to "Thus it is maintained," clearly explains the method for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

Since this boundary is so vast that everyone must assemble there, and because it is difficult to escape from it once established—fearing it would cause hardship for the Saṃgha—the second part provides for the binding of a *śīma-kaṇḍaka* (precept field) by a group of four or fewer monks when necessary.

The third section, beginning with "If a bhikṣu wishes to extensively establish a boundary," clarifies the method for dissolving boundaries (*sīmā*) and explains the meaning of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).
This is analyzed through four gates: first, the intention behind the permission and prohibition of establishing boundaries, the explanation of their names, and the determination of their essence;

second, the assembly of monks regarding distance and the inadmissibility of proxy consent (*chanda*); third, the method of establishment; and fourth, the manifestation of whether the ritual procedure (*dharma*) is present or absent.
The first section, from the third [chapter] onwards, consists of one part: an explanation of the intent behind the establishment, opening, and closing of the *sīmā* (boundary).

The *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are the essential pillars for maintaining the discipline; they rectify and sustain the governance of the community. No dharma exceeds these in importance, and thus they ought to be observed by all in common, for there is no principle that permits deviation.

However, because [monks] naturally gather in such great numbers, it leads to exhaustion and fatigue among the assembly, obstructing spiritual cultivation and causing the neglect of one’s duties. This is truly to be pitied. The Great Sage, knowing the proper time, permitted the restriction of the boundaries.
The demarcation of the boundary (*sīmā*) within this location follows the same dharma; for the sake of such benefit, it is necessary to open [the area].

Once opened, the communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) must be performed, as they cannot be accomplished without a defined boundary. Furthermore, it is necessary to establish the rules for its demarcation. First there is the opening, and subsequently the regulation; the matter lies herein.
Regarding the second [point], the explanation of the names: because the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is restricted and limited, it is called "binding" (*bandha*, *kṣetra-bandha*).

Because it separates this side from that side, with each having its own distinct boundary, it is called a "limit" (*sīmā*). Therefore, it is termed "binding the limit" (*kṣetra-bandha*). In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vinayaviniścaya*), the Indic name is *caturmaśi*.
Translated into the language of this land [China], it is called "separate residence" (*pṛthag-vāsa*). Its commentary explains: "In this [language], it is called the *poṣadha-sīmā*."
What is sometimes called a "precept platform" (*jietan*) is not a literal translation of the term. It means that this dwelling place and other dwelling places do not communicate with one another;
when performing ritual acts here, there is no need to seek the consent (*chanda*) of those from other locations. Therefore, it is called a "separate dwelling" (*bielu*).

There are seventeen types of such separate dwellings, namely: the long circular separate dwelling, the four-cornered separate dwelling, the wave-patterned separate dwelling, and so on, up to the seventeenth.

Regarding those such as the "staying apart" (pārivāsika) due to insanity and so forth: the term "water-wave" (udaka-vīci) is used because the characteristics of the boundary (sīmā-lakṣaṇa) resemble the form of water-waves.

Thirdly, regarding the determination of the substance (dravya), there are no more than two types: first, the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā); second, the Small Precept-Platform (kṣudra-sīmā-maṇḍala). Question:

Why is it that only the small boundary receives the name "platform" (maṇḍala)? Answer: It is explained that the location of the Great Boundary is vast and distant, and furthermore, it is where the Saṃgha resides.

This location is fundamentally not intended solely for the purpose of extinguishing evil and generating goodness; therefore, it is designated by the name "Great" (*mahā*) rather than being called by the name of the site itself.

The intent behind establishing the *karmavastu* (boundary) is fundamentally to distinguish between individuals so that goodness may be generated and evil extinguished, thereby selecting the refined while rejecting the defiled—much like a worldly marketplace.

It is from this analogy that the name is manifested. If this is so, then the other two small boundaries (*sīmā*) are likewise for the purpose of generating goodness and extinguishing evil; why, then, are they not so named?

The commentary explains: "One who erects markers and demarcates boundaries" refers to a place where ritual procedures (*dharmakarma*) are performed with long-term stability; such a site may be given the name of a "precinct" (*sīmā*).

The other two types lack such markers and are not places for permanent ritual performance; they are designated by the number of people seated there, up to the point of full occupancy, and thus receive their respective names.

The term "vast and distant" refers to the *mahā-sīmā* (Great Boundary). How many essential constituents does the *mahā-sīmā* have? According to the text, there are four: 1. Separate *poṣadha* (confession) and separate *lābha* (benefits);
this is also called the "concordance of person and dharma within the same boundary. 2. Common *poṣadha* and common *lābha*; this is also called the "concordance of the two dharmas and food.
3. Common *poṣadha* and separate *lābha*; this is also said to be the "concordance of the two [in terms of] dharma alone. 4. Separate *poṣadha*.

It is the same regarding the sharing of offerings (*lābha*). This is also called "the combination of two single-meal practices. These meanings shall be explained later. The great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is broad and distant. How far is it broad and distant?
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when establishing a boundary, one may do so according to the distance; a monk subsequently established a boundary of twelve *yojanas*.

When it was time for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), he had to travel for four or five days to reach it, or he might encounter various difficulties. The Buddha said: "As with the aforementioned boundaries, this is not [permissible]."
It is established. One incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Now, it is permitted that the maximum distance is three *yojanas*. In the *Ji* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya), two texts both state three *yojanas*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the boundary for the *poṣadha* is at most ten *krośas*. According to the principles of this *vinaya*, this should be calculated as one hundred *li*.
Therefore, the Vinaya below states: "If two dwelling places are far apart, yet they bind themselves to a single *poṣadha* recitation," the Buddha said:

"The bhikṣus perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day; some arrive beforehand on the fourteenth day. Others perform the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day; some arrive beforehand on the thirteenth day.

Since they arrive only after having spent a night en route, one knows that the distance is approximately one hundred *li*. A restricted and narrow area is called a 'small boundary' (*kṣudra-sīmā*). This is the essence of the small boundary."
How many [factors] are there? There are three major positions: first, the boundary of the ritual site (*śīmaṇḍala*); second, the number of persons; third, the completion of the seating arrangement.

Alternatively, as in the case of establishing a minor boundary (*kṣudrasīman*) for the reception of precepts, there may be four distinct factors. The minor boundary is restricted and narrow. As for how much constitutes being restricted and narrow, the *Jianlun* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states:
"The ritual site is extremely small, accommodating twenty-one persons at most; it must not be too large or wide, as that would result in obstruction."

Therefore, the remaining two portions of the limit can be understood according to what has been explained. Regarding the demarcation of a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) during the conferral of precepts, it merely states that "the assembly has gathered and the small boundary has been demarcated," yet one does not know whether the characteristics of the boundary are small or large; thus, this too is difficult to apply. Whether it is correct or not is distinguished as usual.
The second section has already provided a preliminary exposition of the principles. Now, the lecture proceeds with an explanation based on the text. The text is divided into two parts:
first, the introductory sequence up to the point where the formal act of receiving the *karmavācanā* (consent) is not permitted, which explains the meaning of the second section;

second, from "the resident monks" (*pūrvasthavira*) onwards, which correctly clarifies the method of performing the formal act, thereby explaining the third and fourth sections. Regarding the first part, we shall first explain the meaning and subsequently interpret the text. [Explanation]
There are two points of meaning. First, the gathering of the Saṃgha according to distance; second, not permitting the acceptance of *chanda* (consent).

Regarding the first point, "distance," it may also refer to the large and small *prakṛti-sīmā* (natural boundaries). The gathering relies upon the natural boundary. How many types of natural boundaries are there? There are three possible positions.

1. The village boundary (*grāma-sīmā*). 2. The forest hermitage boundary (*araṇya-sīmā*). 3. The water boundary (*udaka-sīmā*). Regarding the first, the village: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Upāli asked:
"If a bhikṣu is in a village and first constructs a monastery (*vihāra*) but has not yet formally demarcated the boundary (*sīmā*), at that time, how large should the boundary be?
The Buddha said: "It follows the extent of the village; the limits of the village constitute the boundary of the monastery. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, Upāli asked: "In a city..."

Regarding the characteristics of towns and villages, it is difficult to distinguish between near and far. Is it not possible for a *saṃgha* to establish a boundary (*sīmā*) and achieve its formal accomplishment?

The Buddha said: "Plant one *āmra* tree every seven *dhanus*. Although there may be different boundaries at intervals of eight trees, if the monks can see one another from afar, they may perform legal acts (*dharmakarma*).
Altogether, this amounts to forty-nine *dhanus*. One *dhanu* is nine feet long; thus, [forty-nine *dhanus*] equals four hundred and forty-one feet, which constitutes seventy [bow-lengths]."

Three paces and a half on each of the four sides; these are the two limits. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this is explained based on what can be distinguished. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is discussed in terms of what cannot be distinguished.

Regarding the boundary of an araṇya (wilderness): according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a bhikṣu is in a secluded place without a village and has first begun constructing a monastery but has not yet performed the formal delimitation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), at that time, how large should it be? The Buddha said: "A square *krośa*. Within this [area], there is no..."

[The boundary] is distinct. If it is distinct, one incurs an offense according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. Regarding a forest-dwelling (*araṇyaka*) bhikṣu who does not know the extent of his own natural boundary (*jātīya-sīmā*), the Buddha said:

"The natural boundary extends two *krośas* from the front of the body. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "For a forest-dweller, the front [of the dwelling] should be one *krośa* as the boundary.
However, the size of a *krośa* is not fixed. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is two thousand *dhanus*; one *dhanus* is nine feet long. Combined [these measurements].
Three thousand paces. Ten *danda*. Five hundred *bow* (dhanus). A bow is four *hasta* long; this calculates to six hundred paces.

According to the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*, one *krośa* is here called five *li*. According to the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, the boundary of an *araṇya* (forest hermitage) is at its smallest seven *paṭala* in circumference.
One *paṭala* is twenty-eight *hasta*. If [the residents] do not agree, it is seven times twenty-eight.
One may perform ritual acts at a distance of one *hasta* (cubit) from the exterior; this amounts to one hundred and ninety-six *hasta*.
Each *hasta* is one foot and eight inches, totaling three hundred and fifty-two feet and eight inches, which altogether constitutes fifty-eight paces and one foot and eight inches.
This is the same as the *araṇya* (wilderness) measurement for the *caturvarga* (four-part) robe. Regarding the water site, it is five parts. [The Buddha] informed the bhikṣus: "All..."

Rivers, all lakes and ponds, and all oceans cannot be demarcated as formal boundaries (*sīmā*). If one travels upon the water, the area reached by the water sprinkled by a strong person among the assembly constitutes a natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*).
According to the *Jianlun* (Commentary on the Vinaya), this is not the case; a formal boundary can indeed be established there. Regarding a natural boundary on the water:
once sand has been thrown [to mark the limit], if there are bhikṣus outside that area, it does not obstruct [the boundary]; if one wishes to assemble [them], they may do so.

The monks each rely on their previous boundaries. This refers to cases where the boundary markers are narrow while the territory is wide, or where the boundary markers are wide while the territory is narrow;
in both instances, they rely on the markers to assemble [the community], because [the territory] is not yet the formal boundary.

Regarding the second gate: why is it that for the *sīmā-bandhana* (delimitation of boundaries) alone the granting of consent (*chanda*) is not permitted, whereas for other legal acts (*karmas*) the granting of consent is allowed?

There are three reasons for this. First, the *karma* of delimiting boundaries is the very foundation of the communal assembly (*saṃgha*); logically, it should be strictly regulated, and thus the granting of consent is not permitted.

As for all other *karmas*, they are merely secondary matters for the communal assembly; therefore, the granting of consent is opened up as permissible. Second, because no boundary has yet been established [at the time of the initial delimitation].

In the *Jìnzìrán* (Natural) procedure, because it is weak, it does not include those who have left (*yù*, *chanda*). Other *karman* procedures rely on the boundary (*sīmā*) to be performed; because they are strong, they do include those who have left. This is for three reasons:

to make known the limits of the boundary, to prevent interference with the affairs of the Saṃgha, and to avoid the difficulty of schism. Other procedures are the opposite; therefore, they permit the presence of those who have left.
According to the *Qīlù* (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya), there is no leaving in the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, for fear that one might avoid being accused of an offense.
Next, regarding the explanation of the text: as for the phrase "striking the *gandī*," it is as described in the *Vinaya-ācāra-sūtra*;

here it is called "striking the *qing*. The ritual procedure is to be understood accordingly. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it says that one should strike the drum, strike the *gandī*, or blow the conch shell.

[When asked], "Who strikes them? the Buddha said, "A *śrāmaṇera* or a garden keeper should strike them. If there is no *śrāmaṇera*, a *bhikṣu* may also strike them. Thereupon, they struck them too many times.

The Buddha said: "One should strike the gong three times to assemble the Sangha; those far and near shall not be permitted to receive [the instruction]. Therefore, one should proceed as described above.

Second, from 'among those who have long resided here' onwards, there is the formal procedure for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). This text consists of four parts. Regarding these four parts: first, the appointment of the person to designate the boundaries;
second, the explanation of the designation of the boundaries starting from 'if in the east' and so forth; third, within the assembly, one should appoint those who are capable..."

The following section designates those who shall preside over the rite. From "The fourth virtuous elder, may the Saṃgha listen" onwards, the text explicitly clarifies the method for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
Although the text consists of four sections, its meaning comprises seven points; this is because the first section contains four meanings, while each of the subsequent three sections contains one.

Before explaining the text, three preliminary points must be added: first, one must first know the location where the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept-field) is to be established. Regarding this *śīla-maṇḍala*, as for the boundary...
Regarding the opening and closing of the *kaṭhina* robe for the internal assembly, this boundary may only be established within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

Once the threefold markers have been erected and the boundary has been formally closed, one must never perform the rite outside the boundary; for if it were permitted, the formal act would not be valid.

There are four textual references concerning the "assembly of bhikṣus" and so forth. When the matter arose and the great assembly became exhausted, the *kaṭhina* field was opened; this constitutes first establishing the boundary and subsequently opening it. Furthermore...

In the two lower realms, there is mutual seeing, hearing, and suspicion; since the Buddha ordained that one must call out [the boundary], how could he have ordained calling out for those outside the realm?

Furthermore, the text of the formal act states: "The bhikṣus residing in this dwelling place proclaim the marks of the small boundary. If they were outside the realm, how could they be said to reside in a dwelling place?

Furthermore, there is no place within the *śīmaṇḍala* (boundary of discipline) where one does not abide. The reason the term "place of abiding" (*āvāsa*) is used here is precisely because it refers to the interior of the established circular boundary.

Moreover, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) has already been established, and after it has been relinquished, the *śīmaṇḍala* is subsequently established, one monk should then proclaim the four directional markers (*catur-diśa-lakṣaṇa*), and another monk should further proclaim the exclusion of the inner area (*antar-bhūmi-varjana*). Then, another monk makes the formal motion (*jñapti*).

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen, etc. Furthermore, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If one does not further establish a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) outside, but establishes only a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), one may not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Based on this textual meaning, it is clear that [the candidate] must be placed within the boundary."
The second is the ritual for establishing boundary markers (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding this Vinaya, there are eighteen or twelve [types of markers], as can be understood from the text.
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are eight types of boundary markers: first, mountain markers; large ones are like Mount Sumeru, small ones are like elephants. Second, stone markers;

large ones are like oxen, small ones weigh thirty *liang* (catty). Excluding natural outcroppings, one must not use them; rather, separate stones must be specifically placed to serve as boundary markers. Third, forest markers; large forests...

Extending even for a hundred *yojanas*. As for small [distances], they reach down to four trees joined together. One must exclude grasses, thickets, and bamboo groves, because their substance is insubstantial.
Regarding the characteristics of the four trees: one must exclude withered trees; the large ones are like the *Jambū* tree, while the small ones are eight inches high and as thin as a needle.
Regarding the characteristics of the five paths: one must exclude paths leading toward rivers, dead-end paths, and the like; these are called "great roads. Or...
The sign of the chariot path: extending even through three or four villages. The sign of the ant-hills: six of them appearing like mountains, the smallest being eight inches high.
The sign of the rivers: if it does not rain for four months, those that flow constantly without interruption and have a depth of two feet shall constitute the sign.

The eight characteristics of the water-element boundary (*āpa-dhātu-sīmā*): whether it is a natural pond that has formed its own characteristics, or water flowing through fields, or water collected in a reservoir—none of these may constitute a boundary.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the eight characteristics are: walls, groves, trees, mountains, rocks, roads, ponds, and rivers.

This resembles the *Samānadṛṣṭi-vāda* (Discourse on Identical Views). It consists of five parts. Taking sentient beings, fire, or smoke as the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), whether they are combined with the boundaries (*dhātu*) or mutually interpenetrate, none of these are established.

The resulting offense is a *duṣkṛta* (transgression). Once these characteristics are known, the classification follows the principle of one text and three layers, as can be understood from the usual practice.
Regarding the *Dṛṣṭi-vāda*, there are five types of boundary shapes (*sīmā-ākṛti*): namely, square, circular, drum-shaped, half-moon, and triangular. This is according to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The meanings of "water," "waves," "separate dwelling," and so forth are said to correspond to the natural realm (*dharmadhātu*). This refers to the circular measurement of seventy-three paces and so on;
other natural characteristics are likewise the same.

Third, the determination of the sequence for binding the boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*). In both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, the boundary of the site (*kṣetra-sīmā*) is established first, followed by the establishment of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

However, there is no explicit scriptural authority for this. Rather, it should be done with the great boundary first and the small boundary later, because the site is established within the great boundary.

Fourth is the appointment of those who designate the boundaries (*sīmā*). According to the text, this refers to those who have long resided there, for the purpose of determining the limits of the seasonal training boundary (*vārṣika-sīmā*).
However, even if they are not former residents, provided they know the characteristics of the boundary, it would logically be established.
Next, from "If in the east" onwards, the text clearly explains the proclamation of the boundaries; the second point therein is the actual meaning.
Fifth, if there is no *sīmā-kṣetra* (boundary site), one directly proclaims the external characteristics (*bāhya-lakṣaṇa*) of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), beginning from the southeast corner.

The wording is as follows: "In the east there is a mountain called Mountain," and so forth. If there is a *sīmā-kṣetra*, one first proclaims the external characteristics of the great boundary, then completes the proclamation of the internal characteristics (*abhyantara-lakṣaṇa*).
Next, one summarizes by saying: "This is one complete circuit of the internal and external characteristics of the great boundary. This is repeated three times.

The fifth section: Regarding the failure to announce the four boundaries when performing the formal act of boundary-delineation (*sīmā-bandha*), the Buddha declared that the delineation is not established and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Next, among the assembly, those who are to be appointed—specifically the person who presides over the ritual—are mentioned; this corresponds to the third point in the text.

Regarding the sixth point, the proclamation of boundaries (*sīmā-uddiśana*): it is not permissible for one who is presiding over the legal procedure (*dharmakarma*) to proclaim the boundaries; therefore, these duties are assigned separately.

Next, the method for formally establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*) is correctly explained below, beginning with "one should act as follows. Within this text, the fourth section corresponds to the actual meaning.
Regarding the four phrases in the seventh *śukla-vākya* (white statement), the second [phrase] restates the cause for the undertaking.

If, on the fifteenth day, the two Vinayas state the names of those who proclaim the boundaries (*sīmā*) in order to formally charge someone with an offense, they cite the characteristics of the boundary being proclaimed—such as "because it was proclaimed by the monk so-and-so" in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.

However, both this Vinaya and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* do not mention the names, fearing that doing so might lead to confusion or the establishment of separate boundaries. One may rely on either version; the meaning should be understood accordingly.

This is not correct. To say they "dwell in the same residence" means their location is the same. If two residences were originally separate and have now become one, one cannot say they "dwell in the same residence.
This case refers to those that were originally together and remain together; therefore, it is called "one residence."
Regarding the phrase "the same recitation of the precepts" (*poṣadha*), this refers to the identity of the *dharma*. Question: Why does it not mention "the same *karmavācanā*"? Answer:

Because the recitation of the precepts possesses both types of identity; that is, there is identity of the boundary (*sīmā*) and identity of the disciplinary rule (*saṃvara*) for those within different boundaries. In the case of the *karmavācanā*, there is only identity [of the boundary].
If they belong to the same *dhātu* (realm), there is no prohibition; because they call out from different *dhātus*, it is known that these are not of the same category.

If that is so, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) also possesses both [conditions] of being within the same *dhātu*. Why, then, is it not said that they share the same *pravāraṇā*? Answer: First, because it is rare;

second, because it would be confused with the regular requirement for *pravāraṇā*. Furthermore, it is asked: while the formal act of granting consent (*chanda*) regarding one matter does not accomplish other matters, why is it that here, when speaking of the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, [it is said otherwise]?

Regarding similar cases of naming the matter (*vastu*), one should specifically be permitted to recite the *Poṣadha*. Answer: Because the sequence of these [cases] differs, some are successful and others are not.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed as usual. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the third section.
The fourth section, "Riding the Explanation," clarifies the existence or non-existence of dharmas. Formerly, based on the theory of perception (*darśana-vāda*), it appeared as if dharmas arose;

just as when water washes away earth to form a pit, one knows its location because water flows there, or as when a structure is erected to stand firm and rituals are performed upon it, one thus knows that dharmas such as [non-informative action] exist.
Now, the explanation is not so. It is like a practitioner performing an action that gives rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*); with respect to the practitioner...

The mind has an attainment (*prāpti*). Because there is this attainment, one may say that there exists an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*). However, this rite of boundary-delineation (*sīmā-bandha*) does not belong to any particular individual;

the location of the boundary is insentient. Since this unmanifest action cannot temporarily reside anywhere [apart from the mind], we know that it is merely the proclamation that establishes the place.

Having finished the *poṣadha*, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, you must not perform the *poṣadha* early. On the *poṣadha* day, one should sweep the stūpa and the interior of the monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma*).

First, prepare pure water, fragrant liquid, lighted lamps, and *śalākā* (voting sticks). According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the voting sticks should be at least as short as the fingers held side-by-side, and at most one cubit when the hand is curled.

They should not be thicker than the little finger, nor thinner than a *kṣura* (razor). Once the *gandī* has been struck and the assembly has gathered, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one intends to recite the precepts:
One should first purify the water. Having washed one's hands, one takes up a tally (*śalākā*) and prepares a fragrant liquid for bathing the tallies; those others who take up tallies do likewise.

Furthermore, one sprinkles the ground with fragrant liquid in five portions. One person from among the junior monks should be appointed to distribute the tallies, and another person should be appointed to collect them.
As for the distributor of tallies, he should first announce the formal procedure (*jñapti*) and then perform the distribution and collection according to the usual practice, step by step.

Understand. Jīvaka, first distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*) for those who have received full ordination; then, after distributing the voting sticks for the novices (*śrāmaṇera*), you should announce:

"There are this many fully ordained persons and this many novices; in total, there should be this many people. Once the five-part collection has been gathered, it should be counted. Having counted them, you should proclaim aloud:
"There are so many bhikṣus, so many śrāmaṇeras, and so many members of the harmonious community of renunciants. This is the ritual procedure therein.

The suspension and reinstatement [of the precepts] may be understood accordingly. With three or fewer persons, the *pratimokṣa* is recited face-to-face; the specific characteristics of the precepts are not extensively displayed, nor is there mutual inquiry regarding purity.

Rather, one simply declares oneself pure, as this serves to represent the others' speech. For a single person, the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) and the verbal declaration of purity have the same meaning as the face-to-face method.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *poṣadha* may be performed during all postures, such as walking or standing. Thus, one who performs the *poṣadha* [may do so in any posture].

If a bhikṣu is traveling and reaches the day of the uposatha, and there is danger or fear such that he cannot stay to perform the uposatha, he should first deliberate upon how far he can recite the precepts before reaching a limit—whether it be a mountain, a rock, or a landmark—from which they can reach one another with an outstretched hand and perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the uposatha;
only then should he perform the uposatha. When bhikṣus perform the uposatha by the water, if the water rises to a certain level...

[The Buddha said: "It is extremely difficult, yet it is finally accomplished. One does not know whether the *poṣadha* has been established. The Buddha said: "It is established. Regarding the *poṣadha* with many beds:

all must extend their hands so that they reach one another. As for the *poṣadha* performed while lying down: those who are old or ill and cannot remain upright for long may join the corners of their beds together and perform the *poṣadha* while lying down.

"Is there no offense? The Buddha said: "This refers to those who pass on the *chanda* (consent). Within the section on the characteristics of what is not [the Saṃgha], there are two parts.

Briefly distinguishing their non-validity in contrast to the three preceding positions: the first sentence contrasts with the aforementioned statement regarding the Saṃgha. According to the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, three persons do not constitute a Saṃgha;

thus, the passing on of *chanda* is not accomplished, which constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthag-jana*). As for the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the recitation of the precepts, this is a ritual procedure performed by four persons; since only three persons are now presiding over it, it is invalid.
This is called "unlawful" (*adharma*). That is to say, this refers to an unlawful separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha*). The following two lines refer to a lawful separate assembly.

From the second section on the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) onwards, there is an extensive and repeated analysis: first, the group of six commits an offense; next, they inform the Buddha; next, the Buddha judges that it is not permitted;

and finally, there is an extensive explanation of what constitutes "unlawful," which has four parts. First, the number four is raised; next, three types of unlawfulness are distinguished, with one being explained in detail.

The first three [procedures] are declared invalid; they are intended to make known what is invalid. The next one demonstrates what is valid, in order to bring about an understanding of the valid. Regarding the "three invalidities," the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
first, performing the *jñapti* (motion) in a place that is not pure (*aśuddha-sthāna*); second, declaring the *jñapti* through an illegal *vinaya* procedure (*adharmika-vinaya*).

These are so called because it is feared that the act will not be accomplished—namely, when four or more persons perform two *jñaptis* without being fully assembled, or when three persons receive the consent (*chanda*) of a fourth person and then declare the *jñapti* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.

These two cases are termed "an illegal separate assembly" (*adharma-vighāta*). If four or more persons are all assembled together yet perform two *jñapti* (formal announcements) simultaneously, or if four persons perform the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) using three utterances, this is termed "an illegal harmonious assembly" (*adharmasaṃgha*).

Or, if four or more persons are not fully assembled, yet proceed according to the rules for formal announcement (*jñaptidharma*), or if three or fewer persons accept the consent (*chanda*) and perform the face-to-face rite (*pratyekamukha*), this is termed "a legal separate assembly" (*dharmavighāta*).

Regarding the term "one accord" (*ekavācika*): if four or more persons have all assembled and perform the formal recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), or if three persons do not receive the consent (*chanda*) but each performs the threefold declaration, or if one person performs the mental recitation (*manasikāra*), this is called the harmony of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃgha*). Next, from the passage beginning with "if that bhikṣu...
onwards, it demonstrates the three types of invalidity and clarifies that such is the method for "one accord. Following that, the text states: "It should be declared in this manner."
Regarding "precepts" (*śīla*): it means exhorting the abandonment of improper conduct. As for "this teaching of mine," this is a double conclusion regarding what is proper and what is improper.

Third is the dharma of granting consent and purity (*chanda-pāriśuddhi*). Within this section, there are four parts: first, clarifying the expression of consent so that the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) may be properly performed;

second, from the passage "at that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts" onwards, it concerns the granting of purity, expressing one's own stainless clarity in order to accomplish the recitation.

Third, regarding the section beginning with "At that time, the group of six gave their consent," this refers to the collective granting of consent for purity (*pārisuddhi*), intended so that the legal proceedings (*dharmakarma*) would not be obstructed or delayed.

if the illness is cured and one regains one's original state of mind, it is termed "abandoned" (*prahāṇa*); no formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is required for its release. Fourth, the resolution of doubts and the re-asking of questions: the reason for asking is as follows.
This is because, as with the previous case of Nandika, there was doubt. The Buddha said: "It is not the same; act further according to the specific illness.
Second, the text on the formal admission (*pāṭidesanīya*) has five parts: first, Ānanda requested that the Buddha speak [the precepts], but the Buddha declined to speak them;

second, Maudgalyāyana unilaterally expelled [the offender]; third, from the words "The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana" onwards, it prescribes the taking of the formal admission; fourth, from the words "From this day forward... onwards...

He ceased speaking and entrusted the teaching to his disciples to explain. From the fifth section, "After the Buddha had spoken," etc., eight extraordinary matters are cited to demonstrate that a corpse was not left overnight, thereby clarifying the reason for not speaking [on this matter]. Second, regarding the text on those who have violated the precepts and are impure:
all four grave offenses (pārājika) are included. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, this bhikṣu adorned the poṣadha hall in various ways, fashioning gold lotus petals. The bhikṣu...
Having all entered [the assembly] intending to perform the *poṣadha*, a gold leaf fell to the ground. This wicked bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, picked it up and tucked it under his armpit;
therefore, he was expelled. This fourth [case] is called the Tathāgata’s final recitation of the precepts. According to the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*, regarding the brief teaching:
for twelve years prior, there had been no initial transgression of the detailed rules, so the Buddha himself recited them. Now that the detailed rules have been transgressed...

Therefore, [the Buddha] ceased speaking and entrusted [this matter] to his disciples to explain the extensive teachings. He instructed the disciples that they must not speak of it to those who have committed offenses.
As for why he entrusted it to the disciples, the answer is: because bhikṣus who have attained purity through what they have seen and heard possess the capacity to understand the meaning;
thus, he entrusted it to the disciples. The fifth section has two parts: first, listing the eight similes of the ocean; second, "In this way, Maudgalyāyana... and so forth.

Below, each provides an analogy to be applied to the Dharma. The third section has two parts: first, the regulation of the *karmavācanā* for reciting the precepts every five years to ensure proficiency;
second, from "From this day forward" onwards, the rule that one must rely on a person capable of reciting the precepts when entering the rainy season retreat (*varṣāvāsa*).

The fourth section has three parts, namely: the censure of the transgression and the subsequent regulation. Within the regulation, there are two parts: first, informing the bhikṣus as to where they should go...

Regarding the "Three Sentences on Restraining the Location" asked by the Master: the second section, beginning with "If the matter to be undertaken is not... and so forth, concerns the method for the Preceptor to evaluate the disciple;
it should consist of eight sentences. The third is a single sentence on "non-action. The second and third, and the fifth, are identical in their two "non-s" [negations].

The fourth and sixth are identical in their one "as" [positive] and one "non-as" [negative]. One sentence regarding "location and non-location" is omitted. The remaining two are as in the second [section].
The seventh and third [sections] are like the *pada* (phrases). The first six must be prohibited; the last one permits going. Regarding the fifth text, it is as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
"If a visiting bhikṣu knows that a *poṣadha* karmavācanā for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is about to take place, he should provide various kinds of offerings and service.
Why? Because in the absence of the Buddha, this serves to fill the Buddha’s place. It further says: "Venerable Sir..."
[The Buddha] said: "Monks should not be made to perform labor for the monastery. They should be provided with clothing and food so that they do not suffer from a lack of sustenance;

furthermore, one should freely provide them with excellent dwellings. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one does not go out to meet a Vinaya-holder who has arrived, or fails to offer him food such as *tambala* before the meal or other food after the meal, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There are two methods for the administration of discipline. First, the method for the expiation and extinction of offenses committed by an individual who has received the hearing of the precepts (*śīla-śravaṇa*).
Second, the method for removing offenses committed by the entire Saṃgha or by a sub-group of monks (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) at that time. The former section further divides into two parts:

first, the procedure for the confession and disclosure of two prior offenses—one recognized and one suspected—prior to the hearing and recitation of the precepts; second, the recitation [of the precepts].

Regarding the section following "at the time of observing the precepts," it explains the method for confessing two offenses committed at the time of the recitation. This involves the rite of mental confession and disclosure (*cittena āviṣkaraṇa*). It explains the first phrase:

one who recognizes they have committed an offense is not permitted to hear the precepts; they must be taught to repent and become pure before they may listen without fault. Therefore, its meaning is analyzed through four sections:
first, explaining the methods of counteractive confession (*pratipakṣa*) for extinguishing evil; second, explaining confession and its resolution (*vibhāga*).
The third [section] explains the number of conditions required for the repentance of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
the fourth explains that while the Mahāyāna extinguishes grave offenses, the Hīnayāna does not.
Regarding the first gate: Generally, the arising of all sinful karma depends upon causes and proceeds from conditions.

Although the actions performed have already passed into the past, because they have been accomplished as causes, they will inevitably bring about bitter retribution. Therefore, that which arises from conditions must, by principle, cease through conditions.

Therefore, one develops revulsion toward evil and applies exceptional earnestness and shame. One establishes the path of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) and washes the mind through repentance (*pratikramaṇa*).

By means of this sincerity, one invokes a pleasant retribution (*sukha-vipāka*), causing evil karma to wither away and the fruits of suffering not to come to fruition. This restores the purity of the precepts (*śīla*) to their original state as they were received;
thus, it is called "repentance" (*chàn*) because it promotes good in place of evil, and it is called "regret" (*huì*) because it seeks to transform past transgressions. Therefore...

Regarding the term "repentance" (*chánhuǐ*): although it carries the sense of repentance, the evil karma one has created must necessarily be experienced within the three types of retribution—namely, the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.

Only that which is subject to transformation upon encountering the right conditions can be eliminated. For example, if one commits a grave evil that is certain to be experienced as retribution in this very life, it may still be transformed.
Now, regarding the superior wholesome karma of repentance, it will certainly result in a favorable retribution.
This also occurs during the time of birth; however, because wholesome karma is powerful, it seizes [the body] and one does not undergo [the results of] evil.

Because the timing is fixed, they coincide at the same moment and thus can exclude one another. Because the retribution is not fixed, once there is a discrepancy, there is a permanent discrepancy and one never undergoes it; the intermediate and lower [karmas] are thus dispensed with.

The principle is likewise. Speaking in terms of seeking retribution, it is called "removal by retribution" (*vipākāpanaya*). Speaking in terms of manifesting repentance, the virtuous mind is able to extinguish evil causes;
this is called "removal by practice" (*pratipakṣāpanaya*). Question: The evil karma one has created belongs to the past. Since it is no longer an existing phenomenon, what is there to repent?
Answer: According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the three time periods exist. Although the evil karma committed belongs to the past, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) exists.

It is accomplished; therefore, confession is possible. According to the Dharmaguptaka school, although evil karma has passed away, it is not as if there was no time when the action was originally performed.
Because that original act serves as the cause for its accomplishment, one now confesses the meaning of that original act which served as the cause.
The second section: Repentance is an action within the realm of existence. It requires mutual confrontation and parity; only when they are equal can [the defilement] be eliminated.
If one possesses superior evil karma but only an inferior virtuous mind, the repentance will not constitute a true confrontation; the stronger force will first prevail and draw one away.
Therefore, they cannot be extinguished; one must instead return to superior goodness and look up toward it while subduing evil causes so as not to invite future retribution.

This applies to the middle [level of understanding] countering the middle and lower, and likewise for the lower countering the lower. If one understands, however, it is not thus: lower understanding cuts off upper delusions, and superior understanding cuts off lower delusions.

Because coarse delusions obstruct the principle only superficially, the knowledge that reflects upon that shallow principle is capable of dispelling them; thus, lower understanding can eliminate upper delusions.

The subtle or the obscured has profound principles; were it not for superior wisdom, there would be no means to refute and eliminate them. Therefore, the higher [level of] understanding eliminates the lower [level of] doubt.

As for what is called "repentance" (*chánhuǐ*), it involves a contradiction within the phenomenal realm (*shìzhōng*) and requires an opposing counterpart to be equivalent; thus, it is not analogous [to the aforementioned].

If one proceeds from the prevention of unarisen transgressions, it is analogous to the path that severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Just as when an initial offense is coarse, it is easy to separate from it, so too is the subtle and lower good.

The mind is able to prevent [faults] from arising. In this way, even until the fifth category of faults becomes slight, one must apply oneself with diligent protection and maintenance before one can finally be free of faults.
Thus, it is known that this [method] is superior.

The Third Gate: If one is a practitioner of Mahāyāna repentance, one must have deep faith in the true principle of the Mahāyāna’s reality-mark (dharmatā), its wondrous function that is empty and pervasive, and the non-duality of defilement and purity.
One should simply know that deluded thoughts are defilement and the absence of deluded thoughts is purity.

Furthermore, the nature of sin does not exist within, without, or in between. When such an understanding is attained, the stains of sin are eliminated; or else, one may resolve to confess with determination.
One eternally severs the continuity [of afflictions], shatters the body [of transgressions] so as not to violate them.
Thus, with mind following mind in succession and thought following thought in continuity, immeasurable stains of sin are extinguished through conditions. Therefore, the treatise says:
"If this single moment of goodness had form and color, the trichiliocosm of the ten directions could not contain it; because it has no form or color, it can be contained."
As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are five gates of roots of goodness through which one attains birth in a Pure Land;

these are namely: prostration, repentance, entreaty, sympathetic joy, and dedication. This is precisely what is practiced today as the six-period liturgy of repentance, which is the method for eliminating transgressions.

It requires the presence of four conditions: first, to invite the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to serve as witnesses; second, to recite the Dharma-medicine of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, such as [the names of] the ten directions... [and so forth].
The measure is according to what the Buddha knows; there is nothing that is not fully encompassed. Alternatively, this refers to the repentances of thirty-five or twenty-five Buddhas and the like.

Third, one declares the names and types of the offenses, which are contained within the text of the repentance itself. Fourth, one makes a vow to sever [the offenses] forever, until the attainment of Bodhi.
Regarding the repentance rituals (*prāyaścitta*) of the Hīnayāna, it is essential to request a *mahābhikṣu* to serve as a witness. When facing a superior, five elements are required;

when facing an inferior, the prostration at the feet (*pādavandanā*) is omitted. This explanation is based solely on the context of formal deportment (*īryāpatha*) and does not fully exhaust the underlying principle. In fact, there are four factors involved, which shall be explained in detail below.

The fourth section concerns the Mahāyāna’s extinction of heavy [defilements]. This is because: first, its principle is profound and its medicine is wondrous; second, its remedial practices are superior; and third, its fruit is supreme.

One cultivates the path through many bodies rather than attaining realization within a single form. Because it takes the supreme fruit as its object, the place where the resolve for awakening (*cittotpāda*) is generated is wondrous;

therefore, [the Mahāyāna] brings about extinction. In contrast, the Hīnayāna has shallow principles and inferior practices, and one attains realization within a single form; thus, its fruit is not supreme. For these reasons...

This merely extinguishes minor offenses. Next, the explanation of the text is divided into two parts: first, citing the circumstances to address the Buddha; second, from the words "The Buddha said" onwards, teaching the method of instruction.
There are four points regarding the meaning: first, requesting a preceptor for confession, as the text says, "One should go to a pure bhikṣu"; second, the actual confession.
The text has two parts: first, the preliminary observance of dignified demeanor; second, the formal words of confession beginning with "Venerable Sir," and so forth.

The offenses to be repented—those of the three categories [of pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, and pāyattika] and below, as well as the *sthūlātyaya* and others—all follow this same procedure. Within the text there are eight phrases: first, addressing the object before one, hence saying, "Venerable Sir, listen";
second, from "I, [Name]," and so forth, which is the denunciation of one's own name; third, "having committed such-and-such an offense."
1. "The offense" refers to the name and category of the transgression. 2. "Now, having approached," and so forth, reveals that one has no blemish of concealing faults. 3.

"Repentance brings peace and happiness" demonstrates its benefit and harm, clarifying that one abandons harm and pursues benefit. 4. "Recollection," and so forth, excludes those things not remembered;
whatever is remembered is fully disclosed. 5. "I pray, Venerable Sir," and so forth, requests for witness. 6. "With my body," and so forth, returns [to the state of purity].
It is purified as it was originally; there should thus be a pure dharma. Third is the treatment through censure; fourth is the acceptance of one's own confession.

Regarding the second [category], the offense of doubt (*saṃśaya-vastu*): "doubt" has two meanings: first, doubting whether an offense was committed or not, or doubting its gravity, lightness, name, or type.
Therefore, one should confess so that the mind becomes pure. Regarding the next two occasions for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*):

since the time for the recitation is already imminent and there is no time for formal repentance, fearing it might cause disturbance or confusion, even if one clearly recognizes the offense, one need only mentally confess it to manifest the purity of the mind.
This applies equally to cases of doubt.

Regarding the second section on offenses committed by the Saṃgha, there are three parts. First, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the method for recognizing a doubt and performing confession and disclosure is explained.

As for appointing someone to go to another location to perform the confession, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one is appointed through a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). Next, at the time of the second *poṣadha*, one performs the confession and disclosure through a formal motion.

Third, on the day of the *poṣadha*, if the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense but does not recognize its name or characteristics, the method for inquiring about the procedure for confession is explained.

Regarding the fact that there is only a day for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) but no specific time for reciting them: the answer is that previously, when one had doubts about an offense and was certain that oneself and others were guilty, it was necessary to announce and confess it.

Now, however, because one does not recognize the name, category, or details of the offense and is therefore guiltless, and because the minds of the assembly are pure, there is no need to make an announcement;
thus, it does not exist [in this case]. Furthermore, another interpretation is that even if it existed at the time of the recitation of the precepts, [it would likewise not be required].
One should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and the confession (*āviṣkaraṇa*); these are omitted in the text for brevity. Regarding "not knowing the name and the characteristic":

it is like lighting a fire on an open ground where seeds have sprouted, yet not knowing what offense has been committed—such as the destruction of the earth—and thus it is said one does not know the name.

Furthermore, because one does not recognize the specific nature, quantity, or distinctions of the offense itself, it is said one does not know the characteristic. This is addressed to those who harbor attachments, for fear that they might give rise to anger or contention.

It is said that one must not forcibly compel another to undergo repentance (*pratideśanā*). This is because the other person relies on their own mind, which is free from contention (*araṇa*); therefore, it is said that "forcibly granting *parivāsa*" is not analogous to this case.

Furthermore, it may be appropriate to administer treatment according to the number of days the offense was concealed, as it does not accord with [the offender's] disposition; thus, it is stated that "forcibly granting" is not of the same category as this.

The fifth section contains four parts. First, up to the mention of the *sthūlātyaya* offense, there are thirty-six phrases concerning whether the days [of the observance] are the same or different, and whether [monks] come from afar or nearby, or in small or large numbers, and what is appropriate or inappropriate.
Second, following the statement regarding the day of the *poṣadha*, there are forty phrases concerning mutual seeing, hearing, or suspecting [an offense] within the monastery grounds (*saṃghārāma*).
Third, following the phrase "in another residence," there are [phrases concerning] the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and the *sīmā-maṇḍala*.

Regarding "seeing, hearing, and suspecting," there are twenty-four permutations. In the fourth section, beginning with "having different residences within the boundary but outside the *sīmā*," there are twenty-four permutations concerning mutual seeing, hearing, and suspecting.
The first part has two sections: the first, up to "it is also thus," consists of twenty-six permutations that distinguish what is appropriate and what is inappropriate;
the second, beginning with "or [if one says]... and so forth, concerns whether or not one should follow [the rule] when performing legal acts (*dharmakarma*) with an evil mind.

Regarding the offense incurred for violating the instructions, there are three sets of twelve cases in the beginning. The first set concerns the different days of arrival, ranging from few to many, totaling twelve.

The second set concerns the time; starting from the day of the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) and below, it concerns the same five types of arrivals where the day of the *poṣadha* is not mutually known, ranging from few to many, totaling twelve.
The third set consists of twelve cases, which differ specifically in that the arrivals are mutually known.
First, I shall explain the initial passage. The fourteenth and fifteenth [days] are treated as one; the first three are guests, while the fourteenth is an old resident.

On the fifteenth, the number of arriving guests is greater than that of the residents. Furthermore, if there are fourteen old residents and fifteen arriving guests, the number of arriving guests is again greater than that of the residents. This is further divided into three parts.
Fifteen and sixteen are treated as one, "sixteen. There are only the last three [cases]: the guest is sixteen and the host is fifteen; the first three are omitted.

This refers to the guest being fifteen and the old resident being sixteen. Question: Why does the ancient teaching state that when a guest arrives, the guest must follow the established rule of the resident?
Regarding this, it is said that when a guest’s explanation is equal to that of the resident, the resident does not restrict the guest; rather, the resident explains.

The explanation is that because the resident is strong and the guest is weak, the resident speaks so as to cause the guest to follow the resident; the guest’s explanation does not restrict the resident to follow the guest.

If that is so, why is there a further explanation for the guest on subsequent days when they arrive with the same status as the resident? The answer is: because in those cases, they sit down immediately and there is no great exertion.
Regarding the statement that "the guest and the old [resident] are not the same on the same day," this is because it would involve much labor and complication. Question:

Among these differences, why is there no mutual comparison between guest and guest, nor between old resident and old resident, as there is for others? Answer: This is to distinguish the relative strength or weakness of guests and old residents;

since there is no such distinction of strength or weakness among guests and old residents when they are compared with one another, this specific text is absent. Alternatively, while the *Pañcavargika* contains this text, it has been omitted here. Next, the twelve [rules]: first—
Third: the resident looks toward the visitor; next, the visitor looks toward the resident; next, residents look toward one another; next, visitors look toward one another; next, twelve cases:
first, three where the visitor looks toward the resident; next, the resident looks toward the visitor; next, visitor toward visitor; next, resident toward resident. Question:

Why is it that when a bhikṣu comes from outside, he may declare his purity (*viśuddhi*) without committing the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*)? Answer: Because he comes directly toward the Saṃgha, having no intention of creating a division.
Because it is contrary [to the rule]. Jīvaka, one is not permitted to recite the *Poṣadha* twice in a single day at a residence, nor may one recite the *Poṣadha* on consecutive days;

one must wait until the next day before the recitation is permitted. Regarding the classification of offenses, there is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). To summarize the above three points: within the first four of the three categories, the *sthūlātyaya* is fully present.
This means that one should have left [the assembly], or even if one should not have left, because [the quorum] was insufficient and so forth, they did not comply.

Regarding the assembly’s holding of the Dharma: if it is due to an evil mind, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if due to negligence, it is a *duṣkṛta*. In the third case, because one knows [the fault], there is both *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*.

In the twenty-second case, because one has not come to know [it], there is only negligence, which is a *duṣkṛta*. Alternatively, within these three positions, there may equally be both *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*.
The second section has four parts. First, there are ten items concerning a visitor perceiving the signs of a resident; this concerns whether the ritual procedure is successfully performed or not.

Second, there are ten items from "having a residence" onwards, concerning a resident perceiving a visitor. Third, from "on the day of the *poṣadha*" onwards, there are items concerning a visitor hearing the voice of a resident.
Fourth, from "having a residence" onwards, there are ten items concerning a resident hearing the voice of a visitor. Regarding the first [section], there are two groups of five.

Regarding the first section on "not doubting upon initial sight," there are five cases. Of these, the first four do not constitute [an offense], while the fifth does. The first four are further divided into two: in the first three, it does not constitute [an offense] but is culpable;
in the fourth, it does not constitute [an offense] and is non-culpable. It does not constitute [an offense] because the conditions have not assembled;

that is to say, since it was absent, it is not a transgression, and therefore no violation occurs. The first three are further divided into two: in the first two cases, it does not constitute a violation, though it is a minor offense, due to a mind of indolence.

Therefore, the third case does not constitute a *sthūlātyaya*, because it was done with an evil mind. Next, regarding "seeing and doubting" (the fifth): having seen [the person], one gives rise to doubt as to whether he is a *bhikṣu* or a *śrāmaṇera*.
The five phrases are the same as before; thus it says, "it is also like this. All other cases are identical to this.

The third [category] has four positions, as determined previously; it differs from the former only in that the phrases are fewer. First, a visitor sees those who are established [in the community]. While there are six types of seeing, three do not constitute doubt.
Of the first two, the offense is established because the boundaries (*sīmā*) are distinct; since one should have called them but did not, an offense is committed.
The third involves calling them together, which establishes the act but incurs no offense, because this constitutes a public manifestation. There is no third [type of doubt] here.
"Cannot be summoned" refers to the phrase of cursing. The fourth [category] consists of the "no-phrase," which likewise has three aspects of non-doubt. This concludes the first set of six.
The subsequent three sets of six may be understood accordingly; the fourth textual section may also be understood accordingly.

The sixth section: The text on the method for determining the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* has two parts. First, it clarifies that the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) examined themselves and found many transgressions;
fearing punishment by the Saṃgha, they fled and absconded. On the day of the *Poṣadha*, they performed the recitation nineteen times for themselves, and subsequently nineteen times for others.

The seventh is the rule concerning the remaining assembly during the administration of disciplinary measures. Because other members of the assembly might provide support [to the offender] at the time of punishment, it was established that one must not preach before such an assembly.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu is in the presence of bhikṣuṇīs and preaches the bhikṣu precepts, he is not permitted to preach them to the bhikṣuṇīs; nor is he permitted to listen to the bhikṣuṇīs reciting them.
If a bhikṣu stands and listens while a bhikṣuṇī orally transmits the bhikṣuṇī precepts, the reverse of the above case applies, as should be understood.

The second major section concerns the *akāla-saṃgha-karman* (the Saṃgha assembly at an improper time). Regarding the term "improper time" (*akāla*), it refers to times other than the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day of the lunar month.
Because the dispute has already been extinguished and the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) has already been lifted, it is necessary to perform the ritual at an improper time.

Thus, one performs the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). This applies when the person who was subject to suspension has remained separate for a long duration.

This is the same as the monastic procedure (*saṃghadharma*). Once the formal accusation has been resolved and one wishes to attain the status of being in accordance with the Dharma, it is simply for the sake of performing the formal motion (*jñapti*) and for the harmony of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
However, this intent distinguishes the untimely recitation of the precepts; because it is merely for the sake of untimely harmony, both types of formal motions are presented.
If one performs this formal announcement (*jñapti*) for an untimely recitation of the precepts (*akāla-poṣadha*), it is identical to the standard announcement used for the regular recitation.

If categorized according to the previous explanation, among the seven textual passages, the single phrase concerning "newcomers and residents" (*āgantuka-pūrvavāsika*) should be omitted; all other elements are fully present. However, in the current text, only [the following] is set forth:

Within the ritual for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), the formal motion (*jñapti*) for gathering the assembly is always performed as a standard motion; this is why it is so. All other procedures are identical, and there is no need to cite them again.
Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Scroll Seven, Part Two;
Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Scroll Eight, Part One. Composed by the Śramaṇa Fali.
● Regarding the third section, the *Varṣā-khaṇḍaka* (The Chapter on the Rains Retreat), the word "listen" (*anuśrāvaya*) is used because it concerns a virtuous matter.

From the second part, "having designated the person upon whom the retreat depends," the rules for the rains retreat have already been set forth. In contrast to the preceding general text, we shall first explain the meaning.
The gates: first, in terms of time; second, in terms of place; third, with respect to persons; fourth, in relation to the Dharma.
First, the analysis by time, which further comprises four parts: first, the summer retreat is not for spring or winter; second, the summer period consists of four months.

The three [seasons] are established, not four. During the third summer retreat, there is an intercalary month; thus, the timing for the fourth establishment [of the rains] differs. Regarding the first point: Question:

If a nun performs an unbeneficial act during all three seasons, it is a *pācittiya* offense for both [the nun and the monk], whereas if there is a beneficial purpose, it is permitted to perform the act without offense.
Why, then, are only the summer retreats established as such, while spring and winter are not? Answer: During the summer...
Wandering about leads to a great deal of the destruction of virtuous conduct and incurs heavy censure and vexation; this is why the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is established.

During spring and winter, the destruction of virtuous conduct is minor and censure and vexation are slight; therefore, no retreat is established for spring and winter. Thus, the text states: "I allow the bhikṣus to observe the three-month summer retreat.

This means that during the summer there is the practice of remaining in one place (*dharmasthiti*); when departing, it is for the sake of benefit that there is the practice of departing. At other times, [the same applies].
It is of no benefit. There is no abiding in the Dharma that is beneficial, nor is there any departing from the Dharma.
This is the second section. Question: Regarding the four months of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), does one only bind the first three months, or does one bind all four months?

The answer has two meanings. [First,] to open the way for those who have not yet attained [the practice]. If there is no formal connection (*pratyaya*), it concludes with the preceding; if there is a formal connection, it concludes with the following.
If one were to conclude the entire four-month period, then only on the sixteenth day of the fourth month would the summer retreat (*varṣā*) be established;

from the seventeenth day onward, the *anvārambhaṇa* (post-retreat) would not be valid. There is no teaching that restricts it to exactly four months, as such a rule is too urgent and difficult to practice constantly. Therefore, he opened this [flexibility].
One month. This is for deliberating whether to proceed or not; it is because the summer retreat (*varṣā*) concludes on the thirtieth day.

during this interval of one hundred and twenty days, it is likewise permissible. Regarding the keeping of two robes:

although the keeping of two robes is permitted, the allowance includes the intercalary month for the purpose of entering the retreat and practicing the Path; therefore, the duration should be many days. If this is so..."

If one does not take the intercalary month into account, it would not be a day within the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). If one goes outside the boundary during an intercalary month, would this not constitute a breach of the summer retreat?
The answer is: No. Originally, a formal commitment was made to remain within the boundary; since one has departed before that period is complete, the continuity of the retreat is broken.

This is because one has left the boundary, which is the very place where the commitment was established. Therefore, it constitutes a breach. Question: If one accepts the days of the retreat including the intercalary month, can one still count forty-five days?

The dates for the conclusion of the retreat (*varṣā*). One person concludes on the first day of the fifth month. If calculated by the date of departure, the former person departs at the end of the seventh month, while the latter departs on the first day of the eighth month.

there is merely a discrepancy in the date of the conclusion, yet the date of departure remains the same—the first day of the eighth month. This applies when facing an intercalary seventh month; this is the position regarding the conclusion.
There are three [types]. Those who form the boundary on or before the first day of the fifth month observe only ninety days.

when departing, they are separated by one month, and so on, up to being separated by fourteen days after forming the boundary for those who observe one hundred and twenty days.
The summer retreat (*varṣā*) is observed within this period. There are cases where the retreat begins one day early, while the departure [at the end] is delayed by as much as one month;

or where the retreat ends fourteen days early, while the departure is delayed by one month, and so forth—this should be understood accordingly. According to the *Vinaya-ghaṭikā-śāstra*, when there is an intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), it is permitted to count [the retreat days] inclusively.
When the days were complete, they would depart; now it is not like that.

This is the explanation according to the specific characteristics of these divisions. However, if one distinguishes them generally in terms of the time for entering the retreat (*pravāraṇā*): if there is no intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*), the retreat is entered within a single month; if there is an intercalary month, it is in the fourth month.

The [observance] is concluded on the sixtieth day; the remainder is combined with the period prior to the intercalary month, such that it is concluded on the first day of the month when there is no intercalation.
The reason one is permitted to conclude during all these periods is that both the thirtieth and the sixtieth days are times for concluding the observance.

This differs from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, which states that the two days—the sixteenth of the fourth month and the sixteenth of the fifth month—constitute the time for concluding the preceding [observance].
Subsequently, because that person’s journey had not yet reached their destination, they entered the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) by relying on trees or vehicles along the roadside.

Treatise: The *pūrvavārṣika* (first summer retreat) is on the sixteenth day of the fifth month; the *aparavārṣika* (second summer retreat) is on the sixteenth day of the sixth month.
This is because the King altered the calendar system. Question: Why does this text state that the formal establishment (*sīmābandha*) is valid for one month of sixty days?
Answer: Because all three months are complete. As the text below states regarding the "later summer retreat," it refers to residing during the latter three months.
Regarding the *pārivāsika* (probationary) period following the preceding *anvāraka* (early retreat), one does not count the years;

rather, the duration is fulfilled by the number of days spent in attendance. Second, concerning the distinction based on location, there is one interpretation: it refers to the *anvāraka* performed in dependence upon a specific dwelling, such as a monastery (*ārāma*) or a house. Thus the text says: "In dependence upon a certain village, a certain monastery, a house, and so forth.

Furthermore, another explanation holds that it depends upon the boundary (*sīmā*). This is known because the boundary serves as the protection for the summer retreat (*varṣā*). The limit of the summer [retreat] is thus defined.
Regarding this, the text below states: "If one foot enters the boundary and one receives [an invitation], then upon leaving the boundary at sunrise, it is again outside.

Furthermore, regarding whether or not an invitation is valid when facing away from it, there are cases where the *poṣadha* is performed within the internal boundary while being outside the external boundary. Moreover, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu who placed a bed within four boundaries; he could travel back and forth without obstruction, yet later he did not know where to retrieve his robes.

The Buddha said, "Take one portion from each of the four places. He further stated, "If many monastic quarters are collectively bound into a single boundary (*sīmā*) for the purpose of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), in which monastic quarter should one reside?

The answer is: "One may reside according to one's preference. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, because Śāriputra wished to benefit his relatives, he went to the village of Nāla to observe the retreat.
Later, not wishing to be separated from the World-Honored One, he informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
From this day forward, I authorize the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha and the village of Nāla to form a single *poṣadha* boundary, so that Śāriputra may dwell in peace and comfort.
This shall be established by the formal act of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. Furthermore, on the day of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) at the village of Nāla, Śāriputra went daily to the Bamboo Grove;
he was unable to carry his robes [to and from there]. Also, there was a bhikṣu who was observing the summer retreat at the Jetavana Monastery; after his meal, he wished to...
They went to visit Kāyabhadraka to practice meditation, or stayed there overnight. The Buddha said:
