The following section concerns how those who heard the Buddha’s brief instruction practiced it and attained realization. The initial text consists of four parts: first, up to the point where he encountered the Buddha and attained the Way by abstaining from drinking alcohol;

second, from "At that time, within the assembly of elders... down to his renunciation of the world and reception of the full precepts (*upasampadā*), wherein his mind became weary of the world and he left the household life;
third, from "His parents [in] both cities... down to his offering food to the Sangha and practicing self-awareness; fourth, [the remainder].
[His] feet [are well-formed]. Having gone down to the hot springs in the fourth [section], if one does not practice meditation with a focused mind, the heart will then become restless.

According to the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, in a past life he gave a single *kambala* garment to a Pratyekabuddha to wipe his feet; by virtue of this meritorious retribution, [his feet are thus].
He was always born into a family of great wealth and nobility. Beneath his feet grew hair, appearing like forms within emptiness.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, he was given the name Vimalakīrti; however, because he possessed two billion coins, people of the time called him Viśākha (Twenty-Million).
Furthermore, during the time of the past Buddha Vipaśyin, he had assembled sixty-eight thousand arhats and made offerings to them at his home, one for each person.
Having sat once and partaken of various foods and drinks, he gave two pairs of leather sandals to the Kapphiṇas. One pair was such that for ninety-one kalpas, hair grew on the soles of his feet;
he never trod upon the ground, and his body was so soft and supple that it could not withstand being mounted.
According to the *Sīla-vinaya*, Viśvabhū’s feet grew hair four inches long and golden in color. During the time of the past Buddha Vipaśyin, [he offered] white cotton cloth...
At the site of the offering, he made offerings to an assembly of eighty thousand people, whereby for ninety-one kalpas hair grew beneath his feet.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, at the time of his birth, there was a golden ring on each of his ears; being made of pure gold weighing one hundred million units, he was called the Śramaṇa Koṭīviṃśa (Hundred-Million-Ears).

Since he previously possessed two hundred million pieces of gold, he is referred to as "Two-Hundred-Million. As the text states: "The various faculties should be equal," [referring to] the aforementioned...
Because one excessively torments the body, agitation arises. The Noble One exhorts the equal application of body and mind; that is, the mind contemplates the true principle.
Therefore, it is said that one should be equanimous toward all faculties.

Regarding the second section on "Recollection of One's Own Realization of the Path," there are two parts. The first part, which begins as before, correctly explains the recollection of one's own realization of the path.

The second part, beginning with "Having spoken these words," correctly explains the recitation of verses. The first of these sections further divides into three: first, the fruit of delighting in the six sense bases;
second, the passage beginning with "Is there anyone who does not rely on faith," which sets forth the causes of the six sense bases; third, "The exhaustion of that desire and the absence of desire."

The following summarizes the two preceding liberations (*vimokṣa*) which serve as the basis for accomplishing the six subtle practices (*ṣaḍ-yoga*). Regarding the text on the fruits of these six bases, there are three parts:

the introduction, the exposition, and the conclusion. Following the specific matters, six [categories] are manifested; yet in terms of their essential nature, there are only four—namely, the two liberations and the two nirvāṇas.

Their wisdom-nature is pure and lucid, capable of eliminating delusion and dispelling [obstructions], such that they are not bound by afflictions (*kleśa*); this is termed "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*). It is what the noble ones delight in and thus it is so called.
This constitutes bliss. Therefore, it is said that one finds bliss in renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*). This is liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).

When the mind is tranquil through concentration (*samādhi*) and all agitation has ceased, it is called "quiescence" (*śānti*); because it is a source of joy for sentient beings, it is called "bliss. This clarifies liberation through concentration (*samādhi-vimukti*).

Taken together, both are conditioned liberations (*saṃskṛta-vimukti*). The third is the state where afflictions are exhausted; it is quiescent, sublime, and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These are the second, fourth, and sixth [liberations].
The three phrases are called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder). Since its cause is absent, the fruit of suffering is also extinguished.

What is called the exhaustion of the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder). These two are not returned by the three characteristics; they are unconditioned fruits (*asaṃskṛta-phala*). Next, to distinguish the three causes:
they are faith, upholding the precepts, and abandoning gain and honor. Faith is the root of practice; therefore, it is explained first as the basis.
Having given rise to faith, one next maintains pure precepts. Among the great obstacles to the precepts, none surpasses gain and honor; therefore, one must sever gain and honor.
In the text, the repeated statement that "one does not harbor such thoughts" is intended to answer previous questions based on one's own understanding, thereby eliminating doubts and misconceptions.

Next, the explanation of the passage on the "wondrous eye" has three parts. First, regarding the section on the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*), the extensive text explains it in detail; the other faculties are to be understood by analogy.
Within the discussion of the eye, the initial section up to "liberation of mind" (*ceto-vimukti*) refers to those who are "doubly liberated" (*ubhaya-to-bhāga-vimukta*).

Among these, the portion from the beginning up to "free from delusion" (*amoha*) indicates that because the three afflictions are absent, one is "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*). The subsequent section, beginning with "such a bhikṣu," refers to liberation of mind.
These two liberations are raised as the supporting factors (*upakaraṇa*). Regarding "the two eyes seeing many forms," this refers to the mutual correspondence of the sense faculty and its object.
From "the liberation through wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*) onwards, the meaning of being undefiled (*asaṃkliṣṭa*) is explained. This section is divided into three parts:

first, up to "neither defiled nor stained," which is due to the presence of mental wisdom and because of liberation; second, after eye-consciousness, it flows into the subsequent mental states (*citta*), yet afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise. Correctly...
This is sublime conduct; therefore, it is said to be "unstained. The two consciousnesses do not mix with form (*rūpa*). This further explains "unstained":
if consciousness were to grasp the characteristics of form (*nimitta*) and arise through successive conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), then the three feelings (*vedanā*) could be called "mixed.

Now, although one sees form, one does not grasp its characteristics, yet the three feelings still arise; therefore, it is said that "consciousness does not mix with form. Third, abiding in the fourth *dhyāna* further explains "unstained."

"Mixed. This is to demonstrate that this person has attained the fourth dhyāna, which is free from all sensations; therefore, it is not mixed. Just as it is with the eye and visible forms, so it is with the ear and sounds, and the rest;
hence it says, "it is also thus. Next, there are three further metaphors: first, up to the metaphor of "not leaking," which illustrates the two liberations;

second, from "the eastern direction" onwards, which illustrates the second [point] regarding the mutual encounter of sense-faculties and their objects; third, "this mountain does not... [is incomplete].

afflictions and delusions are then exhausted, and they cannot be overturned by external objects. Therefore, it says, "not shifting," and so forth. When wind and rain come from the east, since they do not...
It destroys the other three directions, yet even wind cannot destroy it; therefore, it is said, "it is also like this. The remaining metaphors for the [other] faculties are omitted.

This is determined by the holy ones based on the calculation of the number of people taking up residence at this location. Second, regarding the mutual inclusion of the two divisions, it is as explained in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
When a gift is given to the community of bhikṣus outside of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), and there are no bhikṣus present, the bhikṣuṇīs should divide it.

When a gift is given to the community of bhikṣuṇīs outside of the rainy season retreat, and there are no bhikṣuṇīs present, the bhikṣu-saṃgha should divide it. It is further stated that gifts obtained during the rainy season retreat are all likewise handled;
once the mutual assignment is settled, the members of the respective division shall divide it among themselves. Third, [the section on] the *yā* and *zhèng*. Below.

The text consists of six sentences. The first three are distinguished in relation to the Saṃgha. This refers to: having obtained summer robes and then torn them; having torn them and then obtained [new] items;

or having obtained [new items] and then torn them. These three cases all involve distributing [the items] by counting the number of people, as they do not constitute a formal ritual act (*avijñapti*), but are merely determined by the time.
The determination regarding the person who receives [the goods] based on the specific location and time is established for that reason. The following three phrases refer to individuals:

whether one has already obtained or not yet obtained [the goods] in relation to the object, and whether one proceeds from the correct [path], all are determined by the person receiving [the goods] based on the specific time and location.

This is based on the correct assembly (*samyag-saṃgha*) taking possession of the goods; by inferring the meaning accordingly, there should further be three phrases concerning the heterodox assembly (*mithyā-saṃgha*) taking possession.

As for the objects: those that turn away from the heterodox and return to the orthodox should be shared with the departing party; furthermore, each of the six [categories] should be expected to share with the orthodox or the heterodox, but they do not share with the arriving party. These matters are all abbreviated here.

Regarding the fourth category, "that which is acquired by the Saṃgha at an improper time," there are two divisions of meaning. First, the objects given by donors, which clarify what is acquired by the Saṃgha.
Second, the property of deceased bhikṣus, which is treated as being identical to what is acquired by the Saṃgha. Within these two sections, the objects given by donors are explained first.

Regarding the three gates: first, each section has four types: (1) permanent property (*nitya*), (2) property obtained through boundaries (*sīmā-labdha*), (3) property obtained through communal *karmavācanā* (*samāna-karma*), and (4) property obtained by the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-labdha*).
This [latter] refers exclusively to gifts to the Saṃgha. In the first three cases, the application of the rules is fixed; they follow and enter into three categories.

Only the single type, "property obtained by the Saṃgha," must be determined by formal procedure (*dharma*). There are three levels of formal procedure: namely, mental reflection (*cetanā*), face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*), and *karmavācanā*. These are established.
Regarding the meaning, it must be explained extensively; it is now discussed within this section of the text. As for the two groups, there are also four types: first, permanent property;
second, property acquired through the realm (*dhātu-labdha*); third, property acquired through communal ritual action (*samāna-karma*); and fourth, property acquired by the Saṃgha.

The first, permanent property, belongs to the specific location and is therefore divided into two portions according to the two groups of the Saṃgha. The fourth, property acquired by the Saṃgha, requires formal legal procedure (*dharma*), because the two groups... [text ends].

The *sādhāraṇa-karman* (common ritual) is also divided into two parts. Regarding the middle two—namely, the boundary (*sīmā*) and the acquisition of the same *karman*—because these are determined by the location of the site, they are divided according to the number of persons.

Since they may also be called "two divisions," they are both divided into two parts; this interpretation is not contradictory. For now, we shall specifically distinguish that there are two types of *saṃghalābha* (monastic acquisitions).
First, regarding the original intent of the face-to-face bestowal (*saṃmukhavinaya*), the text for the two divisions contains seven phrases. Among them:
The five categories are divided into two parts. Regarding the four and seven categories, there is no mutual inclusion among the groups, as neither group is fully assembled;

thus, one cannot calculate the portion of those currently present. Furthermore, since there is no common ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), they are divided into two parts, each being subsumed under the specific category appropriate to its respective section, just as in the first section of the *Dharmaguptaka* school. The second part is mutually included within the two sections and divided into five categories.
When a gift is given to the bhikṣus outside of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), it should not be divided among those who are neither bhikṣus nor bhikṣuṇīs.

When a gift is given to the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha outside of the *varṣā*, it should not be divided among those who are neither bhikṣuṇīs nor bhikṣus. Although this specific textual passage does not exist, the principle should likewise apply.
Having established the five categories of inclusion as determined above, each [category] obtains its respective dharma. Third, regarding the mutual intermixture of the correct and the erroneous:

As for this, there are six phrases in the text. The first two concern the Saṃgha; they also distinguish between what has been obtained and what has not yet been obtained regarding the object, and thus are divided into three cases.
Regarding "that which has already been divided": it should be divided into two portions. Regarding "the object obtained after [the community] has been split": it must be returned to the donor.

The third phrase—having obtained [the object] after being split, and having obtained it after the split—is the same as the preceding two phrases. As for the first phrase, dividing it into two portions: since it is the Saṃgha...
Objects and persons both possess their respective portions; these are not restricted to the present. How, then, could one calculate the portion of a person based solely on the present?

Since the four directions do not all assemble together, must one apply a formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) to determine the correct portion? Furthermore, there is no principle for a collective ritual action;
therefore, it is divided into two parts, with each side performing the ritual procedure for its own portion. The meaning of the following two lines can be understood by analogy. Next, there is...
There are three cases. First, because the Saṃgha has already been split regarding the shared property, there are three [categories].

These individuals who follow the heterodox path do not share in the portion for those going to the orthodox path, because they have already divided it into two parts: one part belongs to those who have gone to the heterodox faction, and since they already possess that portion, this [orthodox faction] need not give them a share.
According to principle, there should again be three [cases]: those returning from the heterodox to the orthodox should be given a share for those coming.

The text is abbreviated where there is nothing to state. These six phrases refer to the case where the legitimate assembly (*pakṣa*) takes possession of property, or the illegitimate assembly (*vipakṣa*) takes possession of property;
these are the six phrases stated by contrasting the legitimate and the illegitimate. The first three phrases are as explained in the first three [cases] above.
The subsequent three phrases are as explained in the latter three [cases].
The second section concerns the meaning of "person," "clothing," and "goods," which is the same as that for "non-seasonal acquisitions by the Saṃgha. This is analyzed through two general approaches:
first, an interpretation based on this specific Vinaya; second, a comprehensive inclusion of differing points from other schools to supplement these omissions.
Regarding the first section: based on the principles of adjudication according to this Vinaya, there are five stages. First, the category of debt; second, the category of suspension (*ukkhepanīya*);
third, the category of *yāva-d-ajjhāpanna*; fourth, the category of the two assemblies; and fifth, the death of one member of a harmonious assembly, which necessitates the transfer [of the matter].
As for the sequence of these categories, it is because the meaning within the category of the single assembly is the most extensive and manifold. In contrast to...

The commentary explains the meaning for the sake of convenience. First, regarding the debtor: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are seven cases concerning property lent at interest when the debtor dies.
The Buddha ruled that [the debt] shall enter either the boundary where the document was kept, the place where the guarantor resides, or the place where the pledged collateral is held;
those who receive it equally are explained in detail therein. However, when investigated through reasoning, it may differ from that [text]. If one informs...

Regarding items lent out by a robe-donor that remain with the recipient and have not yet been recovered: one may, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, treat this as a debt based on the underlying principle and so forth.
If the items are located within the monastery grounds, after the bhikṣu has passed away, they should all be acquired by the Saṃgha according to where the items are situated;
it is feared that one cannot rely on mutual inclusion across boundaries (*sīmā*) and the like. This initial case involves taking these monastic items and assigning them [to the appropriate party].

Since he does not rely on either "this" or "that," nor on the community (*saṃgha*) as a whole, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one is to assign [the property], it must be done by way of two gates.
First, the procedure for when another person owes a debt to a deceased individual is clarified: the text asks, "Who owes you?
If a member of the Buddha’s disciples owes an item belonging to a sick person, it should be collected as a debt, because that property rightfully belongs to the community. If...

When the gravity of the offense corresponds to the value of the object, each follows the category into which it enters; when light and heavy items are mixed, they are both treated according to their original nature.

If one owes a permanent endowment (*sāṃghika*) of heavy value, it must be entered into the permanent endowment. If one owes a light item, it must be claimed and entered into the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the local monastic community).

If the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* itself is in debt, both heavy and light items must be claimed; the heavy is entered into the permanent endowment, while the light must be formally added [to the inventory] because of its nature. Thus it is.

The second [section] clarifies the method for repaying debts. The text asks: "To whom do you owe? This refers to cases where a sick person owes the Three Jewels, other individuals, or items of heavy or light value.
One should repay each according to its weight; if there is nothing of equal value, it is not an obstacle to repay them interchangeably.

Calculating the general principle, one should first repay those to whom one owes a debt, as it is beneficial to the King (the sovereign). Once these have been repaid and there is a remainder, then [proceed] as follows...

This is the constant rule (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the subsequent text states: "If there is an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), one should repay it by returning the excess. If there is none, one should sell the three robes (*tricīvara*) to repay it;

any remainder shall be given to the attendant. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu who borrowed property belonging to a stūpa for his own private use, and borrowed property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions for his own private use.
The Buddha said: 'The property must be returned; calculate its value and deliver it to the stūpa and the Saṃgha of the four directions. Any remainder..."
The remaining property should be divided among the monks present. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who died before repaying a debt for wine he had sold on credit.
The owner of the wine demanded payment from the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus said, "Why did you not demand payment while this bhikṣu was still alive?
The owner replied, "If it is not repaid, you will suffer ill repute. The Buddha said, "If this bhikṣu possessed robes or other articles, they should be used to repay the debt."
If the master has no property, one should take property from the Saṃgha to repay it. Why? Because it serves to dispel the ill repute of you, O bhikṣus.
However, there is no distinction made between "permanent endowment" (sthāvarika) and "present" (pratyutpanna) property; yet, according to reason, the present property should be considered superior.

Regarding the second type of person subject to suspension (*ukkhittaka*), the Buddha states in the following passage: "The Saṃgha should grant [the act] to whichever monk they perform the formal ritual (*kamma*) together with. One interpretation states:

Regarding those who have been subjected to the same formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*): the reason for this is that after the suspension has been carried out, they no longer share in the same material or spiritual community (*dhamma-vinaya*).

For what reason, then, should their property be permitted to be taken up immediately after death? Therefore, it is not appropriate for the *dhamma*-conforming Saṃgha to take it. If that is so, when one person who has been suspended dies, to whom should [the property] belong?

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it should enter the Saṃgha of Merit (*puñña-saṃgha*), also called the Saṃgha of Efficacy (*guṇa-saṃgha*), because the *dhamma*-conforming Saṃgha has already administered the disciplinary penalty.

Because of this merit, it is sufficient that at the time of the formal act (*karmavācanā*), one is designated for the distribution of property; therefore, it is said: "In accordance with the communal formal act, the Saṃgha should grant [the share] to the one who was designated.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, when a monk who has been subject to suspension dies, his deceased belongings are placed upon a bed and dragged out to be discarded in a wild field.
If a person tending cattle or sheep takes these items and gives them to the Saṃgha, then [the following] is performed:
Because that donor’s property [is dedicated to them], they accept it.

The third [section] on "Heresy" (*yā*) clarifies the two phrases according to the text: turning one's back on the Right and heading toward the Heretical, such that the property enters the heretical faction.

Examining its original intent, the paths of the Heretical and the Right diverge. Regarding the phrase "the robes and bowl may be taken wherever one goes," this should also consist of two phrases, starting from...

Those who return to the True Dharma and enter the community of the True Sect are omitted from the text where there is nothing to record. Furthermore, regarding items carried on one's person, they are judged according to the previous ruling.
As for items outside of these, they may be indeterminate. Moreover, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If one who has received the Dharma dies while being encoffined, one should go before the assembly that has not received the Dharma and seek repentance for purification. I shall act as one who has not received the Dharma. If one dies before the offense has been removed..."

The robes and bowl shall be returned to the community that accepts the Dharma. If [the offender] dies after having been cleared of the offense, the robes and bowl enter the community that does not accept the Dharma.
If a monk of the community that does not accept the Dharma has been encoffined, he may go among the community that accepts the Dharma to seek confession and so forth;

the reverse case is to be understood accordingly. "Encoffined" (殯) means to lift up or place upon a bier. Furthermore, if a monk who accepts the Dharma dies within the community that does not accept the Dharma, his robes and bowl...

The objects are called out to summon the *dharmavādin* bhikṣus to return. If they do not come to take them, then [the items] shall be made into bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions from among the *adharmavādin* assembly.
If an *adharmavādin* bhikṣu dies among the *dharmavādin* bhikṣus, the reverse case may be understood accordingly.
This rule and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* clarify that the first instance refers to the mutual opposition and mutual turning away between the heterodox and the orthodox.

Regarding the third point concerning mutual reversion: based on the mutual presence of the heterodox and the orthodox at the moment of death, once the heterodox and the orthodox have been definitively determined, each respective school returns to its own constant law.
The fourth section on the rules of inclusion: Later, when [the Buddha] arrived at Anāthapiṇḍika Village in the kingdom of Kośala, a person passed away.
He informed the Buddha, who said: "If there is a faithful upāsaka or a park-keeper in that place, they should take charge of it.
If members of the fivefold monastic community come forward, they may take the items from the layperson's location; however, one must fear using them and thereby incurring guilt."

Therefore, among those who have entered the five assemblies (*pañca-skandha*), whoever arrives first receives it. Regardless of whether the offense is grave or light, all are included among those who arrive first.

However, in the case of a light offense, the property enters that person immediately without waiting for formal legal procedures; whereas in the case of a grave offense, because the object does not belong to the individual, it is distributed according to the order of arrival and returned to the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) of the community.

This is because the donated object was originally obtained based upon the two divisions of the Sangha prior to the death; thus, after the person has passed away, it returns to [the communal treasury].

Regarding the two assemblies: if there is no one who has previously sent [the deceased's belongings] to the two assemblies in the vicinity, one should simply take them from the nearby location without distinguishing between monks and nuns.
Cases such as death on the road, death while living alone, or death at a private estate are judged according to the previous rules.

This is because if the items are located in both the monastic and nun locations, they are treated identically. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding mutual entrustment and death: suppose a single bhikṣu dies at a residence. This is...
A bhikṣu had entrusted his robes and bowl to a nunnery. The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu dies, the robes and articles entrusted to the bhikṣuṇīs shall be divided by the bhikṣu-saṃgha present there.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣuṇī died at a certain residence, her robes and bowl were entrusted to a bhikṣu monastery. The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣuṇī dies, [the robes] entrusted to the bhikṣu..."
As for the robes and clothing, they should be divided among the present Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, because both communities know the Dharma and do not reside in the same location as laypeople;

therefore, they are divided according to the place of death, as this is their common category. Furthermore, because there were Bhikṣus at the place of death, this case differs from that of one who dies while living alone.
Since the mutual entrustment of property is thus settled, the same principle should apply to mutual debts.

Regarding the fifth section, there are two stages within it: namely, the distinction between those who possess [the precepts] and those who do not. As for a *śrāmaṇera* who dies, there is no textual passage concerning this in this Vinaya;

according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, he is included among the *upādhyāya*s. Since the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* treats this according to the rules for *bhikṣu*s, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that when a *śrāmaṇera* passes away...

If at the time of death there is someone to whom [the items] should be given, they should be given to them. If they have not already been given away, the *saṃgha* present before him should divide them.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a novice from Kośala died, his inner and outer robes were given to others by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

Light articles belonging to a deceased person should be divided by the *saṃgha*, while heavy articles should not be divided. These three categories of persons are all the same in this regard; however, as for the actual performance of the rite—

At that time, regarding the purity or impurity within the various categories of the *niśraya* (monastic dependencies), there are three types of impurity. The first is the grave offense leading to death; within this, there are three sub-categories:

first, if the body has not yet been enshrouded, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states it is judged according to ordinary rules. Second, once the formal rite of enshrouding has been performed, one enters among the lay associates (*upāsaka*).

Third, one enters among the *śikṣamāṇā* novices. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, upon death, one enters among the *saṃgha* present before them. The second [category of impurity] is censure (*tarjanīya-karman*).
The four types of offenses, such as those involving separate residence (*pārivāsika*) and so forth, are all judged according to the same criteria as a pure death.

Third, regarding one who has been suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), it has already been explained as before. Next, the analysis of a pure death is distinguished by four sections: first, distinguishing whether co-residence and communal treatment are established or not;
second, explaining whether the entrustment (*anuśāsti*) is established or not; third, determining the gravity of the object; and fourth, the reward for nursing the sick.
Regarding the "Exertion" (*lao*), which encompasses the formal methods for establishing the doctrine, there is a preliminary exposition here; the detailed commentary follows the text.

Second, as for the comprehensive inclusion of differing views from other schools to supplement these omissions: within this Vinaya, there are five distinctions regarding the distribution of a deceased person's property.
First, death while in debt; second, death after being subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*); third, death while in either a heterodox or orthodox state...
The fourth is death within two divisions, both monks and nuns. The fifth is death within a single division where the community is in harmony.
There are four other types of death due to differences among the divisions; when added to the preceding ones, there are nine in total. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there is one case:

if someone dies while being swept away by water, and their robes and bowl remain hanging on a tree branch within the boundary (*sīmā*), the bhikṣus see them and enter the boundary, concluding that they should belong to the Saṃgha. The Buddha [said]: [...]

It is said: "Listen; one may take discarded robes (pāṃsukūla). In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are two cases: first, when a training śrāmaṇera dies, his belongings enter the distribution for the *saṃgha* present at the place of death;
second, when one dies while entrusting items to the other community, they are each returned to the respective *saṃgha* of monks or nuns.
In the remaining three Vinayas, there are likewise provisions for the passing of a śrāmaṇera, as already explained above. These four points differ from those distinguished in other Vinayas.

Since the *Caturvarga-vinaya* does not exist, there is no hindrance to applying [the rules] by analogy. Regarding the distinctions between the five schools of the Vinaya and the nine differences, as well as the treatment of property belonging to the deceased—its meaning being identical to that of untimely offerings (*akāla-dāna*)—these have all been explained according to the text during previous lectures. Next, we shall explain the text itself.
In the third section, "The Time for Dividing Robes," the eight lines beginning with "when guests arrive" clarify what should and should not be given.

The first four lines indicate that it *should* be given because the division has not yet been finalized; the latter four lines indicate that it *should not* be given because the distribution of items has already been settled.

Within the first four lines, the second and third sentences are distinguished by comparing the preceding form to the subsequent one; thus, they are designated as two distinct names. This applies when there are two or more [persons].

Because it involves the distribution by means of counting sticks (*śalākā*), it is said that after the sticks have been cast, one enters within the boundary; however, a single bhikṣu takes charge of the goods.

Knowing with whom else he must distribute them by counting sticks, he considers the goods as belonging to himself. Therefore, it is given the name "receiving a portion with joy" (*prāmodya-bhāga-grahaṇa*), rather than referring to the initial mental resolve (*cetanā*) of acceptance.
Since the taking charge of the goods is already settled, those who arrive later should not be given a share. Furthermore, the former two cases are acceptable.
Thus, regarding the third case where there is a remainder but it is not divided: if there is no remainder, it is as concluded in the two cases above;

if there is a remainder but the procedure is not concluded, it is not given; if the procedure is concluded, it should be given together. In this way, the first two cases do not apply. The subsequent phrase is also like this.
Furthermore, since the property obtained by the Saṃgha may be divided even down to a servant, in each of these four cases, [the rule] does not apply.

[The section on] "Completion" is concluded; it is subsumed within the first four [sections]. Now, for the time being, the "Completion" is presented; therefore, it is said that [this case] is not included [therein].

The second [section], "Formulation by Means of a Formal Act" (*dharmena vyavasthāpanam*), consists of three parts: first, the formulation of the method of distribution; this briefly cites the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) regarding communal procedures.

The second section consists of two sentences. Regarding items such as *vāśuka* robes, the Buddha permitted their possession and wearing; this briefly sets forth the nature of the objects to be divided.

From "There are three types of separate residences" onwards is the actual distribution according to the Dharma, which contains three parts: first, distribution through formal *karmavācanā* before the Saṃgha;

second, distribution by means of a threefold statement; and third, acceptance through mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Within the methods for the Saṃgha, it is necessary to include both types of *jñapti*.
There are two methods. First is the method for appointing a person to distribute the robes; thus the text says, "One person should be appointed to divide [the robes].

Furthermore, as in the section on the rules for dwellings where the appointment of a distributor of gruel and so forth is mentioned, the distribution of robes and the distribution of rain-bathing robes require five qualities.

Rebirth in heaven is as previously described. As for "in person," it refers to cases such as when Trapusa was personally appointed to distribute bedding and other items. Why, then, would one never appoint a person specifically for the distribution of robes?

Therefore, it is essential to appoint [the official]. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are five qualities for a person who distributes robes: they must know the color, value, and quantity of the robe-material, as well as whether it has been given or not;

furthermore, they must be appointed through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). There are also five other requirements, namely, that they have not accepted [the position] improperly, and so forth.

In the present text, the appointment via *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is omitted, though it is indispensable for the performance of the rite. Second, regarding the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the entrustment of the robes: this refers to those items listed in the preceding section of the text.
Therefore, the text says: "The Saṃgha now gives this to the bhikṣu so-and-so; he shall give it to the Saṃgha. As for the reason why it must be entrusted to another individual:

it is because it must be circulated throughout the four directions, and thus it must be entrusted to another. As for the reason why it is then returned to the Saṃgha: if it were not given to the Saṃgha, one would not be entitled to share in the distribution.
Formerly, some interpreted this rule as meaning that the act of distribution was completed immediately [upon entrustment]; therefore, in the *karmavācanā* (ritual formula):

To state directly that these two [procedures] are not so is incorrect. Because it is a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) performed by a small number of people, once the robe has been entrusted, its distribution follows that person’s disposition;
this is precisely the method for dividing it. There is no separate formal ritual (*dharma*) to be performed.

However, as for the scriptural statement that "the robe is held and given to one bhikṣu, who is then to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to divide it," this means that the aforementioned person who should be appointed is raised up to divide it, and the *jñapti* is performed.

The term "two *karmas*" is as explained previously. "Assigning and distributing" refers simply to the act of assigning; it does not mean that this person must further perform the formal procedure of distribution (*vibhāga-dharma*).

If there are five or more people, these two methods may be fully employed; however, with only four people, one cannot appoint and assign, because the number of persons appointed and assigned would fail to reach the required quorum.
The Saṃgha should instead perform the *karman* directly to effect the restriction. It should be stated: "Great..."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These robes and articles belonging to this residence are to be divided among the present members of the Saṃgha;

the present Saṃgha should divide them. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding the division of these items by the present Saṃgha.

The *karmavācanā* (formal motion) is to be recited according to the wording of this announcement. The reason for this is stated in the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*: "The practice appropriate for four persons refers to five persons living together, with one person [acting as the steward]."
[The deceased] passes away. When four persons perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide [the property], this is called the "procedure for four persons.

It does not say that it should be transferred as a gift to one person. Furthermore, regarding what is called the "procedure for five persons": five persons perform the *karmavācanā* to divide the deceased's belongings;

four persons perform the *karmavācanā* to bestow [a portion] upon one person, and that one person then bestows it back to the community (*saṃgha*), after which they divide it together. This is called the "procedure for five persons."

Regarding the *dharma*: it is here that the transfer of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) is first mentioned. It is clearly understood that while the four individuals receive only their direct shares, the Saṃgha receives the property.
Since the property is determined by the *dharma*, one must analyze this through four propositions: (1) both the gift and the *dharma* apply; (2) the gift applies but the *dharma* does not.
In the third [case], it reaches the dharma but not the gift; in the fourth, it reaches neither. Among these four, the first three are divisible.

If it reaches the whole or reaches a portion, it distinguishes two dharmas; therefore, it is appropriate to name it "reaching" (*prāpti*). Even if it only reaches a portion and does not reach a distinction, its meaning still involves reaching the dharma;
thus, it must essentially involve reaching both dharmas. The second and fourth phrases are not divisible, because they do not involve reaching the dharma.

Furthermore, although a novice (śrāmaṇera) does not participate in the formal ritual (karmavācanā) alongside others, if he is within the boundary (sīmā) at the time the ritual is performed, he shall be included within the limits of that rite.
If the case involves the lifting of an accusation (pravāraṇā) before the assembled community (saṃgha), this also constitutes four permutations:

first, inclusion in both the gift and the distribution; second, inclusion in the gift but not in the distribution; third, inclusion in the distribution but not in the gift; fourth, inclusion in neither. Among these four...

The first two [methods] result in acquisition, because they involve the formal act of giving (*dāna*) for the sake of establishing a fixed boundary. The latter two do not result in acquisition, because they fail to reach the point of giving.
Next is the method of three verbal declarations in the presence of the recipient. One should say: "Venerable sir, please bear this in mind:

whatever robes or non-robes are present in this residence should be distributed by the Saṃgha currently before us. There is no Saṃgha here; this is our share. This is to be recited three times. Alternatively, some cite another Vinaya [tradition].
"This object belongs to me and is for the Elder’s use"; this is no different from what was stated previously.

Since this text does not mention receiving [the object] through three separate utterances for each individual, when a single person performs the ritual act, saying "this is our portion," it refers to a shared portion.

There is no need for mutual labor; it is not recited together, as it is feared that each might separately manifest the purity of their conduct. Next, one person should perform the mental recitation (*manasikāra*), saying:
"In this dwelling place, whether it be robes or non-robes, the present Saṃgha should divide them. There is no Saṃgha here; this is my portion. This is said three times.
Alternatively, if the Saṃgha receives few items to be given, they are divided into five parts. When the resident Saṃgha divides the robes at a dwelling place, the guests...
A bhikṣu arrived, but the portion to be distributed was small. Not wishing to divide it, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Even if one obtains only a single waist-belt, it should be divided.
If it is too small to be so divided, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) to give it to a bhikṣu who has no robes.
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This robe or non-robe obtained by the Saṃgha is now given collectively to the bhikṣu [Name]. Thus is the motion. Then the *karman* is performed."

This is established according to the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Question: How many types of mental reflection (*cittānuvartana*) are there in this Vinaya? Answer: There are seven, namely: the two types of distributing robes, the declaration [of a robe], the fear of regret, the auspicious [recitation], the confession (*pratideśanā*), and the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*). This is how it should be understood.
The third section, concerning success and failure, consists of twelve statements. The first six concern whether the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is successful or not;
the latter six concern whether it is successful when performed through three utterances or by mental reflection (*manasikāra*).

Alternatively, the first six may be understood as regarding success or failure based on the *karmavācanā* and the presence of a counterpart, while the subsequent six concern success or failure based on mental reflection, since [the rite] can also be divided between three or two persons. Within these two groups of six, each...
The first three [cases] do not constitute an offense; the latter three do. Furthermore, among the four sets of three, in each case one commits the first two offenses but does not commit the third.

The second [case], regarding the loss of another's property, is identical in meaning to what the Saṃgha acquires at an improper time. There are two textual passages for this: the first extends up to the words "all belongs to."

The *Saṃgha-buddha-paññatti* (the rules concerning the Saṃgha) determines that [these items] belong to the Saṃgha. Second, from "all the bhikṣus" onwards, there is a detailed analysis of the gravity of the offenses.
The preceding text briefly cites thirteen items: 1. the monastery; 2. the gardens, fields, and fruit trees belonging to the monastery;
3. separate rooms; 4. the objects belonging to separate rooms; 5. copper jars, basins, axes, chisels, and braziers; 6. various heavy articles; 7. ... [text breaks off].
1. Large and small mats and pillows; 2. Eight types of *elāyanta* woolen carpets and the like; 3. Monastery attendants; 4. Carriages and litters; 5. Water vessels, alms bowls, and fans; 6.
Utensils made of iron, wood, pottery, leather, bamboo, and so forth, as well as razors and the like;
7. Robes, alms bowls, needle cases, and so forth. Regarding those with many acquaintances, there is Upananda; regarding those with no acquaintances, [there is none].
Regarding the Bhikṣu Cunda: according to the text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, when the Bhikṣu Cunda entered *nirvāṇa*, he took his robe and bowl and went to the king to have them appraised.
The price was five coins (*kārsāpaṇas*). [The king] decided that they should be returned to the bhikṣu. The Buddha said, "They should belong to the Saṃgha.
Therefore, it is said that for one with many acquaintances, if there are no acquaintances, everything belongs to the Saṃgha. This statement regarding belonging to the Saṃgha is for...

This is because [the offerings] are made for the Buddha-dharma and other secular purposes. The reason for this is that since those who have left the household life all follow the path of renunciation, whatever they do with their bodies is entirely encompassed by the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*).
Since they originally obtained [their status] by relying on the Saṃgha, it follows that after death they should likewise return to the Saṃgha.

Offerings made to the Buddha-dharma and to individual *bhikṣus* receive no share; for this reason, after death, [the deceased] does not enter the Buddha-dharma. [Thus it is said regarding] kings and ministers.

Relatives: Since there are differences between the monastic and the lay, and differences in how they acquire property, it is not appropriate for [the deceased's items] to enter into those [lay households].

This is explained in detail in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Second, regarding the analysis of the gravity or lightness [of offenses]: the rules governing the category of a deceased person’s clothing and belongings must be treated through four sections. First:
1. Determining whether the ownership is identical; 2. Whether the entrustment is successful; 3. Determining the gravity of the offense; 4. The method for distributing rewards for labor.

Regarding the second and fourth sections, their meanings will be explained in the subsequent text. Here, I shall explain the first section. As for "shared with those born together" (*sahaja*) and so forth:

if the teacher’s original intention was to ultimately provide the disciple with food and clothing and he has already finished giving it, [the property] is acquired; as for the remainder that has not yet been given, it belongs to the teacher after his death.
The Sangha members are not truly co-residents; they falsely claim to be so. If one calculates the value [of the property], one commits an offense.

Alternatively, if the teacher’s original intention was for the wealth and goods to be held in common, then upon his death, whether he returns to lay life or lives separately, the property shall be divided equally among the individuals, with one share belonging to the Sangha and so on down to the one living separately.
If one does not act according to this agreement, one commits an offense by calculating the value. Now, it is stipulated that although they are co-residents, the goods have already been divided.

The remainder belongs to the deceased. Next, the analysis of gravity and lightness has two parts: first, a classification according to the gate of ultimate meaning; second, a detailed examination based on the text.
Regarding the first, the gate of meaning, there are three provisional categories. The first concerns items prescribed by the Buddha for possession, such as the six requisites.
Second, items that are not permitted to be kept, such as fields, houses, gardens, groves, slaves, servants, and domestic animals.
Third, items that are permitted to be kept, such as extra robes and travel provisions. Among these three types of items, the first is categorized as light because it is essential for the path;
the second is categorized as heavy because it obstructs the path. These constitute the two gates of light and heavy. Within the third category of items, there are further three distinctions. First:

There are three types of lightness and heaviness: first, lightness and heaviness by nature; second, lightness and heaviness according to the object; and third, lightness and heaviness according to usage.

Regarding "lightness by nature," this refers to the ten kinds of materials such as cloth, silk, fine cotton, thread, and yarn. Because the garments produced from them are light, the fibers and threads that constitute them also fall within the category of light items.
Regarding "heaviness by nature," this refers to all precious objects, as well as stones, wood, fields, houses, jars, pots, cauldrons, slaves, and livestock.
Items such as living beings, wheeled carriages, the five types of grain, and even all objects that obstruct the path, are classified as heavy offenses.
Regarding those said to be light in nature: examples include all items for the body, clothing, shirts, skirts, woolen blankets, and sitting mats;

these should be classified as light. Regarding those said to be heavy in nature: examples include large woolen rugs, mattresses, various types of canopies, curtains, pillows, fans, and quilts; these should be classified as heavy.
Regarding those items that are light by virtue of their utility: these include the bowl-casket, the cases for the three robes, and the use of needles, razors, and so forth;

these should be classified as light. Regarding those items that are heavy by virtue of their utility: these include door curtains, canopies, tents, bed curtains, palanquins, desks, tables, carriages, front and rear awnings, and curtains;
these should be classified as heavy. Now, by means of the three types of lightness—nature, substance, and utility—they are subsumed.

Regarding the first category of items: they are generally included among the light because their nature and purpose follow their function through three levels of classification. Combined, they are included in the second category of items, which are collectively bound into the heavy.
Within the section on permitted possession, sixteen [types] for nuns are classified as heavy; those such as auxiliary robes and the like are classified as light.
The remainder may be understood by analogy with what was previously explained.
Next, regarding the analysis according to the text: among the preceding thirteen [categories], the first six are combined into three;
the ninth and tenth are combined into one; and the remaining five remain as five. Thus, they are judged by way of nine gates in total.

As for the second gate, which pertains to the property of individual rooms (*pṛthak-śālā-vastu*), this refers to items such as bedsteads, wall-coverings, and screens within the room. If one uses silk or cloth to construct a room for oneself, [it is included here].

Regarding the death of the owner of a dwelling: if it has not yet undergone transformation, it is categorized as light; once it has undergone transformation, it is categorized as heavy. This is because both states pertain to the bhikṣu;

therefore, the determination is made based on whether the state at the time of death was heavy or light. This differs from the case of relinquishing objects for the purpose of burial or other uses for one's parents, teachers, or the Saṃgha.

Because they belong to distinct categories. Furthermore, the relinquishment of items belonging to the class of the Buddha’s Dharma is likewise. As for the statement that they "should not be divided," it is because, as previously examined, they constitute heavy property.

Regarding the third category, the jar and vessel: unlike the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which limits the classification by specific measurements, here there is no distinction made between large and small, nor regarding items such as ivory or horn vessels.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, those weighing half a *dō* (斗) or more are heavy, while those below that weight are light;

although there is no explicit textual authority for this case, all such items are included among the heavy. Among various objects—such as tables, benches, medicinal herbs, stones, dyes, and dyeing implements—none of these [are exempt].
It should be divided. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the robes for the Saṃgha of the four directions are collectively dyed.

In the eighth section, the *Elivata* tradition states that a *pauñja* is a small curtain and a *mauñja* is a large curtain. Carpets (*kūrca*) that are sufficient to cover the body may be permitted for division.

It is the same for the various types of felt. If they are of the proper measure or less, they enter the category of light offenses; if they exceed the measure, they enter the category of heavy offenses. This also applies to single-layered cloths (*maṇḍala*).
They differ from the five-part woolen blankets (*pañcaka-paṭa*), which are judged as heavy offenses if they are whole and as divisible offenses if they are cut.

If the wool exceeds three finger-widths and the colors are distinct, it enters the category of heavy offenses, because garments such as embroidered hand-cloths or brocade robes are not permitted to be kept. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "Whether it be brocade or damask..."
If it is a hair-tassel or a bandage for covering a wound, these are indivisible items belonging to the Saṃgha. Under the ninth category, slaves, laborers, and subjects are included;

whatever private property they possess shall be used for their private needs. Regarding the relatives of the deceased, whether there are no relatives or not, there is no fault in using such items for the Saṃgha.
Under the twelfth category, iron-made vessels and the like—meaning items made of iron, bamboo, or leather—are included as heavy items.
One may also fashion implements of iron; those such as tongs, hammers, and bellows are heavy. The rest should be understood by analogy. A razor is a necessary implement in accordance with the Dharma;
because it is used [frequently], it is light. Its case, the whetstone, and so forth all accompany the razor.

Knife-blades and arrowheads—the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* permits their division. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that nail-clippers, door-hooks, and needles are items that may be divided. Since these...

There is no formal text [on this matter]. Entering [the assembly] repeatedly is not an impediment. Regarding the incense burner, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* permits its division; the present discussion likewise remains unsettled.

When entering the Saṃgha, it should be given to those capable of making offerings. All items belonging to the bags shall follow the incense burner. As for the scriptures, commentaries, and sub-commentaries, they should be given to those capable of receiving and upholding them;

they must not be assigned arbitrarily. As for the chests, boxes, scrolls, and bundles containing the treasured writings and legacy documents, they should be placed within their respective cases and wrappers.
This also follows the commentaries on the sūtras; following the sūtra regarding the bookshelf, there is no loss of meaning. Regarding the thirteen types of robes:
all those that are not garments worn by bhikṣus are included in the category of heavy items, meaning they are equivalent to the robes of laypeople, non-Buddhists, and the like.

As for bowls, water-strainers, lamps, spoons, chopsticks, and so forth, all should be permitted to be divided; this refers to what is stated in the subsequent section concerning the division of *kuñcīra* vessels.

It may be divided into five parts. Copper *tāra* vessels for holding medicinal eye-salves may be divided. If they exceed the prescribed measure, white bowls (*pātra*) must be classified as heavy property.
If that were the case, then exceeding measures of white robes would also have to be classified as heavy. To explain: the nature of a bowl is such that it is heavy when large and light when small.

Now, since this [bowl] exceeds the measure and its white color renders it unfit for use, it is no longer a bowl; therefore, it must be classified as heavy. As for robes, because their substance is light by nature, they are returned [to the owner].

It falls under the category of light offenses (*dukkaṭa*). For other cases, there may be no textual record; one should follow the guidelines of other Vinayas accordingly. Question: What is a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*)? Answer: By principle, it definitely falls under light offenses.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is called a "concomitant object" (*anuvartaka-dravya*). In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is granted as a reward to the attendant who nursed the sick.

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is an item that may be divided, and it should be distributed when present. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* permits the division of leather footwear; therefore, it is known that boots, shoes, and similar items are also permitted to be divided. However, they must not be [retained individually].
The quantity [of the rules] is determined.

Next, regarding the two sections that subsume the legal procedures (*vinaya*), there are three textual parts. First, up to the point where it says "to be sent to a nearby monastery," is the procedure for obtaining the dharma from the Saṃgha of both divisions.
Second, from the passage "The World-Honored One, in Śrāvastī, having instructed them to remain in retreat for three months" onwards, is the permission granted to the Bhikṣuṇīs.
The section on "the two divisions of the Saṃgha being present" (*ubhayasaṃgha-sammukhībhāva*) clarifies that the preceding [rules] pertain to what is obtained by the *saṃgha*.

Thirdly, regarding the passage beginning with "all bhikṣus reflect upon having completed the *parivāsa*," there is a detailed analysis of what is obtained by the two aforementioned *saṃghas* being present. This initial text is further divided into two parts:

first, the inclusion within one division; second, the objects [of the gift]. Now, within these two divisions, there are likewise two stages. First, the property of a donor (*dānapati*) corresponds to the initial text mentioned above.

Next, regarding the distribution of the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu from Kośala, this corresponds to the second passage mentioned above. The first passage consists of seven phrases, as explained in the preceding section on the meaning.
The subsequent passage is also analyzed according to the same categories of meaning. Since it specifies "nearby," there is no distinction made between monks and nuns;

it should be understood that the same applies when a nun dies without a companion. If a bhikṣu has deposited items in a nunnery, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they should be sent [to the appropriate place].
[The property] shall be given to the deceased’s original monastery. If the location is unknown, it shall be sent to the nearest community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*).

It must not enter a nunnery or be used for private purposes. The same applies when a nun entrusts [property] to a monk. This is because if they reside in different villages, there is a fear that laypeople might damage or misappropriate the monastic property;

therefore, the respective communities may mutually receive it. If a monk dies on his private estate and has a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) or a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) guarding [the property], [it shall be treated accordingly].
One must guard these items; the monks of the neighboring monastery may not take them because they are under protection.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*, if there is no local monastery and no one to guard them, they should be brought into the Great Sangha of the neighboring monastery. The same applies when a nun dies.
The second section, "Manifestation," consists of three parts in Chinese. First, the Buddha informs the bhikṣu Śāntamāsa and establishes a regulation.
Second, from "And so on" (*he xian yi*) down to "inquiring after the World-Honored One's well-being," because they recognize the Buddha’s intention, they pay homage, visit him, and offer praise.

Third, from "At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard this" down to "not for the sake of desire," [it is stated that] when traveling together and discarding robes to practice giving, one may give robes to a bhikṣuṇī; this is precisely [the case].

Because it is a gift given in the presence of both assemblies, one must not give it to laypeople. Within this, it is also given to the Buddha and his stūpas; however, this is stated specifically in contrast to the Saṃgha.

The third section, the detailed analysis of the text, is divided into two parts. The first part, ending with the discussion on borrowing robes, concerns what should or should not be given to the seven classes of followers.

Second, Śāriputra explains below the principle of whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to take the property of others. Those in separate residence (*pṛthagnivāsin*) and so forth may give together with those who are pure (*pariśuddha*).

The person performing the sevenfold formal act (*saptakarmika*) should place the object on the ground to give it; this is done so that by not giving it directly, one avoids being subject to censure (*anuvāda*).

It is permitted to give to laypeople (*avadātavasana*) who have rendered service, provided they are compensated for their labor according to its value. These distinctions concern gifts given in the presence of the recipient (*saṃmukha-dāna*). As for the phrase "harmonious śrāmaṇeras": [it refers to those who are in concord].
Regarding "giving equal shares, etc.": when there is one person, they receive the full amount. Next, regarding "giving half":
the bhikṣu receives the whole, while the śrāmaṇera receives half of that whole. Regarding "giving a third": the bhikṣu receives three parts, and the śrāmaṇera receives one of those three.
This refers to what is obtained by the Saṃgha; although it accords with the donor's intention, since it is property obtained by the Saṃgha, it must be distributed individually among the members.
There are differences in their status. If they are not of equal rank, the degrees of their seniority differ. In the presence of the assembly, distribution follows the intention of the donor;

it is determined according to the individual, so no distinction of rank is considered. Although the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) may not be monks, because they have rendered service to the Saṃgha, they must also be given [a share].
Because they differ from the laity, and furthermore because they differ from the śrāmaṇeras, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, they are given one part, or sometimes none at all.

It should not be divided. Next, regarding the gravity of parental kindness, it is permitted to give [the robe]. Next, from the section on Śrāvastī onwards, it is permitted to borrow the robes of laypeople.
One must not say to a layperson while facing them, "I am giving this to you. From the second section on Śāriputra onwards, the above has correctly explained the ritual for giving to others;
by extension, it explains whether or not one may take the property of others. If the person is a relative or friend, one may take it; otherwise, one may not.
It is not appropriate. Regarding the "intention of a close friend" to take a *pārikara* (a small garment): this refers to a minor friend who takes a fragmentary or small piece of cloth.

If one were to take something of great value, or if one were to be resentful over a mere trifle of cloth without being generous, that person is not a close friend; therefore, it is improper to accept such a gift.

Even if one specifically requires this *pārikāra* (a small measure), it should not be accepted; for it would be indistinguishable from what is not from a friend. Therefore, it is said that even if one lacks it, it should not be accepted.

Regarding the third section on the method for rewarding labor, there are three parts. From the beginning until "is easy to see," the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, established the method for tending to the sick.
Second, at that time, the bhikṣus from Kośala [down to] those who "honored me, followed my instructions, and attended to the sick as praised by the Noble Ones.
Third, "those who took the robes and bowls of the six bhikṣus" [and so on], which concerns the rewarding of labor and the gathering of the Dharma. The preceding text further divides into two parts:

first, up to the point where the Buddha personally attended to the sick after they had departed, for the purpose of establishing a rule; [the second part is] the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, wherein the Dharma was attained after the teaching was given.
The Buddha summoned the bhikṣu Bìfáng and ordered him to tend to the sick. He further manifested as a sick śrāmaṇera and said, "You must attend to him;

this shall be a meritorious retribution for you. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this sick person immediately attained arhatship. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, he was a sick bhikṣu.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. As stated in the *Dharmapada*, because the Buddha wished to repay the kindness of the five types of meritorious deeds performed in previous lives, he had to attend to the sick.
Second, at that time, the World-Honored One established the rules for nursing the sick. This section on further observation has three parts:
first, the establishment of the rule for nursing the sick; second, the permission for that bhikṣu [to have an upādhyāya], etc., which clarifies the method of observation.

The attachment of the sick to the seven classes [of practitioners]. Regarding the third type of sick person, there are five matters below that cite difficult cases of illness to manifest the perfection of their virtue.

In the second section on nursing, there are three parts: first, citing the sacred teachings; second, "he then immediately... and following, which concerns nursing the sick in accordance with the teachings.
Then, having taken up the deceased’s robes and bowl, he brought them forward and informed the Buddha. The Buddha immediately praised him, saying:

"This is one who makes offerings to me; this is one who nurses the sick in accordance with my teachings. Because this is the practice of making offerings, and because nursing the sick with a heart of compassion is equal to [nursing them] with a heart of reverence, I have previously said: 'If you wish to make offerings to me, you should make offerings to the sick.'"

Next, the third section on the methods for managing the community’s practice consists of four parts: first, the method for taking the clothing and belongings of a deceased patient and distributing them as a reward for services rendered;
second, whether or not the instructions given by a dying patient are valid; third, the method for repaying debts, beginning with the account of the debtor in Śrāvastī;
and fourth, the prohibition against questioning a patient beyond what is permitted, following the instruction to inquire after the patient’s condition.

The preceding section is divided into two parts. First, from "He took the robes of the deceased bhikṣu" down to "the Saṃgha should divide them," which is a general statement regarding the inclusion [of the property] within the Saṃgha.

Second, from "At that time, the Blessed One addressed [the monks]" onwards, which teaches the method for the Saṃgha’s inclusion [of the property]. This section has three parts: first, the method for distributing rewards to those who remained behind;
second, from "At that time, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there were many [monks with] three robes" onwards, which involves the selection of materials; third...
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having briefly considered whether it was appropriate or not according to his virtue, proceeded with the preceding text in three parts:

first, up to "thus [the Buddha] granted permission for the distribution of labor"; second, from "at that time, the patient-caregiver" down to the third section, which teaches the instructions for the patient-caregiver;

and third, the collective relinquishment before the Saṃgha. Once the relinquishment is complete, one may then determine the co-arising [of the property], followed by determining the entrustment. Next...

First, the determination of light and heavy [offenses]. Next, arriving at the distribution of rewards, this is the general exposition of the established principles (*yì*). Third, from "once the selection has been made within the Saṃgha" onwards, it teaches the methods for the Saṃgha’s inclusion [of the property].
First, it clarifies the rewarding of labor; next, the sub-commentary notes that the formal inclusion of the property by the Saṃgha involves the allocation of these items.
There must be five sections: first, the necessity of bestowing rewards; second, the person to whom the reward is bestowed; third, the classification of objects; fourth, the classification of virtues;
fifth, the method for distributing the rewards. Regarding the first section, we shall first explain the necessity of bestowing rewards.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, when a patient nurses another with resentment, saying, "I did not avoid cold or heat for you, nor did I seek medicine or remove impurities," even if this is indeed the case, who should receive the robes and requisites? It is said that the Saṃgha receives them.
"Yes. The Buddha said, "One should give him the three robes, the alms bowl, and the remaining medicine he received.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, once the distribution of the robes and bowl among the Saṅgha was finished, the Saṅgha asked, "Who will attend to the sick? The caregiver replied, "I will. The Saṅgha said, "Carry this corpse away.
This man said, "I am neither a caṇḍāla nor one afflicted with white leprosy. While the robes, bowl, and goods were distributed by the Saṅgha, they now command me to carry the corpse. This man—
"While he was alive, you honored and loved me; I have now repaid that debt. This is a dead man; whoever wishes to take him may carry him away as they please. A bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, who said:
"One should first give the six articles [of a deceased monk] to his designated heirs; the remaining items the Saṃgha should divide. Heavy items should not be divided.
In the second section regarding the care of the sick, this applies to all seven classes of followers. If a bhikṣu dies, two classes may receive [his belongings]. If it is a bhikṣuṇī...

The three groups [of monastics] receive [the robes] upon death. This is because the remaining laity and householders, as well as the two groups [of nuns], do not mutually fulfill the requirements for labor.

Therefore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when there are many caregivers, one does not know how many people should receive the robes. The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu passes away, the robes should be given to two people: a bhikṣu and a śrāmaṇera.
Even though they may be one's parents, brothers, or other relatives, they should still not be given to them. If a bhikṣuṇī passes away..."

One should give robes to three types of persons: nuns, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇeras. Discussing this according to its underlying principle, the same applies to the death of the other three groups [of renunciants], as stated previously.
When a bhikṣu distributes items belonging to a deceased attendant, he gives one-third to the śrāmaṇera. This bhikṣu claims that the distribution should follow the standard procedure;
however, the Buddha said that it should be distributed equally. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, a śrāmaṇera who has attended to the sick should receive an equal share.
The Great Sangha grants it. The meanings of the following two gates are explained in the *Viniścaya-vibhaṅga*. Regarding the fifth gate, the Dharma, there are further four sections.

First is the time for distributing robes, which refers to cases other than before a corpse. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, in the kingdom of Kośala, while a person was dying, the robes and bowl were distributed in the presence of the corpse.
The deceased bhikṣu arose and said, "Venerable sirs, do not distribute my robes and bowl. He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Do not [distribute them] immediately."

Regarding the portion for the corpse: if [the monk] has already departed, or if the Saṃgha is in another location, it should be divided. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when a bhikṣu passes away, one should not immediately close his door;

rather, those who practice mutual reliance (*niśraya*) should keep it together, or entrust the key to a trustworthy person. If he is not trustworthy, they should take it and give it to someone who is.
Once the affairs have been settled and the śarīra have been honored, and the arrangements are complete, one should then bring out the robes and belongings and perform the *karmavācanā*.
Once it has been ground, one should measure the shadow and allow [the relics] to enter; it should be understood that this occurs either before or after the *karmavācanā*.

Regarding the four permutations—such as encountering death but not the *karmavācanā*, and so forth—among these, one who encounters the *karmavācanā* or encounters both shall receive [a share]; the other two cases do not qualify.

According to this text, it is necessary to enshrine the *śarīra* first, and only then perform the ritual for the distribution. The place where the objects are divided into two portions is the *mahā-sīmā* (Great Boundary).

Because it is not a *sīmā* (boundary). According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*: if six bhikṣus perform a *karmavācanā* on the *sīmā* regarding robes and requisites, they commit a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline).

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: if one takes property acquired by the Saṃgha beyond the boundary, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing). It should be shared equally with other bhikṣus in five portions.
Regarding robes and requisites acquired by the Saṃgha at a single residence that are subject to distribution: if one bhikṣu takes them to the *sīmā*, he may take them for himself alone.
One should receive and uphold [this rule]. The Buddha said that it should not be transgressed lightly; the Saṃgha present should divide it, and only then may one share it with oneself.
However, because this depends on the number of people involved, there are three cases based on the number of persons: namely, the Saṃgha as a large group, and the Saṃgha as two individuals.
"Distinct" refers to the difference between groups of five and four people. Regarding the fourth point, the application of the rules differs according to the number of persons:

if there are five or more, all three procedures are employed—namely, the formal motion (*jñapti*) and second proclamation (*dvitīya-karman*) for appointing a person to distribute the robes as a reward for their labor, and the formal motion and second proclamation for entrusting the robes and collecting the items.

The *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one announcement) procedure consists of only two parts. Regarding the four persons: they perform the single formal act (*ekakarma*) as fully explained in the section on "Acquisition by the Saṃgha.

For three persons or fewer, it is understood that they face each other (*pratimukha*) and perform the mental recitation (*manasikāra*). Furthermore, if four persons or fewer perform the three formal acts accordingly and conclude them, the robe is then bestowed as a reward.
Next, to explain the text: first is the rewarding of labor; this refers to the robes and bowls formally recorded in the *jñapti-dvitīya*. This...

The formal procedure for the distribution of the Dharma-wealth is as follows: it is referred to according to its presence rather than being recorded in full every time. The reason for bestowing rewards through this ritual act is that labor deserves its full recompense;
furthermore, since there may be both good and bad [qualities among those involved], and these items are already the property of the Saṃgha, it is logically improper to divert them for private use.

Therefore, the Saṃgha’s legal authority is entrusted to him. For the third time, the meaning is added by appointing a person; for the third time, the authority to manage the property is entrusted. This may be understood from the text itself.

Regarding the second section, which addresses the objects [of the precepts], there are five gates within it. First is the determination of the objects. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one should be provided with six objects:
