2. Contact but not evil: This refers to contact through inadvertence while observing the precepts, or as when a lay attendant (*śuddhaka-puruṣa*) forcibly attaches [clothing] in great quantity.
Regarding food suspended [from a hook] and similar types: three cases are both [defiled and non-defiled], namely when one harbors an evil mind toward oneself and when one is indolent;
four cases are neither, such as food that is pure by nature. The second pair of categories explains the meaning of defilement and non-defilement from the perspective of the object itself.
This means that items such as those with two-fold precepts or those that are moist and greasy may not enter a clean kitchen for use, lest they come into contact with pure substances.
The details may be understood from the extensive explanations. Furthermore, regarding door-bolts, locks, vessels, non-vessels, and so forth, the extensive explanations are as usual.

Next, regarding cooking for oneself: whether one cooks it oneself or instructs another to do so, provided it is a person possessing the precepts who cooks it—transforming the raw into the cooked—it all constitutes cooking for oneself.

Third, the penetration and obstruction [of the fourfold classification]. There are four aspects to this penetration and obstruction: namely, medicine, time, person, and place. Regarding the first, medicine, there are two parts.

First, it is distinguished by contrasting it with the four types of medicine. Only the *kālika* (timely) medicine possesses all four faults from beginning to end, because its utility is so powerful that it must always be used.
As for the remaining three types, they are only permitted to be accepted when one is ill, according to their respective limits; in all cases, they are free from the four faults.

[The period] has passed; therefore, the text says "seven days. To exceed seven days is to be untimely (*akāla*). One incurs the offense only after the untimely period has elapsed, because there is no transgression within the limit. Second, the distinction between raw and cooked:

cooking for oneself is restricted to the case where both the raw material and the act of cooking are performed by oneself. If the raw material is cooked by another, both constitute cooking for oneself. The other three cases [of meat] pass through the stage of being cooked.
The reason it is so is that transforming the raw into the cooked involves the turmoil of killing and obstructs spiritual cultivation; therefore, it is made [prohibited].

The offense of "cooking for oneself" (*svapāka*) is committed by the resident monks. Regarding food eaten by laypeople, one must distinguish [the cases]: the boundary is not a place where cooking is performed.

Therefore, if food is stored overnight (*antar-śaya*) and cooked within the boundary, it constitutes both the offenses of "overnight storage" (*śaya*) and "cooking for oneself" (*pāka*), regardless of whether the food is raw or cooked. Since the act of preparation involves physical contact, it should be considered identical to "cooking for oneself.

However, because the Noble Ones do not permit contact [with such food], this applies to both cases; for both raw and cooked food must be formally received (*paribhoga*). This is the meaning of "cooking within" (*antar-pāka*).

[The first two] apply to all [stages]. Regarding the two [offenses of] "previous contact" (*pūrva-sparśa*) and "contact" (*sparśa*), they do not apply to growth, development, or those who have not yet reached maturity, nor to self-cooking.
One offense is restricted to the stage of birth; it does not apply to the stages of birth-ending or maturation. As for the third, the classification by time:

if one considers the transgression arising in relation to food, it applies to both appropriate and inappropriate times, and in both cases four offenses are established. However, when based on the specific time at which the conditions for the transgression are fulfilled, the meaning differs. This can be divided into three positions. First...
The first and second [cases] explain the commonality of the cooking. Because one performs the physical act oneself in a place that is not pure, both types of faults are incurred;
this is because the conditions do not distinguish between the proper time and the improper time. The second [case] restricts the lodging to the period of the day by means of the appearance of dawn.

The third point regarding the meaning of "contact" (*spṛṣṭa*) is not fixed. If one does not physically grasp it, the case is similar to the two instances of "boiling," where both [the act] apply equally to the proper time (*kāla*) and the improper time (*akāla*).

However, when it occurs spontaneously through the hand or the mouth, it is equivalent to "storing overnight" (*sāyaṃpāta*); it is established only within the proper time because the hand is restricted to the improper time. Thus, for now, we generally judge that "storing overnight" and "contact" are prohibited.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo-lun), merely grasping something overnight constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*), even before one has consumed it. This is the second [point].

The three types of persons are distinguished by whether they are "fully equipped" (*saṃpanna*) or "not fully equipped. One who is already restricted to being "fully equipped" speaks of the "general" within that state of equipment;

thus, there is the "residual overnight" (*śeṣa-rātri*) rule. When the dawn light appears, all sons of the Śākya are impure. Even if another bhikṣu cooks for them, it constitutes cooking for oneself because they belong to the same class;
none of them are permitted to cook. This is because, in relation to those who ought to cook, [the others] are collectively considered to be cooking for themselves.

Thus it is. Regarding "contact" (*sparśa*), it applies to both internally and externally; regarding "internal boiling," it is restricted by location. Who would distinguish whether a person possesses the requisite? The meaning of "contact" is not fixed;

while "not receiving" and "grasping contact" are restricted, the "requisite" is not a minor characteristic. For those who understand the defilement, the meaning applies to both the Great and Small Vehicles;

therefore, it is judged collectively. To say that "understanding" is internal is a general principle. As for the fourth section on "distinction of locations," there are two parts: first, the mutual comparison of the pure and the impure.

It is further divided into two parts. First, regarding the two locations in relation to one another: the second case is restricted to impurity because it is not the place where food was previously cooked;

thus, the explanation applies universally to both pure and impure. This is so because they arise within the process of preparation. Second, regarding the person in relation to the medicine: this is discussed in terms of location.
If both the person and the medicine are impure, all four faults are fully established. If both the person and the medicine are present [in the same location]...

Regarding the second [topic], the preparation for purity (*parikarma*), there are three cases. Since there is no mention of "cooking within" (*antar-pāka*) but there is mention of "storing overnight within" (*antar-śaya*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) may be established:

1. Both [the person and the medicine] are in an impure state. 2. Both are in a pure state. 3. The person is in a pure state, but the medicine is in an impure state; in this case, it constitutes "storing overnight. 4.

The medicine is in a pure state, but the person is in an impure state; in this case, it is pure. The reason why the third case also constitutes "storing overnight" is because of the distinction between the pure and the impure.
It is not included within the pure grounds of both realms; since it enters into food that is impure and is not subsumed by what is pure, it likewise constitutes "overnight storage.

If one distinguishes the pure grounds, there is "overnight storage" but no "internal cooking"; this will be explained in the relevant passage. Second, we shall again distinguish [the types of food] based on the four kinds of purity.

If one discusses the meaning from the perspective of the self, all four types of purity incur two faults, because they arise within the realm of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) and thus do not constitute pure restraint.
If one says that both [types of] internal [restraint] and the four purities are absent, it is called "purity" because there is no restraint regarding the two internals;
yet this is described as being "blocked. However, the prior state is not necessarily determinable. Regarding the meaning of these three gates, the lecturer should follow the text for each point.
Each of these offenses may be analyzed according to three categories, which is likewise unobjectionable.

Next, the text is explained. Regarding the presence or absence of "storing overnight" (*antarā-sthāpana*), there are three pairs in the text: the first two are mutually overlapping; the next two are mutually inclusive; and the final two are mutually penetrating.
To say they are "mutually overlapping" is to judge them from the perspective of their roots. To say they are "mutually following" [is to judge them] from the perspective of their sequence.

If fruits that have not yet reached full maturity remain on impure ground and undergo constant transformation, they do not constitute "overnight storage" (*antar-śayita*) and may thus enter the pure kitchen.
However, if there is only a bhikṣu who has employed someone on impure ground to prepare the vegetables, he asks the Buddha whether it is permissible for them to enter the pure kitchen.

The Buddha said: "If one has not yet passed the first watch of the night, one may enter the pure kitchen; thus we know that what has not yet been consumed is not considered 'overnight' (sukhita). Question:
"If the production of food constitutes an offense for keeping it overnight, why does the text state that fruit from an impure ground which falls onto a pure ground [is permissible]? The Buddha said:

"Because no one has the intention to take it and eat it after it has been kept overnight with ripe fruit. Answer: "This person never harbors the intent to take and eat it after it has been kept overnight with ripe fruit."

Because it fell due to the fault of being insentient, that which falls of its own accord is pure; since the principle is the same, it is newly acquired from another and thus does not constitute an internal transgression.
If one intentionally desires to eat fruit that has been co-resident [with oneself], even if it is ripe and falls because a bird has pecked it, it is not pure and should not be eaten.
Therefore, the text states: "If one does not intentionally desire it to fall, but it falls because it was blown or struck by wind and rain, or because a bird pecked it, it is pure."

The second phrase judges purity based on the sense organ (*indriya*). Both the matured and the immature are pure; regarding these two phrases, the Buddha stated that both are pure. If one were to state the opposite of what was previously explained, both would become impure.
As for the term "mutual entry" (*anyonya-praveśa*), each is pure or impure according to the location of its respective organ.

The first phrase refers to the matured, and is therefore impure. The second phrase refers to the matured-and-germinating, and is therefore pure. If one were to state the opposite of the former, such that the former is germinating and the latter is matured, [the same logic applies].
"Pure before and impure after"—these two phrases each contain the meanings of both purity and impurity; for the sake of brevity, only one aspect is cited here.
Second, regarding the five types of pure seeds and the two sets of five pure dharmas, they are as stated in the text. The four lines concerning pure fruits are as explained above. Five.

[The fruits] are divided [into five types]. If one eats fruit, it should be purified by the five methods of purification for a śramaṇa: namely, purification by fire, by knife, by bird, by injury, and by non-seeding.
If one eats roots, there are five methods of purification: peeling, cutting, breaking, washing, and fire-purification.
If one eats stalks, there are three purifications: by knife, by fire, and by washing, etc. Furthermore, they should be purified collectively; it is sufficient to purify even one [of these methods].

Regarding the third [category], the presence or absence of a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), there are eight items within it. First, regarding the two items concerning transformation, there is no explanation because they have already been dealt with.
Second, the three phrases beginning with "a young novice" (*sāmaṇera*) concern assisting the intentions of the *kappiya-kāraka*; therefore, there is no explanation.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that when there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one is permitted to supervise food and drink on a boat; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is likewise. Tipping over [the vessel] serves to assist in rectifying [the situation]. Third, the items beginning with the "ghee and oil jar."

Although there was a certain understanding [of this matter], for the sake of protecting the Saṃgha, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one should use new materials to cover [the roots] so that the hands do not come into contact with them.

Fourth: Regarding the group of six [monks] who dared to eat unclean [vegetables] and, upon encountering circumstances, failed to understand that they must wash root vegetables with water—having first washed them, they thought that since water extinguishes fire, it constituted purification.
The Buddha said, "This does not constitute a loss [of purity]; therefore, this washing is indeed purification. Fifth.
The two lines beginning with "Previously there was aversion" do not constitute a formal resolution (*kṣānti*). A resolution is [defined as] impurity.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a certain Brahmin threw a handful of impure rice into a cart and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If it can be removed separately, do so;

if it cannot be removed separately, discard a handful. Furthermore, regarding the carcasses of deer, gazelles, and the like that have been washed away by water, if there is no pure person (*pariśuddha-pudgala*) available, [the same rule applies].

A bhikṣu entered the water himself to retrieve [the food] and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Once it has reached the shore, have a layperson (upāsaka) cut away the portion grasped by the bhikṣu’s hand;

then it may be eaten without offense. Regarding the sixth case, "a layperson forcibly takes more than... and so forth, this is not a valid solution because it is difficult for one to receive and grasp the food.
Regarding the seventh case, "various householders... and so forth, taking another's property is not a valid solution. (*Pañcavargika-vinaya*).

A certain brāhmaṇa entrusted some parched grain (maṇḍa) to a bhikṣu. The bhikṣu placed it on ground that was not pure (aśuddha-bhūmi). After one night had passed, the brāhmaṇa came the next day to retrieve it; he divided it and gave a portion to the bhikṣu.
Because the bhikṣu had placed it on impure ground himself, he did not dare to accept and eat it. The Buddha said:

"Since this parched grain originally belonged to a layperson (avadātavasana), I permit you to accept and eat it; there is no offense. [The eighth case concerns] a sick bhikṣu who required gruel; from here below, the acceptance is permitted.

Therefore, it is not a case of [the rule] being understood. Regarding the fourth point, the text states that one must not cook gruel within the boundary (*sīmā*). It permits cooking for oneself; however, if one cooks for oneself while [the food] is raw, an offense is committed.

Since it is permitted to cook for oneself, one should do so on pure ground (*pariśuddha-bhūmi*). Question: The original establishment of the *kappiya-kāraka* (the one who makes things permissible) was intended to prevent the two types of "internal" [cooking].
Therefore, one commits an offense by keeping [food] overnight, but there is no offense in cooking it after it has been kept overnight. There are several interpretations; here is one explanation:

if the *kappiya-kāraka* (the person authorized to prepare food) cannot be trusted, and if such an allowance were not granted, there would be no means to sustain one's life while maintaining the rules of inspection. For this reason, the rule allows that one may look at the food without committing an offense, provided it is not cooked inside [the monastery].

One must avoid the appearance of dawn (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*); otherwise, one commits an offense for keeping it overnight due to negligence. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that because the act of cooking occurs in a specific location, there is no offense regarding the overnight period.

The original [rule] follows the person; it does not matter whether it is a pure place (*śuddhasthāna*). If one eats together with a person in the same location, it is termed "staying overnight together" (*saha-vasati*).
Therefore, the text says "eating and staying overnight together. As for cooking, it follows the location; it does not matter whether a *bhikṣu* is present or not.

However, if it is an impure place (*aśuddhasthāna*), that is where the cooking takes place; in a pure place, there is no cooking. This refers to the fault of staying overnight in an impure place without a *bhikṣu*. Question: Why is this so?
What is meant by "a prior bias following a person constitutes a prior condition"? The explanation states: A *bhikṣu* is difficult to trust; there may be fear of censure or suspicion.
Because one does not act in their presence, there is no witness to the proof [of the act]. Therefore, it constitutes a prior condition. Cooking is performed wherever one happens to be.

When acting in the presence [of others], there is supervision and witnesses, which avoids censure. Thus, cooking on pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) or watching over the cooking does not constitute the condition for cooking. This concludes the explanation of the fourth section.
Regarding the meaning: next, as for the three phrases concerning "erroneously receiving oil" and so forth, they do not constitute a valid acceptance; thus there is an interpretation.
Next, regarding "forgetting not to accept food," it is because there is no fault of mental contact [with the food]; these two phrases are explained through repeated analysis and selection.
The fifth [category] consists of eight matters; these eight matters comprise five groups. Specifically, there are two internal [matters]: cooking for oneself and not accepting [food].

There are four other methods of food (*kṛtānna-dharma*), which in meaning also include improper contact (*duṣṭa-sparśana*) and so forth. Thus, there are two types of names for these. As for the *pācittiya* alone, the reason it is permitted is that the two internal matters are contrasted with external ones.

External matters involve taking food away, which results in the loss of the meal. The four types—cooking for oneself, not accepting, and the four other methods—are all [prohibited] because they involve harming others.

It is for this reason that [the rule against] eating leftovers from the previous night (*paryuṣita*) is not waived. Regarding "storing within" (*antaḥśāya*), since it was previously purified and stored overnight, it is permitted.

However, regarding "leftovers" (*ucchiṣṭa*), since it was not previously purified and constitutes an offense with every swallow, it is not permitted. Alcohol is likewise not permitted because it is contrary to the Dharma.
Furthermore, eight matters are permitted because they relate to external losses of food; whereas "leftovers" originally relates to what is not leftover, and that which is not leftover is pure food.

Regarding the name "pure food" (*śucibhakṣa*): it is not because one fears others might take it away that one must discard it and eat the leftovers as pure. Therefore, this is not an exception to the rule.

Since cooking for oneself is permitted, it is clear that there is the destruction of living beings; however, fearing confusion with the "external destruction" [of plants], it is not explicitly mentioned here.
This is solely because internal consumption through cooking is already subsumed within the category of "cooking for oneself."

The sixth section clarifies the absence of "overnight storage" (*antarā-sayaṃ*). This passage consists of four points: 1. Regarding a wooden pillar that extends both inside and outside: the Buddha declared it is not "inside.

If materials are taken from pure ground and the house is erected on impure ground, the Buddha declared it impure. If materials are taken from impure ground and the house is erected on pure ground, it is considered impure;
however, the Buddha declared it pure. 2. The second point concerns three clauses regarding moving food at night and so forth.

One who is without mind is not "resident. One who falls between the pure and the impure appears to possess the dharma of a purified ground. Regarding the three instances of the two phrases concerning "doubt":

because they involve the removal of food, the resolution of purity, the warding off of evil, and the protection of goodness, the fourth case—where a guest arrives from outside and departs seeking to leave the boundary—is likewise not a fault of the sentient being;
since both [the arrival and departure] are permitted, it constitutes purity. Therefore, it is said: "The same applies to one who intends to travel far."
The fourth section, which discriminates between what is appropriate and inappropriate, should be understood as follows. [The Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus:
"Even if it is something I have prescribed, if it is not considered pure in other regions, the bhikṣus should not employ it.
Even if it is not something I have prescribed, if it must be practiced in other regions, you must all practice it."
● The Eighth Section: The Kāṭhina Robe.

Regarding the Kāṭhina robe, its name in the Western language (Sanskrit) means "the robe for rewarding the good and punishing the evil. "Reward" refers to the five privileges granted as a reward to those who observe the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat).

"Punishment" refers to the fact that those who observe the *paścimavārṣika* (late rains retreat) do not obtain these five privileges, which is termed punishment. It is also called "firmness" (*kaṭhina*).
It is a "substantial robe" (*sāra-cīvara*). Because many robes are offered, and one selects those that are firm and superior to complete this robe, it is called a "firm and substantial robe.

It is also named the "robe of merit" (*guṇa-cīvara*). If one receives this robe, it can produce five kinds of beneficial merits; as the name is derived from its functional efficacy, it is called the "robe of merit.
A detailed explanation of the methods for receiving and relinquishing it is titled the *Khandhaka*. Within this section, there are three parts. First:
The section on the conditions for receiving robes consists of three parts: first, the five reasons for obtaining the robe and the five benefits thereof;

second, from "From the Saṃgha it should be thus" onwards, up to the rules for receiving the robe according to the Dharma; and third, from "Those six groups [of monks]" onwards, the ritual for relinquishing it.
Within the first part, regarding the conditions for receiving the *saṃghāṭī* due to its heaviness causing exhaustion, there are two sections.
First, the bhikṣus of the Kosalā country; second, the bhikṣus of the snowy lands. Following this, the World-Honored One concludes the explanation of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

There are four matters that ought to be performed, which clarify that the receiving of robes occurs at the same time as the end of the summer. This is followed by the enumeration of the remaining three [sections].
Third, from "there are five matters" onwards, it demonstrates that the efficacy of these robes necessarily secures five benefits. Second, four [matters].

Regarding the matters: for the first [matter], one may receive [the robe] on any of the three days—the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth; for the remaining three matters, it is restricted to the sixteenth day.

Regarding the second section of the third text: first, receiving it for the sake of the five [privileges]; next, after having received the *kaṭhina* robe, as indicated by the phrase "having already received it," one is permitted to perform the five matters.

The second section, the text on receiving the robe, has two parts: first, clarifying the substance and color of the robe-material; second, from "If one dwells in a [specific] location" onwards, the actual method for receiving the robe.

The former part further divides into two: first, the substance of the robe as in the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules; second, from "The group of six" onwards, the color of the robe as in the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.

Regarding the text on the substance of the robe, there are three sections: first, up to the conclusion of the procedure for receiving the robe, the substance of the robe-material as in the rules; second, [the question] "Why?"... [and so forth].

Having completed the formal acceptance (*parigraha*), if the substance of the robe-material is not as prescribed—down to the point where it is not properly constituted—it does not constitute a valid acceptance.

Regarding the third section, "How is it [not valid]? and so forth, this raises the aforementioned substances and explains how they accord with the Dharma, combining them with the intent for acceptance.

In the initial text, its meaning is first explained through five analytical gates: first, the analysis by time; second, the analysis by location; third, the analysis by person; fourth, the analysis by robe; and fifth...
Regarding the classification of the Dharma, there are two times: first, the time of receiving the robes; second, the time of obtaining the benefit.

As for the first time, this Vinaya specifically restricts it to the sixteenth day, because on the fifteenth day the period of labor has not yet been completed. Therefore, it is said that one should receive [the robes] once the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is finished.
If it is seventeen days [after the full moon], there is no fifth month; therefore, the subsequent text permits that one should relinquish [the robes] once the four months of winter are complete.
Even if one were to take days from the following period to fulfill the five months, this would encroach upon the days of the spring equinox.

According to the *Karmavibhaṅga* and the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, those who enter the later retreat (*paścimā varṣā*) are not permitted to receive robes. Thus, we know that the time for receiving [the robes] is also the same as in this Vinaya. If it is otherwise...

The *Three Vinayas* all permit receiving robes for one month and relinquishing robes after one month. The *Ten Vinayas* state: if one obtains a robe on the first day of the month, one should receive it that very day;
if one obtains it on the second, third, or even up to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it is likewise.
The *Five-Part Vinaya* states: there are thirty days for receiving robes and thirty days for relinquishing them. If [one obtains a robe] on the sixteenth day of the seventh month...
If one receives [the rains retreat] on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, it is relinquished on the seventeenth day;

or from the seventeenth day up until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it is received on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month and relinquished on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month, continuing until it is relinquished on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month.

If one enters the later retreat (paścimā vārṣikī) on the sixteenth day of the eighth month, it is received on that date and relinquished on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. This is the second period for obtaining benefits.

If one relies on the *Caturvargika-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the period is fixed at five months. However, regarding the time when the benefit is obtained, it follows the eight [factors], and whether the robes are discarded or kept is not fixed.

As in the other three Vinayas, the period is fixed at four months; because both those who come before and those who come after listen to and receive the robe, the time when the benefit is obtained likewise follows whether they discard or keep them for a long or short duration.
As for the second point, it pertains solely to the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); this is the great distinction.
It is small and moreover restricted to this world-system; if one belongs to another world-system, they cannot receive a robe at this location (according to the *Jianlun*).
Other monks may count toward the quorum but are not permitted to receive the benefit. Regarding the third person, there is a threefold distinction: first, the recipient of the robe;
second, the keeper of the robe; and third, the individual monk. As for the recipient of the robe, there is a primary fivefold classification; the [first] two are not [the recipient].

The lower three [grades] are not [permissible], because for one who practices the path with full completeness, the labor is not heavy; furthermore, there is no *saṃghāṭī* robe available to provide. According to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views):

four *bhikṣus* and one *śrāmaṇera* were about to conclude their *varṣā* retreat. For the sake of the *śrāmaṇera*, they conferred the precepts so that the quorum of five could be met to receive the *kaṭhina* robe.
The newly ordained person also successfully received the robe. [Thus there were] one *bhikṣu* and four *śrāmaṇeras*.

Thus it is clearly known that there is no formal procedure for a śrāmaṇera to receive robes. Regarding the second point, among the two types of "upper" [robes], one may or may not be placed [in the inventory].

If it is not placed, it cannot be received, because the *an-kyung* (the summer retreat) has not yet concluded; this is according to the *Jian lun* (Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra). Even if the later *an-kyung* breaks the retreat, it still does not constitute a valid reception.

Regarding the third, whether at the beginning or end of the *an-kyung*, the fourth, at the beginning or middle, if it is broken, it is not established. The fifth is established within the [proper] period.
If there is a *saṃghāṭī* robe, and it is within the boundary (*sīmā*) and in the presence of the Saṃgha, only then does one become a recipient of the robe.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one who is undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation) is not permitted to receive it; this applies regardless of other types of formal acts (*karmas*). Furthermore, is there a case where the Saṃgha receives a robe but there is someone within the Saṃgha who does not obtain it?
The Buddha said: "There is. This refers to those who have entered the rains retreat (*varṣā*) elsewhere. As for the two persons who hold the robe:

One should also take up the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) in the same location in accordance with the Dharma; there should be few people traveling about. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one must possess five virtues, namely freedom from attachment and so forth.
Regarding the knowledge of who has received [the robe] and who has not: when appointing someone to hold the robes, although there is no explicit text for this, the meaning should likewise be applied.

Thirdly, regarding the distinction of the Saṃgha: this refers to the Saṃgha as distinct from a group of four; however, five persons are required. This is stated in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Question: How many persons are required to obtain [it]?

Regarding the receiving of the *kaṭhina* robe: it may be received by as few as five people, because those who enter the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat) are permitted to receive it. The principles concerning its determination and its effects on obstacles are as explained in the section on the four types of Saṃghas.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if a large assembly of ten thousand or twenty thousand finds it difficult to reach consensus, a great number of individuals may also separately receive the *guṇakaṭhina*.
Everything is the same as for a large assembly, with the sole difference being that "a great number" (*bahujana*) is substituted for "the assembly. If there is only one person...
One may receive [the robe] alone. Regarding the classification of the fourth robe, there are five parts. First, the classification of obtaining through seeking the Dharma, as in the text.

Second, the classification of upper and lower garments; this refers to the three robes (*tricīvara*) and not others such as the *saṃkakṣikā* (breast-cloth) and so forth, because the text mentions "ten intervals" (*daśa-koṭi*). [This is according to] the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

If the robes differ from those of the five assemblies, such as the bhikṣus, they are not termed "received. Furthermore, it is said that if the saṃghāṭī and the two lower robes are not cut into patches, the reception is also not accomplished;

conversely, if they are so prepared, the reception is accomplished. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, a robe that is deficient in measurement does not accomplish the reception of the *kaṭhina* robe.

Regarding the third point concerning quantity: at most, one may possess the three robes. According to the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*, if a person brings three robes and offers them [to another], [the reception is accomplished].

The monk shall take it as a *guṇa-cīvara* (virtue-robe) and say: "If this is taken as a *guṇa-cīvara*, then all three robes shall belong to the person who holds the robe, according to the donor's instruction;
they shall be given entirely to the robe-holder, and the rest of the Saṃgha shall not receive them. If many people send robes, he should accept only one robe."

The remainder should be divided. If it is given to those whose robes are worn out, and there are many such persons, it should be given to those who have spent the summer retreat. Regarding the fourth [category], if it has already been completed, there is no need for further distribution;

if it is not yet completed, it must be made. This Vinaya merely states that one should appoint a person to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal act); it does not provide the text for the appointment itself.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) specifies that one, two, three, or even a multitude of people may be appointed by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sectarian Vinaya) likewise prescribes a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
The first two or three persons who are capable of discerning the principle perform it. The ten *dhāraṇīs* (mantras) at the conclusion are performed by four *bhikṣus*.

They cause [the robe] to be raised, washed, dyed, cut, joined, and sewn; these are the six methods of mental non-deviation. The fifth is the "as-it-is" (*yathā*) classification. One body is to be understood as "like" (*tathā*);
the second is "acting like" (*yathākāra*), such as the six acts of spreading out and so forth according to the text; the third is "measuring like" (*parimāṇa-yathā*).
The fourth is the suchness of form (*rūpa-tathatā*). The fifth, the analysis of phenomena (*dharma-vibhaṅga*), follows the text.
Next, the text is explained according to its sequence. The first section has three parts: first, a general statement regarding the appropriate manner of receiving and listening to the teaching;

thus it says, "The Saṃgha should receive the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit) in this manner. The specific method for doing so follows below. Second, from "If one obtains a new robe" onwards, there is a detailed exposition.

Regarding the characteristics of what is in accordance with the Dharma: once the three groups of monks have accepted it, the following are collectively established as the conclusion. The second section lists seven matters: first, determining the nature of the robe-material and resolving the legal principles;

second, not seeking through improper livelihoods and so forth, but manifesting a request that is in accordance with the Dharma; third, not spending the night [with the material], because it accords with the teaching;
fourth, the substance of the robe is pure and free from the offense of "abandonment" (nissaggiya-pācittiya); fifth, having arrived on that very day, it conforms to the Dharma, and so forth.
This explains the characteristics of robes made during times of clarity. Sixth, the six matters concerning the method of making robes, beginning with "one should wash them oneself.

Seventh, the determination that [the robe] is completed before the Saṃgha. The first section has four parts, namely, because it concerns what is first obtained; therefore it says, "if one obtains a new robe.
"New" contains two types, namely *dīrghalābha* (long-term gain) and *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe). Therefore, next, the two types of robes are listed. Third, regarding "whether new or old," within...
The first three types each have both new and old varieties. The fourth is for the purpose of avoiding attachment to fine garments; it demonstrates the method for accepting patched robes.

The second refers to being free from the five improper ways of seeking clothing, hence it says "not by wrong livelihood. This means not wearing heavy furs during the summer and so forth; hence it says "not by signs. This means not soliciting by agitating people;
hence it says "not by incitement. Regarding "not staying overnight": [it means] not staying overnight at a place where one has already received a robe.

When receiving the robe, it is not received on the fifteenth day; there is no fault, as it can be understood through its purity. Because it is specifically permitted, it conforms to the Dharma upon arriving that very day.
Since the four borders and below are distinguished when the robe is being made, it is said, "upon arriving that very day," and so forth;
the rest is self-evident. Regarding the conclusion of the third section: this refers to the completion of the resolution according to the Dharma; the remaining two [sections] are likewise clear.
Regarding the "color of form" (rūpa-tathatā), it refers to the color of the kāṣāya robe.
The text on the formal acceptance of the robe consists of four parts: 1. After obtaining the *kaṭhina* robe, one requests the Buddha to hold the square cloth;

thus the text says, "not knowing what to do," one raises the matter to inform the Honored One. 2. From the words "The Buddha said" onwards, the actual method of acceptance is shown. 3. Third, Upāli [asks].

The following section addresses the removal of doubts and obstructions. The fourth part provides a detailed analysis regarding whether the robe is successfully established. Within the second section on "Receiving," there are four parts:

first, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to inform the Sangha of whether the robe has been received; second, the appointment of a guardian for the robe after the announcement, where no specific qualifications are required because there is no particular risk of damage;
third, the selection of a qualified person according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; and fourth, the announcement: "Venerable Sangha, please listen."

The following section concerns the entrustment [of robes] based on the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act). This is because those who hold [the robes] at this residence are shown not to be entitled to the benefit of the robes.

From the fourth point, "That bhikṣu... onwards, the actual reception [of the robes] is clearly explained. Question: In the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), one first appoints [an official] and subsequently makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Why, in this procedure for receiving robes, does one first make the announcement and subsequently appoint [the official]? Answer: The *pravāraṇā* is a formal enactment.

First one is appointed, and afterwards it is announced. Receiving the robe is an exception; there is no fault in not receiving it. Because it is unknown whether one has received it or not, it is necessary to announce it first and then appoint [the recipient].
Regarding the formal procedure for receiving [the robe], there are three parts: First, the person holding the robe places the robe crosswise upon both arms;

as the various bhikṣus speak, the signs of its acquisition become clear. The formal act of receiving is recited three times. Second, from the passage "those bhikṣus... onwards refers to the monastic assembly.

"Having received. This is said to demonstrate that the holding of the robe is in accordance with the Dharma; thus it says, "it has been properly received. Regarding the phrase "merit and reputation belong to me":

this means that since the five types of beneficial merit are free from fault, a beautiful resonance is manifested externally; hence it is called "reputation. Because it causes me to obtain this, it is said to "belong to me.
The third response, "so be it," means that the person holding the robe speaks words of assent and compliance. As for its not... [text ends]

Regarding those who receive the benefit: they remain silent in this manner, continuing down to the lowest seat. When the *upāsaka* sees that the robe has been accepted, there are nine phrases: the first refers to the future; the next phrase is the present;
and "already" refers to the past. By repeating these three phrases, do they not constitute nine? This is because there are three for each of the three periods of time.
[Question: In which period of time is the merit-robe (*guṇa-cīvara*) received? [Answer: The Buddha’s response can be understood. This is the fourth section of the analysis.
The summary of what has and has not been [discussed] follows the text. It is abbreviated and lacks the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the appointment.

Regarding the third section, the text on relinquishing the robe (cīvara-pratyākhyāna), there are two parts: first, up to the mention of the *dukkaṭa* offense, which concerns the occasion for relinquishing the robe;

second, from "there are eight causes and conditions" onwards, which extensively explains the method of relinquishment. Within the text concerning the occasion, there are two parts: first, up to the restriction of five months, which concerns the limit of five months; second, that...

Regarding the six groups [of monks] and below, when the time limit has expired, there is no formal announcement (*jñapti*) for relinquishing; this consists of two sets of three. The first set is: (1) the failure to announce the non-relinquishment to the Buddha;
(2) the Buddha’s statement [beginning with "I say... which judges it as improper; and (3) the formal announcement [beginning with "Now, therefore... establishing the rule.

Within the second set of three, the third—the establishment of the rule—further consists of three parts: (1) the proclamation of the rule once the time has expired; and (2) the instruction beginning with "It should be proclaimed in this manner... and so forth.
The method for its enactment. Third, the section beginning with "If it is not enacted" concludes the offense.

Regarding the second part of the text on the procedure, there are two sections. First, the preparatory ritual for the assembly of the Saṃgha and so forth. There are six points regarding what people say:
first, the gathering of the assembly, such as those who should come having come; second, concordant silence. It is said that there are five factors by which one should be considered in concord.
Third, because the assembly is purified, those who have not yet received the precepts are excluded. Fourth, those who do not attend must announce their consent (*chanda*).

Fifth, the inquiry; sixth, the response. Thus, the preceding section is divided into six parts. This meaning is not so [as previously stated]; that is to say, "harmony" (*sāmagrī*) is itself the gathering of the Saṃgha, and there is no separate essence of harmony.
Regarding the five things for which one should harmonize: first, if it is in accordance with the Dharma, one should harmonize; that is, the ritual action (*dharmakarma*) accords with principle.
