Let us discuss this. These four types of *saṃgha* are what uphold [the Dharma]. Among them, the *caturvargika-saṃgha* (four-person *saṃgha*) has many matters to perform, and its incidental transgressions (*pārājika* and other offenses) are also numerous.
The three [groups] beginning with the five-person *saṃgha* have fewer matters to perform, and their incidental transgressions are likewise few. This principle may be understood by analogy.

Eighth, regarding the difficulty of accomplishment when facing a specific matter, there are two sections of analysis: first, in terms of the *dharma*; second, in relation to the Saṃgha. Regarding the analysis in terms of the *dharma*:
what has been taught since antiquity is further discussed by way of the eighteen *dharmas*. First, in response to the *tāḍana* (reproach), they made a mutual request to the Buddha;
because the Buddha judged it to be unaccomplished, he stated that such matters as these are contrary to the *dharma* and do not achieve success. Below are ten [cases].

The remaining three categories, such as "admission by oneself" (*svayaṃ-vāda*), each comprise five [subdivisions] that collectively subsume the eighteen dharmas;
thus, there are one hundred and twenty instances of what is not [the dharma]. If further elaborated, there are one hundred and forty-five dharmas and fifteen instances of what is not [the dharma].

Within the one hundred and two formal acts, such as the *jñapti-dvitīya* and *jñapti-caturtha*, excluding the three *jñapti-caturtha* acts for receiving the precepts, there are fifteen instances of what is not [the dharma].
Regarding the remaining ninety-nine dharmas, each has fourteen faults; thus, there are one thousand four hundred and thirty-one faults in total.
As for the forty-three *śuddha-vidhi* (simple announcements), excluding the two types of *karma*, the three *śuddha-vidhi* of the Preceptor each have thirteen faults.

Excluding the two cases that resemble [the formal act], the remaining forty-one instances of "white" (pure) acts each constitute only twelve instances of non-offense; thus, there are no cases where the required number of persons is not met.

Because the censure does not cease the offense, it results in five hundred and nineteen instances of non-offense. Together with the previous total, there are one thousand nine hundred and fifty instances of non-offense.
If, when facing the actual matter, many [procedures] fail to be accomplished, one falls into this many instances of non-offense. This is stated in relation to the Saṃgha.
This [category] also consists of a group of four monks. Because the matters they undertake are numerous, they are difficult to accomplish when faced with them, and their failures are also many.
As for the other three groups of monks, the matters they undertake are few, and their failures are likewise few.

In the ninth section, regarding the refutation of disputes concerning *adharma* (unlawfulness) and *asamagra* (a discordant assembly), when an *adharma-asamagra-karman* (an unlawful act performed by a discordant assembly) was carried out against a bhikṣu, seven people disputed the matter.
The Buddha stated that what is called "unlawful and discordant" (*adharma-asamagra*) is a statement of the Dharma (*dharmavāda*).

As explained in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one should say that two [of the disputants] speak according to the Dharma—namely, those who declare it to be "unlawful and discordant" and those who declare it "invalid"—while the remaining five speak contrary to the Dharma (*adharmavāda*).
This should also be understood accordingly, as with the following categories. One disputes the remaining four non-[legitimate] acts; one person speaks according to the Dharma. Therefore it is said:
"Up to the point where the concordant semblance of the Dharma is the speaking of the Dharma. Within this, there is a twofold analysis: first, regarding the Dharma; second, regarding the Saṃgha.

Regarding the first, concerning the Dharma: excluding the two groups [of the *pārivāsika* and *mānāpyacārika*], the three methods of receiving ordination possess fifteen non-[legitimate] acts and give rise to seventeen.

Regarding the various types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), among the remaining ninety-nine dharmas—the *jñapti-dvitīya* and *jñapti-caturtha* procedures—there are fourteen instances of what is not in accordance with the meaning (*an-artha*).

To categorize them, one dharma is raised as the heading for the "dispute concerning a single point" (*ekottarika-adhikaraṇa*), namely the "improper act by an incomplete assembly" (*adharma-vinirbhoga-gaṇa*).

This single instance of impropriety (*adharma*) constitutes sixteen types of dispute (*vivāda*), which refers to each of those [members] adhering to the fourteen kinds of impropriety and debating whether their words are established or not. Thus says the Buddha.

If one were to adjudicate and correct these statements, among them two types of persons speak according to the Dharma: namely, those who say "it is not the Path" regarding what is not the Dharma, and those whose speech is not established as a formal proposition.
The remaining fourteen types of assertions are all not in accordance with the Dharma. As it is with the first [type of] dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), so it is for the other thirteen meanings.
Since this one *dharma* is thus, the same applies by analogy to the remaining ninety-eight *dharmas*. This is the single [principle].

Among the *jñapti* (formal motions), because there are no two that resemble one another, the two types of *jñapti* are excluded. Regarding the three *jñaptis* of the Preceptor (*śikṣādātrī*), there are thirteen instances of non-transgression (*avipatti*) and fifteen kinds of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) arise.

As for the remaining *jñaptis*, etc., furthermore, because there are no cases where the quorum is not met, nor cases where a transgression is not stopped by a formal reprimand (*prativāraṇa*), there are only twelve.
These correspond only to fourteen kinds of disputes; this can be understood through comparison. The same logic should apply to the detailed explanation; it is merely abbreviated here in the text.
Regarding the phrase "in the presence of the Saṃgha," this refers to the four-membered Saṃgha, in which there are many matters to be performed and many disputes and transgressions.
In the other three types of Saṃghas, the matters to be performed are few, and disputes and transgressions are likewise few.

Regarding the tenth point, "Doubtful Cases of Non-Resolution," there is a threefold analysis: first, by way of persons; second, by way of dharmas; and third, in relation to the four types of saṃgha. As for the analysis by way of persons:

only thirteen kinds of persons are permanently excluded and cannot be reinstated. Their reinstatement does not constitute a valid resolution; rather, it constitutes a resolution that results in non-resolution.

As for others who are nominally treated as persons undergoing resolution, their resolution is indeed valid because it is not permanent. If they were not treated as persons undergoing resolution, [the case would be different].
This is not an incorrect understanding. Therefore, the text says: "Whether it is accomplished or not accomplished—how is it not accomplished?
The Buddha said: "Thirteen kinds of persons do not accomplish understanding. Excluding these thirteen persons, all others accomplish understanding. This is according to the meaning.

Matters such as accepting gifts that accord with one's desires or acting as a proxy for others need not be explained; to explain them would be incorrect. Question: What are the "thirteen persons"? Answer:
They refer to the four *pārājika* offenses and the eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for monks and nuns, along with the *pratyantika-niḥsaraṇa* (exclusion) for the lower assembly. Question:
If the two higher assemblies [monks and nuns] have twelve [offenses] by dividing the four and eight, why are the four *pārājika* offenses of the lower assembly not added to them to make ten?
Are there six people? Or, if one further follows the specific cases such as the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas* (obstacles), why would there be only thirteen people?
Now, the explanation for saying "thirteen people" is that these thirteen people are so called because the thirteen types of persons with obstacles (*trayodaśa-antarāyika-pudgala*) are questioned;

those established as the thirteen are all subsumed under the category of "borderline offenses" (*pārājika*). If that is so, then among the thirteen obstacles, can they all be expelled through the formal ritual (*karma*)? Or...

It is said: "Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, the release is not accomplished. The answer is as stated in the text: because they are outsiders (*tīrthika*), and for reasons such as having committed murder, it is said that they should all be expelled (*pravāsanīya*).

All other cases are accomplished through release. Regarding the statement "concerning the Dharma": previously, it was explained that if one received [an object] without a formal request, it was necessary to release it;

if one received it with a formal request, there was no need to release it. Now, regarding these two, each has its own case of being released or not released. If one receives it with a formal request...

[The section on] the Middle [Community]: 1) Receiving the bowl through collective practice; 2) receiving confession from the Sangha; 3) disclosure and separation from one's robe; 4) the six-year period of administrative assignment;

5) appointing a person to receive the [formal] days; 6) returning the robe after four months; 7) penalizing him to use the old [robe] while holding the new staff and bag; 8) resolving the seven types of *karmavācanā* for those undergoing penance, and so forth.
It is not necessary to relinquish it. Regarding the single dharma of receiving the precepts, one is permitted to relinquish them for fear of violating them;

thus, the relinquishing of the *kaṭhina* robe is explained as being done out of leniency. In the midst of the formal request and acceptance, whether before the Saṃgha or individually, it may be either relinquished or not.

As for those who are subject to banishment or disciplinary treatment, they are permanently discarded and there is no relinquishing. Although the two-fold formal announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya*) regarding Chanda is called a disciplinary punishment, it is established as a regulation for prevention and likewise does not [constitute a relinquishing].

One must understand that [procedures such as] the *jñapti*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and so forth do not require formal dissolution (*visarga*), because they are acts of admonition or exhortation rather than disciplinary measures. Therefore, these do not require dissolution.

All others do require it; that is to say, for the eleven assemblies concerning the definition of boundaries (*sīmā*) and so forth, there is a procedure for dissolution because their established arrangements must be altered. Regarding persons, there are thirteen types.

This refers to the seven rules for punishing those who commit offenses: the place of punishment, insanity, the overturning of the bowl, the family of learners (*śaikṣa-kula*), not paying respects, and the relinquishing of instruction;

these are all understood together. Why is this so? First, because in all cases there is no intentional request or acceptance [of the offense], unlike the case of being separated from one's robes and so forth.

Second, because in both cases there is no fixed limit for the duration of losing the dharma, whereas after the period has passed, one receives a different [period of] days. Third, they are applied reciprocally as punishments to eliminate doubt and establish the regulations. Not...

The same applies to the appointment of an emissary (*dūta*), the two types of *jñapti-dvitīya* [procedures], the two types of *jñapti-caturtha* [procedures] such as the *cāturmāsika* (four-month) and the formal admonition (*śāsanānuśāsana*), and the four [procedures] for the purpose of discipline, as well as the permanent banishment (*pārājika*) and the training through repentance (*yadbhūyaḥ-kṣānti*). Therefore, all of these must involve the knowledge of the Dharma;

these requirements total twenty-six dharmas. Just as one must relinquish [the precepts] when receiving them, so too does one relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe; this requires a single *jñapti* (motion), which refers to the dissolution of the various [procedures].

Regarding the elements (*dhātu*), persons (*pudgala*), and so forth: there are sixteen *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and one proclamation) concerning offenses such as the *sthāpanārha*;
eight *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and three proclamations). These various dharmas must be understood as they were established by the Noble One.

All other *jñapti* and other triad-formal acts do not need to be understood. In the present text, it speaks directly of thirteen types of persons; the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for expulsion (*pravāsanīya*) does not need to be understood, while the others...
This constitutes the explanation. Such a statement is merely a general one. Regarding the third category, the *saṃgha*:

all that has been listed above—namely, matters that logically require formal authorization (*jñapti*) or do not require it, as well as the affairs performed by a *saṃgha* of four members, with the single exception of the rite of receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*)—are included.
As for the other three types of *saṃgha*, when they act to fulfill the wishes of the assembly, they are all included within those cases where formal authorization is not required.

In the tenth section, "Expulsion and Non-Expulsion," there are likewise three categories: first, with respect to persons; second, with respect to the dharma; and third, with respect to the Saṃgha. Regarding the category of persons:

it is restricted to thirteen individuals, as these constitute the limit for expulsion. Those who are not among them are not subject to expulsion; others do not qualify for expulsion because expelling them would be improper.
Thus, the wording of the *Śāstra* states that [the act] may result in expulsion or may not result in expulsion. If [it concerns] the thirteen...
Regarding the types of persons: once a *karmavācanā* has been performed, the expulsion is accomplished and the person is expelled, with the exception of thirteen individuals;
for the others, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, it is subsequently resolved, and the *karmavācanā* is considered resolved. If the expulsion is not accomplished, it is not an expulsion.

As for what is called "in accordance with the Dharma," there is only the single *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of permanent banishment (*nigarhaṇīya*), which is the method for eternal expulsion; the remaining one hundred and forty-four methods were originally not [meant to be] such.

It is the act of expelling (*nāśana*). Regarding the phrase "in the presence of the *saṃgha*": the four who uphold the legal procedure (*dharmakarma*) constitute the *saṃgha* for the purpose of this specific act;

however, for other matters of the *saṃgha*, as well as other legal procedures (*dharma*), the principle applies to all four types of *saṃghas*. This is as explained in the section on the "Delineation of the *Saṃgha*" (*saṃghabheda-vibhāga*).

Furthermore, this *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal motion followed by three proclamations) also applies to all four types of *saṃghas*, and the composition of those who uphold the procedure is likewise as stated in the "Delineation," namely five persons and so forth, who uphold this act of expulsion.
This is because it is subsumed under the *caturvargika-saṃgha* (the community of four persons).
End of the eighth fascicle of the *Sifenlü shu*;
beginning of the ninth fascicle of the *Sifenlü shu*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fali. Chapter Eleven: The Section on Rebuking (Kṣepaka-vastu). Regarding the superior grade of single-minded diligence, there is no fault;
as for the middling grade, one may be punished; and for the inferior grade, one need only repent within oneself without further labor. Thus, these seven kinds of evils are subdued.

When people have faults that continue in succession, it is necessary by principle to discipline and regulate them; only by following the path of the Dharma can one accomplish the benefit of protecting and saving sentient beings.
Therefore, this is explained next. Within the monastery, double-tongued speech must be rebuked and corrected. Because people delight in such behavior from the outset, it is given its name;
hence it is called "rebuke" (*khaṭa*). Since these seven matters are not single but are collected together in one place, they are called a *khandhaka* (section).

First, I shall explain its meaning through an eightfold analysis: first, the enumeration and definition of the names; second, the reason for establishing seven [categories]; third, the sequence of light and heavy [offenses];
fourth, the distinctions between separate and combined [categories]; fifth, whether the number is complete or incomplete;
sixth, the presence or absence of corresponding [factors]; seventh, the order of confession and resolution; and eighth, the difference between admonishing and not admonishing.
The first section has two parts: first, the explanation of the name; second, the derivation of the name. Regarding the explanation of the term "reproach" (*hā-zé*):

this person treats the monastic community with contempt, harbors intentions for strife and discord, speaks perversely before the assembly, causes division between parties, and refuses to accept instruction.
Because the transgression is grave, it must be met with corrective punishment; therefore, it is called "reproach. One performs the *karmavācanā* ritual to reproach the person before them;
hence, it is called the "Karma of Reproach. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is likewise. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* calls it "subjugation" (*nigraha*). As for "banishment" (*pravāsanā*):
this person has misrepresented the Buddha-dharma in the presence of laypeople, defiling their households with evil conduct and destroying their faith. Therefore—

This is not for the sake of [mere] punishment; rather, it is to impose a formal penalty and expel them from their original location so that they may be subdued and reform, returning to goodness and restoring their faith as laypeople.
Therefore, it is called the *bhaiṣajya-karman* (act of banishment). In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is termed the *nissāraṇīya-karman* (act of expulsion);

in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is termed "expulsion. As for the term "dependence" (*niśraya*): although this person has long been in the Path, they themselves possess no wisdom of liberation and dwell in close association with laypeople.

To speak erroneously regarding these four matters gives rise to faults according to the circumstances; one’s conduct cannot be established by oneself and must be subject to monastic disciplinary measures.
By submitting to those of eminent virtue and requesting their instruction in the Dharma, one achieves personal benefit; therefore, this is called *niśraya-karman* (the act of dependence).

In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is termed *sthāpana-karman* (the act of setting aside), meaning that one is placed under the care of a person of virtue; hence the name. As for the expression "prohibiting [entrance] to the homes of laypeople," it means:

If one preaches the Buddha-dharma perversely before laypeople who possess faith, slanders and disparages the Triple Gem, insults laypeople, and destroys their secular faith, and then departs, this is called "not arriving.

A formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed to impose punishment, and eight virtuous monks are dispatched to deliver an apology so that the laypeople's faith may be restored and to prevent such non-arrival;
because it requires the offender to go in person, it is called "preventing non-arrival" (*āvaraṇa-aprāpti*).

The *karmavācanā* for lay households (*avadātavasana*) is called the *karmavācanā* for censuring offenses (*āpattipratyuddhāra*). It reveals one's faults to others and requires repentance before laypeople;

therefore, it is termed the "fifteenth [type of] censure. The two Vinayas refer to this as "humbling the mind" (*adho-manas*). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, "arousing joy" means causing laypeople to feel gladness.
To say that one does not see the censure is to disbelieve in the two causes—good and evil—and the resulting two retributions—suffering and pleasure. This is erroneous.
The matter remains in his heart and is manifested upon the path of study; he ought to be subjected to disciplinary subjugation. To be removed from the assembly is termed "ejection" (*ukṣepa*).
By instituting this method of ejection, one treats those who do not acknowledge their fault; hence it is called "ejection for non-acknowledgment" (*adarśanāya ukṣepa*).

In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, this is termed the "karma of that which is not yet visible. Regarding the phrase "ejection for non-confession": although offenses have no fixed nature, as they arise from conditions, there is a principle by which they may be repented and eliminated.

They cease based on conditions. Now, the view of self-existence (satkāyadṛṣṭi) remains within the mind; one does not believe that conditions can induce karma, and the defilements and hindrances are particularly deep.

There is no way to progress on the Path unless one is subdued by the Saṃgha, leading one to believe in repentance and extinguish transgressions. Therefore it is said: "If one does not repent... Śāriputra’s explanation is the same as before.
Nirvāṇa is termed the "extinction of karma" (*karmavastu-nirodha*). It is because one punishes the person before them so that they may develop faith, repent, and extinguish their offenses.

As for those who do not abandon evil views: "view" refers to that which desires to obstruct [the truth] and penetrates through with a deviant mind; it is called "view. When such a view and mind contradict the principle, it is designated as "evil.
To discipline and suspend those who harbor evil views, they are distinguished from the community and rendered unfit for monastic functions; therefore, they are called "those of evil views."
"Not relinquishing the formal act of suspension" (*anutkṣepa*) refers to the "suspension for not relinquishing evil conduct" (*apratiniḥsṛṣṭāpattitā-utkṣepa*).

According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*), these three acts of suspension are combined into a single *asaṃvāsa-karman* (act of non-cohabitation). Thus, the verse states: "And the five acts based on [the five] foundations.

There are five matters that serve as the bases, and there are likewise five corresponding acts of discipline (*karman*). If a bhikṣu is arrogant and disrespectful, and this is not toward the rest of the great assembly—for such a person...
The *bhayānaka-karman* (act of intimidation) is precisely what may be censured here. If a bhikṣu is not yet proficient in distinguishing between offense and non-offense within the Vinaya,
or between cessation and non-cessation within the Abhidharma, and he either leaves his formal dependence (*niśraya*) or accepts the dependence of a śrāmaṇera,
or undergoes training under the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), then the *parimocana-karman* (act of refinement) performed by one who is proficient is likewise based upon this dependence.
What was stated above: "Sin" refers to evil karma; "non-sin" refers to the precepts; "extinction" refers to *nirvāṇa*; and "non-extinction" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

One who does not understand this must practice refinement and training. If a bhikṣu commits defiled and evil conduct while residing in a layperson's dwelling, and the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) is performed, that is precisely what is meant by "banishment.
If a bhikṣu slanders or disparages the Buddha-dharma among laypeople, [the formal act of]... is performed.

The *karmavācanā* for wiping away [faults] through apology refers to those who slander the Triple Gem—such as saying that the Buddha lacks omniscience, that the Dharma cannot bring an end to suffering, or that the Saṃgha lacks pure conduct—and must be subjected to this punishment; this is precisely what constitutes "obstructing [them] from approaching.
If a bhikṣu does not perceive his own offenses, or if he perceives them but refuses to practice the remedial methods, or if he does not abandon false views, [he commits an offense].
Regarding the *asaṃvāsa-karman* (act of not living together): the second section explains how it acquires its name. Within this, there are two positions.

The first four [categories] derive their names from the remedies applied, because the individuals being treated have distinct identities. The latter three establish their designations based on the faults [addressed], because the individuals being treated share the same identity.
If one were to distinguish the names of the formal acts (*karma*), they would receive their appellations based on metaphors.
The Second Gate: A Comparative Analysis of Three Gates. First, those who should be disciplined and those who should not; second, whether the discipline is exhaustive or not;
third, the intent behind establishing the seven [categories]. Regarding the first gate, there are generally seven methods for practicing:

namely, when one has committed an offense and, whether before the Saṃgha or before individual bhikṣus, goes to confess eighteen matters, such as the two places and two things, thereby disturbing the great assembly, and [the procedure] for performing [the disciplinary act] against him.

Reproach. If one speaks of the eighteen [grounds for censure] and so forth, causing laypeople to lose their impartiality of mind, one should apply the disciplinary measure of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

If one dwells in close association with laypeople, becoming intimately attached to them, and despite frequent confession of faults, a transgression arises due to those prior circumstances, one should apply the disciplinary measure of dependence (*niśraya-karman*).
Or, if due to the disclosure of prior matters one causes distress or slander toward laypeople, one should apply the disciplinary measure of exclusion from access (*apratisaṃkhyā-niṣkarṣaṇa-karman*).

Regarding the disciplinary measures (*karmavācanā*): if, due to a prior matter, the offense of "not seeing" (*adarśana*) arises, one applies the formal act of suspension for not seeing (*adarśanotkṣepa*). Furthermore, if, due to that [prior matter], a lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) arises, and one does not perform confession (*pratideśanā*), one applies the formal act of suspension for not confessing (*apratideśanotkṣepa*).
If, upon reaching the point of speaking, one says, "I do not wish to obstruct the Path," one applies the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing [the view] (*apratinisargotkṣepa*).

Therefore, two additional phrases are added: "There are two bhikṣus who should be subjected to the formal act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*): those who speak what is not Dharma as Dharma, and those who speak what is Dharma as not Dharma."

To speak what is not the Dharma, and so forth, up to speaking what should not be spoken—thus is the formal act (*kamma*) of banishing one who relies [on another], and likewise the formal act of prohibiting someone from approaching [a teacher] or being censured.
It is also thus for the two locations, the two matters, and the two views. Furthermore, within the three additional textual passages, there are the three factors pertaining to the Saṃgha.
One should perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against those who have violated the precepts, violated the views, or violated the decorum;
it is the same for all such cases, up to and including the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension). Although an offense may indeed be real, it must necessarily have a basis (*mūla*).

Therefore, the fourfold text regarding the four dharmas—performing the *karman* and so forth—that are non-Dharma and non-Vinaya, which are invalid and do not constitute a formal act, refers to what is called "lack of basis" (*amūla*), namely: violation of the precepts, violation of the views, [violation of the views, and violation of the precepts].

Violating the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*) and violating right livelihood (*ājīva*). There are cases where the root offense is established as a formal act of censure (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). The opposite of the above constitutes [the offense].

Furthermore, one may perform the required legal procedures (*kamma*), as explained in the third section of the ninth [chapter]. Regarding the second point, "exhausted" or "not exhausted," there are many methods of disciplinary treatment; for now, these seven are made manifest.

Because of these six meanings, the governance [of the Saṃgha] is not fully encompassed. First, it focuses solely on governing persons and does not address the adjudication of offenses; this refers to the four methods such as *viveka* (separation) and *praticchādana* (concealment).

Second, it concerns the execution of communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*), which differs from the case of the "evil horse. Third, it is intended for the governance of those who have committed transgressions, and is distinct from *pravāsanīya-karman* (expulsion).
Fourth, it is exclusively for governing persons and is not for the purpose of settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), differing from the locus of adjudicating offenses. Fifth, it merely...
As for the methods of governance, they also distinguish between the two communities of monks and nuns regarding the *pātra-nyubja* (the overturning of the bowl) and other matters;

punishments are to be administered before the assembly. Thus, distinct rules of governance are established for those who do not pay respect and so forth. Based on this principle, how could it be that the methods of governance are not numerous?

This does not exhaustively encompass [all cases]. The third category and others do not include the remainder. As for why there are seven: within these seven, two positions involve the destruction of conduct while faith remains undestroyed;
the latter three involve the destruction of both faith and conduct. Among the four types where conduct is destroyed, although such conduct is immeasurable, it is briefly explained in two kinds:
first, internal protective conduct, which refers to those who have left the household life and practice in accordance with the teachings, thereby fulfilling the various dharmas.

To establish [the teaching], to take up the Dharma within oneself, and to ensure it does not fall into ruin for a thousand years—this is called the practice of internal protection of the Buddha-dharma. Second is the practice of external protection:
this refers to laypeople who, with reverence and faith, uphold the Triple Gem and protect the Buddha-dharma so that it does not decline or perish;

this is called external protection. Internal protection is of two kinds: namely, internal protection of the communal Dharma and internal protection through one’s own practice. If one destroys the internal protection of the communal Dharma...

Regarding the practitioner: if they commit an offense, they are subject to the treatment of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*). If they violate their own internal conduct, they are subject to the treatment of dependence (*niśraya-karman*).

External conduct also has two aspects, namely opposition and compliance. If an offense arises through compliance with one's own inclinations—whether it concerns many families or a single family, and regardless of whether it is a general or specific rule—they must all be subject to the treatment of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

This is for the purpose of protection, so as to cause them to give rise to right faith. If, however, they act against their own inclinations and distress others—regardless of whether it involves many or one—all [must be treated accordingly].

Not reaching the point of punishment is itself protection against causing affliction. Since affliction arises from verbal abuse, four methods of governance are established according to the specific circumstances.
Among the latter three, which involve mutual ruin, although the practices are immeasurable, they do not exceed two types:

first, believing that the two causes of good and evil evoke the two retributions of suffering and happiness; this is the initial gateway for entering the Path. Second, based on this belief, one initiates practice. Now...

To speak briefly, there are likewise only two [categories]: first, the practice of restraint through observance (*śīla-vṛtti*), which refers to those who believe in transgressions and repent to extinguish them;
second, the practice of observance through action (*kriyā-vṛtti*), which refers to seeing desire as an obstruction and cultivating pure conduct free from defilement.

These are the three cultivations (*tri-bhāvanā*). Contrary to these three cultivations, one forms the three errors (*tri-mithyā*). To counteract these three errors, the three formal admonitions (*tri-udghāta*) are established. Furthermore, according to another interpretation:
These three dharmas are all [applicable] to those who lack faith and hold wrong views. Such views do not arise in isolation; they arise in dependence upon objects.
Briefly stated, the objects consist of medicine and illness. One type—lack of remorse—arises in response to the medicine. The remaining two views both arise from illness, namely, unwholesome karma.

down to the case of having only one person—this single instance is restricted to the procedure for the removal of an offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) in the presence of the Saṃgha, according to the rules of a single session.
Regarding the fourth direction, the treatise states: one should observe the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) associated with the karma.

For those performing formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) such as the *jñapti-caturtha*, although there are three [levels] of legal status (*dharmapada*), because these matters concerning the treatment of residual offenses (*śeṣasaṃvara-dharma*) are all of the highest grade (*uttama-pakṣa*), they are equalized by the *jñapti-caturtha*.
Within this application, there are at most four legal statuses: namely, *parivāsa*, *mānatva*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, and *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (or *yadbhūyasyārha*). What is meant by "reproach"?
To understand these four, one must analyze them through six categories. Regarding the vertical exposition (*ūrdhva-artha*), the commentator provides an overview here;

for the word-by-word commentary, one should refer to the text itself. Question: Why is the third category called the "Aggregate of Karma" (*karmaskandha*) and the fourth called "Associated with Karma," yet both are referred to as "points of training" (*śikṣāpada*)?
Answer: The Western (Sanskrit) term is *karma*. In this land (China), it is sometimes called "distinguishing matters" (*bian shi*) or "that which is performed."

It is called "action" (*karma*), or alternatively "deed. "Deed" refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act). This points to the section within the *Campa-vinaya* that distinguishes the *karmavācanā*, clarifying the four types of Saṃgha;
therefore, it is termed the "aggregate of deeds" (*karmaskandha*). That which correctly distinguishes between what is proper and improper is the essential substance of the *karmavācanā* method;

therefore, it is termed "correspondence with deeds" (*karmasamprayukta*). Subsequently, the Buddha established the rule that one must recite it; whether one has practiced it or not, failure to do so incurs an offense. For this reason...

These two are both called *śikṣāpada* (precepts). This is because, as stated in the *Campā-vastu*, they distinguish between the monastic community that enacts the rule (*dharmasamādāyaka*) and the legal procedure itself (*dharma*).
Regarding the fifth point, the treatise states: "One should observe, among the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, whether concealment for one day and night, etc., has occurred or not."
To clarify the distinction between those with and without the *saṃvara* (restraint), the stages such as the *pūrvavāsa-mānatta* are established.

"Stage" (*bhūmi*) is a term for a location; it refers here to the four positions beginning with *parivāsa*. Within these four positions, if one possesses the *saṃvara*, one practices the stage of *pūrvavāsa*.

This refers to the practice of the *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (probation); since one must necessarily spend a night while practicing this *paryuṣitaparivāsa*, it is called *pūrvavāsa* (staying overnight). If [one does not possess the *saṃvara*],...

The *kṣaya* (destruction) refers to the direct application of the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness). Thus, it is said that there are those with *kṣaya* and those without *kṛta* (accomplishment), and so forth.

The establishment of the *pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness of recollecting past lives) and so on constitutes the three factors for the obscured (*nivṛta*) applications and the two factors for the unobscured (*anivṛta*) applications; this is the method of correlating the medicinal substances with their respective limits, analogous to the correspondence between disease and medicine.

However, regarding the offenses to be remedied, there is a distinction between those that are concealed and those that are not. Furthermore, even when establishing the positions for the medicines, there are likewise two types.

That is to say: first, the remedy for concealment (*mrakṣa*); second, the remedy for non-concealment. Within these two, there are again two for each, because there are medicines for those of non-degenerate nature (*abhedyadharma*) and those of degenerate nature (*bhedyadharma*), thus forming four distinct categories.
That is to say: among those who conceal, there are both the non-degenerate and the degenerate; among those who do not conceal, there are likewise both the non-degenerate and the degenerate.
First, regarding concealment, as for the non-degenerate and degenerate natures: there are three stages for the non-degenerate nature and five stages for the degenerate nature.
Because they undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) for six nights, each carrying its own original date, this refers to the new offense being combined with the original date.

According to the rules for combining different types of offenses, a heavy treatment is administered. This is explained within the section on the "original dates. If one takes the time factor into account, within the category of repeated offenses, the new and old appear distinct, thus constituting seven methods:
namely, the method for concealing the original offense, first, the method for concealing a newly committed offense, and second, the original date for the previously committed offense.

[The procedure for] parivāsa consists of three [stages], each lasting six nights. Next, because the offenses are combined and the *pārivāsika* is released from his status, it is said that "it may be seven. Thus the text states:

If a monk who is practicing *parivāsa* commits an offense during that interval and conceals it for a known number of days, the Saṃgha should grant him a *parivāsa* (concealment) *karmavācanā* according to the duration of that intermediate offense.
Once the *parivāsa* *karmavācanā* has been granted, they grant him *mūlaparivāsa*. When the *mūlaparivāsa* has been completed, he is released.
[The Buddha said: "Grant him the *mānatta* penance. Once the *mānatta* has been completed, he should be absolved of the offense (*abbhāna*).

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu who intentionally emitted semen and committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which he did not conceal. He requested from the Saṃgha a six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra-mānatta*).

During those six nights, he again committed an offense which he did not conceal and informed the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣu: 'I now permit that bhikṣu to request again from the Saṃgha and undergo the *mānatta* penance. The Saṃgha should..."
[The procedure] for the six-night *jñapti-caturtha* [karma]: When that bhikṣu has completed the *mānatva*, he should again request it from the Saṃgha.

He must perform the original *mānatva*. The Saṃgha should grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-caturtha* [karma]. What is the ritual procedure? It is as follows: That bhikṣu again requests it from the Saṃgha, saying:
"I, bhikṣu so-and-so, previously intentionally emitted semen; I committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and did not conceal it. From the Saṃgha..."
"I request the practice of *mānatva*. The Saṃgha has granted me *mānatva*. During those six nights, I have again committed an offense that was not concealed.
I now request from the Saṃgha the practice of *mānatva*; may you grant me *mānatva* once more. Thus he requests three times.
A single bhikṣu should then announce the formal motion (*jñapti*) and grant it through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. When he has completed those six nights of practice, he again requests from...

The monk requests: "I, bhikṣu [Name], having previously intentionally emitted semen, have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense without concealment. I request from the Saṃgha the practice of *mānatva*. May the Saṃgha grant me the practice of *mānatva*. He shall undergo the *mānatva* for six nights. The formula is:

"I, bhikṣu [Name], having previously intentionally emitted semen, have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense without concealment. I have requested from the Saṃgha the practice of *mānatva*, and the Saṃgha has granted me the practice of *mānatva*."
"During those six nights, I again committed an offense that was not concealed. I have already completed the *mānatva* penance for six nights requested from the Saṃgha;
now I request from the Saṃgha to perform the *mānatva* for six nights. May the Saṃgha grant me the performance of the original six-night *mānatva*.
Thus he requests three times. The granting of the dharma is as before. He then performs the six...
When the night has ended, one should grant the *āśvāsa* (consolation). If one commits the offense of concealment (*paticchādana*), the procedure is also as described above.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, these two texts distinguish between new and old offenses; this must be understood when performing the ritual. However, within the category where concealment does not destroy the [status], there are differences in the methods for obtaining the dharma.
Briefly stated, there are four positions. First: one offense, one method of obtaining the dharma; this refers to the opening text. Second: ...

When many offenses have been concealed by a single person, they undergo the three dharmas of communal practice (*sādhivihārika*). This refers to cases such as concealing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for one night, two nights, or even up to ten nights, wherein one must collectively request the practice of penance.

Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If one remembers the nights but does not remember the specific offenses, one is granted an indefinite period of separate residence (*parivāsa*) for those distinct offenses.
The third case involves many offenses and many instances of concealment, where one undergoes the three dharmas of communal practice, as described in the first seven-point rule.
Among these, the first four lines concern the fourth [category], which explains the acquisition of the dharma through a single offense.

This is as found in the text regarding the concealment of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for two months. Furthermore, it may also be that two, three, four, five, six, or many [offenses] result in the acquisition of the dharma;

for now, the case of "re-acquisition" is cited as its general model, as will be explained extensively below. Within these four positions, each position universally encompasses three aspects, namely: the offense to be remedied...
Whether one knows the number of days or does not know the number of days, or whether one knows the count or does not know the count—by pairing three with four, there are twelve distinct headings.
Now, however, we shall proceed by summarizing according to the attainment of the methods; let us explain this starting from the four stages.

Within the second stage, the "Destruction of Concealment" (*bhaṅga-saṃvara*), five or seven factors are practiced; that is, the aforementioned four stages along with the twelve headings, all of which possess this destruction.
Regarding the five categories of offenses and so forth, within the context of repeated transgressions, there are four temporal stages according to their meaning.

First, by correlating the timing of the concealment of a committed offense with the process of repeated transgression, one distinguishes the methods for destroying, treating, and rescuing [the offender]. Within these four positions and three heads, this results in four groups, each consisting of twenty-seven individuals.
This serves to clarify the distinctions between the categories. Specifically, regarding the repeated offenses according to time, this refers to the general summary.
Furthermore, as for these three heads, each of which comprises nine persons: because their dharmas are identical, they are termed "three heads," yet each head consists of distinct groups of nine.

Alternatively, there may be a second layer of destruction within each position, doubling them again to twenty-seven; this is achieved by adding both the old and the new, or through the combination and separation of factors.
Whether it be the third, fourth, or fifth offense, the principle may likewise be understood. For now, we shall speak of the first;
however, what is said regarding the three periods below applies equally to those who commit a grave offense (*duṣkṛta*) during those times.

Therefore, the text below states that the same applies when the *parivāsa* (probation) is completed, and so on up to when the *ṣaḍrātra* (six-night penance) is completed. Thus, there are sixteen items for twenty-seven persons, totaling four hundred and three.
There are twelve types of persons; since their arising of offenses differs, there are four hundred and thirty-two categories.

As for the distinct methods for each head [of offense], whether they be two, three, or more layers, the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) are all different. Question: In the case of a single offense, if one knows the number of its grades but does not know the number of instances?
These two cases may be so. Since it is stated that there is "one offense," how can one also know that they were not in harmony? The explanation says:

It is possible to commit a single offense and conceal it for one year; however, for the period within the last hundred days, one clearly remembers [the details], whereas for the period prior to those hundred days, the number cannot be fixed.
If one wishes to administer punishment, although it may be remembered, because of the short duration, it does not count.
The number of concentrations is known; since their meanings and their antidotes are also extensive, this section exists, and there is no logical contradiction in this.

These four attainments of the stage of the Dharma each accord with many meanings, as explained extensively in the text. As for the distinctions between five gates, four gates, and so forth, these are vertical classifications made in relation to what is discussed herein.
Regarding the "twelve" mentioned above, they are categorized in contrast to consciousness and non-consciousness, or by way of the gates of recollection and non-recollection, or doubt and non-doubt.

Regarding the section on doubt (*vicikitsā*): its meaning is always no different [from that of mindfulness]. Therefore, within the long and short durations of the remedial methods (*pratipakṣa-dharma*), it is explained by way of three gates—mindfulness, doubt, and cognition—in a general manner.
How could one know or not know that there is a "day of origin" (*mūla-divasa*)? As for the other cases of mindfulness, doubt, and so forth, there is no such thing as a repeated offense.

Therefore, the dharmas that enable [this] attainment are likewise four for each stage. According to the classification by the length of the dharmas, there are three for each of these four, thus totaling twelve.

If one classifies them according to the destruction of dharmas, these dharmas are fully present within the three categories previously mentioned—the sixteen, the twenty-seven, and the recollections—and so forth.
Based on this, the dharmas are indeed infinite; yet, as in the *Karmavācanā-mūla*, only three cycles are cited, following this principle.
As for those who wish to clarify and exhaustively master this, it is like a single drop in the great ocean or a single mote of dust on Mount Sumeru.

Regarding the second section, "The Treatment of Non-Obstruction," within the phrase "the non-destructive destroys": there are three positions of non-destruction; for each [position], there is one offense and one attainment of the Dharma.
That is to say, among the three cases in the intermediate [text], there are two where one incurs many offenses and obtains the dharma once, and one where one incurs many offenses and the dharma.

These two are explained by analogy with the concealment [of offenses], except that there is no case of obtaining the dharma a second time for a single offense; this is because the six-night penance does not vary according to the length [of the period of concealment].

Within the three stages, there are three categories—knowing, not knowing, and so forth; these three sets of three combine to form nine. Furthermore, regarding the three stages of attaining the dharma-position, they are treated according to the same method as the preceding analysis.
If one were to apply the method of "knowing" and "not knowing" here, because the phrasing differs, each of the three would again have three sub-divisions;
however, one does not wish to differentiate them by length. Regarding the second [section], the destruction of dharmas, it is said that there are two periods, each of which has...

There are three groups of twenty-seven persons: those who initiate the offense, those who treat it, and those who rescue from it. The remainder is explained according to the rules for concealment (*paticchādana*).

The reason why one must explain this by way of the five directions (*pañcadisā*) above is that, in the subsequent text, each and every method of treatment requires these five—namely, knowing whether all factors are complete or deficient, whether the concealment is established or not, the presiding monk, the legal act (*dhamma*) to be performed, and the limits of the medicinal application. Therefore, this...

This is the general explanation of the middle section. If one were to correlate this with the subsequent text, one must cite these five directions and apply mental empowerment (*cittādhiṣṭhāna*) to each according to the Dharma;
thus, one will know the signs of success or failure. Next, the text is divided. According to the ancient interpretation, it is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the medicine.
Next, regarding the diseases to be remedied—those such as the three types of concealment and below—the correspondence between medicine and disease is explained by itself:

in the preceding section on medicines and diseases, the disease is cited to establish the medicine; in the section on diseases, the medicine is cited to clarify the disease. This meaning is not so [as you suggest].
In each of these instances above and below, a disease is cited and then treated with its corresponding medicine; each such passage constitutes a single matter.

One should establish treatments according to the specific case; there is no treatment that is not comprehensive. How could it be that the first passage mentions only the medicine while the subsequent one exclusively reveals the illness?
Furthermore, in the third passage, there are instances where the illness mentioned in the second passage is cited, yet the first passage is taken as the basis for each individual point of treatment.

Therefore, it is known that this text and the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (Settling of Disputes) are not of the same class and cannot be compared; one must not recklessly rely on that text to determine [the meaning].

This principle merely enumerates the formal procedures (*dharma*). Although both the abbreviated and the extensive versions may be employed for the *jñapti-caturtha* (the motion with three proclamations), they ultimately cannot be used interchangeably when citing the specific matter (*vastu*).

This is because the procedure herein—whether the object is initially recognized or unrecognized—is likewise [restricted]. To distinguish this from concealment (*chādana*), it must be treated as an extended version of the initial concealment;
otherwise, if there were mutual treatment at the second stage, other faults would all fail to be established as previously analyzed.
Now, this *Khandhaka* is explained. There are two major sections. The first, up to "thus it is held," briefly treats the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.

The second section concerns a monk who has committed numerous *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; some he concealed for one night up to ten nights, and below that, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses are treated extensively.
Within these two [sections], each text contains two parts. Regarding the two parts of the text: the former treats the purification.

[The section on] Concealment (*paticchādana*). Next is the treatment for not concealing. This is because, while the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense itself does not differ, there is a distinction based on whether it was concealed or not;

that is why it is so. The extensive text also has two parts. The first, from the beginning up to "whether recognized or unrecognized is also like this," serves to distinguish this concealment and requires treatment more extensively than the initial concealment mentioned above.
The second part begins with "At one time, a bhikṣu committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and did not conceal it," and continues until the end.

The *Khandaka* has not yet been clarified; originally, there was no method for the subsequent expansion of what was not previously covered. By not covering this [now], the meaning is twofold and the text fourfold.
Thus it is known that after the various summaries, the fifth method among the five methods cited above is expanded upon.

Verifying these preceding and succeeding sections, it is sufficient to know that the first is a summary followed by an expansion. Within the preceding summary, one first explains the initial "covering" (*chui*), which consists of four parts.

The Dharma-text is again divided into four parts: namely, (1) concealment for one day; (2) the six-night penance; (3) the expiation of the offense; and (4) [the fourth]. First, I shall explain the categories of meaning.
These four *karmans* are analyzed according to six gates: first, listing the names and explaining their meanings; second, the analysis of what is remedied;
third, the presence or absence of duration; fourth, the sequence of priority; fifth, the similarities and differences among the various schools; and sixth...
The rules for monks and nuns differ.
Regarding the first section: this refers to the *parivāsa* and so forth, up to the *ajñāpya*. As for the term *parivāsa*, in this land it is called "concealment" (*fùcáng*).
It is so named because it receives its designation based on the emotional transgression that is being remedied. This Vinaya frequently speaks of...

Because of concealment, the Buddha stated that the Saṃgha is permitted to grant the *parivāsa* (concealment) rite according to the duration of such concealment; this is also called *pravāsanīya* (separate dwelling).

As found in the three Vinayas, such as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, as well as in the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, it is uniformly termed *pravāsanīya*. In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is termed *pūrvavāsa* (prior dwelling).

It is so named because it refers to the practice of performing repentance. Since staying together with the community would hinder one's ability to carry out duties and neglect one's work, it was prescribed that the individual must dwell separately.

Dwelling [in this state], one reflects on one's transgressions and reforms one's faults, deeply repenting and reproaching oneself; it is only through such practice that the goal is accomplished, carrying the meaning of "extinguishing karma.
As for *mānatva*, the *Abhidharmakośa* (Vyākhyāyukti) calls it *manada*; it signifies "pleasing the assembly" or "arousing joy."

By performing this rite, one’s own accumulated offenses will be eliminated; because the inner mind is filled with joy, it is called "arousing joy" (*prāmodya*), and it is also termed "lowering the mind" (*avanāmanīya*).
Because this dharma subdues arrogance and renders the mind humble and supple, it is called the *avanāmanīyakarman* (the rite of lowering the mind).

Question: Since both the *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (concealment penance) and the *mānāpya* (probation) do not involve staying overnight [with the community], why is the former called *parivāsa* (separate residence) while this is called "lowering the mind"?

The explanation states: Concealment does not involve staying overnight within the Saṃgha, nor is there a daily announcement; because the manifestation of one’s humble intent is not evident, it is given the name *parivāsa* (separate dwelling).

This *mānatva*, however, involves staying overnight within the Saṃgha and there is a daily announcement; because the meaning of manifesting one’s humble intent is evident, its full designation is retained.
As for *mūlāpakarṣa* (punishment by returning to the beginning), one undergoes the penalty again from the original date; therefore, it is called *mūlāpakarṣa*.
"Knowledge" (jñā) is a word from the Western [Sanskrit] language. What is *āpavarga*? In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it is called *āyāha*.

In this region, it is sometimes called the "rite for summoning one to enter the assembly. Because one was not yet pure prior to the six nights, and is now purified, it is therefore called "summoning to enter."

This also includes the methods for extracting and eliminating offenses. The text of this Vinaya states that one "emerges from an offense" (*pārivāsika*) by performing these ritual acts, because one thereby emerges from the offense, or because the offense is eliminated through the performance of the ritual procedure.
These four are collectively termed *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts). It is not that the *karmavācanā* itself is the emergence from the offense;
rather, it is called such because by performing this *karmavācanā*, one undergoes the period of probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth, until finally emerging from the offense. Thus it is said.
Regarding the second section: there is one dharma to be concealed, yet there are two things that must be remedied. First, the remedy for concealment:

if one does not remedy the fault of the mind, it is because of such factors as failing to remember, doubting, or not recognizing the offense; thus, because the concealment itself is not remedied, the text below states:

"First, one confesses the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) of concealment, and only thereafter is the formal act of concealment (*parivāsa-karman*) granted. Second, the remedy for the fault of improperly intruding upon the pure assembly.

If one is within the period of probation (*mānāpya*), one treats the concealment [of the offense]; however, in cases such as those who have left the order (*pravrajyā-tyāga*), treatment is not required.

*Mānāpya* is the formal treatment for the intentional transgression of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and it also serves as the preparatory means for that treatment. *Mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction to the original status) is the treatment for one's own violation of the rules of conduct and the punishment for disobeying the command of the Saṃgha, which restores one to their original state.
As for new offenses committed during this period, they are treated according to whether they were concealed or not; once the original status is restored, [the offender] attains it.

The procedure for subsequent days is the same as the previous two. The *Vinaya-śāstra* states: "As for 'punishment on the original day' (*mūlāpakarṣa*), it is for the sake of discipline so that the bhikṣus may know:
'This elder was thus; his afflictions were so intense that he committed an offense, but out of shame and remorse, he shall not do it again.'"

*Ātāpana* refers to the merit and benefit of *mānatva*. Because one seeks purification by humbling the mind and subduing oneself, and because one seeks to emerge from the offense, the bhikṣus, out of compassion, grant the emergence from the offense; thus one attains purity and correctly rectifies the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Furthermore, it is said that there are two types of *mūlāpakarṣa* (penance involving returning to the beginning), which serve to make the precepts complete.
The Third Gate: On Existence and Non-existence, and Length and Shortness. Regarding "existence and non-existence," this refers to being obscured (*nivṛta*) or unobscured (*anivṛta*).

First, we distinguish existence and non-existence by contrast with the other categories [of offenses]. Question: Why is it that while the first [offense] of the upper category and the three [offenses] of the lower category do not require treatment for concealment, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* alone is treated as such?
Answer: The offense of the first category is so grave that, according to principle, it cannot be expiated; what need is there to treat its secondary branches?

[The previous offenses] have passed. Regarding the three subsequent articles, since the root offense is light, it does not require confession before the Sangha; one simply confesses the concealment directly, and the minor branches are not separately punished.

This present article is among those where confession is required, yet it is grave. One must rely on the Sangha to extinguish the transgression of concealing and covering [the offense]. It is appropriate to impose severe punishment so that the body and mind are humbled and subdued, thereby enabling the practice to reach fulfillment.
Next, we shall proceed to the four dharmas to explain the presence or absence of concealment, as well as the "original day" (pūrvadina).
Regarding the punishment for improper confession (*adharma-vinaya*): its presence or absence is not fixed. When present, it consists of four or five factors; when absent, it consists of three or two.

This refers to the statement that there are two "threes" and one "two. As for the long and short [versions]: concealment (*paryavasthāna*) and subsequent transgression (*anuvartana*) are called the basis of the punishment, because the offense of concealment is completed by passing a night.
The *mānāpya* (probation) is fixed at six nights, because the offense of residual transgression (*śeṣa-saṃghāvaśeṣa*) does not depend on the passage of days to be completed.
Today follows the previous rain. Regarding the sequence of the fourth gate:
according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, why is the *parivāsa* (probation) performed for six nights? Why does the root text say "to treat"?
It is for the sake of subduing the mind. If one performs this matter starting again from the original date, it causes the mind to be subdued. Why?

This is for the purpose of emerging from the offense (*āpatti*) so that the precepts may be purified. It is the duty of the bhikṣus to act in such a way as to enable this person to emerge from the offense.
Question: Is it a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) to conceal and treat a mental transgression? Should one first confess and then undergo punishment? Does the mental transgression emerge from the offense?

Is it the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) that is being treated? Why is the mental transgression treated first, and only afterwards is the offense itself treated? Answer: Because each case proceeds from the lighter to the heavier.

Therefore, if one were to perform the *pārivāsika* penance while a remnant of the offense still remained, and then, upon first treating that remnant, were called "pure," what need would there be for the six-night penance?
Thus, the two cases are not analogous.
Fifth Section, Part Four, Number Fifty, Item Three: Regarding the Vinaya, if one commits a transgression repeatedly, all instances shall be treated according to the original date;

since begging is an act of disclosure (*viva-raṇa*) and there is no hiding of one's faults, its essence is that very awareness. How, then, could it be the same as a lack of awareness?

If both practices are already obstructed, against what would the phrase "the conclusion of the two" be distinguished? Therefore, this is also an obstruction; it is certainly a mistaken statement. Regarding the second section:

the question asks whether, among the four periods below, the case of "one covering and one confessing" refers to the old or the new. The answer is: this refers to the case where, during the four periods, one commits a new offense again.

For this reason, when those of the old school say that "this is one concealment and one manifestation," they mean it is neither a fundamental offense nor a *pūrvakṛta* (original-day) treatment. If the original rule (*dharma*) is violated, the two subsequent [offenses] arise, and one performs the *pūrvakṛta* treatment.

one must initiate the primary practice. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are eight types: first, a new *parivāsa*; second, a second *parivāsa*; third, a new six-night period; fourth...

The eight modes of conduct refer to the continuous practice, while the four completions refer to the continuous performance. Each of the eight persons acts in this manner; combined, they total sixty-four.

The fifth section concerns the transgression of a second offense regarding whether the *dharma* has been violated or not. As for the methods of treatment and rescue, since it is stated that the *dharma* has been violated, this again refers to the four periods:

the two stages of practice and the two stages of completion. First, regarding the period of concealment during the stage of practice, following the treatment of the root offense below, there are three positions within the category of non-concealment:
first, one who knows the number of days of concealment; second, one who does not know the number of days of concealment; third, one who knows the number of days of concealment.

Concealment (*paticchādana*): These three are all fundamental. Regarding the attainment of the practice of concealment, although the text simply states "at that time there was a bhikkhu who practiced concealment," it is clear that the meaning applies to all three types of persons.
Furthermore, within the category of the first type of person, there are again three types regarding repeated offenses.

One must distinguish between the new and the old [offenses] and certainly grant separate [penances] for each. However, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* appears to treat them separately as well; as its text states:

"When that bhikṣu has completed the six-night penance, he should again request it from the Saṃgha. Based on this scriptural passage, it seems that what was originally intended was the *mānatva* penance.

The separate *karmavācanā* should be performed together. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there is no violation of the rule; the principle is simply that one requests the new [penance], and once the concealment of the offense has been granted, it is to be performed together with the original offense.
This concludes the brief explanation of the three or two offenses involving *mānatva* and the four or two offenses involving *āvarhaṇa*.
