The disciple’s offenses consist of three heads, totaling thirty-three pairs. The remaining two heads likewise each have thirty-three, making ninety-nine sets of *karmavācanā* in total.
If one were to combine and resolve both old and new offenses, there would be only eighty-one. For now, I shall retain the previous explanation, which comprehensively covers the beginning and end;
there are twenty-seven individuals involved here, based on the commission of offenses during the process of *pravāraṇā*. Since the offense has already arisen...

It is so. Within the latter three periods, the commission of new offenses is likewise [treated]. Furthermore, these four periods are not only restricted by stage; the offenses themselves do not overlap.

This refers to the locus from which one emerges to rectify an offense. For example, if one commits a grave offense while already undergoing the *paryuṣaṇā* (covering) period, twenty-seven people are collectively treated for both old and new offenses, with each being cleared of guilt through the process of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
This does not apply when one commits a grave offense during other periods, or when one commits a grave offense during the course of having already completed the *paryuṣaṇā*.

The transgression is likewise not applicable [to others]. The remaining cases should be dealt with according to their respective categories; one must also exhaustively bring about the emergence from the offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). The same applies to the other two times.

Therefore, within each respective category, all three factors—such as concealment (*pracchādana*) and so forth—are fully present. This is explained in reference to a single grave offense (*guru-āpatti*); however, if there are separate second-time grave offenses, [the procedure differs].

That is, one proceeds through the four stages of concealment (*paticchādana*), etc., with each stage doubling the number of twenty-seven persons. Therefore, as stated in the second section below, the second round of offenses is likewise;
this may be understood to apply up to the third, fourth, fifth, and so on. Furthermore, regarding the twenty-seven persons across the four periods:
if one multiplies them by four heads who have attained the Dharma, this constitutes sixteen sets of twenty-seven persons. This is the case for the second round of offenses.

This is known by analogy; it should be understood through the full exposition as being thus. However, because this current text provides only a brief general summary, it simply mentions "a bhikṣu who conceals [his offense]," and regarding new offenses, it names only three cases involving concealment, while the rest are not mentioned.

Furthermore, passages concerning "not concealing an offense" and so forth must have been erroneously included here; there is no need for further elaboration. Next, the analysis of concealment is concluded, as previously stated.
It is so. Regarding the second period, from the bhikṣu next in line to perform the *mānāttā* down to those who likewise do so, it is the same.

Regarding the third period, from the completion of the *mānāttā* for the next in line down to the fourth period and so forth, the detailed explanation is as before. This concerns the case of repeated offenses within the time periods.

Regarding the total number of individuals possessing the *dharmas* [of penance]: taking one offense and one attainment of the *dharma* as an example, if one commits it during three *śīrṣa* or two *caraṇa* [stages], there are twenty-seven persons, and there are ninety-nine rounds of *karma*.

If one commits it during two *niṣṭhā* [stages], there are seventy-two rounds, because twenty-seven cases of *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction to the root) and non-destruction of the two *niṣṭhā* *dharmas* are excluded. The remainder...
The three methods for obtaining the dharma are likewise the same.

In the sixth section on the combined performance of different types, there are four parts: first, the method of concealment (*paryavasthāna*); second, the method of returning to the original state (*mūlāpakarṣa*);

third, the *mānatva*; and fourth, the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*). The first three extensively list the methods, while the final one provides a brief summary. Within the section on concealment, there are four parts, as previously stated in the first.

Regarding "offenses": among those confessed to the Buddha, "not concealing" means that although one may have initially failed to conceal them, they subsequently become concealed again due to attachment.

Regarding "equal or unequal concealment": this refers to the duration of time, such as long or short. Regarding "a single name": this is because they are identical in being *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. Regarding "many types": this refers to the distinctions among the thirteen [categories].
Regarding "intrinsic nature and non-intrinsic nature," this refers to the ten natures and the three negations. Regarding "abiding in distinctness," this means there are four types;

because their constituent elements differ, it is said they "abide in distinctness. Next, within the section on the treatment of the original day (*mūlāpatti*), since both instances are the same treatment for the original day, they are combined into one.
The subsequent six nights and the subsequent expiation of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*) may be understood accordingly. However, regarding the various [sections] above and below...

The text states: "When each individual case has been resolved through the application of its specific medicine for treatment and salvation, one may then proceed to arrange the teachings, concluding with their broad and abbreviated forms.
It is not until this point that one erroneously claims to begin the second section by taking the first ten texts to treat the illness;
to call this 'the correspondence between medicine and illness' is entirely incorrect. The reason for this is as follows: regarding the illness in the first text, the second..."
Regarding the medicinal substances mentioned in the text: what is their intended use? To state directly that they "mutually manifest" one another is meaningless speech.
In response to this, a fivefold analysis must be conducted: first, by way of species; second, by way of the number of transgressions for repeated offenses;

third, by way of the time of repeated offenses and their number; fourth, by way of the number of persons involved; and fifth, by way of demonstrating the ritual procedures for the Saṃgha. As for the first section:
The methods presented in this text enumerate thirteen distinct types of combined treatments; these constitute the prescribed methods. This is intended to demonstrate the excellence of the medicine.

Provided that one can establish a mind of revulsion and follow the teachings, and provided the necessary conditions are met regardless of their number, both general and specific afflictions will be entirely eradicated.
For example, just as frost and dew wither immediately upon encountering the sun, so it is here. When examined through reason, this is not necessarily the case; perhaps [only] five...
The numbers six, seven, eight, and so forth, are all without obstruction; one simply refers to them according to the quantity of the preceding matters. Question:

Since they follow the quantity [of the matters], why are they listed together? Answer: Because in the preceding texts, whether there be one, two, or many, the methods for subsuming and treating them—whether through separation, combination, conjunction, or distinction—are exhaustive;
therefore, they must be listed collectively to demonstrate that the inclusion and regulation are complete. Regarding the second section, the text clearly indicates "the second."

Regarding the repetition of the offense: if one commits a new grave violation while undergoing the *mūla-āpakarṣa* (original-day penance), this does not constitute a "repeated grave violation" (*punar-guru-dūṣaṇa*) because the original text did not discuss such a case.

Alternatively, if during the course of the *mūla-āpakarṣa* one commits a new grave violation and seeks relief through further treatment, how is it that the Buddha stated, "I permit you to undergo the *mūla-āpakarṣa* once more"?
This is because this case differs from the *parivāsa* (probation); since the root [offense] has been violated, that [probation] cannot be granted. Why, then, is a third [instance] not mentioned?

Regarding "repeatedly breaking [the precepts]": the answer is that because the first offense constitutes the fundamental breaking [of the precepts], it is necessary to clarify the *pārivāsika* (probation) for the original day.

If one did not speak of a second repeated offense, it would imply a further, more serious breaking [of the precepts], for which one could no longer be granted probation for the original day; therefore, it says "second repeated offense.
As for the third, fourth, and so forth, since it is permitted to apply probation repeatedly, there is logically no difference [in principle]. Thus, [it is not mentioned separately].
It must be further explained. Regarding the third section: the text only addresses the case of a grave offense committed during the period of concealment, as in the three preceding instances.
If one commits a new offense during the second period of probation (*mūlāpakarṣa*), may one again be subjected to the *mūlāpakarṣa* discipline? Answer:

According to the underlying principle, since both courses of action have been completed, there is the sense of an offense occurring throughout all four periods. Among these four periods, should one commit a grave offense during the period of the original probation (*mūla*), [one must undergo the *mūlāpakarṣa*].

Regarding the treatment (*pratīkāra*): it is also obtained as above by way of the four periods (*catur-kāla*). Among the cases of "ruining" (*bhaṅga*) and "difference of conditions" (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*), both are established by way of the four periods to demonstrate a repeated offense.
Thus, one should know that the second type of "repeated ruining" (*dvitīya-guru-bhaṅga*) also applies to all four periods to clarify a repeated offense.

However, regarding the two types of conduct, for "ruining the original day" (*mūla-divasa-bhaṅga*), if those two have already concluded, one need only address a new offense; there is no [need for] a single "original-day treatment" (*mūla-divasa-pratīkāra*) for a repeated offense.

Because it destroys the dharma that has already emerged; the text relies on the dharma of emergence. For the time being, this is explained by way of the period of concealment, though one must not cling to this as a restrictive definition.
Regarding the number of persons in the fourth section, there are briefly five levels of numerical variation.

First, within the dharma of emergence, it is stated that only new offenses are cited; knowing the number and concealing them, a single person acts for the sake of the dharma. Second, according to the standard...
As for those who are not proficient [in the rules], there are thirteen cases in total when considering new offenses.

There are three categories—knowing the number [of days], not knowing the number, and so forth—and for each of these, there are three further sub-categories based on whether the concealment was total or partial. These, together with the three types of non-disclosure (*avadya*), constitute nine persons.

Thirdly, if one takes the three heads—knowing the number and so forth—and divides these nine persons accordingly, there should be twenty-seven persons. Fourthly, this is then multiplied by the four heads concerning the attainment of the Dharma.
This results in four groups of twenty-seven persons. The fifth [category] encompasses these four alongside [the others], categorized according to the four times, each having a secondary destruction;
this constitutes sixteen groups of twenty-seven persons. These sixteen groups of twenty-seven persons all possess a second secondary destruction.
Because the text of the fifth section collectively cites various types practiced in combination, it says:

Whether it be equal concealment or unequal concealment, concealment or non-concealment, and so forth up to dwelling in separation (*nānāsaṃvāsa*), one who practices the Dharma must fully manifest all these categories.

This is termed "concealment and so forth, long and short. The short follows from the long and so forth; one must request from the Saṃgha a specific number of days for the concealment of the dharma and so on, and only then will it be accomplished.
If it is contrary to this, it is not accomplished—this refers to everything up to dwelling in separation and so forth. Thus it has been stated.
Regarding the preceding text: the procedures for the removal of a monk (*pārivāsika*) and the formal announcement (*jñapti*), etc., are all to be conducted according to this standard.

As for the seventh [case], the person who has completed the period of concealment and is fit for rehabilitation: if the community of monks provides medicinal treatment in an improper manner, it is for this reason that the present text is required.

Previously, the discussion was focused exclusively on distinguishing between concealed (*saṃvṛta*) and unconcealed (*asaṃvṛta*) offenses, as well as those that are remediable (*yukta-pratikāra*) and those that are not.

What is clarified here, however, is that although a remedy may be prescribed for a concealment, if it is not an actual ailment, the remedy shall not be administered; thus, one must discern what constitutes a "non-remedy.

This refers to the explanations given in relation to the *saṃgha*, the *sīmā*, the *dharma*, and so forth. Within this section, there are two parts: first, up to the phrase "is also like this," which raises cases of non-conformity that should be recognized; second, the subsequent portion, which contains analogies.

The passage beginning with "Qiū" (丘) below clarifies this as an exhortation to know. Within the preceding section on "non-offenses," one should list the three headings for the fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*).
However, here we again rely upon different categories to combine them into a unified method of practice, thereby encompassing multiple meanings.

To demonstrate that the inclusion of non-offenses is exhaustive, we shall now follow the intermediate portion of the text regarding the three headings for repeated offenses: first, nine cases of knowing the number of days of repetition; second, nine cases of not knowing the number; third...

One knows the number of days but does not know the count of the nine. Within the first nine, there are again three types of concealment: first, knowing the count but concealing it; second, knowing the number of days but not concealing it;

third, knowing the number of days and both concealing and not concealing it. Regarding the three phrases within the category of concealment: the first two cases involve neither [knowing] the rule nor [the number];

the second case involves concealment as in the lower two [cases], while the third involves concealment as in the six-night [penance], like the non-expiation of the offense. The first statement refers to these three.
Regarding "Non-": first, the clarification of the non-covers (anāpatti) consists of three sections. First, the fundamental offenses and their non-covers are listed.
Second, from "if he commits a grave offense while in the state of concealment" onwards, the concealment of a single grave offense committed during the period of *mūlāpakarṣa* is listed.

Third, from "if that bhikṣu, while practicing concealment, commits a second grave offense in the interim" onwards, the concealment of a second grave offense committed during the period of *mūlāpakarṣa* is raised. This...

Although there are three [types of concealment], they are collectively categorized as concealment of what is improper (*asādhūna*). The subsequent concealment is like the two types of "improper" [concealment] mentioned below; the subsequent concealment is like the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*), and the concealment of one who has been cleared of guilt (*āpattivyutthāna*) is likewise improper.
This can be understood through analogy. Question: When it is simply said to be "not according to the Dharma" (*adharmika*), what constitutes this "impropriety"? Answer:

Because it does not deviate from the two sets of seven types of "improper" [actions] mentioned in the preceding text; furthermore, even if there is a specific time period, if its length is disproportionate, it is entirely an impropriety of the matter itself (*vastu-asādhūna*).
Question: Why is it that "non-middle" is neither obscured nor non-obscured? The same applies to the two lower [categories] and so forth. Answer: The latter "non-" does not exclude the former;

as the former is like the latter, there must necessarily be no "non-" in the former. This is because the latter is raised by restating the former. The second set of three phrases and the third set of three phrases are also like this. Combined, these constitute the first nine.
The second [set] consists of nine instances of "not knowing the number," while the third consists of both "knowing the number" and "not knowing the number."
The nine [cases] are as can be known. If one takes three heads, there are twenty-seven phrases, totaling eighty-one non-faults (*anāpatti*).

Regarding the second [category], there are nine within it: first, knowing the number; second, not knowing the number. Within "not knowing the number," there are three each, thus making nine. As for the three cases of "knowing the number":
first, the three instances of concealing after a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*); second, the three instances of concealing or not concealing; third, the three instances of concealing or not concealing.
The first three "as it was" (*yathā*) cases refer to concealment (*paryuṣita*) and the purification of the offense after six nights. As in the text, different types are cited again;
when combined with the original concealment and the two original days, these constitute the "as it was" cases of concealment. The next two sets of three are likewise treated, totaling nine phrases.
If explained by proceeding through the three heads, there are also twenty-seven phrases, which are the twenty-seven "as it was" cases.
Furthermore, if one considers phrases in relation to phrases: one phrase is opposed to one phrase.
One "as-it-is" (yathā) is opposed to three "not-as-it-is" (na-yathā), which constitutes nine phrases opposing nine phrases; thus, one "as-it-is" opposes twenty-seven "not-as-it-is.
If explained by way of three heads, twenty-seven phrases oppose twenty-seven phrases; twenty-seven "as-it-is" oppose eighty-one "not-as-it-is. However, the present text is abbreviated.

Furthermore, if one takes the attainment of the Dharma as the four heads and rides upon them, it immediately forms four sets of twenty-seven "is-nesses" (如) and reverses four sets of eighty-one "non-is-nesses" (非).
This is merely a brief indication within the text.

The eighth [point] concerns treating or not treating based on the person rather than the rule. Up to this point, we have discussed what constitutes a transgression and what constitutes a remedy to clarify what is appropriate or inappropriate;

however, we have not yet distinguished this in relation to the person. Now, we shall distinguish between those who are treated and those who are not by means of two types of persons. Among these, there are two types of *śrāmaṇeras* (those in the four stages of approach) who both conceal their offenses but differ in their views.
When a *bhikṣu* conceals [an offense], it refers to one who conceals out of shame before a *bhikṣu* whose view is pure; in both cases, this constitutes concealment (*praticchādana*).

However, there are cases where it is concealed and cases where it is not. The following three phrases distinguish this according to the person. First, one person remembers [the offense] and has no doubt;
because they remain so throughout the night, they therefore constitute concealment (*paticchādana*). Second, another person does not remember or doubt on that very day;

although both likewise fail to disclose it, because they lack a hidden intent, it does not constitute concealment. The subsequent cases of doubting versus not doubting can be understood accordingly. Next, regarding knowing versus not knowing, this refers to:
It is a matter of being conscious or unconscious. The reason there are only three [stages] is that, in relation to the two types of persons, there is the distinction between delusion and clarity;
furthermore, as for the other two [stages], they do not involve the mind. Therefore, there are only three.

In the ninth [section], from the perspective of reasoning, one should also distinguish between recollection and doubt; this is explained briefly in contrast to the third [point] regarding knowing and not knowing.
As for the previous statement that "not knowing does not constitute concealment," how is it that one does not know? Thus, one explains what it means to not know. Regarding "one who does not know":

These are merely different names for delusive characteristics. Among these, there are specifically six cases concerning *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (saṅghādisesa). "Residual" (*avaśeṣa*) refers to the remaining six [categories], excluding the *pārājika*, which can be understood by implication.
Furthermore, the other five categories are each distinguished as having six [cases], making thirty-six in total (six times six).

Since it was previously stated that concealment is established through knowledge, one might ask: what constitutes "knowledge"? Therefore, next, regarding the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the explanation follows concerning how knowledge establishes concealment.

The formal petition (*jñapti*) is discussed generally as being of six types. Regarding the sequence for administering the medicine [of penance]: it means that one first performs the confession (*pratideśanā*) for the concealment (*paryavasthāna*), followed by the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
This applies even to cases of "evil speech" (*durvacana*); first one repents the concealment, and subsequently one recollects the removal of the offense (*paryavasthāna-vinodana*).

The tenth section briefly examines the length of the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* (the rite of concealment). Because it follows the specific days [of the offense], the concealment of the original day’s penalty is treated identically to the concealment of the confession itself.
This text is divided into two parts: first, the determination of the length of concealment regarding offenses that are identical in name and kind; second, from "If he remembers one offense...

onwards, the determination of the length of concealment regarding offenses that are identical in name but different in kind. Regarding the first part, the text concerning offenses identical in name and kind is as follows:
Regarding the three phrases within the context of recollection: in the first two cases, because the number of days is not remembered, one confesses the concealment from the time of purification;

this is called "treating the long. In the third case, because the number of days is remembered, one treats it as short. The same applies to the following two cases. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there are four phrases:

first, remembering the offense but not the nights; second, remembering the nights but not the offense; third, remembering both; fourth, remembering neither. The first phrase corresponds to the fourth [of the previous set].

The first case treats the offense as long; the second and third treat it as short. These three phrases in this Vinaya are abbreviated because, within them, the concealment is already established and completed, as they directly manifest the length or brevity [of the offense].
Regarding these three modes of concealment, there are two gates for requesting [expiation]; however, one must not rely upon them, as they merely distinguish the substance of the offense.

Because they serve to distinguish between long and short [syllables], they are omitted and not discussed here. Next, regarding those with identical names but different types, these are also known through three categories.

Thus far, we have briefly clarified the remaining points concerning obscured existence (*nivṛta-bhava*). This concludes the first four sections of the initial part of the "Extensive Exposition" (*vistara*).

The second section below concerns the treatment of those who previously committed unconcealed offenses. This expands upon the three [stages]—beginning, middle, and end—that were briefly mentioned previously.

Within this, there are three types of fundamental offenders: first, those who know the number [of offenses] and do not conceal them; second, those who do not know the number and do not conceal them; and third, those who both know the number and do not know the number, yet do not conceal them.
Each of these constitutes six permutations. Within the first fundamental category, there are three instances of repeated offenses: first, knowing the number and concealing them.
Second, concealment by one who does not know the number [of offenses]. Third, concealment by one who knows the number [of offenses] but does not know the number [of days].

For each, two types of *karmavācanā* (formal procedures) are performed. Within the first—concealment by one who knows the number—the text is divided into two parts. First, up to "grant this bhikṣu *mānatva* and *pūrvakalpa*" (the original probation), which clarifies the new and old *mānatva*.
Second, from "having practiced *mānatva* and *pūrvakalpa*" onwards, it concerns the granting of rehabilitation (*āpattivyutthāna*) for both cases. This is the initial text.
There are two cases. First, regarding the case where one proceeds to perform the *mānāpya* (probation) after the root offense has been clarified:

because the offense was committed again on the very day the *dharma* was obtained, it merely subverts the previous *dharma*; since there are no days yet to be forfeited, one simply records both the old and new offenses together and grants the *mānāpya*.
Second, regarding the case where one has already performed [the probation] for one night or less: because the original *mānāpya* has already passed through a night, there is...
The *pārivāsika* (probation) is for the new offense; the *mānatva* (penance) is for the old offense. This text indicates that the new and old offenses are not combined.

A second time, the restoration from guilt (*ābṛhaṇa*) is granted, and the two methods are performed together. Question: Regarding one who has concealed a new offense, why is there no treatment for the concealment?
Answer: This term "concealment" refers to hiding [the offense] without disclosure. Because it did not extend beyond a single night, there is no mention of treating the concealment. If...
Why do you say "one night up to six nights"? The answer is: this refers to the interval between [the offense and the confession].

That is to say, because the offense was committed within the interval of six days, each case does not involve the passing of a night. If a night had passed, then one would indeed have to undergo the *pārivāsika* (probation) for concealment.

Within these six nights of practicing [probation], if one commits a new offense that constitutes a further concealment, it is as explained in the section on single concealment: regarding a second repeated offense where the number of concealments is unknown, it is likewise [treated].

There are two methods of practice. Third, regarding knowing the number [of offenses] or not knowing the number, and concealing them or not concealing them, there are likewise two. As combined previously, these constitute the first six cases. Second, regarding the original offense, not knowing the number and not concealing them, there are likewise six. Third, regarding knowing the number or not knowing the number and not concealing them, there are likewise six; therefore, it says "it is also thus" for each.
If one considers the intermediate cases of concealing or not concealing, there are likewise three sets of six; the text is abbreviated here, and one should infer accordingly.
The preceding textual passage should be abbreviated as both "as it is" and "not as it is.
● The Thirteenth Chapter on Concealment (*Praticchādana-khandhaka*).
Since one has already attained the Dharma, if one does not practice accordingly, the causal practice will not be accomplished; how then could one possibly extinguish past karma? Therefore—

Next, the thirty-five matters of forfeiture are explained. Because one humbles the mind and softens the will to subdue true pride, it is for this reason that [the practitioner] comes [to the community].

The name is indicated from the end [of the procedure]; it should properly be called the *Mānatva-khandhaka*. However, here it is designated according to its initial reception, hence it is called "concealment" (*paryuṣita*).

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is termed the "Dharma of Separate Residence" (*parivāsa*); in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is the "Dharma of Following the Sequence. Within this text, there are three sections; the first concludes as follows.
The first clearly explains the four types of persons who may not mutually count toward the quorum for performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*).

The second, beginning with "As for those who have performed the *parivāsa*," details the procedure for advancing or halting the practice of concealment (*channa-caryā*). The third, beginning with "The Buddha said:
'I authorize the bhikṣu who is practicing *mānatva*,'" sets forth the six-night practice (*ṣaḍ-rātra-caryā*).

The initial text has two parts. First, up to the section on "expiation of offenses" (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), there are sixteen phrases that clarify four types of persons whose own transgressions have not yet been removed;

such persons may not even preside over legal procedures (*dharmakarma*). Second, from the section "He who practices concealment" (*tad-aticchanna-caraṇa*) onwards, there are sixteen phrases concerning four types of persons who likewise do not count toward the quorum for presiding over legal procedures.
Within the section on presiding over legal procedures, there are four divisions: first, practicing concealment oneself; second, practicing the restoration of the original day (*mūla-pratyāgamana*).

Regarding the treatment [of offenses]: first, performing the *mānatva* oneself; second, performing the *mānatva* for another; third, performing the *mānatva* oneself; fourth, performing the *paryavasthāna-vinodana* (removal of the offense) oneself. Each of these involves four permutations when performed mutually, thus totaling sixteen.
Furthermore, within the procedure for fulfilling the quorum (*pariṣad-pūraṇa*), there are likewise sixteen cases, which can be understood by analogy with what has been explained.

This is strictly because one who is themselves bound by fetters and simultaneously engaged in a formal ritual (*dharma-caryā*) lacks the capacity to generate wholesome states in others or to release them from their bonds; therefore, it is prohibited to fulfill the quorum through mutual participation.

Regarding the number [of monks], one must not separate them; to separate them constitutes a *pṛthakkaraṇa* offense. For this reason, among the four types of Saṃghas, they are clarified as not being counted [in the formal quorum], because they do not constitute a destruction of the root [of the Saṃgha]. Therefore, they are not enumerated in that text.

The text on the procedure for concealing offenses (*pārājika*) consists of three parts. First, from "one should not do so" down to "depriving him of his [status]," this concerns the imposition of the disciplinary measure of subjugation (*tarjanīya-karman*).

Second, from "that person who has practiced concealment, together with pure monks" down to "the Buddha said he may receive [ordination]," this refers to the practice of respectful compliance (*anuvartana-dharma*).
Third, from "that person who has practiced concealment does not announce" onwards, it concerns the eight matters such as the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Regarding the method for confessing and repenting, the thirty-five matters have already been briefly explained.
Within the second section on "Reverence," first is the regulation for showing respect to superiors;

second is that those who practice concealment may think, "We and those below us shall open [the practice] to receiving [offerings] from our peers and other assemblies," and thus they shall mutually pay respects and provide service and support. This concludes the preceding [section].
Regarding the section on "Respectful Service," there are two parts. First, regarding respectful service: whether already present or yet to come, one should serve.

Second, concerning the robes and requisites of the Saṃgha: it is permitted to take them according to the order of seniority. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a monk in separate residence (*pārivāsika*) has three things that are lowest:
he takes the lowest bedding, the lowest dwelling, and walks behind the most senior monk. There are three matters that follow the original [status]; the second refers to...

When receiving gifts, during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, when distributing alms bowls, or when the Saṃgha is convened by appointment—if one receives a bowl full of water, a rain-cloak, or during the *pravāraṇā*, these should all be received according to the order of seniority.

One should be assigned the lowest dwelling, the lowest bedding, and the most humble seat. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "If the Saṃgha is convened by appointment, [the items] are received with a bowl full of water; likewise for the rain-cloak and the *pravāraṇā*. These are all received according to the sequence of the *upādhyāya* (seniority).

one may renounce at this location and practice at this same location; or practice at another location; or renounce at one location and practice at another location, or practice at this location [after having renounced elsewhere].

[The author] explains that the extent [of the rules] is determined by their breadth or brevity. The third [category] differs from the preceding seven and five [categories] in terms of being subject to destruction or non-destruction, and in terms of loss or non-loss.

Regarding the intended meaning of "remediation" (*pratīkāra*): while the two matters of the sixth and seventh [categories], namely the *deśanā-dharma* (the dharma of confession), must necessarily involve such [remediation], the remaining six matters are *vivaṛaṇa-dharma* (the dharma of disclosure).

Therefore, the masters of old named these the "eight matters of disclosure and confession," beginning with *āviṣkaraṇa* (disclosure). As for the rule that one who has committed a *deśanā-dharma* may not stay overnight [with others], this is a prohibition against transgression.

Regarding the method of treatment: because it violates the name of "separate residence" (*pārivāsika*), and furthermore, because it prescribes separate lodging in order to induce reflection on one's transgressions and the amendment of faults.

As for the statement that "one must not be without a bhikṣu," this prevents one from acting solely on one's own authority and ensures the practice of discipline (*vinaya*). If there were no other person present, whom would one show respect to and provide service for?

Furthermore, in relation to whom would one perform the three lowest acts, the four successive acts, and so forth? Moreover, it is only in relation to another that the designation "saṃghāvaśeṣa" (requiring suspension by the Saṃgha) applies.
"Separate" (guāi) means that receiving the three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses regarding dwellings and bedding is termed *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If one commits such an offense, one must undergo this *avaśeṣa* (remainder); because it is not a *pārājika* (immediate expulsion) when committed alone, these two matters constitute the method for repentance.

Regarding the statement "the remaining six are revealed": this is because they are the opposite of the preceding concealment (*paticchādana*). Alternatively, one may interpret it as the first two being concealment and the remaining six being its reversal.

Regarding the second [section], the detailed explanation according to the specific matters, there are three parts: the introduction, the exposition, and the conclusion. If it is prior to the formal announcement (*ñatti*),...

There is no *śayanāsanavastu* (overnight stay) that can be lost; it must necessarily be formally announced (*śuddhika-śrāvaṇa*). Only after the formal act has been performed does an overnight stay become subject to loss.

Since this concerns the rectification of a transgression and not the punishment for an offense, it is concluded with a single announcement; there is no need to announce it day by day. This differs from the case of the two offenses involving the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra-parivāsa*), which requires a daily announcement.
Furthermore, when departing for another monastery, one does not announce it—meaning one does not announce it to the monks of the other monastery—and thus loses that one night.

They shall not be included in the count. When two visiting bhikṣus arrive, intending to come to this place, when they announce their arrival as visitors, it is unnecessary to further assemble the resident monks, because this announcement serves as a formal disclosure (*viśuddhi*).
Question: Regarding those who were previously within this boundary, or visitors from outside the boundary who frequently come and go—is it necessary to announce them again?
Answer: It is unnecessary to announce them, because they are already known; this is unlike the procedure for the *poṣadha*.

Regarding the requirement to inform the resident monks: this is because one must disclose [one's absence]. As for those who do not need to inform when leaving the boundary due to a valid reason, this refers to not informing the monks on the road between two boundaries.
This is why, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one sees a bhikṣu on the road, one must inform him.

Within the monastery, one does not announce [one's arrival] while walking slowly. "Within the monastery" distinguishes it from outside the monastery; "walking slowly" distinguishes it from walking quickly, because the latter refers to passing directly through this boundary.

One who is ill does not send a messenger to announce [their presence]. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a person undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) performs the *poṣadha*, they should enter among the Saṃgha and three times announce their confession of offenses.
If they are ill, they should send a messenger to the Saṃgha and say: "I, that person undergoing *parivāsa*..."

there are three [types of] detailed and two [types of] abbreviated [procedures]. Even if one commits many offenses, one cannot have eight nights forfeited all at once, because they occur on the same day. If one commits eight offenses on eight different days, one loses one night for each, leaving no remaining night.

For a bhikṣuṇī, the performance of the half-monthly ritual must be carried out within both assemblies (the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī saṃghas). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* fully sets forth the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) for bhikṣuṇīs.

If one’s internal sense of shame (*hrī*) is destroyed and they request the Dharma from the Saṃgha, performing the seven groups of five [precepts] and repenting to eliminate their transgressions, they should be granted the pure Dharma and need not be subject to formal censure (*pratisāraṇīya*).

● Chapter Fifteen: On Schism in the Saṃgha (Saṃghabheda-khandhaka).
If one lacks the five virtues within and, in censuring another, does so at an improper time, it will lead to strife and contention, resulting in a schism in the Saṃgha; therefore, this is clarified.

To divide the assembly into different factions and perform religious rites separately is called "schism. To extensively manifest its characteristics, it is termed the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Monastic Discipline).
The main text is divided into three parts: first, from the beginning up to "the assembly of five hundred bhikṣus arrived," which concerns the present schism; second, the Buddha... [text truncated].
Having addressed the bhikṣu Śāriputra, the following section cites past events to harmonize the ancient with the present. Thirdly, from the passage beginning "At that time, Upāli...
onwards, it asks about the current methods for schism in the Saṃgha, as well as the two future fruits of such a schism. The preceding text is divided into two parts:
first, up to the point where it says "not to be saved for an eon," it concerns Devadatta’s schism; second, from the passage beginning "At that time, Śāriputra... onwards.

The current section on "Schism in the Saṃgha" consists of three parts within the Chinese text: first, from the beginning up to the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts, which clearly explains Devadatta’s schism;
second, from "At that time, many bhikṣus... onwards, which records the report submitted to the Buddha; third, from "The Buddha said...

onwards, which contains the reprimand that exposes his transgressions. The section on the schism itself is divided into three parts: first, from the beginning up to "taking the voting sticks," which describes the methods for causing a schism practiced within the city of Rājagṛha.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Devadatta proclaimed before the assembly that there were four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) and not five dharmas.

At the first proclamation, he had only four companions who took up the voting sticks (*śalākā*) for the five dharmas. At the second proclamation, there were two hundred and fifty bhikṣus who took up the voting sticks for the five dharmas.
At the third proclamation, there were another three hundred and fifty bhikṣus who took up the voting sticks; thus, they totaled five hundred.
One hundred [monks] differ from this text. Second, at that time, sixty bhikṣus, including Ānanda and others, did not receive the instruction;
they immediately transformed themselves into five hundred [monks] and took the voting sticks (*śalākā*), with the sole exception of Ānanda and one bhikṣu who was a *srotāpanna*.
At that time, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and all the great arhats were not present in that *poṣadha* assembly. Third, at that time, Devadatta...
Having gone down to Gayāśīrṣa Mountain, the method for splitting the Saṃgha is as follows: [the first part] concerns the fulfillment of faith;
[the second part] concerns the preparation for breaking the true Dharma. Second, the various bhikṣus returned and reported the aforementioned three fulfillments to the Buddha.

Third, the "reproach of the foolish person who splits the Saṃgha" constitutes the Buddha’s words of censure. From "There are eight non-Dharmas" onwards, the faults are revealed. [This concludes] the division of the text.
This consists of two parts. First, from the beginning up to "not saved for one kalpa," it cites the conditions that give rise to the karma of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

Second, from "If I see... onwards, it demonstrates the gravity of the karma committed and the manner in which there is no salvation. The preceding section has three sub-divisions. First, a general enumeration to reveal the fault:
these eight matters are not the true path to liberation; therefore, they are called "not the True Dharma. This is intended to reveal the conditions of Devadatta’s transgressions and compliance.
When encountering gain, praise, fame, and pleasure, one cannot help but covet them; when meeting with loss, defamation, censure, and suffering, one cannot help but resent them.

This emotional grasping and refusal to let go is called "entanglement" (*paryavasthāna*). Because it can manifest unarisen wholesome states [only to obstruct them], it is called "obscuration" (*nivaraṇa*).

Furthermore, it causes already arisen wholesome karma to fail to achieve its fruition as a cause, thereby extinguishing the wholesome mind and perpetually binding one to the three miserable realms (*durgati*); hence it is called "destiny" (*gati*).

By specifying "in what is not the path," other minor offenses are excluded; by saying "within the hells," the time of receiving retribution is revealed; by calling it "one kalpa," the duration is indicated;
and by stating "not saved," the lack of rescue is made manifest. Second, from "What are the eight? onwards, the eight dharmas are listed individually.
To receive nourishment is called "benefit"; to lack nourishment is called "decline. Hence, it is named "lack of benefit. To speak of fame while exceeding one's virtue is [the opposite];

to disparage beyond one's measure is called "lack of fame. The remaining texts mostly refer to these as "disparagement and fame. When body and mind are perfectly compliant, they find delight in its meaning.

To call this by its name is "praise. When the Vinaya refers to approaching an external object, it is called "reverence. To see faults and express resentment or reproach, while the mind does not seek compliance, is termed "ridicule";
in the Vinaya, this is called "lack of reverence. When an enemy opposes one's objective and can produce internal affliction, it is called "suffering";

this refers to the internal mind, whereas the Vinaya focuses on the external, hence calling such a person an "evil friend" (*pāpamitra*). To take pleasure in evil companions and falsely consider them suitable is termed "delusion."
Joy. All sentient beings are without exception not apart from these eight; Devadatta was particularly extreme in this regard.

From "Third, having such eight [factors]" onwards, the text concludes by establishing the karmic conditions (*karmapratyaya*). Because he turned toward these conditions and committed the schism of the Saṃgha, it is called "karmic conditions.

Within the second section, "Heavy Karma Beyond Redemption," there are three parts: namely, the Dharma (the teaching), the Parable, and the Synthesis. Within the textual exposition of the Dharma, there are two parts: namely, the inverse and the direct.

[The Buddha] covered [the matter] to manifest that there was no means of rescue. Regarding the means of rescue, first he raised a counter-argument: "If one sees even a small amount of merit and does not record it as exhausted, then there is no rescue.
Second, he spoke in accordance with the truth: "Because I see that their merit is exhausted and their evil has been perfected, I record that they will not be rescued.

Within the text, there are three parts for each: first, the person; second, whether the merit is exhausted or not; third, the conclusion and the recording. Below, the analogy and its application also have three parts. For example, like the person before us...

The analogy refers to those among people who are initially in opposition or compliance. "Sunk in excrement" is a metaphor for the second stage, where evil is completely exhausted and goodness is perfected.

"There are some people who wish to emerge" and the following passages are metaphors for the third stage, wherein there is no means of medical treatment. From "Third, now observing... and below, the metaphors are applied to the actual meaning.
First, Devadatta—the person who split the Saṃgha—corresponds to the opening simile of "the man. Second, from "not seeing... and below, it corresponds to what preceded.

He fell into excrement. Third, from "Therefore" onwards, it corresponds to the previous section on the lack of means to escape. Next, the present section on harmonizing with the Sangha follows the text as written.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Sundarananda kicked Devadatta with his big toe and reviled him, saying, "Arise, you slave of the Śākyas!
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, by other expedient means, led the bhikṣus away. Startled, Devadatta rose and reviled them, saying, "This..."
A bhikṣu with evil desires harbors good intentions; how could he suddenly give rise to an evil mind?
Using skillful means, he attempts to take my bhikṣu away, whereupon [the victim] is struck with great terror and alarm, and warm blood gushes from his face. He then falls alive into the Great Hell.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when Devadatta saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana approaching, he immediately dispatched Kāḷodāyin to detain Maudgalyāyana.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana departed with their disciples. Once Devadatta had awakened and saw that the lecture hall was empty, he thought to himself:
"I am of the Śākya clan, a descendant of Gautama; as a great man, I cannot be humbled or made to follow another. He then spoke to his four disciples, saying:
"Previously there were the teachings of the non-Buddhists, which had become obscured and were no longer clear. I shall now cause these teachings to be initiated and made manifest.
You should know that from this moment on, I no longer belong to the śramaṇa Gautama. At the very moment one speaks these words, it is called the abandonment of the precepts.

The second section, which cites past events to harmonize the ancient with the present, consists of three parts: first, citing Śāriputra’s past refutation to contrast it with his current reconciliation;
second, from “Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha” onwards, citing past instances of the Dharma to contrast them with the present study of the Dharma;
third, from “the bhikṣus” onwards, citing past instances of ingratitude to harmonize them with the current act of betrayal.

The first passage. Question: Within the discourse on the *poṣadha*, it is said that minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*) obstruct the Path; why then, in this instance, does one who has committed a *sthūlātyaya* attain the First Fruit (*srotāpatti*)?

Answer: Because it is the second [offense], it is an obstruction to the first [fruit] and thus does not hinder it. As for the text stating that he performed the confession for a *sthūlātyaya*: this refers to the fact that these five hundred were acting as a faction;
because they were associates of those who split the Saṃgha, there was no fault in their being the first [to confess]. This was done to manifest the proper rule (*vidhi*).
Therefore, it is said that one must perform repentance.

Regarding the second section on the "Dharma-Image," there are four verses. First, one line recites how, having already encountered suffering and affliction within the past Dharma-images, [one is bound].
Second, one line reveals that because the causes do not cease, it is said: "Even unto the long night, the breath does not extinguish," and so forth.
The three times and three phrases demonstrate that because there is a cause, one now experiences suffering and affliction. The four and five phrases extensively cite their categories and analogies;
because they previously destroyed themselves through evil teachings and perversions, they fall into the ocean of phenomena and drown in death—hence it is said they "drown in the sea.
Now, by means of false expedients, they fall into the sea of birth and death.

The third section contains two parts: first, the inquiry into the methods for causing a schism in the Saṃgha; second, from the question of Upāli onwards, the inquiry into the retribution for breaking harmony.
The meaning of "causing a schism" is analyzed through eight gates: first, listing the names and explaining their definitions; second, distinguishing the essential natures of the agent and the object;
third, the derivation of the name; fourth, the conditions required for the offense to be established; fifth, the determination of the time and place of the schism, also called the "direction."
Thus, the fundamental characteristics are distinguished. The sixth section contrasts with the shedding of blood to distinguish the sequence of its preliminary and consummatory stages.

The seventh section concerns the time and place of falling into hell upon abandoning the precepts. The eighth section contrasts with the schism of the *saṃgha* through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to distinguish their similarities and differences.
Regarding the first category, there are two types of names: first, the schism of the Saṃgha; second, the schism of the Wheel (cakra).

As for the term "Saṃgha," it refers to those within a single boundary who perform separate religious rites. As for the "schism of the Wheel," it means abandoning the Eightfold Noble Path and abiding in the five [wrong] dharmas.
Thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "I would rather now cause a schism in the Saṃgha-wheel. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "You should join me in breaking the Śramaṇas."

"O Gautama, the Saṃgha is united; you are destroying the Wheel of Dharma. Furthermore, according to the *Gāthā-śāstra*: "Either the Wheel is destroyed but the Saṃgha is not, or the Saṃgha is destroyed but the Wheel is not.

To abandon the Eightfold Noble Path and instead propound another path constitutes the destruction of the Wheel. When all members within a single boundary (*sīmā*) assemble together without division, this is not the destruction of the Saṃgha."

Second, there may be a schism of the Saṃgha that is not a schism of the Wheel (*cakra*). This occurs when the Eightfold Noble Path is not abandoned and no other path is taught; thus it is not a schism of the Wheel.

Within a single boundary (*sīmā*), because each group performs its own *jñapti-karman* (formal act), this constitutes a schism of the Saṃgha. Third, there may be neither. Fourth, there may be both a schism of the Wheel and a schism of the Saṃgha.
Thus, one should know that the Saṃgha and the Wheel are distinct. Regarding the explanation of the names: if one analyzes "schism" (*bhedana*) with respect to the Saṃgha, there is...
Regarding these two meanings: first, it is called "schism" (*saṃghabheda*) because of the distinction between what was originally one and what is now divided.

That is to say, the community that was originally unified is now [divided] because Devadatta has claimed himself to be a Buddha; he acts contrary to the mind and turns his back on right thought, preaching perverted and false teachings to seduce the ignorant.
Because the bhikṣus divide the Saṃgha toward what is false, it is called "schism" (saṃghabheda). Second, regarding the explanation of "schism" by way of following the false:

only the faction of the heterodox is a schism; thus the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states: "It is ordinary persons who cause destruction, not noble ones. If one explains "destruction" as the destruction of the Wheel of Dharma, there are also two meanings.
First, explaining destruction by way of causes and conditions: this means that by means of the heterodox assembly practicing two dharmas, they destroy the Tathāgata’s [teaching].

This concerns the formal procedures for the Saṃgha. Therefore, this Vinaya states: "Devadatta, today you wish to sever my four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa). Devadatta, do not sever my four noble lineages.

This first illustrates the schism of the Saṃgha by way of its formal procedures. As for the True Dharma, because [Devadatta] accepted five points with faith, the community followed a different course;
this is the schism of the Dharma. These two types—of the community and of the Dharma—are categorized according to the nature of what is damaged.
It is "ruined" by way of dissolution; that is, one fails to attain what ought to be attained, and thus it is called "ruined. Therefore, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states:

"If one has not yet transcended and departed from the state of birth (*anupapatti-vyutkrānta*), then there is neither the attainment of the fruit nor the cultivation of dhyāna. One merely contemplates the arising of pleasure."
Because the Wheel of Dharma does not turn throughout the great trichiliocosm. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already shattered the Wheel;
because it can obstruct the arising of the Noble Path, it is called 'shattering the wheel' (*cakrabheda*)."

The second section, which distinguishes between the agent and the object, again proceeds by means of the preceding two categories: first, the agent and object of schism in the Sangha; second, the agent and object of the destruction of the Wheel [of Dharma].
Regarding the fundamental path of action (*karmapatha*) of schism, which is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), it takes the form of manifest and unmanifest matter (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) as its agent.

According to the *Abhidharmasaddharma* (Realist Treatise), unmanifest matter takes non-matter and non-mind as its agent. If one includes the preparatory stages (*prayoga*), there are also bodily and mental agents.

According to the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, this precept comprises three factors: the actions of body, speech, and mind. Regarding the destruction of the Saṃgha, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that it is a non-concordant formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) characterized by a nature of non-harmony that is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
It is not capable of existing anywhere [else]. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa* likewise maintain that it is a non-concordant formation.
If one is capable of destroying the Wheel of Dharma, they are able to shatter the teachings on the two factors—the causes and the conditioned formations.

This capacity is exercised through the opposition of form and non-form, as well as non-mind, names, phrases, and syllables. The objects to be shattered—the causes, the conditioned formations, the two factors, and the teachings—are identical in nature to this capacity.

Regarding its practice, it takes the wholesome root of non-attachment as its capacity. If one distinguishes what is impaired according to the methods of practice, the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) are the same as before.
As for manifesting the impairment in terms of persons, it causes them not to obtain what they ought to obtain; this takes non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its capacity.

Regarding the third point, concerning the derivation of the name: it is derived from its functional capacity (*kāritra*). The Wheel of the Dharma of the Saṃgha is the locus of that [capacity], and "breaking" is the function.
Alternatively, it may receive its name from both the object and the function: the Wheel of the Dharma of the Saṃgha is the object, and "destroying" is the function.

The fourth [factor] constitutes an offense when all conditions are met. This refers to the *ānantarya* (immediate) and *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offenses. To explain the meaning of these "conditions," there are generally three:

First, the individual must be a *bhikṣu* (fully ordained monk). This is because he competes with the Buddha in the work of conversion. Furthermore, one who has already committed an *ānantarya* or *sthūlātyaya* offense does not qualify as such for the others; thus, the Vinaya states:

"Nor is it [an offense] for *bhikṣuṇīs* and so forth," because the fourfold assembly (*catur-vidha-saṃgha*) would then be split. Second, he must have defied the three admonitions of the Buddha and the Saṃgha. When facing other matters...
Regarding the precepts: after the extensive teachings were established, the act of schism was designated as the first offense because it is equivalent to the second [offense].
Third, there is no grave illness that impairs the mind. If one understands the term *bhikṣu* (venerable), it refers to a man whose conduct is pure, who is learned, and possesses eloquence;

this distinguishes him from the rest of the assembly, such as those who practice broken precepts, have little learning, or are speech-impaired. Thus, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are nine types of pure persons.

It is not by other groups. Regarding the *Cittavibhaṅga* (Treatise on the Mind), those for whom views predominate (*dṛṣṭicarita*) are those who can destroy the Saṃgha because of their evil aspirations;

those for whom craving predominates (*tṛṣṇācarita*) cannot, because they are fickle and unstable. Furthermore, only those such as those with great learning and eloquence are capable of splitting the Saṃgha.

Second, there are ten specific conditions: first, the boundary must have already been established. Thus the *Cittavibhaṅga* states that if the boundary has not been established, the schism is not accomplished. Therefore, the text says: "If..."
Within the boundaries of a single residence (*āvāsa*), two groups perform the *poṣadha* ceremony separately; it is only then that a schism is established.
Second, while the Buddha is still in the world, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states that there is no schism because there is no other teacher once the Great Master has entered *parinirvāṇa*.

Third, it is not at the beginning or the end; the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* also states it is neither before nor after, because within these two periods, the Saṃgha remains of one flavor. (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*)
The same applies to the *Śāstra*. Since the first pair has already been established, the *Cittavṛtti-śāstra* (Heart Treatise) likewise does not fail to establish the first pair.

This is because the schism of the Saṃgha does not persist for more than one night; it is reconciled on that very day. Fifth, regarding the arising of evil desires and the establishment of false Triple Gems:

this refers to the time when unwholesome precepts and views have not yet arisen, and thus it is said there is no "breaking. In the *Cittavṛtti-śāstra*, it is stated that when [the breaking] has not yet occurred, there is no "breaking."

1. Because it is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). 2. Because the six Buddhas were not present among the assembly; the *Cittaviparyaya-śāstra* states that when the Great Master is present among the assembly, they lack majestic splendor (*tejas*).

3. Because the number of attendants is complete; these are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and not noble ones (*ārya*). As the Vinaya says: "In this assembly there is one bhikṣu, and in that assembly there is one bhikṣu;

they perform the *śalākā* (voting stick) for the schism of the Saṃgha and carry out the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Even if they act thus, they cannot cause a schism; they merely cause dust to arise within the Saṃgha."

"Upāli, it is the same for two or three people. Upāli, if this assembly consists of four or more, and that assembly consists of four or more, and they carry out a *śalākā* (voting stick) to break the Saṃgha and perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*), Upāli, this is defined as 'breaking the Saṃgha.
This is for the purpose of breaking the harmonious Saṃgha. Furthermore, in this Vinaya, young bhikṣus must certainly believe and accept it."

Furthermore, in all the Śāstra treatises, the refutation of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) refers to the refutation of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), because the Noble Ones (ārya) cannot be refuted.
This Vinaya also states that the Elder Bhikṣu, fearing they would not believe or accept it, spoke of the five dharmas regarding the eight heterodox views and heterodox tolerances.
The remaining six [factors]—the leader of the schism and so forth—consist of: (7) casting nine illegal voting-slips; (8) the monks consenting and taking up the voting-slips;
and (9) performing the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* separately within the same boundary. These last two conditions refer to the destruction of the practice of the two dharmas;
therefore, this Vinaya states that Upāli, there are two things that constitute a schism in the Saṃgha: false speech and similar speech. Furthermore, there are two other things.
The schism of the Saṃgha, the performance of the *karmavācanā*, and the taking of voting tallies (*śalākā*)—these points may be understood through the analysis of the deficiency.
Fifth Gate: Questioning according to this Vinaya text, the five dharmas were proclaimed at Rājagṛha, and five hundred bhikṣus took up the voting tallies.
He immediately went to Gayā Mountain and personally performed the *karmavācanā* and recited the precepts; the *Mahāsāṃghika* school is also like this.

Within these two locations, at which place and at what time is the fundamental path of action (*mūlakarmapatha*) accomplished? The answer is: it is at the conclusion of the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the precepts at Gayā.
This concludes the refutation. Why is this so? Because Devadatta broke the Saṃgha by imitating the Tathāgata and establishing two kinds of dharma:
first, he established his own false views as the dharma for practice, thereby deviating from the Buddha’s Eightfold Noble Path;

second, he established illegal *karmavācanā* and *poṣadha* ceremonies, thereby deviating from the Buddha’s correct *karmavācanā* and *poṣadha* ceremonies which constitute the locus of the community's legal procedures. Thus, in Rājagṛha—

In the city, five hundred [monks] drew lots and accepted the five dharmas; they first came to believe in the heterodox practices of Devadatta and ultimately brought about the destruction of the Tathāgata’s orthodox practices.
This was merely a skillful means. Later, at Mount Gayā, they themselves performed the *karmavācanā* and recited the precepts.
The five hundred again believed in the heterodox assembly’s dharma and brought about the destruction of the Tathāgata’s orthodox assembly. This was the beginning of their belief in the heterodox.
It is complete because it possesses the full requirements for destroying the true Dharma. On Mount Gayā, he ultimately accomplished the destruction. Therefore, the preceding Vinaya text states:

"If, before all have been exhorted, one intends to destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha and, through skillful means, accepts the method of destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha, persisting in it without relinquishing it, it is entirely *duṣkṛta*.
If one establishes five types of false doctrines and thereby accomplishes the destruction, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
For this reason, furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the preparatory measures were also taken at Rājagṛha.
Devadatta went far toward Gayā City. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Go and tell Devadatta to come; today the Saṃgha shall perform the *poṣadha* karmavācanā.
Ānanda immediately followed these instructions and went to summon him. Devadatta said, "I will not go. From this day forward, I shall no longer associate with the Buddha."
"Regarding the Dharma and the Saṃgha, we shall not perform the *poṣadha* or *karmavācanā* together. As for today’s *prātimokṣa*, whether you wish to study it or not is up to your own will.
Having heard these words, Ānanda thought to himself: "This is a strange matter; such an evil sound has been uttered.

Will this not cause the destruction of the Saṃgha? Ānanda reported all of this in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha spoke to Ānanda a second time, telling him to go and summon [the monk], and so forth.
"You may go now. [Ānanda] related the aforementioned matters in detail. "As before, will this not cause a schism in the Saṅgha?
After Ānanda had returned, the group of six bhikṣus said among themselves, "The śramaṇa Gautama will surely send messengers three times more.

Let us each set our minds right and together perform the poṣadha ceremony. By doing so, we shall establish a reputation for ourselves in future generations while the Buddha is still in the world. Devadatta..."
[The Buddha said: "Many. The group of six bhikṣus have together brought about a schism in the Saṃgha and have already completed the poṣadha.
The Buddha again a third time told Ānanda to go and summon them. He replied, "We have already completed the poṣadha. Having heard this, Ānanda thought to himself: "How extraordinary!

They have already caused a schism in the Saṃgha. He immediately informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Those who act contrary to the Dharma have already completed their poṣadha; according to the Dharma, it should be as follows..."
They performed the *poṣadha*. Based on such textual evidence, we know that the schism occurred at Gayā and not at Rājagṛha.

In the sixth section, regarding the shedding of blood, we distinguish between the preliminary preparations (*pūrvakalpa*) and the final consummation (*niṣṭhā*). The first two parts provide a detailed analysis.
Regarding "preliminary and final," the *Dharmaguptaka*, *Mahīśāsaka*, and *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* all place the preparations for the schism first, followed by the shedding of the Buddha’s blood.
Blood. Next, he again instigates the schism of the Saṃgha; this is the culmination of his preparatory effort, as clarified in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
First he breaks the wheel of the Saṃgha, and next he sheds the blood of the Buddha's body. Therefore, that text states: "Devadatta received great offerings, yet his followers were few."
He thought to himself, "I possess thirty of the marks [of a Great Man], lacking only two compared to the Buddha. It is simply because my disciples have not yet gathered;
otherwise, how would this differ from being surrounded by a great assembly? Having thought thus, a schism arose in his mind.

He gained five hundred disciples, and while Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were teaching and transforming beings through the Dharma, the Saṃgha was restored to harmony. At that time, Devadatta conceived an evil intent and pushed him [down].
When Śaṅkha Buddha was struck by a vajra-wielding *vajrapāṇi* who hurled a vajra from afar, a splinter of stone flew toward him and wounded the Buddha’s toe.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā rebuked him for this, whereupon he struck her with his fist; she immediately bled from her eyes and died.

This is said to constitute the commission of three *ānantarya* (immediate) sins. The case of Niṃdika was also like this. Furthermore, shedding blood [of a Buddha] constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This is the rule.
This is appropriate. The reason for this is that although Devadatta’s original intention was to take the Buddha’s life, he has now merely drawn blood;
his primary intent has not been fulfilled, and his underlying purpose remains unaccomplished. Therefore, the karma of harboring such thoughts constitutes a skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, as this was the very first instance, it was classified as an *anantarya-thullaccaya* (a grave offense short of a formal transgression), because the broad teachings could still have been violated. Question: Does shedding the Buddha’s blood occur before the precept against killing a person is established?

Is it for later? Answer: It was nine years after Devadatta shed the Buddha’s blood and departed from the Twin Śāla Trees. It is clear that this was established after the precept against shedding blood was promulgated.

If that is so, within the precept against shedding blood, it has already been stated that if the act is completed, it is a *pārājika* (defeat), and if not completed, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

thus the detailed teaching is already manifest. Now, shedding the Buddha’s blood is the second [offense]; how can it be the first? Answer: Regarding the precept against shedding blood, it is a *sthūlātyaya* if not completed.

This differs from the offense of drawing blood in two respects; therefore, it is treated separately as a primary [offense]. First, there is the distinction between what can be expiated and what cannot be expiated;

second, there is the difference between being a heinous crime (*ānantarya*) and not being a heinous crime. Question: If the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) to kill an ordinary person does not constitute a heinous crime, yet drawing blood constitutes a heinous crime, why is this so?

The distinction between "pācittiya" (offense) and "non-pācittiya" is not a case of having a separate beginning. If there were a separate beginning for other persons relative to their fathers, then at the time of killing one's father, there should likewise be a separate beginning.
Answer: There is only the distinction between "pācittiya" and "non-pācittiya," yet they are equally irredeemable; therefore, there is no separate beginning. This principle is somewhat difficult.

Generally, when we speak of a "beginning," it refers to the extensive teachings (*vaipulya*); it is only when something that was originally non-existent now comes into being that one can distinguish a beginning.
Second: Regarding these current cases of *ānantarya* (heinous offenses), whether or not they have been formally proscribed by the Buddha, they are equally *ānantarya* in nature;

therefore, one cannot rely upon them to clarify the first two [categories]. If it were the name "stain" (*pārājika*), it would be the second [category]. If that were so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state that nine pure persons can cause a schism in the Saṃgha?

Furthermore, according to the *Cittaviveka-śāstra*, those who violate the precepts are not "preeminent" (*adhipati*). In response, it is said that "pure" refers to those who have not committed a *pārājika*.
This is a matter of circumstance. It may also be explained further: even if one is the second person [involved], it does not preclude the schism of the Saṃgha.
The Sūtras and Śāstras differ; for instance, in the *Jñānaprasthāna* (as cited in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), one first causes a schism and subsequently sheds blood.

In the four, five, or ten Vinayas, one first sheds blood and subsequently causes a schism. Which of these is definitive? However, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* itself states that there are nine pure persons, and furthermore, it first...

If [the offense] occurs after shedding blood, it constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha; how could this not be contradictory? Therefore, one must know that one cannot rely solely on the words of a single treatise.

If one commits other offenses without such distinctions, one cannot cite the text regarding "schism" to obstruct the various sūtras. A schism in the Saṃgha through stealing is the ultimate offense, not a preliminary stage.
Devadatta’s original intention was to usurp the Buddha’s position, destroy the Saṃgha, and sever the Dharma.

Now that he has succeeded in splitting the assembly and caused them to follow his own views, his objective is fulfilled; his mind’s desire is satisfied, and there is no further progress to be made, thus it is the ultimate [act].

Furthermore, since his transgressions have been made manifest and he has violated the teachings by causing a schism, he is the second person. Therefore, according to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views), this constitutes "breaking the Saṃgha."

There is no "first" [offense], because it contradicts the three-fold admonition of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, regarding this term "second": since the schism of the Saṃgha has not yet occurred, there is no "first";
therefore, the offense is said to be "second" because it is identical to the second [stage]. This does not mean that Devadatta had already previously committed a schism. Question:
If Devadatta’s schism is the "second," then his violation of the admonition for the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense should also be considered so.
Second: The schism of the Saṃgha is the matter to be admonished. When one is being admonished regarding this matter, if one persists in the schism despite the admonition, it constitutes a schism.
Because Devadatta did not accept the second admonition, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for persisting in the refusal of an admonition is the first [of its kind].

Regarding the seventh section on the time of relinquishing the precepts and so forth: According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the hall of Devadatta was empty and only his four companions remained, Kāḷodāyin kicked Devadatta with his right foot to wake him. Upon seeing the hall empty, Devadatta fell from his bed in a state of confusion and distress.
His four companions sprinkled water on him and he regained consciousness. He then thought: "I am of the Śākya clan, a descendant of Gautama. Great...

A person must not be humiliated or brought low. To the point where one says, "From this day forward, I no longer belong to the Śramaṇa Gautama"—at the moment such words are spoken, it is called the abandonment of the precepts (*śīla-tyāga*).

There is no time when one enters hell [immediately]. [In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*,] Śrutananda kicked [the Buddha] with his toe, saying, "Slave of the Śākya," until warm blood gushed from his ear-hole; he fell alive into the Great Hell. There is no... [time when one enters hell immediately].

These are the words of renouncing the precepts. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he first caused a schism in the Saṃgha; next, he drew blood [from the Buddha] and further struck the nun Utpalavarṇā until she died.

He maintained close intimacy with the heretics such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others, severed his roots of goodness, and was devoid of shame or remorse. This was the occasion of his renunciation of the precepts.
Furthermore, he placed a potent poison on his fingernails, intending to injure the Buddha; however, before he could reach Rājagṛha, he fell ill.
In the middle [section], it is said that the earth naturally cracks open and flaming chariots come to meet him; he is born directly into hell.
Although the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* mentions only such things as hot blood gushing from his face and so forth, it does not state that one enters hell at the moment of abandoning the precepts.

The Eighth Section. Refuting the Schism of the Saṃgha through Ritual (Karmavācanā) to Distinguish Similarities and Differences. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-uttaragrantha), there are nine sections.

First, the schism of the ritual is different from the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). This refers to a bhikṣu who views [the conduct] as equal; it is not the case that other assemblies view it as conduct based on affection. If one breaks the ritual...
This applies generally to both assemblies, as both assemblies alike uphold the *karmavācanā*. Second, regarding whether or not one must feign being the Buddha:

the *dharmacakra-saṃgha* requires one to feign being the Buddha by self-proclaiming oneself as such, because the Buddha is the master of the *dharmacakra*, and because the Tathāgata is the master of the *dharmacakra*.
However, in the case of a schism in the *karma*, one does not need to feign being the Buddha, because the Buddha does not uphold the *karmavācanā*.

Therefore it is so. Thirdly, regarding the number [of persons]: to break the *saṃgha* by means of formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), it requires a minimum of eight people—four on each side within a single boundary (*sīmā*)—performing separate ritual acts;
because their respective rituals are not valid and no benefit is obtained, the term "breaking the *saṃgha*" applies even at this minimum of eight.
To break the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), however, it requires a minimum of nine people. The reason for this is as follows:
Devadatta, intending to destroy the true Triple Gem, first established a false Triple Gem. Devadatta claimed the title of Buddha, thereby destroying the true Buddha-Gem.
