The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* establishes these eighteen factors, though with slight differences from this [text]. That treatise states: "Constant practice and impermanent practice;
that which is taught and that which is not taught"—these two pairs are elucidated within the teachings of the Abhidharma. One should analyze their characteristics in detail.

The previous discussion on the schism in the Saṃgha and the precept against defying admonition has already been explained at length. If one follows this principle, it is entirely improper to take "speaking" as the objective basis for a dispute over matters (*vastu-saṃgha-rāṭi*).

Furthermore, to take "constant practice" versus "non-constant practice," or "that which is prescribed" versus "that which is not prescribed," as the objective basis for a dispute over matters—this also contradicts the treatise.

Now, relying on the treatise to resolve and identify the offense, the two bases are as previously stated. As for determining the objective basis of a dispute over matters, one must rely on the Vinaya.
It is not *vinaya*. It takes the dispute over matters (*adhikaraṇa*) as its object, because the communal rules (*saṃghadharma*) constitute the *vinaya*. The explanation of the meaning is as before.

Whether it is spoken or unspoken, it is subsumed within the remaining six [categories] to form the disputes over speech (*bhāṣādhikaraṇa*) and the disputes over seeking [faults] (*anveṣaṇādhikaraṇa*).

The second section, the clarification of the text, has three parts: first, clarifying the person who initiates the dispute; second, from "by means of the three types of formal accusations" (*tīṇi ukkhepanakāraṇāni*) onwards, clarifying the object to be investigated;
and third, from "having acted in this way" onwards, correctly clarifying the deficiency in the formal accusation regarding the contradiction with the fourth phrase.

Within the second part (the object), there are three sections: first, "by means of the three types of formal accusations," which generally indicates the subject of the accusation; second, breaking the precepts...
The following is a detailed enumeration of the objects cited. Regarding the "three [grounds of] seeing, hearing, and suspecting": these are the three bases upon which the accuser relies.
In the third section, "formally accusing based on such characteristics and seeking a companion to speak with," this specifically refers to the power of seeking a companion to support one's case;
that is, the accuser claims to have a companion who corroborates them, thereby reassuring their own mind.
One who, by means of skillful means and gentle words, consoles, encourages, and instructs; one who, when raising a matter for recollection, cites evidence to establish this point;
one who establishes that which has a basis and does not establish that which lacks a basis; one who, regarding that which is not done and is not deluded, clarifies what is being raised;
one who possesses internal understanding and wisdom; and one who, though not yet liberated, uses exhortatory language to manifest the one who raises the matter: "If you..."
By confessing to me, one attains purity and liberation. If one does not acknowledge and confess [the offense] before me, one will be bound by evil karma;

therefore, it is said that such a person is not liberated from the dispute over an offense (*āpatti-vivāda*). There is only the second category of the evaluated object (*viṣaya*), while the remaining three phrases—existence, non-existence, and so forth—are missing.

In the case of a dispute over a matter (*vastu-vivāda*) as well, there is only the second category, and the remaining three are likewise absent. Regarding the dispute over a point of doctrine (*dharma-vivāda*), there is a single explanation concerning the performance of the matter and so forth; namely, the resolution.

When there is a dispute regarding speech, it is settled by means of the "majority decision in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*). Within this process, there is the selection of a person through a formal motion consisting of a single announcement (*jñapti*) and a formal motion consisting of two announcements (*jñaptidvitīya*), which serves to distinguish the assembly.

Regarding the meaning of whether these two—the dispute itself and the act of settling it—are established or not: herein, the matter of the dispute is addressed, and the dispute regarding investigation (*anusandhikaraṇīya-artha*) is thereby resolved.

There are three *jñapti-caturtha* [procedures], namely those concerning these three [types of disputes]. This refers to the formal act (*karmavastu*) within the context of a dispute arising from a search (*paryeṣaṇā-vivāda*).

When resolving a dispute arising from an offense (*āpatti-vivāda*), there is the single-announcement (*ekajñapti*) for accepting confession and the announcement made by a harmonious assembly; this refers to the dispute arising from these two, which constitutes the formal act within the context of a dispute arising from an offense.
To provide such an interpretation is not only logically inconsistent, but it also fails to encompass all types of disputes. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation of...

145. Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, whether the dispute is actually settled or not, if a dispute arises based on principle, it is to be extinguished by the "majority decision in the presence" (*sammukhavinaya*).
This is called the "procedural act within a verbal dispute. It is like performing two formal announcements (*jñapti*) where only one was required;

when one is accused by another, the person being accused does not fulfill the requirements of being accused, yet they themselves claim that the initial announcement was valid and that the subsequent [announcement] was established.
The "act of white waves" (*śvetataraṅga-karman*) and that which gives rise to dispute are also included within the category of the "act of verbal dispute" (*vāda-vivāda-karman*).

For example, when at Campā an illegal *jñapti-caturtha* (fourth motion) *karma* was performed by a separate assembly, and seven people disputed [the matter], the Buddha judged that two of them spoke according to the Dharma while the others spoke contrary to the Dharma;
all such cases are subsumed under the category of the act of verbal dispute. If there are three grounds [for accusation] regarding the raising of that illegal *karma*, [it is likewise so].

When a person who has been accused of an offense is established as guilty, or when one claims that an illegal act was not committed yet the slander is well-founded, or when an act was performed during a state of insanity or delusion, or when a dispute arises because what was previously cited contradicts what follows—such cases must be settled by means of the three methods, such as *smṛti-vinaya* (reliance on memory), and so forth.

Therefore, the one hundred and forty-five *karmas* (formal ecclesiastical acts) and other procedures are all matters to be handled within the category of *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (settlement of disputes). If two people [dispute] arbitrarily...
They criticize another’s performance as illegal (*adharma*) through a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed by a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃvāsika*).

One person says, "He committed a *thullaccaya* offense out of ill will (*duṣṭacitta*)," while another says, "He committed a *pācittiya* offense out of negligence (*pramāda*). Although the matter is the same, their views differ; this is also a case of formal action within a dispute over speech (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*).

Both individuals arbitrarily criticize the other’s performance as illegal through a formal act performed by a separate assembly. One says, "This person committed a *thullaccaya* offense out of ill will."

People may say that this mind of indolence constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; or one person may say that another has performed an illegal act, while through a formal act of concord (*saṃghakarma*), another says that he has performed a legal act, or a formal act of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa-karma*). Or, after the formal act has been performed, the community may become divided into factions and give rise to dispute.

In such cases, where both the matter and the view are discordant, it is necessary to employ the method of "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) based on their own admission, as in other similar instances.
Regarding all *karmas*, those that give rise to disputes in this manner are all matters occurring within the context of disputes involving offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*).
Next, the roots of dispute are distinguished. "Root" (*mūla*) has the meaning of "arising. Since the emergence of the four types of disputes arises from these, they are therefore called "roots."

Regarding the statement that among the types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), three unwholesome minds and three wholesome minds serve as the root: this means they serve as the root by way of being internal causes.

When one evaluates the four types of Saṃghas and gives rise to this dispute, the dispute arises because of the Saṃgha; therefore, it is said that the Saṃgha is the root. This is stated from the perspective of objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Since the dispute arises because of persons, it is said that persons are the root. Regarding the six bases from which disputes arise serving as the root: this refers to...
Because it is taught as the root of karma, as stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*: first, being stubborn and refusing to speak; second, having an evil nature and delighting in strife;
third, being deceitful and crooked; fourth, greed and envy; fifth, lack of shame and lack of remorse; sixth, wrong view. Regarding the eight matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha:
one takes the contested dharma as the root and seeks the root of the dispute. First, regarding greed and non-greed, etc.—this refers to how these [factors] are raised and arise within the mind.

This refers to *adhikaraṇa* (legal disputes). Because it cites the offenses of the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha is the root. Since the offenses of the Saṃgha arise from the *sīmā* (boundary), the root is spoken of in terms of the remote conditions that give rise to the dispute.
Because it cites the offenses of individuals, the individual is the root. Regarding the "three matters of accusation," these refer to the specific acts committed;

because they do not involve disputing over the principles or the nature of right and wrong, the eighteen *dharmas* do not apply here. This *paryeṣaṇā-adhikaraṇa* (dispute concerning investigation) concerns only whether an offense has been committed or not.
This is because it refers to the roots of disputes arising from transgressions. There are only greed and the other [afflictions], as they are based on the causes of transgression.

If one considers the conduct that gives rise to disputes, there should likewise be three types; virtuous minds and the like are as previously explained. The three matters of formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) are also as before.

The six transgressions serve as the roots when explained in terms of the completion of karmic action, as clarified in the "Six Matters of the Saṃgha. Disputes arising from these should be understood by analogy with what was previously stated regarding the three [roots].

Regarding the third point, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): the "search for objects" (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*) pertains to all three natures; the "attainment" (*prāpti*) pertains to all three natures; and "offenses" (*āpatti*)—whether non-virtuous or neutral offenses—pertain only to two [natures].
If one considers them in terms of contentious conduct (*vivāda-caryā*), they should pertain to all three natures. Regarding the three natures of contention:

if it is for the sake of fame and profit, or with the intent to humiliate others, then the passion for victory or defeat in debating the principles is unwholesome (*akuśala*). However, if it is for the purpose of manifesting the truth...

Regarding the Buddha-dharma, those whose intent lies in seeking the principle and who do not seek profit or fame are said to engage in "virtuous seeking" (*kuśala-paryeṣaṇā*), rather than the former two [types of] mental states;

this is neutral (*avyākṛta*). There are two parts to the search for pure texts: first, a general presentation showing that it applies to all three [moral categories]; second, a specific explanation of how it applies to all three. This is divided into three sections.
First, explaining virtuous seeking; within this, there are three parts: first, a general presentation of the person’s virtuous mind seeking and investigating. Second...

Having finished the three matters of formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), the following section specifically clarifies the process of investigation. The phrase "with these three" and so forth correctly explains the formal accusation itself. Regarding the term "specifically clarifying":

the passage beginning with "the three matters of formal accusation" expands upon the preceding investigation; the second section, beginning with "internally there are five factors," expands upon the preceding virtuous mind.
There are three aspects to this investigation: first, the general indication of the three types of formal accusation; second, the enumeration of their violations.
The items beginning with "precepts" are the specific objects sought. The third [category] consists of the three bases for seeking—what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Regarding the second internal category, there are five factors. As for the previous mention of a "wholesome mind," there are two ways to explain it:

first, by presenting what constitutes a wholesome mind; as for how it is wholesome, it is because there are five internal factors. Second, by which means is it known that these five factors exist? This is what follows.

Regarding its characteristics, it is known to be wholesome for two reasons: first, to cause the person before one to practice purity themselves, as indicated by the text "without transgression" and so forth;
second, to ensure the purity of the assembly, so that there are no external criticisms based on what has been seen or heard, as indicated by the text "do not let this person’s ill repute spread.
The third point, the correct explanation of the textual meaning, is as stated above. Next is the unwholesome.

This is divided into three parts: first, a general enumeration of unwholesome mental seeking; second, from "by means of the three types of formal charges" onwards, a detailed explanation of the preceding section;

third, from "in this manner" onwards, the demonstration of what is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). Within the middle section, there are two parts: first, the explanation of "seeking," which is further divided into three:
first, the general indication of the subject matter by means of the three types of formal charges; second, the specific listing of the matters charged, such as violating the precepts; third...
And as for the supporting faculties (*indriya*), there are two internal absences of five factors. The explanation of the unwholesome mind (*akuśala-citta*) has two parts:
first, the unwholesome mind that correctly understands the absence of the five internal factors; second, clarifying that the characteristics of the unwholesome mind have two aspects.

The first is intended to cause the person before one to personally practice what is not pure; thus the text says: "Intending to cause this person to commit transgressions, defilements, and impure offenses."

[He] departs. Second, because he wishes to cause others to perceive the impurity of the monastic community through external reports of his misconduct, the text says "even to the point of spreading [the report].

Regarding the third [point], the formal accusation (*karma*) that is contrary to the Dharma: "not falsely seeking companions" means following one's own deluded inclinations and seeking assistance in an unlawful manner;
"not providing consolation" means internally lacking the five qualities while using harsh words to reprimand and perform the formal act of accusation (*codanā*) and recollection (*smṛti*).

"Recollection" refers to falsely citing evidence to establish this matter; that is, establishing a groundless charge of non-offense. One does not establish it within another matter that has a basis because of a lack of internal wisdom.
"Delusion from which one is not liberated" refers to an illegitimate formal accusation (*adharmika-āropaṇā*), as both fail to escape the burden of entanglement.

The neutral (*avyākṛta*) cases may be understood by analogy. Regarding the text on disputes concerning offenses, there are two parts: first, the general presentation of the headings, which does not apply to those of a wholesome nature.

The second part, the detailed explanation, has two sections. First, regarding unwholesome offenses (*akuśala-āpatti*): these are committed by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*). "Those in training" refers to individuals who have attained the three lower fruits of the path.
Alternatively, this distinction may be made because ordinary persons commit both general and extensive offenses, whereas those in training commit only brief ones.

Regarding neutral offenses (*avyākṛta-āpatti*): these refer to the unintentional offenses of ordinary persons and those in training, as well as the offenses of those free from attachment (*asaṅga*). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, ordinary persons... [text ends].

Human beings may commit offenses through all three natures. An offense committed with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) is, for example, when a newly ordained *bhikṣu*, being unaware of the characteristics of the precepts, pulls grass and the like by hand from the vicinity of a Buddha stūpa;
or, as in the case of killing a person out of compassion (*maitrī*). An offense committed with an unwholesome mind (*akuśala-citta*) refers to intentional transgression of the precepts.

Regarding offenses committed with an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind: these are those that do not belong to the two aforementioned types [of minds]. In this text, the person in training (*śaikṣa*) is not discussed. Upāli asked:
"With which of the three natures of mind does an Arhat commit an offense? The Buddha said: "All offenses are committed with an indeterminate mind.

For example, when an Arhat does not recall that he possesses an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), or forgets to entrust it for safekeeping, or enters a village at an improper time—such matters follow the rules of dispute."
Three [points] may be understood by analogy with what has been explained.

Fourth, the text distinguishes between what is correct and incorrect. "Correct" refers to words concerning the principle of tranquility; these constitute a *vāda-adhikaraṇa* (dispute over words). Other words and other disputes are not *vāda-adhikaraṇas*.
Seeking out the faults of others and thereby giving rise to anger and contention constitutes a *anveṣaṇā-adhikaraṇa* (dispute over seeking); other forms of seeking are likewise [not this].
Other disputes are not "disputes of seeking" (*vitandā-vivāda*). Causing anger through the accusation of an offense is a "dispute of offenses" (*āpatti-vivāda*);

other offenses and other disputes are not "disputes of offenses. There are one hundred and forty-five types of collective disputes. Whether a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) has already arisen and been accomplished or not is a "dispute of matters" (*kṛtya-vivāda*);

other matters and other disputes are not "disputes of matters. Such is the nature of these distinctions; first, regarding disputes of speech (*bhāṣā-vivāda*), the right and wrong have been analyzed and distinguished. The rest...
The categories can be understood accordingly.
Within the context of disputes over speech (*vāda-vivāda*), the text is divided into three parts. First, regarding "disputes over speech" and so forth:

initially, one first engages in mutual confrontation through disputatious speech, which is categorized into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Second, the phrase "or there may be speech" and those that follow serve to distinguish this from the aforementioned [general] disputes over speech.
No. It is divided into seven sections. The third section, beginning with "What is it? and so forth, is a detailed explanation of the characteristics that distinguish the correct from the incorrect.

Regarding the first part, there are four sections therein: first, verbal dispute (*vāda-vivāda*); second, words of dispute (*vivāda-vākya*); third, dispute (*vivāda*); and fourth, words of dispute (*vivāda-vākya*).

Although the established text is thus, some explain these four phrases as follows: in the first and third cases, "speech" (*vāda*) is used immediately for "dispute" (*vivāda*) in order to distinguish it from other types of speech;
in the second and fourth cases, "dispute" is used immediately for "speech" in order to distinguish it from other types of dispute. However, among these four...
The first two constitute one pair, and the latter two constitute another pair.

Within these two pairs, the reason the former pair is called "dispute over speech" (*vāda-vivāda*)—and why "dispute over speech" is used as a distinct term—is to differentiate it from the latter. For what reason, then, is the latter pair called simply "dispute" (*vivāda*)?

The term "single dispute" (*ekavāda*) is stated in order to distinguish it from what precedes it; in terms of actual principle, they are similar. To distinguish between the two pairs, there are both single and multiple [terms], yet none fail to provide the initial [qualification].
The third [clause] equally excludes other speech, while the second and fourth equally exclude other disputes. This interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?
For example, if the phrase "dispute over speech" in the second clause were to use a provisional qualification to exclude what is non-[speech], then it would follow that the text...
It says: "There may be disputes that are not words. Since it says they are "not words," how can this be called a "distinction" (*viveka*) in relation to this text?
If other disputes were being distinguished from "disputes," one should simply have said, "There may be disputes that are not words.

Therefore, by taking up "words" and even distinguishing them as "not [words]," one discards "words" altogether and distinguishes only "disputes. Furthermore, he asks: "In contrast to what was the preceding [statement] made?"
"Speech is itself verbal dispute (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*); verbal dispute is itself speech. How is it that [the text] excludes what is not [speech] and simply says "dispute is not speech"?
Therefore, I shall now further explain these four. The first two form a pair: speech is itself verbal dispute, and verbal dispute is itself speech.

This means that by using general terms to distinguish specific disputes, they are mutually identical yet distinct. To exclude other types of speech, the next two pairs consist of using speech as the dispute itself and the dispute as speech itself;
this means using general terms to encompass both the mutual identity and distinction. This is to exclude other forms of speech.
This also excludes other types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*). How are these disputes and verbal expressions (*vāda*) related in terms of their general and specific characteristics?

For example, the first term "verbal expression" (*vāda*) has the general sense of being either right or wrong; it is "specific" because it refers specifically to the four types of verbal disputes (*vādādhikaraṇa*) among the four [types of disputes].

Regarding the second pair, as stated previously, the term "verbal expression" is used generally. As for "general dispute," this refers directly to the dispute itself; since the dispute applies to all four [types], it is not here differentiated by terms such as "verbal expression. Therefore, [the two are distinguished].
This is termed "dispute regarding names. Question: What is the difference between these two pairs? There are two aspects of difference:
first, a difference in terminology, as was determined above; second, a difference in the specific objects being distinguished. Within each of these two pairs, speech is opposed by dispute.
The remaining terms are excluded in the same manner. Each is contrasted with its respective term for the purpose of exclusion; since that which is excluded is distinct [from the term it contrasts].

That is to say, the second phrase contrasts "specific dispute" (*viśeṣavivāda*) with "speech" (*vacana*) to exclude other types of speech. The fourth [phrase] contrasts "general dispute" (*sāmānyavivāda*) with "speech" to exclude other types of dispute.
Question: If one relies on the latter pair, it already constitutes a complete [definition] that distinguishes speech from dispute. Why then is the former pair necessary? Answer:

If there were only the lower pair, one would merely obtain a general term for general disputes. To distinguish them from other types of speech, and because other [types of] disputes have not yet arisen—lacking both general and specific disputes—one must exclusively distinguish other types of speech.
That is to say, by pairing "general dispute" with "speech," one distinguishes dispute; by pairing "specific dispute" with "speech," one distinguishes speech.

Therefore, two pairs [of categories] are required in order to fully exhaust the principle. If there were only one pair, the differentiation would not be comprehensive; this is why it is so. Fundamentally, these are not paired with "contention" (vivāda);
they concern the difficulties and ease from beginning to end, as well as the fixed number of contentions and so forth.

The second pair serves to exclude what is incorrect and opens up the preceding four chapters. Regarding the division into seven gates: if one were to rely solely on the first gate for the correct interpretation of their respective characteristics, there would only be four;
however, by citing the incorrect [alternatives] to clarify each, they should total eight—namely, the four preceding lines, each citing one instance of the incorrect.
Thus, it is said that the second line cites the incorrect as one gate, which is identical in its citation of the incorrect to the fourth gate. Text.

Because [the negation] was omitted and not explicitly stated, there were only seven [categories]. Now, the explanation is not thus: the first [phrase] and the second [phrase], these three phrases, all involve citing what is incorrect to reveal what is correct;
thus, they constitute six gates. As for the second phrase, it merely presents what is correct; it should also cite what is not the Path.
To say "there may be verbal dispute that is not verbal" means that "not verbal" refers to nothing other than that which does not give rise to disputatious speech; this constitutes...

Regarding the eight sections: since the first has already been called "dispute over words" (*vāda*), it is stated again as "not [a dispute] over words" for fear of confusing it with cases that are not excluded. Thus, it is only the seven sections that are distinguished.
Since these differ from the original and are not identical, if the eighth were like this and identical, it would not be excluded; therefore, the first phrase serves as the initial point.

The second raises what is non-meaningful (*anartha*), which is the same as the third section’s exclusion of what is non-meaningful. Why? Because the first phrase is also identical in its phrasing for raising what is non-meaningful, such as "speaking with children" and so forth. (2)
They exist in the same category. If this were not an objection, why would the second [category] alone be abbreviated by stating "it is not"?

Therefore, we know it is not so. As for the seven categories: first, some say that "speech" (*vāda*) is itself "contentious speech" (*vivāda*); this is the first phrase, intended to distinguish it from other types of speech, because speech is itself a dispute.
Second, some say that "speech" is not "contentious speech"; this mentions the negative to reveal the positive, citing that [other type].

The phrase "it is not" serves to preclude [the possibility that] it is a dispute over speech (*vāda-vivāda*). This clarifies that the aforementioned adherence to a position constitutes a dispute over speech.

Regarding the third category, "there is a dispute over speech which is itself speech," this refers to the second clause above; it demonstrates that the two are identical. One should likewise have cited cases where it is not [a dispute over speech].

Alternatively, there may be disputes over speech that are not themselves speech; these are not cited here to avoid the confusion of including other types of speech. Or perhaps they cannot be cited because their underlying principle is unattainable. Regarding the fourth category, "there is a dispute over speech... [the text continues].
Regarding "that which is itself contention": this correctly explains the third section. Some say that the word "speech" (*vacana*) mentioned above is itself contention;

thus, within the third phrase, the character for "contention" (*raṇa*) below is used to distinguish it from other types of speech, thereby identifying speech itself as contention. Fifth, regarding "some say it is not contention":
this employs the negative to reveal the affirmative; by citing "good speech" as being its [true] contention, it clarifies that the aforementioned "evil speech" is what constitutes it.

This refers to "dispute" (*raṇa*). Regarding the sixth [category], "having dispute," it is stated as "immediate speech" (*sadyovāda*). This correctly explains the "having dispute" within the fourth section; that is, the character "dispute" (*raṇa*) in the fourth phrase.

It is stated as such because the character "speech" (*vāda*) has not yet been mentioned in the fourth phrase. To distinguish it from other types of dispute, the term "immediate" (*sadyas*) is applied to "dispute.
Regarding the seventh, "having dispute but not immediate speech," this cites the negative to reveal the positive; that is, by citing other disputes, it shows what is not [immediate].
This statement reveals the preceding dispute; it is precisely that statement.

The third section provides an extensive analysis, which is the characteristic of distinguishing the correct from the incorrect. Based on the seven preceding gates, it is explained in successive order.
What is meant by "the statement"? It refers to the dispute over words. Having restated the initial question, it is then extensively explained: "If a bhikṣu," and so forth, serves to cite [the case].

Regarding the person who initiates the dispute: this distinguishes them from the rest of the assembly. They dispute with those of a different class, as they are not bound by the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
This applies to monks; it is the same when contrasted with nuns—that is, when nuns dispute with nuns. For now, however, we shall explain this by way of reference to monks.

As for the term "disputing speech" (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), it distinguishes this from the other three types of disputes. By the phrase "by means of eighteen matters," the objects of dispute are collectively enumerated, such as what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma (*adharma*), and so forth.

The specific categories of the disputes are listed separately. Regarding those who dispute with one another by means of such characteristics: this collectively reveals the nature of dispute as mutual combat and mutual discord;

it generally demonstrates the faults of dispute, wherein each party clings to their own view and does not follow the words of others, mutually accusing and destroying one another—hence it is said, "up to and including discord.
This constitutes the concluding summary. What is meant by "disputes concerning speech and non-speech"?
The second formal inquiry: If one cites common worldly virtuous speech and uses it as an analogy for the virtuous speech of a bhikṣu, this is not a "dispute over speech" (*vāda-vivāda*);
this constitutes the lower conclusion. What, then, is a dispute over speech? It is precisely that which speaks. This is the third formal inquiry.

The explanation and conclusion are the same as before. What is meant by "it is precisely contention"? This is the restatement of the fourth question; the explanation and conclusion are likewise the same. What is meant by "it is not contention"? This is the restatement of the fifth question;
the explanation and conclusion follow the previous pattern. What is meant by "contention is precisely speech"? This is the restatement and explanation of the sixth.
What is "dispute that is not speech"? This is the seventh [section], which restates and explains [the topic].
Next, the dispute of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā-vivāda*) shall also be explained by way of three gates: first, a general presentation of four propositions by cross-referencing dispute and seeking;

second, distinguishing the correct from the incorrect by means of these [propositions], opening up seven categories; third, a detailed analysis and explanation of the characteristics of distinguishing the correct from the incorrect. Now, within this text:

There are only four general propositions at the outset: first, seeking for what is sought; second, what is sought for seeking; third, seeking for what is sought; and fourth, what is sought for seeking. The first two form one pair, which generally refer to seeking while specifically referring to disputes;

they differ from one another in their mutual relationship and are intended to distinguish them from other forms of seeking. The latter two form another pair, which generally refer to both seeking and disputes;
they differ from one another in their mutual relationship and are intended to distinguish them from other forms of seeking as well as from other disputes. This is why [the distinctions must be made].

Regarding "exclusion" (*vinodana*): since other types of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*) do not give rise to disputes, there is no need to eliminate those other disputes through this principle, as they are eliminated by other remedies;

therefore, they are not included here. If these instances of seeking were themselves disputes, they would have to be eliminated through methods such as "recollection" (*smṛti*); for this reason, they must be excluded. Next, seven sections are opened.

Following that, the two categories of dispute regarding matters of offenses (*āpatti-vastu*) previously mentioned are explained; because the underlying principles are the same, it is stated: "it is also as above."
From here below is the third section, concerning the method for extinguishing [faults] through the correspondence of illness and medicine. This is divided into three parts:

first, up to "the Sangha is also like this," which generally clarifies the right and wrong of what is present; second, from "Ānanda" onwards until "all are extinguished," which clarifies the specific methods of extinction.

This section clearly explains the method for extinguishing disputes through the correspondence between medicine and illness. From the third section on Upāli onwards, there are general inquiries regarding self-accusation as being either valid or invalid;

since this constitutes the foundation of the "present assembly" (pratyakṣa-saṃgha) medicine, one first discriminates between what is valid and what is invalid. That which is invalid is to be discarded.

This [section] follows the practical application; as for the section on disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), it need not be further elaborated here, as it refers back to the preceding text, being concise and essential in meaning.

Furthermore, the subsequent requirement to inquire whether one admits to being right or wrong arises because this had not yet been examined above. Within the initial section on "manifest before the assembly" (*saṃmukha-vinaya*), the text is divided into two parts:
first, up to the phrase "the Sangha is also like this," which generally clarifies what is improper and exposes the faults so that they may be abandoned. Second...
If a bhikṣu has already correctly understood the Dharma as it is, this constitutes the practice of settling disputes through speech (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).

Within such disputes, two factors—the facts of the case and the application of legal procedures—serve as the basis for evaluating right and wrong, thereby giving rise to contention. Since the principles of the Dharma are revealed through the teachings, the *Tripitaka* masters rely on the scriptures to determine whether the principles are right or wrong;
thus, the underlying sentiments of the dispute are eventually pacified. Therefore, by directly confronting the present situation, one is able to...
Extinction is attained. The remaining two types of dispute are not adjudicated by evaluating the right and wrong of their underlying principles through the *pratyakṣa* (presence) method alone;

these cannot be extinguished independently, but must be resolved according to the appropriate prescriptions. Herein, "presence" (*pratyakṣa*) is explained in a general sense regarding right and wrong, rather than specifically referring to what is currently intended for resolution.

For the time being, I shall employ a single method to explain this passage; it does not mean that it refers to the minor category of verbal disputes (*vāda-vivāda*) that are to be formally settled. It is as follows: one...
In the *jñapti* (motion), two *jñaptis* are made; the assembly of monks then sits in dispute. Regarding this *karmavācanā*, one person says:

"The initial *jñapti* was already established, and the subsequent *jñapti* was redundant; by performing this rite, it is accomplished. Another person says: "The performance of the rite is not accomplished. Thus they quarrel and contend with one another.
A mediator is taken to determine right from wrong. Among the sixteen phrases, they are divided into two positions; the first consists of twelve phrases.
Three are non-dharmas. Next, there are four phrases. Five are non-dharmas. Three are non-dharmas. Regarding the twelve [cases]:
first, one bhikṣu; second, two bhikṣus; third, three bhikṣus. Each serves as the head for four phrases, as in the text. Therefore, the text says: "If it is one bhikṣu..."

This refers to the person who settles disputes. Next, the phrase "in the presence of a single bhikṣu" means that the disputing parties, regarding the meaning of what they say, come together before one person.

"One who speaks with skillful instruction" means one who falsely establishes principles to reconcile both sides, summarizing their intentions and asserting what is wrong as being right. Therefore, "if it is confused" briefly refers to the matter being disputed.

This does not mean that what has already been settled is invalid; rather, it refers to the person who adjudicates the matter acting contrary to the Dharma, up to and including acting contrary to the Buddha’s teaching.

This statement serves to exclude those matters that have been settled, because the preceding legal principles are established as being truly in accordance with the Dharma and thus cannot be rendered invalid. The passage beginning with "He speaks such words" and following explains why [the previous ruling] is not correct;

hence the phrase "speaks such words. Up to the point of "this is contrary to the Buddha’s teaching," this is what constitutes non-Dharma (*adharma*). When the Dharma is manifest, one should act accordingly.
To accept and practice [this] is to falsely encourage the acceptance of [an invalid] decision. This is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; it is manifest as such.

Regarding the phrase "the matter of dispute having been settled," this concludes its illegality: namely, that what was previously not established is falsely judged to be established, which is inconsistent with the Noble Teaching.
Because it is a procedure for the dharma that is currently ceasing, it is called "non-dharma" (adharma); yet because it also possesses three factors, it is termed "resembling" (pratirūpa).
The subsequent eleven categories are likewise the same. The following four or five dharmas that are non-dharmas are also to be understood by analogy with what was previously explained.

Next, the sixteen phrases within the section on "Suchness" (*tathatā*) are distinguished. The first twelve phrases concern the suchness of the three dharmas; the next four concern the suchness of the five dharmas.

Regarding the single monk: within the section on the monk, there are four parts: (1) the citation of the three factors being present before one's eyes; (2) the conclusion establishing the suchness, beginning with "If he has acted in this way...";
(3) the restatement of the names followed by their explanation, beginning with "In this regard..."; and (4) "If a monk... and so forth.
The following section establishes the offense for the initiator. Regarding the first passage, "the three factors being present before one":

if a monk who is resolving a dispute stands before another monk, the initiator [of the dispute] must have a person present, because such a person is required. This constitutes the presence of the person consisting of both the agent and the object.
Second, regarding the phrase "having spoken with kind words," etc., this is discussed by way of a single example. For instance, as if one person were holding...

If one wishes to forget [the formal motion] but does not announce it, and the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is nevertheless performed, that person says: "Since the *chanda* (consent) was not announced, the assembly is incomplete (*abhikṣu-saṃgha*) and the act is invalid. This other person says:
"Since one has already arrived within the assembly, even if the announcement is not made, it is nonetheless accomplished. This dharma is entrusted for the purpose of settling the dispute.

As for the phrasing of the text—using "good words," "instructive speech," and first stating the underlying principle—it is because it harmonizes both parties; thus it is said to be "as between those two" and "in accordance with the Dharma."
"Even unto what has been taught by the Buddha": this indicates that the *karmavācanā* (formal procedure) under dispute is actually accomplished.

Therefore it is said: "In accordance with the Dharma," because it can eliminate evil and give rise to good; "in accordance with the Vinaya," because it accords with the Noble Teaching; and "in accordance with the Buddha's instruction.

Following the phrase "having spoken thus," it refers to the one who terminates the dispute, who likewise approves of the preceding method as being correct. Therefore it is said: "even unto what has been taught by the Buddha."
This is the presence of the Dharma (*dharmasammukha*). You should accept this with forbearance and be exhorted to uphold it;

this is the presence of the Vinaya (*vinayasammukha*) for its circulation. Next is the formal conclusion of the presence; next is the explanation of the presence, which may be understood from the text. Fourth is the conclusion regarding the offense of instigation.

Three types of persons initiate [a dispute]: first, the person who sits and interrupts the proceedings; second, a person who arrives later; and third, one who has newly received the precepts—meaning this refers to the initial disputant. "Initial" here means "new.

This means that in relation to the two others, such as the one who arrives later, [the interrupter] thinks: "I was not present when they were sitting; I should expect that the dispute, which has not yet been extinguished, would apply equally to me.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha judged this to be an initial dispute. However, provided that it has been extinguished, all [disputes] are [resolved].
This has already been extinguished; it does not mean that, in relation to what has already occurred, it is not extinguished. Therefore, it is called the "first. Both incur the offense of *pārājika*.
The next eleven cases are the same as before and may be understood accordingly. The Sangha constitutes one [category], while the bhikṣus are divided into four: (1) the five factors being present;

(2) from "if it is thus" onwards, the establishment of the name and its accomplishment; (3) the citation of the name and its explanation; (4) the manifestation of the originating offense. First, the five [factors].

In the context of "being present" (*sammukha*), the specific boundaries are omitted for brevity. Regarding the three types of "being present": as for the "Dharma being present," it refers to upholding the principles of what is right and wrong.
As for the "Vinaya being present," it refers to upholding these principles in order to encourage the acceptance [of discipline] and the cessation of disputes.

Regarding the "person being present through the exchange of meaning," this clarifies the matter by encompassing both the subject and the object together. "The Saṃgha being present" refers to those who are in harmony.

This refers to internal formal acts (*karmavācanā*). "Establishing a restriction" means establishing a ritual boundary (*dharmasīmā*), in order to distinguish it from the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*). Regarding the four types of individuals who initiate [the act]:
these are those who grant their consent (*chanda*), those who later regret [granting it], and the three subsequent categories.

Next, the second method for settling disputes is explained. There are four [methods] corresponding to the extinction of the four types of disputes. The text states that there are three types of disputes.
First is the general question and answer regarding the quantity of the medicinal remedies used, which serves to distinguish them from the other five remedies.

Next, from Ānanda onwards, there are specific questions and answers that demonstrate the methods for thorough extinction. Third is the comparison of the superiority and inferiority between the mediators who settle disputes and the five types of partisans. Regarding the former:
Regarding the general question and answer: Since the intent of the question involves seven remedies, it was not yet known how many remedies are applied to verbal disputes (*vāda*).

Therefore, it asks, "By how many cessations are they ceased? The Buddha also answers generally: "Among these seven remedies, only two types are used—namely, presence (*sammukha*) and the majority opinion (*yadbhūyaḥkṣānti*).

Thus, he says, "They are ceased by two cessations. The reason for this is explained as follows: verbal disputes arise from evaluating whether principles are correct or erroneous. Regarding the Dharma...

They disputed over right and wrong, each claiming their own position was correct and unable to reach a definitive conclusion; consequently, they gave rise to contention. However, the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and their underlying principles are recorded in the teachings.

Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master, relying on the principles of the Noble Teachings, edited, corrected, and adjudicated the matter, using the consensus of the majority present to determine what was right and wrong.
Once the correct and the false were distinguished, the contentious emotions were extinguished, and the medicine [of the teaching] was applied to the illness [of the dispute].
Therefore, these two [methods] are employed; the remaining five are not the remedies for this. It is like the three *vinayas* used in the search (*mārgaṇā*):

a dispute arises from persons when their purity or impurity has not yet been distinguished, and thus the dispute is produced. One must employ *smṛti-vinaya* (recollection) and *amūḍha-vinaya* (absence of delusion).

When those who are pure are determined and those who are turbid are determined, once purity and turbidity are distinguished, the dispute is thereby extinguished. This is their remedy; hence it is called "the adjudication of disputes" (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*).

[The dispute] arises from principle (*nyāya*). Even if one employs the three methods such as recollection (*smṛti*) and so forth, although they may determine whether a person is pure or turbid, they do not distinguish the characteristics of the principle;

thus, disputes still arise spontaneously. Since these are not the remedies for this [situation], they need not be employed. Furthermore, regarding the arising of a dispute over an offense, it concerns the lightness or gravity of the offense committed by the disputant.

Moreover, because a dispute arises from treating someone arbitrarily based on an adherence to their commission of an offense, it is necessary to have the person themselves state their own transgression in order to establish the legal determination.

Regarding the gravity [of offenses]: if individuals conspire with one another over the years, claiming that their transgressions have not been extinguished, they must employ "covering with grass" (*tṛṇapraticchādana*).

This refers to disputing the underlying principle rather than disputing the specific offense; it is not the case that all violations are identical in their gravity. Why, then, would one need to employ "self-accusation" (*svavacana*) or "covering with grass"?

Furthermore, if the fundamental principle is pure, what use is there for self-accusation, which involves taking the fault upon oneself? The principle must be made manifest; why resort to "covering with grass"?
Now, these two types of cessation merely resolve disputes; they do not punish the person or extinguish their offenses.

Next, the text is explained below. As in the previous interpretation of the text, there are three parts. First, up to the point "the Saṃgha is also like this," it concerns the settlement through simple presence (*sammukhavinaya*).

The minor grade of verbal dispute: second, when those disputing bhikṣus cannot endure the first [method], it is subsequently extinguished by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya* (extinction in the presence of).
The middling grade of verbal dispute: third, at that time in Śrāvastī and below, it is extinguished by employing both medicines in total.
It is said that this is the highest grade of verbal dispute (*vāda-vivāda*). This is not necessarily so.

If one examines the categories in detail according to their sequential order, from a single individual up to the speech of a multitude, there are nine successive stages of progression. Within these nine, if the matter is clarified, it should be resolved and extinguished at its very source.
This constitutes the cessation of the nine grounds. If it is not settled as such, the procedure for the majority (yadbhūyasikīya) is concluded.
Since there is a sense of mutual circulation among these three types, he [the proponent] should take back the voting sticks (śalākā) he himself distributed and go to a secluded place.

If the count is not according to the Dharma and the sticks are in the majority, he should cause them to rise again and sit at a distance from one another, whispering privately: "This is the speech of the Dharma; this is the speech of the Vinaya; this is what was taught by the Buddha."
"Venerable sir, you should relinquish this; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha.
Having spoken thus, because the voting sticks were cast once more, the current interpretation need not be restricted to an explanation based on the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior.

The main text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of settling through *pratideśanīya* (confession) alone. Second, from "At that time, in Śrāvastī... onwards, the settlement by means of the two *vinayas*.
The first part is further divided into two: first, a question and answer concerning whether, although it was previously stated that [the *saṃmukhavinaya*] is used, it can be used alone;

second, whether the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (majority decision) is not used when the *saṃmukhavinaya* is employed. This is not a separate inquiry. The Buddha said: "There is," thus providing a specific question and answer.
Why did he not ask further: "Does the Buddha ever have disputes regarding speech? Does he employ the 'majority' (yadbhūyaḥ) rather than the 'presence' (sammukha)?
The explanation is: Ānanda already knew that the "presence" is the root of all medicines; therefore, he asked about employing the "majority" alone.

Because it is not separate from what is present before one, there is no need to ask about it. However, as for the *bahujana-vāda* (the majority decision), it is exclusively capable of resolving disputes within the Saṃgha;

because there is a distinction [between this and other methods], the "present before" (*sammukha*) Saṃgha refers to those who have not all assembled within the boundary (*sīmā*). In the case of the *bahujana-vāda*, only those who are wise and upright are selected to resolve the dispute.

In the case of the Saṃgha where all have assembled, there is no need for such selection; they may assemble from the entire boundary, with the sole exception of those who have granted their consent (*chanda*).
As for this, the principle of external exclusion (*bahiṣkaraṇa*) is largely the same as that of the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Therefore, the *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (decision by the majority) may not be applied separately. Second, regarding the question "What is...? and so forth, there follows one question and answer:

the essence of the Buddha’s dharma of arising and ceasing can be categorized into eight types according to the person who effects the cessation: first, cessation by a single bhikṣu; second, by two bhikṣus; third, by three bhikṣus; and so on.
4. When the fourfold assembly has completed the act for the bhikṣu, the meaning of "being present" therein is as explained above; in this case, the saṃgha is dissolved. 5.

If those disputing bhikṣus are unable to proceed according to the Dharma on the road, [the offense] from the phrase below down to "pāyattika" is as explained above regarding the dissolution of the saṃgha in a different territory.
6. If those disputing bhikṣus are unable to proceed halfway, [the offense] from the phrase below down to "pāyattika" is as explained above regarding a different [territory].

The first [type of] *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is extinguished by three persons who are *tripiṭaka*-holders within the same boundary (*sīmā*). The second is extinguished by two persons who are *tripiṭaka*-holders, down to one or two persons.
The third is extinguished by one person who is a *tripiṭaka*-holder within a different boundary, down to one person. These eight [cases] are capable of extinguishing the offense among human beings.

If distinguished by boundary, the first four concern persons within the same boundary, while the latter four concern persons in different boundaries. If categorized according to those present, there are five types; the first...

The three [cases] at the end [are resolved] by means of the three dharmas being present for extinction; the two assemblies of four and five [members] are resolved by means of the five dharmas being present for extinction.
As for the number of persons: the first four proceed from one person up to a *saṃgha*, while the latter four proceed from a *saṃgha* down to one person.

Now, regarding the eightfold division into upper and lower [categories], this does not depend on whether the dharmas are three or five, nor is it restricted to the number of persons or the identity of the boundary (*sīmā*); rather, it depends solely on...
The person who adjudicates disputes according to the Tripiṭaka establishes the sequence based on the superiority or inferiority of their practice and realization.

First, it clarifies the extinction [of a dispute] by means of a single bhikṣu, which is also divided into four sections: (1) extinction through the presence of the Three Jewels; (2) the establishment of extinction by assigning names to those from Ānanda downward;
(3) the explanation of the meaning of "presence"; and (4) the section on the offenses that should be initiated, which is abbreviated. If there is one bhikṣu...
When persons such as the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra appear before us, and after favorable words have been spoken down to the point that "this is the Buddha’s teaching," the Dharma appears before us.

Since one wishes to establish a definitive resolution (*viniscaya*), one must first bring forth the points of contention (*vivāda*). What constitutes these points of contention? They are, for example, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) found in the *Dvādaśadvāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Twelve Gates), where the phrasing is identical but the meaning differs, or the meaning is identical but the phrasing differs.

Through these, the definitive resolution is fully attained. For now, however, we shall discuss this by way of the distinction between the prohibitive (*pratiṣedha*) and the essential (*svabhāva*). As for those who establish the formal argument (*sthāpanā-vādin*), they speak in broad terms.
The gravity of offenses regarding the nature of equality is heavy, whereas those concerning prohibited acts such as acting as a matchmaker for marriages are light.

As for the "discussant," since both parties belong to the same chapter [of the Vinaya], how can there be a distinction between light and heavy? Before right and wrong have been distinguished, they give rise to dispute. This matter is then submitted to the Tripitaka masters to determine what is right and what is wrong.
"One who delights in the words of the teaching" refers to one who judges right and wrong based on the formal teachings. "This is Dharma and this is Vinaya" refers to a general statement.

Regarding the "one who establishes the meaning" (*vādī*): because they speak in accordance with principle and propriety, and are able to extinguish evil and give rise to goodness, it is said that "this is the Dharma and this is the Vinaya.
Because it does not contradict the teachings of the Sage, it is called "the instruction of the Buddha. As for the phrase "he speaks thus," it refers to the one who settles disputes.

The Master of the Establishment of Meaning (Siddhāntavādin) was thus certified; because this accords with the Buddha’s intention, it is said that "that which is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya is the teaching of the Buddha.
As for the preceding statement, "the Dharma is present before you; accept this, endure this," it is an exhortation to embrace it, to settle the mind upon it, and not to abandon it.

This is the *vinaya* [settlement] in the presence of others. The remaining meanings are as above. Two bhikṣus effect the settlement; three bhikṣus effect the settlement as above; therefore, it is stated in both cases, "it is also thus.
Regarding the fourth, the settlement by the Saṃgha, there are two parts. First, it is said that the Saṃgha is also thus; this refers to the judgment of settlement before the Saṃgha.
Second, from the passage "The Buddha said to Ānanda" onwards, the settlement occurs on the road without being before the Saṃgha. The first three instances involve settlement in specific locations.

The *mārga-pratyaya-nirghāta* (extinction by way of the path) is omitted. Within the *saṃgha-purataḥ-pratyaya-nirghāta* (extinction before the Saṃgha), there are four [cases] regarding the object of the action;

as above, there are four texts for the first case where one person is confronted. The same applies to two or three members of the Saṃgha. In the *mārga-pratyaya-nirghāta*, the text contains the first three [cases], while the *samutthāna* (origination) is omitted.
Although this involves going to another location, if it is now extinguished, it is still due to the power of the previous Saṃgha; thus, the fifth [case] is the Saṃgha.
Chinese Text II. First, up to the *pāyattika* [offense], it is extinguished as in the case of the *saṃgha*. Second, from "those disputing bhikṣus" onwards, it is deliberated upon while on the road;
it is not extinguished in the presence of the *saṃgha*. The preceding section has three parts: first, up to "abandon this matter of dispute," it concerns the method for entrusting the dispute.
Second, from "this *saṃgha* should speak to that bhikṣu" onwards, it concerns how one should accept the dispute in this manner.
The Ritual for Teaching Monks to Accept a Dispute. Third, following the acceptance, this section demonstrates the methods for the Saṃgha to extinguish a dispute.

Within this, there are four parts: first, up to "abandoning this dispute," it explains the origin and basis of the dispute already arisen, its general underlying intent, and the request for its extinction and abandonment.
Second, from "If the Elder cannot act according to the Dharma" onwards, it correctly clarifies the illegal methods of extinguishing a dispute, thereby causing the dispute [to persist].

Profound and grave. [The Buddha] fears that they will not extinguish it according to the Dharma. Third, the section beginning with "If not according to the Dharma" clarifies that it is not merely the arising of disputes, but that they may lead to a schism in the Saṃgha and cause dissatisfaction in one's dwelling.
Fourth, the section beginning with "Those disputing bhikṣus" concludes by exhorting them to abandon the matter.
The first part has three sections. First, from the beginning up to "to the elder," he states his purpose for coming; herein there are five sub-phrases.
I have here summarized this matter of dispute. Next, I shall explain its fundamental cause; thus it says, "In this way it arose," and so forth.
Next, "The Saṃgha acts in this way to extinguish [the dispute]" introduces the aforementioned extinction by the Saṃgha. Next, "I do not accept" expresses my own refusal to accept [the decision].
Since the dispute has not yet been quelled, next, "Therefore," and so forth, concludes the underlying intention. Second, from "Excellent, Elder," and below, is the request.

Regarding the extinction of a legal matter (*dharmavinaya*) by means of its opposite, as opposed to the previous method of extinction: the third section, beginning with "If, Venerable Sir, you can for our sake...

and so forth, demonstrates the ability to relinquish and accept the fourfold resolution of disputes. From the first point up to "extinguishing this dispute," it correctly clarifies the exhortation to speak according to reality.

I shall now deliberate on what is appropriate and evaluate which [method] is in accordance with the Dharma. Within this, there are four parts; the first concerns the "Venerable One" and the "matter of dispute."

1. Regarding the person who has initiated the dispute: this refers to summarizing the matter of the dispute. "If it is thus," and so forth, refers to investigating the root cause of the dispute. 3. "As that Saṃgha settled the dispute":
this refers to investigating the legal procedures used by the previous Saṃgha to settle it. 4. "If one can speak according to reality," and so forth:

this encourages reliance on truthful speech and recommends evaluating and settling the matter accordingly. Second, "If the Elder, regarding the matter of the dispute," and so forth: this correctly clarifies that the statement made was not in accordance with the facts.

[The first section] concerns the reality [of the matter]. It does not examine whether one has grasped the meaning in judging a dispute; rather, it seeks to ensure that the purification is profound and heavy, and to cause fear so that one speaks according to the Dharma.

The third section, from "that which is non-Dharma and non-Vinaya" onwards, serves to demonstrate that there is not merely the arising of a dispute, but also the harm of causing a schism in the Saṃgha and distressing the assembly;

thus, it explains the necessity of the true intent. The fourth section is the formal conclusion and exhortation regarding the method for accepting disputes. The text on the settlement of disputes consists of two parts: the first concludes the preceding [section]. The second...

The text on the two *samyak-prahāṇas* (right abandonments) consists of four sections. First, up to the phrase "one should thus extinguish the dispute," it establishes the correct method for extinguishing disputes.

Second, from "if one has acted in this way" onwards, it clarifies that the name of the settlement is "extinguished. Third, from "the meaning of being present before" onwards, it explains the meaning of "being present before" as above.
Fourth, it clarifies the offense of the instigator as above. Within the preceding section on extinction, there are four parts. First, it states [the procedure] as taught by the Buddha...

1. Instruction on the place for settling disputes among bhikṣus. 2. If the Saṃgha, having formed such a thought [as described below], assists this bhikṣu, they must select a person capable of adjudicating the matter.

3. If that disputed matter has not been settled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, down to the point where they acknowledge the matter as such, they should instruct the Saṃgha whether to proceed. 4. The Saṃgha should then speak to those disputing bhikṣus... [and so forth].
This clearly explains the cessation [of disputes]. First, the placement of the disputing parties is as stated in the text. Second, the section on the examination of persons has five parts:
first, it clarifies the Sangha’s deliberation and discernment; second, from "The Buddha told Ānanda" onwards, it prescribes the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the assembly of wise bhikṣus.

Third, regarding the ten qualities required of a person to be appointed as an official: according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, two monks must be selected from among the assembly for each of the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) that require resolution;
both are to be appointed by a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). This *Vinaya* (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*) and the seven hundred items [of the *Karmavastu*] are likewise the same as that.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one should first reflect upon one’s own physical strength, the power of merit, the power of eloquence, the power of fearlessness, and knowledge of the conditions of the matter.
[He] rises. There is such power as this that the strife of the preceding minds may be extinguished.
Among the four types of monks who settle disputes, [the procedure] begins with the formal motion (*jñapti*) to dismiss three individuals; the procedure for these three is as stated in the text.

Fifth, regarding the person of complete virtue among those sitting in the assembly of monks who settle disputes—one who follows the correct principle and acts as a virtuous companion—if the one previously performing the formal motion [is not qualified], [then...]

They are excluded from the category of those who adjudicate legal matters (*adhikaraṇa-vinaya*). If they are within the boundary (*sīmā*), their consent (*chanda*) must be obtained in its entirety, as explained in the *Saptavargika-vastu*.
Regarding the path, it is not included among the "extinguishments before the Saṃgha. Furthermore, there are four [cases] as mentioned above.

The sixth case, concerning the extinction by a multitude of bhikṣus, clearly explains the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) as detailed above. As for the two cases of extinction by seven or eight [bhikṣus], they are to be understood according to what is stated in the sixth case.
It is stated that it is also thus. Furthermore, when comparing six to seven, and seven to eight, the "pathway-extinction" (*mārga-nirodha*) is omitted.

From this point downward is the second section, which employs the two types of extinction (*nirodha*). This text has two parts: first, up to the point where he rebukes [the offender], raising and manifesting the circumstances of the transgression;

second, from the point where he addresses the bhikṣus onward, prescribing the use of the "decision by a majority" (*yadbhūya-vāda*). Within the former [section], there are three parts. The first ends as above.

Regarding the monk who manifests contention and does not accept the eight methods of settling disputes: herein, from the beginning up to "does not accept," it refers to the Saṃgha’s settlement of the matter of dispute;
that is to say, the monk cannot be settled by the first four methods. Next, from "having heard that he resides there" onwards, it means he cannot be settled by the [first] four.
Second, from "those monks who are disputing" onwards, they bring the case forward and report it to the Buddha. Third, from "the World-Honored One" onwards, he rebukes him.

In the second section, "The Extinction of the Right Teaching," there are two parts. First, citing the fundamental tenets and establishing the application of the *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (majority decision) through multiple persons, two topical headings are set forth:
first, the heading on the application of the *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti*; second, the heading on the appointment of persons, specifically the appointment of those who distribute the *śalākā* (voting sticks).
From "The second [section] has five dharmas" onwards, the ritual procedures are explained in detail. Within this, there are two parts: first, the method for the cessation [of disputes];

second, from "There are ten ways that are not according to the Dharma" onwards, the correctness or incorrectness of taking voting sticks (*śalākā*) is distinguished. In the former part, there are two sections:

the first is the selection of persons based on their virtues, which extensively explains the second section on the procedure for appointing persons; the second is from "There are three kinds" onwards, which extensively explains the previous section on using the majority vote (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*).
Within this section, there are three parts: first, stating the number; second, listing their names according to that number;
and third, from "How so" onwards, a detailed exposition of the three characteristics. These constitute three sub-sections: first, the manifest; second, the concealed; and third, the whispered.
In the first section, "The Manifest," there are four parts. First, from the beginning up to "thus the dispute is settled," which correctly demonstrates the settling of disputes.
Second, from "This is for Ānanda" onwards, which summarizes their names. Third, from "How so? onwards, which cites the names and provides an explanation.

Fourth, from "If one acts in this way" onwards, which concludes by identifying the fault of the instigation. Within the section on settling, there are two parts; the first extends up to "the matter of dispute."

Extinguishing [the dispute]. One should extinguish it by means of the assembly at that very place. Second, if there are few monks who act according to the Dharma, one should seek another assembly from outside to extinguish it.
The preceding text has four parts: first, explaining the five kinds of *śalākā* (voting sticks);

second, "one should perform two kinds," etc., which prescribes the making of two kinds of *śalākā* in order to manifest the distinction between the two types of dharmas—right and wrong. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are two kinds of counting sticks (*cūḍā*): one long and one short.
Short [version]: One black and one white. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* is also like this. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "Dharmic voting sticks" and "non-dharmic voting sticks.
After three times performing the *śalākā* (voting sticks), one proceeds with the formal motion (*jñapti*) for the distribution of the sticks. Above this, the Dharma is made manifest.

After four times performing the *śalākā*, one proclaims the cessation according to the Dharma; herein, the *vinaya* is made manifest. The other three [types of] manifestation may be understood accordingly.
Knowing this, he seeks elsewhere for another to extinguish the internal turmoil; having caused the disturbance, he then departs.
He leaves it to the five virtuous men to judge whether he should be promoted or not, and he is categorized as one type and sent away. The final three sections are as in the text.

Next is *parivāsa* (concealment), and next is *mānāpya* (probation). Regarding these two types, they follow the fifth case in the section on "non-manifestation" (*aprakāśana*), because in that assembly, those who act contrary to the Dharma are numerous, and thus it is entirely invalid.
In the section on the "proper extinction" of *mānāpya*, there should be five textual items;
one must add the procedure for performing *mānāpya*, while the remainder follows what was explained previously.
Next, the "As-Non" (如非) is explained. First, regarding the "As-Non," ten categories are listed; second, from "How so? onwards is the explanation.
The distinctions between the *jñapti-dvitīya* and *jñapti-caturtha* [procedures] refer to the differences in *karmavācanā*.

As for the determination of minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*), it refers either to the recollection of having committed an offense—meaning the fifth category of transgression was not intentional—or to an offense that may be settled through face-to-face confession. Or...

To "act with the intention" means to give rise to the thought of wishing to commit [an offense]. This is not an offense at all. If one were to evaluate these cases, it would be improper to cast the voting tally (*śalākā*), for if one casts it, it is not done intentionally.

Furthermore, it is said that if one evaluates a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), one may either perform a confession before another person (*pratyekapratideśana*) or perform a mental confession (*manasā-pratideśana*).
Both [procedures] are according to the Dharma. If, when distributing the voting lots (*śalākā*), one is certain to be right and the other wrong, it is termed a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
If the distribution of the voting lots is in accordance with the Dharma, the opposite case may be understood as wrong.

Third, regarding the adjudicators of legal cases, there are five points as in the preceding section: first, the enumeration; second, the listing of names; third, the explanation of the names starting from "How" (*kathaṃ*);

fourth, the analysis of the four permutations, such as "not acting with the body but acting with speech," and so forth; and fifth, the illustration through the *Caturvarga-vinaya*. As for the adjudicators of legal cases, they are as described in the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
The fourth category consists of those who manifest harsh speech and provide instructions while sharing the same views. This refers to the manifestation of evil through body and speech;

that is, sharing the same views as those who do not act according to the Dharma. This may be manifested through bodily expression or verbal expression. Such individuals are not fit to adjudicate legal matters.

The remaining phrases may be understood by mutual analogy. The fourth section, from "Among these" onwards, compares their relative superiority and inferiority, enabling one to resolve matters when in an assembly.
The fifth section serves as the conclusion for the subsequent part.

The second section, the text on seeking [a resolution for] disputes (*mṛga-vivāda*), has two parts. First is the general question and answer regarding the quantity of the medicinal application, intended to distinguish it from the other three [types of disputes]. The question is:
why are only these four used, and why are the other three unnecessary? To explain the *mṛga-vivāda* under discussion: disputes arise from persons.

One must employ the presence of witnesses, recollection, non-delusion, the specific offense, and the location; these determine whether a person is pure or turbid, whereby the contentious emotions are eventually stilled.

Because the medicine and the ailment correspond, seeking those who do not adjudicate according to principle is not the appropriate remedy; what use, then, would there be for the *mahājanavāda* (decision by majority)?

Furthermore, since one does not dispute whether a prior offense was grave or light, why would there be a need for self-accusation or the *tṛṇapraticchādana* (covering with grass)? Therefore, only four methods are employed: the two types of separate questioning and separate [decision].

Answer: Regarding the ritual for administering medicine, it is divided into three parts according to its application: first, mindfulness (*smṛti*) that is present before one; second, the place (*sthāna*) that is present before one;
and third, the inquiry as to why [the latter] is not asked. Is there perhaps a case where mindfulness alone is employed without the presence [of the other factors]?

This question is not raised because the presence [of the object] is essential as the foundation of all medicines; thus, these three—mindfulness and so forth—are not to be understood as occurring simultaneously.
In this section on recollection (*anusmṛti*), there are four parts: first, the preliminary questions and answers that distinguish the ritual procedures and their respective proportions;

second, from "Furthermore, having asked... onwards, the actual presentation of the essence of the method; third, within this [second part], there are four sections: (1) the actual cessation; (2) from "If it is thus...
onwards, the summary of its names; (3) from "Among these... onwards, the citation of names followed by their explanation; and (4) the conclusion identifying the originator of the teaching.
Regarding the offense, the text on its formal extinction consists of three parts. First, from the beginning up to "the interrogation did not cease," it reveals the faults of his dispute.

Second, from "Ānanda, the Saṃgha should grant" onwards, it explains the granting of the *smṛtivinaya* (discipline of recollection) as described above. Third, from "there are three kinds of illegality" onwards, it distinguishes between what is correct and what is incorrect.
First, it clarifies the three types of methods that are not correct; next, it distinguishes the five types of methods that are not correct, as can be understood from the text itself.

The enumeration of names and the explanation of this offense do not include *karma*, *smṛti*, or *amūḍha-vinaya*. These are also *vinaya*. *Pratyakṣa-amūḍha* is explained according to the rules for *smṛti*.

Next, within the section on the presence of the offense and the location, there are likewise four [categories] as above. Within the first, "the actual extinction," three [categories] are also as above.
Regarding the third, "that which is non-accordant" (*asādhu*), first concerning the non-accordance of the three dharmas: first non-accordant and later accordant; each has [its own sub-categories].

The third [point] is as stated in the text. If "as" (yathā) were not "not-as" (ayathā), then the relative relationship between "more" and "less" would be like what is explained in the *Campa* [Sūtra]. Next, regarding the five dharmas that are "as" and "not-as":
among these five "not-ases," if one does not state it oneself from the outset, there would be no basis for the subtle blue to be perceived; therefore, it must be stated by oneself.

If one has already made a confession, how can one be assigned a formal charge (*sthāpanārha*)? Answer: Because of the previous confession, which was made with a desire to conceal [the offense], the wording was not pure;
