that is to say, because he had previously cited a *pārājika* offense as having been committed, it was improper to take him for disciplinary action.

If the wording had been pure, it would have been proper [to proceed], yet it was improper to treat him [as such]. Such treatment would have been contrary to the Dharma, because he was concealing his offense. Therefore, it is said: "This offense is further..."
One must perform the formal act of *ukkhepana* (reproval) and *sativinaya* (remembrance).

Regarding the third section on the text for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), there are two parts: first, the general question and answer; and second, the determination of the application of the medicines [of settlement].

Only three methods—the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (presence), *patisāraṇīya* (verbal confession), and *tassapāpiyasika* (covering over as if with grass)—are employed. The reason other methods are not used here is that within this context, the entire community has collectively committed an offense.

Regarding offenses, one must deliberate upon their gravity. If one were to arbitrarily evaluate the circumstances of another’s transgression, it would cause the monastic community to fall into prolonged dispute.

To extinguish such strife, it is essential to accept the individual's own confession as evidence; thus, one does not unjustly punish those who are pure. Furthermore, by discerning the gravity of the offense, the contentious emotions will subside.

If parties support one another and the dispute remains difficult to quell, one must employ the "covering over with grass" (tṛṇaprastāraka) method, so that the medicine and the disease may correspond. Therefore, these three methods are utilized. Since [your] reasoning is not permitted, how can you claim otherwise?

The *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (majority decision) is employed. Furthermore, since it has already been stated that the evaluation determines whether an offense is light or heavy, rather than disputing over its purity or impurity, what is the use of the three methods such as *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection)?
In the second section, beginning with Ānanda, there are separate questions and answers, which consist of two parts:

first, the question regarding *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused), and second, the question regarding *tṛṇaprastāraka* (settlement by covering over as with grass). Within the former, there are two sections; the first consists of a question and answer that distinguishes the quantity of medicine to be administered.

The Delimitation (*maryādā*). Next, what is the method for administering the medicine [of confession] as set forth below? Within this, it is divided into two parts according to the delimitation of the Dharma:

first, the *pratyakṣa-svavavāda* (confession in the presence of others) regarding three objects and three dharmas; second, the *pañca-dharma-pratyakṣa-svavavāda* (confession in the presence of five dharmas) if one wishes to do so within the Saṃgha.
Now, with respect to the person capable of effecting the cessation [of the offense], it is divided into four parts, which may be understood from the text. First, the confession in the presence of...
Each individual offense also has four parts: first, the confession of the offense in person; second, the formal conclusion of the name of the offense, beginning with "If one has done such [a thing]";

third, the explanation, beginning with "In this regard..."; and fourth, the arousal of the offense. Within the section on the actual extinction of the offense, this is a confession performed before another (pratideśanā);

therefore, one may only obtain absolution for offenses ranging from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to the light *duṣkṛta*, as well as for offenses involving human skin and so forth, including *sthūlātyaya* and *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*.

Nun. The remaining cases are not subject to this confrontation. Regarding the method of confession for a single person, the four points are distinguished as usual. As for the confrontation between the agent and the object: the person must be present.
Second, from the beginning until "having thus recited three times," this constitutes the presence of the *dharma*.

He should then say to himself: "Reprove your own mind," and so forth—these two constitute the presence of the *vinaya*. Next, one confronts two bhikṣus; next, one confronts three bhikṣus. The fixed text is as follows.
Each of the preceding categories possesses five dharmas. Regarding the confession of offenses, one may only obtain *deśanā* (confession) for those that are light;

for those involving *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting), *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses requiring forfeiture), or *saṃghabheda-prayoga-vyatikrama* (the preparatory act of schism resulting in a *duṣkṛta*), and so forth. All others are excluded from this. Next is confession before the *saṃgha*;

this excludes only the *pārājika* (defeat) and the most grave *sthūlātyaya*, as well as the four types of associates, the schism of the *karma*, and so on. This also excludes *sthūlātyaya*, *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the schism of the *saṃgha*, and the *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses.

Minor preparatory offenses such as *duṣkṛta* and others are not included in this category. As mentioned above, there are four textual stages; however, within the actual procedure of confession (*pratideśanā*), there are five elements:

first, the request for confession; second, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) by the one receiving the confession; third, the actual confession; fourth, the administration of censure and discipline; and fifth, the acceptance [of the confession].

The text lacks the second section on requesting the *sāṃghika* for confession; by calculation, there should be six sections. Regarding these four positions, they are all analogous to the two types of *vinaya-pratyakṣa* (manifestation of the discipline);
the remainder are cases of *dharma-pratyakṣa* (manifestation of the dharma). The second section on *pratyakṣa* and *tṛṇastāraka* (covering with grass) consists of two parts.

The first concerns the inquiry and response regarding the amount to be used. The second, beginning from "Furthermore, having asked," concerns the method of application. This section also has four parts: first, the actual cessation.
1. The two fetters are named "extinction. 2. Explanation. 3. The arising of offenses regarding the limbs. 4. The text for the formal confession (*pratideśanā*) consists of four parts:
First, up to the point "not dwelling in peace," this reveals the fault of their divine dispute. Second, from "Ānanda, within that one assembly...

onwards, it correctly describes the two assemblies mutually deliberating on how to seek the "grass-covering" (*tṛṇastāraka*) procedure. Third, from "Ānanda, that bhikṣu... onwards, it prescribes the *jñapti-karman* (motion) for reconciliation.

Regarding the two groups: the fourth [section] concerning Ānanda is one group; herein, the text below establishes the formal regulation for these two groups, each performing a "grass-covering" (*tṛṇastāraka*) confession to extinguish disputes arising from offenses.

The Mother [of the Vinaya] says: "This extinguishes the dispute but does not extinguish the offense. That which is to be confessed refers to the aforementioned characteristic of the non-extinction of an offense through self-accusation within the *pātimokkha* (self-assertion), specifically that which is difficult to determine regarding factions; it does not apply to all cases. For now, this is explained according to such instances.

When the assembly eats together and praises the food, if one half [of the assembly] perceives it as a *pāyattika* offense and the other half perceives it as a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (or *deśanīya*) offense regarding the instruction for food, they each hold to their own view;

thus, the names and categories of the offenses are indeterminate. Since such cases cannot be settled through formal confession (*pratideśanā*), the Buddha permitted that the specific names and categories need not be recited, and that one should perform a "grass-covering" confession (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).
The leader of the assembly should rise and speak as follows: "Venerable sirs, regarding this matter of dispute..."
This refers to restating a prior dispute regarding an offense one has committed—the very offense under dispute.

It refers to restating a grave offense, such as a *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, which cannot be confessed in private and for which there is no legal procedure for extinction through face-to-face confrontation.

Furthermore, because it necessitates confessing before a layperson rather than being resolved by merely apologizing to the Saṃgha, it is not extinguished by the "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*). Such an offense must also be removed; it may likewise be addressed upon a grave offense.

Regarding disputes: if they are not extinguished through the "covering with grass" (tṛṇapraticchādana) method, they must be removed. As for those who perform the repentance by covering with grass, they mutually apologize to one another;
beyond this point, all matters are removed through the "covering with grass" method.

The fourth matter is the dispute (*adhikaraṇa*). Because it is distinguished by its specific status, one must raise the general question; this is because, following the three origins of dispute, it has no distinct characteristics of its own.

Therefore, the general answer states that "all are extinguished by extinction. If one were to ask further specific questions, they would not differ from the previous three, as they correspond to their respective categories;
thus, there is no need for separate questioning. Furthermore, fearing confusion with those used collectively, it is said: "according to what has been committed," which serves to distinguish them.

The similarities and differences among the various schools regarding the four types of disputes (*catur-vivāda*) in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: first, disputes over speech (*vāda-vivāda*); second, disputes over instruction (*anuśāsana-vivāda*); third, disputes over offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*).

If a bhikṣu commits an offense ranging from a *pārājika* down to a *durbhāṣita*, or if they engage in quarreling and mutual abuse, giving rise to evil conduct of body, speech, and mind—this is called a dispute over offenses.

Fourth, disputes over matters (*kṛtya-vivāda*). Following this, the medicines are enumerated, beginning with the *sammukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and continuing through to the *yadbhūyaḥ-karaṇīya* (settlement by majority decision).

It is the seventh [chapter]. Regarding the ten *vinaya* rules on the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): first, disputes arising from contention; second, disputes concerning groundless matters; third, disputes concerning offenses;

and fourth, disputes concerning routine matters. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the four disputes are: first, disputes regarding verbal expressions; second, disputes involving slander; third, disputes regarding offenses; and fourth, disputes regarding routine matters.

If one were to distinguish these by correlating the medicine with the ailment, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, verbal disputes are extinguished by two methods of settlement: *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and...

When many people have cast their voting sticks (*śalākā*) and it is found that the majority has acted according to the Dharma, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to properly extinguish the dispute concerning instruction (*anuśāsana-vivāda*) by means of the four methods of settlement:
presence (*saṃmukha*), recollection (*smṛti*), non-delusion (*amūḍha*), and the original statement (*yadbhūyaḥ-prakṛti*). There are two kinds of the original statement:

those that are subject to confession and those that are not. Regarding those that are not subject to confession, one should grant them the status of being "irreversible for life" (*yāvaj-jīvam-avivāda*) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations).
Regarding the offense committed through *karmavācanā*: there are three methods of pacification—*pratideśanīya*, *pratyāpatti*, and *yadbhūyaiṣīya*. As for *yadbhūyaiṣīya*:
when monks are engaged in quarreling and mutual abuse, this monk kneels on his right knee and addresses the Saṃgha, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

We have been quarreling and abusing one another, performing evil deeds of body, speech, and mind. Furthermore, we thought: 'We have been quarreling and abusing one another, performing [evil deeds] of body, speech, and mind...'"
"This is an evil deed. Would it not be better now to expiate this offense within the Saṃgha by performing the 'grass-spreading' (tṛṇastāraka) confession?
I now beg the Saṃgha for the 'grass-spreading' confession. Having said this three times, he extends his hands and feet and prostrates himself toward the *karmadāna* (the master of the ritual).
Listen with a single mind. The *karmavācanā* master proclaims: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen," and so forth; this is the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya*) for the actual settlement.

What is meant by "spreading grass upon the ground" (*tṛṇastāraka*)? Those bhikṣus no longer speak of the origins of the dispute, and the Saṃgha likewise does not further inquire into the root of the matter.
Regarding disputes over matters (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*): these are the regular procedures of the Saṃgha, including all formal acts (*karmavācanā*) and whatever actions are undertaken.

Because these lead to disputes, they are extinguished by means of the seven methods for settling disputes according to the specific matter. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, disputes are settled by two methods: presence before the assembly (*sammukha-vinaya*) and searching for the truth through majority decision (*yadbhūya-sammuti*).

The four types of disputes arising from rootless [accusations] are settled by four methods of resolution: presence (*sammukhavinaya*), recollection (*sativinaya*), non-delusion (*amūḷhavinaya*), and investigation according to the facts (*tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*).

The three types of disputes arising from offenses are settled by three methods: presence, confession (*pratijñākāraka*), and the covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*). Disputes concerning habitual conduct are settled by all [four] methods of resolution.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, disputes involving verbal accusations are settled by three methods: presence, majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*), and the covering over as with grass. Within the method of majority decision and the covering over as with grass, the dispute extends to both monastics and laypeople.

Together they shall extinguish matters of contention; only through the cessation of the factors of the Path is there true cessation. One who confesses their own offense must undergo the *tassapāpiyasika-kamma*.
Once the *tassapāpiyasika-kamma* has been completed, eight privileges are revoked and may no longer be exercised. As for the regular duties of the Saṃgha:

whatever matter the Saṃgha performs must be settled according to the Dharma and the Vinaya—being properly convened, properly resolved, properly relinquished, and properly bestowed—just as is done for the bhikṣus who are disciples of the Blessed One.
Regarding the matters practiced by the assembly, each and every matter is settled through the seven methods for settling disputes (*satta adhikaraṇasamatha*).

Among these, within the dispute of mutual recrimination (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), there was a case involving the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī who first disputed whether water contained insects or not, whether grass was pure or impure, and whether a person possessed a sense of shame or lacked it.
Regarding disputes over what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya:
first, if the dispute is not settled through discussion by a majority regarding the precepts, one should next extinguish this matter by the "spreading of grass" (tṛṇastāraka) method.

If a junior monk has committed an offense, he should go to where a senior monk is, prostrate at his feet with his head and face touching them, and say: "Venerable Sir, that which I have done was contrary to the Dharma; it was an offense of transgression. I now repent."
If it occurs again, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should stroke the head with his hand, support him as he rises, and embrace him, saying: "O Venerable One (āyuṣmat), I too have faults toward you;
please do not be angry. If the senior monk himself has committed a fault, he should go to the junior monk, take his hand, and say: [as above].
"The unrighteous acts I have committed exceed yours. I confess them and shall not do them again.
The junior monk should rise and pay homage to the senior monk, confessing as above. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"All such matters of dispute—such as those involving mutual striking, dragging one another out of the room, the types of divisive speech, groundless slander, and so forth—all should be settled by the 'spreading of grass upon the ground' (tṛṇaprastāraka) method."
This should be settled through the "covering over as with grass" (tṛṇaprastāraka), yet it appears that the offense has not been extinguished. A verse in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states:
"Having understood the four types of formal acts (karmavācanā) and the robe for tranquility. The commentary explains: In the Vinaya, it is taught that there are four bases for formal acts:

first, formal acts based on disputes; second, formal acts based on wholesome instruction; third, formal acts based on offenses and transgressions; and fourth, formal acts based on specific tasks to be performed.
These four *niśraya-karmas* are extinguished by means of seven kinds of *santi-niśrayas*:
first, *sammukha-vinaya*; second, *smṛti-vinaya*; third, *amūḍha-vinaya*; fourth, *yadbhūyaḥ-sammuti-vinaya*; fifth, *tatsvabhāva-vinaya*; sixth, *yati-vinaya*;
and seventh, *tṛṇaprastāraka-vinaya*. By means of these seven *santi-niśrayas*, how are the four *niśrayas* extinguished?
Regarding *karmavācanā*: if it concerns a *karmavācanā* based on a dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), its characteristic is the differing adherence to [the nature of] an offense;

it is pacified by two bases, namely, through the *pratyakṣavinaya* (settlement in the presence) and the *yadbhūyaḥsādhika-vinaya* (settlement according to the majority). If it concerns a *karmavācanā* based on a formal instruction (*śāsana*), its characteristic is interrogation;
it is pacified by four bases, namely, through the *pratyakṣa-uttarimanuṣyadharma* (settlement regarding the claim of superhuman states) and the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection).

The *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one not insane) and others arise based on the formal act (*karmavācanā*) concerning an offense or a transgression; these take as their characteristic the sequence of events leading up to the matter at hand.

They are extinguished through the three bases of tranquility, namely: the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of), the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), and the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (settlement by sweeping under the rug).
If a formal act arises regarding a task to be performed, this takes as its characteristic all the formal acts concerning the tasks to be performed, according to the appropriate path.

The principle is that it is extinguished by the seven bases of tranquility, as explained at length in the Vinaya. It should be understood that this passage first lists the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), followed by the seven medicines;

it then pairs the medicines with the diseases. Regarding the third [type of dispute], one asks about what is right or wrong based on one's own admission, whereas for the remaining six, no such questioning occurs.

He asked alone: "What is meant by 'speaking for oneself'? He replied: "Regarding other matters of discipline (*vinaya*), both right and wrong are clearly explained as in the section on 'covering with grass.

Within the context of speaking for oneself, one merely cites what is right. Upāli raised a doubt because it was not clarified whether this was done for the sake of being in accordance with the Dharma, or because there was no fault to be found in what was wrong.
Therefore, [the Buddha] did not distinguish them. The Buddha replied: 'Not everything is in accordance with the Dharma; there are also [cases that are not]. "
This is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). This section is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of an improper self-accusation;

second, from "Upāli" onwards, the explanation of a proper self-accusation; third, from "At that time there was a bhikṣu... onwards, the formal explanation of the gains and losses regarding Upāli’s self-accusation.

It may also be applied to other bhikṣus, thereby clarifying the matters where a self-accusation is invalid. Within the section on what is contrary to the Dharma, it is further divided into two: first, [the case] regarding...

Not committing an offense that is contrary to the Dharma. Second, Upāli: herein, after a bhikṣu has committed an offense, the following explains the non-Dharmic nature of the formal accusation (codanā).

Regarding the two cases of non-offense, first, there are forty-nine permutations concerning not performing the formal act of recollection (smṛti-karaṇa); second, there are [permutations] concerning performing the formal act of raising the charge (udghāta) and performing the recollection.
There are forty-nine phrases. These correspond to the seven groups (*sapta-varga*), each having seven as its heading; thus there are seven times seven.
Because one confesses an offense when in fact one has not committed it, this is explained as "confessing what is not an offense," which is divided into two parts.

First, when one has actually committed an offense but does not initiate a formal accusation (*codanā*) nor a formal reminder (*smṛti-codanā*), there are forty-two phrases. Second, when one has actually committed an offense and both initiates a formal accusation and a formal reminder, there are forty-two phrases.

It also corresponds to the seven groups (*sapta-varga*). Although these may constitute actual offenses, because the respective citations do not correspond, they are likewise not in accordance with the Dharma.

Each of the headings has six [subdivisions], thus forming seven sets of six. Within the section on "In Accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*), there are two sets of seven phrases; both constitute actual offenses. Regarding the first set of seven:

one does not perform the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepana*) nor the act of calling to mind (*sativinodana*); conversely, for each of the first four [of the second set], there are twelve [cases]. Regarding the subsequent set of seven: one performs the act of suspension and the act of calling to mind.
This reverses the previous cases [where the numbers were] two, forty-nine, and forty-two. Because the respective grounds for accusation are equivalent, it is called "speaking according to the Dharma.
This refers to the case where, in the presence of Upāli, a formal confession (*pāṭidesanīya*) was rendered invalid; this may be understood from the text.

Regarding the remainder of the various practices, those that have been collected above and shown to be exhaustive are the same as for the Great Saṃgha; these have already been distinguished as above.

As for the rules that differ [from those of the monks], they must be treated as separate items. Therefore, they are explained next. If one were to name this according to its subject matter, it should be called...
Regarding the Method for Receiving the Precepts: currently, as the Dharma is hidden and follows the person, it is called the Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka. This is divided into two parts:

first, from the beginning up to "the precepts for those who have received both organs," which clarifies the method for receiving the precepts; second, from "all the bhikṣuṇīs having gathered in one place" onwards, which concerns the miscellaneous practices of the bhikṣuṇīs.

The section on receiving the precepts is divided into two parts. First, up to "this is the reception of the precepts," which correctly explains the preparatory methods for requesting and receiving the precepts.

Within this section, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that Mahāprajāpatī wept with streaming tears, which serves as the occasion for Ānanda’s request;

second, from the words "At that time, Ānanda... onwards, it shows his intention to make the request. Second is the actual prayer and entreaty, which is divided into three parts. From the beginning up to "then [the Buddha] permitted... [is the first part].

thus it says, "Women are many, and their families decline. The second analogy reveals her inability to respect others; thus it is like frost and hail. Next, [the text] raises...
The reflection on the invitation: First the invitation, then the response. There are four aspects to this response: first, because of me, one comes to know the Three Jewels;
second, because of me, one gives rise to faith in the Three Jewels; third, because of me, one receives the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts; fourth, because of me, one attains the Way.
This cannot be repaid by providing worldly sustenance such as food and clothing. Having thus manifested the completion of my repayment, next—
Regarding the request for equality between cause and effect: first is the request, followed by the Buddha’s words below, which constitute the Tathāgata’s acceptance.
This is because their merit is equal and their realization is identical; since the principle is difficult to contravene, there is no reason he would not grant it.

The second section, on the formal acceptance [of the eight weighty rules], consists of two parts. First, from the beginning up to "having circumambulated, she departed," which concerns her respectful departure after receiving the eight weighty rules from the nun Mahāprajāpatī.
Second, at that time, there were other women who received the precepts through the *karmavācanā* ritual. This section on the eight weighty rules consists of four parts.

First, from the beginning up to "as explained above," which is the actual conferral of the precepts. Within this, there are two sub-sections: first, it clarifies how the Tathāgata spoke the eight weighty rules and used analogies to entrust them to Ānanda; second, [the subsequent portion].
At that time, Ānanda and those below him transmitted the meaning of the Eightfold Respectful Precepts to Mahāprajāpatī; this has already been explained previously.

After the two Mahās (Mahāprajāpatī and her followers) had spoken, they received [the precepts] with joy and veneration, speaking parables to express their own celebration. This was not like the case where only Mahāprajāpatī alone received the precepts according to the *Vinaya of the Five Hundred*;

rather, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred others all received them through the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Thirdly, Ānanda and those below him transmitted [the teachings].

Having completed his mission, he returned and informed the Buddha. After the four Buddhas had finished speaking, the following section from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* demonstrates the disadvantages of ordaining women.

Ānanda further addressed Mahāprajāpatī, saying: "I pray that you will once again enter [the city] on my behalf and inform the World-Honored One, saying: 'I have now received the eight rules upon the crown of my head.'"
"Among these eight rules, I wish to request one favor: may you grant that bhikṣuṇīs be permitted to pay homage to bhikṣus according to seniority.
How could a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years' standing pay homage to a bhikṣu who has only recently received the precepts? Ānanda again made this request to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to Ānanda:
If I were to permit a bhikṣuṇī to perform prostrations to a bhikṣu according to seniority, such a thing would be impossible. Women have five obstacles;
they cannot become Śakra, King of Devas, Māra, Brahmā Devānām Indra, a Cakravartin King, or a Dharma King of the Three Realms.

Had I not permitted women to go forth, the Buddha’s True Dharma would have remained in the world for a thousand years; now that I have permitted their going forth, it will be reduced by five hundred years.

"O Āyuṣmat, if women had not gone forth and received full ordination within my Dharma, then after my parinirvāṇa, the upāsakas would have carried the four types of offerings and followed behind the bhikṣus, accepting them out of compassion for me. Ānanda was filled with grief and regret, thinking: "I did not hear or know of this before. Had I known of it earlier, how could I have made three requests?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Do not weep any longer. Māra obscured your mind; that is why it happened thus. According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, Kāśyapa requested ordination on this account.

Women. There are ten matters for which they are punished regarding Ānanda: First, if women did not go forth [into homelessness], donors would kneel on their hams by the roadside and offer food from vessels to the śramaṇas.

Because it concerns seeking refuge, the opening section is for the purpose of dispatching a messenger. From "the third [allowance] for one who has already [received]" onwards, it specifically concerns the matter of dispatching a messenger according to the original *dharmas*.

Since these matters differ from those in the *Nitya* (Constant) [section], they need not be cited in detail here; instead, I shall clarify directly the procedure for approaching the assembly of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*). This ritual should consist of seven parts: first, measuring the purity or impurity of the area beforehand;

second, within the assembly, a person should be appointed—this is done by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one announcement)—and the verbal act constitutes the essence of the appointment; third, receiving...
1. She causes the bhikṣuṇī to go down and request the three [refuges] on her behalf. 2. The fourth [step] is for the preceptor to perform the formal announcement (jñapti);

the text is abbreviated and not detailed. 3. In the text concerning the examination before the assembly, one only asks about the name, the upādhyāya, the bhikṣuṇī’s training in the precepts, and so forth; the rest is likewise abbreviated.

The sixth [section] serves as the formal text for receiving the precepts; it consists only of the *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations) and the description of the characteristics, while the subsequent matters are all omitted and not explained.

From the seventh [section], "That messenger... onwards, it merely informs [the recipient] directly, which differs from the three Vinayas. According to other Vinayas, one must fully recite the *bhikṣu-karman* (formal act of the great monks) before the precepts can be generated.
Next, the various practices and other dharmas are explained. Regarding dwelling in an araṇya (hermitage), it is permitted to trade with laypeople.

Regarding dwelling in a village, it is permitted for the sake of the Saṃgha. If, within a private residence, buying and selling and the like are not permitted, it is because it is not for the sake of the Saṃgha.

As for a bhikṣuṇī who administers the *karmavācanā* of non-prostration against a bhikṣu, this does not violate the Eight Respectful Rules (*gurudharma*), because the Buddha has permitted it. If one exceeds [the limit] without prior consultation...

Regarding the term "nun" (bhikṣuṇī): its meaning is not [as it appears]. The text mentions beating, reviling, and deceptive speech; here, "deceptive" means contrary. That is to say, speech that is contrary to principle and evil.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, a bhikṣuṇī may perform the four types of formal acts (*karmans*) for a bhikṣu, yet she does not prostrate to him, nor does she converse with him.

They did not offer him worship, nor did they inquire after his well-being. A bhikṣu may perform three *karmas* for a bhikṣuṇī: the ordination, the half-monthly confession (*poṣadha*), and the expiation of offenses.

Alternatively, if a bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense and a *karma* for the relinquishment of instruction is to be performed for her, this means that because she no longer receives instruction, the *karma* for relinquishing it need not wait for further formal procedures to be enacted.
My current interpretation is that this is not so. Furthermore, it is said that one should perform the *karma* for the relinquishment of instruction for her.
Since it is stated that "it should be performed," this clarifies that a formal procedure consisting of a motion and a second (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) must be established to discipline the nuns.

If one were to claim that no further action is required and that simply abandoning the instruction constitutes "abandonment," then while it might be acceptable for the community as a whole to commit an offense, how could it be right for the remaining nuns—perhaps only one, two, or three individuals—to be disciplined?

How could the rest of the nuns be entirely excluded from receiving instruction? Furthermore, how could the entire assembly be subjected to disciplinary measures merely because one, two, or three individuals have committed a transgression? Therefore...

One should deal with them according to the *dharmakarma* (legal procedures). If śrāmaṇeras or śrāmaṇerīs mutually cause offense or disturb both assemblies, and they do not reform even when directly disciplined, the elders shall likewise discipline their two teachers as described above. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, a bhikṣuṇī must not revile or slander a bhikṣu;
however, she may speak of a bhikṣu’s transgressions, saying: "Do not associate with evil friends, wicked companions, and the like. Furthermore...
It was said that there were a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī who, playing and laughing together, disturbed the other bhikṣus. The Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha shall perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for these two individuals for the offense of disturbing the Saṃgha and being impure.
Once this *karman* has been performed, whatever these two consume shall be considered as theft; however, if these two confess their transgression before the Saṃgha...

Regarding those who request release: they shall request it from the Saṃgha three times; the Saṃgha shall grant it through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. This releases them from the *akalpa-karman* (the formal act of impurity).

As for the food consumed, let it not be like theft. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when a Bhikṣuṇī receives the sūtras, if there are coarse or vulgar expressions within them, she is permitted to write them down and transmit them.

If one does not know how to read or write, it is permitted to receive instruction through a partition; if there is no partition, it is permitted to receive instruction while facing away from each other.
One should not perform the *poṣadha* together with the bhikṣus. Every half-month, one should request a bhikṣu to come and ask for instruction in the precepts.

If the bhikṣus are unwilling to do so, the Buddha said that it is permitted for the bhikṣuṇīs to provide offerings such as alms-bowl bags, waistbands, fragrant oils, and food for before and after meals. Or...
[If] the *poṣadha* has not yet been performed, one makes the announcement; or if it has already been performed, one then makes the announcement. The Buddha said: "It should not be done in that way.
When the time comes for the proclamation regarding the purity (*pāriśuddhi*) of those bhikṣuṇīs who have not arrived, one should rise from one's seat, stand before the Saṃgha, and announce:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This community of bhikṣuṇīs of this monastery, having prostrated at the feet of the harmonious community of bhikṣus, requests instruction.'"
Regarding the person who instructs in the precepts: if the Saṃgha has already appointed an instructor, the presiding elder (upādhyāya) should reply, "Receive it from such-and-such a bhikṣu.
If no one has been appointed but there is someone capable of preaching, he should reply, "Go to such-and-such a person and receive it.
If there is still no one, he should reply, "There is no instructor here, nor is there anyone capable of preaching the Dharma; do not be negligent. [He should add: "Tomorrow..."

The bhikṣuṇīs asked whether it was permissible; he replied to them with these same words. Furthermore, if there were no bhikṣus in the bhikṣuṇī village, or if there were bhikṣus in the āraṇya but the bhikṣuṇīs could not go because of the distance or various difficulties, or if those bhikṣus did not act as a harmonious assembly so that they were unable to invite [them for] the *pravāraṇā*, the Buddha said:
"I allow a learned (*bahuśruta*) bhikṣu to perform [the *pravāraṇā*] on behalf of the bhikṣuṇīs."
When coming into a village, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* together. Afterwards, the bhikṣuṇīs should invite [the monks] for *pravāraṇā*.

Furthermore, during the ordination ceremony, after the eight conditions have been explained to the bhikṣuṇīs, one should generally explain the four similes. Next, one explains the eight rules that must not be transgressed.

Next, one explains the four reliances (*niśraya*). A bhikṣuṇī’s latrine must be very deep; the opening should be made small by folding back the edge by one cubit (*hasta*). If a bhikṣuṇī sells wine, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. [The bhikṣuṇīs...]

He sells *lān* (fragrant grass) after pressing oil from it. If a *bhikṣuṇī* does not announce that she will eat at her own discretion (*svairakāra*), and one eats, there is an offense of *pāyattika* for every mouthful.

The Eighteenth Chapter on the Dharma-Section (*Dharmaskandha*) on the Rules of Decorum (*Iryāpatha-vinaya*). This is the essential core of practice; it can internally restrain the activities of the mind and externally engender goodness in sentient beings. It is because of this [that it is taught].
It is for the sake of the Dharma. Within this section, seven types of disciplinary practices (*dharma*) are extensively explained;
because they are collected in one place, it is called the *Dharmavastu* (Section on the Dharma). In general terms, there is nothing that is not Dharma, which is why this receives the name "Dharma.

As for the other sections (*vastu*) not being called "Dharma," the commentary explains that this is to manifest the distinctions between the characteristics of the various Dharmas; thus, the other sections conceal their general name and establish their titles according to their specific subject matter.
In this context, the specific is subsumed under the general; therefore, it is called "Dharma. Within the text, there are seven sections.

From the beginning up to "governing according to the Dharma" (*yathādharma*), the primary purpose is to clarify the rules for visiting monks (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*). The reason these are explained first is that those who have left the household life are guests of the triple world.
One should maintain a composed demeanor and conduct oneself in accordance with the Dharma. This ensures that the inner mind is pure and that outward faith and respect increase;

since the essence of practice lies in excellence, it must first be clarified. Second, from this point forward, for the sake of senior bhikṣus and others, the method for senior bhikṣus to attend to guests is taught.
Third, from "The Buddha was in Rājagṛha" onwards, the proper procedures for defecation and urination are clearly explained.
1. Rituals: The toilet (śikya) must not be situated in the east; it should be constructed in the north.

It should have three holes, each one hand-span wide and one and a half cubits long. Fourth: From "At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī" onwards, this concerns the rules for the bhikṣus' practice of begging for alms.
Fifth: From "The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha" onwards, this concerns the dharmas for forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka). Sixth: The Buddha was staying at... [text breaks off].
From the passage "In Rājagṛha... onwards, it describes the majestic deportment in coming and going when accepting an invitation, as well as the rules for conduct at the meal;

one must wait until these have been proclaimed according to this Vinaya before eating. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) must not eat first, but should wait until the proclamation has been made throughout and then eat.
The *Vinaya-kaṅkṣā-viśodhana-śāstra* (Wǔshí jiālùn) likewise says that after the food has been distributed, one should loudly proclaim the *saṃghabhedaka*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states:

"Waiting until it has been heard everywhere," etc., refers to eating together with those who have made the sound [of the announcement]. From "The seventh Buddha was in Rājagṛha" onwards concerns the rules for dyeing robes and so forth;
this concludes the fourth section below.
The Nineteenth Khandhaka on Lodgings (*Vihāra-khandhaka*).
The preceding section clarified the rules of deportment and the conduct of movement; yet such conduct does not achieve itself independently, but is established by relying upon material requisites.

Among the essential requisites for the Path, none surpasses the lodging. Therefore, this section follows next to examine them. Within this, there are two parts; the first extends from the beginning up to the allowance for pillows.
For those who are superior practitioners, he taught such practices as dwelling under trees or sitting in the open air, according to their respective dispositions and faculties;
by relying on these, they cultivate the path and give rise to the conditions for becoming noble. These are called the "conditions for the noble" and are termed the "noble lineages.

Second, at that time, while the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha, he permitted those of the next lower grade to dwell in rooms with roofs and coverings; this refers to the fourth of the four reliances.
"If one obtains long-term benefits, such as small houses or stone chambers, they may be accepted," and so forth.

The second section is divided into six parts: first, up to the point of "according to one's wish" (*yathāsukham*), which correctly explains the method for accepting long-term benefits regarding rooms and dwellings;
second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha" onwards, which describes the signs of [the Buddha’s] honoring and recommending [the practice].

[Year. The senior monks should receive the best rooms, bedding, and so forth. In the third section, from the householder down to the permission to keep [possessions], various rules regarding rooms and other matters are clarified.
In the fourth, from Rāhula onwards, it is taught that giving before [the formal act] is a gift, while giving after is not in accordance with the Dharma.
In the fifth, from "The Buddha was in Kāśī" onwards, it is taught that the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions should not [be used inappropriately].

Regarding the distribution [of dwellings] and so forth: the sixth section concerns the Buddha’s stay at Śrāvastī and below, concerning the rewarding of those who manage construction projects and the rules for the distribution of rooms.

The initial text is divided into four parts. First, from the beginning until "having paid homage to the Buddha, they departed," it describes how King Bimbisāra offered the Bamboo Grove to the Buddha and the Saṃgha of the four directions.

Second, from "at that time, the bhikṣus, having risen early in the morning" and below, up to "they constructed various types of rooms," the Buddha said, "I authorize you to build them. This is the correct [text].
He clearly understood the inclination toward giving and constructed separate rooms as offerings for the bhikṣus.

At the three times of day, when the bhikṣus wished to build rooms, [the Buddha] even permitted down to the provision of water vessels, all of which were to be placed together in one location. Regarding the extensive requirements for these rooms, at that time the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha;
[the account continues] from the householder Sudatta in Śrāvastī, who provided food for the solitary ones (Gautama) for the sake of the Buddha.
The construction of the vihāra; the second section concerns the Elder Maṇibhadra’s offering of his chamber, wherein he is exhorted with verses.

The first one and a half verses concern the efficacy of the chamber as a general condition for both defilement and purification. The second, beginning with "upholding the precepts," in one line reveals the practitioner supported by the chamber, who accomplishes the practices of the three trainings.
The third consists of one and a half verses concerning the praise of the noble ones, which demonstrates its excellence through comparison. [End of] the five sections. All.

When a layperson (*avadātavasana*) offers fields, houses, or shops to a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu does not accept them, fearing censure that says, "These bhikṣus are unworthy of receiving offerings," the Buddha said:

"I permit the Saṃgha to accept them, provided they are managed by a *kappiyakāraka* (pure person). In the third section concerning the interior of the quarters, it is stated that a small śrāmaṇera may be placed inside a partitioned room;
the Buddha said: "I permit this. Because of this text, it appears as though one door leads to multiple rooms where one may stay overnight together.
There is no offense. He was doubtful about boarding a boat with a woman. The Buddha said: "Except for crossing directly [to the other side].

Whether sitting, standing, or lying down"—according to this text, the rule regarding boarding the same boat is explained above; it appears that this precept should be applied equally to nuns and women. Regarding the fourth point:
why is it that the merit of giving does not equal even one-sixteenth of the merit of going a single step to listen to the Dharma from the Buddha? Answer: Giving...

The karma of giving is a wholesome deed that constitutes a portion of merit (*puṇya-bhāga*). To approach the Buddha to hear the Dharma, to open and transform the mind, and to give rise to the supreme understanding that severs birth and death, is a wholesome deed that constitutes a portion of the Path (*mārga-bhāga*).
Since these two principles cannot coexist, it is said that the former does not equal even one-sixteenth of the latter.
Even when merely resolving to go and listen, such merit is produced; how much more so when one hears and understands with faith, and practices according to the teaching? Thus it is said in contrast.
The verse concerning the Elder Sudatta is divided into three parts. The first two lines state that because he has cultivated the path and realized cessation, he attains peaceful sleep.

The next four lines state that because he has abandoned the origin [of suffering] and eliminated its suffering, he attains peaceful sleep. The final two lines conclude the attainment of peaceful sleep.
For these reasons, I am indeed different from him.

The second section, on mutual veneration and respect, consists of four parts: first, up to the point where [the monks] address the Buddha, raising the occasion of their transgression to inform the Buddha;

second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason... onwards, examining the monks' understanding of the matter; third, from "The Buddha addressed the monks... onwards...; fourth, [the conclusion].

Having concluded [the previous section], the text may now be circulated. This section uses what follows to illustrate what precedes it, similar to how a lower case serves as an illustration for a higher one.

Fourth, from "From this day forward" onwards, there is a two-part analysis distinguishing between what should be manifested and what should not. First, the circumstances are presented. Second, from "You all... onwards, the propriety of paying homage or not is clarified.
Within this, first, four reasons why one should not pay homage are given: (1) because laypeople and women differ in status from monastics; (2) ... [text fragment].

Fourth, because those who receive the precepts later differ in their status as Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna; third, because those who have committed the "borderline offenses" (*sīmā-baddha-āpatti*) and so forth differ in their purity or defilement;

fourth, because all improper speech differs in being heterodox or orthodox. Next, from the words "What [kind of person]... onwards, the text clarifies the passage concerning those to whom one should pay homage; this section has five parts.
The junior *śrāmaṇerikā* should perform prostrations to twelve objects: six for persons and six for stūpas. Next, the junior *śrāmaṇerī* should perform prostrations to eight objects:

four for persons and four for stūpas. Next, the junior *śikṣamāṇā* should perform prostrations to six objects: three for persons and three for stūpas. The junior *bhikṣuṇī* should perform prostrations to four objects:
[two] for persons and [two] for stūpas. The junior *bhikṣu* should perform prostrations to four objects: [two] for persons and [two] for stūpas.
Because there are two of each. Next, regarding the statement that "there should also be five great [categories]," each should be treated as a primary heading for the purpose of paying homage;

since all [others] are to be excluded as being minor, the objects of homage are narrow, and thus the text is abbreviated and does not distinguish them. For example, there are two types of persons and stupas to whom a great bhikṣu should pay homage.

This refers to the Buddha and his stūpas, up to and including the great śrāmaṇerikās; there are ten such objects to whom one should pay homage, namely five for humans and five for stūpas, because one does not pay homage to those of one's own class.
The rest may be understood by analogy with this.

The third section, a miscellaneous clarification regarding matters of the dwelling, consists of three parts: first, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for a donor’s dwelling and the adjudication of disputes concerning monks;

second, the construction of a dwelling by monks, including the completion of all necessary requisites for the dwelling; and third, the clarification of all legal procedures (*dharma-kriyā*) required for the dwelling.

Third: At that time, the World-Honored One traveled from Vaiśālī. He then clarified that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered his park to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, along with all the necessary requisites for the monastery.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, shaving the head was not permitted within the *jantāghara* (hot bathhouse) or the lecture hall, except for those who were elderly or ill;
however, it was permitted to shave the head within the *jantāghara*.

Regarding the fourth [point], "the former giving" among these types of giving: from the beginning up to the passage "if the body is defiled," and following the words "World-Honored One, by this cause and condition," the text correctly analyzes the aforementioned "former giving. As for what is called "unlawful giving":

when a long-standing lay devotee relinquishes a dwelling to give as an object of use to the Saṃgha, it must be that their three karmas are pure and they accept and maintain it in accordance with the Dharma. If the three karmas...

If one sees that there is something blameworthy in the subsequent redirection of the gift, it is not called "unlawful" (*adharma*). If one does not see anything blameworthy in the subsequent redirection of the gift, then it is indeed unlawful.
For this reason, the Buddha did not make a definitive judgment. He required that Rāhula be sent to intervene between the previous donor and the recipient;
only when he saw no blameworthiness in Rāhula’s three karmas did the Buddha finally judge it to be unlawful. In this matter, first...
The establishment [of the categories] is not like the two preceding chapter-gates. Second, regarding "How so? and below, the text first explains the *adharma* (non-dharma) in three parts:
namely, the citation, the explanation, and the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are five chapter-gates: first, a single individual; second, multiple individuals;

third, the Saṃgha; fourth, one's own school; and fifth, establishing a different school. If these five are applied according to the text under each of the four gates, they form twenty propositions in total.
If one seeks the meaning, there are five phrases for each of the gates, totaling twenty-five phrases.
Beginning with giving to one person, then giving to another, and so on up to the fifth person—it is the same for each—though the text is abbreviated and lacks these details.

Next is the explanation of the gate of "giving, receiving, and abiding according to the Dharma," which also consists of three parts as in the text; the five phrases within the explanation can be understood accordingly.

Fifth, regarding the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions, which "should not be divided," there are three parts. First, up to the point where he informs the World-Honored One of the matter and reports the transgression to the Buddha;
second, from "The World-Honored One, by this... onwards, which generally refers to the property of the Saṃgha and extensively prescribes what is improper;

third, from "What are the four? onwards, which cites the aforementioned four categories and analyzes why they are improper. Second, there are again four parts, the first of which provides a general summary.
Regarding the four directions: it is improper to employ the property of the Saṃgha for four kinds of matters;

that is to say, it is improper to divide it, improper to take it for oneself, improper to set it aside, and improper to sell it. Since it was previously stated only that it is "improper," for whom does this apply?
Next, it is not for the Saṃgha, nor even for a single person; these three types of individuals are all improper to perform these four [actions]. Furthermore, it is not yet known...
Because of whether [the act] is accomplished or not. Next, thirdly, as for these three types of persons: if each performs this division for themselves and so forth, none of them accomplish it;
that is to say, they do not accomplish the purchase and so on. Therefore, it is said: "One should not [act] because it is unaccomplished. Next, fourthly, regarding the determination of the offense:
because it is an evil mind that obstructs the Saṃgha’s acceptance, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). This applies generally to all three persons; however, this is merely temporary.

Because it is divided, if one seeks it, one obtains it with greater weight. If that is the case regarding the division, when there is a temporary sale or purchase, could one also say "obtained" even for a temporary instance?
Answer: These refer to groups of wicked bhikṣus who falsely employ the four methods to obstruct the use of guests. How could this sale be considered equivalent?

Furthermore, it does not constitute a permanent determination that would result in a grave offense. Within the third section of the detailed analysis (*liaojian*), the *Caturvarga-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) is specifically cited, each point corresponding to what precedes it.
The four texts [of the Vinaya] conclude that the offense is established because the distribution is invalid; this may be understood from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Fearing the arrival of visiting bhikṣus, [the resident monks] divided the bedding and furniture of the monastic quarters, as well as the flowers of the gardens, into four portions and performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to give them to four bhikṣus, or even to a single person.
The Buddha said: "It is not valid. Since the division is invalid, [the recipients] commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."

The sixth section has two parts. The first part, ending with the Buddha’s statement that "the transfer is permitted," correctly clarifies the management of affairs: when a person has labored, they must be rewarded.

The second part, beginning with "There are five dharmas," distinguishes between what is appropriate and inappropriate based on merit. If one lacks the merit of construction work and possesses no commendable virtue, it is not fitting to reward their labor.
[For example,] there was a bhikṣu who built a private room on land belonging to the Saṃgha and guarded it, refusing to give it to the Saṃgha.
One should demand the land back. One should tell them to return the land to the Saṃgha; there is no further justification for taking the Saṃgha’s land as one's own.
By this standard, it can be known whether what was privately planted within the Saṃgha’s land is right or wrong.

When a bhikṣu was building a grass hut on the Saṃgha’s land, the senior monk came and assigned rooms in order, yet this bhikṣu did not give [the space] to the other bhikṣus. He reported this to the Buddha.
It is called a *duṣkṛta*. If it is not so, one should take grass and wood and go elsewhere. Furthermore, the person managing the construction undergoes great hardship;

first, one must request permission, and next, one should grant it by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*) followed by three proclamations (*trivācanā*). One may then dwell for five years in a cell built by oneself, and subsequently, one should receive a communal monastery (*saṃghārāma*) in due order.
If a senior elder (*sthavira*) arrives, one who receives [the dwelling] next should not give it to one who has obtained it through a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
If one is traveling far away, the [responsibility] is entrusted to the Saṃgha; when one returns, they should take it up again, provided that the full period of the preceding days has been completed.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The administrator said, 'I have settled the matter through reasoning, yet I am instead unable to remain. The Buddha said: 'One should measure the amount of labor performed. At most, one may stay for twelve years, residing there as one pleases.

Grant this to him via a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: 'If one repairs a dilapidated dwelling, [the period is] six years.'"
Regarding dwelling: if one builds a new house or residence, one may dwell there for twelve years. According to both the *Mātṛkā* and the *Vinaya*, one may dwell there for twelve years;

thereafter, one must follow the assignment of the Saṃgha. Regarding the *kappa-kata* (temporary) hut: having requested materials from the Saṃgha, if one does not build a permanent hut, it is a *kappa-kata*.

Having built another's hut, if one dwells in it as a *kappa-kata*, it is likewise. If one has begun building but not finished it, and then dies, or if one says of oneself, "I am a śrāmaṇera," "a eunuch," or "one with two sexual organs," [the rules apply] extensively.

The explanation regarding the *śikṣādattaka* (one who has been granted penance) is as follows. Within the section on duties (*guṇa*), there are two parts; the first part up to this point should be understood accordingly.

Regarding those who are to be appointed and those who are not to be appointed, the text enumerates the following: 1. distributing rice porridge; 2. distributing *khādanīya* (hard food); 3. appointing someone for the invitation assembly; 4. distributing bedding and seats;
5. distributing lay clothing; 6. distribution [of other items]; 7. what may be accepted; 8. what may be given; 9. appointing a monk as a messenger; 10. appointing a *śrāmaṇera* as a messenger.

Eleventh: Since it is stated that one who distributes the robes must possess five qualities and should be formally appointed, this clarifies the necessity for the method of appointment. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the person distributing the robes must possess five virtues:
(1) knowing the type of robe-material, (2) its value, (3) the number of items, (4) whether they have been distributed or not, and (5) the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

Furthermore, there are five qualities required for such an appointment, namely being free from favoritism and so forth, up to knowing what has already been distributed and what remains undistributed. Moreover, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*...
In the forest grove, there was no bhikṣu who knew the proper timing to announce the time, strike the *gandī* gong, sweep and sprinkle the ground, or repair the lecture hall and dining areas.

Once the people had gathered in succession, there was no one to arrange the beds and mats. There was no one to instruct on the purification of fruits and vegetables; as for the lack of anyone [to handle] the fermented rice wine, it contained insects.
At the time of eating and drinking, there was no one to distribute water. When the assembly became disorderly, there was no one to snap their fingers and make the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

The Buddha said: "One who possesses five qualities—such as being free from favoritism and so forth—should be appointed as the *karmadāna* (steward) by means of a formal motion and a second resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

No monk of great virtue or high standing should be made to perform such menial service. Regarding the subsequent passage on the five qualities for distributing rice gruel and the resulting descent into hell, this is intended to demonstrate loss and gain based on the presence or absence of such virtues. This explains why it was previously necessary to appoint a person endowed with these qualities."
● Section on Miscellaneous Matters (Kṣudraka-vastu), Chapter Twenty:

The conditions for supporting the Path are immeasurable and cannot be individually detailed; they are collectively termed "Miscellaneous," hence it is called the "Miscellaneous Dharma" (Kṣudraka-dharma).

Regarding the Chinese text, there are two parts. First, from the beginning up to "having brought forth the storehouse," it correctly explains the miscellaneous rules (*miśraka-dharma*) concerning what should and should not be kept for use.
Second, from "at that time, the Buddha was in Kauśāmbī" onwards, it correctly explains the rules of conduct regarding the observance of the precepts for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
In the preceding text, the miscellaneous rules lacked a systematic structure; thus, they are fully organized into two sections. The first section extends up to "one should use a waistband."

The first section, from "Tying [the bowl] to the dragon-tooth wood" (*nāgadantaka*) up to "Having washed it, one may eat," clearly explains the rules for the alms-bowl (*pātra*) while also clarifying other related items.

The second section, from "In Rājagṛha, at the Āmrapālī Grove" onwards, generally explains various matters. Within the former [section], there are four parts; the first extends to the point where it is permitted to wash [the bowl] and then eat.

The rules concerning the alms bowl (*pātra*) are distinguished as follows. The five bhikṣus asked the Buddha for permission to possess them. A *kālapātra* is a black-colored bowl; a *śarapātra* is a red-colored bowl.
During the second period, when the hair of the bhikṣus grew long, they were instructed that it should not reach down to their fingers; this was the rule regarding the application of the finger-mark.

Regarding the clarification of requisites, the statement "if it exceeds one [unit] by length, it should be cut" does not mean it must be exactly one barley grain [in length]; rather, it means that exceeding that measure is permissible.
This was retained so that [the hair] would grow only as long as a barley grain before being cut. Thus, when the hair reaches its maximum length of two finger-widths, it is shaved once;

this occurs every two months. Thirdly, at that time, outside the city of Rājagṛha, the World-Honored One—beginning with the six heretical teachers and continuing down to the restoration of the *pātra* (alms-bowl) rules—contained two sections within the text.
From the beginning up until the preparation of the eye medicine, he manifested supernatural powers for the sake of Piṇḍola.

Because he took a wooden bowl, the Tathāgata established a precept prohibiting its display at will. A wooden bowl is not in accordance with the Dharma; it is the ritual implement of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

Since displaying supernatural powers to take one is of no benefit, [the Buddha] prohibited it. After the Buddha had rebuked him in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, he declared that he was to be expelled for life.
"You should not remain in Jambudvīpa; go instead to Aparagoyānī. Furthermore, for the purpose of performing Buddha-work, he established the precept against possessing eight kinds of bowls:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, maṇi, copper, white wax, wood, and stone. To possess these constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, to possess a wooden bowl constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense; the rest is the same as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. During the second period, there were various non-Buddhist practitioners."
Having heard this, because [the Buddha] had previously established a rule regarding Piṇḍola, the non-Buddhists invited him to compete in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

This section clearly elucidates how the Tathāgata extensively displayed his miraculous transformations to deliver beings, as it was beneficial. Furthermore, regarding the preceding established rule, there are four parts within the text.

First, up to the point where [the power] increased twofold, it clarifies the non-Buddhists' adherence to their claims; then, it describes how the rule was prepared and the Buddha was requested to undergo a trial of power. Second, at that time, the King...

The city of Śrāvastī is vast and expansive... [from here until] rising from his seat and departing. This clearly explains the conversion and prediction of the lay follower (dānapati) of the non-Buddhists.

Third, from the passage beginning "At that time, the various non-Buddhists... until the end, covering the period from the first day to the fifteenth day, they traveled throughout the six great cities;
this describes the scope of the conversion of the non-Buddhist kings and their vast assemblies. Fourth, at that time, the World-Honored One...
From the passage beginning "facing east" onwards, it extensively demonstrates the transformative deliverance [of sentient beings]. This reverses the previous restrictions.
On the fourth day, he took a handful of water from the Buddha and cast it upon the ground in front; immediately, that spot became a great pool.

The water was clear and cool, free from all impurities, and those who drank it suffered no harm—this refers to the manifestation of the eight meritorious qualities of water (*aṣṭāṅgopeta-vāri*). As for the "eight," they are: lightness, coolness, softness, sweetness, purity, lack of foul odor, [non-harmfulness], and [clarity].
Drinking it brings no affliction; once drunk, it is harmonious and soothing. Among the eight qualities, the first six constitute its essential nature as water:

the first three are the tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*), while "exquisite" refers to taste (*rasa*), "pure" refers to color (*rūpa*), and "not foul-smelling" refers to fragrance (*gandha*). The final two qualities are the functional capacities of the water:

first, coolness; second, freedom from dust and impurities; third, freedom from affliction. In the text, however, only four [qualities] are mentioned. Please [note]: first, coolness; second, freedom from dust and filth; third, freedom from affliction.
These refer to the four gates and the remaining four. On the tenth day, he taught through miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*). On the twelfth day, he taught by means of mental intimation (*cetanā*);

this corresponds to the "intimation" (*saṃjñā*) and so forth. On the thirteenth day, he taught by means of instruction; this refers to the "all-blazing" (*sarvajvalita*) and so forth, which constitutes the third wheel.
Fourthly, after the World-Honored One had permitted the bhikṣus to enter the palace in Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra [listened], and thereafter [the text] proceeds to explain the return.
Just as when the Nirgrantha Śīlavat was struck and killed by a stone, the Buddha said that there are five qualities of speech that enable one to defend oneself and avoid being reproached:
first, speaking well; second, speaking according to the Dharma; third, speaking with affection; fourth, speaking truthfully;
and fifth, speaking for the benefit [of others]. Regarding these spoken verses, there are five; the first verse summarizes these five qualities, while the following four...

This is the general introductory section of the commentary. First, the commentary explains the word "good" (*kuśala*); next, it explains the word "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*); next, it explains the word "truth" (*satya*);
next, half [of the verse] explains the word "speech" (*vāc*); and the final half explains the word "benefit" (*hita*).
Second, from here on, there is a miscellaneous explanation of what should and should not be done. One should not travel half a *yojana* without a water filter (*parisrāvaṇa*).
If one has none, one should filter the water using the corner of a monk’s robe; it should be shaped like a hook, or triangular, or made into a guest-pitcher, or made into a filtering flask.
If one is troubled by minute insects, one should place them inside a sand bag. He [the monk] should discard that water containing mixed insects onto dry land. Thus said the Buddha.
It is said that one should return it to the water. Regarding incense, one may light up to ninety sticks; if one carries them inside, one must announce: "Venerable sirs, the lamps are about to enter.
Having announced this, one lights them and enters. The extinguishing of lamps is likewise. If they must be extinguished, one must not blow on them with the mouth;
rather, one should fan them with the hand, a cloth, or a fan. As for the lamp before the Buddha, it is as described in the *Maudgalyāyana-āśīti-praśna*.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "The five divisions [of the Vinaya] do not permit it; to use the Buddha’s words as the language of secular texts constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "To recite a sutra with a complete [secular] accent constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mātṛkā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* records: A bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying, "Bhikṣus come from various lineages and various countries."
Those who have left the household life employ incorrect pronunciations and thereby corrupt the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras.
I pray that the Buddha will permit me to use the treatises of the icchantikas to rectify the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras. The Buddha said: "In my Dharma, we do not prize flowery and ornate speech.

Though it be plain and simple, provided it does not lose its true meaning, the essential thing is to enable people to receive understanding. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when the group of six [monks] lent money to laypeople, they demanded double."
[If one does so], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one causes a living being to be thrown into [water], or if one throws oneself into [it] to escape, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
A *bhikṣuṇī* is not permitted to borrow a monk’s room; if a *bhikṣuṇī* borrows a private dwelling, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* brews her own alcohol, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding food offered at the stūpas of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, when it was not known who should eat it, the Buddha said: "Whether a *bhikṣu*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or an *upāsaka*..."
Regarding those who manage the *sai* (monastery), they should eat [the food]. Next is the food of the *stūpa*. The Buddha said: "Those who built the *stūpa* should eat it.

Regarding the treatment of the overturned bowl (*pātra-nyubja*), there are four sections in the text for laypeople (*avadāta-vastra*). The first is as explained above: having received the instruction, one acts with slander. The second concerns the time of *Dharmadatta* and those below him, as [described] in the text.
[The Buddha] came to reprimand [them]. Thirdly, after the Buddha told the bhikṣus [the rules], he established legal procedures (*dharmakarma*) for dealing with laypeople.

This section contains two parts. First, it clarifies the establishment of legal procedures for punishment, which involves three types of evaluation. First, one who possesses five qualities evaluates the layperson (*avadātavasana*).
Next, from "one who possesses ten qualities" onwards, he evaluates the offense committed. Third, from "having acted thus" onwards, he evaluates the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

The second [case] involves a messenger conveying the notification. The fourth [case] states that he immediately said, "I have truly obtained Ānanda in this way," which explains the subsequent compliance after the phrase "having killed me.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when performing the formal act of overturning the bowl (*pātra-parivartana*), one uses a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation); when resolving it, it is called "begging for the upright bowl" (*utkṣipta-pātra*) and requires a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations).

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, both overturning and uprighting use the *jñapti-mātra* (simple motion) procedure. According to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, it is a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this is the rule.
Yue was an upāsaka who, because he understood the Dharma, frequently debated with the bhikṣus and emerged victorious.

He mocked the bhikṣus, whereupon the Buddha decreed that they perform the *pātra-āvartaṇa* (turning-over of the bowl) through a formal *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. The Buddha sent him to question a certain bhikṣu regarding the meaning of "salt";

Yue did not understand it and mocked him, saying, "This man is an arhat. When he questioned another bhikṣu, the latter understood the name and its meaning thoroughly, yet he was merely an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
The Buddha said: "For this reason, those who do not understand the meaning must not mock [the offender] lightly; they should first perform a confession (*pratideśanā*). The Buddha said:

'Grant them the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for the resolution of the staff-bag (*daṇḍa-kośa-karman*). All three Vinayas contain the words for requesting and admonishing.

The reason one must observe silence in this matter is that, in general, when discussing the fundamental basis for maintaining the communal Dharma, since the monastic Dharma is practiced with harmony as its priority, if..."

If the Sangha performs what is improper, or acts in a manner contrary to the Sangha’s proper conduct, it is appropriate to reprimand and interrogate them. However, even those capable of reprimanding must first consider whether they should proceed or not.
If one perceives that others do not discern right from wrong, or if one lacks virtuous companions, then even if one witnesses an unrighteous act, one should remain silent and refrain from speaking.

Therefore, the text states: When Śāriputra saw the Sangha performing an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) and no one agreed with him, he wished to remain silent and let it proceed. The Buddha [said...]
He said: "Listen! Why? For fear that the Saṃgha might become divided. Furthermore, there are those who ought to be rebuked;

one uses words to examine things, and since there are virtuous companions, it is logically necessary to rebuke them. Thus, the text below says: "Among the assembly of disciples, Aniruddha would settle disputes but would abandon the task of instructing and rebuking.
The Buddha said: "Aniruddha, how could you possibly instruct and rebuke? Is it not because of you, Śāriputra?"
This is not the case with Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. Now, regarding these five and three: the first ten are "silent," while the subsequent five are "in harmony. Why is this so?

When the mind perceives right and wrong, yet one remains silent without manifesting it through speech, it is called "silence. When the object and the mind correspond, and one honors patience by approving, it is termed "harmony.
According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, when the bhikṣus assemble to perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*), if within that assembly there are those who act contrary to the Dharma...
If one sees the assembly of monks, the ritual act will not be accomplished. If this person has one or two companions, they may be exhorted;

if he is alone, there is no need to exhort him. Why? Because the power of the great assembly is great; it might even expel him, which would be of no benefit to the Dharma and would only result in suffering for himself.
For these reasons, one should remain silent.
Next, regarding the explanation according to the text: if distinguished by whether they are silent or not silent, the first ten are silent, while the latter five are harmonious.

If distinguished by whether they are "as it is" (tathatā) or not, the first five are not in accordance with the Dharma, while the latter two sets of five are in accordance with the Dharma. This clarifies what is not in accordance with the Dharma, analyzed from the perspective of the mind.

It does not depend on the object. The reason for this is that within the accomplishment of the initial five formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), three involve objects that are non-Dharmic and thus possess both right and wrong, which are termed the "five non-procedures" (*pañcādharmāḥ*).
Therefore, we know that it refers to the mind. The first phrase refers to seeing another as acting in accordance with the Dharma.

It is appropriate to remain silent and maintain harmony, yet if one’s mind does not accord [with the assembly], one incurs offense oneself; this is called "unlawful" (*adharma*). The second case refers to the "unlawfulness of others.

If there are companions who agree with one, it is appropriate to reprove them and correct their errors; to remain silent and allow them to act unlawfully constitutes the third case, which is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense.

It is improper to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for confession unless one remains silent and fails to reprove them; therefore, it is declared unlawful. As for the fourth case, people... [text ends].

[The assembly] gathers completely. Because one remains silent and does not rebuke, it is not [a valid] *naivāsika* (resident) [act]. The fifth phrase concerns the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*).

If one does not gather at the boundary of the precept-field (*sīmā*), but knows [the situation] alone and does not inform others, although the act is accomplished, the statement is invalid. Next, regarding the five objects, there is both validity and invalidity;

yet because the mind remains as it was, in the first phrase, even if a guest has good companions, if they merely speak without discerning the object and remain silent—rebuking what is accomplished so as to reconcile a breach—the mind therefore remains as it was.
