this is because it is seen to be entirely exhausted [in its potency]. As for medicinal substances kept for the duration of one's life, they do not incur the offense of "overnight contact" (*sthāpana-saṃsarga*) with salt; those cases where consumption is prohibited are as stated in the text.
At that time, the group of six monks ate food mixed with salt that had been kept overnight. The Buddha said, "One should not eat food mixed with salt that has been kept overnight at a stūpa.
Therefore, it is as prescribed in the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*. Furthermore, in the text, it is stated that only medicines for life-long use (*yāvajjīvika*) are permitted;

thus, the *Pañcavargīka-vinaya* says: "Salt and ginger may be kept overnight. Regarding the eight types of *jañjala* liquor, the *Pañcavargīka-vinaya* refers to them as "unfermented liquor" (*amadya*).

Now, as for the statement that one may drink it: this is because one sees that the sap of the wood is originally not something that has not been fermented. Furthermore, since the seasonal laborers have not yet changed their beverages, drinking is permitted;
this refers to the time when it was originally fermented, which, after a long duration, has transformed into [the current state], yet it remains no different from the original wood sap.
Why is it that one may not drink? Therefore, it is said that one may drink *jaḷu* liquor; yet the regulation states that one must not drink it.

If it is categorized as a fermented beverage (*pāna*), the Noble Ones permit its consumption. However, if it is originally a distilled spirit or has undergone fermentation, it is categorized as wine (*madya*), and the Noble Ones do not permit its drinking.

For this reason, among the eight [types of intoxicants] mentioned in the preceding text, the first four—which lack the actual appearance of wine—are all prohibited from being drunk. Thus [it is concluded].
It is said: up to the case of the *bāga-ja* (or *vāgaja*) as in the *Kṣudraka-vastu*. When the monks obtained *āmra-prasāda* (mango juice), the Buddha said, "I allow you to drink it.

If it has not yet fermented into wine, it is permitted to be drunk even at improper times; if it has fermented into wine, it should not be drunk. If one drinks it, one is to be dealt with according to the law, as prescribed in the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*.
In a poor dwelling, we [the monks] purified our own quarters. In a poor place, they made wine and drank it. Ninth: one may possess an uncut sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).

This is based on the principle of the *saṃyama* (sewing) rule: if one does not cut [the cloth], there is no offense. Likewise, if one possesses a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) that exceeds the prescribed measure without having cut it down, there should likewise be no offense.

However, if one follows the principle of the *asaṃyama* (non-sewing) rule, a transgression (*āpatti*) may arise; for the regulation states that one must not possess [a mat] without cutting it to the proper measure.
Therefore, the text specifies the measurements: the length is two *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha’s hand, and the width is one and a half *vitasti*. Furthermore, the width may be increased...
Each is half a span in length, because the Buddha established this as the prescribed measure. Therefore, it is said that the rule was promulgated even for the group of six bhikṣus.

Once gold and silver were accepted and precious objects were possessed, they were relinquished and entrusted to laypeople; the laypeople then returned them to me. It was permitted for me to hold them on their behalf.
Although I received them, according to one dharma, I immediately took possession of them with the intention that they belong to those people. Knowing this clearly, there is no violation of the rule.

It is said: "If the treasure were on that person's side, it might be permissible not to incur an offense; however, if one immediately forms the intention that it belongs to that person and accepts it, then since the treasure is now on my own side, what difference is there between this and accepting it from Baddhananda himself and placing it upon the shop counter? Therefore, this is what is meant.

Second, one must understand the settling of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), namely the eight types of disputes such as those concerning the two fingers and so forth, regarding whether an offense has been committed or not. It is permissible to deliberate on these later within the monastery; thus, the two types of disputes are established.

This is not established, because in both cases the facts are identical while the views differ. Furthermore, in the section on "Extinction" (*nirodha*) below, it specifies that for one who possesses the wisdom of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-jñāna*), extinction occurs when five factors are present;

thus, we know that both are subsumed under verbal disputes (*vāda-vivāda*). Even if we were to provisionally grant that they are subject to disciplinary procedures (*karmavācanā*), they would still constitute a formal act (*kriyā*) within the category of verbal disputes.

The third category is named "Types" (*jāti*). Within this, there are ten matters and seven types. There are two names for offenses: namely, *pāyattika* (defeat) and *duskrta* (wrongdoing). Regarding the seven types:
the first, second, and sixth constitute three types of "sufficient food" (*pūrva-bhakta*). The third and fourth matters are two types of "separate assembly" (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).
"Blessing" (*puṇya*) refers to "storing indoors" (*antar-vasita*). The "excessive sitting mat," "drinking alcohol," and "accepting precious objects" are constant rules (*dharmatā*). One.

Regarding the matter: if one says that when a permanent dharma (*nityadharma*) is grasped as conventional, it is driven by the validity or invalidity of the teaching, yet no auspicious result is verified—this is still because of the planting of the seven [types of karma].
Now, to explain the permanent dharma: it means causing the opening of the eight matters; the seeds of the self [consist of] four, namely:
not receiving harmful contact, and the two internal boilings. Combined with the previous [four], there are ten.

The second [section], on the formal extinction (*pratisaṃharaṇa*), is divided into three parts. First, from "all the senior monks (*sthavira*) having assembled" until "making clear the selection of persons and the taking of the consent (*chanda*)," it explains the procedure for selecting those who will perform the formal act.

Second, from "at that time, all having departed" until "the senior monk goes to a secluded place in the Nāli Grove so that everyone knows," it explains the method for resolving and extinguishing the dispute. Third, from "those elders having all gone there" onwards, it corresponds to the formal response.

In the presence of the great assembly and the quarreling bhikṣus, five matters were brought forward to settle the dispute, so that the entire assembly might know it was wrong and distinguish the wrong from the right.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Upāli asked the Elder Sarvakāmin: "Is it pure for salt and ginger to be kept overnight together?
He replied, "It is not pure. He asked, "Where was this prohibited? He replied, "At Rājagṛha; it was established because of a forest-dwelling (*araṇyaka*) bhikṣu."

Question: What offense is committed? Answer: One commits the *pāyattika* (offense of eating stored food). Again, it was asked: Is it pure to eat by pinching food with two fingers? Answer: It is not pure. Up to:

One commits the *pāyattika* for failing to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) rite. Eating while sitting behind [the meal] is pure; eating beyond the village boundary is pure—it is also like this.
Furthermore, is it pure to mix ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar with curd? Answer: It is not pure. Question: Why? Answer: Because it is at an improper time (*vikāla*).

He drank it. [The other] replied, "It is impure. [The questioner asked], "Up to what offense does this constitute? [The reply was], "It constitutes the *pāyattika* offense of eating at an improper time.
Again he asked, "Is other *jāloru* liquor pure? The Elder asked, "What kind? He replied, "It is fermented liquor that has not yet matured.

[The Elder] replied, "It is impure. Up to [the conclusion]: "It constitutes the *pāyattika* offense of drinking alcohol. Again he asked, "Is a sitting mat, regardless of its size, pure? He replied, "It is impure. Up to...
It is said that this constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. Again, he asked whether what was previously practiced was pure. The Elder asked, "In what way?

He replied, "I practiced what was done during my time as a layperson. The Elder said, "Some things may be practiced, while others may not. Again, he asked whether seeking permission was pure. The Elder asked, "How so?
He replied, "One performs the *kamma* separately, and only afterwards comes to seek the permission of others. [The Elder] replied, "It is impure."

...up to the point where it is said that an offense has been committed. What follows the *karmavācanā* (formal act)? Furthermore, he asks: "Is the acceptance of gold, silver, and money pure? He answers:

"...up to the point where it constitutes an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. This concludes the questioning by means of counting sticks regarding the ten lower [offenses]. Together they return and assemble once more;
subsequently, within the great assembly, they again engage in question and answer one by one as above. Once a counting stick has been cast down, the *naiṣadyika* proclaims: "I..."
The discussion on the Vinaya is hereby concluded. That which the Buddha has not prescribed should not be arbitrarily prescribed; that which has already been prescribed must not be contravened.
At that time, all those present in the assembly rose from their seats: Upāli had one hundred and thirty *vassa*;

Revata two hundred and twenty *vassa*; Sambhūta three hundred and ten *vassa*. In total, there were seven hundred [monks]. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, this is the section on "Single Defilement."

The first is not [the case]. That is to say, at the time of the *poṣadha*, Yaśas taught others to accept gold, silver, and precious objects, and having received them, they divided them among themselves.

Yaśas joined in this and a dispute arose. After the formal act of suspension (*ukṣepa-karman*) was carried out against him, he sought out a great assembly of those of noble virtue. Once the *Vinaya-piṭaka* had been compiled and verified, it was proven that there was no such precedent;
only then was the rule established prohibiting the acceptance of gold and silver.

The section following "Non-Section" (*Atthakavagga*) clarifies the circulation [of the teachings] during the Buddha’s lifetime. This is divided into two parts. First, regarding the "Section" (*Vagga*):

this properly clarifies that Upāli was the primary custodian of the transmission, who resolved doubts and removed obstructions by inquiring about transgressions and other matters. Second, from the "Ekottara" (*Aṅguttaranikāya*) onwards: it clarifies the circulation by means of numerical limits and their mutual interconnections. As for the term "Section": [Note:

All matters of doubt within the sections above are consulted and resolved one by one, so that they may be understood, transmitted, and upheld;
thus it is called "Sectional Chapters" (Tiao-bu). Question: Among the various sūtras, all inquire after the title before circulating them. Why is it that this Vinaya does not inquire after the title?
Answer: The Sūtras are teachings that transform through signs; they clarify the depth and shallowness of principles, and their titles are not uniform. However, [the Vinaya]...

Because there are immeasurable [names], it is necessary to ask for the name to determine the scope of the school. Since this Vinaya practice and teaching is restricted to the Piṇi-piṭaka, there is no confusion with other names;
therefore, it is unnecessary to ask. Within this, the first four precepts are asked about in detail. Regarding the second category:
One need only inquire about these six; all else is omitted. Regarding the precept against impure conduct: suppose there is a crow or a vulture that seizes a woman and does not release her.
There is no offense if the owner has relinquished their claim, such that she has come under the possession of the bird, and one lacks the intention to steal another's property.
Therefore, there is no offense. This is not like a rat stealing a walnut; since the owner was unaware and had no intention of relinquishing it, there was no offense.
Later, however, when one perceives it as a peach and takes it, one commits a grave offense.

Furthermore, regarding the case of others' "side-born" or "single-born" children, because there was no intent to steal or cause harm, but only a heart of compassion and pity, there was likewise no offense. Because such an intention arose later, an offense was subsequently committed.

Regarding the precept against stealing: secondly, if one perceives a male as a female and takes his property or the like, and thereby commits an offense, this is because while there is a discrepancy in the mental state regarding the male or female, the underlying intention to steal another's property remains unchanged; therefore, an offense is committed. This applies equally when one perceives a woman as that very woman and so forth.

This case also involves a woman; it is a *sthūlātyaya* because there was a discrepancy in the perception regarding the name, but no discrepancy in the mind. The Buddha said: "The one who obstructs commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

Thus, there is no need to consider whether the number of persons reaches or does not reach five, as in cases such as burning or burying [the goods], where the offense is established merely by the completion of the damage of five *kārsāpaṇas*. Therefore, the theft is light.

Regarding "the grave offense": the meaning is as explained above. If one intends to steal another's robe but mistakenly obtains one's own, this refers to the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) due to a discrepancy in the object (*viṣaya-viparyāsa*).

There is no offense at all for obtaining one's own robe, because it is not an object from which an offense arises and there is no distinct harm [to oneself]. Regarding "and obtaining one's own robe, there is *duṣkṛta*":

this means that if one intends to take two robes belonging to another but only succeeds in taking one, one commits a grave offense; yet, by also mistakenly obtaining one's own robe, [there is the aforementioned *duṣkṛta*]. Due to...

If there are different owners, it may be considered a mental severance [of the connection], yet one incurs only a minor offense (duṣkṛta), because the two karmas are each incomplete as five [factors].
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed theft and then seized the property of that thief; he felt doubt. The Buddha said: "It is a pārājika."

This principle is analyzed in detail as previously explained in the section on the precept against stealing. Since these two aforementioned acts have not yet been relinquished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. As for guarding and watching, or receiving food when it is given, once it has come under one's own control, it becomes one's own property.

the Buddha stated that this constitutes a *pārājika* offense because the teacher did not send him to take it; thus, it is called "groundless. Because one acts with a thieving mind toward a donor (*dānapati*), one commits a grave offense.

Alternatively, it is called "groundless" because the teacher did not send him to take it. Once the donor has finished giving to the teacher, [the bhikṣu] takes it from the teacher’s possession with his own mind.

Because one acted with the intention of being a friend toward the person from whom it was taken, a grave offense is not committed. Taking by deceiving a donor constitutes a *pācittiya* due to the lie.

However, because one acts with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion for a small child, and lacks any intent to steal or cause loss, no offense is committed. This may be difficult for ordinary people to understand.

Regarding the term "exalted and superior bhikṣu": this is intended to demonstrate the absence of any intention to steal or cause harm. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Ānanda did not participate in the *poṣadha* for six years.

Skin, flesh, bone, and blood—if a woman does not give birth to these, they are said to be "transformed persons" (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*).
This is the second category of leakage. Whether it be from between the breasts, under the armpits, or even held within the mouth—all such cases are included.

Examining this textual explanation, one must also consider the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) to determine the degree of gravity. Regarding the four permutations mentioned above concerning harsh speech:

*Saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding the *Vinayottaragrantha*, as for the term "vinaya," it refers to the collective title of one section intended to encompass the Great Teaching.

It organizes the dharmas by number and connects them so that no aspect of the dharma-characteristics is omitted, thereby manifesting the entrustment; it takes the number one as its fundamental principle.
Adding one to one, it is thus called the *Ekottarika* (Incremental One). In this manner, it proceeds up to twenty-two.
However, within the text, seven sections—namely the fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, eighteenth, nineteenth, and twenty-second—are omitted; these are abbreviated so as not to be overly prolix.
This means that by taking "one" and connecting it to all "one-dharma" topics, "two" to all "two-dharma" topics, and so on for the three-dharma [topics] and beyond.
The same applies down to the twenty-two categories. There are those who maintain that there is a structural outline (*ko-vibhaṅga*) for their arising; this is a numerical method.
As for those that correspond to a single dharma-gate, they are collected in one place—how could there be a sequential order? Therefore, know that this objection is invalid.
Now, proceeding according to the main text, we establish fifteen sections based on the increasing number of items. First, within the section on the "increase of one," we divide [the text].
This is the explanation of the text. Within this section, there are two parts. First, from the beginning up to "the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada," the sequence is correctly elucidated.
Second, from "The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus" onwards, it points out the teachings—both false and correct—that were heard, stating:
"You should believe, abandon evil, and practice good. This is precisely the Dharma that is to be believed. Within the first part, there are again two sections; the first is as follows:

It is called "separate" because it refers specifically to the disciples' recounting of the event after the sutra has been authenticated;

Regarding the meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*), those who transmit the Dharma now cite it here to further establish proof and inspire faith. Since this meaning encompasses both aspects, it is called the "General Introduction" (*sāmānyanidāna*).
First, we shall explain the phrase "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth through a fivefold analysis: first, the reason why [the teaching] exists; second, the necessity for its existence.
The meaning [of this]. Third, the placement regarding the breadth and brevity. Fourth, the placement regarding the location. Fifth, the formal explanation of the text.
First, as for "having a source": by what cause is this statement possible? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is an omniscient person (*sarvajña*). He appears spontaneously;

"This is what I have heard. The answer is: "It was spoken by the great disciples, such as Ānanda and others. For what reason did they speak it? Because of the Buddha's instruction.
By what means did the Buddha instruct them? Because of Ānanda’s request. Again, for what reason did he make the request?
Because of the instruction of Aniruddha. For what reason did he instruct him? Because he saw that the mind of the bhikṣu Ānanda was distressed with grief. Why [was the bhikṣu Ānanda] so?
He was distressed by grief because he saw that the Tathāgata was entering parinirvāṇa. As the Buddha was about to pass away, he lay between the twin trees with his head to the north.
At that time, Ānanda, whose bonds of kinship and affection were not yet severed, was submerged in an ocean of sorrow and could not master himself.
Aniruddha then awakened Ānanda, saying: "You are the one who guards the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha; you ought not to be like an ordinary person, drowning yourself in an ocean of grief.
All conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of impermanence; do not be sorrowful or anxious. Furthermore, the Buddha has entrusted the Dharma to you in turn;
if you now fall into distress and despondency, you will fail in your duty. You should ask the Buddha regarding the period after his parinirvāṇa."
"Regarding these matters: how should we practice the Path? Who shall serve as our teacher? How shall we dwell together with the foul-mouthed Chandaka?
What words should be placed at the beginning of the Buddha’s sutras? Such matters concerning future events ought to be asked of the Buddha.

Having heard these words, his distressed mind was slightly refreshed; aided by the power of mindfulness regarding the Path, he questioned the Buddha concerning these matters by the side of the Buddha’s final bed.
The Buddha said: "After my passing, rely upon the Dharma as your own refuge—that is, the four foundations of mindfulness—and do not rely upon anything else.

if his mind becomes supple and virtuous, you should further preach the Dharma to him, and he will then be able to attain the Path. This is the Dharma I have accumulated over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*."

The *piṭaka*. This Dharma-gate begins with the words, "Thus have I heard. Therefore, when it is now traditionally transmitted that one is about to proclaim a Buddha-sūtra, it likewise contains the phrase "Thus have I heard.
Second, there must be a purpose for this: for what reason did the Buddha originally instruct that these words be placed at the beginning?
It is to generate faith in sentient beings. How do such words as "Thus" and so forth generate faith? Ānanda and others, through their own faith and compliance with the Buddha’s words, declare—
The Buddha’s words are indeed the Buddha’s words; therefore, they cause other sentient beings to give rise to faith just as he himself has.
When one says, "I have heard," it means that faith is born. Ānanda and others are but ordinary persons; if they were to say, "This was spoken by me," most people would not believe them.
Because it is said that this Dharma was heard from the Buddha, everyone believes it together. Such is the arising of faith. Faith.
For what purpose is faith generated? Faith is the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma and the foremost means of receiving the Dharma.
Whenever one enters the Buddha-dharma, one must first give rise to faith; therefore, the sūtras and śāstras refer to it as the "hand of faith. It is like a person who possesses hands.
When one reaches a place where treasures are gathered, one may collect them as one pleases; yet if one has no hands, one will obtain nothing at all.

Likewise, those who enter the Buddha-dharma possess the hand of faith, by which they may collect the treasures of the Path’s teachings as they please; yet if they lack faith, they will gain nothing at all.
Therefore, one must give rise to faith. This is called "right faith. As this may be the commentary of a later transmitter, I have now set it aside as such.
These words were spoken for the sake of such a person. If they neither believe nor disbelieve the truth, then even such words as these would be insufficient to encourage their faith;

Third, regarding the extensive and the abbreviated: A question arises concerning why at the beginning of all sūtras there is the single phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), which serves as a certification for the entire section.

This is because the person, time, place, and event are, in every case, one and the same. Alternatively, within a single section, many such phrases may be placed, as in the *Āgama* sūtras and others, because the persons, times, places, and events are each distinct.
Now, this Vinaya prohibition applies throughout the entire dispensation; furthermore, it concerns the persons, places, and events.
It is distinct. Why is it that we do not establish multiple "Thus" (evam) for each individual precept? If there were only one, what would be the meaning? To explain the term:

generally speaking, the word "Thus" serves as a basis for authentication and faith. If there were multiple "Thus" statements, it would imply a lack of uniformity in direction; therefore, only one is established.
Furthermore, if multiple were established based on differences in person, time, place, or matter, there would be the aforementioned confusion. Moreover, it may be said:

"The characteristics of these are exhausted. Regarding the phrase "by reason of a single principle," this also collectively summarizes the intent behind the formulation of the precepts throughout the entire section.

One should immediately believe one section; its text is concise and its exhortation essential, which is why it is placed here. Next, the terminology will be explained. Upāli says: "The Buddha’s words are 'thus' (evam)";
this points out the Dharma as it was heard. When the teaching of the specific school is set forth without error, it is called "thus" (yathā).

Question: Within the Buddha-dharma, all phenomena are empty and devoid of a self. Why, then, do you say "I have heard"? Answer: The disciples of the Buddha deeply understand...

The offenses are numerous; they are subsumed under the categories of light and heavy, for there is nothing that is not encompassed by them. To cite one example each: two light and two heavy.

That is to say, the *pārājika* offense is considered heavy, while the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and others are considered light. The term "two places" (*dvi-sthāna*) refers to the fact that these two cases—where [an action] gives rise to light [retribution] and where it gives rise to heavy [retribution]—are distinguished by their relative gravity.

This can be understood through their mutual explanation. Next, let us distinguish them by means of annihilationism and eternalism. Those who perceive the light of the world are those who, having detached from the aggregates (*skandha*), reckon the self as existing within the aggregates;

Therefore it is said that there is no such thing as the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) in the world. This is based on the present life. To see the world as having a limit is the view of annihilation;
to see it as being without limit is the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). These two are based on the future. To hold that "this body is the life" is called the view of annihilation;

to hold that "the body is one thing and the life is another" is called the view of eternity. These two are the roots of annihilationism and eternalism. To say that the Tathāgata passes into extinction (*parinirvāti*) is [the view of] annihilation.
To see that there is no parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is the view of eternalism; this is said with reference to the past.
To hold that there is or is not a parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is the calculation of annihilationism and eternalism: the coarse self is extinguished, while the subtle self eternally persists.

That there is neither existence nor non-existence of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa is the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As for the next two *vinayas*, these refer to the *vinaya* concerning offenses and disputes, which are designated according to what is to be extinguished.

The third major section concerns those who slander and those who do not slander. This section contains seven pairs: first, slandering versus not slandering; second, not receiving wholesome teachings; third, opposing the Tathāgata;
fourth, stubbornly clinging to views while maintaining purity before the Tathāgata; fifth, failing to honor the Tathāgata; sixth, failing to encounter the Tathāgata;

and seventh, being harsh and lacking a compassionate heart toward the Tathāgata. Within the category of slandering and not slandering, there are five [points], the first of which is a general [statement].
This clarifies slander and non-slander, and demonstrates that the offense of slandering the Buddha is grave. Second, it is discussed in terms of the eighteen dharmas;

third, in terms of two locations; fourth, in terms of two matters; and fifth, in terms of two views. These latter four pairs each cite the initial text to explain them. First is lack of faith and delight.

This refers to the intensification of jealousy. It means that one’s own mind is distorted, and being exclusively attached to one's own views, one speaks in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma; therefore, it is called "slander.

Furthermore, it is called slander because one lacks faith and understanding, yet claims to accept and uphold [the teaching]. However, the principles of the Buddha-dharma are profound and beyond the comprehension of ordinary beings.

If one’s understanding is merely superficial, yet they claim to have exhausted its depths, or if their minds lack discernment as they discourse upon the words of the Sages, it is for these reasons that it is so named.

This constitutes slander. If one recognizes the limits of one's own understanding and realizes that one’s comprehension reaches only this far, then speaking according to one's own capacity based on conventional reasoning is permissible.

As for all other profound meanings, only the Sages know them; such [limited] discourse increases one's merit and wisdom—how could there be any fault? Now, those who claim to have reached the ultimate limit are what we call "slanderers.
Therefore, when it is said to you that slandering the Tathāgata incurs great and heavy retribution, it is stated in order to manifest this truth.
The sin of slandering the Buddha is grave; it cannot be compared to anything else. Within the twenty-eighth dharma, there are two parts.

these are collectively termed the "Eighteen Dharmas. Next are two locations, next two matters, and next two views. If these are explained in summary, they are called the "arriving at the explanation of three from the *Ekottarika-āgama* corresponding [to others]."

Those petty kings of the bordering states who do not obey commands are like the analogy of minor bhikṣus who do not obey the commands of bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma as they have taught for practice.
The people and industries of the five kingdoms being abandoned and ruined are like the upāsakas... [text truncated].
The "Sai" (塞) and others cannot purely cultivate the five precepts and ten wholesome acts; this corresponds to the analogy of the cessation and abandonment of one's livelihood.

Next, those who possess power through unrighteousness correspond to the second preceding analogy of the flourishing of a multitude of thieves. These Dharma-monks being powerless correspond, in reverse order, to the first phrase of the analogy regarding the weakness of the Dharma-king’s power.
That the monks who act according to the Dharma do not obtain peace and happiness corresponds to the third [preceding] analogy of the Dharma...
The analogy of the king not obtaining peace and happiness: "If he is among the multitude, he may not speak" corresponds to the entry [into the womb].
"If he is in a secluded place, from this point downward, these dharmas do not function" corresponds to the exit [from the womb].

"He does not practice with diligence" and so forth corresponds to the fourth analogy, that of the minor kings of the bordering states. "Then the various devas and people" and so forth corresponds to the fifth analogy. This is the second analogy.
Within this, there are also five [analogies]. First, the analogy of the powerful king’s force being superior to that of the powerful, righteous bhikṣu;
second, the analogy of the weak force of the bandits of the multitude, from the point they flee in hiding downward, representing the powerful force of the unrighteous bhikṣus;

third, the analogy of the Dharma-king and those below him, representing the peaceful and secure coming and going of the righteous bhikṣus; fourth, the analogy of the minor kings of the bordering states and those below them, representing the various minor bhikṣus.

Qiu complies with the instructions; this corresponds to the analogy of practicing as taught. From "within the five sense objects" onwards, it corresponds to ordinary people obtaining the opportunity to freely practice the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten wholesome actions.

Next, the powerful *dharmika* bhikṣu corresponds to the first analogy above regarding the king’s superior power. The *adharmika* bhikṣus and those below, including all manner of evils, correspond to the second analogy above.
Regarding the phrase "those who are non-Dharmic and powerless" therein: this corresponds to those who join forces with bandits and are weak.

As for the previously mentioned non-Dharmic bhikṣus who come to follow their commands, this corresponds to all those who come to submit and say, "If we were to flee and hide, we would not commit evil."

The phrase "fleeing together" corresponds to the above. At that time, from the "monks who act according to the Dharma" down to "those who do not practice according to the Dharma," corresponds to the third analogy, the "King of Dharma’s Peace and Happiness.
From "diligently practicing" onwards corresponds to the fourth. From "then causing all devas and humans" onwards corresponds to the fifth.
These two analogies of "like" and "not like" collectively illustrate the aforementioned two assemblies in their entirety. Second, the contemplation.
The text consists of three sections. First, up to the phrase "they do not obtain peace and happiness," it explains that they are harmed because of mutual contention.

Second, from "If a bhikṣu disputes with another bhikṣu" onwards, each examines their own faults and benefits. Third, from "After the Buddha had spoken" onwards, they receive and uphold [the teaching] with joy.
Each section of the Chinese text has three parts. First, a general examination of the faults and benefits for both the subject and the object. Second, from "How should the bhikṣus...

onwards, there is a specific instruction on the method for the subject and object to examine their faults. Regarding the person who has been formally charged (*ud-dhṛta*) examining their own faults: they should reflect as follows:
"It is because I have committed an offense that I have been brought before others for formal charge; had I not committed an offense, I would not have been subjected to such a charge."
He feels deep compassion for me; I should repent and wash away my past and future transgressions. One who can bring forth another’s fault must first examine their own shortcomings;

since it was due to that person’s own offense that they were censured by me, if one censures another with a mind of anger, their own fault exceeds that of the other—how then could they save the other?
For this reason, one should give rise to a good heart and benevolent intent, ensuring that the offense is removed and the dispute is settled. Third, if a bhikṣu has already engaged in a dispute...

The following summarizes the benefits of contemplation. Regarding the third point, "the two types of persons—the ignorant and the wise"—this refers to the passage concerning liberation and non-liberation, as has already been explained above.

Regarding the fourth point, the section on the rules for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), there are three parts: first, it sets forth the benefits of establishing these rules for settling disputes, illustrating them through one specific approach.
Other benefits are for the most part non-existent. Regarding the two obstacles, both the subject and the object must internally possess the requisite virtues;

thus, one gate is briefly cited. Fifth, concerning the duration and cessation of the True Dharma (*saddharma*): hitherto, the "is" and "is not" have been explained in conjunction. Now, in this passage, as with the "is not," they are distinguished.
First, it clarifies the rapid extinction of the light; second, it distinguishes the long endurance of the True Dharma. In the first section, there are seven gates, the first of which is:
The True Dharma will be swiftly extinguished. Second, one cannot produce wholesome states. Third, one destroys oneself. Fourth, one commits offenses.
Fifth, one is rebuked by the wise. Sixth, one incurs many transgressions. Seventh, one falls into hell like an arrow shot. These seven points are divided into three sections:
the first section clarifies how the True Dharma is swiftly extinguished; the next five sections demonstrate the harm to persons; and finally—
First point: Because the previous causes have already established a transgression that invites a grave root [of demerit]. Second point:

Regarding the "destruction of the five" among the five aggregates, as for the statement that "wholesome dharmas do not arise," this is because one has reached the point of expounding the eight [wrong views]. When one's view does not rely on principle, then even wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen cannot arise;

this is what is meant by "self-destruction. As for the statement that "already arisen wholesome dharmas no longer continue to arise," it is therefore called "destruction. As for the statement "committing an offense":
This is because [the offense] arises according to what one perceives, rather than being intentional. The Noble Ones have spoken of its faults; therefore, it is said to be "reproached by the wise.
Since the violation arises conditioned by contact, it is said that "one incurs many offenses. These seven gates each correspond to their respective explanations.

Within the two increases, there are two dharmas, two locations, two matters, and two violations—four pairs making eight. There are seven superior defects; when categorized individually, they should amount to seven. However, in the present text...

In the middle [section], the first two and the seventh are each explained individually, while the remaining four are analyzed collectively. What is here termed "two transgressions" is analogous to the two aforementioned views;
"transgression" is stated in reference to the object, whereas "view" refers to the cognitive mind. Next, the analysis of long-term abiding also consists of seven gates, each having four pairs;
when stated in reverse, these constitute six.

The sixth section, "Legal Procedures for Rescinding a Formal Act," consists of three parts in the Chinese text. First, it clarifies the conditions under which a formal act of censure may be rescinded;

this refers to the case where, upon being censured, one manifests that the fault was indeed present and thus the censure was appropriate, hence it is called "proper. Second, from "if the formal act was performed according to the Dharma" onwards, it clarifies the rescinding of a formal act in relation to the specific matter;

"according to the Dharma" means that the person censured is one who can be trusted, and the remedy was applied appropriately to the illness, hence it is called "according to the Dharma. Third, again...

Regarding the passage beginning with "There are two dharmas that should be followed by a formal reprimand," there are six types of disciplinary measures for treating illness through medicine and proper practice.

Among these, the first [category] consists of six kinds: (1) *udghāta* (formal accusation), (2) *smṛti* (remembrance), (3) *svavāda* (self-accusation), (4) prohibition of the *pravāraṇā*, (5) prohibition of the *poṣadha*, and (6) prohibition of the *pravāraṇā*.
Within the first [category], the *udghāta*, when it reaches the exposition of the two dharmas, its five meanings—such as *smṛti* and so forth—are identical; therefore, it is said "also."
Thus it is. Next, regarding the second [category], there are two locations, three matters, and four offenses; as these all apply to the preceding six, it says, "it is also thus.

Next, within the six sections concerning formal censure (*pratisedha-udghāta*) according to the Dharma, each has four pairs. In the text, first its censure is manifested, which consists of four pairs;
next, from "having performed the recollection" (*smṛti-karaṇa*) onwards, the remaining five sections each have four pairs. Furthermore...

Regarding the statement that "the two preceding passages should mention *udghāta* (formal accusation) and so forth," this indicates that the four faults (*doṣa*) are to be countered by the six remedies (*pratipakṣa*) beginning with *udghāta*.
Therefore, the four faults constitute the stages (*avasthā*), and each must be supplemented by the six remedies such as *udghāta*; thus, there are four sets of six.

Now, within the formal procedure of *udghāta* according to the Dharma, the Saṃgha maintains the ritual in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, the six remedies beginning with *udghāta* are established as the stages, each counteracting the four faults, thereby forming six.
This is the fourth [category]. Next, within the seven types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts of discipline), four instances of *tarjanīya* (reproach) are extensively listed with their characteristics.

Following the section on *pravāsanīya* (banishment) and below, these are treated more briefly as before; that is to say, if one appears before the assembly of monks and speaks of these four grounds, yet lacks shame and causes strife between superiors and subordinates, the *tarjanīya* rite is performed against them.
If one appears before laypeople and speaks of these four, it destroys the faith of those people at that time.

One must administer the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment). If, upon being addressed regarding these four [offenses], one continues to commit them repeatedly and does not desist, nor does their resolve become established, one must administer the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence).

If, upon being addressed regarding these four, one reviles, slanders, or causes distress to laypeople (*avadātavasana*), it is necessary to require a formal apology; one must then administer the *apratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of exclusion).
Because of having been addressed regarding these four, there is an offense. If, when questioned, one says "I do not see [the fault]," or if one sees it but does not confess, or if one speaks...
Regarding the arising of afflictions such as the hindrance of desire, they are treated according to the three groups.

Within the seventh [category], the increase or non-increase of outflows (*āsrava*), it is briefly explained by way of seven pairs: namely, shame (*hrī*) and lack of shame (*ahrī*), and purity (*śubha*) and impurity (*aśubha*).
It is like the passage on the two views: transgression and non-transgression, grave and light, with remainder and without remainder—this is precisely what is meant by "residual" and "non-residual.
It refers to the Dharma and non-Dharma, the prescribed and the non-prescribed. Extensively citing such passages on the two views and so forth, there are many varieties.
The eighth [section], "Renouncing the Precepts," consists of two pairs of dharmas, which may be understood accordingly.
The ninth [section], "The Benefits of the Precepts," has two parts. First, its benefits are set forth; there are nine pairs. The first four pairs may be understood.

Regarding the two types of outflows (*āsrava*) in the world, they are categorized as five pairs of adversaries. Speaking in terms of being oppressed by external objects, the latter [part] speaks of fear.
This refers to taking the apprehension of circumstances as the cause. As for the term "outflows" (*āsrava*), its meaning extends to both cause and effect.

"Unwholesome dharmas" refers to present karmic causes; "grave offenses" refers to future evil results. For the second time, the precepts are cited, referring to the two hundred and eighty rules of training.
Each consists of nine sets of two dharmas; within these, the extensive texts are censured, while the rest are briefly indicated.

Furthermore, from the "Three Increases" (*vṛddhi-traya*) downward, regarding the benefits of the precepts, each contains numerous instances of three, four, five, and so forth; all should be understood according to this explanation.

Within the text on the "Three Increases," there are five sections. The first, up to the *karma* for breaking proper deportment (*īryāpatha*), clarifies how the three types of *karma* remove offenses and extinguish disputes.
The method of subduing [the mind] consists of five parts: first, the general introduction; second, the explicit clarification of the merits of practicing the three trainings (*śikṣā*) and below;

third, the separate elucidation of the characteristics of compliance and opposition regarding the various practices and the three aggregates (*saṃgraha-vastu*) and below; fourth, the relinquishing of the precepts;
and fifth, the benefits of upholding them.
The initial section has two parts. First, the analysis of the validity and invalidity of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures), along with the clarification of the teacher’s qualifications.

Second, from "There are three matters regarding the loss [of the precepts]" onwards, there is an extensive discussion on the distinctions between transgressions and non-transgressions across various precepts. The former part further divides into two. First, regarding the three types of *karmavācanā*:

these take the essential substance (*tattva*) to encompass the functions (*vyāpāra*), and according to their functional differentiation, they branch out into the hundred-and-one specific variations. Based on this, the *Vinaya* contains one hundred and four [procedures].
The fifteen [categories] and so forth are subsumed within the three bodies; there is nothing they do not encompass. Therefore, it is said that they "include all.

Second, regarding the broad application according to specific matters and their respective functions, one distinguishes between what is in accordance with the Dharma and what is not. Within the context of "mindfulness according to the Dharma," "broad mindfulness" refers to one who has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and is capable of receiving it.
This means broadly searching for one's own transgressions; because this is done intentionally, it is called "broad mindfulness."

Regarding the statement that one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), one should repent according to the Dharma and request [forgiveness] from the Saṃgha; this is called "repentance according to the Dharma" (*yathādharma*).

This refers to the weighing of the gravity of the dispute, which gives rise to a *vitandā-vivāda* (contentious dispute). As for the "three methods of reconciliation," these refer to the methods for disciplining and subduing individuals.

Because there are three sets of three methods, the first three of the seven are briefly cited here as the methods of treatment. As for the "three methods of settlement," they refer to the [first] four... [text ends].
This is because it brings an end to disputes. There are three procedures for performing a *karmavācanā*: first, summoning the bhikṣu to be present; second, making the formal announcement (*jñapti*);

and third, performing the three proclamations (*trivācanā*). Because this bhikṣu delights in quarreling and, by performing the three proclamations against others, causes discord within the Saṃgha, he is subjected to censure.
Furthermore, because he causes discord among laypeople in the village, leading them to lose faith, he is censured.

Therefore, the *parivāsa* (probation) discipline is administered. Specifically, for those who delight in strife and contention, because they are ignorant and repeatedly commit transgressions, the *niśraya* (dependence) discipline is administered.

Next, the qualifications of the precept-conferring master (*upādhyāya*) may be understood through this analysis. Regarding what is called "breaking the precepts and undergoing censure," this refers to committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).
Because of this grave matter, they mutually slander one another and cause discord within the Saṃgha; thus, they commit an offense of the second category. This is [the meaning].
This is termed "breaking the precepts" and merits censure. If one has committed a *pārājika* offense and conceals it, they must logically be subject to formal expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*).
If, however, one does not conceal it, they may personally undergo training and repentance; this is not what is being clarified here.

If, while in a village, one sits or rises on the same bed as a woman and utters coarse or evil speech, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and should be subjected to expulsion. If, on account of having committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one reviles [others]...

Slandering laypeople, obstructing others from undergoing disciplinary treatment, and failing to establish one's own resolve due to the violation of precepts—because such individuals have broken the precepts, they require the granting of formal dependence (*niśraya*).

Because they have broken the precepts, it is said that [the offense] was not seen, or that there was no confession. Or, because of committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one speaks of "desire" and "non-obstruction," and so forth;

these must be treated by means of the three types of formal accusation (*tri-udghāta*). For those who have broken right view or broken dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), all must be treated by the seven methods. The various types of punishments can be understood through similar explanations.
There are three dharmas that should be understood as liberation: that which should be seen is seen, that which should be repented is repented, and that which should be relinquished is relinquished.

Since it is said that one "should see," once it is seen, it constitutes liberation; thus we know that when one "should repent," once it is repented, it likewise constitutes liberation—this is logically unobjectionable.
For the teaching of repentance directly contradicts the original [wrong] view; how could it be otherwise? As for the scriptural statement, "one should have faith," it does not [apply here].

Regarding "faith" (*śraddhā*) and those who are "accused and disciplined": this refers to arriving at the formal proclamation of the eighteen [grounds for accusation] and so forth. Is this also [a case of] "wrongdoing"?

It broadly applies to all phenomena, yet it is not established within the third ground of accusation. Alternatively, that which follows this ground shares the same principle as the previous two, because it is not restricted to matters performed out of compliance with one's own inclinations.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "weighing the bhikṣu": if he is a good person and is suddenly reviled or slandered...

The layperson (avadātavasana) immediately feels shame and remorse; one should not discipline them. If they lack shame and remorse, and do not discipline themselves, there is no way to cease their transgressions;

therefore, it is said that one must weigh [the case of] the bhikṣu. Regarding weighing the layperson: if they possess sincere faith and profound compassion, and are endowed with the five qualities, they are fit to discipline the bhikṣu.
If these five qualities involve strife, there is no need to discipline them. As for weighing the matter: if...

If one reviles [the offender] for the sake of their benefit, this does not constitute a formal disciplinary action (*karma*). However, if it is done with the intent to cause harm, then disciplinary action must indeed be administered;
therefore, the *dharma* should be applied in harmony. For this reason, it is called a "weighed" (*tulita*) *karma*. Regarding the weighing of the offense:

if one has committed an offense of the first category (*pārājika*), administering discipline would be of no benefit, and thus there is no need for it. If one has committed an offense of the lower four categories, then disciplinary action must be administered. This distinguishes between what is real and what is unreal.

The presence or absence of the three roots, and whether an act was committed or not—meaning the reality or unreality of the offense—the third point, weighing the status of the layperson (*avadātavasana*), is the same as above.

Next, the explanation of the second section, which distinguishes according to the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), has three parts: first, a brief treatment of the two characteristics of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pārājika*;

second, from "there are three kinds of persons who have committed [an offense]" onwards, which relies on the person to distinguish between the agent and the object, and between what is appropriate and inappropriate; third, the three kinds of correct speech (*samyag-vāk*).

Below this, the text examines the roots and objects of the offense to clarify what constitutes a transgression and what does not. Regarding the first point, it is established that one cannot claim to have attained what has not been attained;
such a claim is subsumed under false speech. Since the attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) is not an isolated occurrence, it necessarily depends upon both body and speech.
Therefore, the following five sets of three phrases precisely distinguish the differences between transgressions of body and speech. Karma is... [text ends].
It is self-established because it arises from [the preceding]. The next three phrases clarify the three afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding "bodily desire to harm" and so forth, there are three [sections] that correctly clarify the completion of karma through the manifestation of thought: first, bodily transgression, which refers to having already performed a written expression through bodily action;
verbal transgression is easily understood; and both bodily and verbal transgressions together constitute the second phrase. As for the three types of characteristics, the body manifests...
As for "the one who," it is like putting on or taking off the *saṃghāṭī* robe and so forth. As for "manifesting signs through speech," it refers to saying to a layperson:
"Tomorrow I shall go to your house and preach the Dharma; he is a holy man. Then, on the following day, one goes there and preaches the Dharma for them, causing others to understand and realize it.
This is what is meant by "both body and speech being easy to recognize. Regarding the third line, the three kinds of spells: first, the bodily radiance; second, the body itself...
"Mantra" refers to the practice of writing talismans and performing incantations or exorcisms to represent that one has attained holiness, thereby causing others to understand and believe this.

"Verbal" refers to speaking mantra words with the mouth to effect transformations, manifesting that one has attained holiness. "Both body and speech" refers to performing both types of action simultaneously.
The fourth phrase consists of three types of non-dignified conduct (*anairyāṇika*). Regarding non-dignified bodily conduct:

this refers to such acts as piercing the body with a thousand needles, practicing breath-holding, or abstaining from grains, all performed to manifest that one has attained saintliness. Regarding non-dignified verbal conduct: this refers to reciting scriptures claiming they emerged from the Buddha’s own mouth.
Non-dignified conduct involving both [body and speech] occurs when these two modes of action are practiced together. The fifth phrase consists of three types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Regarding the "vitality of the body": this refers to manifesting the form of a Buddha, sitting upright and motionless, thereby acting as a holy one. Regarding the "vitality of speech":

this refers to declaring that one is in a place of peril, such that lions, tigers, and wolves cannot harm one, and that various deities also constantly come to make offerings to one, thereby manifesting that one possesses holiness.
Regarding the "vitality of both body and speech": these two types of karma are practiced simultaneously. From here below, [the text] proceeds by way of...

Regarding persons: first, there are three types of persons, explained below in the section on the *pācittiya* rules and those following. Next, regarding the three types of transgressors, these are contrasted with the *naiḥsargika* rules.
As for the three types of silence, they are categorized according to whether persons are dull-witted or wise.

"Silence despite knowing" refers to one who well understands right and wrong and remains silent out of patient forbearance. "Silence due to ignorance" refers to an unlearned bhikṣu who does not comprehend what is correct or incorrect.
"To silently acquiesce out of delusion while remaining silent" means that although one has studied, one lacks understanding; it refers to the foolish mind silently accepting [the teaching].

Having already spoken of the emptiness of arising, one then fulfills the categories of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) so that they are not destroyed by conditions; this is called "abiding in the precepts" (*śīlasthita*).

Attaining true emptiness and the untainted (*anāsrava*), with perfect understanding becoming clear and bright, firm and non-retrogressive—this is named "abiding in vision" (*dṛṣṭisthita*). Skillfully understanding all phenomena in accordance with the teachings...

Because it cannot be destroyed by *ākrośa* (abuse), it is called *karmasthiti* (abiding in formal action). Because one is free from the subtle transgressions of the lower three categories [of offenses], it is called *īryāpathasthiti* (abiding in dignified deportment).
Because one has severed the five types of wrong livelihood and dwells in right livelihood, it is called *ājīvasthiti* (abiding in livelihood).

Regarding the three types of persons who dispute, there are seven sets of three phrases below; these positions are organized into four groups. The first three sets of three phrases are spoken in reference to the disputing parties. Next...

The fourth [section] consists of one and three [subsections] concerning the relative relationship between the subject and the object. Next, there are two and three [subsections] explaining the persons who resolve disputes.

Finally, the last one and three [subsections] cite the three types of persons who initiate disputes mentioned above, so that they may be eliminated. The details are as in the text. This concludes the four types of disputes and the three types of persons.

The *utpanna-adhikaraṇa* (arisen dispute) is resolved exclusively in the presence of the Saṃgha; the remaining three types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) are extinguished by any three persons. These distinctions should be understood through reflection.

If one consults the seven medicinal applications (*bhaiṣajya*), the *sammukha-vinaya* (resolution in the presence of) and the *pratijñā-kāraka* (acting on confession) apply to any three persons, while the remaining five medicinal applications are restricted to the use of the Saṃgha.
These distinctions may be inferred and explained accordingly. Next, below this, the first of the three correct modes of speech (*vāk-samyak*) is as follows:

Regarding the objects sought: next, there are three types of faculties that serve as the basis for seeking; next, there are three cases concerning those about to break the precepts and so forth, contrasted with concealment versus disclosure, right, or wrong.
Next, there are one and three [cases]: if one does not disclose and repent within one's own mind, one undergoes formal disciplinary punishment, namely, the performance of the three *karmavācanās*.
Because these punish three kinds of negligent persons, they are called the "Threefold Karmas for Negligence."
Because there are three dharma-gates, they are provisionally referred to as the "three forms of negligence.
In the second major section, the cultivation of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), there are four parts:

first, up to the point where these three trainings are briefly explained in terms of their abandonment and attainment; second, from Ānanda onwards, the three trainings are taught specifically for three individuals; third, at that time...
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are three trainings," and so forth, explaining the three trainings in detail, excluding their attainment. Fourth, there are again the three trainings;

below this is the essential nature and characteristics of the three trainings. The first section has two parts. The second part presents the essence of the three trainings, namely, the dharmas that are to be trained in.
Second, from the passage beginning "At that time, a great number of bhikṣus... onwards, the text employs a series of questions and answers to clarify the training and its attainment. The former...

Within this, there are further two sections. First, the essence of the three trainings is revealed; second, the three trainings themselves are presented. Regarding the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), it is distinguished by way of its practice. First, concerning its essence:

beginning with the stage of the ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), one single-mindedly applies effort to guard and maintain [the precepts]. Upon realizing the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*), this support becomes firm and solid, surpassing what came before.

Therefore, it is called the "increased training in ethical discipline" (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). The four [foundations] manifest the principle of stillness, severing all agitation and movement; this is the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is the beginning of accomplishment. Therefore, it is said that after increasing the training in concentration (*samādhi*) and entering the signless (*animitta*), one realizes true emptiness and the untainted (*anāsrava*), becoming definitively clear and lucid;

thus, it is called increasing the training in wisdom (*prajñā*). Next, regarding the practice of discernment: this refers to practicing the three lower sections [of the *Śrāvakabhūmi*], which are the practices of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).
In the movements of body and speech, there are respective rules and methods; therefore, it is called the training in increased majestic demeanor (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).

When the former two [trainings] are well-cultivated, the practice of their antidotes is perfected, and one eliminates all contrary defilements; this is named the training in increased pure conduct (*adhicitta-śikṣā*). One skillfully recognizes the characteristics of the precepts, distinguishing clearly between the light and the heavy;
therefore, it is called the training in increased *prātimokṣa*. The second section has two parts: first, the bhikṣus request the Buddha; the Buddha answers the bhikṣus.
The Buddha briefly clarifies what is to be eliminated. Second, the Buddha examines the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu answers the Buddha, briefly manifesting what has been attained.
Among the three questions posed by the first bhikṣu, the first question asks the Buddha: "What is meant by 'training'?

Second, from "The Buddha having spoken" onwards, the Buddha answers regarding that which is to be trained in, thereby clarifying what is to be eliminated. From the beginning up to "therefore it is called training," he explains the cultivation of the three trainings. Third...

Regarding the statement "this training is the training in the precepts": this is to demonstrate that the two trainings are not outside of "cessation" (*śamatha*) and "application" (*pragraha*), as both are subsumed within the gateway of the precepts.

As for the phrase "that training in higher ethics, training in higher mind," which indicates there is something to be removed first until the exhaustion of delusion: this refers to the removal of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Next, regarding the passage "Having exhausted greed and so forth," it means that one does not commit unwholesome acts; this clarifies that karma is neither arising nor being performed, meaning that various evils and bitter fruits follow oneself.
Third is the joy of receiving and upholding [the teachings]. Second, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣu Śreṇika with two initial questions:
first, "What is a learner? which asks about the method and practice for the bhikṣus who are learning; second, "For what purpose is one a learner? which asks about the objective of learning.
"O Bhikṣus, for the sake of seeking what kind of fruit and retribution? First, in response to the initial question: "As the World-Honored One has taught, we practice according to those teachings;
this is called 'training' (*śaikṣa*). This answers the method of cultivation and training. Furthermore, from "There are three trainings" onwards, it responds to the second question:
"We study these three trainings in order to pray for the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], not seeking worldly rewards."

The second section, which treats three individuals separately, first clarifies the case of Ānanda. Acting as a *brāhmaṇa*, he practices the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) to manifest the Buddha’s intention in establishing the precepts.

Second, for the sake of Kāśyapa, who was performing repentance, [the text] uses praise and censure to clarify the three natures. Third, for the sake of Vatsa, it provides a brief exposition of the three trainings.
Regarding the second part concerning Kāśyapa, there are four sections. The first, extending up to the point where he says, "I fear that we are foolish,"...
1. Lacking faith, one incurs the fault of slander. 2. Thereupon, after the World-Honored One had moved his residence to Rājagṛha, [the disciples] sought pity and offered repentance. 3.
Thirdly, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "You yourselves must repent," and so forth, until the Buddha accepted their repentance. 4.

At that time, after Kāśyapa had prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, [the text] contrasts the praise and censure of the bhikṣus to demonstrate the resulting benefit and loss. Within this section, it concerns...

"Persons are not like two threes," meaning that each is categorized as superior, middling, or inferior. Next, the three trainings are illustrated by means of a metaphor. This is not merely in contrast to the aforementioned person;
it refers to how a precept-breaking bhikṣu differs in monastic deportment and even in his gait from one who maintains the precepts.
Thus, the metaphor is as follows: the precept-keeping bhikṣu’s advancing and halting accord with the Dharma, and his speech establishes a standard of conduct, which is likened to an ox. Second.

Because various dharmas are gathered together in one place, it is called "practicing in common. To say of oneself, "I am a bhikṣu," [is to claim] that one is a "good bhikṣu. The hair is a metaphor for precepts (*śīla*);
because purity and defilement are distinct, they do not resemble each other at all. Thus, hair does not resemble a cow's hoof;

this is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because stillness and agitation are different. A cow's hoof does not resemble a cow's sound; this is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*), because the ignorant and the wise are not alike.

Because they are different, the sound does not resemble that of an ox. Such foolish people are fit to follow after donkeys; whereas a bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma is fit to walk together with those above him.
He claims for himself, "I am a bhikṣu," yet he is fit only for those above him to say of him, "This is an ox. He lacks the monastic precepts (saṃgha-śīla) that correspond to the hair;
he increases his mind [of concentration] which corresponds to the hooves; and he increases his wisdom which corresponds to the voice.
The third section has two parts. The first clarifies the fulfillment of training through pure cultivation alone, excluding attainment.

The second, beginning with "Furthermore, there are three trainings," clarifies the fulfillment of training through combined cultivation, including attainment. The preceding text has three parts. First, the Buddha tells the bhikṣus that there are three trainings.
This raises the essential nature of the dharmas to be studied. From "First, what is it? and below, the three types of persons are listed individually to demonstrate their removal and attainment.

From "Third, the practitioner who has fulfilled [the training]" and below, the preceding section on pure fulfillment is concluded. Regarding the second part, which specifically clarifies the three persons: the first person purely cultivates ethical discipline (*śīla*);

the second person cultivates ethical discipline together with meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the third person fully cultivates all three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). For the first person, there are five...
Section. One: A brief inquiry. Two: Raising the mind to seek [the precepts], not cultivating the other two because one follows one's own capacity.

Three: "He, regarding these precepts... and below, correctly clarifies the training in the precepts. Four: "He abandons... and below, the five messengers; this reveals what is eliminated. Five: "Regarding the aforementioned nirvāṇa...
and below, this manifests what is attained. Third, regarding the training in the precepts: if one commits a minor offense, it refers to the four lower [offenses].
Section. Because it does not constitute a permanent obstruction for a single lifetime, it is called "light. Since it can be removed through conditions, it is referred to as a "text for repentance";
the metaphor is clear. If it were a grave precept—meaning a *pārājika* offense—one would be permanently obstructed upon its commission, like a broken vessel or a shattered stone;
therefore, it is called "grave. It is logically appropriate to maintain it with singular diligence; thus, it says "abiding well in the precepts."
Generally speaking, the Dharma of the precepts is the foundation for giving rise to concentration and wisdom, and the correct path for proceeding toward Bodhi. Therefore, the treatises state:
"In the towered pavilion of the factors of enlightenment, the precepts serve as the pillars; in the city of the mind of meditative concentration, the precepts serve as the ramparts.
To enter the assembly of virtuous people, one must wear the seal of the precepts. Thus, they must be upheld with reverence, not merely in thought, but practiced in accordance with the Dharma.
The characteristics of the five branches may be called "skillfully upholding the precepts. As for the five branches: first, the precept of purity regarding the fundamental karmic actions;
second, the precept of purity regarding the remaining ancillary factors before and after [the action]; third, the precept of purity regarding the absence of unwholesome thoughts;

fourth, the precept of purity regarding mindfulness that guards and maintains right recollection; and fifth, the precept of dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Branch" (*aṅga*) means cause.
This is distinct. Among the five stages, two are intermediate; the first four constitute practice, while the last one consists of generating the resolve and dedicating merit.
Within the first four, the initial three involve the cessation of evil, and the fourth involves the production of goodness. Regarding the preceding cessation of evil, there are again two parts:

the first two involve the cessation of karmic evil, and the third involves the subduing of afflictions. As for the evil of karma, the first part involves abandoning the fundamental paths of karmic action, such as abandoning the taking of life.
The evil of taking life; the evil of theft, such as lifting an object and moving it from its place, and so forth. Second, the evil of the preparatory actions (*prayoga*) for abstaining [from these].

For example, at the time of killing, dragging [the victim] forward, binding them, striking them once or twice, and so forth—these are the preliminary preparations (*pūrvaprayoga*). Subsequently, there are acts such as flaying their skin or cutting them apart.

These are the subsequent preparatory stages (*pūrvaprayoga*). These two establish the preceding fundamental stage; therefore, they are called "the remainder. Now, regarding the wholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*) of ethical discipline (*śīla*):

when one abandons the preceding fundamental stage, there is "fundamental purity" (*maulaviśuddhi*); when one abandons both the preceding and subsequent preparatory stages, there is "preparatory purity" (*prayogaviśuddhi*).

It is by means of this that the karma is accomplished. This occurs because, through the absence of unwholesome thoughts (*vitarka*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) are subdued; or, since the root is already absent, the karma does not arise. Why?

How does one abandon unwholesome thoughts? Their accomplishment depends on right mindfulness. This means taking as an antidote the mindfulness of the functional power of the essence of the precepts, as well as the merit of the Three Jewels arising from wholesome states and their objective qualities;
thus, there are no evil thoughts. The preceding practices have been established. If one does not dedicate [the merit], it may instead result in rebirth within the three realms of existence.
Therefore, the fifth stage is the dedication toward Bodhi. According to the *Cittaviveka-śāstra*, this constitutes the fundamental and its attendants, whether pure or impure.
They are destroyed by ignorance; therefore, one should embrace right mindfulness and follow the path to Nirvāṇa. Each and every precept is fully endowed with these five qualities.
In this Vinaya text, only the first two are briefly mentioned. Regarding the statement "one should associate with those who practice":

this refers to the skillful means of upholding the precepts, which counteract the preliminary conditions for unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*). It concerns conduct that is untainted by evil, namely, a mind of wholesome sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), which serves as the antidote.

The subsequent preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the subsequent completion (*pṛṣṭha*) are the two that constitute the retinue (*parivāra*). The remaining pure precepts constitute the second: the practice of non-deficiency.
This correctly abandons the evil of the fundamental paths of action (*mūlakarmapatha*), which is itself the root of the wholesome paths of action;
therefore, it is called the practice of non-deficiency. The other three are omitted here. To summarize the training in the precepts, it says: "One should constantly cultivate these in this sequence."

The four [factors] that sever those five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are what is to be eliminated. Question: Since morality merely subdues karma, why is it said here that it severs the five lower fetters?

Answer: This is stated according to the fundamental principle; in reality, they are not severed. As for the "five lower fetters," these refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), and hatred (*dveṣa*).

They are called "lower fetters" for three reasons: first, because they belong to the lower realm; second, because they pertain to the minds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); and third, because they are inferior in nature.

Regarding "arising in the middle": the first three [defilements] arise within the minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have abandoned the views of the three realms through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The two fetters of greed and hatred arise within the minds of those who have abandoned [the defilements] of the desire realm through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Therefore, the first two [types of] "moistening" (*puṣṭi*) arise within the minds of those who have attained the lower two fruits [of stream-enterer and once-returner].

The first three moisten the births of ordinary beings in the three realms; the latter two moisten the lower two fruits. Regarding the birth in the lower [desire realm], there are three obstacles to the lower fruit. The former...
The first three fetters constitute the first fruit; the latter two fetters constitute the second and third fruits, namely the Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin.

Therefore, they are called the "lower latent tendencies. If one attains the state of Anāgāmin, one must necessarily eliminate these; hence it is said that the five lower latent tendencies are abandoned. As for the phrase "five among the higher," this clarifies what has been attained.
Having already severed the lower fetters (*anuśaya*), that is to say, because one has realized the state of a *anāgāmin* who does not return to the desire realm.

The second person is as described above. The third person has three points: first, they fully cultivate the three trainings; second, they attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), which is what is to be eliminated;

third, having attained the liberation of mind through the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the following clarifies what is obtained. Regarding "the practitioner who fulfills the fetters," this refers to the third person.
Regarding those who practice without contentment: by combining the two preceding types of practitioners, it is shown that the cause of practice must inevitably result in its fruit.

However, depending on whether the causes are complete or deficient, there will be degrees of excellence or inferiority in the fruit; it is never established in vain. Therefore, it is said that there is no empty pointing.

What has been explained above concerns the practice of the complete training (śikṣā) through exclusive cultivation; this is the teaching for those who practice according to their respective capacities but do not yet fully comprehend the instructions.

Below this follows the teaching for those who cultivate the complete training through both means and who fully comprehend the instructions. This section contains two parts: first, the presentation of the essential nature of the trainings to be practiced, hence the statement "up to the training in increased wisdom";
second, from "What are they? onwards, the specific enumeration of the three types of persons. Within the first of these, there are three phrases.

This refers to the three levels, which are categorized according to the three fruits. Because their power and capacity are insufficient as described in terms of the fruits, and because their practice is incomplete, they do not attain the fourth fruit.
Looking back at the *nāga* [stage], there are three types: first, those who possess the full precepts while concurrently cultivating the two practices.

Second, by stating that he has severed the five lower fetters (*anuśaya*), it clarifies what has been eliminated. This is then contrasted with the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) who, regarding the higher realms and *nirvāṇa*, is distinguished by having something further to attain.
